Good game. I've got it on sale so I feel like it was worth it. The problems that I had with this game... where to begin... First of
all the game only auto saves when you travel across certain areas of the game which can take more than an hour and so I have lost all my progress in one place because I forgot to save! Always save often because this game has a bad habit of crashing. Almost everytime it tries to load it crashes and so you loose your progress if you didn't save prior to the loading screen. To get around it, I discovered that the game loads fine when used in windowed mode so try that before the game loads, otherwise it will freeze for some people at least. Also the game never remembers my settings in the menu, like the controller settings or subtitles, resolution, etc. Now, on the gameplay side, the game is pretty sweet. What I didn't like was that there were some portions of the game, especially at the end when you had to escort the little sisters without a single bullet because enemy's kept spawning and spawning. Also, the little sisters voices kept reapeating the same lines over again and gain to frequently. There are some portions when you feel like you're going mad because of so many enemies. It's a pretty lenghty game as well. On the positive side, it was pretty easy to complete objectives and search for objects and certain items and I never had to resort on searching online for a walktrough or anything so I really loved that. There are some other little things that annoyed me but on the long run, I had fun with the game and I completed it on medium setting. Would I play it again? Nope because there are too many games that I still haven't finished or played. Other than that, the game has replay value because of the RPG elements like making your character better. Cheers :)

Absolutely amazing and well kept with pretty much all the features and objectives this game offers.
AI:
The AI system is awesome and better than any game i know of. The AI have a great connection with the environment and the island. They have features that would include:
- Being passive and aggressive given the decisions you make
- Progressively get harder to deal with if such decisions make them aggressive
- Different types of enemies that are very unique to the story and difficulty the game presents
Weapons:
The weapons in this game are very suited to the environment and are very diverse. From axes to bows to even swords the game adds a fair amount of combat options against enemies that may be tougher to deal with or suit a better option such as survival that may be the reason you survive your exploration. Along with diverse and unique placement to find such weapons, the combat options offer a high risk high reward factor that can overall help your survival experience and make the game much more enjoyable and fun :0
Exploration:
The games island is medium sized however it is compensated with more diverse exploration systems such as snowy biomes, beach biomes as well as cave systems. The cave systems is overall my favourite part of this game as it truly tests your survival capability and truly questions whether you should dive deeper or prepare just a touch more. It is where most of the exploration takes place as well as the screams that you will lash out from the terrifying monsters and large hordes of enemies that await every corner.
Base Building:
Along with exploration this is a great part of the game as through every update new features are added. This helped it be fresh and got your mind focused on many building aspects and allowed you to be very creative from escape options or new base building ideas. The possiblities are virtually endless is this regard.
Combat:
The combat system is very basic from attacking and blocking attacks however there are other combat ideas such as fire damage such as molotovs, bow and arrow, sword, axe even explosives. The point is even though the combat system is basic, there are various ways to combat the enemies and allows for great ideas and ways to evade, attack or defend against enemies.
Crafting:
The crafting system is AWESOME! It took a while to understand especially from a noob perspective but that idea was very intriguing. The system is great right-click items and craft them. It doesnt lend you a hand in discovering how to craft a specific item e.g. arrow but lets you know whether youre on the right track.
Hunting:
This aspect is very important as food eventually becomes a problem and hunting is the only resort. There are many ways to hunt such as bow and arrow, spear or even traps and makes it interesting everytime. Overall great system and is very unique in some cases.
CONS:
The only con i can really think of is that the game can get boring from building especially if you have finished exploring everything there is, but i wouldnt consider this to be a MAJOR or even minor issue as the game is still in Early Access and lots of features are still to be added.
Overall Rating 9.7/10
TL:DR
If you love survival games that are tough and exploration/ base-building heavy--- 100% recommend

This game is sort of like Half Life 1, in terms of atmosphere and tone. You really will learn to love the weapons and plasmids, and how/when to use them. Combat feels like you use slick combos (Similar to other fighting games like Super Smash bros or Mortal Combat) stunning with a plasmid and shooting them down with the revolver all on your own. The game can be TENSE, the entire game puts you on edge, and some parts I had to actually put it away and come back to it when I felt ready. However, it is sort of like exploring one big enclosed place, so if you don't like games like Dead Space, you might not like this game. It really is great though, 9.2/10.

Overall it's a good game (worth getting on a decent sale) but the reviews are always subjective. In this case, I am comparing this game to Tropico 4 to which it seems like a step backwards overall. There are some new interesting mechanics that look very promising like research, dynasties, and etc. but it feels a bit shallower overall.
Maybe the game will get more depth after a few DLC but it just doesn't feel right yet.

Katamari Damacy meets Echo the Dolphin... a cliché way to describe a game, perhaps, but accurate nonetheless. Fortunately, it lacks both the stress-inducing time-limits of the former, and the obnoxious difficulty of the later. You're graded according to how quickly you get through the stages, so if you wanna three-star every level, you're gonna have to move your tail - but if you just wanna take it easy, enjoy the sights, and stop to eat the flowers, nothing's stopping you.
Of course, unless you DO want to do exactly that, it's going to be a fairly short game. Don't expact days of entertainment here - you can blast through the whole thing in an evening if you're so inclined. Still, it's a fair ammount of fun for the price, and worth owning just for the experience of going straight from chomping on zytoplankton to eating the moon within the space of a single game.
The only real critique I can level at it is that some of the levels have you hang around the same area, eating the same endlessly-respawning objects for way too long time - but that's ultimately a minor quibble. The controls are tight and responsive, particularly if you're using a controller, the physics are tuned more towards 'fun' than 'realism' (which is how it SHOULD be), and there's a huge variety of things to eat - from bottlecaps to aircraft-carriers. So if you're looking for an afternoon of anarchic, all-devouring fun, look no further than this clever little game!

Simply the most immersive, challenging, and beautiful survival experience to date. Survive and adapt to a frozen dying world... until one mistake too many ends it all. Mother nature takes center stage as a neutral passive antagonist. Sometimes providing breathtaking views of a coastal sunrise only to threaten you with a fatal blizzard hours later. Stumble into a cave to shelter the storm and hope it's not an angry bear's den. The unscripted stories that can unfold in the sandbox may keep you coming back for dozens or hundreds of hours.
Having purchased this title nearly two years ago, I can say the developers have been very active throughout early access. The amount of content and depth of gameplay that has been added since the original release is astounding. Some may complain that "story mode" has been delayed several times, but there is no shortage of value to be had for the $20 price tag in it's current state.

Tasy Blue is is a smaller arcade game, a mutant fish simulator with
cute graphics and entertaining gameplay.  It operates on a star system,
which encourages replayability, but I feel the game would have benefitted
from having a leaderboard.
Your objective is to eat smaller items or fish, and the more you eat,
the larger you grow.  The comedic aspects comes when you may find yourself
large enough to eat small boats or buildings within the missions.  The
mechanic is simple, but is solidly supported by the music, which helps
keep the atmosphere, and the level design, which mixes up the levels so
you don't feel like you are replaying the same mission with small variations.
This is a small, simple, game with solid mechanics and an entertaining
arcade feel.  I can easily recommend this for those that enjoy this
sort of game.

Ok, so.  The game is currently rated Overwhelmingly Positive, and there's tons of gameplay footage and hype surrounding this game, so you probably already know if you want this game and whether you'll enjoy it.  But in case you're one of the few who doesn't know already, lemme just lay it out for you.
This is a platformer bullet hell lite game.  Dying carries no penalties.  Which is good because you die a lot.  There's a guy on isle 2 that keeps track of just how much you died.  I hate that guy.  Still, it's hard.  Bosses have patterns, and the patterns are difficult to master, and sometimes you still screw up even when you know exactly what's about to happen.  It takes several tries on each boss, and each boss is its own type of challenging.  A lot of people struggled with the flower guy, but I breezed past him.  But then I had trouble with the candyland chick, and she's supposedly super easy.  So give yourself some slack.
But not too much slack.  The tutorial is easy.  If you struggle with the tutorial, you have a problem.  If you don't understand the reference, look up the cuphead tutorial videos.  I promise you'll find it.
Anyway, winning feels super rewarding because it's hard.  But it's not maddening and unforgiving like dark souls.  You get an instant retry, with basically no lost progress.  And when you finally get it, you'll get that really satisfied feeling that has me addicted to this game.  And every boss is beatable, and no boss move is broken or undodgeable, you just have to learn how, and that's part of WHY it's so rewarding.  You really feel like you earned it.
The game is very focused on boss fights.  There are some side scrolling levels with the same general feel to them.  The controls are intuitive, the animations are honestly the most fun and entertaining out of any game I've played, bar none.  The soundtrack fits perfectly.  I laughed at the shift between boss forms several times.  It's just... fun.
Try it.  You'll know before 2 hours if you like it or not.  Obviously, most people did.  Personally, I think it's the most refreshing game I've played in a while.

Most likely you won't like the "game" (note the quotation marks). For the most part of the game you simply walk from room to room and do as you are told by the narrator. In consequence a) it is very (very) short, b) at the same time it feels overly long - e.g. you cannot run c) the narrative is slow and most importantly d) it is not Stanleys Parable Part II - in case you were looking for that.
All in all, one can finish this in less than 90 min. Is it rewarding? No, you have zero impact in this game. Your "choices" do not matter and there is nothing below the things placed right in front of you. Does the game tell you something on a meta level? Depends on yourself -  it does reflect a bit on how a story is told, but that is more likely than not irrelevant to most of you out there. Again, 9 out of 10 will not like this game - if you believe to be this one person out of a group of 10, go ahead and play it. But be warned, you might get disappointed.
Edit:
As the review sparked a comment pointing towards the game description as redeeming evidence, I feel compelled to add a few lines, reflecting on that.
I read quite a lot, meaning I come acroos a range of stories from a broad spectrum. I am willing to be let into other worlds and ways of thinking. What is placed in front of you here is framed as a struggle the narrator goes through. The downside is, this is deliverd as a blunt force instrument. There is nothing to discover for the person in front of the computer and this in turn means, the game would play out nearly identical as a slide show. Meaning as well, you are given no reason to go astray or explore on your own, as the game does not offer any insights beyond what is placed directly in front of you. It is therefore different from other games "without an objective or goal".
Whether the conflict outlined within the game is real or just a plot device is not for me to tell, the amount of positive reviews suggest that a number of people enjoyed the experience. With the label "not recommended" I make a sweeping generalization about the player base on this platform, including all the obvious drawbacks this implies. As others are entitled to their fair judgement, I assume that this short trip appeals only to a fraction of people visiting. For the reasons stated above, I find the product lacking - even with the disclaimers put in the description. An assessment that does not need to be shared, but I want to caution those, trying to judge whether to by the game or not.

Visually it took my breath away. The lush forests, the vast caves, and the huge map make for endless ways to play the game. From walking on mud, rocks, sand, or metal, to cutting down trees, big and small. To the tree's rustling from the wind. The eerie noises at night of distant cannibals and wildlife. I definately suggest playing the game at night if you want to get really immersed in the game. Put some surround sound headphones on and try not to get scared by a deer getting startled by you in the night.
Playing with friends just makes it even more fun, as you all are either teaming up against cannibals, wildlife, or nature. Or you all play as lone wolves, eeking out a life, rarely meeting one another, even if only to trade somethings then part ways again.
Among the horde of survival games, this stands out above almost all of the rest. 10/10.

Where to start on Evolve ... I think this will be a polarising game; forget all the whining about day one DLCs the haters are idiots, who cares about some skins its a non-issue with people trying to find something to be e-angry about the most important thing comes down to "is this game fun?"
You'll also hear people whining about content, that it doesn't have some great long campaign, or NPCs ... or crafting  ... or fishing. Its not that type of game. Chess, after all only has 6 unique pieces on an 8x8 board. Evolve is built like any older arena based game with a single simple core where the real game is not just the popping skulls but map knowledge, movement and lots and lots of tactics, etc.
I think the main point to take away about Evolve is that it is BRUTAL and unforgiving, both sides need to play well or you will get slaughtered. Many new players will definitely get discouraged by coming in and being torn apart, especially in no-mic pug games (this game is 100x better with a mic and a bunch of friends).
After all the above disclaimers though, I have to say this game is really sucking me in. The vein-popping rage of losing to a L3 Wraith is offset by the oh yes moments after pulling off a sweet win. The atmosphere and the sense of hunting is fantastic, running through pouring rain avoiding carnivorous plants and trying to out-think the monster player is incredibly engaging. A 5 round match of Evacuation mode disappears before you know it and you realise you haven't looked away from the screen for anywhere between 30 mins to almost 2 hours. Every round you learn a little more and become a little better.
So ... if you have low tolerance to failure and just want a super straight forward game of shoot heads then I would seriously suggest that this game might frustrate you. If you are prepared to think and have a certain level of fortitude then this is an absorbing, rewarding game.

This review is about the game, not about the marketing decisions of the company.
That being said, this is a great game.  It's easy to play, but hard to master.  Each match is tense and exciting, with just enough frustration to flavour the experience without being so bad that it sours it.  Character progression comes in multiple flavours, and even losing nets you points towards ranking up.  Multiplayer is easy to get in to, and works really well.  The game does a good job of trying to give you the role you want, but sometimes you'll get shifted to a new character and it's actually really good to see how the other side lives.  I didn't realize I liked support until I didn't get my assault pick.
The first time I played the monster was exhilarating and awesome.  I lost and it didn't even matter because I felt like I did a good job and really made the hunters work for it.  The first time I won?  Amazing.  Tricking those hunters into a narrow cavern to make best use of my powers felt really good.
Evacuation mode was a good idea.  Making it so you can play it online or solo or just with some friends was brilliant.  It's fun and dynamic.  Having a way to learn playing the classes without being forced to embarass yourself in front of other people is super.
I think there might be some balance wrinkles to sort out, but that's not surprising in such a complex and multifaceted game.  Stasis grenades seem pretty OP the few times I've seen them used.  On the flip side, the Kraken monster has always been overwhelming every time I've encountered it.  But then, maybe I'm still fresh and don't know the right strategies.
That's what makes this a really good game.  It's fun with friends, it's exciting, and it rewards being clever.  I don't know how much staying power it's going to have, but for right now, it's a blast.

Cuphead is a fantastic old school platformer, and it is one of the best games of 2017.
At first, I was a bit afraid that apart from the art style, it would be lacking in the gameplay department. I hoped that Cuphead would not be the classic case of style over substance, and man, it really wasn't. Not only did we get a game that is beautifully animated and it is really a joy to look at, but we also got a game that emulates old school run'n'gun games really well.
The twist on the forumula is pretty simple: over the course of the game, you will be pretty much fighting bosses rather than run'n'gunning through different levels. It is like Shadow of the Colossus meets a Contra game from the SNES era. However, all of these bosses are very different and fighting a new one feels so refreshing that you will never get bored of the whole thing. Whenever you fail (and you will fail a lot of times), you will jump back and try again without hesitation. Everything in Cuphead is so tightly crafted that even if you lose to a boss, you will never feel that the game is unfair.
To put it simply, if you like classic or old school run'n'gun shooters, you have to get Cuphead. Period. Here is hoping that with enough support, we will again get a gem of a game from Studio MDHR. The time it took for them to meticulously craft this world and create such a good game must have been immense.
Cuphead is one of my most wholehearted recommendations I've ever made.

LYNE can best be described as a minimalist puzzle game.
Essentially it is a series of logic puzzles generated on a grid, consisting of coloured nodes and permeable gears.  Each puzzle must be solved on the fly by connecting paths from one primary node to another through the same coloured nodes and transitional gears.  The goal is to ensure that all nodes and all the slots on each gear are used in the eventual solution.
There are twenty-five individual puzzles grouped into twenty-six sets, which grow in depth and complexity the greater the progress made.  As you can imagine the puzzles start off deliberately simple allowing players to grasp the basic elements of gameplay.  Later puzzles require an ever increasing amount of convoluted paths to be drawn in order to use all the available nodes and gear slots.  In addition the game also generates a set of daily time-limited puzzles which vary in complexity and must be finished each day or they disappear until they are generated sometime in the future.
Finding the solution to each puzzle can take between a few seconds and a few minutes depending on your ability. If you become stuck a combination of trial and error will eventually lead you to your goal.  If you really dislike puzzle-solving take heart, for what I found truly amazing about LYNE is that it that solutions become intuitive.  Drawing the correct paths take on an almost organic feel.  Someone on the forums said that 'it feels like LYNE rewires the way your brain works,' and it does feel like that.
Despite the graphics feeling simplistic they are cleanly drawn and totally appropriate.  While there is no music to speak of the game uses a series of medolic sounds with every mouse stroke that rise in frequency the the faster the connections are made.  Together these sounds have an almost hypnotic quality which Im sure sublimally urges you on to complete the next objective.
If you dont like solving puzzle or find that your brain just isnt suited to play such games then this might be an exception.  It is such a wonderful distraction from the plethora of online shooters, RTS and RPG/adventure games out there that you should really give it a go.  LYNE is everything it says it is on the store page and worth the cheap price.  Glad I made this purchase.

I'll start by saying normally I don't write reviews. However after seeing all the negative bashing its receiving, I'll take my chances at being flamed and I'll go ahead and throw in my opinion.
Bottom line is, is this game worth $60? Depends on what you expect. Like L4D,  the game is repetitive after awhile, however the replayability comes with the different scenarios and situations you can get yourself involved into. The base line is you as a hunter, will chase the monster, some games you'll catch him early, some games you won't. The scenario changes if you enroute get eaten by a man-eating-plant, and suddenly your team is one man short, or two if they send someone to retrieve you, so you don't get so far behind the monster losing most of your time. Or if you aggro one of the wonderfully aggressive, and frequent animals that are around the maps. Choices in characters come into play depending on one of four classes, each that have 3 choices within each class itself, assault, trapper, support, or medic.
As the monster, you will be running during the beginning of the game, if you don't like that concept, don't buy the game. You're goal here is to evade, and eat the local wildlife as to gain armor, and evolve until hopefully stage 2 or 3, when you can actually, 1) take a hit, 2) deal some good damage to the hunters that are no doubt on your rear. Also amusing, is letting them catch up to you right by a super agressive powerful wildlife, taking their attention off of you for a few moments allowing you to catch your breath, or gain enough distance to evolve without worrying about being locked in animation taking damage. Does the game have enough content to be worth $60 by itself? I don't think so. Does it have enough replayability to be worth $60? To me? Entirely. I thoroughly enjoy the game, I haven't had any negative games thus far, however I am aware they are out there.
Regarding the DLC bashing, if you look, the DLC is all skins. Optional Skins. They've stated that future maps will be free of charge, thus far the only thing costing money are skins, so all the bashing about day 1 DLC, I wouldn't even classify as DLC since while it may be content, its not adding anything meaningful to the game. It doesn't alter the game play in any way, doesn't give an advantage, it's there if you want to look different. I'm perfectly content playing on my base version of the game without it, and getting my moneys worth.
I'm really surprised at the negative bashing its received over this type of DLC, since I've seen games released on Day 1 with DLC that alters the game in huge ways, such as weapons or powerups. Regardless, I'm thoroughly happy with my purchase, even at $60. If you want to wait til it price drops, I couldn't blame you, but I'm all about wanting to get into it now so I don't mind paying a little bit more to save myself months of time waiting for it. Hopefully this will enlighten someone whos thinking about purchasing it, but is just seeing all the hate.
Have fun, and good luck!

Let me say that I will willingly change this review as is warranted if the game develops, but as of now, I wouldn't recommend it.
Visually, the game is stunning- it is a work of art with an unparalleled level of immersion that draws you in...but it is not a good "game."
Frankly, it becomes a stressful chore after awhile, and I never really felt like I was progressing (I acquired stuff, and my skill points went up, but with no appreciable effects).
Probably the biggest negative is that I picked this title up a few months ago, played it over a couple of days, formed an initial impression, set it aside, only to pick it back up again now and...nothing has changed.
To be fair, I'm sure the game world is bigger and richer now, and I noticed some UI polishing, but Story mode is still teased at, the UI is still clunky, the game still becomes the aforementioned chore, the bug where your character suddenly starts speaking in demonic tongues is still a thing (Linux) and modding still doesn't exist.
A word on modding: I don't see it happening any time soon either, since the developer has stated they want to "wait till they can do it right" which is a complete blow off. This is a title based on the Unity game engine - tons of titles in Early Access (with Unity especially) have vibrant moding scenes, with tiny development teams (e.g. RimWorld).
I predict (and I'm ready to eat this statement) that this game will languish in the EA development doldrums for quite some time. I would love to be proven wrong though.
TLDR: Get it if you want to interact with an immersive work of art. Avoid if you want a survival game. Might be a title to hang onto though, if you get it on sale.

A clever and unique game, Reigns is essentially a resource management game but with a simplistic yet addicting design.
Basically you're the King of the realm and your job is to live as long as you can.
The game is played by having cards appear as your choices regarding a certain matter. Your decision, which is not just a yes or no, will reduce or increase one of your 4 resources. Faith, People, Army, Money. Certain desicions might please or displease several of these resources at any given time. Get one of them to either the lowest or its highest mark and your
is over! Every choice matters, every decision might affect a future one is some degree so you need to be careful. Appeasing the Army constanly will have detrimental effects on the People although they might be circumstances which will benefit both.
The game also features sort of miniquest and a dueling mechanic. Completing the miniquests will unlock more sets of cards to play around with during your reign. There are also sort of items (and I'm using the term loosely here) which will help you or hinder you depending on said scenario. Some of them will persist even if your current king dies for some years and some might have a use further down the road.
Reigns is delightfully minimalistic at a first glance, but once you get into you'll begin to understand how it excels at keeping you hooked to play some more. There are many secrets to discover within the game, there's plenty of humour and meta humour to go around and at this price it's a definite recommendation if you're looking for something different and refreshing to play.
Long live the King!

A special survival game focused on the raw struggles of living innawoods. There are no exotic dangers around; it's just you against nature. There will be wild animals, some dangerous and some peaceful. The UI is minimalist in design so that you can be immersed in the game easily, and unfortunately some of the game is pretty simple too. However, it is really easy to get immersed in the game. The game artstyle is very pastel-like, which gives it a unique flavor. There isn't much detail on the individual textures, but the game enviroment will look absolutely stunning. Some of my fondest memories of the game were just standing, looking up into the night sky or at the valleys below. The hard part about the game is surviving in general. You must learn how to scavenge for food, supplies, and wood while going up against the weather, the terrain, and time.
I'm not the biggest fan of the genre, and that combined with how slow the game has been developed, I say you should buy this game at a discounted price. I certainly hope Hinterland Studios can add more content in a timely order.

Although I am a huge fan of the Stanley Parable and experimental games in general, I feel let down by this game.
Whereas the Stanley parable actually can be classified as a game because it actually lets you make choices along the way that have a significant impact on the outcome, the Beginner's Guide does not employ decision trees in any way.
Bereft of choice I am a spectator, this is not a problem in and of itself. I enjoy mysteries and sad stories such as The Vanishing of Ethan Carter or "enlightening puzzle games" such as The Witness more than anything.
But what these games offer is the indirect, but profound satisfaction of the epiphany. The rush of of the a-ha erlebnis, the feeling of: before I did not have understanding, but now that I've been through this, I do.
This fundamentally human mechanic rewards you for going through tedious, tough or unpleasant activities, which can sometimes be found in these games, and thereby making these activities worthwhile.
The Beginner's Guide to my disappointment offers none of those rewards. While at the same time bothering you with long walks through unimaginative and unaspiring levels. The narration, although at times sounding sincere, quickly blends into this sea of greyness.
Possible <Spoiler>
Yes I can accept Coda is sad, lonely, lacking in productivity and purpose. Yes I can see this is the Narrator projecting his own failures and/or limitations on somebody else through that person's work and yes I can surmise  some sort of social commentary on both game developer and player to which all those negative attributes might be attributed.
</Spoiler>
However none of these insights are particular deep, helpful or well delivered and therefor none of it excuses the lack of captivating visuals or creative puzzles the player is being dragged through.
I do appreciate the effort to make something out of the ordinary and I might give the next product of the developer another go on the basis of the Stanley Parable, but The Beginner's Guide simply does not work for me.

Edit 6/11/16 at about 7 AM Texas Time. So. Im editing my review as me and a few buddies have attemtped to get back into this game after what was....a little more than a years absence. Things have changed. Mr. Enigma has proven to be a real dude of sorts and helped me through a technical issue. Hats off. The whole "Kill the top stair" thing apparently has been addressed, at least to some degree, as me and my friends have been to several servers and not fallen through anymore top floors of staircases. So theres that. The community....still kinda sucks. I guess thats because of the types of servers....of which there are VERY few in my neck of the woods. HOWEVER....I get to host my own server on my less than average machine perfectly well. Hats off again.
They seem to have actually read my review...or maybe it was popular vote....who knows. All I know is thats another fix. There are added features, better building mechanics. I mean....you can REALLY pimp out yer home now. Edit yer own settings if you dont like the regular ones. The community has a set of really great mods to choose from and it appears that not only are they readily available and easy to install...theyre supported. Sweet. Community support goes a long way to a games longevity. Look at Fallout New Vegas. Its been like 5-6 years since that came out. People still play it.
The game seems to be developing. At a snails pace but at least its in actual development. The character creation still needs work though. I mean...I made a character today and wanted to create a strong person who is weather resistant and can do carpentry as well as take care of an axe. So...Im a half blind, disorganized, slow reader, that needs 3 times the amount of water to live. Just for 2 points of strength.....weak sauce. Still takes like 3-5 hits from a bat to kill a Zed. The extra carrying capacity was worthless too. I get 2 extra carrying units in total. So....no. I dont see this character living much longer. Might do a suicide run and clear out the warehouse with her.
Do I recommend the game? I wish I could say yes. Im not recommending the game. I would if I could. Heres why I cant. The people behind the game. Theyre not schysters. The people behind the game generally seem like they care about the product. They seem like regular guys living a life trying to put out a product. As an artist / guy whos just trying to put food in the fridge and stay out of the hospital I empathize. However. I cant expect anyone to endorse my drawings because of my charming personality. If the product is weak then its weak.
Here is the core problem. No one plays. I have a server up and friends on, after a few hours of building a house and stocking it there just isnt any more interest. I mean, Im interested but even my general want to open canned goods while fending off the hordes wanes after I look at the empty server. Try to join a different server you say? Well. Thats a great plan. Cant find any with a ping less than 350. Seems like this is a big game across the pond. I honestly think that me and my friends are the only Americans that bought into this.
Its a good game with a few faults. The bugs are being worked out and a year ago my review was venomous. The community sucked hard....still does on the servers I actually manage to get on. The game had SO many exploits. Still does to a degree but it seems to be more controlled now. Certain items never spawn in. Honestly. I could literally write a 20 page book on those stupid Hunting Books that never...I mean NEVER spawned in.
Anyhow. Im not slamming this game. More like...just delicately pushing the hand away from the cookie jar with a friendly smile and saying "No no no sir." It can be a good game. Who knows...in a few more months it might be a great game.  Until that time I say keep this one in the back of your mind. I wouldnt buy in just yet. Dont write it off...if it can get the support it needs and if the fire heats up so the iron strike is hot....this game could be fire! For now its just a smolder. Still. Hats off gents. Keep on doing right.

This being an HD remaster of ps2 era games, its probably not for everyone. I was a fan of the original .hack games, and surprisingly hadnt even heard GU existed until maybe a year ago so it was a "Duh" purchase the moment this was released.
Would I recommend this, even for non fans of the series? Definitely. Buy it. Now. Or wait for a sale, buy it twice, and gift the copy to someone. K, Its not THAT amazing, but I liked it alot. In comparison to the original 4, I feel that the story is much more involved and overall better, but as far a gameplay mechanics go I think they dropped the ball in a few spots:
1. Combat system is much more fluid. Thats a bonus, but as you progress through the volumes you get different forms that allow you to use more weapons. By the time I got to the end of 2 and around the middle of 3 I realized its almost pointless to use anything other than dual swords as your primary weapon. Everything else is just slow, until Xth.
2. There is a victory scene after every regular fight that you cannot skip. They build up your annoyance after playing the game for hours on end trying to grind to a certain level. The only way to avoid that is to get to volume 3, which by then its probably been over 40 hours...little late.
3. Combat difficulty is...low. At the start of every volume, if you level up 10-20 levels (and that doesnt take long), literally the rest of the volume is a cakewalk. Basically enemies below a certain threshold simply dont do damage to you, and your damage counter ramps up to 9999 just to show you how OP you are for that current area.
4. AI of party members is borderline mentally handicapped. Its been a while since I played the original 4, but it felt like you could tell your members what to do with a little more detail. In GU theres only 4 commands, and healing is the one I had the most issue with. You set a party member to heal and they about vanish from the battlefield and blow through their magic just to heal you for every speck of dirt that damages you, yet ignore people who die.
5. Activating story progression is the most tedious thing you will ever do. The game forces you to check your email for one message, to then have you log back in, change servers, warp to some 3 to 4 layer dungeon that you have to go to the end to for a 20 second cutscene that has -86% impact on anything, to then repeat it all for actual progression...
6. Status ailments arent so well defined as they were in the first 4. I didnt care enough to look it up, or pay close attention if it tells you in game, but I still have no idea what curse does. They also dont seem to affect enemies very much but will just about annihilate you without proper armor effects/items.
I can give all of those a pass for the most part considering the game's age, the reason I consider them cons is because I'm comparing them too much to modern games. I know there's been some 'controversy' regarding how the pre-purpose and advertisement for the game has been handled, but that is not what this is about, putting that aside, this will be a review of the game itself, not it's marketing.
The planet of Shear is underseige, as "Monsters" run amok on the world. 12 of the Galaxy's best "Hunters" are hired to help hunt down these creatures, and evacuate the colonists. Will the Hunters remain the Hunters, or become the Hunted? Welcome to Shear, happy hunting.
Evolve allows the player to have a game of 'cat and mouse', but spun on it's head, with 12 playable hunters, against 1 playable monster. The result creates a very interesting dynamic to the game; team work vs cunning, firepower vs brawn. With 1 Assault, 1 Medic, 1 Support, and 1 Trapper, work together to kill the Monster. The Monster, must first hide from the hunters, eat to 'Evolve", and become strong enough to kill the Hunters.
The bread and butter game comes with Currently;
12 Hunters
3 Monsters
16 Maps
5 Modes of play
Single player and Multiplayer
Turtlerock Studios (who created Left 4 Dead I believe), have stated they wanted to do this before L4D, and they've put effort into working to balance this game out. It's not perfect, there could be some balancing and bug fixing in the future, but all in all, it's a solid game. I could write a HUGE review, but I'll try to some it up with pros and cons.
Pros;
+ Single and multiplayer support
+ Fun gameplay, unique feel
+ Multiple modes of play, keeping it fresh
+ Gameplay can be fast and frenzied, tense, or slow and methodical
Cons;
- Little buggy off release
- Like Left 4 Dead, sometimes you may run into players who are less than 'friendly'
- Minor balancing, nothing to grip about too much
All in all, before anyone puts down the game and denounces it over how it was handled for release, give the game a try. It grows on you, and you appreciate the thought into this game and why you want to keep playing it. It's a fun hunting game that's spun on it's head, and it's all for the better.

Evolve is a great game as it stands, yes there are microtransactions but these currently are only skin packs. Later down the line there will be added monsters and hunters but I wouldnt recommend buying them. The game is very balanced as is and a very fun game to play with and without friends. The detail put into the game is wonderful, from the sounds to the graphics. As a monster you really feel like a powerful beast but never so powerful that you are over balanced. In the beginning you start at weak and need to be stealthy to survive and outwit the hunters. If you can outlast and evolve you can over power the hunters in a battle but only if you target the right people during the right time in battle. As a hunter the mechanics of the game allow you communicate well with and without a headset, being able to mark targets and send messages quickly. The different characters within each class makes for a great way to mix things up during each play through as well as create great teamwork between players. No 2 matches are the same and the base game is great. The micro transactions do not hinder the games gameplay and do not slow down your progression. IF you are worried about all the DLC bundles then buy this game and no other DLCs as a well to boycott this marketing plan. Overall Evolve is a great multiplayer game and is masterfully crafted.

The game attempts to explore the relationship between games desginers, their games, and, primarily, how people interpret the designer through those games.
Ugghhh.... I would describe it as an interesting concept, that wasn't executed with enough finesse;
I felt it ended up as a pretentious load of meta-drivel, possibly derived from semi-real personal experience.
Summarily, by its end, the game creates a discussion about the game designer, fueled by what people interpreted through the game's narration, plot and design. It is clever, but that is all it is. I really feel it is a series of ideas copied and pasted with narration thrown in to make sense of it.
The narration and writing is too heavy handed. I feel the developer has created characters whom are not nuanced, real people, but simply archetypal. This was likely to make these characters "generally" relatable, to reach the most people possible. Throughout the story, if you pay any real attention to the narration, the ending becomes obvious part way through. It barrels onwards, often with exposition, in order to direct your thoughts and emotions in a particular direction. These are things that should come about naturally through the exprience, but I never felt this was achieved. It was akin to an "Applause" sign lighting up, so you know it is now the appropriate moment to do so.
Anyway, it started interesting and became completely unrelateable as the fallacies of the game became blatantly obvious. Unfortunate.

Or you'll die because a bullet from a far away enemy just happened to go through a window hitting you in the arm instantly killing you (your bullets through windows don't kill by the way). You're bombarded with random black and white screen flashes, replays are covered with "SUPERHOT" playing over and over, and some lame tacked on creepy pasta "story" about DOS and old school modems and stuff.
Ultimately, the game boils down to you constantly just doing the same thing over and over. Shoot a few times, throw your weapon, stun an enemy, grab their gun. Rinse and repeat forever. Yawn.

"There's always a bigger fish" sums up the whole game for those who don't want to read, now on to the review for those looking for a more in depth look.
Okay, so, Tasty Blue sound familiar? Well if you ever heard of tasty planet way long ago then you'd know this is that game.

The first part I'll talk about is what is it? Well it's what it looks like a game where you eat things that you can until you grow enough so that you can eat bigger objects and then when you eat enough of those you can eat the evven bigger objects and so on. Your character will occasionally make these accented sounds like "yummy" "yum-yum" and everytime you finish a level he goes "oompa!" that's just the first character though but I'll get to that later. As far as the two predecessing games go, the sound assets are the same throughout with screaming people and animals and crunch noises when eating, as far as I know they haven't made any different sound clips. There is a local co-op that allows you to use the other controls. The controls are simple, you either move with the mouse, the WSAD keys or arrow keys(the game won't mention the wsad keys but they works just fine)

Now I think I've talked about the original titles enough now I shall discuss what makes this differ from the other games. For starters, it's based in the ocean so there's water physics and the ability to launch yourself out of the ocean. instead of it being 2D top down it's a sidescroller so it may look a bit off in some places. The story as far as I know is about as descriptive as any of the others and uneccesary at most. now the strange thing about this game is that there's no clear chapters anywhere, you know there's 3 different fish types but there's no clear definition where one starts or ends. Now how the fish work, beign that you control a fish and not a grey blob, you can generally move forward with better ease with a challenge for doing a 180 some people might not like this but the only real issue I found was when I tried to eat an object and I ended up looping around it for a bit before I had to turn off. The game seems to have a star scoring system involved, there's a timer on the top right so if there's any obsessionalists who strife for completion the game has that. There's at least 5 difficulty setting that change the damage ratio on enemies.
The setting are simple but more than what the other two games had, you got graphics with aspect ratio but everything else is just a checkbox. Something different they decided to do is include a "carnage" system where you use a slider to change how much "blood" shows when you eat something that's alive. Control options are bare minimum with only mouse sensitivity options, with no rebindable keys.... could be an issue

That's about all I can think of for information, I guess if you either played the original tasty planet games 10 years ago or are curious to play a katamari esqu title then this is your game, it's not for everyone though clearly with visual quality not high in depth. At it's current price and estimated play time of about an hour or two it's definitely a fair price range. And even then if your not satisfied I'm certain this game will be on sale either with the weekly or seasonally.
I really do reccomend this though, I'm having fun with it

Summary:
Classic PS2 JRPG with a fairly engaging story, though game is left marred by slightly weak gameplay and level design when compared to other similar JRPGs of the era.
Pros:
+ Fun yet simple combat
+ Great story with well thought out characters and storylines for each
+ Plenty of content on offer and plenty of things to do
+ SImplistic yet charming artstyle
+ Great character designs
+ Avatar battles are pretty awesome (much better than the main combat IMHO)
Cons:
- Three different level types that don't have many permutations to distinguish each dungeon. Gives game a repetitive feel at times.
- Although fun, combat isn't very mechanically deep, challenging or well balanced. Didn't die or come close to dying once.
Mixed:
-/+ Apart from a few standouts, music is servicable but unmemorable
-/+ Levelling is kind of fast. Whilst this means you don't spend nearly as much time in repetitive dungeons/fields, this does give you less chance to smell the roses if that's what you want.
Overall probably about a 7/10 for the first volume.

One giant monster. Four hunters. Hunters chase monster, and if the game goes on long enough, monster chases hunters. Sort of. The game changes the objective of the hunters to defend a point when the monster hits stage 3 of evolution, which should really be called the "♥♥♥♥ the Hunters So Hard" stage.
All in all, that is the entirety of the game, a game that costs 60 USD, and doesn't really deserve to.
Is it fun? Sort of.  Between in game voice chat bugs, a cursor that just wont quit in game, and a sense of general balance issues here and there, the game has a lot of problems. The core idea of the game is a good one, and has potential to be fun. Killing Floor and Orion Prelude have similar ideas, and both are a hell of a time.
However, this game has more problems than good to it right now, a problem that I can't say for certain will be fixed.
As far as the ludicrous DLC amounts, look no further than the 99.99 USD PC Monster Race pack, that gives a fifth playable monster, two aditional hunters and four monster skins. It also includes the base game, but that is a lot for release day DLC in a game that lacks as much content even when compared to "free to play" MMORPGs by Aria Games (somewhat legendary in their lack of content in games), and even worse, when compared to the often times $1 Orion: Prelude where at least you can enjoy the sensation of killing dinosaurs, across more maps. Bare in mind that the fact that it costs 60 base, they are asking 40 for the privelage to play an entire monster type and two hunters.
If you, like me, bought this game; I am sorry, but at least you weren't the only one, and assuming the bugs get worked out, it can even be considered a good time. I will still be playing it occasionally, if for no other reason than a boost to my own self esteem, a desperate ploy to make me feel like I did not waste my money. If you were lucky enough not to, don't. Wait on it, and see if this game becomes worth the $60 price tag or not.

I first played Tropico back in 2010 on the Xbox 360. Tropico 3 blew me away and to this day is still one of the best games I have ever played. When I heard Tropico 4 was due to release, I was ecstatic. I was let-down by the lack of Juanito which was a big deal at the time. However 4 was still an amazing game, it took 3 and improved upon it.
As you've probably guessed, when I heard Tropico 5 was due to release I was elated. When I found out it had multiplayer, I pre-ordered instantly. Everything they showed just seemed to be an improvement in so many ways.
And then it released.
Tropico 5 is a downgrade in many places to previous titles. I will start off with the negatives first and end on a high.
First of all, the most noticeable and probably most significant change is that they've done away with El Presidente completely, essentially. No more elections, no more♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off factions to please others or just for fun, no more replacing shacks with statues of the glorious ruler. Happiness and votes have all been streamlined into a more casual experience.
Many buildings and features are absent, which were later added as paid DLC to monetise the game further. No more prisons, a lack of tourist attractions, wind farms, etc. These are each added as DLC priced at around $5 per building. It's sad such a brilliant franchise had to result in such petty practices.
Sadly the above issues turned me off the game too much. I couldn't find it fun and enjoyable at all because it just changed the formula too much for the worse.
However, Tropico 5 is at least still a good city builder. It's still one of the top recent ones on the market and I would recommend it to fans of city builders. There's still quite a lot to build and enjoy, big islands to democratically lead or rule with an iron fist. The soundtrack is great as ever.
I would recommend the game to those who haven't played the previous (though IMO you're better off with Tropico 4 + Modern Times), and fans of city builders which aren't OTT on micromanagement strategy. But fans of the previous games, stay away.

This is the first game of it's type (broad world, realistic graphic simulator) that I've played.  This is about the limit of what my Mac Laptop can safely handle, but it made me decide to get a gaming consule so I can have such an immersive and intense experience again in more complex games.
First off I will say that I was there. It felt very real and present, and it didn't hurt that my avatar sounded a lot like me IRL. The landscape was intensely beautiful, with broad starry scars at night, and breathtaking sunrises. It was also brutal, and the panic and ease of being caught in an endless blizzard was a stark reality.
This is a meditative game, and one that took me out of my own place and time, and put me in a stark Canadian wildnerness. It was the ultimate escapist game, also calmed my natural rapid thought process, and led me to focus on the single aim of survival. In spite of the sometimes foreboding music, it eased my mind. I have always wanted to go on a survival expedition (though perhaps not one THIS dangerous), but am currently disabled, so this allowed me the closest thing possible, and for that I am grateful.
It was intensely addictive and kept me up way too late to the point, and sometimes I forgot to eat and wondered if the grumbling stomach was my own. (The chewing noise made me feel like a zombie)
However, I feel this game, at this point, does have its limitations as far as extended replay ( That said, I did play for a looong wonderful time, and do feel I got my money's worth). It became frustrating to enter the locations with the same design over and over, and pick up the same materials.  Though I realize the work involved, I would have liked more variety in interiors, foodstuffs, clothing, crafting, and even possibly wildlife, so I feel that each world is unique. While I realize this is a game about survival, and not building to a  cushy atmosphere, being able to craft increasingly useful items from rare or difficult to attain supplies would be a great incentive to keep playing.
Anyway, transcendent experience and wonderful work from Hinterland.

I really want to like this game because of its interesting concept, but I just can't justify a recommendation.
(1) Plants die way too easily, and for no clear reason. Because of the simplicity of the graphics, you sometimes see plants die, but other times, they just disappear when your back is turned. Was it eaten by a microscopic herbivore? Did it not have enough water in the all-desert arena? Did it not have enough sunlight in the long night? Did it just get too old, since apparently you can't make ageless redwoods? Similarly, because they all look the same, it's hard to tell what species a given plant is.
(2) Is there a mutation dynamic? I honestly don't know, because none of my creatures (mine or randomly created) tended to survive long enough. For an "evolutionary sandbox", there seems to be a lot of reliance on the player to balance it just-so. It seemed like half my playtime was just scattering randomly generated seeds and herbivores (at about a 50:1 ratio) to try to keep the ecosystem from collapsing, and usually ended up lagging my high-end PC in the process.
(3) As others have mentioned, the interface is really difficult to work with. You aren't given any information on what various settings do, and yet you pretty much need to have a fully balanced ecosystem running before you can really test anything easily. (How do you test how efficient a new predator is if the herbivores have already eaten all the plants and starved to death? That happens surprisingly quickly.) And especially for designing plants, this dovetails with point (1) on how difficult just understanding what you're watching can be.
Suggestions for the Developer (if you see this):
(a) Please implement a pause button. going through the menus to pause is much less convenient than just having a simple P/start button pause control.
(b) Please allow us to look at/clone a creature by seeing ALL it's (discovered) values, not just one at a time. I would suggest using a pop-up window for it, as the existing interface is very clunky.
(c) Can we get some simple elaborations on the plants? It would be much easier to work with (and prettier) if there were just a handful of sprites (or sprite pieces that could mix and match for greater diversity for minimal work). For example, "broad leaf", "pointy leaf", "three point leaf" would allow a player to visually see the difference between species at a glance much better than color alone.
(d) Likewise for animals, such as "thin body"/ "fat body", "no legs"/ "four legs", and "tail"/ "no tail". That would give 8 combinations, multiplied by the existing color/size combinations. A simple yawing motion would probably be sufficient to not go into the uncanny valley with the addition of legs.`

Cuphead is an exceedingly difficult game that takes the utmost delight in busting your kneecaps with a metal crowbar and then making you march. It is frustrating and twisted, but more often than not, quite fair. This game is somewhere between a Bullet Hell and a Platformer, having you run 'n' gun in a '30s animation film strip world as you dodge enemies and bullets all over the screen.
There's a satisfying release in besting a difficult challenge in this game. The levels are rarely unfair, and so when you fail, it's usually your fault. Every level takes one of two forms: a battle with something you could call a boss, or a "run 'n' gun" platforming challenge where you have to make it to the end of a level as enemies jump, run, and fly in all around you, trying to take you down. I expected to have an easier time with the latter than the former, but frankly, these platforming challenges are extreme; it's a lot harder to focus on where you're jumping and where you're landing while also trying to pay attention at the swarm of enemies and bullets all around you.
As far as style goes, Cuphead has it in spades. It takes its visual appearance from the advent of color animation, the 1930s, and it takes it full cloth, oddities and all. Even the smallest details are carried over, from a small, inconsistent outline on the boot of King Dice to the small highlight on the eyelids of characters. Almost every major fight is with something that shifts and contorts and transforms, like a clown whose head inflates into a balloon as he accosts you with balloon animals, or a zeppelin woman on a unicycle who transforms into constellations.
The soundtrack too takes much from the source material, composed of the same sorts of melodies, and throughout the game, you'll sometimes hear lyrics attached to the score. Every level starts with an old-timey announcer shouting out something about a high-class wallop or a brewing battle, and the game moves so quickly, even in its menus and loading screens, that the only reason you ever want to put it down is that sheer frustration its high difficulty bar provides. (Which is, incidentally, a reason you may also
want to put it down.)
All in all, Cuphead is a very good game. At a few rare instances, it becomes unfair, but such instances are hard to come by and tend to be, more than anything, an unfortunate convergence of unlikely events rather than an intentional implementation in the game. If you like a difficult, challenging game that will force you to hone your focus, this is the game for you.

In this game, you play as a team of stuntmen who play Power Rangers on television, and they've gotten fed up with their director and open their own studio doing the exact same thing instead. The plot is rather tongue-in-cheek and "dorky," but with a fun tone and some pleasant music along the way. The gameplay is a bit like the Shadowrun turn-based strategy games on PC if those were all about melee combat instead of ranged. You might say "oh, like Banner Saga?" but I would reply "No, this is actually kinda enjoyable, so it's not that much like Banner Saga." As with Shadowrun, you have abilities with cooldowns that give you a nice edge in combat, and the further into the game you get, the game shows you that there are higher tiers of skills to unlock, making things more interesting than just "run over and punch a dude" each turn.
The game has three difficulty levels: one intended to just get through the game without challenge, one to get through it with a little challenge, and a tough version. I played the middle of these three options and found it to be a nice experience that does a good job of teaching you the basics. In between missions ("episodes"), you can buy new equipment for your team, as well as upgrade your studio to incur running costs that give you bonus attitbutes on missions (worth it, from what I experienced).
I personally lack the interest in the narrative and the gameplay hasn't fully hooked me in enough for me to want to really continue, but this game has the rare condition of being one I'm stopping playing that I would actually recommend. I could totally see myself playing it through to completion and liking it if I had more time to spend on games that don't pull me in strong. It commits no grave offenses against the player, seems well-balanced, has a lot of heart, and seems fully intended to be a fun and different experience for gamers. If turn-based strategy, goofy/dorky plot, and/or Power Rangers put a smile on your face, this could be a good buy for you, especially on sale or Humble Bundle.

The closest thing to Zombie Apocolypse SImulator 2015.  I've never seen a game go so deep into the mechanics of it all..  from having to keep both physical and mental health up, realistic looting/scavenging and zombie behavior.  This is one of those games where the simplicity of the graphics hide a deep and realistic system.  It almost plays like the Sims and old-skool isometric action-RPGs.
This is a game where you can actually watch the seasons change and where the zombies will slowly weaken with decay.  You can actually go from the minute after the start of the apocolypse to years later.  From desperate survivor to reconstruction.  There is just one thing it lacks...
and that is NPCs.  From my understanding, they used to be in the game, but the behavior was so wonky they were removed while a new behaviorial model is being developed.  If they can pull off what they want, and that is a dynamic, behind-the-scenes system that governs their behavior and actions, this game will simply be amazing.  It needs interactivity to truly bolster it's gameplay...otherwise it just becomes depressing and rather boring over time.  Also, the sheer size of the maps (the default one is the size of a U.S. county) requires some form of vehicular transport.  I also hear this is being worked on, and it is sorely needed.
What this game can do is provide a deep multi-player experience.  I have yet to try it but I understand there are communities of players that treat PZ like a pen-and-paper RPG.  It definately has that feel.  You couldn't get deeper gameplay without busting out some D20s and rulebooks.  So in the meantime, while we wait for the world to come alive again, there are always private and public servers and roleplay groups.
With the right people, (and mods and maps) you could simulate the Walking Dead act for act.  Details matter.
I recommend this game as a survival/zombie sim and platform for multiplayer gaming.  However, if it's a SP experience you are looking for, I would recommend you wait until at least NPCs are added or you are in for a lonely, quiet time stockpiling supplies and waiting till the power goes out  :)

I'll never forget my first game.
We're the Russians, and we're losing... badly. I'm a member of one the few remaining Soviet fireteams, and we're holed up with our commander in a bombed-out building. Over the rumble of approaching panzers, he's shouting to us his plan to retreat to the final objective in waves and take as many Germans with us as we can.
As the bullets begin to fly overhead, he turns to me, drops a German SMG at my feet, and tells me to cover my squad's retreat across the street. I'm to shoot anyone who comes through the door until the ammunition runs out, then... ahem... make my own retreat to the final objective.
As soon as he says it, I know exactly what he means. I'm just a cog in an immense, brutal machine, and I've found myself in the wrong place at the wrong time. As soon as I've exhausted my usefuleness...
No... I can't think about it. No time. The best I can hope now is to go down swinging. Take a few facists down with me. Go out in a blaze of glory, as they say. I silently bid my squadmates good luck, and take one last deep pull of sooty, frigid air as I resign myself to my fate.
I look at the door I'm supposed to be covering. Then to the SMG. Then at the hole in the wall my squad just escaped through. Then back to the SMG.
...Wait, what key was it to pick something up again?
My tonsils are turned to wallpaper by a Mauser bullet.

Every level in Superhot is an exciting, self-contained, time-bending puzzle that turns typical fast-paced first-person shooter mechanics on their head. Every time you move, your enemies and their bullets do, too – but if you stand still, so will time. It’s a unique idea that creates a smart, tense puzzles where, in between reloading and lining up a shot, you can sometimes dodge every individual bullet in the spray of a burst rifle by moving one small step - and therefore a fraction of a second.
Even as you learn that painful lesson, near-instant respawns keep Superhot’s pace feeling addictive, rather than frustrating. The levels are also designed in a way that compliments both replayability and trial and error: they’re small, self-contained combat instances that would be a tiny part of a level in most games. The real-time playback you get when you complete a level might only be five seconds long, but Superhot’s real gameplay exists in those moments where time has stopped and you have to carefully calculate your next movement based on a heightened situational awareness of what the enemies around you are likely to do while they can move, too.
Tough decisions happen in those moments: Is it worth picking up that object to throw, knowing that picking something up is the most time-consuming action you can take, and your enemy might have moved three feet to the left by the time it lands? Something that an action hero would have to do by instinct in a split second is, in Superhot, a carefully thought-out move.
While the difficulty does increase throughout the 32 levels by introducing environments with less cover to hide behind, multiple entry points for enemies, and usually a lot more enemies armed with shotguns and rifles instead of clubs or pistols (just like other shooters), Superhot also presents scenarios that would likely be impossible without the ability to slow time. One of the later levels, for example, has you standing unarmed in a small room with three armed enemies. You’re not Batman - there aren’t any fancy takedown moves, so you have a few intense seconds to rely on your own attention to detail, and take tiny steps that let you see which enemy might raise their gun first, whether one of their bullets will be inside your head in the next second, or whether the one you just disarmed has recovered behind you and is ready to punch you out before you can shoot the others.
None of my deaths in Superhot felt unfair, though - with white, plain environments that starkly contrast with glowing red enemies that shatter when they’re dead, with a sound effect that makes sure you know they’re out of the picture, every aspect of its visual design is catered to your success, so long as you’re meticulous.
But while every scenario offers a unique challenge, and every level is wholly worth playing, there’s a very significant lack of them - Superhot only takes around four hours to finish, and never significantly evolves its concept in that amount of time. Unlike a puzzle game like Portal or Braid, which constantly introduce new spins on their novelty mechanics, Superhot always functions based on the same time-stopping principle, just in different environments. It doesn’t bother to introduce new weapons or effects to master, except for a ‘possession’ style action that you’re never overtly prompted to use because no levels are designed around it. In its lack of variety and brief length, Superhot feels underdeveloped – a good first step toward a great game, but not quite there yet.
Finishing the main story will unlock some very basic challenge modes in the same levels, but also an ‘endless’ mode that’s fairly addictive in its near-ridiculous difficulty. Hopefully we’ll eventually see some leaderboards, but they weren’t available at the time of review - the difficult-to-decipher menu is actually full of holes and links that lead to nothing, or things that aren’t explained well.
That’s if you can manage to get through the story without wanting to quit, though - what starts out as a laughably cheesy 90s-style hacker story turns into an annoyingly corny roadblock in between the enjoyable gameplay. While it uses its premise in some creative ways - like telling you to quit but rendering your ‘esc’ button useless - it’s largely just nonsensical in its ridiculous hacker hyperbole, like telling you your body is disposable, and you should submit to the software. The entire experience also feels very skewed towards the upcoming VR headsets, as opposed to the 2D screens it’s playable on right now, and while it’s easy to imagine playing these levels and experiencing some of the pixelated software-inspired cutscenes in VR, I doubt it would make the story any more impactful or intelligent.
Superhot’s clever time-manipulation idea delivers consistently fulfilling challenges by turning blink-of-an-eye action into carefully considered and cautious tactical decisions. It avoids potential one-hit death frustration with quick respawns and deaths that always feel earned and avoidable in hindsight. Its unique brand of puzzles are complemented by simplistic but helpfully high-contrast art and sound design, yet undermined by a tedious, intrusive story and a reluctance to put new game-changing spins on its ideas to extend their lives.

“I’m you from the future! There’s no time to explain!”
Thus begins No Time To Explain, a game which seems so promising as you chase your future self through the first few levels as he screams about being horribly mangled by the giant enemy crab who sets off the whole story.
While this is funny – and a very strong start – unfortunately, the game rather goes downhill from there. This is not because the gameplay becomes any worse, but because, while the silly story continues, it just isn’t as continuous after that point. It mostly takes place after zones, rather than getting those reminders in-zone of what is going on and what your goal is, and consequently, it basically ends up boiling down to the puzzles.
Now, this isn’t entirely bad; the game is built up around the 2D platforming puzzles that make it up. There are a number of zones, and in most of the zones, you gain a new ability unique to that zone to help propel you through that zone – or else, there is some unique new gimmick the new zone has. Both work decently enough, and the variety means that the levels seldom feel too samey. All of the areas are quite short as well, meaning that you never end up spending too much time on any given level, and the respawns are pretty generous, with frequent checkpoints (with a couple of exceptions which largely make sense).
But a big part of the charm of the game is the ridiculous plot of you from the future warning you from the present, and the various silly things that happen as a result of that recursion, and without that in a lot of the game, it just kind of feels… there.
However, the biggest flaw with this game is that it is a puzzle platformer with deliberately poor controls – that is to say, it is intentionally difficult to control your character and get them to do exactly what you want them to do. The primary challenge is making whatever janky ability you have in a new area work for you and aid you in getting through the stages without struggling too much. While the controls are not “loose” in the sense of being inconsistent, they are certainly finicky, and it is often more or less trial and error in getting just the right angle on your abilities to clear many obstacles. It isn’t that you don’t know what you’re supposed to do, it is that actually executing on what you’re supposed to do is quite hard – ultimately, the game is more of a technical challenge than an intellectual one.
The game itself feels a little bit cheap as well – the graphics are unimpressive, and the whole thing feels like it was made in Flash. There’s just nothing really there to impress, and while there are a few levels later on – in particular, the art level – which do more, it just isn’t really something that changed my mind about the game.
For all its flaws, the game isn’t bad. But it is kind of mediocre. I don’t regret my time playing it, but it isn’t anything to write home about, either, and your life will not be forever less for not playing it. It is passable, but no more.

tl:dr: Another great concept with less-than-awesome implementation.  The game itself is a great idea.  However, the UI is clunky, graphics could use some work, and the controls are confusing and, even once learned, error-prone.  It looks barely more polished than the projects I see coming out of Oregon State's online CS degree.  I'm sure all the algorithms under the hood are very cool and fancy, but the gamer experience (controls, etc) leads MUCH to be desired.
Neat: You can generate random organisms, see which ones succeed, and then read out their genetic values (for any genes you've unlocked) to try to mimic them/make them better.
Annoying: To do so, you need to read/set each value one-at-a-time.  There is no editor to allow you to view all gene settings for an existing organism, or view all gene settings for a new one.  This would make a HUGE improvement to the game.
Annoying: Small values changes seem to make a big difference, but the sliders are adjusted by very large values.  There is no way to manually enter a specific value
Annoying: Since the premise of the game is tweaking small things to make your ecosystem more effective, the feature allowing the player to to 'clone' an existing organism, make tweaks to genes, and then place is missing and sorely needed.  This makes the game tedious at best.
Annoying: There's a 'limit population' option that seems to cap out populations at 1500.  This is required, because anything over 1500 rapidly grows and slows the game down to unplayable speeds.  However the maps are so large that 1500 plants still result in sparse enough population over the area that herbivores starve.  There is no way to adjust this limit to, say 2500 (which is still playable, but dramatically less sparse).
Annoying: Force fields don't work as expected; plants regularly escape them... so trying to limit the play area to a smaller space (to deal with the population cap) fails over time.
I got this as part of a bundle, which is always a gamble, so I'm not terribly upset about the whole thing.  However, if the developer were to put a bit more time into the player experience (UI, controls, maybe some better looking models) it could be seriously amazing.  Not bad for a small, indie shop, but probably not worth more than a few dollars.

Personally, as a casual strategist, I think that this is a really great and fun game. Overall, most of the controls and mechanics are solid, and of course it doesn't look fabulous, but the graphics are not bad and, to me, the game looks fine. Besides, a little less graphical quality helps it run better on non-dedicated gaming machines. The AI in the game are not super hard, and you will find things about bad ground AI, but to me the AI in ground battles has been fine, and the space battle AI is still good. Really huge Star Wars fans would love this game, as well as many casual strategists.
Rebel campaign, in my opinion, seems a little harder early on - you don't really have a ship equal to light Imperial cruisers, though you do have bombers.
Besides, some of the space battles can get pretty awesome, with large fleets of Star Destroyers or Mon Calamari ships.
For those who don't want to do a lengthy campaign, there is a solid skirmish mode.
Overall, a solid game that looks alright and is pretty fun for most strategists.

this game is interesting enough in its mechanics, to me, to give it a thumbs up, although seeing the general opinion and commentary on this game i see there are just as many reasons to give it a thumbs down, a neutral vote would be amazing here.
all in all this is a fairly simple looking game, but not very optimized for what it needs to do, especially when populations start going into the thousands the game grinds down to a snailspace or worse, this is because of the many calculations going on while the game is not multithreaded, leaving it incapable of processing its own data at a fast enough rate,besides that, and if you keep populations low enough (amount depends on your pc's cpu power) you will have a fun time for a while.
this is a game where you try to play a balancing act with the 3 types of available creatures, in my opinion its not the greatest thing in existence, and will get dull pretty soon, but its fun enough and will keep you busy especially if you are going after the achievements, which once you understand how the game works are easy to get, but before that moment you will fail and struggle a lot.
weird as it is, as the deciphering  has little to do with the game's actual content, the most fun i had was hunting for the codebreaker achievement, the content you unlock is however very very relevant to the game and will greatly help you understand the games core mechanics ;).
if you are into a game that uses the concept of evolution/genetics or just like something different for once, then get this game, preferably when discounted.
its not everyones cup a tea, but surely worth checking out, also there are not many games in this type of simulation genre anyway so give it a try.
