Conceptually, this game is interesting; create a balanced ecosystem to terraform worlds, via genetic tinkering. By examining what survival strategies work, and which ones don't, you can create more adapted, survivable organisms more likely to flourish. Unfortunately, the game makes achieving it's own goals difficult ENTIRELY through being opaque about data.
Genetic traits are not explained. Some are obvious, some are not. Changing traits and observing differing outcomes between species is difficult, because you can't view an organism's traits after it's created and you can and often will lose them amongst other organisms, making gathering data impossible. Further, you can't track individual populations, so two near-identical looking populations coming into existence instantly means you are unable to observe the success of either group; they could both be flourishing, or one might have gone extinct immediately.
The end result is that simply spawning vast numbers of random organisms, and waiting the few minutes it takes for natural selection to choose succesful organisms is both faster and more efficient than attempting to make your own; making it a game that rewards you for not playing it.

Chroma squad is power rangers meets Xcom with pixle art. Yes it is as good as that sounds to the ten year old inside you thats been bludgoned to near death by the cynical you of today.
The plot of the game is simple. Five stuntmen quit their job at a sentai tv series studio and decide to make their own. From there, the plot thickens in the same way watery milk turns into tasty cheese. In other words, the plot starts out weak, but gets stronger the further on you go, just don't expect anything other than pure cheesy sentai goodness.
The game is split into two parts, base management and combat. The base is your studio, from here you can buy new gear for your heros, craft new stuff for them, build new parts for your mecha, view your heros and change their equipment and abilities, upgrade the studio, check emails, and lastly, hire a sponsor. Upgrading your studio gives benefits in and out of combat, from HP boosts, to shop discounts. None of the upgrades are Game changing, but they are all useful. The sponsor however does change things up. Each sponsor can be hired, and you can only have one at a time. Each one offers various benefits, with additional benefits being added on top of those by spending fans (i can only assume its their tolerance your expending). These can have positives and negatives. for example, one of them will cost you alot of money each episode, but give you a big conversion boost. Overall, you want to check what kinds of episodes you'll be shooting during the season before you hire them on. The emails are also worth checking, as you make choices in them that can effect the game. some of them provide no options, others allow you to possibly change the plot or gain more fans and items.
Combat is square grid tactical turn based. during your turn you can move and do one of four things with each individual hero. Attack, weapon attack, activate an ability, or engage teamwork mode. Each hero has an entirely different skill set and should be used appropriately. For example, the techie is good at long range combat and a solid support, while the lead is the guy you use to set up team moves. Each ability has a certain amount of cool down time, that can be decreased by using specific bits of equipment. Weapon attack is exactly what it says on the tin, your hero attacks with the weapon they have equipped instead of their fists. Certain weapons can only be used by certain cheracters, and once used they go on cool down. The ability to use teamwork abilities is what makes this game different from others. When you set a character into teamwork mode, their turn ends, but you can still move your other heros around. You can do three things with two team members when one of them is in teamwork mode. Joint attacks, acrobatics and joint weapon attacks. attacking an enemy that is next to hero in teamwork mode causes both of you to attack at once, causing a greater amount of damage. Weapon attacks do the same thing, but both characters must have their weapons off cool down in order to pull off. Acrobatics are a little different. Each character can only move a certain amount (unless you equip them with gear that increases the distance), but, they can extend the distance by being thrown, allowing them to reach beyond their movement. They do this by walking over to a hero in team mode and then getting thrown higher than a crack addict on a spring board.
The combat is simple at first, but after each season it gets more and more complex, adding on new abilities, new gear and new options at the base. This prevents it from getting stale, always adding in something fresh.
Visually the game isn't all that impressive, certain areas are reused several times, the sprites aren't extremely detailed and you can really see each pixle. But, the number of different sprites there are for the heros is impressive, as it changes with each helmet you wear and each outfit you put on. There are in total about five basic enemy types, two of which get three different sprites. However, the game has alot of bosses, each one is rather different and challenging, save for a few who were rather lacking. The final bosses are really challenging and require you to really plan out your moves, they don't feel unfair though, more like a reward for getting that far, given how much fun they are to fight. The music of the game is limited to a few tracks, none of which are particularly memorable, but they aren't bad by any means and serve their purpose well enough.
The game does allow you to change the names of your characters, your studio, your mecha and pretty much everything else that your in game studio owns. Nothing felt better than seeing my dudes yell "taste the rainbow ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!" before shooting a guy with a traffic cone on his head with a laser powered by crappy special effects and friendship.
That little moment sums up the game, its charming, and it allows you to add your own spin on it to an extent. Its obvious this game came from a place of love and it really does shine despite its flaws, the few complaints i have with it don't outweigh the number of good qualities this title has and i would recommend anyone who loved, or loves power rangers get this. Anyone who likes Xcom, but wants an easier experience, this is for you. Hell, if you like turn based rpgs, this is worth checking out.

Chroma Squad is an amusing romp through sentia silliness - a bunch of sentia (re: a show in the vein of the Power Rangers) actors, fed up with their poor treatment, set up their own studio and follow their dreams...with a tongue firmly in cheek the entire way. And Then Things Get Weird. The game itself plays out through 5 "seasons," each containing 6 episodes - an opener, a closer, and 4 stages that can be done in any order. Each episode consists of one or more turn-based scenarios with several optional conditions - for example, your goal in a stage might be beating the boss, but you get a bonus if a particular character hits them every turn. People familiar with the Disgeae series will be pretty comfortable here. Outside of battles, you spend the income you earned thanks to your legions of adoring fans to buy upgrades for your studio, actors/costumes, and the mech suit, hire advertisers, and respond to fanmail.
The controls are nice and solid, though you will be occassionally frustrated that a throw doesn't pan out the way you want (the rules for when one person can assist another by catapulting them across the field aren't clear, though they are consistent). There are also a few occassions when there is a mechanic that isn't well explained - for example, during a giant mech/monster fight, your audience can save you if you run out of life - but nothing mentions this effect.
The graphics are fun and clear, with a pleasantly pixelated presentation, and while the results aren't exactly spectacular, they are very firmly in line with the source material.
The music and sound effects are pleasant if not particularly memorable.
The story is interesting, if incredibly silly, and not terribly written (or, rather, it's terribly written in the way sentia series are, so, good/bad writing).
There is some replay value - there is clearly a fair number of alternative routes to take, for example, and multiple levels of difficulty. I will certainly play through at least twice more.
TLDR: 8/10 light fun turn based strategy with a solid sense of humor and a nice degree of self-awareness. It isn't trying to be an epic blockbuster AAA, and it certainly doesn't need to be. Some of the elements are a little iffy, but nothing is "badly done," and, if you like the source material, there are a fair number of places and nods to keep you amused.

I'll never forget my first game.
We're the Russians, and we're losing... badly. I'm a member of one the few remaining Soviet fireteams, and we're holed up with our commander in a bombed-out building. Over the rumble of approaching panzers, he's shouting to us his plan to retreat to the final objective in waves and take as many Germans with us as we can.
As the bullets begin to fly overhead, he turns to me, drops a German SMG at my feet, and tells me to cover my squad's retreat across the street. I'm to shoot anyone who comes through the door until the ammunition runs out, then... ahem... make my own retreat to the final objective.
As soon as he says it, I know exactly what he means. I'm just a cog in an immense, brutal machine, and I've found myself in the wrong place at the wrong time. As soon as I've exhausted my usefuleness...
No... I can't think about it. No time. The best I can hope now is to go down swinging. Take a few facists down with me. Go out in a blaze of glory, as they say. I silently bid my squadmates good luck, and take one last deep pull of sooty, frigid air as I resign myself to my fate.
I look at the door I'm supposed to be covering. Then to the SMG. Then at the hole in the wall my squad just escaped through. Then back to the SMG.
...Wait, what key was it to pick something up again?
My tonsils are turned to wallpaper by a Mauser bullet.

Evolve is a great game as it stands, yes there are microtransactions but these currently are only skin packs. Later down the line there will be added monsters and hunters but I wouldnt recommend buying them. The game is very balanced as is and a very fun game to play with and without friends. The detail put into the game is wonderful, from the sounds to the graphics. As a monster you really feel like a powerful beast but never so powerful that you are over balanced. In the beginning you start at weak and need to be stealthy to survive and outwit the hunters. If you can outlast and evolve you can over power the hunters in a battle but only if you target the right people during the right time in battle. As a hunter the mechanics of the game allow you communicate well with and without a headset, being able to mark targets and send messages quickly. The different characters within each class makes for a great way to mix things up during each play through as well as create great teamwork between players. No 2 matches are the same and the base game is great. The micro transactions do not hinder the games gameplay and do not slow down your progression. IF you are worried about all the DLC bundles then buy this game and no other DLCs as a well to boycott this marketing plan. Overall Evolve is a great multiplayer game and is masterfully crafted.

Unfortunately, when I was younger I never had the chance to get into the .hack games.  Years down the road I played the G.U series on an emulator.  Now, several years later, I was fortunate enough to see this remake come out on steam.  I love .hack for its story and the G.U. series does not disappoint.  IMO the story was quite interesting, I enjoyed the character development that happens throughout the series, and compared to the original series, G.U. felt very polished by comparison.  This remake takes something that was already wonderful and made it even better.
If you are new to .hack or at least the G.U. series.  I would suggest watching the .hack roots anime.  If you don't like anime or have time to watch it, you can still very much enjoy and understand the events in this game as they touch on past events that were important anyway.  The game is set up to simulate a real computer environment.  You have "the world" (the name of the MMO being played in the .hack series), your e-mail, online news and forums, etc.  All of this helps to set the tone for the game as well as create the actual world you are playing in.  You actually roleplay the person that is playing an MMORPG.

There are several random NPC characters running around that act as simple player characters.  You can talk to them, trade with it, and gift them items as you would expect to be able to do with players in an MMO.  You party with various characters and go on quests and explore dungeons, as you might expect to do in an MMO.  I was actually quite surprised how far they went to make it feel that you were a person communicating with other players online and playing an MMO with them.  Now, is it completely realistic or a perfect simulation of this?  Of course not!  However, it does the job and does it quite well.  Read the news articles and forum posts as you progress throughout the game to see what is going on in the world, some events being a direct result of things happening in the MMO.
.Hack was truely ahead of its time.  Perhaps to it's detriment.  Hopefully it will see a bit of a revival as the "trapped in an MMO" thing has grown in popularity the last couple years.  If you have the money, you don’t mind playing a single player game, and you want something fun with active combat (this is not turn based), a decent story that is pretty well told, something that feels larger than the game itself, and actually has character development (yes it exists) then try this game out especially if you are a fan of anything .hack!

One giant monster. Four hunters. Hunters chase monster, and if the game goes on long enough, monster chases hunters. Sort of. The game changes the objective of the hunters to defend a point when the monster hits stage 3 of evolution, which should really be called the "♥♥♥♥ the Hunters So Hard" stage.
All in all, that is the entirety of the game, a game that costs 60 USD, and doesn't really deserve to.
Is it fun? Sort of.  Between in game voice chat bugs, a cursor that just wont quit in game, and a sense of general balance issues here and there, the game has a lot of problems. The core idea of the game is a good one, and has potential to be fun. Killing Floor and Orion Prelude have similar ideas, and both are a hell of a time.
However, this game has more problems than good to it right now, a problem that I can't say for certain will be fixed.
As far as the ludicrous DLC amounts, look no further than the 99.99 USD PC Monster Race pack, that gives a fifth playable monster, two aditional hunters and four monster skins. It also includes the base game, but that is a lot for release day DLC in a game that lacks as much content even when compared to "free to play" MMORPGs by Aria Games (somewhat legendary in their lack of content in games), and even worse, when compared to the often times $1 Orion: Prelude where at least you can enjoy the sensation of killing dinosaurs, across more maps. Bare in mind that the fact that it costs 60 base, they are asking 40 for the privelage to play an entire monster type and two hunters.
If you, like me, bought this game; I am sorry, but at least you weren't the only one, and assuming the bugs get worked out, it can even be considered a good time. I will still be playing it occasionally, if for no other reason than a boost to my own self esteem, a desperate ploy to make me feel like I did not waste my money. If you were lucky enough not to, don't. Wait on it, and see if this game becomes worth the $60 price tag or not.

If you are in any way serious about science fiction and/or FPShooters then just get this game. It is one of those cult classics that doesn't get old and something you simply must experience.
Set in the 1960s, somewhere under the Atlantic ocean is the underwater city of Rapture, a supposed Eden for creative minds from the tyranny and oppression of Democracy, Communism and God.
Presiding under the waves is Andrew Ryan, the self proclaimed visionary and hero of the entire project.
However things in Rapture are not as they should be, bodies line the walkways, the tunnels are stalked by insane 'splicers' and the streets are patrolled by the infamous Big Daddies and their terrifying charges: the Little Sisters.
You find yourself in the water as the plane you were in litters the space around you. A lighthouse tower stands above, intimidating any soul that sees it. You enter and your adventure begins.
Bioshock was, and still is, revolutionary. It's intelligence and style do not fail to captivate and horrify. This is not the kind of horror filled with jump scares and the dark. In fact the city is very well lit. This is slow horror, the kind that only works on the minds that stop for thought.
Sure; insane, serial killing, masked mutants do jump at you with sickles implanted in their hands. But it is the pervading sense of no control amid false security and eerie calm that makes you clinch your buttocks for what is around the corner.
The gameplay is fantastic, you have an entire arsenal of - upgradeable - firearms and it doesn't stop there. You can manipulate your very DNA with plasmids. Freeze, burn, shock, fool and launch a hornet hive from your own fingertips. You can make some pretty neat combos too. However, your enemies level up with you (not level 1,2,3,4 etc. they just stay tougher than you).
Killing that guy was easy, and her, and him. What about them? I could really use a health pack. Damn, I've ran out. Oh great, my ammo is almost dry, I could really use some money....
In short, this game is not some crappy FPShooter like COD where you just tank and click on men. It's not some jump scare fest like Outlast where you soil yourself at every turn. It is it's own game, and a brilliant one at that.
The graphics are dated, but have aged well. The soundtrack is minimal and the effects like to emphasise the 1960s setting. My 2014 laptop had no problem with this on medium settings. This game can be played offline with no difference whatsoever. It has provided me with far more than 2.3 hours of entertainment when my internet connection has shorted out.
This game is often on sale for 80% of at around £2.79p or $4.12 cents.

Intelligent design may look simplistic but there's great complexity beneath the surface. You take control of a drone on an uninhabited planet tasked with creating a stable ecosystem. At first it feels like an incremental or idle game; spawn some things, gather resources, upgrade and repeat. However, as you gather research you'll unlock genetic manipulation; a great tool for everyone's inner mad scientist.
Starting with simple mutations – how high your plants grow for example and working your way up to the kind of genes that let you build the ultimate predator (e.g. their speed, manoeuvrability or even how ravenous they are).  Tapping into the very core of the simulation in this way can have some pretty heavy consequences. You may be pretty proud of your freshly crafted apex predator, but it could soon wipe out your entire herbivore population! Adapting to these changes is the main challenge of the game as you progress through sets of three objectives.
The objectives only provide limited direction in an open sandbox so it's up to you if you follow them or go off on your own, striving for the most efficient ecosystem or just tinkering with a single species. Often you'll find correcting your own mistakes to be the most satisfying objective.
This can be tricky without knowing what each genetic trait actually does, and the game purposefully doesn't explain them to you. This encourages science. You can either go full scientist and use forcefields to set up test chambers, run a control and tweak each variable to discern its effect or you can take part in the budding online community as they investigate and experiment to develop theories together.
There's even some delightfully meta gameplay of discovering the games inner workings and players have only recently (at time of original review for Niche: Treat Your Geek) cracked the formula used for the World Efficiency Rating which forms the basis of the online leader-boards. Players were then rewarded with a peak behind the curtain and screenshots of the game's source code and so science intensified as the community started to break it down for clues to the inner workings of the simulation. If you feel like joining in the game can even generate .xml files from your play data.
It may not look like much but if you're looking for a well thought out simulation to toy with (or you don't get enough genetic manipulation and experimentation at home) then this may be what you are looking for. However that does mean the game isn't suited for people that like to mentally switch off while playing or anyone who needs amazing visuals or a deep story. Intelligent Design: An Evolutionary Sandbox is great at what it sets out to do and offers great value for those that will enjoy it most.

Interesting concept, but flawed in practice. The game is a platformer where you chase yourself, and you move around by shooting a beam in the opposite direction. Its kind of novel and fun at first, but then the levels get tougher and it just ends up being more of a frustration than fun. The problem is its a super strong beam that sends you flying. You have very little control, and its hard to maneuver in the air. Also, it stops sending you up very quickly. Also, you can jump, but you barely go off the ground, which doesn't do you any favors. Also the controls of L2 jumping is less than ideal and finnicky.
Then theres the beam itself. So if you want to go up you have to shoot. But the problem is when there are destroyable objects above and below, which the game likes to do. This means jumping destroys the objects below you. But you have to shoot the objects above you, but this sends you flying. Its super hard to aim it to destroy specific blocks, and since you barely can jump, but you can't get up high because you have to destroy the blocks below you. When you try to be precise the gun's super large beam with destroy everything around the single block you want to, also because it moves you. Then theres the boss fights. What should be simple fights of you dodging and shooting, turn into anything but. This is because of the stupid beam. When you try and shoot at the enemy above, below, or to the side, it sends you flying, usually into a spike or to your death. So you can neve just stand your ground and shoot him above you, because.....you know, the annoying unnecessary beam. Also the jump sucks and barely moves you, so you are forced to use the beam to get around. With single mistake deaths and only 3 lives, while the boss has lots of health, it just makes the bosses harder than they should be. After playing this game it makes me appreciate simple jumping and movement, and being able to shoot someone above you without it auto-killing you. Avoid unless you like things that are unnecessarily harder than they should be, just to be different.

The tagline is "Deceptively Simple"... I think they forgot the "Looks" at the front.
Lyne was originally a tablet app, so it has basic mouse-driven controls, and rules so simple you could easily let a child play it.  The first few sets certainly are so simple that how long they take you are more a measurement of manual dexterity than intelligence.  A child will probably find the later levels frustrating, however.
Somewhat like a Sudoku, I found Lyne's puzzles to be relatively simple and logical, even when they were occasionally time-consuming, they were rarely as frustrating and unforgiving as some game's puzzles are.  It's a puzzle game for relaxation, and when I found myself incapable of solving the puzzle the first try, often, just undoing my moves and starting from the other end made the solution apparent.
It comes with a daily update of about 50 new quick puzzles every day, so that you have a little something to unwind with whever you want, and that's a nice plus.  I beat the static puzzles (650 puzzles, excluding dailies) in about 15 hours of playtime, without ever feeling like it was a chore.
If you're someone who likes doing puzzles because the act of thinking something through several moves in advance is relaxing to you, this is a great place to sink a little cash for a lot of leasure.

I've only spent a few hours on this game so far, but it has me quite intrigued.  As of late June, 2017, it is a fairly new game, and the developer has decided to allow the players to do most of the figuring out of how the game's genetics (and other factors) work.  This is very much a "Sit down and sink your teeth into the mechanics" kind of game, and it is very, very much focused on genetics, evolution, adaptation, and extinction.
You can create plants, herbivores, or carnivores.  You 'earn the right' to control some of their genetics over time, but you can create random individuals without controlled features whenever you like.  Once something starts to survive, especially if it is a plant, well there you go - good luck getting rid of all life in your place again.
I really like the study of genetics.  I don't want all the factors explained to me, and I want great depth and complexity.  This game offers me this.
For example, plant color.  Sure, the graphics are simple and representative of the genetic differences... but there are visible phenotypic differences.  Some plants are a different color - but there is no "color" gene.  It's something else making the change.  And through study and comparison of individuals, I can see where it clearly isn't, and where it probably is... and lo and behold, it is likely from the interplay of two different genes...
Such studies entertain me.  Real genetics are as or more complicated than this, and real genetics are not labeled as doing whatever until scientists figure them out - and even then, it is not certain everything has been understood yet.  The game mirrors this well.  I like it.
Additionally, once you earn the right to control some genes, you can only partially control them.  Natural variation extends outside of the range you can create. Want to get exceptionally low or high values?  You can start in a direction, but that's the end of the "intelligent design" - it's the environment and random happenings that take over.  I have noticed gene values can go negative as well.
What does -1.4 "seed drift" gene mean?  I don't know yet, but the game has just enough visual detail combined with genetic detail and space for individuals to play out their phenotypes that I think I can puzzle it out.
I highly recommend this game for those who want to sink their teeth into a genetic drift and gene function simulator, who want to figure it out from many, many examples instead of being told.

Growing up, I was a huge fan of the .hack//SIGN anime and the original games. I never played the PS2 .hack//G.U. games, so I was very excited to see them remastered, and have the chance to log back into The World.
The 'world' of .hack// is immense. That being said, if you aren't familiar with the franchise, this game makes it easy to enter into the series. The "Terminal Disc" included also provides a synopsis of the original .hack// games (usually referred to as .hack//IMOQ), if you weren't able to play them when they originally released. Even so, that information is still background, and won't hinder your experience if you don't watch. I have been supplementing my gameplay by watching the .hack//SIGN series again, then the Terminal Discs, and now .hack//Roots (an anime that takes place right before G.U. actually begins).
I'm currently working on Vol.1, so not sure how this will change, but so far I am enjoying the game. The characters are all memorable; most are cliché, but in a way that remains humorous. Some users have complained about the game being too easy (esp. those who played G.U. on PS2); while I cannot advise on the difference, I have found that often the combat is not difficult, unless encountering enemies that are quite higher in level. I don't have an issue with the pace of leveling, although the Weapon Skill leveling (separate from Character Level) isn't as transparent as it could be.
Something that I have always enjoyed about the .hack games is the 'meta' game. The MMO where most of the action occurs, "The World," is just one aspect of the actual game - you also have access to the Official and Community Forums, News Site, and Email. In essence, you're playing the person who is playing the character of Haseo. While this adds to the immersion, it can occasionally become inconvenient - for example, after reaching a certain point in the area, in order to progress, you have to Log Out, check your email to see that you've qualified for the next step, and then you can log back in and proceed.
It is worth noting that there are some issues with this port, which hopefully the developers will patch soon. This game is clearly made to be played with a controller, but it only has Xbox controls native (odd given that steam supports DS4 controller, and the game is originally from PS2 and has a PS4 port). There are some mods which address this, but it's unfortunate that it wasn't included. Many people encountered issues with the 'anti-aliasing.' I personally play on a laptop not geared towards high-end gaming, so I had to decrease the resolution, but once done was able to get consistent 60fps.
I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys JRPGs, people who are interested in learning more about the .hack franchise, and definitely to those who are longtime fans of the series.

SUPERHOT is one of the most unique games I've played in awhile. From gameplay, to visuals, to sound design, I can't say I've ever played anything quite like it and I play a lot of video games. It's fun, stylish, intense, and it's one of those games that, by gameplay alone, gets into your head and sticks with you--think Super Hexagon--to the point where for days afterwards, I'd be playing more conventional FPSs and wondering why time wasn't moving with me.
The biggest thing to note is that you should NOT buy this game hoping for a standard FPS experience, or you will be disappointed. There's only a small variety of weapons available to you, the only firearms of which are a pistol, a tommy gun, and a shotgun. Aim is not important; your enemies shatter like glass, so a bullet to the foot is just as effective as a bullet to the head. And you are going to be CONSTANTLY outgunned anyway, since you're facing multiple enemies who, unlike you, never run out of ammo. Instead, this game plays much more like a very intense puzzle game. Each level, you are given a small environment, a smattering of usable items, and a group of enemies that spawn at specific times with specific weapons. Rather than blow them away with superior firepower or marksmanship, you have to come up with a strategic solution that takes into account a number of smaller, calculated decisions. How many fractions of a second will it take me to disarm this enemy? Should I throw my gun to temporarily knock this enemy back, or should I risk waiting the extra second it takes me to reload? If I move two paces forward, where will my enemies be positioned afterwards? In many of the earlier levels, these puzzles are pretty easy to solve, but in later levels, they become really challenging and nerve-wracking, and as a result, very rewarding when you finally find a solution that's both efficient and gorgeous in the automatic replay afterwards.
Speaking of gorgeous, this game looks incredible. Between the sight of red, glassy enemies shattering into flying shards against a high contrast backdrop, to the glitchy, increasingly abstract "cutscenes" scattered through the game, I could barely tear my fingers away from the F12 key to snap as many screenshots as possible. In a review I read before I played the game, the reviewer complained of the writing and aesthetic as "hacker hyperbole," and though that is a completely apt description, I found it delightful rather than obnoxious. Go in looking forward to an over-the-top and psychadelic glitchscape, and don't worry if the plot doesn't stand up to scrutiny.
As for the negatives, my biggest complaint about the game is it's length. It ended far earlier than I expected, taking just 3-4 hours to beat the main campaign. This was especially frustrating because at least half of that time was spent on levels that I didn't find all that challenging. It left me feeling like it ended just as I was starting to break a sweat. To be fair, there is bonus content at the end, but all of it involves riffing on the same few levels provided in the main campaign--speedruns, weapon restrictions, harder enemies, etc.  There is also an "endless mode" with constantly spawning enemies on a few new maps, but without any leaderboards or new content/mechanics in this mode, I didn't feel motivated to play it for very long.
A much MUCH more minor complaint is the lack of sound in sharable playbacks you can make at the end of each level. With a game as good-looking as SUPERHOT, I was taking tons of video to show my friends my coolest moments in-game, but I feel that a lot was lost just by virtue of there being no sound--especially because the sound design for this game is so awesome. The low buzz of time passing, the whoosh of bullets passing by in slow-mo, the sound of breaking glass as you shatter your enemies--all of it is so damn cool, and I was disappointed when I found out that all the videos you take in game are muted.
In sum, SUPERHOT is a super stylish and unique violence-puzzle that I loved playing, but that ended much too soon. After playing both the main campaign and some of the challenge modes, I'm not sure I would've bought this game at full price, but I feel the sale price of $15 that I did pay for it is quite fair. If you want a puzzle game that makes you feel like a time-bending badass, then I would definitely recommend giving SUPERHOT a try.

The tagline is "Deceptively Simple"... I think they forgot the "Looks" at the front.
Lyne was originally a tablet app, so it has basic mouse-driven controls, and rules so simple you could easily let a child play it.  The first few sets certainly are so simple that how long they take you are more a measurement of manual dexterity than intelligence.  A child will probably find the later levels frustrating, however.
Somewhat like a Sudoku, I found Lyne's puzzles to be relatively simple and logical, even when they were occasionally time-consuming, they were rarely as frustrating and unforgiving as some game's puzzles are.  It's a puzzle game for relaxation, and when I found myself incapable of solving the puzzle the first try, often, just undoing my moves and starting from the other end made the solution apparent.
It comes with a daily update of about 50 new quick puzzles every day, so that you have a little something to unwind with whever you want, and that's a nice plus.  I beat the static puzzles (650 puzzles, excluding dailies) in about 15 hours of playtime, without ever feeling like it was a chore.
If you're someone who likes doing puzzles because the act of thinking something through several moves in advance is relaxing to you, this is a great place to sink a little cash for a lot of leasure.

Pros
+ The single-player MMO gimmick is one of it's best features. You can read and respond to emails sent by your companions, read up on current events in the dot hack universe through the news system, play a  pretty decent card game or read the game's many forums and respond to some of the topics. Some of the banter in the forums was top notch.
+ Pretty decent story that flows well through all four volumes.
+ Memorable characters, most of the characters get a good amount of development throughout the games. Either through in game cinematics or emails.
+ The combat is pretty good, similar to 'Tales of' action RPGS.
+ The restored textures look great and for a PS2 era game it aged very well.
+ Lengthy game (if you are playing all 4 volumes for the first time). There is a lot to do in each volume besides the main story.
+ Soundtrack was excellent, and the voice acting ( I played with the Japanese dub) was solid.
+ Good port, had no real issues worth mentioning. Assuming you don't have a toaster you should be able to run this fine.
Cons
- While the majority of the cast is pretty great there a few characters (GASPARD!!!!) that are insufferable. The main character, Haseo, falls into this category for most of the first game. Thankfully he grows out of it later. Same could be said for Atoli.
- Do not go into this game expecting a complex dungeon crawler with an amazing combat system. One of the game's biggest issues is its repetitive nature.
- This is especially prevalent with the dungeon/quest design. You will get very sick of seeing this one cave dungeon that the developers just love to use for so many of the quests and side quests over and over again. To add to that most of the story missions are set in the worst most repetitive and boring dungeons (out of the 8 or so dungeons styles there are in the game).
- The boss battles and overall difficulty of the game is pretty low. I never found a need to grind other than to raise my level enough to use certain weapons that I acquired. The game is very easy, there were a handful of moments were I felt pressured and that was mostly due to not bringing a dedicated healer (Atoli) or purposefully fighting bosses several levels higher than me.
- The crafting/upgrading system was pretty meh. I hardly ever used it or had need for it.

I began playing The Long Dark during its Early Access phase, and reviewed it favourably after just a few days!  However, I thought I should update my review because the game is released now and is quite different than when I began playing.
I can only recommend it even higher now!  After the introduction of custom difficulty settings, this is the best purely-survival game available, in my opinion.  It's possible to tailor your gaming experience to suit your unique playstyle, *and* you can share a code with your friends that enables them to try your difficulty settings too!
There is so much to love in this game!  If you're new, I still recommend you play the Survival mode sandbox to learn the game before trying the Wintermute story mode.  You might like to learn by starting at Mystery Lake with this code:
8h4x-AkBQ-NZAh-1u5o-xgAA
With this difficulty setting code, you will still need to be careful around wildlife--unlike Pilgrim--but it's less intense than the Voyager difficulty setting, in terms of wildlife threats.  To compensate, you'll be able to get cabin fever, which is not a risk in Voyager mode.  So think of it as an in-between setting, but with cabin fever.  ;)

The Forest is an alpha game with lots of content and even more potential. Playing alone can quickly become boring or scary, but playing with friends almost never gets old and there is dozens of hours of playtime. A group of friends and I did a playthrough a while back where we built an entire fortress complete with walls, attempted to cut down a small section of the forest, battled hordes of cannibals and mutants to defend our base and even led some in to catch in a rope trap until we eventually finished the game. Hundreds of crafting reciepes, building options, a large open map, dozens of caves and weapons, pre rendered loot packages, skyscraping mountains and even cannibal villages littered across the map all allow for over 30 hours of playtime (thats how long it took us to get curious and beat that save, so you can potentially double it.) until you and your friends decide to figure out the entire mystery...
TLDR;
Epic game with limitless goals and challenges that can be played easily with friends to give you up to hundreds of hours of playtime, and even has a satisfying ending. I absolutely adored playing this game with my friends, and its always something you can go back to and play again since the devs still update on the regular.

There is art here, despite what many would say isn't possible with games, from Roger Ebert to game designers like Hideo Kojima. But it's in BioShock - it's in the gorgeously realized, watery halls of Rapture. It's in the way the characters develop, in the testimonials of the recording boxes you pick up along the way. It's in the way the narrative is structured, and the way it blends so seamlessly with the action.
Irrational had a clear vision with this game, something pulled off with remarkable precision in every department. They didn't just deliver something that's fun to play, a criterion so often cited as the benchmark of what makes a game worthwhile. BioShock stands as a monolithic example of the convergence of entertaining gameplay and an irresistibly sinister, engrossing storyline that encompasses a host of multifaceted characters. This is an essential gaming experience.

Science!
This is a game for people who enjoy patiently solving puzzles. Completing all the game objectives is not the end game, it's where the game starts. Once you know how everything works, you spend time trying to develop genetic recipes for plants, herbivores, and carnivores. You can conduct experiments inside the contained forcefields. You tweak the balance until it stays stable. You observe how random mutations either help or hurt the design.
I spent an entire day developing my "stepping stone" plant recipe. Over the next few hours the plants mutated into taller "fat candles" that were better able to stand up to the stresses of wild fires and getting munched on by herbivores. This weekend I've assigned it as a science project for my homeschooled kid.  I haven't figured out how to get the herbivores and carnivores into a stable balance yet. I have lots of experiements left to run!
The down sides are in the simple graphics and unpolished UI. Framerates do drop when populations get high. This is because every plant and animal has its own genetic profile and behavior.
The game is still new and the developer is rapidly working on improvements. The lastest update, allowing you to scan existing organisms to see their genetic values was a big help. (Keep up the good work!)
If conducting experiements and tinkering with variables is your thing, you will love this game. If you're looking for a polished commercialised adventure game, this isn't it. The $6.99 price tag is pretty decent considering the hours I've put in so far.

I'm sick to death of early access survival games on Steam, so for that reason I almost passed on The Long Dark. Yet another game where you're collecting wood while fiddling around with a hunger and thirst meter. *Yawn*
This is one time when I'm happy to have been wrong. You will do those things in The Long Dark, but they keep the gameplay interesting and rewarding.
Pros
- Resource collection is time-consuming, but doesn't feel like a time-wasting slog. It's not an overly long, drawn-out process where you have to chop a tree and then chop up the log and then chase down sticks as they roll all over the environment.
- No zombies! Thank god for that. The enemies are natural and the fact that they're animals like wolves and bears makes them no less menacing. I'm so grateful that this isn't yet another zombie survival game.
- The enemy AI makes them pretty intimidating. They don't just charge you from across the map every time the second they see you. A wolf might approach slowly, appearing and disappearing from your sight. It adds to the stress.
- The environment does a great job of making you feel cold. It's not just because it's snowing in game. The sound design and lighting and everything just gives off the perfect wintry vibes.
- The inventory system forces you to make tough decisions and choices. Picking up and moving camp isn't a simple decision if you have a lot of stuff stashed in your current hideout. Walking is dangerous and time and resource-consuming. You actually have to put thought into your wandering.
- I personally like that there's no map. I printed out a physical map, but I actually quite like that you can't just open a map and see a little map marker moving around that you can mindlessly use to navigate. You have to put thought into where you're going. I do wish they would add a simple, hand-drawn map to the game that your character crudely adds to as you discover new locations. It makes sense to me that a survivor would try to keep some sort of map. I would, but I would like if it didn't have a player marker. Or at least had the ability to turn the player marker on and off.
Cons
- This is a temporary con, but no story mode yet. This is what I'm waiting for more than anything.
- The art style doesn't appeal to me personally. Things, especially bodies, are just lumpy and devoid of detail. Lots of games manage to make low or medium detail appealing, but this doesn't.
- Sometimes the hunger mechanic seems a little out-of-whack with reality. People, even people who are in physically stressful condition don't need to eat multiple times a day. In this game you'll eat two or three entire fish and then you're still hungry and your hunger meter is still going down! You do start to get worn out by trying to get the amount of food the game thinks you need.
- I wish you could interact a little more with the buildings. It would be nice if you were able to clear the dead bodies out of the bedrooms, for one.
Overall, a fun game that I'm looking forward to playing more of when it's out of EA.

A tactics game where you play as a Power Rangers TV studio. Game is split up into episodes (where you do battle) and in between episodes you spend your cash/craft upgrades. It has a silly story with silly enemies and plot. Story is mostly told through dialogue so doesn't get very deep. A lot of 'just because' reasoning so you have to go with the flow. Things that happen outside dialogue are often just quickly summed up by the narrator to set the scene. Graphics are good enough and sound fits well.
Episodes are often split up into 1-3 tactics battle segments and sometimes finished off with a mecha battle. The tactics system is pretty standard and simple. There are only damage and status effects, no damage types (no physical vs magic attack, no elemental resistance/weakness). The mecha battle is a regular RPG slugfest where you take turns attacking each other. You can do multiple actions in your turn and each action builds up your combo meter (which increases the effect of your next action but decreases the accuracy). In normal mode, the enemy mecha usually just does 3 regular attacks one special attack. You reduce damage taken through a timing minigame (there's a bar that fills up, stop it at the right time and you block more damage).
It feels like you want mecha battles to be over as soon as possible so it feels better to go for as many 50%+ accuracy attacks as you can rather than ever defending. It seems like enemies usually do 3 attacks of ~5k damage each and defending (maybe unless you go for max defense) only blocks a total of ~5k of that. It feels like a race against the clock so the less turns you take to defeat the mecha, the less turns the enemy has to deal 15k+ damage.
However, it does get a little frustrating when you miss your 2nd attack (~85% accuracy) twice in a row, which is brutal because of your missed damage output (especially if you're holding onto your finisher for a high combo) and it means you take free rounds of damage. But I guess that's why there's the mecha audience meter (DBZ spirit bomb-esque gathering the energy of your fans). When you lose all hp in a mecha fight, your hp meter refills with audience points (though losing hp from then on doesn't seem to affect audience score later). Assumably, the more fans you have the more HP you get.
In tactics battles, your performance is calculated by an audience meter which goes up through combat actions and by following the episode's director's instructions (which are bonus objectives like 'win in 5 turns' or 'keep all members above 50% health). In normal difficulty, clearing missions wasn't too hard but clearing them while following the director's instructions was sometimes pretty challenging. However, you don't need to do every instruction to max out your audience meter and it doesn't seem like failing them matters if you fill the meter anyway.
Boss enemies sometimes have line attacks but they feel unpredictable. The attacks don't hit a standard grid-based area (not clean 45 degree directions) so it's more realistic but you can't tell what it'll hit. One boss has a burst aoe (starting from himself) that usually hits allies hidden behind other allies but there were rare times where it didn't (only the one in front got hit). Sometimes the cubes served as cover, sometimes his attack hit despite the cube being in the way. Maybe there is no such thing as cover and it just randomly misses without showing the 'miss' text. He burst twice in the same spot on one turn and hit 2 on the first and all 5 on the second.
The only real indicator I could see of how much damage you'd do is the enemy health bar (which shows how much remaining hp would be left after the attack). It can be a little tough to see if an attack really finishes it off or if there's a pixel left. It would've been nice to see an obvious indicator (like the bar turning gray) to show the attack should finish off the opponent.
Alternatively, you could check your attack stat for how much damage you'd do (only for single attacks; I'm not sure how teamwork attacks affect damage).
Seems to let you retry missions relatively easily (via abandon mission) so if you like to retry there's no need to quit/restart the game. If you don't, then you can personally choose to make your own hardcore mode by accepting whatever result you get. It's pretty nice for me because you go into episodes without knowing what you're really up against so you can abandon and customize/upgrade as necessary so you can beat the mission. Also, some director's instructions (mission goals) can be ruined by unfortunate events outside your control.
It allows you to fast forward through cutscenes which is very nice. However, it sometimes speeds through the first text bubble even when I didn't intentionally click or skip through. It may have captured a click several seconds before during a cutscene or something. It would be nice to also have animation speed options in settings to make quicken actions and be able to fast forward in-battle quips.
[Side note: why is 'go' and 'fas' blocked by steam? Wanted to type 'go' and 'faster']
Other thoughts:
Worth a try if you like the theme (a studio making episodes of Power Rangers) and are fine with simple tactics games. I don't think I would like it as much if it were a generic tactics game (the combat system isn't very deep) but I think they play up to the theme very well. Reminds me of Punch Club (silly story, good-enough game) though I think I enjoyed this experience more.

Chroma Squad is a turn-based, tactics RPG from Behold Studios. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
The Power Rangers were a huge part of my childhood. I’m not talking about the newer, crappier Power Ranger series’, I’m talking about the original that started in 93. The Red Ranger was on of my idols as a child. Chroma Squad has all the same Power Rangers vibes in all the right ways.
The story is not what I expected it to be. While I was ready to dive headfirst into a tactical, turn-based Power Rnagers styled game, I was surprised to find that I was diving into a tactical, turn-based you’re playing as stuntmen filming a Power Rangers styled show game. Total curve ball. That’s what I get for not watching the trailer beforehand. I’m still trying to figure out how I missed it.
Gameplay is simple, but not too simple. There’s the right amount of everything for you to take into consideration while you’re in the heat of battle.
The music is great and the dialog is actually pretty funny.
The Bad
I’ve got nothing here. Move along, please.
The Meh
It’s not actually the Power Rangers.

* Amazing Entertainment Value for a Tiny Price *
I love little indie games like this.  Inexpensive and widly entertaining considering what one paid for them, even at full price.  While it doesn't look like much, this simple game combines an expanding RNG with a few twists and encourages experimentation.  Death is effectively meaningless aside from setting a high score and a few objecitves, and discovering some new stupid way to die is actually encouraged.
This creates the unique experience of not only having the strategy of trying to stay alive as long as possible, but at the same time rewarding decisions to go out in a blaze of glory or at least some new way of meeting one's demise (which sometimes manage to pay off anyway).
The poker-like element of knowing how to play any given situation keeps the game fresh, and for the tiny price tag I can safely recommend it to anyone -- even if the play style isn't really for you, the actual risk in miniscule!

The definitive zombie survival game. There is a learning curve but it is a very rewarding game once you understand its core mechanics. And to think this is early access.
I joined a online server and holed up in a house boarding up the windows and laying low but thats just my strategy. You could find a group and work together, be a bandit or a lone pyschopath. Zombie numbers can vary from a few shamblers to several massive hordes.

There is a rpg/sim like element to this game as well. You can read books to learn how to trap, fish, peform first aid, cook amongst other skills. You also have to maintain your character's wellbeing like eating, drinking, avoiding getting bored or stressted which is not a far cry from the sims.
You also get to create a character from some different models and choosing the hair type, skin tone, profession which have certain perks and traits where you can pick negative ones in order to get positive ones (like lucky trait or eagle eyed) or you can just skip the traits altogether.
For an early access game this has a lot going for it. It's a great experience and i look forward to future updates

SUPERHOT is one of the most unique games I've played in awhile. From gameplay, to visuals, to sound design, I can't say I've ever played anything quite like it and I play a lot of video games. It's fun, stylish, intense, and it's one of those games that, by gameplay alone, gets into your head and sticks with you--think Super Hexagon--to the point where for days afterwards, I'd be playing more conventional FPSs and wondering why time wasn't moving with me.
The biggest thing to note is that you should NOT buy this game hoping for a standard FPS experience, or you will be disappointed. There's only a small variety of weapons available to you, the only firearms of which are a pistol, a tommy gun, and a shotgun. Aim is not important; your enemies shatter like glass, so a bullet to the foot is just as effective as a bullet to the head. And you are going to be CONSTANTLY outgunned anyway, since you're facing multiple enemies who, unlike you, never run out of ammo. Instead, this game plays much more like a very intense puzzle game. Each level, you are given a small environment, a smattering of usable items, and a group of enemies that spawn at specific times with specific weapons. Rather than blow them away with superior firepower or marksmanship, you have to come up with a strategic solution that takes into account a number of smaller, calculated decisions. How many fractions of a second will it take me to disarm this enemy? Should I throw my gun to temporarily knock this enemy back, or should I risk waiting the extra second it takes me to reload? If I move two paces forward, where will my enemies be positioned afterwards? In many of the earlier levels, these puzzles are pretty easy to solve, but in later levels, they become really challenging and nerve-wracking, and as a result, very rewarding when you finally find a solution that's both efficient and gorgeous in the automatic replay afterwards.
Speaking of gorgeous, this game looks incredible. Between the sight of red, glassy enemies shattering into flying shards against a high contrast backdrop, to the glitchy, increasingly abstract "cutscenes" scattered through the game, I could barely tear my fingers away from the F12 key to snap as many screenshots as possible. In a review I read before I played the game, the reviewer complained of the writing and aesthetic as "hacker hyperbole," and though that is a completely apt description, I found it delightful rather than obnoxious. Go in looking forward to an over-the-top and psychadelic glitchscape, and don't worry if the plot doesn't stand up to scrutiny.
As for the negatives, my biggest complaint about the game is it's length. It ended far earlier than I expected, taking just 3-4 hours to beat the main campaign. This was especially frustrating because at least half of that time was spent on levels that I didn't find all that challenging. It left me feeling like it ended just as I was starting to break a sweat. To be fair, there is bonus content at the end, but all of it involves riffing on the same few levels provided in the main campaign--speedruns, weapon restrictions, harder enemies, etc.  There is also an "endless mode" with constantly spawning enemies on a few new maps, but without any leaderboards or new content/mechanics in this mode, I didn't feel motivated to play it for very long.
A much MUCH more minor complaint is the lack of sound in sharable playbacks you can make at the end of each level. With a game as good-looking as SUPERHOT, I was taking tons of video to show my friends my coolest moments in-game, but I feel that a lot was lost just by virtue of there being no sound--especially because the sound design for this game is so awesome. The low buzz of time passing, the whoosh of bullets passing by in slow-mo, the sound of breaking glass as you shatter your enemies--all of it is so damn cool, and I was disappointed when I found out that all the videos you take in game are muted.
In sum, SUPERHOT is a super stylish and unique violence-puzzle that I loved playing, but that ended much too soon. After playing both the main campaign and some of the challenge modes, I'm not sure I would've bought this game at full price, but I feel the sale price of $15 that I did pay for it is quite fair. If you want a puzzle game that makes you feel like a time-bending badass, then I would definitely recommend giving SUPERHOT a try.

Dragodino is a colourful, family friendly multiplayer platform game with nice audio and simple yet fun gameplay mechanics.

****************

- Can become repetitive after about an hour or two.
- Audio can become overwhelming after an hour or two.
Final Thoughts

Okay, first of all, I received the game in Humble Bundle's June Monthly bundle. That means, I actually didn't buy it on purpose, even though it's been on my wishlist for quite a while.
But let's get to the point: Superhot is a fun shooter. It really is fun, but it tries to pull off a serious story which can be completen in less than an hour. And has to be completed if you want to play things like Endless Mode. And for me, the story takes the fun away. I wanted Superhot just to make some fancy kills in slow motion (basically what it advertised), but forcing myself through the "campaign" really killed my motivation for the game. It basically felt like an hour long tutorial.
The story itself was pretty generic meta stuff. I'm not going to spoil anyone here, but halfway through the story, the game reveals that it is  - surprise - more than just a game. Afterwards, Superhot takes you hostage, disables the Esc button, ... Nothing other meta games didn't already do much better.
Don't get me wrong, I'd be really happy if the game had a good story mode. And for 23€, I'd expect more than one hour of half-hearted depth. But I don't like to get forced to play something that feels like a way too long tutorial before I can do what I actually wanted to do.
The shooting part is fun. Time only moves when you move, so you can do some pretty sick shots. The replays afterwards are in real-time, so it looks even more epic. But halfway through the game, you learn to "hack" enemies and take over their bodies. This feature doesn't have to be used very often, but it - for me - defeats the purpose of a shooter.
Recommending it or not is a hard choice. It really is fun, especially if you unlocked Endless Mode. It is innovative and looks pretty, but it doesn't offer nearly enough for it's price. If you want it, get it on sale. But I'm not going to recommend it for 22,99€.

Evolve (Just the base game, not the DLC, not the season pass) is a fun game for myself. I enjoy the game modes that they  implemented into the game (Hunt, Rescue, Nest, & Defend) and then Evacuation (combining the 4 modes into an interesting 'plot' over 5 days). The 12 hunters all have their own personality and kits/weapon loadouts making each of their gameplay different from the other (from Markov and his lightning gun to Parnell with his rapid fire shotgun). There are all sorts of playstyles mixing up the hunters. A fun game in my opinion though I do not know if I would charge $60 for a multiplayer only game (yes even the 'solo' campaign mode is the same as multiplayer, just with bots instead of other players). I felt thats the bots both fellow hunter bots and the monster bot are really well done in the game (though they can bug out occasionally). The game maps are interesting though some feel a bit simialr to others, though all in all the 12 different maps make for interesting and varying gameplay. To add onto the game, future maps and game mode will be free, making the base game amazing
Now for the cons. While the game itself is fun, there are some parts of the game, or parts to be added that drag it down. The first would be the three ways of obtaining the game. A flat $60 for Evolve, the $80 delux edition, and the $100 PC Monster race all three do not include the day one DLC. Given it is JUST COSMETIC, so it isn't that big of a loss though trying to sell the season pass or the 100 dollar order without the added DLC leaves a few questions to be asked. On top of the DLC, future monsters as well as hunters will be an added cost so while the player gets new maps and modes, the new characters are locked less you pay. Given they are fun, Hunt, Rescue, Nest & Defend get stale after a while.
All in all, if you can find the game with everything included (all they have to offer in one package) then jump all over it. Outside of that, either just get the game and enjoy it for what it is and try to ignore 2K trying to sell you DLC which merits the negative review

Ignore how many hours I have logged on steam, I had this game on disc before and easily have hundreds, possibly a thousand hours unlogged on it.
Onto the review:
I have only played Star Wars: Empire at War, not the Forces of Corruption expansion that also came with the Steam version, thus that makes this review for the core game itself, not the FoC expansion!
The game itself is an RTS. Rebellion vs Empire in the Star Wars universe that features a galactic map system (Something people might be familiar with in the old Star Wars Battlefront games). However EAW features both land and space battles in a two-step invasion system to conquer a planet. The ultimate goal is to take control over the entire galaxy, but to achieve it smaller, and much more tedious and annoying goals must be finished. The online multiplayer last time I checked no longer functions due to gamespy shutting down their multiplayer servers (RIP). But back when it was online there were a few gamemodes, none I really played. It had a fairly sizable modding community which provided custom maps, Which I am not sure you can get anymore as they were hosted on filefront. Not to say this game is boring, but just throwing out there that there are custom maps for this game you could find.
Every planet (Excluding one, the astroid fields.) has it's own space and ground map, which will lead to hours of gameplay alone as you battle through each of them for either faction. But be aware a lot of them have native species which will either side with you, your enemy, or themselves. There are build pads scattered across the maps in key locations and choke points where you can build turrets (AA, AT, and AI), radar scanners (Sensor Nodes), or a medical station/vehicle repair station.
The graphics on thisgame show their date. The game itself is pretty old. But like I stated before, there are mods for that. Just use google and you can probably still find them.
This game has very few custom songs, maybe none at all from what I know. All the music I have heard in this game is recycled from the official movie's soundtracks.
I would especially recommend this game for newer players getting into the RTS genre as it is a very forgiving game on the easier difficulties. RTS veterans would still have a bit of a problem playing on the hardest difficulty as I have found the AI player does not really have many restrictions on it, meaning it will start producing units from multiple locations at the same time and have dozens of fleets moving at the same time, leaving the player at a severe disadvantage.

I could probably list a couple dozen PS2 games which were better in all ways than these and came out before.  When you stack it next to games like Grandia, Dark Cloud, Tales of Symphonia, SMT: Nocturne, Shadow Hearts, FF12, and Persona 3, it falls flat on its face.  It just seems
.

TLDR: This game is very misleading and has nothing to do with anything evolutionary and should NOT be picked up anywhere close to $7.
Later in this review, I will be reffering to an Imgur album of screenshots I've made to properly explain what exactly I'm talking about, though I'll try my best to explain it for those who don't or can't use the album.
Imgur Link:
The description of this game is misleading at best. Name anything that you could possibly find fun or interesting as you read about it. There's a 90% chance it's not what you think. This game has absolutely
to do with evolution. You start the game by planting plants with random genes, and later on you can manipulate genes adn create your own super plant if you want. Cool. Except it's literally just that simple. You place it down, it generates random stats that you can't even see, and then that's it until it dies. Same with any animals, but I couldn't even get them to survive long enough for them to matter.
The game also boasts about it's complex weather system that it has, and how it affects the species that live in your biosphere. How does it affect them, you'd ask. Well I have no idea. You can bring up a graph of how the wind, heat, and humidity has been, but I don't think that makes any difference to the game at all except wind carries plant seeds that you generate. Heat and humidity seem to have no affect at all, as there's not even genes for heat or humidty resistence in the game as of now.
The game has a "clicker" type style to it, meaning that the only use for the currency in game is to buy buildings which collect more currency. Once you're more than like a half hour into the game, you have more currency than you know what to do with. Other than that, the gameplay as a whole is dull and unresponsive. The only thing there is to show progression is your "research" which only gives you more options on how to customize your custom species. And that system also sucks (we'll get into that later.)
Frankly, what the♥♥♥♥♥♥do half the mechanics in this game exactly do. If you look at the first picture in the Imgur album you'll see just how cluttered and nonsensical the UI is, and I'm not even sure what any of it means. In the top right it shows a progression bar that goes up randomly, along with a "gen" count that also doesn't mean anything. There is a World Effeciency and Score that the game praises as mysterious and boasts about how it will be fun to figure out. But no, it's not fun to figure out, because why would anyone care about it if it seemingly doesn't even mean anything?
But the main lack of clarity comes from the custom species system that allows you to generate a custom species. It gives you about 10 sliders that are all different genes that you can manipulate. I finally unlocked all the genes for plants and thought "Awesome, maybe I'll be able to a biosphere of species that all look cool and act interesting!" But again, that isn't the case. Some of the sliders are very straightforward, like Height or Life expectency. But what exactly does Biomass mean? Or what about competitiveness? How do plants compete? And wouldn't the Effeciency gene just be overall how well a plant will survive? No explanation in game. Even the crown jewel of this game, the custom species creator, falls short due to a lack of exploration.

Watching the things grow can help some with seeing what the genes do, but many of them aren't obvious, and there are enough environmnetal factors that it can be nearly impossible to tell if something is actually helping or hindering, or if it was just blind luck that something went well.  The interface is also rather clunky to navigate.  I think this is to make it easier to operate with a controller, or perhaps with VR or something, but as it stands with mouse and keyboard it just  seems like a chore to do what you actually want.
Long story short, I love the idea, and it has a lot of potential, but a lack of feedback on what your actions accomplish leaves you blind to what you're doing.

Antes de Bioshock creía que los FPS carecían de historia profunda, tenían una estética genérica y sólo consistían en dejar como coladera cuanto NPC o jugador se te cruzará en frente. Estaba muy equivocado. Es cierto que el único FPS que disfrutaba en aquél momento era Unreal Tournament y su versión UT2004, por lo que mis prejuicios con el género tenían sentido, aunque no me mal entiendan: despanzurrar gente con el Flak Cannon a quema ropa es endemoniadamente divertido. Halo me parecía lento, y por ello no surgió el amor con la franquicia de Master Chief; por lo tanto no tenía mayor referente además de House of The Dead y Time Crisis (Hate is Coming).
Bioshock marcó un antes y un después en mis prejuicios hacia los First Person Shooters. Comencemos por decir que lo primero que conocí sobre el mundo distópico inspirado en la literatura de Ayn Rand y George Orwell fue la historia. Todo el mundo incluía el juego en tops, artículos y recomendaciones; la razón de tanta alabanza fue clara cuando vi la serie Bioshock: The Complete Story hecha por Eligible Monster narrando la historia del juego. La serie de videos está llena de spoilers así que evítala como la plaga si no quieres saber nada de la historia.

I own at least two survival games within my steam library, "The Forest" and "Stranded Deep" but this one caught my eye the most. While the other two games are great to play I keep returning to this one for an odd reason, Everytime I start the game up and hear that beautiful tone play and when I get to the menu and just hear the roar of the wind for me its something that I oddly enjoy watching and listening to.
The good thing that I can say about this game is the visuals, while most games have state of the art graphics, the style here in the game feels amazing and beautiful to look at. Graphics here don't matter, in my opinion its the world we're all playing in and how brutal it can be.
Another good thing is music, when a theme plays it's stunning, you feel a sense of wonder but feel lonely in the world wondering if there's a survivor, even when your in caves the music tone feels dark and unsure, you don't know if there's a black bear or wolves that call that cave home.
One final thing I will say that is good is gameplay, trying to find food and water and watching your basic human needs is a fun thing. For some it may seem boring but for survivalists it feels real and that we're trying to survive a catclysm and look for survivors to find answers. The journal in the player's inventory feels like a personal log, you can create a story out of it and for me that's exciting for some reason.
However there are a couple things that the developers could improve on.
One would be the skybox, Now I understand they're working on it I just want to stare into the night sky and see these auroras dancing across my screen giving me a show that is both spectacular and worrying at the same time. I know this will be implemented in the near future, I just hope they can nail it the first try.
One more thing I would say needs improvement is diversity. Right now there's only deer, bears, wolves, rabbits, fish and frozen corpses. The world feels empty and I know that they're working on adding more things I think small updates to include new biodiversity would be really cool and improving the landscape instead of seeing the same rock in a cave. This will be added in the future but maybe through small updates it can make the game feel more lively.
If you were intending to purchase this game, first watch someone who has it play and then you try and play it yourself, if you think your going to enjoy it then buy this game. So far this game is on a good trail, the website says it's going to include a copious amount of stuff when the big update rolls around and I hope the developers will keep their word.
In its current state my review for The Long Dark would be an 8.5/10. While it nails human survival almost really well, the world just feels empty and lost in the snowstorm but sooner or later the storm will dissipate and then that's when this game will shine as bright as the sun hopefully.

This game is...
I'm just doing this for a badge
After playing this whole game, I wrote this review.

This game has a nice idea at it's core. Unfortunately, it is flawed in many key ways that basically make it unenjoyable.
First lets talk about bugs:
Now, annoyances (minor):
Now for the major annoyance. The unbelievable level of obscurity in this game. Yes okay, I'm supposed to figure things out. I did quite well for a few things (like world score or world efficiency), however it would be nice to know what half the genes in the genetic engineering this game proudly boosts as one of it's key features, actually did. Height, root spread, max speed, turning speed. Those are all pretty obvious genes to alter, it makes the plant grow taller or it's roots wider and makes animals move or turn faster.
What about absorbtion? Is that absorption of water from the soil or CO2 from the air? How about "efficiency" and how does that relate to a plant? More importantly, why am I given a choice as if it pertains to what I think it means (how well a plant manages it's resources) then surely I want to crank that up to 100% all the time, which makes this busy work at best (make a note of this, we're coming back). Cohesion, how does that pertain to animals? Apart from making them resistant to Star Trek diseases that affect cellular cohesion.
And that's not taking into account genes that have obvious names (like competitiveness) but you're given very little clues as to how it relates to the biosphere in general, as yes competitive plants will kill off less competitve ones, but what about an ecosystem completely full of competitive plants? Will they all metaphorically strangle themselves to death, or will it be okay?
This obscurity around one of the key mechanics is infuriating, as even in an "explore it for yourself" style game, one mess of one of these genes could create a species that annihilates your entire biosphere. Not to mention you can have plants that are perfectly fine until they spontaneously combust. And the fact that animals will breed, lay eggs but never hatch. Had that a couple of times with no feedback as to what I was doing wrong. The developer says they want you to experiment, but to experiment you need a hypothesis; and mine begins and end with "I'm left with a bunch of burned plants and no idea what caused them to spontaneously combust, as it definately wasn't the environment as they made it through midday just fine".
Back to that busy work, in game that actively punishes you for adding things manually there is a surprising amount of stuff that you are required to do that by all rights you shouldn't. For example that efficiency gene from above, if it's entirely beneficial why should I have to manually set it to max? And the science system is a joke, where you only unlock one gene at a time, in a fixed order, but you have to go and manually click the unlock button. I can forgive the generic science buttons, as that has a choice between plants, herbivores and carnivore unlocks, but for the dedicated unlocks, it's unnessecary. Espcially for a key mechanic.
Also, the whole thing carries a cookie clicker vibe of using numbers to make numbers go up faster and nothing really to do with those numbers except make other numbers go up faster. Don't believe me? You spawn plants. You place a collector to collect biomass. You use that biomass to make a research station to generate science. Science unlocks a gene called max biomass that increases the biomass you get. The game even hits the "leave it by itself for a while" vibe pretty nicely as I got my best score by getting up and getting a drink. Came back, can of coke in hand to find my score had doubled and I'd unlocked two achievements for high efficiency.
Finally, I can't rate their story as the method of delivery is so poor. At most I can tell you that you work for a company, and they may be nebulously evil, going from the store page description and some odd dialog in the tutorial. Other than that, occasionally a small green square on a black circle with some text on it will appear on the ground with some text on it. One felt like a sentence from another player confused as to what they were doing, one was a length of random characters in a code and one seemed like a message from the Dev asking for feedback.
Oh and if you though that I was going to whale on the GUI and graphics, I won't. I can understand that. It's the general bad ideas in what otherwise could be a good game.
