I love what the game is trying to do, but I feel that it fails.
The combat is very shallow for a turn-based RPG and too much of it comes down to random chance (particularly the mech scenes). It varies between frustratingly easy and frustratingly difficult, and never really feels like a rewarding challenge.
The writing would be a lot funnier if they didn't call attention to every single joke and reference that they make (Seriously, they throw in a "see what we did there?" at least once per cutscene, and it feels like a laugh track.)
And for a game that is supposedly about running a studio, it really doesn't do anything original with its combat. I think it would have been a lot more interesting if we could choose the extras for them to fight and increase the challenge level on our own, and get more audience points for having a dramatic battle.
Instead we're only rewarded for winning the fight, and that's no different from every other tactics RPG in existence.

The last thing I remember is darkness. As my car overturned on the highway, all I can remember is being dragged out onto the lonely road, then darkness. As I open my eyes, I notice surroundings that are unfamiliar to me. It is dim in the room, but I can make out a few shapes in the shadows. I try to move my arms and legs, but cannot. I struggle for a few moments, before giving up and taking note of how cold it is. I try to call out for help, but my mouth is gagged with some kind of cloth. Suddenly, the lights turn on. I look down to realize that I am dressed like a mime from the stomach down, but the bra I am wearing is not mine. I look up and see organs lining the wall, and... Is that a head? Oh my god, I have to get out, I have to get out, I...
Oh, thank god, another person! He toddles up to me in a strange fashion before screaming at me to start dancing. Fearfully, I comply. The strange figure, though he is a few feet away, smells awful, his shirt streaked in what I hope isn't feces, his clothing in tatters, dirt caking his skin. His mouth cracks into a smile, his teeth missing. He reaches into his pocket, and I cringe in pain as he starts throwing change at me. The coins bounce off of my skin, leaving small welts, tears streaming from my face. The stranger moves back and forth, as if avoiding some object I cannot see, before ducking, getting back up, and starting over again. Flinching as the coins pelt me, the stranger takes this for agreement, and throws more coins at me. I fear I may die here.
2/10.

I wish Steam allowed for more nuance than yes or no, but lacking that I considered which one was best. And the sour taste in my mouth at the end of the game have me leaning towards no.
A lot of people complain about the length, but I don't mind a short game if it brings a good experience to the table. Initially, it seemed like Superhot would do that. But in the end, three things hold it back.
First, as many people have mentioned, the story is painfully pretentious. I found myself constantly groaning and rolling my eyes, thinking there might be a point where actual options were presented. Without them, the game's smug and self-congratulatory manner is just grating.
Second, the sound design. When one of your inspirations is the sound of a dial-up modem, you've made a terrible decision.
More than that, though, the gameplay is hampered by one simple thing: It's inconsistent. I've seen people describe Superhot as more of a puzzle or strategy game than a shooter and I agree. Plenty of levels required me to figure out enemy positions, weapon locations and routes to take. I like that. But the further I got, the more niggling annoyances would come up. The main one is that the throwing mechanics are simply unreliable. And since that makes up about a third of your arsenal, you'll more than once find yourself dying because the weapon you threw spun awkwardly and hit a low wall or corner that it shouldn't. Enemies seemed to spawn differently at times, weapons would remain clipped in their arms instead of dropped on a hit so they could go straight back to shooting, bullets would hit invisible walls or corners, the list goes on.
Don't get me wrong, none of these things are extreme. It's not an incompetantly made game. The core game idea is creative, the visuals are striking and the set-up of a lot of levels is great. But the flaws just piled up and the final level of the game was pure frustration and riddled with deaths that felt unfair. I can still recommend checking it out when it's cheap or if you think these flaws don't seem that bad (some might see it more as a chaotic shooter and prefer it that way.)
But personally, I won't be touching the game again.

>>>Mostly spoiler free<<<
Only spoils are estimates on how long the game would take
TL;DR if you're wanting to play all the games, you can expect about 80 hours of content (Not counting the longer grinds). But it's not worth it just for the 4TH game.
If you want to play just the NEW GAME, don't bother. It's only about two or three hours tops. They even literally disable al lthe side content and even though they updated the models to look more modern (Only in this game for some reason?), only having like two dungeons to run that are both generic is pretty boring. There's no side missions, no events, no special thing you can do. Just a short epilouge plot that expands on the lore some and ties up loose ends kind of nicely. They even got most (or all?) of the old voice actors for returning characters, so the voices soudn fine.
New game aside, the old games were HD'd in a nice way that doesn't take away from them, but it's also pretty clear it's just HD'd PS2 games, so the models themselves look old; but they overall hold up decently since thanks to a lot of care being put into them back when they were first made; you'll just notice hair clipping or blocky hands outside of cutscenes.. A lot of clear love was put into it to make sure it all translated well. I dind't have any major issues with the games, Only crashed once in over 80 hours, No audio desync issues (in the first three games anyway), everything functions the same, and the games actually hold up fairly well when compared to modern games. There's plenty of secrets to find, optional grind quest with fun little rewards but nothing mandatory, the games can be as hard as you make them (if you just do story it can be pretty hard, but it's easy to go and out grind them to easily breeze through the story).
If you're looking for a really long game experience and want a game that looks pretty nice and is fairly actiony without much filler plot, this is a decent game to pick up. It's got multiple twist and turns ot the story with a pretty deep and complex world where they actually took the time to make fake forum post by people, even having a bunch of random artist make art for the game so people on the forums could post their own art in various different styles. They made anime news videos to look like actual news reporters talking to you about stuff, and a decently long news series where you kind of get to see how people in the real world respond to stuff going on in your game world (and see what the effects are, it gives nice context to what you're doing).
Honestly what befudles me is how the New game had them go through the trouble of updating all the models of characters you don't get much time with and making them look nice, but they didn't just put that in the older games and left those mostly un touched. The new game mostly just plays the same as the old ones. You eventually get the New Form you see on the cover art, and it has a clear amount of love put into it with very unique attacks and combos that are a ton of fun to watch and use.... but again, the new game is so short and you don't have any areas to really go and enjoy it.
Hopefully we'll see more from this series, I'd love it if .hack made some big comeback, and it does kind of hint that there's possibilities for a new story to start, but I'm finding it really unlikely as of right now.

I'm sick to death of early access survival games on Steam, so for that reason I almost passed on The Long Dark. Yet another game where you're collecting wood while fiddling around with a hunger and thirst meter. *Yawn*
This is one time when I'm happy to have been wrong. You will do those things in The Long Dark, but they keep the gameplay interesting and rewarding.
Pros
- Resource collection is time-consuming, but doesn't feel like a time-wasting slog. It's not an overly long, drawn-out process where you have to chop a tree and then chop up the log and then chase down sticks as they roll all over the environment.
- No zombies! Thank god for that. The enemies are natural and the fact that they're animals like wolves and bears makes them no less menacing. I'm so grateful that this isn't yet another zombie survival game.
- The enemy AI makes them pretty intimidating. They don't just charge you from across the map every time the second they see you. A wolf might approach slowly, appearing and disappearing from your sight. It adds to the stress.
- The environment does a great job of making you feel cold. It's not just because it's snowing in game. The sound design and lighting and everything just gives off the perfect wintry vibes.
- The inventory system forces you to make tough decisions and choices. Picking up and moving camp isn't a simple decision if you have a lot of stuff stashed in your current hideout. Walking is dangerous and time and resource-consuming. You actually have to put thought into your wandering.
- I personally like that there's no map. I printed out a physical map, but I actually quite like that you can't just open a map and see a little map marker moving around that you can mindlessly use to navigate. You have to put thought into where you're going. I do wish they would add a simple, hand-drawn map to the game that your character crudely adds to as you discover new locations. It makes sense to me that a survivor would try to keep some sort of map. I would, but I would like if it didn't have a player marker. Or at least had the ability to turn the player marker on and off.
Cons
- This is a temporary con, but no story mode yet. This is what I'm waiting for more than anything.
- The art style doesn't appeal to me personally. Things, especially bodies, are just lumpy and devoid of detail. Lots of games manage to make low or medium detail appealing, but this doesn't.
- Sometimes the hunger mechanic seems a little out-of-whack with reality. People, even people who are in physically stressful condition don't need to eat multiple times a day. In this game you'll eat two or three entire fish and then you're still hungry and your hunger meter is still going down! You do start to get worn out by trying to get the amount of food the game thinks you need.
- I wish you could interact a little more with the buildings. It would be nice if you were able to clear the dead bodies out of the bedrooms, for one.
Overall, a fun game that I'm looking forward to playing more of when it's out of EA.

What is LYNE? It's a game about associating lines. It seems simple, but like most puzzle games, the more you advance, the harder it gets. I love LYNE. Why is that? Well, I like the way it's simple, but at the same time intelligent. The game is addictive and you will find yourself coming back to challenge your brain. The art is simplistic, but it fits the game just right. You can change it as you advance with smooth combinations of colors. It's simple and intelligent just like the game. There is not much music, when you interact with the levels, sound comes out of your interactions. Sometimes it can create an appeasing melody. The goal is just to relax your mind, while at the same time working it.
In LYNE, you have two options, to play the pre-built levels which go from A to Z with 25 levels in each (650 levels, if you feel lazy) or do the dailies which are levels generated everyday for you to play. You guessed right, the longevity of the game isn't bad. While LYNE is a mobile port, it is a good one. Both are the same things, except for the Steam features (achievements and cards).
I highly recommend LYNE for everyone who would like a game that chills your mind, but exercises it at the same time.

As a fan of puzzle games, particularly ones I can pick up for just a few minutes at a time,
is an instant classic. Minimalistic in terms of gameplay, graphics and audio, it is reminiscent of
, which I used to play on the original Gameboy. Although these two games differ in terms of the puzzle design, they share a purpose on the parts of the designers to create a game that is both relaxing and challenging. This simple approach means the game is easy to learn, and has great replayability.
Easy to learn does not mean easy to finish, however. As one progresses through the game, new elements and larger fields of play increase the difficulty. Additionally, there are daily challenges that range from laid back to aggravating, which again, adds to replayability.
If you enjoy puzzle games, give this one a go. It may not be the biggest time sink, but makes for a great distraction while taking the train home, or sitting on the can. It's also fairly cheap, which is a bonus. So kudos to Thomas Bowker for having the focus and discipline to create an instant classic.

A nice, fast placed 'hard platformer' comedy with a lot of psychological elements. The game is constantly trying to trick and troll you by subte means. It's very short, about three hours long (also includes a map editor for user made screens, but I'm not too fond of that stuff for most games). It plays rather much like a flash game, with the elements of complexity revolving around left-clicking and things like direction and moment.
There's a fair ammount of variety to the game mechanics. There are decent boss fights which tend to range from too long to too easy, but still manage to be enjoyable and use the game mechanics well.
There's a rather lengthy reference to the 'are video games art' debate, which I think is outdated to the point where only people who play nothing but Madden and people who are so liberal they think Burney Sanders is a fascist would bother arguing about. Anyway, those levels are very easy and aren't really funny, even though it constitutes about 80% of the game's unspoken dialogue. It slows down gameplay, and just annoyed and distracted me.
Otherwise, the spoken dialogue is funny, but there's not a whole lot of it. No Time to Explain, in general, is very creative, but they could have done a lot more with the open-ended concept. The level editor leaves a lot to be desired, with no way to design full level campaign, the editor can only make a single screen. There doesn't seem to be a way to add any of the game's various 'suit powerups' in the editor.
For a short game, I'd say it's worth a playthrough, and is somewhat iconic of the cheap indie spectrum. It could have done a lot more, and it's pretty flash-game like. Still, definently a step ahead of even the best flash games. That said, for games this short I generally want more of a story, something with more context than a platformer with about 8 worlds and 25 levels.
I would not recommend it at the silly price of $15. Not for a 3 hour platformer with an editor that's an afterthought.

This is an evolution sandbox where you create random plants, that feed random herbivores that feed random carnivores. You will spam click to create as many plants as possible because not all will survive or reproduce successfully. Once you have plants growing you can harvest some of their biomass with these devices you place that are stationary on the map. Biomass is currency for buying buildings. There are 3 buildings, the generator, research lab and radar. You will get 1 free generator which you use to snowball all future building costs. Research stations study the species around them and give you species points (Plants, herbivores and carnivores all have their own points) which unlock genetic traits that you can edit.
Genetics is a huge part of the selling point of this game. You can create an apex predator, an invasive plant species and herbivores which will eat all plants until their population crashes from short food supply.
You can create these species by adjusting a slider with values such as "Move speed, Turning speed, Growth rate, metabolism, absorption, senses, caution, hunger, reprduction rate, seed drag, seed force"
The list goes on.
With that said I've pretty much explained the entire game and will tell you that you can learn all mechanics within 30 minutes of play. The game isn't complicated to learn or control but I think beating the game is hard and would require a lot of micromanaging. (beating the game meaning getting a completely sustainable ecosystem with no input from a player)
My first day of play:
I enjoyed spawning random plants for about 10 minutes while finishing the tutorial. Around 30 minutes in I was starting to research all the genetics for plants. Around an hour in i experimented with different plant variables and was able to create 2 species which were able to reproduce on their own forever, or so I thought. (One species is basically grass and the other was like a tree)
Anyways once I had a certain amount of plants and saw the number steadily growing without my input I decided to spawn a couple herbivores.
The herbivores reproduced out of control so I started making carnivores to eat them, but only a couple because I learned from my herbivore spawning mistakes. They completely killed a plant species that I custom made and ignored the other one all together. As of this review I've tried recreating the original species but with no success.
Anyways the herbivores ate all their food because their population was booming. So they started to die because of this.
They also started to die because they carnivore population was booming and eating them.
Eventually the system reset because the carnivores ate all the herbivores and then they starved to death. The plants began to grow back.
It took around 10 hours for my ecosystem to crash, meaning there were no more herbivores or carnivores in the game. This isn't game over and there really isn't an end to this game. However, I believe that you can beat the game if you're able to make an environment where all Type of Life are able to grow indefinteily without your input.
Anyways I woke up to find my ecosystem wiped and I started my 2nd days worth of inputs.
This time around I decided to spam plants until my computer couldn't handle it. Which basically meant that there was so much activity on screen that my frames dipped to 3FPS and the overall game world slowed down. There are some workarounds to getting the game to run fast, turn off the sound, turn down the settings and save and reload whenever it gets laggy.
I did all of that and managed to see all my plants settle, I then started planning out a slow herbivore with a low hunger and reproduction rate so that they wouldn't grow out of control.
Hour 13 : The herbivore population is growing again... added some carnivores
Hour 15 : All herbivores and carnivores dead.
Hour 16 : Randomly spawn a bunch of plants and herbivores
Hour 17 : Herbivores all dead
Review Time Hour 18ish --- Sometimes you can get very unlucky with the randomly generated herbivores and they'll just die out because their genes suck. Around this point into the game I've had about 3 hours of solid focused, micromanaging play and it's all been very gratifying.
The best part about this game is that I can leave it open on my laptop and place off in the corner of my room and go about my day. I can come back and see meaningful change in the ecosystem. Sometimes I see the error of my ways and sometimes I'm left wondering what happened. Overall, I find the game very rewarding when you check on it from time to time.

The Long Dark is an atmospheric survival game set in the Canadian wilderness. You must survive by gathering resources and defending your self against the forces of nature.
*No Spoilers*
Pros:
-The atmosphere of this game is absolutely amazing. I felt like I was actually in the game. I was genuinely scared at certain points, something that most scary games can't do for me.
-The gameplay was overall very good.
-The graphics were nice and fitting.
-The survival aspects of the game were great. Managing temperature, food, and other resources is done perfectly in the game.
-The performance was good and I experienced no major bugs.
Cons:
-There are sometimes when you get no resources from any of the chests that you find. You will eventually die from hunger before you can actually find anything.
-Sometimes you spawn in large places that are completely empty. The result is once again death before you can find any chest or hut.
Final Verdict:
Apart from some problems with spawning, The Long Dark is a phenomenal game. It has an amazing atmosphere and the gameplay is great. I totally recommend that you buy this game, just be prepared to get scared to death. I will give The Long Dark a 8.5/10.

The setting and writing is excellent, although it's dragged down by stiff, clunky combat. This wouldn't be an issue if, like System Shock 2, it allowed multiple alternatives to straight-up shootouts, but the game frequently forces the player into combat - expect lots of corridor shooting and being dropped in mini-arenas while enemies swarm you. ADAM, the game's equivalent to Experience Points, can only be obtained by taking on absurdly spongey armored enemies.
As mentioned earlier, the writing and setting is fantastic. Few games pull off audiologs well, but Bioshock does it perfectly, fleshing out an entertaining cast of characters in a fairly logical and convincing manner. Rapture is eerily beautiful, and the enemies are so entertainingly macabre that it's easy to forget that there isn't much variety among them.
Overall, expect fantastic presentation brought down somewhat by mediocre, stiff shooting galleries with bullet-sponge enemies. It'd be better if it had fully committed to being either a System Shock-style RPG or a straight-up shooter instead of occupying a weird middle-ground, but it's a hard game not to like.

Why do I have to be ashamed to admit I enjoy these games?
The fanbase has gone to complete crap, and no where seems to be safe. These youngin's are trying to ruin my horror games! Seriously, don't bother trying to find a good community.
Without any of that into consideration, the game is good. (Depending on who you are.)
As for the horror part, it's great. It's dripping in atmosphere, and while you could call it "jumpscare-bait," the jumpscares would be meaningless without a good build up. The sound design is superb, it's haunting and the game rewards you for listening closely as most of the sounds mean something.
The gameplay is great and very original. It's very well thought-out, you can really tell that a lot of effort went into making all the mechanics. That being said, many people don't like it and just feels as if it's micro-management. The animatronics all move and act mostly randomly which is great and unexpected in Nights 1-4, but on 5 it just feels unfair. You can play the game perfectly, yet it'll screw you over because... why not? It feels like a fake added difficulty, when I die I should feel like I made a mistake! Not because the random number generator screwed me over!
The visuals are simple and not overly detailed, yet they are good enough and give the game it's own style and character. Each room is well put together and can be really spooky, especially at night! The graphics are all pre-rendered images, and while it is rough around the edges in places, it isn't too easy to notice. It's done very well to trick you into think it's actually 3D. (Though more observant players will notice.)
The story is what some would call the only part worth playing in this game. The story is presented very well, and is very mysterious. It's a lot of fun to try and put the pieces together and search for clues throughout the series. Yet, despit what some think, the story itself is very simplistic.
It's not about the destination, it's about the journey.
Even with all that, it is far from perfect. The jumpscares look laughably silly, and it could remove all the built up tension you had. The game is well designed, but not well made. There is no pause button. Pushing escape instantly exits the game. (Like, what?) There are no options what-so-ever. (No subtitles for people who like them) There are no resolution options, the game is not widescreen so if you play it fullscreen on any monitor that isn't decades old, it'll just stretch the image. This is 2015, widescreen should be the standard.
If you can ignore it's technical flaws, the community, and want a unique and fresh horror experience, play this game. If you've seen videos and don't think you'll enjoy it, then you probably won't, so don't bother. And if you do enjoy the game, then I recommend the sequels!
The sequels are great, and they don't feel like shameless cash-ins. Each game brings a new gameplay twist making each one stand out as it's own game. I say you should give all of them a try, but if you only want to try one I would say go with the fourth one. It's really good. (Unfortunatly, they all suffer from the same flaws as this one. Except for the jumpscares, those got better to the point of actually being freaky.)

Chroma Squad
Behold Studios
Behold Studios
SRPG/Economic hybrid
Perhaps I’m just nostalgic about those simple and happy times I used to watch the Power Rangers on TV as kid. For me, Chroma Squad really shed a new light on what a modern pixelated video game can achieve. The title I’m reviewing today is a far cry from your run-of-the-mill 2D Simulation Role Playing Game (SRPG, for short) since it incorporates a well planned economic component to it. You have to supervise  a team of stunt actors looking to promote their own studio and projects. And that is no easy task, given how cutthroat the show business is in general terms. You control everything from the production of the shows and even the advertising and human resources department of your firm. It’s not just a faux Power Ranger simulator in which combat takes center stage.
You need to carefully manage your total funds and some compromises shall be made when hiring actors or sacking older ones which contrary to their skill sets, lack any appeal towards the audience. And you will certainly have to entertain your public. That is where the core tactical side of the game, comes alive. You have a surprisingly complex turn-based battle system that relies on literal teamwork between the squadmates you control, since boss fights are never easy. This really is a rare case of a title that can be used to demonstrate independent creativeness and show the gaming industry that you don’t require an overinflated budget in order to create a fun and captivating game.
+ Beautiful pixel graphics and equally pleasant soundtrack.
+ Clever use of pop culture references and humor.
+ Unique type of gameplay.
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements.
- Some elements get repetitive over time.

An overhyped mess. It rides on the nostalgia train but crashes ingloriously when it comes to gameplay.
This is written after haven finished the highest difficulty.
In essence it consists of 4 core elements: Tactical RPG, economy / money management, crafting, and bugs.
-On the tactics side we have a squad of 5 actors / heroes fighting enemies in turn based combad on a planar field. During the first few levels it works perfectly. You have your classes like assault, support and scout who each do different things. But the more you play the more a mess it becomes. Suddenly everyone has heals, buffs, damage, etc. It lacks imagination. This is even more emphasized when it comes to enemies. You have to face melee, ranged, healers and coloured variations with more hp / damage. Even the bosses play the same way (almost) every level. They each mainly use the same attacks / abilities. It makes for a very tedious gameplay experience all the way to the end.
-Economy. The better you do the more money you get. That's the premise. It falls apart very early in the game when it becomes clear that it's almost impossible to miss the mark. Probably due to the very easy difficulty even on the highest setting. Same with director instructions during missions. Basically sidequests that make you do something. Mostly it doesn't even affect the gameplay and furthermore the boost they give becomes negligible the further you progress.
-Crafting is a big part of the game. The more this hurts. It is horrible and completely missed the point of crafting.
You get materials from slain enemies or you can buy random packs in the shop. So good so far. But crafting is a lottery. You pick your base and it adds random properties. That's not crafting, it's lottery. When you want a defined outcome. That's crafting. It makes sense very early in the game pretending that your actors are improvising. But when you suddenly deal with high tech components the immersion falls apart. It doesn't hel either that most of the game the shop sold items are just far superior and don't have you hurt yourself through the atrocious interface.
-Bugs. This one is really dissapointing. We are talking on an Ubisoft level of bugginess. Nothing so far has been gamebreaking, but considering this whole thing rides on tropes and the passion for the genre one would think the devs would put more effort into this. Originally I would list the bugs here, but I simply lost track of them and at one point didn't bother to write them down. From economy, to battle, loot drops. Hell, even the basic text bubbles have a minor word wrap bug. It really becomes a joke when you realise there is a permanent bug report button on the top right.
This is a very sad case. I really tried to like this game, it's not bad, but it is below mediocre. It became painfully obvious during the game that all they cared about was the athmosphere and design. They got that perfectly and then stopped doing anything else. Don't get me wrong, most of the things I mentioned are very minor, but they are so numerous you wouldn't believe the devs actually played their own game (and those peeves are not even all).
For the price tag of 15€ I cannot recommend this game. Too short, lackluster gameplay. Even fans of the genre are better of just buying a DVD of their favourite series.

I can't describe how happy it made me.
I feel exteremely bad for waiting this long to pick up this game, and through a humble bundle no less. The developers of this game deserve full compensation for doing such a magnificent job.

I've never experienced another MMO with this many bugs.
First, in order to log in with  Steam there is a separate launcher from the game. This only works half the time and there is no way to manually log in. After every update it stops working or sometimes it just stops working for no apparent reason. Second, quests are bugged. I've had a main storyline quest just break with no way to recover it and no other quests available, effectively making the entire character useless. Google revealed that there are several quests in particular that have been broken for years without anyone working on them. Third, the prices for items are different depending if you are on the Warp Portal website or if you're on Steam. The best deals are on their site. Also, some items expire after a couple of days (which is bad if you can't log in half of the time.)
The game has been doctored so that Warp Portal can make more money. In the original Korean servers, there are quite a few Tiger mounts that you could purchase for in game money. All of these have been removed and put in a cash shop were you have a CHANCE at getting them permamently in a box. (There is only one mount available that does not require real money.) Costumes are not permament either. Most costumes expire after 30 days and you need to buy extenders to keep it. Both these items cost real money. If you want a permament costume the only way to get it is by more chance items, or by getting a lot of rare stones to play a pyramid game (which has an extrememly low chance of getting an item.) Inventory / Bank space is severely limited. Only 'medium' bags are dropped / purchasable which hardly have any slots. You will get these at level 10. If you want actual space, you need to buy bags from the cash shop. RO2 may not be a 'pay to win' but it sure is a 'pay to do anything fun' sort of game. Server population is pretty low. No one seems to be socializing. In fact, all the social interaction I had was a creepy guy hitting on me. So, if you play MMOs in hopes of finding some new buddies to talk too, you won't find them here.
If you insist on plaything this game, do not do it through Steam. Go to the site itself, or better yet find another company / private server. Warp portal is not doing a good job integrating RO2 with Steam. If the game actually worked as intended I might suggest it for someone looking for a casual game to play with friends (if you don't mind old school rpg grinding) but since Warp portal provides such a terrible service, I suggest trying one of Aeria Games' anime MMOs instead. They have a cash shop too, but they are more fair about what they give you.
Overall RO2 is a HUGE DISSAPOINTMENT and I am not saying this because it is different from the first game. I am saying this because of the bugs, Warp portal's poor choice of business model and all the issues I've been having. I've played a ton of f2p mmos and none have quite been this bad. You have been warned!

I played the tech demo of SUPERHOT back when it came out and it impressed me, but I didn't really see how they could really make a game out of it.  I got SUPERHOT as part of the humble monthly bundle and man, I'm glad I did because it was a unique and fun game.  SUPERHOT is an interesting concept--time moves as you move and when you're still time is at a crawl.  Also, one shot (a bullet from a pistol, assault rifle, or even a single shotgun pellet) will kill anything--you, an enemy, or an object (you can pick up some stuff in the environment and thow it at an enemy).  This design makes SUPERHOT a kind of puzzle game as you're constantly trying to decide what to do next.  Maybe you have a few armed enemies you have to deal with.  You could pick up a painting off the wall, throw it at an enemy causing them to drop their gun, grab that gun out of the air, shoot the guy whose gun you just stole, then throw that gun at another enemy to steal their gun as waiting to shoot your gun again would waste precious time.  The story mode was also surprisingly fleshed out.  I expected just a few levels and the endless mode, but the devs actually made a really neat story to link the levels together (though it'll only last you an hour or two).  I recommend this game, but probably for $15 max.

Santa Rockstar is a Christmas-themed homage to games like Guitar Hero & Rock Band.
The game has 15 rock covers of classic Christmas songs. They actually sound pretty awesome, and although I wouldn't listen to them in my spare time (just like any Christmas song) I enjoy the hell out of listening to them while playing this game.
The game's gameplay feels almost identical to the games it is inspired by, and the graphics and cutscene look straight out of the Guitar Hero series, and capture the feeling quite well. The graphics aren't amazing, but I honestly think they look absolutely fine, and don't look any worse than games like GH3. Besides, you'll be concentrated on the notes coming towards you.
There isn't any sort of character creation or unlock system, so the game is simply for playing music, which is fine by me. There's a campaign mode which has you play tracks in a set order, but you can also play any of the songs right from the beginning in the quickplay mode, which is nice.
The intro cutscene is awesomely animated and fun to watch.
Now onto the main problem I had with the game. Getting my Xbox 360 Wireless Guitar controller to work with the game properly.
The developers have stated they used a GH3 xbox 360 Wired controller while developing the game, so I'm unsure if because mine is wireless things started not working just right. I play Guitar Hero just fine on my PC, but it doesn't work properly in this game, for me at least. The problem is that the strum bar isn't detected, and the strum command is instead given to the whammy bar. As soon as I loaded up the main menu, it was scrolling through the options as if I was holding up on the strum bar constantly. I eventually figured out that it was happening because the whammy is in a default up position. As soon as I held the whammy down it would scroll down, and if I centered the whammy it wouldn't move at all.
Luckily you have the option to rebind both your keyboard and controller controls, so I rebinded the strum to my starpower button on my second GH5 guitar. It hurts to play after a while, but it's a solution until the developers fix this issue. Which definitely needs to be fixed. There's a guide on the community hub for how to get your controller working, but after following it I still couldn't get it working properly.
My game still scrolls through the options in the main menu, but at least I can play now without failing instantly. it's still annoying.
Alternatively, you can play with a keyboard, in either the basic or rockstar mode. The first being playing with your keyboard as it is right now, on the desk. The second option being you pick it up and use (by default) the numbers at the top of your keyboard, and the return key to strum. This isn't as fun as the guitar in my opinion, but it can work for some people, depending on how comfortable your keyboard allows it to be. I found rebinding to the F keys at the top made life a bit easier.
One final bit of information, the game has a decent selection of difficulties. Each step up has you add one more button. Eg. easy has you play with 3 buttons, and hard has you play with 5. There is no expert, so for those of you like me, looking for really challenging stuff, you won't really find it here, but it isn't too easy to the point that I couldn't have fun, so it's fine.
Overall, I think the game does what it wants to very well, and captures the whole atmosphere and feeling of playing a GH game, which is great. The music is fun, and the art and graphics are funny to look at. It's a cheap game too, so if you are looking for a music rhythm game, I'd recommend trying it out!
I just really hope an easier solution is found for the guitar controller problem I'm having, so I can enjoy the rest of the game!

They claim Scéal is an adventure game but it’s rather a visual novel which looks like a movable book with pop-up pictures.
In Steam Joint Custody, the only game’s developer, concisely describes Scéal as being «steeped in supernatural Irish folklore».
Scéal means “Story” in Irish language ( Gaelige or Gaelic) so Joint Custody tells you a story about a girl’s spirit who seeks to find her memories with the help of the raven named Branna.
The game puts you in the shoes — or rather the soul — of a little girl who has no memories of her previous life.
It’s a simple but interesting story but it’s so short that you can complete it less than two hours.
The Irish folklore is represented in the game through some forms of the girl ghost (angel, banshee) and a mythical raven named Branna.
In Scéal, there’s simple and symbolic mechanic: wherever a heart goes, the soul must follow. This becomes your method of movement in the game. Players pull an ethereal green heart around the map, and the floating soul chases it to the destination.
You make the girl’s spirit float around a small island consists of two villages and paint some objects (buildings, stones, trees).
As you can see the game is focused on its story rather than gameplay. This would be completely fine if the story really pulled you in but it doesn't manage to do this.
I liked the graphics of this game. Designed to resemble a storybook, Scéal’s pages are filled with pretty watercolor artwork. Upon opening the town map, ink spreads outward to complete the entire picture

The soundtrack of this game is what shines here because it tells the story more through its music. I enjoyed the Irish folk music here as it was high quality and definitely fit the game's tone.
There’s an outstanding soundtrack featuring Irish folk singers such as Aislinn Duffy and Florence Glen. If you have an interest in Irish folk music (like me), you’ll like the Scéal’s soundtrack for sure.
I ought to say Scéal is more of a narrative than a game and besides very short one. I do not recommend Scéal to anyone except those who are keen of Irish folk music.

Scéal хочет быть приключенческой игрой, но это скорее визуальный роман, который выглядит как книга с подвижными частями - всплывающими иллюстрациями.
В Стиме Джойнт Кастоди, являющийся единственным разработчиком игры, кратко описывает Scéal как «погружение в сверхъестественный ирландский фольклор».
Scéal означает «История» на ирландском (гэльском) языке, так что Джойнт Кастоди рассказывает историю о духе девушки, которая стремится найти собственные воспоминания при помощи ворона Бранна.
В игре вы оказываетесь в шкуре - или, скорее, в душе - маленькой девочки, у которой нет воспоминаний о ее предыдущей жизни.
Это простая, но интересная история, правда настолько короткая, что вы можете завершить ее менее чем за два часа.
Ирландский фольклор представлен в игре посредством различных форм девушки-призрака (ангел, банши) и мифического ворона по имени Бранна.
В Scéal простая и символичная механика: туда, куда движется сердце, должна следовать и душа.
Это будет вашим методом передвижения в игре. Игроки двигают эфирное зеленое сердце по карте, а парящая душа следует в указанное место.
Вы двигаете парящий дух девушки по небольшому острову, состоящему из двух деревень, и рисуете (закрашиваете) некоторые предметы (здания, камни, деревья).
Как видите, игра ориентирована на повествование (историю), а не на геймплей. Это было бы прекрасно, если бы история действительно затягивала, но ей это не удается.
Мне понравилась графика этой игры. Страницы Scéal, разработанные, чтобы напоминать сборник рассказов, заполнены прелестными акварельными рисунками. Открывая карту города, чернила постепенно распространяются, чтобы дорисовать всю картину
Саундтрек к этой игре - блистателен, так как история рассказывается больше посредством музыки. Ирландская народная музыка в игре понравилась, поскольку она - высокого качества и определенно соответствовала игровому стилю.
В записи этого выдающегося саундтрека поучаствовали такие исполнители ирландских народных песен как Айслинн Даффи и Флоренция Гленн. Если вы интересуетесь ирландской народной музыкой (как я, например), вам понравится саундтрек Scéal.
Должен сказать, что Scéal – это скорее рассказ, чем игра, и, кроме того, очень короткий. Я никому не рекомендую Scéal, за исключением тех, кому нравится ирландская народная музыка.

Scéal: The Irish Folklore Adventure by developer Joint Custody, is a supernatural adventure game centered around Irish folklore and music, which places the player in a watercolor storybook world on a quest to help a lost soul find her memory. The gameplay requires you to click and drag your character while navigating the map, which can be a little confusing at times. Other than that, I really liked the paint brush mechanic and how it sometimes would reveal memories. I just wish that this occurred every time you painted something and that the object you painted related to the memory. I also wished more information on Irish folklore to be integrated into the game because as someone with no knowledge I found it difficult to see the ways it was incorporated into the storyline. Still, I found the gameplay to be creative and the story to still be entertaining.
The ending features three choices, which does add some replay value to the game. The choices are a little obvious though and leave the player hesitant to pick the other two. I will say that all three do offer interesting insights into the conclusion and are worth pursuing. It is really not a hassle to replay the game as it goes by much quicker once you know what to do.

Scéal describes itself as a “living storybook.” It tells the story of a young girl’s spirit, wandering the world without any memories. Aided by a magical raven, the player guides the ghost to uncover her forgotten past. The story begins with the girl waking up on a lonely pier. Exploring the village and the surrounding area reveals that the book isn’t quite finished. A number of buildings must be “colored in” before the story may proceed. While this may sound like an opportunity for the player to put their own creative stamp on the game, the mechanic is, in fact, much less exciting. All that’s required is dragging the mouse over the screen to reveal the finished version of each illustration. After the book is completed, it comes alive with villagers emerging from their homes to wander the streets. By finding key people from the girl’s past and completing their individual quests, the player uncovers the truth surrounding her death.
The game is made up of many 2D watercolor illustrations layered against one another in a 3D world space, much like a pop-up book. Houses, trees and ships spring up and down as the camera shifts, giving the impression that the games “pages” are being turned. Not only is the environment kinetically alive, the quality and color of the illustrations are also in flux. As the player explores, the world comes to life in their wake, as though an invisible artist were putting the finishing touches on the watercolors. Depending on the time of day or the emotional tone of the story, the hue of the illustrations also change. The difference between the same landscape on an “uplifting” night verses a “melancholic” dawn is striking.
More memorable than its unique visual elements is Scéal‘s soundtrack. Despite its small scale, the game boasts an original soundtrack composed by traditional Irish folk musicians Lorcan Mac Mathuna, Aislinn Duffy and Florence Glen. With 14 tracks, the musical landscape is rich, beautiful and at times haunting. In the final chapter, when the player must decide the ultimate fate of the girl, each choice has its own song. While a positive outcome is rewarded with a lively jig, a negative one results in a gut wrenching dirge. Combined with the story book illustrations, the music feels like a lullaby meant to accompany a bedtime story.
Here we come to the real heart of the problem: is Scéal better off as a video game compared to a traditional paper and ink book? Its certainly more memorable. It wouldn’t have taken more than 5 minutes to read through the text and glance at the key images. No, Scéal is much more special for being “living.” While its core mechanics are nothing to write home about, the dynamic nature of the environment and music makes it a real treat. It’s difficult to say exactly who the target audience might be. Scéal seems fitting for young children. After all, it is a “story book.” The controls are also perfect for a tablet port. I’m left wondering whether the ultimate goal was to have a tablet based game that parents could share with their children like an interactive story book, with the child doing the coloring while the adult helps with navigation and reading.
TL;DR: Is Scéal worth $5? Yes, without a doubt. The music alone is worth the price tag. I probably wont revisit the game now that I have played it through 3 times, once for each ending. Still, it’s a memorable experience and one which I hope will be emulated by future games.

*VERY LONG REVIEW, YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED*
Let me first start off by saying this game is 100% a niche game, it is meant for fans of the .hack property and its various adaptations. That is not to say that people who dont know the .hack brand will not enjoy this game but it will be very hard to overlook its many flaws.
1. This game is a set of 3 games + an epilouge (which is brand new I might add), which originally were released back in 2006-2008, they were originally on the ps2 and were fairly advanced for the standards back then, with some truly impressive graphics for the pre-rendered scenes and even the character models were nicely designed (for some of the up-close shots).
2. This game is very dated in its design. It captures the essense of playing a "single-player" MMO perfectly. You are an average person playing this fictional game. But that in and of itself brings about some odd continuity problems. Such as having to log out of the game to check email, then logging back into the game immediately for a cut scene and then logging out to check email again. The progression is OK by 2006 standards, but very archaic by 2017 standards (which is where the game is supposed to take place as an odd twist of fate)
3. Combat is repetitive. sure, this could be said for every game for the most part, but in .hack its especially so. Since the game is modeled after an MMO, which is by nature repetitive, it does take a while for the combat to pick up, and once you have unlocked everything thats it, there is nothing else to get. Combat revolves around mashing or holding the X (A for you Xbox pad players) and occasionally hitting R1 (right bumper) to activate a skill. The battles are highly skewed in the player's favor, with time coming to a complete stop during these skills and being completely invulnerable during thier animations. This is somewhat alleviated in volumes 2 and 3 with some very smart additions, but it does not take away from the simplicity of the combat. It is nowhere near as rediculous as the first set of .hack games (original quadrilogy), but its got its share of problems. thankfully theyve fixed a number of them with this re-release.
4. Story and Voice acting. This game has some very high production values, but there was something they could not avoid when they were re-releasing this and that was how voiceovers were handled. Because of how the old games were formatted in a 4:3 aspect ratio, the subtitles were done in such a way that they would constantly cut people off the in the middle of sentences, the middle of thoughts and it would just sound awkward if you read the line in its entirety. Since they did not go back and re-record the voies for 10 year old games, there are absolutely spots in the game where the voice acting is slow, and plodding, and the tone is not quite right. But there are also spots where the emotion of the characters is properly conveyed because the voice cast is very very high quality.  The story itself is hit or miss. You will either be completely on board with this non-sensical way of handling computer data and dealing with viruses and bugs. or you will not be impressed by the intersocial aspect of how this game handles its characters. But one thing this game does very well is character development. Main and side characters all get some kind of development, with haseo being the best example.
5. Remake quality. As a fan of the original series and someone who played the games on ps2 to death, i can say that this game does the originals justice by fixing some issues with translations, fixing alot of gameplay issues, but it does bring up a few new ones. Simply because of how easy it is to level and how much more damage you do to enemies, some fights have lost thier challenge, and its easier than ever to over-level and completely trivialize the game. However, a big problem I personally found was that since on the ps2 you had alot of time in between releases to grind out weapon proficiencies, it was very easy in the re-release to be UNDER leveled in those areas. Sure you'd be capped out in the game but you'd be using weaponskills from the beginning of the game still because you blew through it so fast.
In most cases this would not be an issue but it does take away from the joy of being "well prepared" for the subsequent volumes. You could very well grind out weapons and stuff before progressing but the allure of the story (at least for me) was too powerful for me to consider dumping extra time into the older volumes, espeically considering I knew where the story was going and what to expect.
In terms of how well the game performs on PC, I give it an A-. I had one problem with a bug during my play time that cost me an hour, but after that I never encountered a bug again. Load times were fast, and I played the game on the highest settings I could achieve through the game without mods (however I did mod in Playstation button icons, why this was not an OPTION at the very least is criminal) .
There are many issues with .hack as a series. But this set of games is completely and fully enjoyable if you are looking to get yourself lost in a self contained story, with compitent but repetitive combat, and un-even voice acting.

If you enjoy Evo sim style games, this one is one of the better one's I've played in awhile.

- Not a game con per say, but know it's pretty CPU heavy once things get going, your "hour of play" vs mine or anyone elses will vary greatly in terms of actual sim-speed time. The only con here is if you're interested in the leaderboards as in this case, it makes an uneven playfield in relation of output vs relataive time investment.
This featured was added ina recent patch- great addition.
Pros:
+++ The Gene mechanic: If you're one that enjoys critical thinking then its utility is incredibly intuitive- designing flora or fauna to fill/meet specific ecological niches is easy to visualize once you see the traits unfold. There's a couple intentionally vauge descriptors, but nothing difficult to figure out.
++ Game pace: there's really no pressure in the game outside of setting your own goals. The very early portion you deal with a small resource grind but within 10 mins or so things get rolling and its a non issue- funding's no longer the focus allowing you to instead focus on tailoring your ecosystem to what you have in mind.
+++ The Force-field mechanic: Isolation can breed just as much diversity as direct competiton, and though the scoring systems is pretty vague- it's already obvious to me that utilising this feature to maintain balance long term has been incredibly useful.
??: + / -

This is one of those rare little indy gems that I'm really glad I grabbed.
It's an ecological balancing act, and a fairly classic one if you've done your reading.  At its most basic, you've got plants, animals that eat plants, and animals that eat animals.   The trick is to have enough plants to support a population of herbivores, and enough herbivores to support a population of carnivores. Everything evolves. You can also impact that evolution directly.
If your balance is off, then you might have a situation where the herbivores are breeding too fast and eat all the plants, and then die out, leaving the carnivores with nothing.... and the next thing you know you're flying over a barren planet.
Or you might be fine, but suddenly your carnivores start breeding too fast, and wipe out your herbivores... then they starve themselves, and you're flying over a planet full of shrubbery and nothing else.
Graphically simple, but quite pleasantly charming. Audio is almost non-existant apart from some music. The UI could use some polish and is a little cludgy... but the game itself is nice.
I would like to see a bit more transparency around the genetics side of things, and I would like to see some more aesthetic variety on the life forms - which tend to be represented by quite simply polygonal shapes - but it's early days yet, and these things may come.
The game slows down a little in later stages - but that might just be my relatively poor rig.
It's one of those rare games that lets you choose your level of involvement. You can micro-manage your colonies, or you can throw your life-forms onto the planet and come back in a couple of hours to see what you've ended up with... both have so far been quite satisfying.
Do I recommend this game?  Absolutely - with caveats.
It still feels a bit early-access - though I understand work is continuing - and if you're after an action-packed roller-coaster ride, you should probably give this one a miss.   This is a game which requires you to quietly observe what's going on and figure things out which might feel a bit opaque to start with.

The game gives you a huge sense of liberty alowing you to really do whatever you want and leaving you to survive a zombie apocalipse the way you want to, it doesn't tie you up into a single way of surviving, it gives you the tools and it's completely up to the player how you want to survive. Want to go guns blazing, shoot away. Want to make an impregnable fortress, build away. You want to try your luck living like a nomad, follow the wind.
Techincally speaking although the game is still in early access it doesn't show the ridiculous amount of bugs many games have, it's already quite polished and although it is still missing a couple of features this features will only make it more enjoyable.
Considering the gameplay it's really hardcore survival, a single mistake can get you killed and overconfidence is always a big enemy. Take things too easy and you won't last winter, risk your life for food and most likely you'll get yourself killed, the game is really rewarding and punishing at the same time on that aspect yet it still mantains realism considering survival mechanics.
For an extra challenge on your gameplay I'll suggest using sandbox mode, use the already implemented 8 month later option and change the zombies properties, I won't say to use sprinters that's just plain suicide, but add the option on the zombie navigation and allow them to use doors. Good Luck and Have Fun playing :3

Not to be memetic, but it really
the most innovative shooter I've played in years. With that out of the way, I'll explain why. Time comes
to a standstill if you stand perfectly still and don't move your mouse. This turns a frantic firefight that would normally be twitch-based, into a "thinking man's game," as it were. It shows you bullet trails so you can step out of the way, or even fling an object in front of a bullet that would otherwise hit you. Heck, you can even slice bullets in half with a katana mid-flight!
When you complete a level (kill everyone else), the game will exclaim "SUPER HOT SUPER HOT" ad nauseum, with those same words alternating across the entire screen in all caps. Behind this, a replay of your playthrough of that level will loop in real-time, which makes you look like a badass if you watch it, because you're killing everything and miraculously surviving what looks like a fast battle. The biggest disappointment here for me is that the words flashing across the screen block out a significant portion of your view, making it annoying to watch the reply. Supposedly, I could upload the footage online, but I just want to watch the stuff myself instantly without obstacles after beating a level, and the game doesn't seem to want to let me.
The sound effects are quite nice, and the music in the credits was pretty good, though I don't recall there being any other music in the entire game. If there was, it was "subtle ambience" at best. There is a story, though I didn't find it super interesting or delightful. The gameplay is the absolute draw to this title. Once you finish, there is an endless mode and there are challenges, but whether you bother with those depends on if you are into those kinds of things or not. Campaigns are my jam, so the main game's levels in their original format are all that appeals to me.
$24.99 is the game's current, undiscounted pricepoint, and to me, that is outrageously high. I would only recommend getting this at $9.99 or lower if you're a campaign-only kind of person, or $14.99 - $19.99 if you're a total endless mode junkie in most games.

*VERY LONG REVIEW, YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED*
Let me first start off by saying this game is 100% a niche game, it is meant for fans of the .hack property and its various adaptations. That is not to say that people who dont know the .hack brand will not enjoy this game but it will be very hard to overlook its many flaws.
1. This game is a set of 3 games + an epilouge (which is brand new I might add), which originally were released back in 2006-2008, they were originally on the ps2 and were fairly advanced for the standards back then, with some truly impressive graphics for the pre-rendered scenes and even the character models were nicely designed (for some of the up-close shots).
2. This game is very dated in its design. It captures the essense of playing a "single-player" MMO perfectly. You are an average person playing this fictional game. But that in and of itself brings about some odd continuity problems. Such as having to log out of the game to check email, then logging back into the game immediately for a cut scene and then logging out to check email again. The progression is OK by 2006 standards, but very archaic by 2017 standards (which is where the game is supposed to take place as an odd twist of fate)
3. Combat is repetitive. sure, this could be said for every game for the most part, but in .hack its especially so. Since the game is modeled after an MMO, which is by nature repetitive, it does take a while for the combat to pick up, and once you have unlocked everything thats it, there is nothing else to get. Combat revolves around mashing or holding the X (A for you Xbox pad players) and occasionally hitting R1 (right bumper) to activate a skill. The battles are highly skewed in the player's favor, with time coming to a complete stop during these skills and being completely invulnerable during thier animations. This is somewhat alleviated in volumes 2 and 3 with some very smart additions, but it does not take away from the simplicity of the combat. It is nowhere near as rediculous as the first set of .hack games (original quadrilogy), but its got its share of problems. thankfully theyve fixed a number of them with this re-release.
4. Story and Voice acting. This game has some very high production values, but there was something they could not avoid when they were re-releasing this and that was how voiceovers were handled. Because of how the old games were formatted in a 4:3 aspect ratio, the subtitles were done in such a way that they would constantly cut people off the in the middle of sentences, the middle of thoughts and it would just sound awkward if you read the line in its entirety. Since they did not go back and re-record the voies for 10 year old games, there are absolutely spots in the game where the voice acting is slow, and plodding, and the tone is not quite right. But there are also spots where the emotion of the characters is properly conveyed because the voice cast is very very high quality.  The story itself is hit or miss. You will either be completely on board with this non-sensical way of handling computer data and dealing with viruses and bugs. or you will not be impressed by the intersocial aspect of how this game handles its characters. But one thing this game does very well is character development. Main and side characters all get some kind of development, with haseo being the best example.
5. Remake quality. As a fan of the original series and someone who played the games on ps2 to death, i can say that this game does the originals justice by fixing some issues with translations, fixing alot of gameplay issues, but it does bring up a few new ones. Simply because of how easy it is to level and how much more damage you do to enemies, some fights have lost thier challenge, and its easier than ever to over-level and completely trivialize the game. However, a big problem I personally found was that since on the ps2 you had alot of time in between releases to grind out weapon proficiencies, it was very easy in the re-release to be UNDER leveled in those areas. Sure you'd be capped out in the game but you'd be using weaponskills from the beginning of the game still because you blew through it so fast.
In most cases this would not be an issue but it does take away from the joy of being "well prepared" for the subsequent volumes. You could very well grind out weapons and stuff before progressing but the allure of the story (at least for me) was too powerful for me to consider dumping extra time into the older volumes, espeically considering I knew where the story was going and what to expect.
In terms of how well the game performs on PC, I give it an A-. I had one problem with a bug during my play time that cost me an hour, but after that I never encountered a bug again. Load times were fast, and I played the game on the highest settings I could achieve through the game without mods (however I did mod in Playstation button icons, why this was not an OPTION at the very least is criminal) .
There are many issues with .hack as a series. But this set of games is completely and fully enjoyable if you are looking to get yourself lost in a self contained story, with compitent but repetitive combat, and un-even voice acting.

Its like Super Meat Boy in that its a cutsie indie super-hard platformer, but without the tight controls that made trial and error stress-free. Often times you know what you need to do, but because the game is, by design, hard to control, its just dying over and over to perform the task. Hard-to-control games can be fun; Surgeon Simulator and Octodad are both examples of that. But those games instead always make sure that you're making progress. You can be careful and even mess up, but you can slowly make progress. You can slowly get a better idea of how to play those games.
No Time To Explain does not do that. No Time To Explain is not that. You will die a lot, not because you made mistakes, but because its designed to do that. While there are plenty of checkpoiints through the short levels to make sure you don't have to retry the crazy difficult maneuvers a second time, you don't ever realy learn how to control it better. The checkpoint system is merely a mercy call.
Maybe this game is better for short spurts. A game to slowly chip away at. Its fun, sure, but its not worthy of great admiration. Get it on sale and kill time with it, but I can't imagine it'll be on anyone's favorites list.

After encountering hundreds of 'survival/craft' games, one thing remains constant. That is, the game's tendency to make things easier over time, to the point where you feel a little OP. Not with this little gem. you're character never adapts, only YOUR mind as the player. each waking day is a constant battle of survival. In other games, wolves are the weakest of enemies. But in this game,they are a terrifying monsters alone, and impossibly cunning deathbringers in packs. this is a game that brings survival back to it's root.. you dont sit and build 10 story wooden forts, you dont build firearms and armour, you scrounge what you can together to make a bandage, or repair a torn jacket. cos without that, you'll bleed or freeze to death. permadeath and random spawnpoints create a unique story with each playthrough. You end up feeling for your charachter, willing them to make through another hour in a blizzard, or with only a few candy bars. As much edge-of-seat excitement as a brilliant novel or tv series with it's atmospheric music and sound, and it's constant near-death experiences. and the final blow comes when your little survivor finally succumbs to the cold whilst lost in a blizzard, or is ravaged by a wolf that has stalked them for days.. your only memoir that they existed.. their journal. detailing where they went, what they found, what their state of health was and what finally ended thier story. collect enough journals of survivors that never made it and you get a sneak peak into the final days of a few desperate individuals as the harsh, gritty wilderness swallowed them all up.

This is a game for people who like observation over interaction. The game starts off by giving you the option to place randomly generated plants, plant eating animals, and animal eating animals. Each creature has a bunch of genes they are made of. At first those genes are hidden, but as you place research stations near activity, you reveal the hidden stats and are allowed to modify them for future plants and creatures.
After you unlock new genes, you can start placing your own plants and creatures. From there you get to observe how they interact with each other. You can make plants invasive, so that they spread fast and take over, or you can make plants that spread slow but are giants, or giants that spread fast! It's really up to you and what you want to see or experiment with.
So far I have really enjoyed watching the enviornment grow and change over time. The graphics may be simple, but the game is definitely enjoyable to watch. Personally I have it running on a second monitor to see what happens over time.  The game is definitely not for everyone, but for those who like to watch a world grow and change, you might want to consider picking this up.
PS. The leaderboard is a great addition that compares your world score with other players.

I think that BioShock is a wonderful story based game. You start the game being a passenger in an airplane that crashes on the sea. You find a lighthouse with a submarine inside near the plane wreck zone and you decide to get into it. Because of that you find an underwater city named Rapture that is the glorious construction of Andrew Ryan. When you get inside of Rapture, a person named Atlas contacts you via a radio and demands for help in order to save his family. On the way to do this you find a large variety of weapons, such as a wrench, a revolver, machineguns, rocket and grenade launchers and more. In addition, you have to change your DNA structure to get superpowers (plasmids) like telekinesis, incinerate and more. There are also some mini bosses, the 'Big Daddies', who protect some little creatures named 'The Little Sisters' who keeps the vital essence of life in Rapture, ADAM. Once you defeat a Big Daddy, you will be able to extract the ADAM from the little sisters by harvesting them or saving them (like Ms. Tenenbaum told you to do). On the other hand, once you are close to meet Atlas and his family, you find out that Andrew trapped them. Now your mission is to eliminate Mr Ryan. After you do that, your 'friend', Atlas, joins the other side and, with his acolyte, Mr Fountaine, takes over the city and infects you with a deadly toxin. Ms Tenenbaum, the 'mother' of the Little Sisters helps you finding a cure for the toxin, but it has some side effects. It f**ks up your entire DNA System, causing it to switch between plasmids without meaning it. After that, Tenenbaum gives you the second part of the antidote and helps you to survive. Now, your main goal is to escape from Fountaine. Ok, during the entire game i tried to survive against those zombies around here, i even modified my DNA structure, and now, and now am i supposed to transform into one of those smelly... Big Daddies? Are you serious? How many compromises should i do to escape from this god damn place? (By the way, don't get me wrong, i was still playing the game while i wrote those lines). With the help of the little sisters, you get into Fontaine’s Private room and you extract all of his ADAM and you let the little sisters killing him. After that, you turn on them to harvest their ADAM and become the lord of Rapture. But that wasn’t enough. After that you get your army and yourself to the surface starting a war.
Ok, that’s not the end that I expected, but I know where I did wrong. I shouldn’t harvest any one of those sisters; that’s the key for the happy ending. If you proceed like me, just kill yourself. You are a horrible person :D
In conclusion, i recommend this game for its amazing story, not for the shooter feature, because it's a little annoying then you are in combat and you lose half health by one shot in the body and then, on your screen, it appears a lot of sparkles which makes you not seeing anything.

It's been a while since I last properly sat down and played an SRPG, and I was honestly weary to a degree with the whole Super Sentai's Powers Rangers theme Chroma Squad employed. Needless to say fact I beat it in under three days after I actually began playing should tell you I was way off that mark.
You create and assume the roles of your five-strong Super Sentai group, process which is done through choosing which character will assume each role (Lead, Assist, etc) and there are quite a few cameos ranging from actors to pop icons you may recognize. I had fun naming my totally-not-Weasley-Snipes “Eyes-Open”, but that's beside the point. After that's done and over with you find out they're disgruntled stunt actors on a related show who decide to create a new studio and show of their own. These are the humble beginnings game presents you with and it's customizable down to Ranger colors, studio name catchphrases team will employ. Far be it for me to say that's ALL there is to this story, and oh boy does it escalate, but it never loses that sense of “we're running a show here” which is further enforced by character's comments, episode setups and constant camera crews on the set.
This illusion is never broken because no matter what happens you're still making a show which nets you fans and money. Both are important for keeping your studio successful because it lets you craft gear from materials your enemies drop; things like tape, cardboard and glass, or straight up buy new stuff from the store. You will also want to invest in your studio for things like HD cameras which net you more audience per-episode, better health insurance for HP bonus, etc. It's definitely sensible and tongue-in-cheek with the mood of the game. As befitting a Super Sentai team you will also acquire a wise MENTOR and Mecha at your disposal, latter which also gets its own separate upgrades and is used in 1v1 fights against giant opponents.
As far as actual meat of the game goes, that being combat, you'll quickly discover your team of five is constantly outnumbered usually 3-to1 if you're lucky and keeping your gear up snuff is a good idea. As each of the five seasons go by your characters unlock another tier of skills you can choose form so you're not just brute-forcing it. In fact, I'd argue game is somewhat on the easy side unless you really want to do all of Director's Instructions aka specific set of objectives in each episode which may be on the tricky side but are also a great way to get more audience, except in the very last part when that difficulty spike becomes too real. It does make for a fitting conclusion, but also drags down what should've been a way more intense end game. I will say that send off itself is amazing and no game that plays the theme track can do wrong by me in that regard. It turns out your show is pretty radical and watched worldwide.
If there are any negatives they are very few, mostly on the side of some Unity engine shenanigans like some scripts not being timed correctly which leads to some delays, hang ups when game has to display things like a ton of audience bonus gained from healing and alike, but I would probably point out overused Mecha fights in the last episode or so as the worst offender for me. You don't have to end each episode like that and especially not because you'll notice hit percentage is still RNG-driven so it'll eventually turn on you. I also wish game was longer, but you can also have too much of the good stuff.
So, did I like Chroma Squad? I loved it. Really got me motivated to play some more SRPGs when I get the time and had me grinning like a maniac at times. You gotta accept it is, well, episodic at times because that's the source material it draws from, but stellar soundtrack really kicks in at times and does wonders for overall impression. If you're even remotely interested in these games give it a go and remember to GATTAI at your earliest convenience.

Dustforce truly is a work of art. I don't mean that lightly. The way it's animated plus its music gives it that title in my book. I can find myself playing one level for an hour, maybe even hours at a time. The frustration of losing levels is filled with relaxation and calmness because of the ambient music. The way the levels are crafted is truly mindblowing. They had a system in which you had to perfect a level to earn a key, and you would use that key to earn more levels. In layman's terms, to earn more levels, you had to perfect current levels. They ditched that and added an XP system in which you gain more XP to earn a key the more levels you play and perfect. I'm very glad they added this system and was skeptical about buying it. But now that I did buy it, I do not regret it even for a second. One thing I really love about this game is how you don't have to unlock base levels. In a sense, this game is open world. That sense is that many levels are available to you, and you can choose whether you want to advance into more challenging levels, or stay where you're at. To get an S in completion, you have to sweep up EVERY leaf, and to get an S in Finesse, you have to maintain your combo throughout an entire level.
Another thing I absolutely enjoy about Dustforce is its expasive community. There are lots of Community Workshop maps for you to sharpen your skills on, and lots of people who can set a good example. I'm sure most of the people who get best times on all the levels have a Youtube channel, so you can probably catch them there. The community may or not be active, but it sure is good and friendly.
Overall, in terms of gameplay, music, artstyle, animation, and difficulty (it's not an easy game, but it's not that hard of a game either. It just depends on how much you want to play it), I rate this game:
10/10

The expansion pack to this game, Forces of Corruption has containd a game breaking bug since it was initially released; to this date it has not been fixed.  The issues is noticed during the main campaign of the FoC; where, if a player corrupts a planet that one of the main characters is suppose to do a campaign mission on, then there is a chance that the character will become stuck on that planet, invisible.  The player will have no way to interact with the character or start the mission.  How you will notice, is that the character will suddenly vanish off of the map after completing the corruption mission.  No matter where you look, it won't be visible.  If you click on it's icon in the upper corner, it will direct you to the planet where the character was suppose to do the mission.  The reason is, because that character is stuck on the planet; just invisible.  This breaks the game.  The only thing you can do is return to an older save and avoid using corruption when you last did it.
The fact that such an aggrivating bug exists in a released product, is enough to earn it a poor rating.
Edit: I deleted some comments due to fallacies.  Just because you never experience a problem with a product; doesn't mean no problems exist.  You can go to the Star Wars wikipage for FoC and see the campaign bug mentioned on the page.  Granted it says that it was patched; but, obviously it wasn't done so effectively if it still persists for players.  There is literally a recent steam community discussion you can look up, where someone is describing the exact issue and multiple other members are trying to help them trouble shoot the issue.  The final concensus was: you guessed it, restart the campaign.
