But, you know, we live in an era where Mighty No 9 happened. Not to mention a lot of talk about "dumbing down" from the old games (hint: it wasn't dumbing down).
I'll go on about this, but for now here's a tl;dr: it's just as enjoyable as it was back then, looks better (mostly), and gameplay wise is vritually indistinguishable despite it's changes. I will not talk too much about the plot or core gameplay, other than this is a surprisingly story-heavy game for those of you who are not familiar with .hack, and it's gameplay can best be described as solid hack-and-slash, in my opinion. It is an EXTREMELY fun game to play, and a very fun universe to unravel and learn as well. Rather, I want to talk about the derisive changes people are debating, as well as some issues people are having with the game lagging or not starting up.
Let's start talking about some of the gameplay changes:
>Attacks deal more damage
>More EXP
>Retry function
>Chim Sphere cap increased
>Bullets faster in avatar battles
>Reduction in hitstop and battle tempo inscreased
>Cheat mode
>Movement speed increased
In conclusion, after playing Volume 1: virtually nothing has changed between now and the PS2 with these functions in mind.
Go into a high level area well before your time? It's not gonna save you. Infinite retires can't save you whene very enemy oneshots you. The reality is this: G.U. was never hard franchise. When I was only 13-15, outside of Doppelganger fights (mostly because I was really dumb in how I approached them back then), I don't think I got more than five game overs as a child. If I did, it definitely wasn't more than 10 (excluding the final Avatar battle of Vol 3, which I doubt will give me as much issues these times).
These changes were not "dumbing it down" it's making the game go faster. The difficulty is roughly the same as back then. To clarify what this means, the game has greatly increased in it's speed, which is a boon as the PS2 versions sometimes... slagged a bit. Level grinding (btw, G.U. to this day remains the only game I enjoy level grinding in) is less tedious if you aim to go that route (I can't help but reccomend trying to "stay" at story-level to keep some fun bosses being a cakewalk, but it's usually not that bad). Clearing areas is quicker, and it definitely does not feel easier than before, granted it already wasn't hard.
If you find Last Recode easy, you'll find the originals easy too.
"Dumbing down," is an immensely annoying phrase that's entered gamer lingo, one that is tossed at this game often before it was even relased, which is disheartning. This is not a game that has experienced of it: these changes make the game a little less slow and tedious, not "dumb it down for casuals." If you could play G.U. back then, you can play it now. Having more Chim Spheres is good: you can stock up on them for long dungeons where you don't care about the Chim reward for a mission rank and you just want to level up or get the beast statue treasure. I doubt you'll need retries, but at least the option is there. If you bit more than you can handle and you want to Retry just so you can use a smoke screen and not lose your progress?
It's a video game. Do what you want if it's fun! You want to use cheat mode? You bought the damn game, go nuts if it lets you have fun.
If anything, I'm disappointed they didn't change how Duel Swords and Broadswords function in Vol 1. In pre-release material it was reported that "Improvements that were made in Vol. 2: Reminisce and Vol. 3: Redemption will be reflected on Vol. 1: Rebirth in the HD Remaster." You know, maybe this one IS just me not remembering, but quite frankly? I don't see ANY changes. Duel Swords still only combo 3-4 hits, and you still can't move while charging a power attack with a Broadsword in Volume 1. While it was still immensely fun to play after so many years, I can't help but see myself not returning very often to Volume 1 as a result, sadly. I still cannot speak negative of it: while the beginning of Volume 1 is still a bit slow in my opinion, that's a story issue and not a gameplay one.
The graphics are something else I've seen some people mixed on. It's important to remember this is not a remake: it's an HD remaster. They took the old graphics and booted them up to 1080p and made them prettier. It's still a ten year old PS2 game though.
I will comment on Vol 4's graphics when I get there.
Yes, there's some clipping issues. Sometimes it's very blocky, and doesn't look too great at times. Something I had never noticed when I was younger actually is the fact that in a lot of cutscenes, lots of people's mouths didn't move. Probalby a mixture of me being directly at my screen unlike the PS2 days with some distance and being 1080p. So don't expect this looking like a game made brand-new from scratch during 2016-2017. It's not, and it's on you if you're expecting the best visually looking game ever made.
There are two issues I have heard people talk about, and I will give my opinion on both:
>Unusually high lag
>Doesn't seem to start up
I admittingly at first had a lag issue, even with all graphics set to low. I was surprised as this is a good gaming laptop that can play Dark Souls 3 at high graphics with relatively little problem. However, I have a laptop with Nvidia: after doing a little fix (I have posted about this in discussions) I was able to discover this was an issue with Nvidia chosing not to run the game on high settings for some reason. After that, the game runs fun on high graphics, and my girlfriend with a good PC has no issues either.
It's weird, but I think it's more of a "you" issue than a bad port. Still, more than one person has reported such issues, so I suppose beware: in a worst case scenario, don't play more than two hours if you cannot get it to work at all.
I don't know this issue with the game just not starting or crashing. Again, neither me nor anyone I know who has played this game has had this issue. I want to say it's a "you" problem, but more than one person has happened. Saddly, I can offer no real input or advise on it.
In conclusion?
I love this. I loved it back then, and I love it now. I was genuinely happy to buy this game, and I'm genuinely happy to play it. If you'd liek a story-driven anime hack-and-slash with a plot, character evolution (one of the most important things by far is how much Haseo grows up between Volumes 1 and 3 from this edgelord seeking revenge to someone who truly cares for his friends, and Atoli's progression from a doormat into a woman who can stand on her own and even confront the one who ruined her life), a fantastic universe with commentary on the rise of the internet era and the internet's impact on the real world, then I cannot express my encouragement to play this game.
If you are a returning player, then welcome back. 'The World' is ready for you, with a brand new adventure to boot.
And if you are a new player, one who is interested in .hack because you heard about it but could never find a way to play it before (PS2 exclusives each worth a fortune), wanted to play it because you wanted to play the OG "this setting is about an MMORPG that's scewing up the real world," because you're a fan of SAO and wanted to try something you think is similar, or because you hated SAO and heard this was a better version?
Welcome to 'The World.'

I've been slowly adding to my list of relaxing, (mostly) casual puzzle games that I can play both to wind down or get the brain active, and my current list consists of - Kami, Ichi, and Lyne. Of those games, Lyne is easily my favorite, and one that I see myself playing over and over, for the rest of my life. The daily challenges add a lot of replayability to the game.
If you like circuit-based puzzles, you will really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are very simple, but also very easy/nice on the eyes. Different shapes of varying color on a basic background make for relaxing gameplay, completely at your own pace. There isn't really any music, however, the sounds made when you clear a level is very soothing, and when you get in the zone, clearing levels very quickly provides good, positive feedback. After you complete several levels, you unlock the ability to switch the background theme to different color palettes, unlocking more options as you progress through the game.
The controls are super simple - you just click and drag the mouse to move your circuit to (applicable) areas on the grid. The learning curve is minimal to moderate, however, the higher-difficulty levels can be extremely challenging. Difficulty is indicated by the number of triangles.
Each "set" of levels consists of 25 levels, and there is one set for every letter of the alphabet (26). On top of that, there are daily challenges that are changed throughout the week, starting at the easiest difficulty on Mondays, and increasing to brutal, oh-my-god-just-kill-me-this-is-so-hard-and-I-haven't-slept-yet-trying-to-finish-this-level torture on Sundays. Achievement hunters will have a grand time trying to 100% complete this, and I play this regularly whenever I have some time to fill. As mentioned before, I see myself playing this game for the rest of my life.
The goal in Lyne is to get all same-shaped circuits to connect to each other - the two bold shapes are your start and end points (you cannot miss a non-bold shape, and you cannot continue the circuit if you connect the start/end points). As you progress, more colors/shapes will be added, increasing the difficulty. Nodes will eventually appear (double, triple, and quadruple sockets), and these must be filled completely for you to solve the level. Nodes are also critical in the later stages, as they will allow your circuits to cross otherwise uncrossable pathways (ex: if you have a green connection going diagonally, you cannot have other circuits passing through that diagonal line). You can undo your connections at will with no penalty, and there is no time limit - everything is completely at-your-own-pace.
One of the best attributes of this game is how it rewards patience, perseverance, and trial-and-error. Many times, I have solved a puzzle by trying every possible route/solution I can think of. Other times, I will go back a few levels and have a sudden moment of clarity because you will realize that most levels in set follow very similar "themes" to solve the puzzles. For example, one set may have a pattern of having you use the longest path (or the shortest path). There are numerous ways to solve each level, and this is also a great thing, because it ensures that you have multiple ways to complete each level.
Overall, this is a great puzzle game that any puzzle enthusiast must try out - especially if you like circuit-based ones.
Highly recommend!
Cheers,

Day one:
I scrounged everything I could from the wreckage, lots of lugage, lots of supplies. Walked in one single direction and found the tree line leading to a cliff, found the beach, good.
Day two:
Collected more supplies from the wreck that had missed the previous day, explored further into the forest, keeping my bearings, nothing of notice apart from vegetation, went back early to build a proper shelter for the night, used a fire axe to chop trees along the beach to do it.
Day 3:
Time to start thinking about an S.O.S. sign, but first I want to delve deeper into the woods, find a source of fresh water.
Walked into a clearing in the middle of the forest - well past the wreckage - and I saw something... someone? His back was facing me, he couldn't see me, he didn't hear me, I thought of reaching out, but he was crouching, hunching, pretty much naked, filty covered in dirt, and making growling noises like as if he was munching or gnawing at something. In front of him, lying on the side was some sort of game animal, a deer perhaps, are those antlers, or bones? Can't make it out, too far away. Decided to go back.
Day 4:
There's "people" here... Maybe not the type I want to make contact with, I'm sticking to the coast for now. Walked by the beach to find anything worth taking, or better shelter, maybe fresh water. There was a sailboat! It was anchored in not far from shore, I can swim there. As I kept walking to get closer to it I noticed a big 'dead' oak tree on the top of a rock formation, could be useful for a tree house, big foundation.
Swam to the boat, yelled 'hello' to no response, walked in, nothing but scatered clothes, no people, no... blood. Found some supplies, found some fresh water bottles, thank goodness!
As I was swiming back to shore and getting out of the water I saw 'them'... Running on the hill that leads to the oak tree to my left, two of them in the distance.
...They were running on all fours, this is very disconcerting.
Day 5:
Chooping more trees along the sealine for a few hours, the consistent noise must have attracted 'him'. I was chopping away when I heard a very close "shriek", it was inhuman... 'he' found me! I ran as fast I could towards the beach, I didn't see him, but I can't fight on the trees, I want a clear shot at him,I wan't to see him clearly without clutter and land my axe on him if it comes to that.
I'm on the beach, standing my ground, shaking, alert, looking at the tree line. Bushes and dry leaves rustle, 'he' doesn't come...
I head back to the boat, I'm sleeping there tonight.
Day 6:
I swim to shore and head to the natural rock-pier where the old oak tree is, go over it to see what's on the other side. Nothing but beach... I need to head in again, I have no choice, I need water.
I head inland, forest is dense, eventually I arrive at a tree line, a massive 500m wide clearing, with more forest to my right side and in front on me in the distance. To my left there's an enormous rock formation and hill, can't see the other side, so I hiked it, it wasn't steep.
...Two of 'them' pop right in front of me, from behind the hill while I was navigating some rocks to climb, they are so fast in all fours! How is it possible? They attack me fast and relentlessly, I had no reaction time. I feel sharp pain, I taste blood, my blood. I thought I was going to die.
Day 6, or 7?
I wake up in a cave, a whole of some sort, no exit but a hole on top of me, the sun is out and bright, is it still the same day? How long have I been out?
My left arm hurts, massive "claw'ish" looking marks, bruising, might be broken. No, just dislocated, I grab a piece of clothing from the floor and stuff it in my mouth, I don't want to scream and attract them. I hit my left harm hard - whilst holding firmly with my right hand - against the rock wall, excruciating pain shoots through it, but it's back into its place.
Chest hurts on the right side when I breathe, could be a broken rib rubbing at my lung, lets hope it hasn't pierced it. My entire face is sticky with caked blood, face covered in it, I feel large slashes and cuts on my face. Neck has a lump of flesh peeling off, lots of blood, dry now. They thought I was dead...
Nothing in the cave but the odd items here and there, a shoe, wallet, hat, glasses, clothing, no bones or bodies, this is not where they throw away the dead or dying, this is where they 'storage' prisioners, or... food.
The hole above me, it's not that high, I climb my way out, it's easy enough even with the broken rib. 'They' aren't using these holes in the ground thinking that whatever they throw in there would climb out, they definitely tought I was dead already when they knocked me out or fainted from my injuries.
I peek with my head side ways before revealing myself, no sign of movement so I climb out. I'm in the middle of a village, around me are 5 or 6 huts or triangular bungalows with no walls, just their skeletal structure, beams and columns. Lot's of luggage and briefcases are scattered around, and in the centre are.. body parts, impaled arms and legs.......
Where the f*** am I? What is this place?
10/10 would continue to play!

[h]This review is based on Early Access Gameplay. Because of the changing nature of the game, parts of this review are very likely to change.[/h]
When you first start the game, you are greeted with a disclaimer:
This game starts by greeting you with a disclaimer.
"The Long Dark is a post-disaster survival simulation. Although we strive to provide an experience steeped in realism, the game is not a replacement for proper wilderness survival training. As the result of the geomagnetic disaster which serves as part of the fictional foundation of the game, we have taken liberties with the potrayal of wildlife behaviour. Hinterland Studio Inc. does not condone the wanton destruction of wildlife."
And then you are taken to the main menu, with a delicious quote from one of many inspirational people that set the tone of the game.
Since this game is in early access, there are parts of the game that are being worked on or missing entirely. The Story Mode is nothing more than a button at this point on the main menu, which tells you that it will be available upon the game's final release when you click on it.
So you're forced to play in the Sandbox.
Which I love - because you pick a starting location, and then from there you let your own story unfold.
And what is the Long Dark? It is entirely Man vs. Nature. And nature will always win. It's simply a quesiton of how much you can take.
Taking place in the Canadian wilderness after a geomagnetic disaster that throws
out of balance, you find yourself fighting for your life against frigid temperatures, debilitating weather patterns, starvation, fatigue, disease, and wildlife.
This game is so spot-on with its survival requirements, that it reminds me of my own small adventures in the area around Lake Pend d'Orielle in Idaho. To combat the dangers of cold (read: exposure), you first need shelter. You start with little more than the clothes on your back and your mostly empty backpack, with a gallon of water and maybe a couple snack bars or a sewing kit to start you on your journey. That hoodie and jacket aren't going to keep you warm in the zero-degree gusts of wind blowing in your face for long. A car is better than being outside, but not by much - you'll be far better off in a house or a mineshaft, but sometimes you will have to make do with the lee of a rock.
I so want to continue on with a lecture of what you need to do to survive - but both in this game and real life, it's not just knowing what to do, it's having the tools to prevent whatever might befall you. And that's part of what I love about this game - there's so much that can happen, from eating only half-cooked venison you hunted yourself and getting sick, to falling too far and breaking a leg, to freezing to death in a building that was the only source of shelter but was still far too cold, and you couldn't get that fire going in time. Or, perhaps, a chance encounter with a bear that was going so well - but went south far too fast.
And that's the thing. All the dangers in this game are purely what you might face in nature - save, perhaps, getting charged by wolves. There's no special monster, no group of cannibalistic tribesmen, no mechanations out to kill you simply to provide a focal threat. Because nature is fearsome enough.
And yet, there's so much to love about nature. The visuals in this game are simplistic on the Unity engine - but it's a distinct, appealing world, desolate but so vibrant all at once. There are crags with frozen rivers that you just can't help but look down; iced-over forests that sparkle in your eye; and vistas provide some amazing views, especially if there's a frozen lake nearby where you can see the ice stretching off to the horizon.
And when you find your flow - not if, when - you'll be able to appreciate those beautiful moments more and more, as you find the systems that tax your character's body less obtrusive, less wanting to kill you as you find your own place in this frozen paradise. Your choice whether you wish to keep some of the modern amenities, or go full tribal and make your own clothes from animal hide and fashion "primitive" tools that get the job done just as effectively as the factory-made ones we use today.
I enjoy Miasmata, but The Long Dark is the survival game I'll be coming back to again and again five years down the line after I've played through it a dozen times. Especially since the developers keep adding more to the systems of this game, fine-tuning things that are working but need that extra bit of polish, and adding whole new systems that could easily turn the tide for or against you in your next playthrough and make it more interesting. This is easily my favorite singleplayer survival game of all time, and I'd be hard-pressed to find one better.
Can't recommend it enough.

If you need something that is constantly changing, this is not the game for you.
That being said, I do thouroughly enjoy this game. The gameplay itself is a bit redundant; make a fire, melt snow, cook food, go outside, search buildings, shoot some stuff if you have the tools, go back inside, repeat... maybe make some tools & clothes, but basically it's all the same aside from different areas having a different landscape and different buildings.
Starting on the easiest setting, you should be pretty much good to go for the long haul. Finding resources is much easier, you don't have to wrry about wolves or bears that you happen to come across trying to attack you, and finding a gun and ammo shouldn't be terribly difficult.
Going up the the medium setting, you should still have an pretty easy time getting by for a good while. You'll need to move onto different areas faster, and you may not find a rifle and/or enough ammo quiet as easily depending on your luck. I've had games where I had enough ammo to start and end a war on my own, and I've had medium setting games where I could barely get enough ammo to help my crappy accuracy land more than a couple deer. The snare is where my home is, for the most part haha. You'll just need to sort out avoiding wolves if you don't have a gun/ammo, or sort out making sure you have a good enough light source to ward them off until you can retreat into a building and wait out the threat.
Hard mode, not going to lie, I haven't gone into that much yet. I like games to be easy enough for me not to rage out on them haha so I usually stick to Medium difficulty. Hard mode, you will find significantly less resources. Finding a gun will be difficult, and in return you will rely on finding food sources in buildings and other searchable places. Wolves and bears will actively seek out attacking you. Avoiding wolves by using light as a source to slow their attack down will be difficult because you will have a difficult time even finding the resources to have said light source, and when you do you will want to use it sparingly as finding more will be difficult as well.
All modes are the same as far as deer-- they will not attack you, but they will run away if you get too close to them. To shoot them, you will need to attempt to get them to run to a dead end so that they turn around and come closer towards you for a good shot, or you will have to get a shot in so you can track them down later once they bleed out.
The landscapes are pretty nice. Obviously snow is all over-- I would have loved to see maybe an end-game area with less snow, but then it wouldn't be a post-apocolypic winter, so that's fair enough for me :P
The main downfall in the game, in my crappy memory's opinion, is there is no map. I don't mind that there isn't a map right off of the bat, but I would have loved to have been able to unlock areas of a map as you discovered them so you could find your way around easier. I have a terrible memory, and I realize they probably did this to be more realistic... but hey, some people draw maps when they are in the wilderness, so why can't we??
Overall, two thumbs up from me.

As I was playing this game, my brother and his friend came over to me and asked what I was playing. They began asking: "Is it a puzzle game?" "Is it an adventure game?" "Is it a horror game?" I hesitated to respond, as I could not decide if it was a game or not. There is nothing to gain here if you seek a complete experience, or even a positive one. Markov scanned the jungle floor, searching for monster tracks hidden under the darkness of the verdant jungle canopy.
The other hunters lied dead behind him - friends, now reduced to piles of meat by the ravaging beast they had come to kill.  It had torn through his suit and his stomach, but one hand was enough to hold his gun as he used the other to stop his innards from spilling out onto the ground.  They had weakened it, but it fled from him, and he just needed to find it and put it down to avenge his friends.
It was only when he heard the growls behind him that he realized he didn't have to find the beast.  It had already found him.
Markov screamed, "Goliath!  I will hang your head on my wall!" and pulled the trigger on his assault rifle.
As the bullets plinked harmlessly against the bleeding beast's thick skin Markov realized with horror that he hadn't paid the extra $20 for the "Damage-dealing-ammunition" DLC.
The monster swung its powerful arm, thick as a tree-trunk, into Markov and sent him flying through the air, where he glitched out and started breakdancing for no particular reason as his mouse cursor suddenly appeared on his screen.  Markov watched helplessly as the monster swaggered over, holding bags of money in each claw, and crushed him to death under its preorder bonuses.
Storytime over.

Cons:
- Literally one game mode with custom game modes so indistinguishable from the basic mode that it would take modders two weeks to create them in their free time, like if Halo had been sold for $60 with no campaign or non Deathmatch game options.
- I have played $20 games with more content and passion put into them than this $60 game.

The game serves a series of loosely related vignettes set across varied stages, steadily introducing new gameplay tweaks along the way. Each set piece lasts only 5-10-15 seconds through its action-packed yet gimmicky real-time replays. Actual play time is obviously much longer, not least due to continuous restarts, but also because this game is decidedly more about thinking than twitching.
Controlling time and dodging bullets is quite exhilarating but it does take a while to fully appreciate the mechanics. Initially, I felt SUPERHOT was not nearly as cool as I hoped, finding it hard to tell where bullets would actually hit. I was also not playing it right.
Without the slow-motion it doesn't really feel like a competent shooter but all its elements combined nevertheless create a particularly efficient mix.
The unlockable katana-only challenge is actually more empowering than the base game, since you're not hampered by the perceptibly slow firing rate of most guns. Multiple alternative game modes and a good list of optional challenges surprisingly offer a lot of diversity and replay value as they force you to completely rethink your strategies.
A mildly intriguing meta hacking story emerges but its overly pretentious tone can be off-putting, such as when it pesters you to leave the game and stop playing. It also leads to an objectionable ending.
The game's developers are very much self-aware and they also made the game constantly self-referential. They knew they were onto something original but they ended up trying a little too hard here.
The presentation is awesome, with a convincing DOS-like old-school OS used throughout the menus, very stylish but ultimately sterile low-poly environments, with additional 3D ASCII levels, and a perfectly selected color scheme. Time well spent!

Before we start: I'm only saying that I recommend this game because there's no middle-ground answer, and I don't think it's bad enough to say that I wouldn't recommend it at all.
The good:
*Cool concept
*Beautiful graphics
*Fun banter dialogue between Hunters (when it isn't just replaying the same crap over and over)
*Fun gameplay (when it works)
The bad:
*The gameplay often doesn't work like it's supposed to
*The crashes
*Balance issues...
*...especially with the Wraith
*The DLC plan
*Monsters are boring after a bit
So all in all, Evolve is a fun experience - when it works. I can't tell you how many times I've gone to attack a creature as a Monster and swung five or six times (without hitting anything) before finally just giving up and running away. Where is the hitbox for the Monster melee? Does the game even know? I certainly don't, even though it seems to work about 75% of the time. Sometimes my placed items will randomly vanish (I tested this - as Griffin, I watched a sound spike disappear  for absolutely no reason, three seconds after placing it) and on occasion the hitboxes on things apparently disappear. And to top all of this off, my game has now crashed five times since I got it. I'm not rocking a toaster here - my rig exceeds the recommended system requirements.
Even more frustrating, though, are the balance issues. The Wraith has already been nerfed from the beta, but that has done almost nothing to stop its rampage. God forbid you should ever fight a Wraith unless it's their very first time playing that Monster. I have defeated a Wraith exactly one time, and in the finished game I've fought probably ten of them. The one I defeated, I'm positive, was brand new to the character.
And my last disappointment (I won't talk about the DLC plan, because everybody else already is) is the generic nature of the Monsters. Yeah, I know, right? But rather than making something cool and interesting - say, for example, a Tremors-themed Monster, or something that spawns little Monsters to fight for it - we have carbon copies of the Warrior (Goliath), Mage (Kraken), and Rogue (Wraith) classes that show up in every MMO and RPG ever. Nice. Way to be creative. That's not to say that it isn't fun to play the Monsters (when they work, of course) but could Turtle Rock not pull its head out of its cloaca for three seconds to come up with something original, or at least a little bit unique?
But yes, the game is fun to play. When everything is working properly, the experience is buttery smooth in addition to being absolutely beautiful, both visually and auditorially. Killing the Monster with epic teamwork feels like a real victory; likewise, killing the Hunters through guile and cunning leaves me with a Hannibal Lecter-esque sense of satisfaction. When you manage to find good players all across the board - not as uncommon as you might think, surprisingly - the games are exhaustingly intense and fun. And believe it or not, I've yet to encounter a single person who is anything less than nice and sociable. My biggest fear going into Evolve was that, with no friends who play this on PC, I'd be the odd man out and a weak link. Not so. Everybody seems to understand that teamwork is key, and they're more than willing to cooperate. I just wish the game would cooperate with us.
So: as of right now, I don't recommend the game unless you really, REALLY want to play it. Wait a few months for things to not be so f*cked up. I'm sure it'll come into its own by then.

TL;DR = Hell yes you should buy this game, you start out with a laser powerful enough to propel you around.
A LASER.  THAT MAKES YOU FLY.  I MEAN SERIOUSLY GUYS COME ON.
Now, the real review.
It ain't heavy on plot (or if it is, I haven't seen much of it), but that's okay - the bits that you do get give you enough "wait, WTF?!" moments to keep you eager to get moving.  They make you want to see what's over the next spike-studded hill.  And those hills *will* be spike-studded: this is something of a hardmode game in the vein of VVVVVV, Super Meat Boy, and the like, requiring both skillful control and a degree of planning in what you're going to do next.
It also ain't really combat heavy.  There are bosses, and the ones I've fought were fun and challenging, but aside from some detours from the standard play style it's mostly navigational challenges.
What it has in spades is STYLE.  Every stage presents something new you have to work around, and the interaction between your character and the stage just makes things that much more interesting (especially when you end up in a different pair of shoes - or hat).
So yes, I have had a blast with the time I've already spent with it - and I intend to spend more still learning what more it has to offer me.  I most strongly recommend picking it up; it has the feel of that rare sort of game that would cause one to brave the wilds of Newgrounds to find the diamond in the rough.

I was thinking if I should write a brand new review or just add what is new in the remaster so here goes. Here is my original review for No Time To Explain

No Time To Explain is the remaster from the developers Tiny Build games. No Time To Explain is a puzzle physics platforming game where the main goal is to use a physics gun to launch yourself across levels.
The original game was very fun but now we have a remaster but is it worth your money ?
For people who haven't bought it already it's must own and for people who own it, I'll run down the fixes.
The game now has a very solid frame rate which was  a big problem in the original game. It was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to fight some of the bosses and some of the levels were a complete nightmare with the unstable frame rate.
The graphics are fixed up and look a little high res than the graphics from the original game which looked like a very poor flash game.
They added a life system which makes the game a challenge which the original game lacked off. The original game was really easy and the challenge is a nice touch.
But there are a few issues about this game too. The game is still kind of buggy. I found myself stuck on platforms and sometimes the gun wouldn't shoot, but overall it's not too bad.
No Time To Explain Remastered is a really good upgrade to a really fun game. For people who don't own it, this is a must pick up and for people who have this upgrade this is really worth another playthrough. The game is kind of difficult but this is still a very fun game. I give No Time To Explain Remastered a 8,5/10

I want to give this one a neutral rating. Everything is here for a great 4 player vs game. Bots, varied ships and weapons, fast menu.
The game feels like some things were rushed. There are about 9 maps, each feels the same and most have background objects that seem like foreground obstacles to new players. You can't play on a map without obstacles, can't make your own maps, can't download new maps and can't adjust the variables on the map (besides choosing small, medium, or large map size).
There is a singleplayer training mode that feels more fleshed out than the multiplayer mode. I found myself wishing for a singleplayer challenges mode that is along the lines of Worms Armageddon with the interesting tricks you need to pulloff using what they equip you with.
Online multiplayer would really benefit this title. It's hard to get 3 other players who will play enough rounds to start getting into the depth the game could have to offer, if they could only keep you playing long enough. Bots are okay but even on hard they seem to move erratically.
If you've got 3 local buddies that are into this type of game (and would be willing to invest a few hours to become slightly seasoned) then this is great at around $2.50. It's not good if you have casual gamer buddies or would play mainly against the bots.

The Long Dark is a survival game developed by Hinterland Games. The game is an absolutely brilliant concept where permadeath survival in a beautiful snowy environment completely made on the Unity Engine!

The game does offer many difficulty settings and a story mode is on its way. The game also offers challenges to make the game more interesting
The game is very complex. The cold weather can change in an instant during your travels which can easily kill you! Calories also play a huge factor during your survival, you have to hunt, gather and cook to stay alive!

The concept is great, the games are boring and dull. You'll play for about half an hour before moving onto something with more substance.
Yeah, getting a good jumpscare every now and then is fun, but ALL these games are is jumpscares and a few lame easter eggs like posters on the walls changing, or things suddenly disappearing from a room. Sometimes animatronics will look at you when you're looking at them, or they make noises. More than likely some of these easter eggs that involve disappearing items are mislabeled glitches that the game's creator didn't notice until the game was released. What I really hate the most is the lack of substance in every game.  Not to mention, you are either totally stationary or confined to one room during gameplay. To me that is lazy game making. It'd be much more interesting if you could actually do something other than look at cameras and in the 4th game, run around your bedroom looking in the halls, the closet, and the bed. The plot of the game is a trainwreck which really makes the games suck even more. During the first game (out of game mostly) it is revealed that several children who were patrons at Freddy Fazbear's Pizzaria were brutally murdered by a staff member dressed in a costume. He lured them into a back room and killed them all at the same time. The bodies were never located, but after awhile, the other patrons began complaining that the animatronic band reeked of death and had stains that resembled blood/mucus. It is never made clear whether the patrons were aware of the fact that the childrens' bodies were stuffed into the animatronics or not, but it is likely that despite the overbearing evidence, they were never any the wiser. That's a great plot. Nobody has ever done anything like that. Too bad it got ruined as time went by. The game's creator likely mass produced so many of these games to satisfy his juvenile fanbase that he forgot what the games were supposed to be about. That would explain the ungodly amount of plotholes in the game. Numerous fans have tried to piece the plot together only to be told that they're wrong-I have a feeling they're all wrong because once again, I really think the creator doesn't even know what is going on at this point. That is typically what happens when you don't put much time/thought into creating something. Some people think it's cool that the storyline is masked and muddled, most people think it's stupid and frustrating. I am part of the latter group. Part of what makes a horror game/movie so scary is understanding the situation you're in. Fully understanding that is. Mass produced games usually wind up being garbage and that's exactly what FNAF has become. It had a chance to be a great franchise but a combination of sloppy game creation, reusing material endlessly and needlessly,promotion from idiots, and a cancerous fanbase made up of disgusting furries and little kids has turned it into a joke among most horror gamers and gamers in general.
If you're a little kid looking for your first jumpscare game,go ahead and buy it. Everyone else-go look at something that actually has a plot,dynamic characters, objectives that challenge you, and an overall purpose.
To be clear, I don't hate the game's creator nor do I truly hate the game, I am just incredibly disappointed that the games went in the direction they did. I hate it when something with lots of potential just doesn't work out.

Chroma Squad is a decent turn-based tactics parody RPG that might not be complex enough for some people. It probably helped that I grew up on Power Rangers so my appreciation for the setting and tolerance for its issues might go a bit further than some. You can expect around 12 hours of playtime on the normal difficulty if you engage a bit with the crafting system and take time to equip everyone optimally.
I’ll start off by going over Chroma Squad’s problems. This game is weighed down by its boring mecha fights and gameplay repetitiveness. The mecha fights are 2D encounters where you take turns beating each other up instead of taking place on a grid. Imagine missing attacks with 80-90% accuracy against monsters that need to be KO’d three times and you have the early mecha combat experience. The fights become more tolerable later as you can equip different mech parts that increase accuracy (a must), other stats, or grant new abilities. Still, they’re too long and not mechanically interesting. I also didn’t enjoy the timing mini-game when you defend.
The gameplay repetitiveness comes from the pacing of acquiring new abilities and the common enemy variety. The bosses are fine and some of them have interesting gimmicks. New abilities are unlocked at the start of a new season which felt too long since you can only have one active out of the two or three choices at that tier. Some choices felt obvious, but I did do some switching around later in the game. What helped me was playing in short bursts of 1-1.5 hours. Otherwise, the gameplay might wear you down since you’ll often be using the same strategies against the same baddies. I noticed areas being reused often too. I recommend deliberately setting out to acquire the Rider path for season 5 to experience some very interesting gameplay changes relative to the rest of the game.
Chroma Squad allows for some silly customization. Since the theme is that you’re running a TV studio, you’re able to select your actors, name their characters, name the studio, customize catchphrases, name the mech, and more.  I highly recommend personalizing everything to have more fun with it. I went with Friendship Squad and named the mech Big Friend. The power of friendship can overcome all, don’t cha know.
The gameplay itself involves recording episodes (going out on missions) and managing your team in-between shoots. Episodes involve combat and following the Director’s Instructions as best as you can since you want to have a high audience rating for more money and fan conversion. The combat involves you making squad members move twice or move and then attack (attacks end the character’s turn). You can use certain abilities that count as free actions so that you can still attack and/or move. The Teamwork ability that any class can use lets you gang up on an enemy or toss teammates around which lets them move farther. The gameplay becomes more interesting later with more abilities unlocked while the start is a bit slow.
An example I can give is the having the Assault use Teamwork to toss the Lead away from danger, then using the Lead’s Join Up ability (free action) to gather everyone without making them use any actions, followed by the Support’s AoE heal, using the Lead’s Lasso ability to rope in a weak enemy for a kill, and then making the Scout cloak for something sneaky-sneaky.
The team management aspect involves crafting gear with materials found in episodes or from crates, deciding on what studio upgrades to buy, deciding which marketing agency to hire (income buffs, combat buffs) so that you can spend fans on even more buffs, buying gear from the shop, deciding on what abilities to use, and reading fan mail. Crafting can be a little time consuming considering that some stats are RNG which leads to multiple attempts if you have a poor roll.
Well, that’s it. I liked the game overall, but it does have some problems. I think it’s worth a look.

A decent remake of the previous Flash prototype. This game is a fun platformer with unique mechanics. And every now and then the mechanics change a little, while still keeping the same idea. And several jokes and over-the-top stuff (no spoilers here)!
Pros:
+ Graphics (smooth 60 fps! except on cutscenes)
+ Music
+ Gameplay
+ The several jokes spread through the game
+ Local co-op (requires gamepads)
+ Keyboard+Mouse and/or Gamepad controls
+ Steam Cloud and Steam Workshop
Cons:
- No in-game resolution setting. You must hold SHIFT while starting the game to change the resolution. But the game looks uglier in higher resolutions.
- The "beam" sound/noise can get annoying after a while.
- No way to skip to a single specific level. We can skip to a levelset, but not to a level inside the levelset.
- 1.2GB seems a bit too large. I believe the assets could have been better compressed/optimized.
- Restarting a level takes a bit too long. The screen slowly fades to black, and a couple of seconds later the level restarts.
- Cannot drop "guest" players without quitting.
- Cannot change between gampad and keyboard+mouse without quitting.
Misc:
± The jump is useless. But you are not supposed to use the jump, anyway.
± Collectible hats spread throughout the levels.
Yes, I recommend this game!
The "cons" are minor stuff (in my opinion), and are not deal-breakers.
Still unsure? Wanna try it before buying it? Look for the in-browser "No Time To Explain" Flash game, it works as a demo/prototype for this game.

Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad with the paid DLC Rising Storm.  If you like World War 2 themed PVP first person shooter simulations, this is a good game to get.  This game is slightly less realistic than the original Red Orchestra, but the graphics and the gameplay is whole lot better.  The single player is WW2 combat like the original Call of Duty and Medal of Honor games.  Comes with a separate Singleplayer campaign game.
You can play as infantry or tanker only.  The tank combat here is better than the original Red Orchestra, because the tank crew bots listen to your detailed comands that you can give, and you have more viewports to use.  The tanks models looks limited to the Panzer 4 and T-34 in the few original tank using maps.  As Commander, you can issue useful commands to your teammates.
Server Maps can have AI bots filling out the team roster.  You can command the bots squads to take objectives, defend objectives, or go to locations but not give artillery targets.  The bots are slightly more smarter, and have better shooting skills but still no substitute for real players.

RO2 multiplayer servers are German vs Russian maps.  With the Rising Storm DLC you have access to Japan vs American maps, (Using the Flamethrower is fun).  Has great multiplayer maps and a single person campaign.  A lot of multiplayer servers have bots filling in for real players.
The single player campaigns are German vs Russian or Russian vs German, it is a separate game bundled with your purchase.  The single player game is sort of buggy and cheats.  You can also use console comands in the single player game to complete the achievements there.
Has Steam Achievements with badge trading cards. Has Steam Workshop with modding community making new maps using the included Level Editor.

Where the hell do I even begin?
Well, I remember playing the original only because I watched Game Grumps play it.
The original was okay, given that you can turn off the guy screaming all the time (which was very ♥♥♥♥ing annoying), and only cause I was lucky enough to play it on a pc that ran it perfect. But then I got a new computer (Which was better than the old one) and it runs even worse. I learned it the hard way that the original engine was absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Anyway, they use a new engine now, and the game runs smoothly, which is great. However there are too many different physics and features that actually♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.
First things first,
Now, I remember playing the original, and it's like any old platform indie game. Challenging levels, bosses here and there, and infinite lives. Now they apparently decided to add in a "finite" life mechanic where when you're on boss levels (or certain levels), you have a limited number of lives. That number would be 5 (or 6, I didn't count how many exactly). 5 lives would seem plentiful, but there's only one problem with this.
How, you may ask? Well, let's just say, now whenever you're standing still, and you start shooting, you slide. Doesn't sound like a big deal, but I had a lot of trouble on second boss (SECOND BOSS MIND YOU) because you have to shoot the shark, but, you have to avoid him, the pit below you, and the spikes. Plus the platforms they provide are extremely small, and you will fall to your death if you don't pay attention.
Next thing,
Yes, it's all fine and dandy that they got a new one. Certainly runs better than the original (as I stated before). However, my only problem is when you jump, it kills the momentum from your laser. Why? In the original, you were able to jump, and get even higher when you shot your laser when combining the jump and laser. however, now,  it gives you less height, and the only real way to get good momentum is if you do it frame perfect, or you just start shooting when you're standing on the ground.
Another problem I have with this, is the fact that in the original, when you shot the laser, you could see it shrinking, thus telling you that you are running out of laser power and you would need to touch the ground again to regain the momentum. In this game, there's no visual of that, therefore, if you relyed on it in the first, then yeah, have fun without the visual. It's only really frustrating because in the water levels, you would REALLY need the visual to be able to tell whether you can jump over a spiked wall or not.
Now, I have beaten the game before, mind you. However, I feel that this new engine is just frustrating with the little tweaks and changes that have occurred. Even though the changes are minor, it's still very frustrating. It can (and does) change the entire flow of the game.
Oh, and another con with the new engine is with the football guy, you can't spam the shotgun when standing on the ground. It sends you flying and you have to wait before you can do it again. That was honestly fun to me. But this actually affects the game because in the level where you first play football guy, you have to use the shotgun to blast through the blocks in your way. In the original, you could keep shooting and keep moving forward. The new engine disagrees, and doesn't allow that. Thus taking more time to complete the level, and increasing your chances of death (♥♥♥♥ing spikes).
Long story short, the new engine has its ups and downs. Really annoying for boss fights, levels, pretty much the entire game, and life system really shouldn't be there either. It runs smoother, which is the only upside I see in this.
If you already have it, cool, but I really don't recommend wasting $15 to play this, unless you really want to.

Hate me if you must, but I just could not get into "Outlast" no matter how hard I tried.
It's not because I wasn't impressed with the graphical content of the game or the immersive atmosphere. On the contrary, both those things are a major plus in my view and continue to be. My problem with it though is the game's dynamic. I'm all for Stealth-Horror gaming. I am. "Forbidden Siren" is one of my favourite Horror games of all time and that's all about stealth. However, there isn't really that much to elevate "Outlast" above the the rest of the pack in this regard, at least not in my view. The game is a simple case of open door, fumble around in the dark, cower in a locker while the lunatic looks for you and then edge your way out hoping in vain that he doesn't catch you.
And, try as you might, the homicidal nutjobs almost always catch you, which would be fine if you could defend yourself somehow. Now I realise that there is a message at the start of the game telling you that your character isn't fighter. I get that. I get that in that sort of scenario most of us would be overwhelmed with fear and fly into a blind panic. However, in a game where you are being stalked by a host of crazies who want you dead and you are surrounded by potential weapons, you do tend to find it a little frustrating that you can't simplay pick up a lead pipe and cave the lunatic's brains in.
It's probably also got a lot to do with the fact that, if you are going to make a stealth game, I think it makes more sense to make it in third person. First-person stealth games tend not to work very well in my experience because you really aren't doing very much in them so character detail is important to maintain audience interest.
As I said, "Outlast" is great as an atmospheric experience and on those grounds alone, I know a lot of people love it. Me, not so much. I felt very similarly about SOMA as well, so I don't know...maybe it's just me?

I should hate this game.  It should be something I refunded after 20 minutes.  I hate super difficult games.  I refund many games in under an hour because of their difficulty.  I love platformers, and they are maybe my favorite genre next to puzzle games, but I haaaaate the bosses.  I have played entire games only to not finish them because I didn’t want to finish the final boss.
This game is amazing!  Every boss demands new thinking, new strategy, new management of weapons and abilities, and a new test of patience and wishing to whatever gods you worship for a lucky run.  Including resets because of an early fatal flaw, I probably attempted to defeat the dragon over 200 times.  I changed weapons, bought new upgrades, and changed strategies numerous times.  Yet I never rage-quitted.  I just wanted back at another chance again and again.
Why if I hate bosses, and I love platformers, would I love a game that is only a platformer in order to play bosses?  Because the bosses in this game are so varied and complex that they each present a new puzzle of strategy and gameplay to defeat, that to call them traditional bosses is an insult to the design.  Maybe that and the fact you know that that is entirely what you are signing up for?  But absolutely everything else is executed with such love and detail that you are enticed to experience more of the game.  The graphics are gorgeous and unique.  The soundtrack (so perfect) and sound effects are amazing, and I wish I had purchased the version with the soundtrack.  The game may have been in a mini version of development hell for a long time, but you can tell it is only because the developers wanted it to be pristine.  That it is.
Only the run and gun levels seem a bit out of place.  But even they are still fun challenges, and just as challenging indeed.  This game gets a 10/10 from me, a player who hates bosses yet can't wait to finish every boss in this game (I'm almost there).  If this game even remotely seems like something you would enjoy, just scroll up and buy it.

Solid run-and-gun gameplay with uninspired levels and no indication of how the game is progressing. Are the levels randomly generated? Does the game go on forever? I got bored with the same-y levels before I could find out. Also, the game has some of the worst screen-tearing I've ever seen.

In space we brawl is sort of like a mix between rocketsrocketsrockets and stardust vanguards.
Pick a ship and a secondary weapon, each with their own unique attributes and styles, and brawl out in an open arena with obstacles.
In space we brawl has a strong scoring system that takes into account multiple achievements during each match, a progressive and appealing system that only a few other titles have explored.
This game wold benefit somewhat from a little extra something during matches to make them a bit more interesting, such as dynamic events - however as it stands it is quite enjoyable.
Following the release of some fairly dissapointing space battle games In space we brawl offers perhaps one of the strongest indie space battle arena experiences. The price tag is fairly reasonable for the content.

Life conspires to take a massive dump on Lorraine, a single mother who loses track of her son Callum at Atlantic Island Park, then loses track of her sanity in an exquisitely presented downward spiral of increasingly chaotic scenes, images, warbling music, and mementos from Lorraine's personal life.
Unfortunately, the fascinating artistic representations of the game's disjointed themes are the highlight of what is on offer. There is little in the way of interesting gameplay; the story's throughline bears references to The Secet World that can be safely ignored without significant loss of context or content, in large part because there is little among the insubstantial fragments provided that the audience can relate to as human beings.
I enjoyed the three hours I spent in The Park despite the expensive price tag and a plot trajectory with all the navigability of a silk web spun by a spider on cocaine, but I can't recommend it. Your money is better spent on an actual psychological horror thriller novel or a video game with the storytelling chops of What Remains of Edith Finch. Lorraine is a character driven by the plot, not the other way around, and like Lorraine, The Park stumbles about in the dark before coming to an abrupt, disquieting end.

Honestly Steam needs more than a yes/no option.
This game is great, some might even call it a masterpiece and i'd be hard pressed to disagree, hence the recommendation. You probably have enough people telling you the strong points about this game: the plot/ gameplay/ atmosphere/ aesthetics/ voice-acting etc. are all top-notch.
However... its a shoddy console port that has tonnes of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ issues related to UI and such. While I was fortunate enough to experience only a few less severe one (i managed to launch the game after all), it was still significant enough to hamper the experience, to the point where I was considering not recommending this game.
A list of problems:
1) Borderless Windowed mode does not exist, it takes a lot of manual configuring that I just couldn't be arsed to do, so I played in fullscreen, and as a result..
2) Alt tabbing is ♥♥♥♥ed up, sometimes it works fine though it feels jerky and slow every time, but other times the game crashes, or returns to the default smallest resolution in one corner of the screen needing a restart of the game to get it fullscreen again.
3) Speaking of crashes.... ♥♥♥♥ crashes really. Every single time the game crashes, all my settings in the options menu were completely reset to default, it has something to do with the game loading a separate ini file for first launch/crashes, but it was really annoying as ♥♥♥♥.
4) Terrible mouse acceleration/lag, you can (partially) fix this problem by tweaking the ini files a bit (google), AND DO NOT SET MOUSE SENSITIVITY TO 1, its bugged and ♥♥♥♥ed up, anything else is fine.
5) The plasmid controls reek of console port, there is ABSOLUTELY no way to configure which hotkey you want to assign a plasmid to, its just done for u at random every time you change/add a plasmid etc with no real pattern at all, it doesn't even follow the order you specified in the gene bank. This creates a♥♥♥♥♥♥tonne of confusion due to muscle memory working against you.
So all in all, i'm trying my best to provide the necessary information to anyone that reads this, in order that you can make an informed choice. Now that steam refunds are in place, i'd absolutely recommend giving this game a go and requesting a refund if the game gives you too many issues,

When I saw info for Reigns, my interest was immediately piqued. I expected a choose your own adventure game based around cards with numerous possibilities and in the loosest sense I guess it is.
You have some text, explaining the scenario and two options on how to handle it. There are four bars in the shape of an icon, like sword/money/food/etc, at the top which increase and/or decrease based on your choice. If one of them drops too low then it's game over.
I know the game needs mechanics beyond a choice of two options but this can be very frustrating:
* You're going to lose repeatedly and feel like there was nothing you could do to prevent it.
* Some choices feel out of touch with their consequences, why has person/sword decreased for me declining to a princess to build a bigger castle?
* Scenarios you're given seem completely random and what comes next after a choice usually has nothing to do with what you just picked
* You can also lose by filling a bar too much - have a full money bar? Apparently you had a feast and choked to death, every time.
* There's no story or character development
* Little depth as you realize the game is nothing more than picking things to stabilize four bars.
The presentation is lovely, the concept is great and I want to like the game more than I currently am. It's very cheap so you may want to give it a try - you'll definitely have a more positive experience if you go in with the mindset of this being resource management rather than meaningful choices.

The original is pretty fun. Really interesting game, scratches the "star wars galactic conquest" notion but there's some weird mechanics.
Hero units are ridiculously overpowered. Remember when Chewbacca and Han Solo killed a swarm of stormtroopers and ATSTs? Me neither.
During battles the defending base generates a free unit, and will regenerate the unit whenever it dies- giving the defender a suicide trooper to constantly use. You'll see this in the first battle-- xwings constantly flying to their deaths. Random troops constantly charging your ATST. The attacker brought 100 stormtroopers? Well, you're going to get a free unit every 10 seconds so send that SOB in. If the attacker doesn't rush you basically win. But then this gets ridiculous when you have a higher-end factory and you get a free tank squad constantly.
And then the expansion breaks the game. Red Alert 2: Yuri's Revenge was a great game. Yuri was pretty imbalanced but still beatable. In this, the "whatever they are/pirates" basically can cast spells to literally "take over entire system"-- and you're constantly "uh... why'd I just lose that system?"
And then they're on a different research tree. The Rebels and Empire research new/upgraded units and build those. The "pirates" research upgrades and then the units receive those benefits. Suddenly the 10 fighter swarms that die in seconds have shields and bombs and are decimating your forces. And the pirates are still dumping those level-1 units out for the same price.
Stick with the original. Or find a game with mods.

At its very least, Reigns is a charming, casual resource-managment game with cute visuals and funny dialogue.  At its best, Reign is a deceptively simple yet interesting puzzle in and of itself, as its seemingly-pointless central mechanic gives way to a meta-game that puts you up against a ticking clock.
Played strictly as a "king simulator," it can become tedious or frustrating over time, since most of the choices you make as a king end up feeling like they have no consequences or meaning, but as I mentioned, there are plenty of opportunities for the meta-game to capture your attention.
It's not as deep as some other games and it's not as long, but for a few dollars and a few hours of enjoyment, Reigns definitely gets my recommendation.

You are to gather Audience during each Episode (mission), so alongside trying to make sure you win (which on the medium difficulty I never felt too pressured about), you are also to coordinate team attacks and acrobatics, fulfilling the optional objectives of that mission, trying to get the last blow on the boss to be a Finishing Move, and whatever else will excite your audience, and thus gain you Fans and Money.  You can customize your super group down to their respective color themes, names, catch-phrases, and so forth.  The songs fit the mood of the moment splendidly, and I'll likely be buying the soundtrack later.
Seeing as I usually prefer more complexity to my RPG's, it's hard for me to indicate exactly what drove me to like this game as much as I did.  Maybe it was just fighting an obvious reference to Barnie to Dinosaur in my Mecha as we towered over the city, combo-ing fists and lasers before I miss and lose the initiative.  Maybe it was the progression of starting as a low-budget series fighting a guy with a traffic cone on his head, up to a full-fledged studio.  Maybe I'm just vain, and desire as many Fans as I can get by being Cool Guy in front of a camera, with a charisma and acting talent I could never attempt in real life.
The point is, I got genuinely excited during some of the pivotal battles in this game, and that's deserving of praise.

The Park had pretty good visuals, and an overall unsettling vibe. It's not necessarily super scary, but it doesn't use jumpscares and still manages to make you feel like there will be one around every corner. The story is okay, nothing too special, although my opinion of the protagonist shifted quite a bit during the short duration of this game. Towards the ending it had a really nice PT (silent hill) thing going on. I can't remember what I paid for this game, but I remember buying it on sale, and if it's around 5 dollars / euros / pounds and you're into psychological horror games (with a special fondness of creepy amusement parks) you should definitely buy it. There is no combat in this game, so if you're looking for a more action focused horror game this is not for you.

Let's get this out of the way:
The DLC optional skins amount to about $60. Then there's the season pass, and the cost of the core game. Should you be concerned? Probably not too much. It's a sad but increasingly common way of pushing AAA games out the door. Can you thoroughly enjoy the game at the base $60? Yes.
Let's talk about the actual game. It's an intense game of Hide N Seek with a graphically pleasing world.
Hunters offer enough variation within classes and characters to ensure that you actually feel at an advantage for having chosen Hank over, say, Bucket.
I personally don't put too much emphasis in story with multiplayer centric games, but the story of Shear is uncovered through snips of dialogue between characters. There's enough variation in conversation to keep things interesting, but you'll likely be more focused on chasing down the monster.
The game's lesser known mode Evacuation plays out like a mini-campaign and ought to have been in the limelight.
5 Days, with each day offering players to vote between two modes for that day. If the monster wins, an effect will occur in favor of the monster for the next day. If the hunters win, they might score an advantage like medical stations, teleportation gates, or hardy turrets for the next map.
Should either side win consecutively, a boon is given to the losing team. This acts like a check against higher skilled opposition, but isn't enough to guarentee a loss. At the end of the day, the figurative people saved / killed during the Campaign grants experience. During each day, a cinematic unfolds explaining the consequence of your winning or losing, and there's a lot of variation to be found here to keep the game interesting.
I've only a couple of times ran into performance bugs or getting caught on terrain. It hasn't been enough to affect my gameplay whatsoever, so I'm omitting it. While it might not run great on all computers, it runs well on my GeForce GTX 780 Ti with a few tweaks for higher framerate.
Although I felt overpowered as the monster during the alpha and beta tests, I felt adequately challenged during release. On either side, I never felt like the game was giving me a victory, I had to earn it.
Progression to unlock some new characters can seem bogged down compared to other classes, and the unlockable perks as you level do grant you significant advantages depending on your play style. Each of the new maps made available on release are extremely well crafted, and offer many positions that are to the benefit of the hunter or monster at all stages and modes.
I also haven't played this game on release with friends, so my experiences are either solo as the monster or with a public group with the hunters. Even with that, I still found it balanced out nicely. I like it, and I think you will too. Set aside the panic of the DLC long enough to try the base game and there's a gem of entertainment to be had.

Kurt Vonnegut said that anyone who has attacked a piece of written work with genuine loathing is being ridiculous, that they are behaving as someone who has "put on full armor and attacked a hot fudge sundae".
What I'm about to do is kind of like that, but imagine me duct taping pink polyester all over my body and wandering into a public park to hunt down an anthropomorphic version of a video game called Chroma Squad, a tiny freckly kid with jubilantly blue eyes, offering me an ice cream cone, his diminutive hands aquiver with timid goodwill. I will proceed to karate kick that child in the face, and as he reaches for the ice cream again (mint chocolate drizzled with galaxies of cake sprinkles), I will remove my plastic helmet to let him gaze on my dreadfully expressionless face as I level a long gentle stare into his brilliant, innocent eyes, grinding his delicious confection into the pea gravel with the heel of a nylon boot.
I came to Chroma Squad for obvious reasons. Chroma Squad begins with what we are to take as the stunt actors from the actual Power Rangers set staging a revolt and opening their own studio to shoot their own martial arts children's show, or in other words, to do everything exactly as before but with a rigorous simulation of creative control. The thing that really drew me to it, though, was the rumor that it was a Final Fantasy Tactics-esque Tactical RPG with a splash of XCOM flavor, full of cheek and wit and heart-warming hilarity to bring home to the whole family.
I'm going to have a total XCOM-snob conniption right now, so be sure to click the 'not helpful' button if those words don't mean anything to you at all. This game's combat is wearing tactical RPG clothes for what appears to be no reason apart from the fun of having made a game that aesthetically resembles a turn-based tactical RPG ala Disgaea or FF Tactics. Battles are much more comparable, however, to those of Diablo or Torchlight, in which you click somewhere on the screen, your little fellows amble (or here, cartwheel and cheer-lift one another) in a direction, swing their fists around, and that's it. This, of course, places Chroma Squad on the tactical combat spectrum nearest to "something you idly click through."
It's all about positioning your team just right so they can perform the same finishing move again. And again. And again. All for the entertainment of the type of children Chroma Squad must think we all were at a certain age: the kid who got up early every Saturday morning to sit at the TV with eyes pressed directly to the glass. Combat is shockingly boring, special abilities don't really synchronize, and there's basically no reason to attempt to play "tactically," because the experience is much closer to being babysat by a kind teenager who thinks she's way cooler than she is. You are given a laundry list each mission of little hoops to jump through, such as "defeat 3 enemies in the same turn," "keep all your heroes alive," or "attempt to figure out how to do that same team attack again," but all of these come off as suggestions on the level with "wouldn't it be really cool if you brushed your teeth and went to bed at exactly 8 PM per your parents' instructions? We're really on the same side here."
I found myself cranking the difficulty down from its highest setting midway through, not because I felt particularly challenged, but because I just couldn't bear the thought of spending more time seeing this thing through than I had to. Yes, sometimes you'll get so bored watching each reskinned enemy type spawn in one-at-a-time and run into positions that will have no effect on how you'll fight that you phase back into paying attention to learn that your healer is dead, and things get a little bit tricky. Then you can halfheartedly attempt to survive the mission or suffer some consequences featuring a number that represents your supposed fans, who have opted, instead of watching your onscreen incompetence, to get stoned and watch Godzilla vs Megalon again, which is about 1/4 as stoned as I'd need to be to enjoy this game or find it compellingly difficult, a state of I mind imagine as a hypothetical level of brain-myopia in which I lose the ability to read or control my bowels.
What you'll never see in Chroma Squad, at any rate, is any indication that the AI knows that it's supposed to try to win. Chroma Squad is every bit the tactical RPG that Battletoads & Double Dragon was way back when.
The game's interface is by far the worst enemy--not much is communicated clearly, and features stand a very real chance of remaining hidden in plain sight well into late game. The explanations of some abilities don't make sense--one has you dealing damage to enemies along your traveled path, but the ability doesn't path through enemies, so I never figured out what the hell that ability is supposed to be doing.
One could argue the game is challenging given that you'll feel underpowered most of the time. But I'll counter that by saying that making a sloppy, unresponsive mess of a studio management screen does not tactical gameplay make. Your resource management screen seems wilfully designed to confuse you--you'll spend money in an attempt to get at least one aspect of your television enterprise functioning competently, but little seems to help. You cannot sell equipment and are instead forced to reduce items to scrap materials you'll probably never use. Everything is a one-way street to a sort of long suffering.
Somehow, the novelty of the game's customization options wears off extremely fast, and even turning your heroes' "morphin time" catchphrase to HAIL SATAN fails to drum up much enthusiasm when you know more deadening combat is coming.
THAT'S THE WHOLE JOKE, you say. It's all LOW RENT and also DID YOU NOTICE that EVERYTHING IS A REFERENCE. Yeah. And it's extremely hilarious or something. Don't get me wrong, there are some sensible chuckles strung throughout in the form of a draconian director barking Backstreet Boys lyrics as stage prompts, an anonymous "biggest fan" innocently emailing the studio to ask if Halliburton had any involvement in the design of the Megazord, or the sudden run-in with the star of Colin's Bear Animation, who unaccountably transforms into a send-up of Yakra and Heckran from Chrono Trigger.
But when I start to sense that the game's wit is wringing itself raw with the exertion of transmuting "Nick Fury" to "Rick Anger", or naming a large sentient iPod enemy DOPi, or reaching -just- -one- -more- -time- for another Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles shoutout, I start experimenting with how much mileage I can get out of the handy fast-forwarding key. I swear to god, nothing tells me more about how quick this game's lights and camera went up around its ramshackle production than having a character recite the Taken monologue verbatim and the villain responding with "Hey Sentai fans, did you catch that that comes from somewhere else? Thanks so much for playing our game, guys, and HEY MACARENA, AHA."
Best of all, I watched the everloving♥♥♥♥♥♥out of Power Rangers as a kid and got into my share of schoolyard trouble for it, and I don't know if it's me or the developers of this game who are supposed to be more♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off that the fact alone does not make this game good. It is all heart, goddamn it, all heart through and through, stuffed with beautiful art and infectious music, and for all those elements I will certainly place a crisp gold star at the top of this game's construction paper project plastered with hot glue and macaroni.
Pure flavor, bad content, like a Fruit Roll-Up or a new season of Full House. Buy it as cheap as you can.

Really compelling game about ruling over a kingdom, and essentially playing a grand balancing game, with a two-choice system of picking outcomes. Every time you die, you start playing again as the succeeding king, and this goes on ad infinitum, so far as I've played, but this never really gets to be annoying, in fact, I always felt the urge to play another 'round' of the game, if you will.
The characters, albeit quite simple, are compelling, and along with the surprisingly robust world building the game preforms, makes for a kingdom you actually care about ruling properly, and in my own experience, I always wanted to get better; I wanted to be BETTER than the previous generation's king, and I wanted to do the tasks set out by the game.
This is all made far easier to digest and appreciate by the game's simple and unique art styles, consisting primarily of colorful geometric shapes used in unison to form the characters and scenery of the game. It's really memorable, and I always find myself remembering the characters I've seen before BECAUSE of just how unique they look (Like ♥♥♥♥ing hell I can remember any of the names, though)
I can't honestly level any criticism at the game. I guess any would-be critique of the game would come down to personal grievances with it, and that's fair, but I dont have any of my own. The games sets out to do what it does and it does that well.
This game, in all its simplicity and almost utter practicality, manages to be a memorable, enjoyable title, that's worth so much more than its minute asking price. I'd highly reccomend this to anyone; It's the kind of experience you won't find elsewhere, I'd wager, and again, the game's price is definitely a positive in this regard.
So uh, yeah, it's alright.

While I love everything about the game and the nostalgia it's bringing me, the fact that the thing continiously crashes on me is really bringing me to stop trying with it.
The graphics look bad? That's not my issue, graphics don't matter if a game is good or bad.
Clipping? Meh, not really bothered by it.
Constant crashing for no apparent reason within 15 minutes of starting the game up?
That's just me being unable to enjoy the game. And until that's fixed, thumbs down.
And of course it's not the game, it's my computer. Mine and plenty of others having this issue, who have attacked the problem as a community to try and fix just what's going on, but nothing seems to work.
EDIT: So the reason for the crashing isn't the game, nor is it my computer. Or maybe it is.
It's a conflict between the controller, the game, and Steam Overlay.
Deleating GameOverlayRenderer64.dll actually ended up fixing all my issues, and then some.
So now I can give this a thumbs up and play for more than 20 minutes without crashing. Huzzah.

Lyne is a very satisfying puzzler game.  The game, effectively, is to find a route through all the nodes on a grid, such that "router" nodes are used the stipulated number of times.   Colourful, relaxing, and very very satisfying.
Most levels have multiple solutions, which grants a very rewarding gameplay.  Most of the levels can be solved with about 10 seconds of observation, and about 5 seconds of swiping.  There are some, however, which require far more consideration.  The longest I spent was about half an hour trying and re-trying paths through the level, until I ended up giving up and cheating, using a hint online.    Other than that one slip, the rest of the game was quite solvable with patience.
Perfectly suited to casual gaming, I left the game minimized, until my tea breaks, when I'd do a level or two.    There are hundreds and hundreds of levels, and with daily levels offering a "quick fix", there's a lot of enjoyment packed into this little puzzler.
Highly recommended for anyone who likes things like Sudoku, or quick crosswords.. i.e. that short, quick puzzle fix.
