Outlast is, in my personal opinion, a good game. It definitely has some flaws (as all games do), but I don't think they truly ruin the experience.
PROS: Outlast is pretty scary. You will constantly be scared and spooked out of your mind. The story is, contrary to popular belief, not that bad. I thought it was pretty interesting, but I guess some other players might not agree. It's mysterious and a little weird, which fits Outlast rather well. The chase scenes can be spooky, but are a little repetitive. I like all the characters and, when you learn their backstories, it's even scarier. Overall, Outlast does a lot of things right and the locations and characters are pretty scary and well done.
CONS: The chase scenes can be, as I said before, a little repetitive. They start out pretty scary but later just become annoying. Chris, a spoopy fat guy who chases you around, starts out pretty scary. You'll run from him with tears in your eyes, screaming, "OH NO! I'M NOT READY TO DIE!" The developers, however, end up using his character too much in the game. His scenes end up feeling like annoying and cheap ways to scare the player. Apart from the enemies, I was a little confused sometimes in the game. I'm not very great at video games, so maybe that's my fault, but I was a little lost at times. Luckily, I had my friend with me (who memorized everything in Outast, for some reason), so he was able to guide me.
Overall...
Outlast is a good game. I would definitely recommend it to anyone looking for some scares. Some scenes aren't as great and are presented poorly, but Outlast makes up for those scenes with scenes that are legitimately scary and spoopy. The characters are pretty great and the story is interesting. This game isn't worth twenty dollars, so wait for a sale. I would recommend getting it for five dollars or, at the most, ten dollars. It's short, but thrilling and occasionally horrifying.
8/10, would recommend.

The original is pretty fun. Really interesting game, scratches the "star wars galactic conquest" notion but there's some weird mechanics.
Hero units are ridiculously overpowered. Remember when Chewbacca and Han Solo killed a swarm of stormtroopers and ATSTs? Me neither.
During battles the defending base generates a free unit, and will regenerate the unit whenever it dies- giving the defender a suicide trooper to constantly use. You'll see this in the first battle-- xwings constantly flying to their deaths. Random troops constantly charging your ATST. The attacker brought 100 stormtroopers? Well, you're going to get a free unit every 10 seconds so send that SOB in. If the attacker doesn't rush you basically win. But then this gets ridiculous when you have a higher-end factory and you get a free tank squad constantly.
And then the expansion breaks the game. Red Alert 2: Yuri's Revenge was a great game. Yuri was pretty imbalanced but still beatable. In this, the "whatever they are/pirates" basically can cast spells to literally "take over entire system"-- and you're constantly "uh... why'd I just lose that system?"
And then they're on a different research tree. The Rebels and Empire research new/upgraded units and build those. The "pirates" research upgrades and then the units receive those benefits. Suddenly the 10 fighter swarms that die in seconds have shields and bombs and are decimating your forces. And the pirates are still dumping those level-1 units out for the same price.
Stick with the original. Or find a game with mods.

A brilliant Concept:
Permadeath Survival in a beautiful DX11 Environment on the Unity Engine!
2019 - A geothermal Disaster made you one of the last Survivors in Canadas Outback during Winter.
-Massive Exploration combined with an infinite Replay Value due to random Starting Points on many different Region Maps (which are linked by Tunnels, Mines and other Gateways inside this Game, so you are able to wander all the Regions in one Playthrough).
-Random Loot Appearance, random frozen Corpses, random Animal Placement at the Start of every new Game! Infinite Replay Value!
-Deeply immersive Surround Sound!
-Many Difficulty Settings, so you are able to play this Single-Player Experience your way.
-A Sandbox Mode to dive into the Game, a Story Mode and several totally different Challenge Modes to play the Game endlessly.
In those Challenge Modes the Game changes to a totally different Experience: Be hunted by a HUGE Bear and try to reach the Trappers Outpost to get a special Rifle, before this Being can find you on the large Maps.... or... try to survive the coming Blizzard of the Century by gathering as much Ressources as you can! You only got 30 Days for that!... and many more of these quest-like Game Enhancements!
-No Aliens, Russians (no offense XD) or Nazi Zombies but starving Wolves, Cougars and aggressive Bears!
Those "Enemies" got a beautiful and complex AI Behaviour and will not just simply attack you on Sight. It all depends on your Difficulty Settings and your Movement ingame. Tools and Weapons will also change your Experience with them, the Hunter can easily become the Hunted! (Which counts for both Sides: The AI and your Character itself!)
But the real Enemy is your own Player Character:
-The cold Weather, which can change in an instant during your Travels, can easily kill you! Stay warm by using Fires, Shelters you are building out of Snow and Ice or hide some Hours inside an abandoned House.
-Calories are a large Factor of Survival! You got to hunt, gather and cook to stay alive!
-Gather and maintain your Survival Gear!... but also consider the Weight of every Item!
-Fight Infections, broken Wrists, craft Bandages for your Wounds... the Number of Things which can happen is nearly endless. No HP Regeneration a la CoD! XD
Rating: Minus 20 out of Minus 10 - The next Blizzard will freeze your dead Body to the Ground!

This is a great game for strategy fans, the fact it's Star Wars is just gravy. It's very similar in ways to Space 4X games, like Endless Space. Of course it's not that deep, but Empire at War is a nice mix of RTS and 4X. You Start out on the Galactic Map in most cases, in which there are numerous planets, each producing a certain amount of Credits, this games only resource/currency. You use Credits to purchase buildings on the planets you control, and Space Station upgrades once you purchase a Space Station in Orbit around the planet. You then build/recruit land units like tanks and infantry, or build spaceships ranging from small Fighter Ships, to large Capital Ships. You can create fleets containing Ships meant for battle, or just transport ships to carry troops. You can keep troops on your Battle ships, but I find it better to send the fighting ships first, THEN send the transports to take control of the ground.
One thing I like is that in ground battles, you can only bring the units you had brought with you beforehand, and not magically drag them out of you♥♥♥♥♥like most RTS games. The only exception to this is the Skirmish game mode, which tries to make itself more similar to traditional RTS games.
Another thing I like is that at the start of the battle, only a handful of units are on the battlefield. To bring in reinforcements, you must capture Reinforcement points, which will allow you to bring in more of your troops from orbit. If you have any that is. Normally for the defenders, they're stuck with what they had on the planet at the time, since in order to engage in ground combat, you must first clear out the Space around it. Not always though, as it's possible to sneak past the Orbital Defenses in certain instances.
Space battles are similar in mechanics, except that(don't quote me on this yet) you aren't restricted to dropping(flying?) in reinforcements into Reinforcement Points. I'm still not very well versed in space battles yet, though. I've mostly played the tutorials and mostly ground combat in the campaign, and haven't done space battles as much. They're gorgeous though.
Also, In space battles, the larger ships have whats called 'hardpoints', where you can target these smaller areas to disable/hamper the ships shields/weapons/etc.
Both land and space have a decent amount of units, however it's not as high as some RTS games.
All in all, I definately recommend this to any Strategy, RTS, or Star Wars fan. Especially if you're any combination of those three.

TL;DR: Mediocre MMO, but the nostalgia's still nice for those who played RÖ1. Better with friends, boring alone.
As a MMO, RÖ2 is below average, quality-wise. Some might chalk it up by saying it's Free2Play, but I've played better F2P MMOs before; RÖ2 gives an aftertaste of unfinished game, a Forever Beta whose developpers bit more than they could chew. The character design isn't particularly original, and the voices are standard. The graphics are okay at first, but get rather dull after the tenth hour. However sometimes you will stumble upon a beautiful scenery (and sometimes, stumble through), but it's not often enough to make it acceptable. The gameplay is entirely standard; the good thing is that you won't be lost with the controls, but if you were looking for something original/different: look somewhere else. As for the story, it isn't grandiose, but if you played the first game, you might like some elements of it.
One big issue in the game, that I hinted at earlier, is how buggy it is, and how little the GM support is. In all the time I played, I managed to contact a GM only once, and managed to get stuck in [trees, houses, mountains, invisible rocks, broken stairs, dunes, out of bound, water, wall, boat, ...] more times than I can count. In one occurence, I got stuck in a mountain; when trying to use a move skill to get out, I warped through the map, fell under it and stayed stuck. When I logged out and back in, I was 3 zones ahead, monsters were 10+ levels above me. Another time, I simply swum my way out of the map, then fell again; same scenario. Although it was hilarious when it was discovered, this kind of bug quickly grew annoying.
That being said, if you've played RÖ1 before, and have some friends who did too, you might want to give it a try; despite everything, it's still fun to play it with friends, even if only halfway through.

Perhaps the last old skool RPG in the spirit of Ultima Underworld and others where there is little to none hand helding. If you don't find that crucial small non-blinking key from those messy grey-toned textures then its too bad, your quest stops there. There is no arrows to point you to right direction, automap is rudimentary and doesn't log places, log book only logs quests at a very high level, and if you miss that important line from cutscene, you don't know what to do next. So pay attention, and use your brains. There are somewhat nasty puzzes here and there but most of them are quite logical and solveable without going to walktrough. I admit I had to use walktrough in a couple of tight spots, but only after wandering around all places and ticked all objects few times over. The level of difficulty is just right.
Graphics are a bit dated today (reShade recommended) but the game is still very athmosperic and textures and lighting are really well made. Ambient music is unique and fits the style. Level design is excellent, and what I especially like is that the areas are not open like in Elder Scrolls and such where you wander around endlessly spending hundreds of hours. I don't have so much time to waste so the length of the game was appropriate to me unlike many other modern games. Just give me 10-50 hours of excellent and well thought single player game and I'm in. Game contains lots of hidden areas and items so it is replayable too. Only real gripe I had was the user interface which is a bit crappy at modern standards but I eventually got used to it. Never learned the spells by hart. thought
Highly recommended and unique gem for those who seek well made RPGs with old school feel and gameplay. Just one question, where is the sequel / remake?

TL;DR: I felt The Park captures the atmosphere of a cursed Amusement Park really well and delivers multiple scares in the process. However, multiple stories in the game with only loose ties to each other resulted in a somewhat ambiguous narrative.
I thought The Park did a really good job of capturing the atmosphere of a decrepit, cursed park, and the horror elements reminded me of going to a haunted house or Knott’s Scary Farm. In many ways it felt like a cross between Donny Darko and Eternal Darkness. There were definitely moments where I screamed out loud (stupid chipmunk) or got the chills (tall-man), so I appreciated the game for effectively conveying a creepy setting.
I found the history of the park and the backstory of Mr. Winter compelling, however, that story doesn’t seem to get fully explored and seems to be dropped towards the end to focus on Lorraine’s story.
In regards to Lorraine and Callum, I was initially compelled by the story of a mother chasing her son into a haunted park. Why is this park haunted? How am I going to catch Callum? What else is in here that’s going to prevent me from finding him? While I found the supernatural aspects of the park creepy, I felt like they jumped into the “single mom is going crazy” storyline too quickly. I would have appreciated a little bit more of a slow burn in that respect.

This game feels Kickstarted as all hell.
The mass-appeal and cheap pixel art aesthetic, the barebones gameplay, the stupid pop culture references in lieu of humor, everything points to Kickstarter. Most damning of all is the numerous systems and mechanics that were obviously bullet points on a pitch list first, and fully fleshed out or interesting ideas second. There's crafting, but it's really simplistic and boring. Ditto the teamwork system, the fans/money interactions, and just the combat in general. This game could really have stood a few more (6+) months in the oven, because it's not truly bad, but it's definitely not living up to its potential.

Really compelling game about ruling over a kingdom, and essentially playing a grand balancing game, with a two-choice system of picking outcomes. Every time you die, you start playing again as the succeeding king, and this goes on ad infinitum, so far as I've played, but this never really gets to be annoying, in fact, I always felt the urge to play another 'round' of the game, if you will.
The characters, albeit quite simple, are compelling, and along with the surprisingly robust world building the game preforms, makes for a kingdom you actually care about ruling properly, and in my own experience, I always wanted to get better; I wanted to be BETTER than the previous generation's king, and I wanted to do the tasks set out by the game.
This is all made far easier to digest and appreciate by the game's simple and unique art styles, consisting primarily of colorful geometric shapes used in unison to form the characters and scenery of the game. It's really memorable, and I always find myself remembering the characters I've seen before BECAUSE of just how unique they look (Like ♥♥♥♥ing hell I can remember any of the names, though)
I can't honestly level any criticism at the game. I guess any would-be critique of the game would come down to personal grievances with it, and that's fair, but I dont have any of my own. The games sets out to do what it does and it does that well.
This game, in all its simplicity and almost utter practicality, manages to be a memorable, enjoyable title, that's worth so much more than its minute asking price. I'd highly reccomend this to anyone; It's the kind of experience you won't find elsewhere, I'd wager, and again, the game's price is definitely a positive in this regard.

The pros:
The game is quite fun and very addictive. It's a strategy RPG with a unique concept that is pulled off extremely well. It's the perfect application of crafting mechanics, too. The graphics are beautiful, and the music is impressively good. The concept of going from small-time to big time is a brilliant idea for a game of this manner.
There is a lot of attention to detail in the game, with secret things to find both graphically and plot wise. It's easily worth the MSRP, and is one of those things you don't know you want until you have played it for yourself.
Protip: Don't try hard mode on your first playthrough. It's really unbalanced hard.
The cons:
The programming is so glitchy the game feels like a beta version. The textboxes overflow when people are talking and transitions are often jarringly abrupt, just cutting out and flickering when a level ends instead of having a proper "you win" screen. The controller controls need major work as they just operate the mouse cursor instead of having true controller support.
The writing is mediocre, with very poor grammar that could have used major proofreading. Some of the scenarios are sort of nonsensical due to the writing. The appearances of numerous Kickstarter backers break the immersion of the game, it would have been better if they didn't have to awkwardly say their full names every time someone appeared. The backer characters all look like the same nerdy white guys, and dont make sense in the setting.
With the lack of characterization you'd think there'd be some kind of character creation for your team, but instead there is very little in the way of choice if you want a decent team, I wish you could choose from more diverse appearances and just assign certain personalities to them, instead there are kind of obvious "best characters", so if you didn't want a cartoon beaver on your team youre flat out of luck.

A pretty fun,cheap and charming pick your own adventure game where you play as a king that keeps getting reincarnated after each death as the next king of the land, stuck in an endless cycle of rulling the land and getting murdered in various ways.
In Reigns you're trying to balance the happines of your people,the church, the military and your own finances via a simple two choice option system that gets present to you by your advisers. If one of the bars gets full or empty, you're done. If the military is not in good shape you get invaded and murdered but if the military is too strong your own general will start a coup and take over while you rot in a dungeon.
So, enjoy getting locked up in prison by your own milittary due to a coup, choking to death due to eating too much expensive food, getting butched by regilious nuts job and having Satan as a dog .
It's just 3$ and it's completely worth it, great way to kill a bit of time while waiting for something, in-between other games or when you're just feeling bored and don't know what else to do.

Damn... what an experience.
At first, I thought this game was just a collection of really interesting, thought provoking games. Like the one where you can only walk backwards. It really got me thinking about what it could mean. All of the games were really unique and just... odd. They were so different and interesting, and I absolutely LOVE games like that.
But then it started to get more interesting (stop reading now if you don't want to see spoilers. I HIGHLY recommend playing this for yourself first). The games felt very lonely and just kind of... hopeless. I felt really similar to how Davey felt, just so worried about Coda and thinking about the depression he must've been going through while making these games, and I was just so scared for him, and I felt so helpless knowing there was literally nothing I can do to help this person.
When I saw Coda's message to Davey, I started crying. I realized that every time Coda said something about how he needed to make games for people, he was probably talking about needing to make games for Davey, so Davey could enjoy them and feel good about himself when he shared them with people. He had to keep making games for Davey and he felt like he would hurt him if he didn't (At least that was my interpretation. I don't actually know how Coda felt). God  damn it must've been so hard to loose a friend that way, being directly told that HE was the reason he struggled so much. And hearing Davey talking directly to Coda... god my heart just broke.
I don't know if it was a good idea for Davey to publish this game for everyone to see, especially since HE'S making the money for the games CODA made. I honestly feel kind of bad for playing them. Coda didn't want anyone to see these, and I voilated his privacy by playing them. But at the same time, it was such a powerful and moving experience that I never would've had if he didn't.
This game is truly unique, because the characters are REAL. Every so often I had to remind myself that these were REAL people and these were their REAL stories, not just a fictional story with actors. Knowing that fact made the experience so much more powerful.
I hope Coda's okay. I wonder if he's seen this game, and what he thinks of it. I hope he's not upset that people played it. I hope I didn't violate his privacy.

Outrun an enemy and hide in a locker? The enemy will look around for 30 seconds then open the locker beside you, same with hiding under beds. While this is fun for a few segments (like evading the wandering doctor) it grows old, especially when paired with the few large pitch black areas that make navigation very frusturating. Despite the repetitive nature of the gameplay I was pretty impressed by it, and think most horror fans would enjoy the journey if you can look past the repetition. 7/10

How to Accept Your Autism
Being autistic can be rough. People tell you that you're embarrassing, that you're rude or insensitive, or that you're a puzzle that needs to be completed in order to be whole. But that doesn't mean that they're right. This article will help you come to terms with your autism so you can focus on being the wonderful human being that you are.
Meet the autistic community. This can be done by contacting a friendly support group, or through a search online. Learn what autistic people have to say about themselves, their symptoms, and the way they interact with the world. Autistic people in general are very welcoming to newly-diagnosed or self-diagnosed people.
Autistic people can offer advice and tips to those in need (and often do so, especially online)
The general positivity of the autism community can help you feel better when you are feeling sad or have low self-esteem.
Read about the strengths that come along with autism. Autism is a complex neurological condition that comes with several blessings along with its impairments:
Deeply passionate interests. These can lead to tremendous expertise, and a very successful career.[1]
Helpfulness. Autistic people in general have a high sense of social responsibility, or the desire to solve problems and help others.[2]
Precision. Autism is often noted to lead to focusing on small parts, rather than the big picture. This can lead to remarkable detail-oriented work, where a neurotypical might be unable to focus so clearly on individual aspects of something.[3]
Visual intelligence. Autistic people have tested higher on visual and nonverbal intelligence tests.[4]
Sincerity. Autistic people tend to mean what they say, and act as a "voice of reason" without becoming mired in social complexities.[5] Your honesty and genuine spirit can feel refreshing to others.
A unique perspective. Autistic people can learn in unusual ways.[6] This provides insights that neurotypicals may never realize, and can become a great asset in collaboration.
Find therapies and treatments that work for you. These will help you work on your weaknesses so that you feel more comfortable and happy. You can also learn coping mechanisms, alternative methods of doing difficult tasks, and how to capitalize on your strengths.
Options include sensory integration therapy, seeing an autism expert (for coping strategies), occupational therapy, special diets in case you are allergic or sensitive to something, behavior therapy, and seeing a psychologist for emotional issues.
Always check with a doctor before altering your diet or attempting an alternative treatment.
Be careful about behavior therapies. Some therapies are based on compliance and may hurt more than helping.[7] If your therapist's goal is to make you more normal (rather than more comfortable or more competent), or if you feel upset and anxious about seeing them, then find a better therapist.
Make autistic friends. Along with the usual benefits of friendship, you can share coping strategies, discuss autism together, and be yourselves without any fear of repercussions.
Read about successful autistic people. Plenty of famous people have been diagnosed or thought to be autistic.
Historically, Einstein,[8] Thomas Jefferson, Emily Dickinson,[9] Mozart,[10] and more people were thought to be autistic.[11]
Famous autistic people today include Tim Burton,[12] Susan Boyle,[13] Adam Young (from Owl City),[14] Jerry Seinfeld,[15] and more.[16]
Focus on your skills and character strengths. This will help you spend less energy mourning your disability, and more energy on doing positive things and enjoying your life.
Spend time on your hobbies and things that you're good at. Enjoy the feeling of competence and expertise.
Make a list of your positive traits. Consider both personality traits and skills. Place the list somewhere where it'll be easy to see when you're feeling sad about yourself.
Help other people. Prepare food for the hungry, raise awareness for important causes, or volunteer for online projects like wikiHow. Effecting a positive change in the world will distract you, help others, and make you feel happier about yourself.
Avoid people and organizations that dehumanize you. You are not broken or lesser. People like you do not deserve to be abused, coerced, silenced, or eugenically aborted.
It is okay to cut toxic people out of your life. You don't need their negativity, and you're much better off without them. You are not required to argue that your existence is worthwhile, and it's okay to decide not to waste your time and energy on them.
If you're stuck with these people, you have two main choices: to educate them, or to avoid them. Educating them can be done by showing them an article, and making an appeal to their desire to be a good person. If you try this and fail, or if you know that they won't respond to reason, it's better to avoid spending time with them, and avoid autism-related conversations. You don't deserve to listen to toxic ideas about your existence.
Practice self-care. Being disabled can be difficult, and it's important to treat yourself well. Cut out energy drains from your life so you can focus on what matters most to you.
Pushing yourself to meet neurotypical standards will only take a toll on your health. It is okay to ask for academic accommodations, take extra breaks, or quit doing things that are too stressful to achieve.
Pay extra attention to general health advice: sleep for at least 8 hours, eat fruits and vegetables, limit junk food, minimize stress, and exercise regularly (taking walks counts). Self-care is extra important for you, to mitigate stress and help with meltdowns.
If you have trouble with self-care, it's okay to ask for help. Assisted living, a group home, or living with your parents might be better for you. Talk with a doctor, social worker, or therapist if you're struggling. There's no shame in meeting your needs, and it'll free up time for things you love.
Stop apologizing for being autistic. You have the right to ask for accommodations, stim in public, and do what you need to do in order to function. Toning down your behavior is your choice—not something to be pushed or coerced out of you. You are not required to act more neurotypical just because everyone else is used to it.
Get involved with positive autism-related organizations. They will help you understand yourself better and make a positive contribution to the world.
Many autism self-advocacy groups have a large online presence. You do not need to physically go somewhere in order to get involved.
Recognize that autism is just a thing of your imagination. People can not love you and your autism. You are a lesser person for it.

There's an awful lot of nonsense being said about this game - which is a pity, because it's actually quite fun.
I'll begin by answering a few criticisms I've seen which are flat wrong: I don't know if this will change anyone's minds - I hope it will - but surely it's better to have the proper info.
1) Yes - there's day one DLC. That is pretty sucky. I'll get over it. The stuff currently avalible is all skins - with no gameplay effect. Yeah - if you want the prettiest monster or a multicoloured gun it's going to cost you. They are selling the first four expansion characters too - or the first six if you get their super-mega-ultra-hunter-death-crazy game edition. But they're not avalible right now, ergo they're not day one DLC. If I stopped buying games that have a season-pass for sale on release, I'd pretty much stop buying AAA games. That's also pretty sucky.
2) 'There are only two game modes': Completely False. There are four game-modes - not two. Hunt, Rescue, Nest, and Defend. It's a little annoying that they've provided a random queue for 'Hunt' and the 'Evacuation' campaign (which combines all four modes in the format 2 hunt/2 rescue or nest/1 defend) - and not, specifically, queues the other two, but they are in there and you can play them in Evacuation or Custom Games.
3) You start with one character of each class, and one monster - and can buy another one. Technically True: but misleading. You do start with one (the easiest one from each class) UNLOCKED but you can pretty quickly unlock the other two characters for each class and the other two monsters to end up with three for each, plus three monsters WITHOUT PAYING ANYTHING. Heck, you can do it quickly in one-player mode in one sitting, and then the unlocked stuff will carry over to online play. It's not as bad as 'you get one, and can buy one more' - it's actually 'you start with three and can buy one more'.
4) It has a 5-mission campaign that can be completed in an hour. Technically True: but misleading. It doesn't have 'a 5-mission campaign'. It has 14 possible missions (by which I mean a small story attached to each map which changes slightly due to the game mode), of which 5 random missions are made into a campaign based upon what the players vote to play. Each has a different win/loss event which makes things different on the following map depending on who won. I've played at least half-a-dozen of these, and have never played the same 'set' - and if I did, the win/loss effects would make it different.
What do I think: It's not perfect - but after 12 hours, it's still really good fun and I don't think I've fully explored half of the classes I've got.  I'm proably going to hit 30 hours which makes it pretty good value for money in my eyes.
It's doing somthing new with the FPS deathmatch framework, and has done it well and introduced somthing genuinely entertaining that I've not seen before - and for that alone I'd reccomend giving it a go.
The Evacuation missions are a genuine unexpected treat - it's great to see somthing genuinely innovative being introduced and explored beyond the new '1v4 mechanism'.
I wholeheartedly reccomend it.

A great, and more modern take on the Ultima Underworld formula.  Really draws you in. I love that they merged the real time combat with the classic dungeon crawler cursor movement.  Because of this we get this awesome mishmash Action/Puzzle RPG. You can cast spells by drawing symbols with your mouse, slash your weapons in real time, drag and pick up objects, drop food by a fire to cook it up, solve object oriented puzzles, etc.  It really scratches the itch for a methodical, slow paced first person dungeon crawler, but with fast paced action combat.
For me, Arx Fatalis is right up there with the likes of Thief: The Dark Project & Thief 2, System Shock, and the original Deus Ex.  Dated or not, it's still a fantastic and immersive first person RPG, and it's still much better than the games that came after it in the same vein like Dark Messiah of Might & Magic.

Starts strong, with an amusing story and good base mechanics.  By season 3 or 4, the scarcity of new and interesting mechanics turns the combat into a dull grind, full of reskinned enemies that you've fought again and again and again.
I played through the end of season 4, on the highest difficulty.  The game balance seemed reasonable but not overly challenging at first, but by the end, it felt like I was constantly underlevelled and underequipped.  Even though the game has no concept of experience (season number does function as a sort of "level") and my gear was the best on offfer.
As a result, the game became a tedious slog of repeatedly sending 2-3 people after each enemy (for multiple turns, if it was the defensive type), keeping everyone's health up, and the occasional weird "because the director told me so" goal to get more audience.  The strategy varied *slightly* depending on the exact configuration of enemies, whether you could hit a few with an AOE, and if there was a boss.  For bosses, the standard procedure was to ignore them until you killed the enemies, then repeatedly wail on them with 2-3 people and heal up from their inevitable "knock one or all nearby people back, move, attack again" attack pattern.  And with a boss in most episodes (stages), even that became completely routine.
The end boss of season 4 was particularly dull.  Every few turns, he summons two enemy-summoning portals.  The portals have about as much health and defense as a normal enemy, and they spawn an enemy every turn (except the turn when they are spawned).  So you spend half or more of your time cleaning up the portals, rather than handling the boss.  The boss also has an assistant, who (for plot reasons) the game suggests not killing.  The assistant heals the boss periodically.  I ended up killing the assistant eventually, because it was taking far, far too long to win when I kept having to go kill portals and watch the boss get healed.  I had even tried letting the portals spawn for a few turns and just focusing on the boss, but had to regroup and clear them out, as the ever-spawning enemies were threatening to overwhelm me.
The mech battles similarly stagnate.  The first one is neat, and the next few are also cool as you customize your mech.  But by the end of season 2, you're mech has basically reached its final form, and it's just a matter of making numbers go up to try to keep pace with ever-stronger enemies.
I liked the game.  It had charm, an amusingly-cheesy plot, and solid mechanics.  But while the plot progressed and got better, the mechanics didn't,  I don't regret buying it, but I do find myself saddened and disappointed that it couldn't follow through on the solid experience it started.

Arx Fatalis, in Latin "fatal fortress", is set on a world whose sun has failed, forcing the above ground creatures to take refuge in subterranean caverns. The action in Arx Fatalis takes place in one of these large caves, where inhabitants from all races such as Trolls, Goblins, Dwarves, Humans, etc. have made their homes on various levels of the cave. The player awakens inside a prison cell and, after making his escape, eventually discovers his mission is to subvert and imprison the God of Destruction, Akbaa, who is trying to manifest itself in Arx.
Arx Fatalis has a somewhat open-ended gameplay style, allowing the player to allocate skill points for the character type such as spellcasting, weapons and armor, stealth, and so on. There are several side quests that can be undertaken. Simple crafting involves enchanting ammunition and weapons, or creating items, such as a fishing rod (fishing pole and rope), keyrings (key and ring), or pies (dough and rolling pin, optional apple and optional bottle of wine). Raw food can be cooked, like rounds of bread, chicken drumsticks, or pies. The main plotline is non-linear with the player collecting the various items to forge a sword required to defeat Akbaa in a final showdown. Additional goals come up such as dealing with the rebels of Arx, the snake women and The King of Arx. The player can resolve the conflict between them all and experience several different endings to the conflict with different consequences somewhat affecting the story.
There is no dialogue system in Arx Fatalis. Rather, the player is able to make choices through actions which lead to different consequences. There are also multiple ways to finish quests and the player can progress through the game in several different ways. For example, the player can use force to kill enemies and break down doors, or they can use stealth and avoid enemies.
One of the intuitive interfaces in Arx Fatalis is the spellcasting system. Using the mouse and the Ctrl key, runes are drawn in mid air with mouse gestures, which must be correctly drawn, in order to successfully cast a spell. The player can find or buy different runes as gameplay progresses, combinations of which unlock new spells. A queue of up to 3 spells can be cast in advance, ready to be activated at the press of a button. There is also an instant magic mode that allows the player to simply select the desired spell they want to cast from a list of learned spells during gameplay.
In addition, Arx supports a stealth mode that is active when a stealth icon is visible on the interface. In stealth mode, usually when a player is in dark or shadowy areas, non player characters cannot see them.

think you should burn the heretics or not, your 'faith' meter makes that decision for you. If you run out of any resource or
you instantly lose, and this happens very frequently. This is the core gameplay experience that you will essentially repeat for as long as you're playing Reigns.
-Cheap

-Charming visuals
-Interesting premise

A solid port of a classic RPG series. As a veteran of the games, it took me 16 hours to beat Vol. 1's main story, plus an additional 10 hours of (fairly repetitive) grinding for 100%. My playtimes for the other volumes were:
Vol. 2: Beat the game- 25 Hours. 100%- 38 Hours.
Vol. 3: Beat the game- 22 Hours. 100%- 45 Hours.
Vol. 4: Beat the game- 3 Hours.
Total: Approx. 112 Hours.
Again, I'm a veteran, so if you're new to these games and want to go for 100%, you should probably expect 120+ hours of playtime across all 4 volumes.
(You may notice my actual playtime is higher, I played through Vol. 1 a second time on release for a stream.)
A few comments, take them as you will:
-Except in certain instances, characters' mouths do not move when they talk.
-There are a few very minor glitches and I have experienced the occasional crash while playing; not nearly enough to stop me from continuing.
-The previously-limited-edition Terminal Disc is included, which will help bring you up to speed on the lore and the story of the original series for new players, and expand on the existing lore for veterans.
-The trailers claim to have taken the various improvements made in Volumes 2 and 3 and applied them to the first game. This is only partially true; some features from the 2nd and 3rd Volumes are still not present in Vol. 1, such as the improved combo mechanics of the twin blades or better charge attacks of the broadsword, or, perhaps most importantly, the quick-switch mechanic.
-Some of the Bonus Content cutscenes (Terminal Disc included) are not updated to HD, and are displayed in a small window within the game. This does not apply to the cutscenes seen throughout the games themselves; only the extra ones you unlock at the end.
-The game's EXP, Skill Points, and Attack Power have been rebalanced to provide a much smoother leveling curve. This version, therefore, is much easier than the originals.
-Features a "Cheat Mode" that allows you to play through the story at max level. Considering the point above, this is mostly inconsequential, as you will rarely have to grind in a normal playthrough anyway.
-Textures and models still look decidedly old, but passable. The lighting engine and cel-shading go a long way to help this.
-The game was made for the PS2, as such it is meant to be played with a controller. It does support DirectInput, as well as all the modern controller APIs.
-Keyboard controls can be re-mapped, but mouse and controller cannot.
-There are 6 new BGMs (available in Vol. 4) and a total of 31 new Backgrounds (Throughout all 4 volumes) that can be used to customize your ingame Desktop. The original Desktop Backgrounds are not updated to the new widescreen format, and are letterboxed in order to maintain their original aspect ratio.
Volume 4 is EXTREMELY short, and many of the features of the first 3 volumes are missing. It is entirely focused on the story, with the only side-content being one final dungeon after beating the game. Its story and presentation are decent, but because of the short runtime it falls flat in my opinion.
The game also features "Parody Mode", a series of cutscenes from the games with edited dialogue. It's probably the best new addition in Last Recode, to be honest.
All-in-all, I think this collection has been well worth my $50 so far, if only for the first three volumes.
(Edit: Updated to reflect my playthroughs of the second, third, and fourth volumes.)

I reasonably well done remaster of a great trilogy originaly designed for playstation. A few things did happen to be lost in translation, however, which causes the game to behave quite differently in some parts and its very obvious if you have played the originals. Overall, definately worth getting if you liked the original series and want to play on the PC. Below is my list detailing all the faults and counterrarguments I've noticed so far. If you've never played this series, I would definately suggest this purchase! If you already have a way of playing the original, I would probably say stick with the original unless the convenience of having it on PC is desired.
Because the game actually runs faster than it did on the playstation, the beast awakening is quite hard to use because the faster attack speed causes you to drop combos very often unless you are outright mashing the button.
The voices and sound affects were changed slightly, which annoys me personally.
The increased graphical quality makes the lack of detail in the faces of many character models painfully obvious, which i guess overall is good?
The game tends to crash and cause a lot of problems with the PC. Just recently when I quit out of the game, it caused the monitor to read "input type not supported" until I restarted the graphics drivers. Although if you think of this as part of the game coming to life....maybe you will become more immersed? Just make sure to save before doing anything so you dont lose your progress, and hopefully soon they will patch out the crashing (I think some people are overexxaggerating just how much it crashes, In my 8 hours of play so far, it has actually crashed once.)
There is no way to adjust many setting in game (because they were designed for a console, you could never change these settings in the game themselves) so you have to quit out to adjust anything. Protip: turn on vsync or your screen will tear like paper.
Some people are suggesting to run on an emulator, I would definately NOT suggest this! Almost all the graphical effects and cutscenes run like garbage on an emulator!
Some people are saying the game is too easy on this version...but the game was easy to begin with. Its maybe a little less grindy on this version, but in terms of actual difficulty its more or less the same.

I am a huge World War II fanatic.  With my World of Warcraft days set aside, I have easily sunk more time into this game than any other.
Red Orchestra 2, even with some minor, forgivable bugs that still remain after years, is one of the best games I have ever played. I come from the age when video games were challenging, and RO2 is as challenging as it gets. When people say "it gave me PTSD," although they may be joking about something which they have no clue, this analysis still isn't quite far off. The sense of immersion that this game provides is unmatched. It feels like you are part of a real World War II battle. You will be afraid to pop your head out of the trench because it will get blown off immediately. You will see glimpses of the fear and horrors that real soldiers might have felt in real battles. You will see how terrible of a thing war actually is, and by proxy, you will see how dumbed-down and desensitized modern games like Call of Duty and Battlefield have taken war and made it into a streamlined cash cow franchise. This game was clearly made by people who had a heart for the real-life heroes of Stalingrad, on both sides of the war.
The community is by-and-large very helpful to new players and dedicated to teamwork and cooperation. This game is not for everyone because of its massive maps and a very steep, unforgiving learning curve. Be prepared to put in many, many, many hours to climb in the ranks, and be prepared to play a "lowly" bolt-action rifleman while you learn the ropes. So much fun. As of the date of this writing, this is easily my favorite game of all-time.

No Time to Explain is a comedic puzzle platformer that features ridiculous amounts of "rocket jumping". You have an extremely powerful and exaggerated laser, though sometimes the game will change it up with different weapons, such as an equally powerful and exaggerated shotgun. Rather than using these weapons to combat creeps, you'll be using them to traverse and solve the level.
The mechanics are simple and easily understood. You can move left and right, jump, aim, shoot, and do a little jig (there is a dance button. Why? Reasons). It's really just that simple. You'll be using the game's weapon that it provides to work out a solution to the end of the map, with the map and the game's physics itself as your adversaries. As mentioned before, there are no mobs to fight (at least from what I've played). The only combat that I've experienced so far, with almost 2 hours in, is the boss fights them selves. The puzzles are satisfying and the map designs are smart, but I do feel the game could of gained rather than detracted if it threw in a few combat scenarios. It feels almost like a waste, that the player can't use these impressive weapons in more meaningful ways, other than traversing. Luckily, the puzzle and platforming aspect is quite well done and serves well as the game's main dish.
The presentation is a little simplistic but it does the job. It goes with a flash cartoon look, something similar to say Castle Crashers, but the characters and animation has a charming appeal to it. The game's focus on comedy really helps out with it's overall feel and atmosphere. It's probably not the best looker of the year, but there's something really lovable about the characters and the animation.
Overall, No Time to Explain is an interesting take on the puzzle platform genre, with smart level design, charming animations, and ridiculous weaponry. I can safely say, I've enjoyed my time with the game.
Pros:
- Charming and comedic characters and animation
- The weapons feel very powerful
- Smart map design
Cons:
- Under utilizes the awesome weapons

At least with RO2, the Axis and the USSR is pretty balanced and teamwork usually wins the game regardless if the map is more in favor of one team.
So in total, I recommend Red Orchestra 2, not so much Rising Storm.

There's been a fair bit of whingeing on behalf of some on the large number of DLC skin packs available at launch, as somebody who is studying multimedia development, I can safely assure you that no, they did not parcel away content from the game to sell back to you, what happened was this, for the last months of development pre-launch, half the team had literally nothing to do, these people were the artists, they can only spend so much time playtesting to help the designers balance the game, and they need something to do, so they create skins. This continues right up until the game launches, including past "content lock", a point at development (also known as Gold) where nothing is added and  the game is finished, being shipped to stores or set up with Steam. There are a whole bunch of actual in game skins, at least one for each character, and the skins themselves are harmless. Overpriced, maybe, that's debateable, but harmless.
It's too early for me to tell what negatives the game will have, so this section we be revisited over the coming weeks.

I'm conflicted. Tropico, if you didn't know, is a series of island-nation-building games, under the theme of banana republics. You'll have rebels to crush, an international community to help when the natural disasters hit, and superpowers to patronize and threaten you. You export everything from bananas and tobacco to cars, cigars and CD players. You build up a military and actually use it. You build your nice beaches into tourist locations, keeping them well away from your personal death squad.
The music and elections in Tropico 4 are VASTLY superior to this game, so much so that I play a youtube playlist of T4 music in the background and mute 5's.
The elections... they're confusing, and whereas 4 allowed you to give a rousing speech to boost your election night chances, 5 only lets you "slightly tweak" the outcome, if you do anything at all. The confusion comes from having to pick a dynasty member to run as presidente, at which point the approval rating changes, but not immediately; any factions that dislike his or her class will vote for the opposition, and you can't know who that is ahead of time, or how well your choice will be recieved.
This, of course, means nothing to people who play as dictators.
Due to some slight gameplay improvements, like the Era system, this game is in some ways superior to 4, but in other ways inferior.
It's hard to recommend this game over 4, but, it's still better than any recent SimCity or even Cities Skylines.

It's another Hercules game. If you like one of them, you'll like them all, because there aren't any drastic differences from one to the next. They're colorful, involve a lot of clicking, and sometimes some thought if you want gold on every level, but they're also perfect for when you just have a few minutes to spend.

TL;DR: This is not a good sequel to Tropico 4. Go play Tropico 4 instead.
Tropico 5 adds some things, removes many things, and doesn't fix any of the issues the previous game had.
Most of the witty writing is gone. Whereas Tropico 4 had many characters with clever jokes about their stereotypes, this game relies on "haha Penultimo is dumb" jokes and lame puns. You also won't interact with those characters as often, since Tropico 5 dumbed down the political factions by a whole lot. Appeasing them isn't that difficult, and simply ignoring their rare demands is enough. Occasionally, there's a blurb of text that was meant to be said by a different character during development, but was then rewritten for the voice line to be spoken by a different character, with the old text left in. That's just silly.
The game is very bad at telling you the information you need to know. It doesn't really give you financial data over a period of time, so you only usually notice something is wrong when you're 20k in the hole, and then you can't figure out what is wrong quickly because you don't know if your expenses rose or if your revenue sunk. It also won't tell you why people are homeless; I've had a well-off person live in a shack next to perfectly adequate open apartment slots.
Speaking of things going wrong, teamsters are awful. No matter how many teamster offices you build, if your city reaches a certain size, they will just sit in a corner and sniff their farts while your industry buildings run out of input resources. The game doesn't tell you at any point that your teamsters are overburdened, and it has no statistics page to show you how much material was moved.
Small things also annoy me. Destroying roads is needlessly fiddly. If you can get your click to register (good luck!), you'll sit there wondering why the road won't disappear until you realise that you need to unpause the game for it to take effect. And you'll be needing to destroy roads a lot, because they never want to work the way you want them to work.
And the worst part is that under all of this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, there still is a fun game somewhere hidden deep beneath, overshadowed just by how bland the writing is and by how fiddly the game mechanics are.

This game is so beautiful. It's the first thing I can think to say, because it feels most important. This game touched me not only because of its stunning visuals, but through the whole sensory and narrative atmosphere it manages to create - and in Sandbox mode at that, since Story Mode isn't out yet! Snowy, poetic, harsh, powerful, intense, difficult, meditative, inspiring - these adjectives are probably my best shot at describing how this game feels. "Feels" is also a key word - this game makes me FEEL things, and I love it. I've loved it since I first saw it and even more since I first played it. I've played it for hours and do not regret a cent of my purchase, even in its current state of development.
However, yes, this game is a work in progress, and I do have some complaints (lack of interesting long-term goals and balancing issues regarding survival being the most significant). But I have no doubt that Hinterland Studios will pull it off and solve them in due time. The addition of Story Mode alone should be huge. The studio seems to be working hard at putting out new content, and that's all I could wish for.
In summary, TLD is already very strong and cohesive from an artistic standpoint, and despite its unfinished state, I was very happy to immerse myself in it for many hours. I can only imagine what this talented group of people will come up with in terms of long-term gameplay that will pull me back in :) Good luck, Hinterland! I know you can do it!

The obvious elephant in the room with RO2 is indeed the number that follows it. Being treated as a sequel there should be expected certain standards. People held Ragnarok, the first, in very high regards. Be it by it's uniqueness in the, at the time, not as saturated MMORPG world, or by simple nostalgia.

The game is however generic and bland, with repetitive gameplay mechanics that a lot of korean mmos suffer, it's safe to say taht RO2 early stages before it was redone were more original and different. The mmo market is filled with games like this, so the game makers were forced to adapt.
The best part however, aside from the visuals and classes, is the soundtrack. How they landed Yoko Kanno I have no idea, but good choice, still, can't live up to the nostalgia given by the original title in the series.
All in all the game suffers from a very generic formula, something that did not with it's predecessor.

This has been the best "Early Access" experience I've had with a game since Mount & Blade. Like M&B, there is one single exceptional mechanic that just continues to shine through all the updates and continually make this a wonderful experience.
In The Long Dark, the reason you play is for the atmosphere. No matter what happens in the game, the atmosphere is what continually sucks you in and delivers unforgettable moments -- of which there are plenty. This is what first-person is all about - making you feel like you're actually really there.

Five Nights at Freddy's is an indie survival horror game, with the unique twist of being mostly point and click. You play the security guard in a pizza restaurant that has a bit of a problem...
Its life-sized animatronic mascots like to roam about at night and kill anything that has a security guards badge.
The aim of the game is to make it through five night shifts.
To stay alive, you flick between different security camera feeds in the hope of catching the killer robots on the prowl. You need to manually shut the two doors to your room to keep them at bay, but you can't leave those doors shut forever...
The doors that save you from time to time drain power from the restaurant's generator. And when the power goes out, so do the lights...
Five Nights at Freddy's doesn't have half of the production values as other games in the horror genre do, but it's just those eyeballs in the dark...  Big, murderous, googly eyes....
Scott Cawthon really targets those childhood fears of your old worn out dolls coming to life to eat your face.
It's no wonder there have been millions of Let's Plays of this game already, because it's loaded with jump scares and unsettling audio such as the pirate fox singing, Freddy laughing at your attempts to save yourself and Chica clattering around in the kitchen.
You're in a permanent state of tension, because you can't keep an eye on everything at once and you inevitably become more paranoid with the eerie sounds playing in the back ground.
Of course, copping a jump scare means it's already too late - you're dead. So it's all the tension in trying to avoid the ever looming death that makes this game effective in its tactics.
The visuals are not as polished as the audio, but what do you expect from one man?
They serve their purpose, and give a semi cartoon look to the Animatronics.
It's clever how managing that one resource - your electricity level - has been made so stressful. It's a constant balancing act, juggling your use of the cameras, the lights in the hallways, and the security doors ... as you watch the power drain and the clock tick to the safety of 6am... you're not always sure you're going to make it. And each shift only gets harder as the animatronics become more active.
If you like spooky scares, this might be for you.

Reigns is a simulation game in which you play as the kings of a medieval kingdom. The main game loop is centered around reading cards of texts and picking one of two choices that the character speaking to you - it could a jester, a doctor, a general, or any one of a lively cast - offers. Your decisions affect four factions, although not each faction
will be responsive to every decision you make. The game doesn't tell you whether one particular choice will
have a positive or negative consequence on your relationship with that faction. This, in turn, yields to an element of uncertainity which makes the experience both enjoyable and replayable. In a market full of simulation games trying to take themselves super seriously, Reigns is a breath of fresh air. While the gameplay might be simple and the atmosphere almost comical at times, the choices you make have an immediate impact both within your reign and across your lineage.

[Build 36 commentary, Feb. 9 - 2017]
So... It's time to update this review I reckon. Six builds and two years after my first comment on this game, I return to it again. So... What's changed?
Well, since my last visit, there's come a few new skillsets, electricity for those interested in making and breaking radio devices, as well as metalworking, which is currently nothing more than a fancier way to build/fortify your base, but opens up a great potential for future updates.
There's also been a few traps developed that are meant to kill or distract zombies rather than catch wildlife, mostly bombs. The zombies have also been tampered with so that they don't simply stand idly by wherever they happen to turn; but congregate into small clusters which move around from time to time, which makes running around in the streets more hazardous than before.
Some mod support has also been added, for those of you who prefer to improve this game yourselves with more or less realistic additions.
...I'm not gonna lie, not very much has changed as far as gameplay goes. Respawning zombies means that there's always going to be some manner of threat if you go outside, but in the end... most of the changes seem to only try and hold off on that boredom moodlet affecting both the character and the player.
I realise that in my last review, which you can read below if you like, I was being very generous with the developers and praising them like they were the next Notch. I still have a lot of respect for them and their ambitions, but... I'll have to admit that their standing with me isn't quite as high anymore, simply because any significant changes they've made are not great enough to make this game as entertaining as it could and should be. They've introduced a few good changes, like more realistic zombie behavior, but most of it is just too subtle to make a difference in what is essencially the same problem this game has had from the start: Hoarding and waiting.
And just to get it out of the way: NPCs are really hyped and would likely make a huge impact on gameplay. But while everyone wants it to happen as quickly as possible, remember this: The only thing worse than no NPCs are broken NPCs. Left for Dead, anyone?
But make no mistake! I wouldn't have put in almost 1000 hours (as I'm writing this review) into this game if it was bad. This is a good game, although many will agree with me that it suffers from a dragged out development process filled with a lot of redundancies, and gameplay that can get stale quicker than your unconserved vegetables if you're not playing multiplayer. It's the big problem with any game that focus too much on realism: They forget that they're meant to be games, not outright simulators.
With all that said... I still recommend this game. Yes, it's likely not gonna be finished by the next year, and yes it can wear itself out once you know what you're doing. But for all its flaws, there's a lot to see and do in Project Zomboid and there's gonna be even more in the future. So whether you're like me and prefer to play these things on your own, or you wanna play around with friends or even strangers (you masochist) in multiplayer, I think you're gonna find a lot of enjoyment in this.
And as always, remember: Don't drink the bleach!
[Build 30 commentary, Feb. 18 - 2015]
Ahh, this game... So many complex feelings, so little time! Well, for starters: This certainly isn't currently a game for everyone.
Yes, it's quite playable and the amount of bugs is kept at a minimum, the developers are dedicated and keep in constant touch and the community is quite excellent at snapping up the details as they keep pouring out. So yes, this game IS going to be finished, one way or another. And as far as I'm concerned, it's going to be grand!
This game is dedicated to creating realistic gameplay, so you'll have to contend with much more than zombies to survive. There are currently no human NPCs, but just trying to keep yourself alive is a challenge as you have to manage hunger, thirst, disease, fear, various kinds of wounds, (damn you broken glass!) and even boredom if you can get that far.
I'm afraid, however, that boredom isn't simply a modlet, it can also affect the player. The main problem with this game is poor pacing.
It's quite nerve-tingling, trying to sneak around without being overwhelmed by the undead horde and get bitten, resulting in slow, unavoidable permadeath. You look for tools, supplies and weapons to stay alive and defend yourself. How you do this is up to you, though some strategies are more likely to succeed than others. With some careful scavenging you can even cut down trees to barricade your house, or even build your own if that's more your style. You can grow crops, fish, trap small animals and generally get by well in the apocalypse. You can even learn to build rain catchers. And if everything else fails: Flee to the woods and forage for nuts and berries, sticks and stones. There's always an option for survival, but there's no zombrex...
And from what I've heard (and experienced) all of this means that players usually end up barricading themselves, stockpiling a huge amount of resources, set up some water catchers, start a farm and just rest into infinity... or get bored really quickly and go out hunting zombies, get overwhelmed and/or bitten, end of story. So yes, the pacing herein is far from perfect...
But the developers are very aware of this flaw, and are working on it with about the same vigour as with their human NPCs. So worry not dear gamers. This game is far from complete, yet it already presents you with a surprisingly engaging survival scenario. And if you're a survivalistic hoarder like myself, then I think you'll understand exactly what makes me hopeful for the future of both this game, and anything else these brilliant developers will create in the future.
Also, I don't care how desperate you get: Don't drink that bleach! Just don't do it!

Cuphead is a 2d shoot-'em-up sidescroller, developed and published by StudioMDHR Entertainment Inc. on the 29th of September 2017. This will be a short critique of the game, as the Steam review section doesn’t fit this style of review, and it would rather belong on a blog, or something similar. This critique will be focusing on 4 sections of the game, with me summarizing my main gripes.
The audiovisual design of the game is based on the rubber hose style of animation originating in the 1920’s with the music playing like something straight out of looney tunes.
Personally, I believe the game to be gorgeous with an amazing soundtrack, and from what I have seen, few disagree with that statement. The game does, however suffer in some ways, for example, the soundtrack is looped in every part of the game, and this is causes annoyance with the game if a player finds a boss fight rather difficult.
A nitpick I have with the games visuals, while not being an issue, is how the “knockouts” are handled at the end of the boss fights, with every boss emitting some smoke animations. The issue I have with this is how imperfect and lazy it looks compared to the rest of the game.
The reason I found the aesthetics appealing was due to the numerous boss fights that the game relies on. There are 28 bosses in total if you count the “secret” bosses at the end of the game, where some fights are better than others.
That’s the greatest problem with having so many bosses, thus forcing some to either feel uninspired or as if they are repetitions of others. One of my least favorite bosses resides in the theatre, just feeling like a mixture of the attacks that the bosses of the candy land have.
Some attacks are also very trial and error, making some fights feel more random and unforgiving than they are, one example being the arcs of the fire parade during the dragon fight, another being the dogs during the boat fight.
One of the weak points of the game is in my opinion the platforming stages. While the controls generally feel responsive, these stages just are not cutting it for me. One of the levels I am talking about would be the treetop stage, where all enemies feel unnatural, and the stage just feels like filler.
I believe this is a symptom of the fact that the developers decided that platforming was required due to all the positive attention the game received after its public announcement. This is not entirely the fault of the game developer, it is also the fault of the consumer pressuring the developer to do something that was never planned for their game.
I believe that most upgrades are useless to any player, with the only two viable ones being the auto parry, and the dash upgrade. In the same sense I also believe that only three shot types are viable for normal play, and only one of the supers is useful if the player chooses to use the supers at all.
This makes the shop practically worthless in my opinion, with any use he might have resides only on the first island, where he supplies you with your first set of upgrades.
I did not enjoy Cuphead as much as another player might have, that is not to say that I do not see the appeal for others, Cuphead just was not for me, as these issues simply made the game more bothersome than it had to be.

I'm conflicted. Tropico, if you didn't know, is a series of island-nation-building games, under the theme of banana republics. You'll have rebels to crush, an international community to help when the natural disasters hit, and superpowers to patronize and threaten you. You export everything from bananas and tobacco to cars, cigars and CD players. You build up a military and actually use it. You build your nice beaches into tourist locations, keeping them well away from your personal death squad.
The music and elections in Tropico 4 are VASTLY superior to this game, so much so that I play a youtube playlist of T4 music in the background and mute 5's.
The elections... they're confusing, and whereas 4 allowed you to give a rousing speech to boost your election night chances, 5 only lets you "slightly tweak" the outcome, if you do anything at all. The confusion comes from having to pick a dynasty member to run as presidente, at which point the approval rating changes, but not immediately; any factions that dislike his or her class will vote for the opposition, and you can't know who that is ahead of time, or how well your choice will be recieved.
This, of course, means nothing to people who play as dictators.
Due to some slight gameplay improvements, like the Era system, this game is in some ways superior to 4, but in other ways inferior.
It's hard to recommend this game over 4, but, it's still better than any recent SimCity or even Cities Skylines.

TL;DR: This is not a good sequel to Tropico 4. Go play Tropico 4 instead.
Tropico 5 adds some things, removes many things, and doesn't fix any of the issues the previous game had.
Most of the witty writing is gone. Whereas Tropico 4 had many characters with clever jokes about their stereotypes, this game relies on "haha Penultimo is dumb" jokes and lame puns. You also won't interact with those characters as often, since Tropico 5 dumbed down the political factions by a whole lot. Appeasing them isn't that difficult, and simply ignoring their rare demands is enough. Occasionally, there's a blurb of text that was meant to be said by a different character during development, but was then rewritten for the voice line to be spoken by a different character, with the old text left in. That's just silly.
The game is very bad at telling you the information you need to know. It doesn't really give you financial data over a period of time, so you only usually notice something is wrong when you're 20k in the hole, and then you can't figure out what is wrong quickly because you don't know if your expenses rose or if your revenue sunk. It also won't tell you why people are homeless; I've had a well-off person live in a shack next to perfectly adequate open apartment slots.
Speaking of things going wrong, teamsters are awful. No matter how many teamster offices you build, if your city reaches a certain size, they will just sit in a corner and sniff their farts while your industry buildings run out of input resources. The game doesn't tell you at any point that your teamsters are overburdened, and it has no statistics page to show you how much material was moved.
Small things also annoy me. Destroying roads is needlessly fiddly. If you can get your click to register (good luck!), you'll sit there wondering why the road won't disappear until you realise that you need to unpause the game for it to take effect. And you'll be needing to destroy roads a lot, because they never want to work the way you want them to work.
And the worst part is that under all of this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, there still is a fun game somewhere hidden deep beneath, overshadowed just by how bland the writing is and by how fiddly the game mechanics are.

Just a bit too buggy, and not quite cognizant enough of its own stability
The game itself is rather enjoyable - your standard Tropico fare, with a good bit of historcal pizazz thrown in. It's nice to actually progress through the ages, and the economic system seams well balanced from what I've seen so far. However, the big issue, the main problem for which I am not recommending it, is its instability. It crashes all the time. Now, this in itself isn't too terible. If the occasional crash was enough to ruin a gaming experience, Bethesda wouldn't be in business. But the save system in this game *sucks*. There's no quicksave hotkey, and the autosave seems to think "Eh, maybe once or twice a decade seems about right". I lost two hours or so of progress on my first playthrough when I got nearly to the point of declaring independence and then my game crashed. When I went back, expecting atleast *some* of my progress to be preserved, and saw that all that had been saved was my Dynasty, I had something of a table flip moment. I was, ofcourse, more conscious of saving from that point in, but between the fairly common crashes, the out-of-the-way save controls, and the game being really easy to "get into" and lose track of things, I still lost an annoying amount of progress to crashes. Also, I failed a mission on a technicality, and when I went to reload a save (yes I savescum sometimes, don't judge me), the most recent save was like three years ago. Which was really really annoying.
tl;dr, if they fixed the nearly useless autosave function and added a quicksave hotkey, and also made the game a bit more stable, I'm sure it would be fantastic. But until then, I can't honestly recommend purchasing it.

I reasonably well done remaster of a great trilogy originaly designed for playstation. A few things did happen to be lost in translation, however, which causes the game to behave quite differently in some parts and its very obvious if you have played the originals. Overall, definately worth getting if you liked the original series and want to play on the PC. Below is my list detailing all the faults and counterrarguments I've noticed so far. If you've never played this series, I would definately suggest this purchase! If you already have a way of playing the original, I would probably say stick with the original unless the convenience of having it on PC is desired.
Because the game actually runs faster than it did on the playstation, the beast awakening is quite hard to use because the faster attack speed causes you to drop combos very often unless you are outright mashing the button.
The voices and sound affects were changed slightly, which annoys me personally.
The increased graphical quality makes the lack of detail in the faces of many character models painfully obvious, which i guess overall is good?
The game tends to crash and cause a lot of problems with the PC. Just recently when I quit out of the game, it caused the monitor to read "input type not supported" until I restarted the graphics drivers. Although if you think of this as part of the game coming to life....maybe you will become more immersed? Just make sure to save before doing anything so you dont lose your progress, and hopefully soon they will patch out the crashing (I think some people are overexxaggerating just how much it crashes, In my 8 hours of play so far, it has actually crashed once.)
There is no way to adjust many setting in game (because they were designed for a console, you could never change these settings in the game themselves) so you have to quit out to adjust anything. Protip: turn on vsync or your screen will tear like paper.
Some people are suggesting to run on an emulator, I would definately NOT suggest this! Almost all the graphical effects and cutscenes run like garbage on an emulator!
Some people are saying the game is too easy on this version...but the game was easy to begin with. Its maybe a little less grindy on this version, but in terms of actual difficulty its more or less the same.

If I want to describe this game in short, then it feels like as if the series finally grew up and left the kiddie gloves at home. There are no more cheap gimmicks like thieves, evil clones, or even needless road art, just pure time management challenge. The road layouts and the resource placement ensure that the workers do not travel needlessly long distances, but in return the game expects forward planning, careful stock management (probably the strongest aspect), and meticulous execution.
Achievement hunters will (justly) complain about the new requirement of beating all developer records to 100% the game, which is another indication of how the series moved past casual game territory. Those whom dare to tackle the challenge will find one of the purest and best entries of this long series, one that can be a source of frustration but also many triumphant moments.
