The Long Dark is a very niche game. So before buying it, you should ask yourself: "Just what kind of game do I want to play?".
As someone who thoroughly enjoys survival games, and had become rather good at staying alive (at least most of the time), The Long Dark provides new challenges, and a new atmosphere. To me, there are key points to consider when you are contemplating getting The Long Dark. These are the sense of realism, the atmosphere, the art style (for those of you who care about that), and, of course, the challenge.
Realism: As far as games go, TLD is very, very realistic. So much so that it can be a double edged sword. Perhaps the main goal of the game is to keep your calories up, while avoiding death via cold, wolves, or even bears. Or falling off of cliffs. As far as food consumption goes, the game is about accurate. You need to consume roughly 2000 or so calories per day to stay healthy. I am currently in a trapper's cabin leaving snares out for rabbits, because I used all of my ammo for my rifle, and lost my only arrows for my bow. The constant need for food is a pressing matter, and realistically done. The same applies to the cold. The cold itself will make you cold if you're unprepared (not wearing adequate clothing), but the wind will expedite the process. What was interesting to me, is that I found that by standing by a wall of other surface while the wind was blowing (on the other side), it actually created a wind shield. This can become very important for when you need to build a fire. You can't do so in the middle of a gale of wind. The realism as far as mechanics go is really solid. However, then there is the other side of it. Playing TLD is not a rapid paced game most of the time. You often choose to walk to avoid burning necessary calories, you will often have to stop traveling and find shelter when a blizzard comes in, and avoiding the hostile wildlife is often better than fighting, as things can go wrong really fast. What you end up with, is a very realistic experience. This is a battle against the elements, not tangible foes. As such, the game can sometimes feel like work. It can feel slow and lonely. You have to be ENTIRELY self-driven. If you are the type of person that likes this level of realism (like me), then you will likely enjoy this aspect of the game. If you are the type of person that prefers faster paced games, then TLD may not be your cup of tea.
Atmosphere: The atmosphere of TLD is phenomenal. From the sound of the wind, to the voice actor's brilliant work, to the gradual lighting of a sunrise or sunset, TLD have a fantastic atmosphere. I first really noticed during a blizzard in the game. I had gone inside of a camp ground cabin to avoid the cold. As I stood there, I could hear the wind raging outside, the house creaking under the wind, and my character's labored breathing (I had sprinted to the cabin). The general lack of background noise is often a boon as well. It is just you, surviving-not thriving, but surviving-in the middle of nature. When the background music occasionally surfaces, it only adds to the feeling of cold and isolation. The atmosphere is a strongpoint for TLD.
Art Style: TLD uses a paint-esc art style (I'm not sure what you would name it). It is consistent, and achieves a good effect. Rather than focus on core realism, the art style comes across as realistic, without having to be as graphically intense. If you truly care about the art style though, watch a video rather than read a review :P
Challenge: The challenge is always there in TLD. Whether it's food, warmth, or safety, you will unlikely become a Fat-cat while surviving. Thanks to a sort of leveling system for various skills, such as fire-starting of carcass harvesting, your character will gradually get better at survival skills. This is a boon. There is also a wound and sickness system to watch out for, and bleeding to death or getting mauled by a wolf sucks. My one complaint, however, lies with the perishability of food and items. Things spoil in TLD. This normally wouldn't be an issue. However, when you pick up matches, canned food, or even a freaking sardine can, you would expect those to last for a dang good long while. Instead, as if your character has some kind of entropic aura, everything you touch (aside from tools) gradually goes bad. I found this out when I examined my canned food stockpile and it was all going close to rancid. Even lighter fluid goes bad. You can maintain certain tools, light a lantern, a hatchet, a gun, etc. But your means of doing so are limited, and I am sure that once my magnifying glass, fire striker, and matches go bad (because in this game a magnifying glass breaks via using it), I will end up shivering in a shack and eating raw rabbit meat, as I fist fight wolves for the rabbit's intestines. It's not a pretty picture.
All in all, The Long Dark is a fantastic survival experience that I would strongly recommend. If you are willing to overlook the attrition rate of items, it will make for a wonderfully good time.

Game Mechanics:
The game continues the time and resource management trend of the previous installments of the series, but at the very least there's no thieves now. The hidden objects within the levels also make a return, though not every level seems to have them. Another returning feature are the additional characters and the puzzle pieces, which (when collected and after solving a simpole jigsaw) unlock a bonus level.
Plot: the plot is incredibly simple, as has become the standard with this series, Zeus is missing from Olympus and it seems that the other Gods are responsible. With the leader of the Olympian Gods missing a poll will be held to decide on the next ruler. Hercules sets off to find Zeus and punish the one responsible.
Presentation:
The game looks and feels like a mobile game, but the visuals are crisp and well-designed, and I can't help but mention the rather enjoyable mellow music (especially within Poseidon's realm and the desert). Some hidden objects blind in quite a bit with the background and some of the level design makes the layout confusing, but it's not actually a big hindrance.
Completion:
All achievements, except for beating the developer's score, are pretty easily obtainable. That last one seems require a bit of grinding and a good grasp of the game's mechanics and precise planning.

This is going to be a rave review, get ready for it.
Like a lot of the community, I've come to be suspicious of early access titles after so many half finished products and broken promises - but this game functioned as a full and polished game a year ago when I bought it, and since then it's just gotten more and more great content.  It is truely one of my favorite games of all time.
Now I loved books like Hatchet as a kid, these realistic-ish wilderness survival novels (also I'm so sick of zombies I could vomit), so the setting and premise of the game were perfect for me.  And the game captures the wonder and the desolation of being stranded in the wild beautifully - although the "wild" in this case also includes abandoned buildings, often complete with frozen corpses.  The environment design is excellent, each corner of the world unique and memorable, even with a lot of repeating assets.  Two to four word location names (which appear on your HUD when you enter a location) add an amazing amount of depth to simple places: picture a cabin just over a hill off a wheat field called the Draft Dodger's Cabin.  It's clear that every house and convenience store and glade was lovingly crafted, and given a colorful history of human use.
Whether in town or deep in the woods, every hill and stream and ruin has so much life and personality, aided also by the incredible weather and lighting systems, which can make the view from your front door dramatically different every day - fog, snow, cloud cover, wind, the path of the sun, all combine and recombine to create a vibrant and changing environment - And one that has a strong relationship with gameplay.  Restricted visibility from fog or from falling dark can be the difference between making it to shelter in that trailer on the horizon or getting lost in the woods with the temperature dropping - and heaven forbid that a blizzard catches you off guard.
You'll learn to pay attention to the weather, and you'll feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥wilderness survival guru doing it - which is something this game does really well: Every time you make a discovery about the game's mechanics, it feels like making a discovery about real wilderness survival.  Even dumb interface discoveries somehow feel like this (Oh there's a button there?  Wait, you can turn this into tinder??).  You'll discover new gatherable items, you'll discover new uses for the items you have, and you'll keep discovering more and more of these things even long into the game; and yet it was never frustrating not to have known those things.  Each discovery is an exciting surprise, and one that lets you survive just a bit longer.

I don't like jumpscares. At least not the ones in movies, television or games. Strangely, I enjoy events like Universal's Halloween Horror Nights which are entirely predicated jumpscares, but there's at least a high production value and good spooky atmosphere present in the many scare houses and other attractions at the park. And that, to me, is the key. I think jumpscares are at their most effective when a good atmosphere is constructed that makes you a little nervous and on edge. Then just when you least suspect it - BAM! Something pops out and scares you. And that's it, now you've got your audience terrified. It's tempting to keep going back to the well and get more jumpscares over and over, but each subsequent jumpscare loses some effectiveness as they become more frequent and expected - especially in the case of Halloween Horror Nights where something pops out at you every 5 seconds. Which now that I think of it is probably why that event doesn't get to me. But most games/movies/TV shows know how to use jumpscares effectively, which is when I start not to like them. I just don't enjoy being scared that way... Which is why I've been hesitant to play Five Nights at Freddy's for a while. It's a game entirely predicated on jumpscares and it uses them effectively
The premise of this game is that you are a security guard who takes a night shift at a restaurant known as Freddy Fazbear's pizzeria. During your shift, it's revealed that the establishment's mascot animatronics have come to life and of course are trying to murder you. Your job is to last from midnight to 6am which is approximately 8 minutes of real time. In order to complete the game, you have to survive five consecutive nights, hence the name of the game. My question is: after surviving one night and knowing the animatronics are homicidal, why would you ever come back? Anyway, you're instructed that the animatronics only move in the dark when you're not watching them, so you're safe as long as you keep an eye on their locations. Your player is stuck at their guard post so your only defenses are checking security cameras, turning the lights on in the dark hallways adjacent to your guard post and closing the electronic doors, but each of these actions consumes electrical power, of which you have limited supply. If you run out of power, you're totally defenseless and more than likely are going to get jumpscared. This game is particularly effective at using audio, or more specifically the lack thereof, to create atmosphere. It's really unnerving to only hear the quiet humming of the security cameras or the buzzing of the florescent lights while your're waiting for what seems like an inevitable loud and disruptive jumpscare.
Since people love to watch other people get scared, this game got a huge boost in popularity from "let's play" videos on YouTube. This first game in the series was relatively critically and commercially successful and has spawned 3 sequels with an upcoming RPG spinoff as well as a movie adaptation from Warner Brothers pictures coming soon. All of this is a little much for me, especially considering the game came out only a little more than a year ago. Don't get me wrong, I liked the game well enough, but having 3 sequels and a movie deal in less than a year seems a bit excessive, no?
Summary
Five Nights at Freddy's is a game that knows how to use jumpscares effectively. It creates a tense atmosphere and keeps the player busy tracking the locations of multiple homicidal animatronics which pop out to scare the player when least expected. I think it's a good enough game, but this game's relative popularity has always been a little confusing to me... I suppose most other people a good jumpscare a lot more than I do.

I used Arx Libertatis (a mod to fix stuff and make the game actually run without crashing), so my actual playtime on this attempt was somewhere around 5 hours. I've played for similar lengths two times in the past on the disc version, so my Steam playtime will be tiny considering the normal exe fails to load as it does for a lot of folks.
This game has a cool fantasy premise in which the various races have gone underground where it's warmer since the sun fizzled out and the surface is supposed to be an arctic tundra. There is an awkward peace between the races, though goblins sometimes violate that, while rat-men don't seem to care about peace efforts at all, being somewhat murder-y and hiding most of the time (probably because they murder folks).
Arx Fatalis plays like a dungeon crawler with non-hostiles from time to time, and the mini-map is fairly helpful for being sure I've gone everywhere on a floor. Locked doors and other barriers you cannot yet get through are bothersome because none of the in-game maps update to highlight the door, nor do they make it readily apparent that there's an unexplored space just beyond, as much of the map is often a bit darkened in spots on the edges, like you haven't been there, just because of how it's programmed to fill in despite your best efforts at wiggling around to make the map fill in completely.
Controls are clunky, requiring that you hold a button before clicking to pick items up, double click to interact with certain things and people, open inventory, double click an item in the inventory, then single click the object or person to use the item on, etc. Also, magic is cast by moving the mouse around in various patterns, which the game is somewhat wishy-washy about accepting or registering as the correct rune. Do this in battle, and you're likely to get demolished, meaning you store three pre-cast spells (probably all fireball, which does crazy damage and everyone says playing as anything other than a mage is suicide unless you
know what you're doing), but even then your mana pool keeps you from casting too many of them. I think spell cooldowns and mana pool could have helped to limit casting if this rune system was the developer's intention, because although it's a very memorable quality of Arx Fatalis, it's not a good one for me.
NPCs are rather one-note and uninteresting, including the most important ones, like kings of factions and named characters. Your main character is, of course, suffering from amnesia, which is no doubt plot-related. However, despite remembering nothing, and this being an RPG, the game won't let me choose his dialog lines, and often has his tone of voice and words be sassy, evasive, confrontational, and other emotions/intentions that I, the player, never wanted my character to use, nor are they terribly consistent. I am actually a proponent of main characters with personality, but this one seemed to just be randomly bitter and manipulative without any input from me, and without being intriguing.
You do gain experience and levels as you go through the game, though leveling up is rare and offers little reward in regard to your attributes. Although that's also the case with Dungeons & Dragons, more than skills improve in D&D at level-ups, making that progression system far more interesting in my opinion. The player's inventory, though huge compared to what you could carry in real life, is pitifully small and requires annoying micromanagement unless you know what you're doing and what you need/should carry.
Although the premise is cool, the actual story is slow-moving and has not yet hooked me in. The flat/dull characters don't get me interested and I can't name one person I like so far. Without a story or characters that I really like, this makes it difficult to find a reason to compel me to complete the game. Making sense of where things are is also difficult for me. While it's true that I naturally have a terrible sense of direction, everything seems sort of spread in an odd fashion with maps that are too broad to easily view and make sense of when studied in the player's journal, and stairs up and down down show up well enough, nor are they labeled with where they go, making it tough for me to tell not only
there are stairs around, but where those stairs even lead to, resulting in a lot of wandering, especially when the quest log is deceitful.
What I mean by that is, for instance, the last quest I started, requires that I obtain an idol. The quest log states that it's in the goblin area. Okay, cool. I'll head back to the goblin area and look for it. WRONG. If you do that, you won't find it. The quest log could cost you hours of time wandering around thinking you're doing the right thing because the quest log told you where to go and you did. The correct course of action is to get the quest, then talk to a goblin you already saw a few minutes prior, who is in the
area, and then a chain of events which the game doesn't explain has anything to do with the idol, proceeds to occur, which will eventually net you the idol. In a game with this much square footage, well-hidden objects, and no freaking sprint button, sending the player in the wrong direction is just dirty and disrespectful of someone's time.
Like I said, the premise is excellent, but no matter how many times I keep starting this game up again due to other players raving about how good it is, each time I walk away dissatisfied and finding the game to be a disappointing experience and hope that I won't let other peoples' opinions blind me to my own realization that I do not enjoy this game, despite having tried it for several hours on three separate occasions, years apart each time, with no enjoyment to speak of on any one attempt at the game thus far.

This is a hard one to describe - I wouldn't particularly describe it as a game, but I would say that it's fun.
You are one king in a long lineage of kings, every time you die you come back as the next in line. You are presented with choices each year, and these choices are purely binary. They can range from things such as "Should we have a feast this year?" to "Should I follow this dog?" and there's a great deal of different choices involved. You'll unlock more as you 'defeat' certain situations (very similar to Hand of Fate if you've played that).
To remain as king, you must balance 4 factions - Religion, Citizens, Army and Merchant. If the power meter for any of these factions gets too low, you'll be ousted. The crux is, if you let any of these factions get too powerful, you'll also be ousted. For example - Let the army's power get too low and you'll end up having your Kingdom overrun, but let them get too powerful and you'll end up with a coup on your hands.
The game hints at what your decisions will affect but don't outrightly tell you, you'll need to figure this out yourself (or you'll likely memorise some of the more common ones over time). The game will show you if your decision is going to slightly affects or greatly affect a faction, and which faction(s) they are, but whether that's a good or bad thing is really down to how you interpret the decision. There's rarely been a decision where I've thought "Huh... I didn't expect THAT to be positive/negative".
There are other different aspects to the game, duels, passive effects and other bits and pieces but really the mechanics are pretty flat to discuss without actually seeing it in action. In summary, this is an incredibly imaginative text-based game where your choices are binary and what sounds like an incredibly boring premise actually turns out to be a really intriguing, surreal and absorbing game.

Project Zomboid is my most recent foray into the world of survival horror. With so many games of this ilk now, does Project Zomboid walk down the street with its head held high, or does it simply shuffle along, stale & decomposing with its asinine brethren in an already overcrowded street littered with hundreds of other; possibly better zombie games?
As of right now, it is still in Early Access so like all games mirroring this state; should be taken with a grain of salt as the facts of today may not be true tomorrow, post-update.
Project Zomboid, or 'PZ' as Developers 'The IndieStone' call it, follow the 'survival model' much in the same vain as high profile games like Day-Z and H1Z1, but where it differentiates itself is in its utterly bleak tone and top down perspective that isn't often tried in the AAA mainstream gaming of today, which works wonders in delivering a fresh look; while retaining the familiarity of so many game titles that have come before it.
PZ presents you with the opportunity to live out your life, your way in the midst of a full blown zombie apocalypse. Customize, stratergize and survive in any way you want, going solo or cooperating with friends either via online or local split-screen, which is relatively straightforward to setup and a preference of choice if you want your limbs & brain matter to remain intact and relatively unmunched.
Getting started, you are offered a slew of game modes and customization features specific to 'Sandbox Mode' which allows you to tailor your experience and create your ultimate zombie heaven (or hell).
PZ supports both Mouse & Keyboard or Controller to choose at your leisure, swapping between one or the other on the fly if you so choose to see what works best for you. Two controllers are heavily recommended though if you intend to play splitscreen, just to keep things simple and fluid. Although setting up Player 2's Controller can be met with some trepidation and it gets equally hairbrained when swapping between Controller and mouse & keyboard as some UI features in the game are not yet fully supported, which can be incredibly frustrating in the heat of the moment when zombies are nipping at your heels and wanting some of that tasty, tasty flesh that is wrapped around your bones.
Button prompting right now I have noticed; is also a slight issue when for example you are stood next to a window attempting to break into a house that could be full of useful supplies such as food, medicines or weapons and the 'Open Window' or 'Smash Window' button prompts appear on screen. Often, my character did not respond until I had shuffled myself into a pinpoint spot on the ground to begin the animation, despite the so called option having been available on screen. I would have suspected my little avatar to have slid into that position to carry out what I asked of him, but alas this is not the case. So awkwardly fumbling about is a survival concern right now and is one that is not appreciated when I am being pursued by reams of the undead.
However it can lead to entertaining (albeit stressful) scenarios that take you in a direction you didn't expect, one playthrough in local coop for example had my girlfriend and I raiding a Motel for medical supplies of which we were desperately running out of. I decided to move up to the top floor where a balcony overlooked the street, trying each door with no succession due to the (once living) populace being careful to lock their front doors, I took it upon myself to smash through the window in order to coax any zombies out of hiding in the apartment. As I stumbled through the dark looking for the light switch I accidentally opened the bathroom door to three maybe even four sets of gaping great jaws coming at me in true Romero fashion. In blind panic I ran back through the apartment and jumped out the window, cutting my hand and bleeding profusely. It didn't stop there however as I must have hit 'B' to vault over twice and I ended up taking a dive right off the upper floor balcony, breaking my ankle in the process and falling into the clutches of one more zombie who must have heard me breaking the glass window upon my initial entry. After my girlfriend arrived to batter the zombie attackers brains into the pavement (and not a moment too soon!) I was heavily bleeding, with a broken bone and worse, I was now bitten.
In agonizing pain, I bandaged my wounds with a ripped sheet covered in disinfectant and munched down on pain pills like they were tasty sweets, desperately trying to calm my avatar down from the mortal death that now loomed its ugly head in my direction. My girlfriend took off down the street in desperation to find me a set of crutches or a splint that might set my broken foot, leaving me with the First Aid box she had managed to scavenge in another room. Slowly, I walked along behind her, wracked in terrible pain and fear as she played human shield, clearing the way as we moved down the infested streets with the shambling of undead corpses. We eventually made it into a local doctors surgery where we attempted to perform some kind of medieval practice of fixing up my character with any and all types of unknown medication we could find. Suffice to say it was all in vain as no more than a mere hour later, I had succumbed to my fatal wounds and passed away in the most ironic of places.
PZ has a clever mechanic of dealing with peripheral vision in which it allows you to see only what is in front of your line of sight meaning in order to see what is behind you; you will need to turn around and face that direction. You can use this to scout through windows of buildings to see what rooms you are breaking into and more importantly, if there is anything nasty lying in wait, but you will not see what is behind a locked door or around a corner for the obvious reason that the human eye cannot see in four dimensions. Making cooperative play with friends an absolute necessity. This is a game where you need to coordinate with your partner/s and treat every building and every room therein, as a potential deathtrap, but an oh-so rewarding one if you can find a can opener for those twenty cans of tuna and baked beans you have been lugging around the past half hour.
There is an abundance of lootable buildings in the game, ranging from the aforementioned doctors surgeries, hospitals, churches, trailer parks, cabins, shops and so on and so forth, all littered with supplies that up your chances of survival, but just because you have a few hiking bags full of orange juice and watermelons, will not be what saves you nor should you take the brazen cocky approach of assuming you are now untouchable because you have a gun or a hammer or even an axe, this style of thinking will punish you with death and wipe hours of playtime.
You can fortify most any structure in the game and craft items like bandages from sheets of cloth, wood plank barricades from scraps of wood and grow a garden and cook your own food and full meals at that if you have a gas stove or microwave on hand! effectively turning John Doe's house in the suburbs into your own private Fort Knox. From here you can monitor your supplies, treat injuries with time and careful practice, potentially build up communities and bring order to the chaos of the apocalypse around you. Its enthralling, time consuming and so much fun.
So what has been learnt from this experience? That even the best laid plans can go awry. Inventory management is key in knowing what you have, what you need and when you need it and that often one supposedly safe escape route can lead to a quick death.
In a world so harsh as depicted in Project Zomboid, friends and family can boil down to nothing more than trust and a good exit strategy.

While I'm not sure where to actually begin contemplating what this game meant or tried to do, very few games have made me feel emotionally confused in so many different ways throughout and after finishing. This is especially impressive given the one hour window it takes up.
There is very little here to nail down as an element worthy of recommendation but I feel that the whole experience deserves to be had by anyone with a vague interest in its premise.

Let's start with the good things.
The gameplay is exactly how I remember it from the original, game-jam, tiny Superhot game that is still available for free on the internet. They take the concept of "Time only moves when you do" to an awesome action-movie extreme, and there were levels that stood out as awesome B-movie action sequences - for example, exiting your cubicle at the office, throwing your suitcase at an enemy with a shotgun before he can shoot at you. It's great.
Unfortunately, that's the end of the praise, and it isn't much. The only good thing I can say about this game is that it takes the gameplay from the original Superhot, and adds in a couple of good moments. Most of the levels in the game are boring, unimaginative, and poorly executed. One level starts with a car rushing at you, and basically guarantees you'll fail it at least once - the level can only be competently tackled after failing it, which is pretty dumb. Other levels (especially at the end) are just a slog, sending hordes of red guys at you with no interesting environments or weapons at your disposal.
The slog levels come in more frequency and more headache towards the end of the game. I'm pretty cynical, so I think this is to artificially increase the playtime of the game. Which it desperately needs. I took my time with this game, and frequently rewatched my playing a level because it looks awesome in realtime. Despite all this, this game took me a whopping
to play through in its entirety. But there's more. I didn't time it, but at least 20-30 minutes of that playtime was spamming enter or click to skip through the atrocious game narrative.
The narrative itself is not only extremely boring, but extremely poorly executed. The game frequently takes you out of the exciting, fun gameplay to put you in a jail cell, or walk you through featureless hallways without any reason whatsoever. There's one point where it literally requires you to quit the game completely, and launch it again, in order to progress. I felt like the story was supposed to be something like Hotline Miami, but instead of intriguing, it just felt stale, recycled, and uninspired. And it was constantly being forced onto me in annoying, unskippable format.
What's worse is that the game breaks the 4th wall in these sequences, recognizing itself as a game, and acknowledges that it is prohibiting you from playing the actual FPS gameplay. It's almost like it thinks it's clever for taking you out of the only part of the game that is actually any good.
And that's just the thing - you look at the positive reviews for this game, and they describe it as innovative and unlike anything they've ever seen. But that's absolutely wrong. We have seen this game before - the original Superhot prototype, which as I have said, is free on the internet. Innovation requires taking risks, and the original Superhot prototype's "time only moves when you do" was a huge risk. When the developers learned that the risk paid off (the prototype was an instant success), they decided to make a full game.
But this full game doesn't take any more risks than the prototype, which is a huge misstep. It doesn't expand on the original gameplay or add anything of substance - the only change is the inclusion of the shotgun and assault rifle (both of which just create slog moments instead of cool moments) and the very late-game ability to swap places with an enemy (which sounds cool but is really pretty useless, cheap, and boring in practice).
To wrap it all up, I'll return to what I said was good about this game. It uses the same gameplay from the free original prototype, and it adds some cool moments such as the cubicle. However, for every cool moment or level, there are 2 frustrating moments and 3 extremely boring levels. Because this game frankly doesn't add anything substansive to the original prototype, you're better off playing that instead. It only lasts about 10 minutes if I remember correctly, but every map is interesting, fun, and a nice mix of action and strategic puzzle-solving, and it costs exactly $0. This game lasts about 70 minutes, about half of which is tedious and stupid narrative, and is mostly a safe FPS with little to no strategy involved, costing an outrageous $25. In my mind, it is absolutely unacceptable.

Time moves very slowly when you stand still, regular speed when you move.  This means the levels focus primarily on efficiency of movement rather than your ability to aim.  SUPERHOT is really more of a puzzle game than FPS, though the FPS aspect is one of the key puzzle-solving mechanics.  Enemies always spawn at the same locations but move depending on where you are in the area, so your task is to figure out the best order to maneuver, disarm, and kill enemies while dodging their bullets and melee attacks.  Many levels take multiple attempts to figure out the best order, and the slow moving time means it is possible to get shot by an unseen enemy behind you while you're standing still, but overall it is a very fun experience.
Many new game modes open up after beating the campaign.  You can replay the campaign with certain modifiers to the rules.  There is also an endless mode that allows you to take on waves of enemies for as long as you can survive.  These are interesting and provide some additional replay value to the game.
I also really liked the poly-art and minimal color scheme.  Gives the game a very clean look.

Let's face it, the only appeal for this game is its omage to golden era of hand drawn cartoons and animations; it is visually stunning and the music is superb; the gameplay however, is a very different story.
If this game didn't feature this visual style and music, it wouldn't be as positively reviewed as it is; it is a very flawed game from a gameplay standpoint.
This game isn't difficult by nature, it's RNG based, which makes the game more difficult than it needs to be.
You will often land in a situation where if you didn't move quickly enough through a section, you can get stuck between a rock and a hard place, somewhere where you inevitably have to take a hit in order to progress.
The game comes with a "co-op design", however, in many levels, especially the "run and gun" ones, you end up realizing that the levels were not designed with 2 players in mind:
- if one player makes a mistake, you both pay (which can be a good mechanic, but its executed very poorly here)
- it gets harder to distinguish your placement on the screen (and to tell yourself apart from your partner) since everything is pretty flat and in a state of chaos.
- you will more often than not be halting progress from your team mate since you hold the camera back (or vice-versa).
If this game was any other game, these flaws would be pointed out and it would be called a bad game, however, the visual style and music is what shines here and that is probably the only thing that should matter to you.
One thing you do have to take into consideration is that, because the game is so fast paced, you don't get to analyze every environment and fully enjoy the details (but you will be familiar with it after your 50th retry).
Whether you should buy this game or not begs one question: Is the pain of enduring poor game mechanics worth the treat for you?
Well here is my answer:
- if you are a nostalgia child, go for it, a few bloody stools didn't kill anyone... well... it did kill people with bowl cancer, but that's beside the point!
- if you cannot stand bum bum torture, then skip this and watch a playthrough.
But it's worth a try, worst case scenario, you can ask for a refund. (Steam refund T&Cs apply.)

If you haven't figured it out already, this game is essentially Power Rangers. With a bunch of comedy, hilarious dialogue, memes and 90s pop culture references thrown in for good measure. That is to say, it's a lot of fun to play, especially if you're old enough to remember the 90s.
Fundamentally, the gameplay is a tactical turn based RPG. You pick your squad members at the start of the game (and use them for the entire game) and upgrade them along the way. There's no levels, you can buy new equipment and unlock new skills as you progress through the story.
Unfortunately, this game is not perfect and I have a few issues with certain aspects of this game. Hopefully the devs can address some of these issues at some point.
1. Tutorial
The tutorial is very light on details and skips over certain fundamental game mechanics entirely. It doesn't provide any information on what the Chromatize button does, or that you need to use it to use your finisher move. Additionally, there is very little information on what the different audience stats and numbers mean in terms of gameplay and what the different stats from the advertising agencies actually do to affect that.
2. Movement and combat
Each character can generally perform two actions per turn (outside of certain free action abilities marked as such). This is fine, but the implementation is quite annoying at times. You first move action, regardless of whether you moved the full distance or not, takes up a full action. So if you moved closer to use a ranged ability and found yourself one tile too far away but still had enough movement range to do it with your first action, you have wasted the turn since to move the one additional tile will take the full second action and you will not be able to use your ranged ability.
It's also hard to see where to position squad members to use abilities and teamwork without actually moving them and seeing what they can do next, compounding the frustration from the abovementioned issue. I would like to see some kind of move planner that lets you plan out all the moves for a turn (with an undo) to queue up all the actions, and when you're done setting it up, it all happens at once when you end the turn.
3. Crafting
Random item drops might sound good on paper and work alright in a game with infinite random monsters to farm to eventually get what you need, but in this game it pretty much means that you'll generally be buying most of your equipment, especially since crafted items have random stats that may or may not be what you actually want/need. Save your resources for upgrading the mecha.
3. Snowballing failure
Because of the story structure of this game, if you don't have the right equipment to do a mission and don't have money to afford it, you're stuck. If you do poorly on an early mission, you'll be short on cash for later missions, leading to a snowball effect of frustration with no solution other than starting over. The game is long enough that this could become rage inducing, especially given the difficulty spike at the very end. Thankfully on casual difficulty the game is easy enough that this isn't an issue at all, but could become a major problem on higher difficulties.
Related to this is the major difficulty spike for the last mission, especially the final mecha battle. Tactics and equipment that worked just fine earlier in the game suddenly become useless since you're now faced with lots of new enemies and abilities. The final mecha battle has no rounds where your mech can recover, so if you didn't equip your mech with an active heal ability, you will lose, even on casual since you won't be able to heal at all, but the boss can and has a lot more health than you.
Overall though I had a lot of fun playing this game in spite of my enthusiasm being dampened by the difficulty spike of the final mission. Easily recommended, especially if the devs keep working on this game and address some of the aforementioned issues.

The Park is a first person horror walking simulator made by FunCom, the makers of The Secret World. The game is about Lorraine, who returns to the titular park to search for her son, Callum, who has run off into the park in search of his teddy bear.
Well, maybe.
This is one of those games that relies rather heavily on mind screw, and at the end, it isn’t really clear what is real and what is fake, or even what actually happened. The protagonist is clearly going crazy and being messed with by The Park, but in the end, the whole thing feels slightly pointless – you walk around the park in a disguised linear loop, but while you see stuff and get to know Lorraine a little bit, ultimately I was left feeling cold. Why should I care? What greater context is there? Some bad guy built an amusement park on bad land and something bad happens as a result. All of the horrible stuff doesn’t really touch me because I’m left wondering why I should care about any of it; there’s no greater connection to the world, and Lorraine isn’t a particularly sympathetic protagonist.
As a walking simulator, the only gameplay is walking around and clicking on stuff; there’s a few dozen interactive objects within the game, including a few rides that you fade to black to get into rather than organically climbing into them for whatever reason. There’s a couple weird scenes that feel kind of inconsistent with everything else and make little sense until you get towards the end, and even then, you might not realize what it meant unless you think about it (I didn’t realize what a certain scene involving electricity meant until I was writing this review).
As there isn’t really any gameplay, and the story is confusing and kind of hollow, I’m not really left with a whole lot here. The game looks nice enough – the parking lot at the start of the game looks nice, as does the park at times (especially when first entering), and there is a nice “blood running down the walls” effect, but the game is a rather generic haunted park, and while some moments are nice visually, on the whole there’s nothing particularly memorable about the game.
As a fan of The Secret World, I did enjoy the nod towards that game in the ending, and indeed, the whole game takes place in a location in that game (or at least an analogue thereof), but, really… I just couldn’t bring myself to care about this game.
My recommendation? Avoid this.

I have a love/hate relationship with Five Nights at Freddy's.

Probably my best (worst?) and first experience with Bonnie resulted in a couple of broken computer accessories and very sore kneecaps.
Seriously, the rabbit might not appear all that from a distance, but that's no ordinary rabbit. Just look at the bones, he's got a vicious streak a mile wide.
All in all, I definitely don't regret buying this game, nor do I regret playing it.
I do, however, regret not being ready for Freddy.
Definitely worth a play or fifty, whether you're prepared or not.

A game built as Art seldom succeeds as Art, and this is no exception.

To be clear to anyone curious about this: This is very much an "Art Game". You're in this for the experience. There's very little gameplay to be had beyond walking around and flipping an occasional switch, and hearing the narrator's commentary. If you're down for that, you'll probably get a 6/10 artistic experience out of it, while if you're in this hoping it's a Game, well... not so much.
Overall: Maybe the message that it wants to share with me is facile, or it's a lesson that I've already learned in life, so overall I found the artistic impact of it limited and at times the experience was tedious. On the flipside, hot *damn* is there some beautiful aesthetics hiding in this game, especially nearer the later half of the story. An interesting take on "weighed decision-making" roleplaying. At first, I read other reviews and agreed about 30 minutes in and thought "Yeh, this is mostly luck based". And that is partially true. Most cards come up at random, and its really the luck of the draw. But believe me: when you are sitting at home playing Solitaire, it is ALSO the luck of the draw, is it not?
Anyway, the game is fair, and when you begin to balance the weighed choices to the point where your rule is lasting over 30 turns/years, you get what the game wants. The turn-based style works very well, and allows different effects, such as establishing trade routes to increase money the more you think about the next decision. But what's more intriguing is that unlike most RPG's or Strategy games where if you get a max out on everything it just stays there, it actually causes your reign to end. If you become too rich in power, you end up choking on food from the lust of power and greed of welfare. You become over-populated? Your kingdom riots the streets. Your army too strong? They overthrow you. Religion becomes too Zealous? You become a martyr for the church.
All in all, it's a really interesting game, and definitely am enjoying it so far. It can be frustrating at times, but what is nice is that you can only move forward as you fail, and the more you fail, the more you learn what choices NOT to make.
Definitely a hidden gem of a game, and definitely worth $3 (which is what I like most about this well-rounded game).

Reigns is a sort of choose-your-own-adventure crossed with a collectible card game in which you take the role of a monarch making decisions that affect that state of your kingdom. It essentially boils down to resource managment, with each decision either making positive or negative effects on your church, people, army and wealth. To succeed for as long as possible, you have to balance out your priorities, as having too much or too little in any one 'resource' will result in a untimely death. Learning the effects of card choices lets you make strategic decisions and extend your reign, but the longer you play, the more new cards you will unlock, with new consequences. When you eventually die, you start again with the next in line for the throne, and the game begins again with the card deck randomized, meaning  that, although you know what the cards do, no two play throughs are quite the same.
The game has a nice, minimalist aesthetic, and although it seems to have been designed primarily for mobiles, it works perfectly fine on PC, and even has controller support, which was a surprise. For the price, it really is a steal; the minimalist style really belies the games systems and it is hard to stop playing once you get into it.

The Long Dark is a very niche game. So before buying it, you should ask yourself: "Just what kind of game do I want to play?".
As someone who thoroughly enjoys survival games, and had become rather good at staying alive (at least most of the time), The Long Dark provides new challenges, and a new atmosphere. To me, there are key points to consider when you are contemplating getting The Long Dark. These are the sense of realism, the atmosphere, the art style (for those of you who care about that), and, of course, the challenge.
Realism: As far as games go, TLD is very, very realistic. So much so that it can be a double edged sword. Perhaps the main goal of the game is to keep your calories up, while avoiding death via cold, wolves, or even bears. Or falling off of cliffs. As far as food consumption goes, the game is about accurate. You need to consume roughly 2000 or so calories per day to stay healthy. I am currently in a trapper's cabin leaving snares out for rabbits, because I used all of my ammo for my rifle, and lost my only arrows for my bow. The constant need for food is a pressing matter, and realistically done. The same applies to the cold. The cold itself will make you cold if you're unprepared (not wearing adequate clothing), but the wind will expedite the process. What was interesting to me, is that I found that by standing by a wall of other surface while the wind was blowing (on the other side), it actually created a wind shield. This can become very important for when you need to build a fire. You can't do so in the middle of a gale of wind. The realism as far as mechanics go is really solid. However, then there is the other side of it. Playing TLD is not a rapid paced game most of the time. You often choose to walk to avoid burning necessary calories, you will often have to stop traveling and find shelter when a blizzard comes in, and avoiding the hostile wildlife is often better than fighting, as things can go wrong really fast. What you end up with, is a very realistic experience. This is a battle against the elements, not tangible foes. As such, the game can sometimes feel like work. It can feel slow and lonely. You have to be ENTIRELY self-driven. If you are the type of person that likes this level of realism (like me), then you will likely enjoy this aspect of the game. If you are the type of person that prefers faster paced games, then TLD may not be your cup of tea.
Atmosphere: The atmosphere of TLD is phenomenal. From the sound of the wind, to the voice actor's brilliant work, to the gradual lighting of a sunrise or sunset, TLD have a fantastic atmosphere. I first really noticed during a blizzard in the game. I had gone inside of a camp ground cabin to avoid the cold. As I stood there, I could hear the wind raging outside, the house creaking under the wind, and my character's labored breathing (I had sprinted to the cabin). The general lack of background noise is often a boon as well. It is just you, surviving-not thriving, but surviving-in the middle of nature. When the background music occasionally surfaces, it only adds to the feeling of cold and isolation. The atmosphere is a strongpoint for TLD.
Art Style: TLD uses a paint-esc art style (I'm not sure what you would name it). It is consistent, and achieves a good effect. Rather than focus on core realism, the art style comes across as realistic, without having to be as graphically intense. If you truly care about the art style though, watch a video rather than read a review :P
Challenge: The challenge is always there in TLD. Whether it's food, warmth, or safety, you will unlikely become a Fat-cat while surviving. Thanks to a sort of leveling system for various skills, such as fire-starting of carcass harvesting, your character will gradually get better at survival skills. This is a boon. There is also a wound and sickness system to watch out for, and bleeding to death or getting mauled by a wolf sucks. My one complaint, however, lies with the perishability of food and items. Things spoil in TLD. This normally wouldn't be an issue. However, when you pick up matches, canned food, or even a freaking sardine can, you would expect those to last for a dang good long while. Instead, as if your character has some kind of entropic aura, everything you touch (aside from tools) gradually goes bad. I found this out when I examined my canned food stockpile and it was all going close to rancid. Even lighter fluid goes bad. You can maintain certain tools, light a lantern, a hatchet, a gun, etc. But your means of doing so are limited, and I am sure that once my magnifying glass, fire striker, and matches go bad (because in this game a magnifying glass breaks via using it), I will end up shivering in a shack and eating raw rabbit meat, as I fist fight wolves for the rabbit's intestines. It's not a pretty picture.
All in all, The Long Dark is a fantastic survival experience that I would strongly recommend. If you are willing to overlook the attrition rate of items, it will make for a wonderfully good time.
Pros:

SUPERHOT is an innovative game where time only moves when you move. Whether that be physically moving, shooting, punching, or whatever else there is, your enemies and bullets pretty much stay in limbo until you move.
The gameplay for this game is pretty fun, and you can take your time or rush through it. There many ways to kill enemies, and the game is very smooth, even when playing in 4k resolution. I played the SUPERHOT demo back when it was still an infant a long time ago, and I hadn't bought it and played it until now. The main mode is a level based system with an odd story (if there is really one at all), and each level gets harder with more enemies.The game also introduces a body swap feature later on into the game. Once you beat the "campaign?" you can unlock endless mode, which is debatably more fun because you can just keep shotting and killing red enemies. SUPERHOT also features a replay mode where you go through what you did in real time, instead of delayed time when you were playing. Overall, I can say nothing but good things about the gameplay.
The art of SUPERHOT is simplistic but good. I enjoyed the sleekness and color scheme of the games. It made the game very easy to go through on the eyes, and it definitly made my game run smoother on 4k resolution. I know there is a VR version of this game, but  can just imagine how cool it would be. Apart from the art, the "SUPER HOT" narration was actually kind of annoying after a certain amount of times.
Overall as a game, the "campaign" isn't very long and you can easily finish it under2.5 hours. However, there are other things to do after the "campaign" ends, including challenges and endless mode. Although these things add to the value of the game, the game is still SUPER SHORT as a whole.
I would strongly recommend this game as it is very fun, just not for full price as it is a bit short for the price tag.

This a pretty grim zombie survival simulation with the same tone as the original 1968 Night of the Living Dead.
The game (in its current state) is still bare-bones in a lot of areas, but it is certainly playable and very fun.
I find it comparable to the roguelike Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead, but with a more focused theme and, of course, graphics.  If you've heard of Cataclysm:DDA, you're probably already familiar with Project Zomboid.  Both games require you to manage your health (mental and physical), supplies (food and water), comfort (dealing with heat, cold, rain, sleep, etc).  In my opinion, PZ is more visceral.
Zombies in the basic game (Survival Mode) are dangerous and scary without resorting to "modern zombie" gimmicks like fast running or supernatural powers -- aside from being, you know, undead.  You can customize the zombies to your liking in Sandbox Mode, as well as other scenario options.  There is also a Last Stand game mode where you fight never-ending waves of zombies, if that's your thing.
The interface can be somewhat clunky, especially managing storage containers, and there are some bugs here and there.
I have only tried multiplayer as split-screen co-op, which is apparently experimental.  However, this is easily my favorite part of the game.   We played using Rock Candy XBox 360 controller for one player, and the regular keyboard and mouse for the other.  One thing to be aware of is (at the time of this review), certain important functions are not accesible via the game controller -- specifically, the ability to zoom your view in/out, and frustratingly, the ability to view your character's Health or Skills.  You can work around the health issue by having the other player "examine" the one using the controller and apply first-aid/bandages as necessary.  However, not being able to access your skills to level up is a big pain in the rear.  If/when they fix these issues, the game would be worth the purchase price for the co-op alone.
Update: Apparently you can access a bunch of menu items using the controller by pressing the Back button (the button opposite the Start button), including the Health and Skills menu.  My gripe is that this info is not readily available to the player, and I only figured it out by accident after pressing all the buttons at random to see what they did.  Still, being able to access the skills and health status means that co-op is very viable!
Intellectually Challenging, Makes You Think Differently Than Just A to B.  Overall Great Game, Especially, If You're Playing Offline.

I'm going to lead with the strong points: It's funny as hell if you like absurdist humour. The presentation is good, the animated assets are pretty simplistic but fluid, music is pretty great, it's a novel concept, and there are times when I had fun with it. But despite all the blood, sweat and tears that have gone into making a more functional release of the game, it turns out that even functioning (mostly) as intended, the design of the game makes for kind of a crapshoot experience.
In a nutshell, the crippling blows are inconsistency and frustration factor. Jetting around on that laser pulse is not an accurate science, and the hitboxes of spikes and other hazards are extremely unforgiving. When you die, you will typically reappear on the last patch of solid ground you stood on, but the detection for this is picky sometimes, the laws of mechanics change from level to level, and some levels require you to make a series of ridiculously precise jumps and hovers before touching down, making for some insane difficulty spikes. On certain levels or when dying to certain hazards, death will restart the level entirely. Sometimes level elements STILL don't behave as intended, particularly in the candy world. Level design as a whole often feels redundant and amateur, making you do the same sorts of jumps with different mechanics and layouts, rather than exploring more varied ways of using the existing mechanics like the laser-bending bolts.
Besides the laser, there are levels that give you similar but varied means of propulsion, some of which are more fun than the laser but you see very little of, others which are interesting in theory but due to their implementation are just a further frustration in control factor.
The Remastered edition has done this much: it stabilized the game, and retooled the boss levels and chase sequences to give you 3 spare lives, rather than switching back and forth between "infinite lives" and "no lives" on a case-by-case basis. It also added several new lines for the characters, which unfortunately stand out rather blatantly and don't sound as good, but whatever. I was, finally, able to complete the game rather than throw up my arms somewhere around the halfway point after falling through the level and breaking the scripting for the Nth time. I would even say it's maybe worth picking up at the $3-$5 level if you have a high tolerance for frustration factor.
Personally, I'm just glad to be done with it, able to watch the ending, and not have it lurking in my half-completed games list forevermore.

Hah! This game is too much fun. For anyone who enjoys turn-based strategy RPGs, with plenty of customization, cheesy chiptune music and intricacies that are easy to learn but difficult to master... Pick this up, even at full price.
Here we have a game where you manage a crew of actors/actresses of your choosing, filming a television show with a brand new studio. The two big elements to this game are when you're in the studio (business management mode), and when you're recording (combat mode). Both are fleshed out quite well--when you're in the studio, you *will* spend a while making tactical decisions as to what agency to sign with, what to craft/buy and for whom, and how to gear up your mech for the upcoming fight.
Combat is a whole 'nother beast. It isn't *terribly* complicated on the surface, but the addition of being able to enter a "Teamwork" state where you can either combo with others or, more importantly, catapult off them to gain some extra movement and set yourself up, that's where it gets interesting. It's a little reminiscent of throwing people around in Disgaea (similarly, the whole game has a Disgaea-ish feel to it). In fact, if I didn't know any better, I'd think this was a direct offshoot of the Super Sentai-esque characters from Disgaea, but that's just because this is also a tactical RPG and it's a common trope.
In addition, adding a layer to combat, in each scenario you have a pair of "Director's Instructions," which net you bonus points (referred to as "audience"). These are tallied at the end to give you money and "fans" (which are effectively points that allow you to benefit from more of your chosen agency's bonuses).
PROS:
* Though it's not for everyone, and can get a little repetitive, the cheesy, chiptune, over-the-top music is great.
* Also subjective, but I find the combat to be just plain fun, and hard difficulty will provide no small amount of challenge for the perfectionist. Mech combat is no exception.
* Very deep game overall. Seems like something I'd give another playthrough.
* It's funny and cheesy without pushing either of those too far.
* Nicely animated for 2D sprites.
CONS:
* Some of the stats are a little unclear, and there seems to be no in-game explanation for most of them. Some of them are self-explanatory, some aren't. This might not really count as a con, but the UI could have used some cleaning up.
* Can't undo accidental misclicks in combat. In fairness though, that can be chalked up to human error, it's not like it's easy to misclick.
* No toggle to see the tactical grid, which has led to some poor choices in gauging how far away I've been from an opponent (another reason I wish there was an undo function).

Especially in this current paradigm of expansive, open-world games with so many distractions that detract from the key focus, Bioshock could be deemd a claustrophobic masterpiece. A city of dystopian corridors under water, where the scene from each step tells its own unique and horrifying story. Everything has environmental purpose, and it feels like the developers carefully, lovingly, touched all of it.
The sounds are a constant barrage, signaling danger, adding to paranoia, informing pending challenge. They give the tight hallways a great and enexpected depth.
I played through first time on Hard. But only because I'd watched friends play it years ago. I still regret not just giving myself the time and space to enjoy the game more. It was really hard. Rosie was always the most effort. Ammo felt weak and sparse. So the bulk of my playstyle adapted to sneaking around and using the wrench.  Some people have mentioned they ended the game with loads of cash and excess items that they didn't know what to do with. Playing it on hard, I ended with like $9 and went in to the final battle with no rounds in my pistol.
Exploring all of Rapture was an endless curiousity. Never did I feel like a dead end had let me down. There was always several well-balanced rewards given for venturing into a side room. They always added depth to the story and usually offered rare items. The hacking puzzles were a welcome break from the game play.
The disorienting maze of the city adds to the insanity of Rapture. Viewing the map was almost no help. Sometimes I would look out the windows and notice a marquee for a part of the city I had recently visited. I thought, "Okay I'm next to that place, I guess!" Otherwise, I felt lost on every level and it was only when it was time to move on that I felt like I was just beginning to know my way around. I relied heavily on the golden arrow at the top of the screen to point me along.
Quick Points:
-I don't prefer any of the crosshairs. I wanted to turn them off. I think they made the whole experience feel less important.
-The physics framerate needed to be patched, but that was a quick fix.
-The sound was choppy during heavy action. I didn't look to see if there was a patch for that.. It wasn't so bad.
-The golden arrow navigation thing was not my favorite way to move forward. It did feel a bit like part of the "Would you Kindly?" story, because I had to think less about where I was going. It worked in the sense that I almost never got lost or frustrated with getting lost.
Overall:
After 8 years this game holds up. Maybe even a beacon... Despite the city's dim-lit environs.
Its good to be back!

Reigns is a sort of choose-your-own-adventure crossed with a collectible card game in which you take the role of a monarch making decisions that affect that state of your kingdom. It essentially boils down to resource managment, with each decision either making positive or negative effects on your church, people, army and wealth. To succeed for as long as possible, you have to balance out your priorities, as having too much or too little in any one 'resource' will result in a untimely death. Learning the effects of card choices lets you make strategic decisions and extend your reign, but the longer you play, the more new cards you will unlock, with new consequences. When you eventually die, you start again with the next in line for the throne, and the game begins again with the card deck randomized, meaning  that, although you know what the cards do, no two play throughs are quite the same.
The game has a nice, minimalist aesthetic, and although it seems to have been designed primarily for mobiles, it works perfectly fine on PC, and even has controller support, which was a surprise. For the price, it really is a steal; the minimalist style really belies the games systems and it is hard to stop playing once you get into it.

A suprisingly good starwars game despite the glut of terrible ones produced by the late Lucas Arts.  It has a very strange system that I have not seen in a game that I remember.  You have the campaign map, but it is not static.  You generate money pretty quick and the enemy can attack you at anytime.  The land and space battles are similar to say what total war is on a much smaller and different scale, but there is no pause after on the campaign.
The difference in difficulty between the rebel campaign and the imperial campaign is huge.  As the empire you should have no problem steam rolling the alliance.  Imperial ships are heavily armored, carry free tie fighters, and have more fire power than most rebel ships.  Your land units will also destroy people.  ATATs can produce squads of free storm troopers meaning you have the best anti veicle and decent anti infantry that cost nothing.
The alliance campaign on the other hand can be frusturating.  Get read to have the auto resolve tell you that your fleet can own 10 victory star destroyers only to play it out and be destroyed.  Because you rely on figters so much, and the Y wing is your only chance against imperial capital ships, its devastating when a Tantun cruiser kills almost all of them in 10 seconds.  Managing ships is hard.  With the empire you just send in your gugernauts and they kill everything.  With the alliance untill you get the assault frigate expect to see your capital ships blown out of orbit.  The nebulon B frigate (medical frigate) is really only good at giving Luke a robot arm and being blown to peices.
Luckily even if you cant hold space, you can hold planet surfaces if you invest in defenses.  The battles can be tense though.  But just as shields are hard for you, they are for the enemy.  Rebel infantry are really good, just watch out for the over powered tie maulers who can just run your entire army over at 60mph.
Still the best starwars RTS I can think of, and there are lots of mods.  I think there is even a 40k mod.

A solid title that stays true to the survival genre, and stands out in a sea of overdone zombie games.
+ Highly interactive world, with lots of choices and a lot of freedom (e.g. you can fish, cook, farm, craft, build a safehouse, drink bleach and die, etc.)
+ Good number of realistic and detailed survival mechanics
+ Lots of items, with many uses (e.g. you can form a rope by stringing clothes together to descend from higher ground safely, or rip said clothes to create makeshift bandages)
+ Unique traits system (balance good and bad traits when building characters)
+ Very large maps with a variety of locations (e.g. neighbourhoods, town squares, beaches, forests)
+ Includes a very flexible sandbox mode that allows players to customise the world, the zombies, and player settings (you can even go against running zombies for the whole 28 Days Later experience)
+ Ability to speed up time up to 3x, reduces wait time for time-consuming tasks
+ Supports both online (up to 64 players) and local (split-screen, up to 4 players) multiplayer
+ Zombies can jump scare you
+ Has official modding tools and level editor
- UI design is not very user-friendly and intuitive, may take some time to get used to
- Controls are not very intuitive, and gamepad does not play well with some UI elements
- Lack of map system to see where you're going, with many long roads that lead nowhere - you may sometimes go for long walks and never come back (although vehicles are planned for future releases)
- Currently, lacks a storyline or at least objectives to work towards (purely sandbox as of now), so like most survival games (The Forest, The Long Dark, DayZ, etc.) you pretty much make your own goals - may be dull for some; but from what I understand, there
be a story mode in the final version

This game, although I've only played 5 hours up to this review, has the best magic system I have ever seen in my life. Although the effects are not great, obviously due to its age, the way you cast spells is quite fun. You literally draw runes in the air to cast spells. It's very innovative and I'm surprised that nobody else picked up on it. If it were to be put into another game with more spells with modern graphics and effects, the game would definitely win many awards.
The dungeons can be confusing, for there are many tunnels within a dungeon and you have no sense of direction where you're supposed to go. You have to keep up with the story to know what you're doing. If you aren't going to use a walkthrough for this game, you may find it quite difficult. For example, for one of the quests you need to get back a Troll idol. To do that, you have to go to the Goblin fortress. You then, without an actual direct hint, after a long time of just wandering around in there, may decide to move a pillow to find a key to continue the quest. Where does the key go? Just try it on everything that's locked there. It's very confusing. Although, the dungeons do have quite a dark ambience. The only thing that may give you fright is when you don't have sound on and are not expecting a monster to creep out of the dark or attack you from behind, then making you panic as you're trying to gesture the correct runes to cast a spell and kill them. Another example is when you didn't know you had to stake zombies to actually kill them and they end up creeping up on you from behind. I mean, it's not scary, but the fog, darkness, and old style graphics and sound just give you anxiety (not that it's a big deal).
The combat is pretty good. It's not too easy or too hard. The runes, in my opinion, are not hard to do and I only have 5 hours into the game. I don't see why people are complaining about it in their reviews. It most definitely does not take long to get good at casting. It may take some practice for some people, I guess. Melee weapons are nice and take some skill to use. One must avoid being hit whilst trying to go on the offensive, and the only real way is by hit-and-running or attacking from long range, such as with spells are archery. I have yet to use a bow, so I can't really go into that. Along with magic, you can precast spells. You can precast up to 3 spells so you have them ready when you're actually going to fight so you don't have to gesture a spell while you're trying to stay alive against some monsters.
The story is pretty good. There is plenty of humor in the game, such as goblin kings with digestive issues and horrible goblin mom jokes. The lore behind the entire story is quite interesting. Humanity and monsters live underground, due to the sun disappearing and the freezing of Earth, making the ambience darker yet, knowing that your character has probably never even seen the sun. Although, with that, there is a loophole. You can find and buy plants that somehow feed themselves without the sun and the fact that humans need the sun to survive. If the lore means that there is no sun, at all, then their "solar" system would just be flying wherever they want in space or attracted to another planet's gravity. I guess it makes level design easier, simply needing walls, a roof, and a ceiling, not a background of trees and hills and a sky with clouds. Thinking outside of technicality, it's pretty good.

The Arx Liberatis patch goes to your steamapps->common->Arx Fatalis-> (drop contents of zip here). One other tip- do not cast Raise Dead in a public place before you acquire stakes. It's not a good idea. Neither is casting Summon.

It is nice to see a survival game that has a different premise than zombies. This game is about a geomagnetic disaster that caused your plane to go down in the Northern Canadian wilderness. A story mode is in the works about some aspects of the game (including the plane crash) as of this review being typed. That mode has been stated to be giving a backstory on the disaster occuring...and will hopefully be super awesome.
Even then, the sandbox mode itself is great. Before you start a game you decide what difficulty you want to play on and where you would like to start out. Then, you show up in the cold, desolate wilderness.
After that it is all about survival.
You can explore where you want and choose what you would like to do. Making decisions can leave you feeling lucky or completely out of luck.
For example, you can drink dirty water and feel fine, but the chance of suffering from dysentery may be too big of a risk to take.
And to be blatantly honest, there is no luck in this game. Every decision comes back to bite you in the butt at some point because the wilderness in this game is despicable. And that is what is so unique about this game.
There are no exceptions.
There are no do-overs.
You will feel the full vengeance of Mother Nature whether you like it or not.
The world is beautiful looking and the sounds will truly make you feel like you are surviving in the unforgiving Canadian wilderness. The weather changes too (and affects how easy it is to survive). I remember there being a blizzard one night where you could barely see anything and barely tell time and then there being a clear day the next morning. The sound and visuals are truly 10/10.
You can play in the same areas over and over and get a different playing experience each time too since loot and your starting location are randomized. Also, you can still venture in a different direction than before and hope for the best.
By clicking spacebar you can see all of your items in your backpack and all of the items you are able to craft. Your backpack has some items in it to start, but they are given to you stringently. They are just enough to keep you going for a several days if you're lucky.
The crafting system is easy to learn since everything is laid out in such a way that in a few clicks you have what you need. This isn't to say that you can just craft whatever you want when you want. Of course you need the adequate supplies to craft something, but you need something more: energy.
Crafting, sleeping, walking, and basically everything else for that matter will cause you to burn calories as well as time. You have to be strategic in when you decide to do certain actions. From a game standpoint, this game nails realism as best as it can.
Even injuries will affect different game mechanics. Sprained wrist? You can't hold weapons. Sprained ankle? Walking sucks. And so on.
~~WHAT I WOULD CHANGE~~
If I were to change anything I would rather have the temperature and day/night hours always on the main playing screen (still having the question marks there when a blizzard occurs).
~~OVERALL~~
This game doesn't reinvent the survival genre. This game is reshaping the survival genre to meet different needs. This game isn't for people who want to come by resources easily and just enjoy the outdoors. This game is for people who want to feel like they are walking knee-deep in snow, avoiding a bear, struggling from a sprained wrist, and hoping to get warm...all at the same time.

I thought this game was excellent.. for conflicting reasons. I thought the philosophy behind the individual "games" themselves were extremely unique and beautiful, I really liked the phonebooth and cleaning one. I loved the first half of the narrative, up to around the theater game. *SPOILERS* I don't like the way the narrator flipped the narrative and made it about himself. I thought the first half was a really beautiful admiration piece and the second half felt kind of self indulgent (of course, in a negative way but self indulgent nevertheless). I felt that the creator did a really sh*tty thing to Coda by telling people he was depressed and sharing his games against his asking. I do not know however what conversations did occur between the narrator and Coda. Having said all that, I do think that even though what the narrator did was pretty sh*tty, ultimately it was probably the best decision to make. I feel that Coda's games probably reached people who really needed them and people who could really appreciate them. I liked the way the narrator guided me through them and hacked them to make them more accessible. Being somebody with depression, I know what it's like to feel suffocated by somebody who just wants to help. I definitely see a lot of good in the narrator but the self depricating cry for help at the end felt unnecessary. I think this game could've been a very touching tribute to Coda (Rather the subject became the narrator) I also  can understand the anger felt in response to that last game. This review has kind of spiraled into my opinions on the narrator but overall I think it's a great game. Very clever game composed of very clever games with very clever narration and direction. The end took a spin for the worst in my opinion (feeling meaningless, self indulgent, flat and anti climactic) but still a very well executed first half. Extremely interesting character study on someone who perhaps didn't want to be studied. This game felt very vital, charming, and comforting. I think Coda's work opened some things within me I hadn't felt before and will most likely do the same for anyone with any sort of psyche. Useless numeric score: 8/10
