An absolute little blast. It starts off with a bang and throws you head first into your time travelling alternate dimension journey.
It starts of silly, and gets crazier as time goes on. I think this is a real little gem of a game, although it could do with being priced a little lower.
Your basic weapon is a giant laser like beam weapon you both use to fight the giant beast attacking your future self, and to propel yourself around the map and obstacles. The mechanics are simple, propel yourself around spikes, traps and and platforms to catch up to your currently being mutilated future self and save him. It's not easy though, it's really not easy; but the music, sense of urgency, and cries from your future self are hilarious and blood pumping.
Did I mention there are hats? Yes, you can collect hats through the zones, and secret little areas and become all the fashionable rage as you travel through space and time battling space crabs and saving yourself. You can also press spacebar and do a little jiggle dance. For extra awesomeness get the funkiest hat, and jiggle and laser your way through dimensions.
After finishing a set of areas and a boss battle, you get to the starting area with floating orbs. Blow these up and you have a portal to yet another dimension, with new enemies and yet another self that needs saving as they're being mauled.
It really is a fun little game, it might not look like it has a story but it does. As convoluted and confusing it might appear as you play at first. Things do make a bit more sense as you progress.
It's darn fun, the looks well and plays well. If it has a leaderboard I'd probably always be at the bottom, but hell it's fun.
Biggest issue is the price, it's a good game. Is it worth €14,99 though? That's hard to say.

A really good semi-realistic 'Battlefield like' World war 2 first person shooter game. If you like World War 2, good weapon feel and cooperation with your teammates give it a try.  Full review follows.
"The earth shakes by artillery shells, bullets whistle around your head. Where is your squad? Alone you're just a piece of dead meat. Eventually they will find you. And kill you."
Red Orchestra 2 Heroes of Stalingrad is set during the battle of Stalingrad in 1942 in conflict between the Third Reich and the Soviet Union. Red Orchestra 2 Rising Storm takes place in hot and wet jungles of Pacific where United States and Japaneese soldiers are struggling for their lifes.
The game offers three basic play styles: Realism (semi-simulation, but not as 'hardcore' as Arma series e.g.), Custom (with modified parameters) and Action (less realism, more action and shooting! It plays a little bit like Battlefield games), and three game modes: Territory (similar to Conquest in Battlefield), Firefight (basicly Team Deathmatch) and Countdown (this mode isn't played at all as much as I know).
It has fair variety of well known period weapons like K98k, M1891, MP4o, PPŠ-41, MG42 (RO2HoS) or M1 Garand, Arisaka type 38&99, Thompson, Type 1oo or B.A.R. (RO2RS). Weapons in RO2 have real kick - if not aimed or even proped by the wall, it's sometimes really hard to hit something. Especially when you're under fire and heavilly supressed.
The game offers also wide variety of maps. From destroyed city of Stalingrad and wide steppes of southeren Russia to dense tropical forrests of Pacific islands or barren black beaches of Iwo Jima.
Red Orchestra 2 puts a lot of emphasis on cooperation with your squad and whole team. You're useless alone.
There are also classes in the game: Rifleman (the backbone of the army, always in the first row, carries a bolt action or semi automatic rifle, holds and defends positions), Sapper (or Enigneer, know how to handle explosives, carries a submachinegun), Assault (storms enemy positions armed with grenades and submachinegun or automatic rifle), Marksman (armed with scoped rifle so that he can spot or pick out defending enemies), Anti-tank (armed with heavy and most of the times useless anti-tank rifle), Squad leader (commands a squad, armed with submachinegun or semi-automatic rifle, smokegranade and binoculars, he  can choose artillery bombardment spots) and Team leader (this gentleman commands whole team).
Every class have separated progression system which grants you some bonuses when playing as the class. The ultimate level is 'hero' level, which grants you unique appearance and special combat buffs for your teammates.
Weapons in RO2 have also their own progression system: this have three stages (worn - well used - new). When unlocked, the second and third stage grants slightly better handling of a weapon (less recoil, faster reloading speed) and different appereance too (Stage 3 - new - weapon looks better than stage 1 - worn-). These weapon stages (or levels) also unlock some features of the weapons such as bayonets, better optics or alternative firemode.
(I don't think this progression system for weapons is necessary in semi-simulation game, but some people likes to unlock new things. Howewer, I can't imagine playing a game just for unlocks.)
In RO2 are also vehicles - T34/76,  T60 and Panzer IV. Vehicles have very detailed interiers, you can see other members of your crew and the rest of the tank.
RO2 has also really good soundtrack - personally I like the original 'Heroes of Stalingrad' one. It has real punch, created by singing of army choir (similar to Alexander Ensamble). When this plays and you are loading your last clip to the rifle and the Germans are coming, it adds truly heroic feeling to the game
My overall rating of RO2 is 8/10 - really good game, but your gaming experience depends on people you're plaing with. If you're in a uncoordinated team and your enemy is just a bit more coordinated, it is frustrating as hell. You're still in the spawn queue and that's really not fun at all.
But if you play with your friends on teamspeak or skype or whatever you like to use, it's really great. And if you'd like to play in organized group and if you're interested in army stuff, find some of 'divisions' (or clans/guilds) and ask them if you can join. Try 29th Infantry division. They're tough guys and they demand obedience and discipline under fire, but playing in 'real army' like organised group is interesting expirience that I can only recommend.

A spunky, cool game featuring a squad of stuntmen and -women who set out to make a POWER RANGERS-style series.
As far as the gameplay goes: It's a mix of isometrical turn-based tactics and one of those management games where you get to buy stuff and outfit your office. Stuff like MAD TV. If you remember that one, then you're an old fart like me and you probably just missed the super sentai-craze of the mid-90s, because you considered yourself too old and prefered mature stuff like those XTREME era IMAGE comics. You know... the ones where superheroes hat 5000 pouches. But I digress. Gameplay-wise, CHROMA SQUAD is really nifty. There are three difficulty levels and the middle one is just right in my opinion. I'm too old to get really good at any game - once you pass the magical 30, you come to find that life won't allow you to play video games for ten hours a day. And when I say "life", I mean "spouse", you know what I'm sayin'? Not that I'm complaining! Just saying it like it is, yo. Droppin' knowledge. Yo, yo.
The thing I like best about this game, is its sense of humour, though. Really. Usually, I find games that try to be funny annoying. There is something so endearing about CHROMA SQUAD that I just can't bring myself not to chuckle. You can see that the makers are not trying to make fun of POWER RANGERS and the like, they are paying hommage, but in an oddball way that really has heart. As referential as the game is, its references are never ham-fisted and they don't pander to geeks moe-stlye. They're actually quite cute.
So. There you go. If you were to ask me "Gaston, shall I buy this game", I'd answer: "Go for it." And then I'd add that if you remember MAD TV, you should google it, because there is an online version of it that you can play in your browser.
Peace, out.

It looks back on it with modern eyes, pokes fun at it's own expense, but completely embraces its nostalgia. I loved it!

Seeing as how my old review was over a year and a half old, and TRS decided to shock some life back into the game by making it free to play, I figured I might as well rereview the game.
- - -
Excellent game
Thanks to TRS, this asymetrical multiplayer shooter / wildlife eating sim has returned. The relaunch is featuring redesigned versions of old maps, a complete power rebalance, and more. Some changes include more powerful early monsters, meaning even a Stage 1 can wipe the hunters, should they play their cards right. Everything in the game, with the exception of a few skins exclusive to Founder members (people who bought the game before the release of Stage 2), can be bought with Keys, the free currency you get from playing the game.
Not a huge fan of the reduced match timer; I've been barely able to get halfway to Stage 3 before the 2 minute warning starts pestering me. Also, gameplay in hunt has been retooled for faster and more action-packed, which means monster stealth has been nerfed considerably. The reduction in monster stealth means that the Trapper, once the person in charge of locating the monster, has been relegated to the position of CC monkey, which is unfortunate.
Overall, it's still a good game; plus, since it's now F2P you probably have very few reasons not to at least give it a try.

From the open-endedness of the game to the challenging enemies in the atmospheric environment, The Forest deserves every praise it gets. The developers prove their commitment to the game with its continuous updates that keep in mind the feedback given by the players.
I've played this game for a good amount of time, and I am not even close to finishing it, mainly because I keep getting distracted by the sheer amount of objectives you can accomplish and items you can create. After all, this is a crafting game as well. I cannot emphasize how many different things you can do in this game. Do you try to find your son? Or do you build a gazebo?
The players will be taken aback by the plethora of environments within The Forest and the many things they must and can do to survive- deer skin to keep warm in the snow, a rebreather to go spelunking in caves, and fire to increase your vision in the night.
It has also earned its rightful place as a Horror game. When the sun sets and there is nothing to be seen for yards away, the player will find themselves finding the nearest shelter as soon as they hear the howls of the cannibals and the scurrying of whatever bumps in the night.
However, for those who aren't big on the demented wailing of cannibals or the sudden jumpscares that happen when they suddenly appear behind you at night, there is also the 'peaceful' mode. Peaceful mode takes away the human enemies and emphasizes the focus on its crafting feature. Or you can just take a stroll in the woods, there's that, too.
It's a perfect single-player and an even better multiplayer game. I certainly believe it is worth more than its normal price of $15, so writing this review during the Autumn Sale makes it a steal.

This is a fairly straight-forward tactical RPG. It has an interesting twist where you run a TV studio filming a "sentai" style action show. For those unfamiliar, that means it's a Power Rangers style show. You get to make a few personal touches as far as Squad name, transformation name, Mech name, and a few other options. You're also in charge of upgrading your studio, some basic marketing options, as well as purchasing or crafting new equipment.
If you've ever played a tactical-RPG, you know what to expect. You get a movement and an action, or two movements. There are free actions which are the exception. There's also a teamwork feature. A member of your squad can throw you further increasing your initial movement. If they are adjacent to an enemy and you attack with another member, they combine their attack and do increased damage. There's also a finishing move if you have 4 members using teamwork and you attack with the 5th.
The pixel graphics are actually well done. Most of the sets look very nice. The details in the character models are nice, as well. Some of the suits look cool. The retro soundtrack is also nice, but you can mostly just play it with the sound off as it gets rather repetitive. Of course, graphics and sound aren't the important part of a game like this so I'm sure you won't be drawn to get this game just because they're not amazing.
This game supports a controller, but it thinks my Xbox controller is a Playstation controller. A minor complaint, but a little weird. Also, and this is annoying, you can't use the controller for the Mech fights. Pretty aggravating to have to use the mouse.
So, if you're interested in the genre, and the theme appeals to you, go for it. Especially if it's on sale.

Reigns is a relatively fun game. It's not without it's flaws, but it has it's moments. I think the problem is that it feels kind of repetitive, there are apparently about 1000 cards to swipe through in total. Having played for about 90 minutes, I experienced just under half of them. A lot of the cards you read will be the same card you've read several times over, and while the game's progress seemed to be moving along at a decent pace for the first 40 or so minutes, it hits a plateau around then. What I mean by this is that you end up with a checklist of goals that you're supposed to accomplish to progress the story and unlock new cards. You end up waiting for well over a hundred years in game for the corresponding card to appear, and there's little or no noticeable reward for performing the tasks to complete your goals. The other aspect of the gameplay is the resources management, which is seemingly nonsensical, but it serves it's function adequately. You need to balance your citizens, the power of the church, your treasury and your military powers to keep everybody happy. For example, your Bishop may ask to buy executive power, causing your religious and monetary spheres to rise. If any of these spheres raise too high or drop too low, your monarch will die and your heir will take over at the beginning of the next year. It's worth mentioning that you will automatically have an heir, so you can die during your first year in power with no consequences. Each new year is marked by a new event, represented by a card. You control the response to the events of the card by clicking to the left or right of the card. Sometimes, you trigger an event with a side effect like "Money is perpetually rising on a timer which operates opposite and contrary to the rest of the game's mechanics to make life more difficult". The game is structured in such a way, typically, that you can take as long as you'd like to decide which reaction you'd like to pick in response to each card drawn, and the timer implemented by these events makes it damn near impossible to form even a rudimentary strategy. Especially because of the way the UI is laid out, which makes it wholly unclear whether your decision will lead to increases or decreases in each sphere.
Taking into consideration that this game is only $3, these things are likely forgiveable. It's got a nice art style and minimally irritating audio. It's a good time killer for a few hours, maybe more if you really enjoy the mechanics of the game. I guess I'll give it a cautious recommendation. Worth a try when it's on sale.

So this is going to be a bit tricky in terms of whether I recommend this or not. On one hand I absolutely adore the .hack series and was really excited when I heard about a remastered version was coming out on Steam. But on the other. . . I'm very unimpressed with this port. Don't misundertand, it boots up and doesn't crash and the graphics resolution is clearly way better than it was on PS2 but just about everything with this "remastered" version screams laziness. The interface is so wonky and not at all designed for a PC and getting back to the main game menu requires restarting the game. Incredibly stupid way to go about things since that's the only way you can change the game to match your screen resolution or activate V-Sync and Jesus are you going to need it. Without V-sync this game tears like crazy. Also, so many of the game asssets weren't upgraded at all when it comes to thier texture resolution. On top of all this if you plug in a controller you have to use an Xbox controller since a play station controller just doesn't work at all. In addition the controller will just randomly stop working and you will have to use keyboard and mouse again and only restarting the game will get the controller to work. Another problem in terms of visuals is the god damned cutscenes, which were not reworked at all, will run fine and then slow to a crawl randomly. No clue why this is happening. I've got a pretty high end rig so this kind of performance dip just makes no sense at all. Very poorly optimized and, overall, it looks like CC2 just went for a quick cash grab with very little effort whatsoever put into making this for PC gamers. So if you have already played the .hack series and have the Ps2 disks . . . use pcsx2 emulator and play them on your PC it will run way better in my experience although you will have to fiddle with the settings to get it just right. If you've never played the series before and don't have a ps2 then this isn't that bad and you might find it to be an amazing game with perhaps a few frustrating caveats with the interface.
Edit: The issue with accessing the steam settings was not well explained on my part. You can get to the title menu from within the game but for whatever reason you cannot change the settings without a restart in my case. Not sure why, hopefully a patch will come out that solves that inconvenience.

- No maps that highlight buildings or areas of affect. Want to know where your religious buildings are, or how far they're effective? Me too. Pity it's not possible. Making people happy is practically guesswork.
- No insight into where your money is going. At one point I was haemmoraging money. No idea why since I can't see where my budget is going so I couldn't see where I could save money.
- Rebels. It took me literally 4 hours saving every few minutes to get past one particular rebel uprising. I had to build a hospital at high priority and upgrade the army a bit and even then I only got through on pure luck. Again, maps would have helped me make the population happy. It turns out a supermax prison with the upgrade to automatically capture rebel leaders and crime bosses makes a massive difference.
This is the first Tropico game I've played and it took me a while to realise what it was all about. It's not detailed enough to be a city sim (it'd be nice to get hints like if I imported more steel I could output more cars and make more profit for example). Also game mechanics like you get one ship per dock = 1 trade route, the fact you need lots of schools/colleges for an educated workforce, etc. weren't obvious, and you're not really helped with some things until too late.
Overall I'd recommend this game, but really the lack of maps showing the types of buildings really surprises me. It's a basic feature of a city builder and without them the game is frustrating. On the plus side, it runs on my laptop where Cities Skylines ground to a halt after a few hours.

This is a great game. A fantastic RPG inspired by Ultima Underworld, with a fully realized world and lore and smooth gameplay, especially considering its age. It's kind of an open world as well, but taking place entirely underground in labyrinthine dungeons and tombs and mines and caves and ruins and all the kinds of locales that are vital to a game of this nature. A good story, fine plot and action, and no grinding or tedious quests. Everything is tightly related to the story or worldbuilding, and quests are often complex, with interesting puzzles unlike I've seen in any other RPG. The rune magic system is unique, MYSTICAL & ENIGMATIC, the combat is a little clunky and slow, but considering the game came out around the same time as Morrowind, it's a step ahead of the competition in that regard. Exploration is rewarding and enjoyable, enemies are challenging, progression is steady, and there's really nothing bad or mediocre to say about the game.

It is nice to see a survival game that has a different premise than zombies. This game is about a geomagnetic disaster that caused your plane to go down in the Northern Canadian wilderness. A story mode is in the works about some aspects of the game (including the plane crash) as of this review being typed. That mode has been stated to be giving a backstory on the disaster occuring...and will hopefully be super awesome.
Even then, the sandbox mode itself is great. Before you start a game you decide what difficulty you want to play on and where you would like to start out. Then, you show up in the cold, desolate wilderness.
After that it is all about survival.
You can explore where you want and choose what you would like to do. Making decisions can leave you feeling lucky or completely out of luck.
For example, you can drink dirty water and feel fine, but the chance of suffering from dysentery may be too big of a risk to take.
And to be blatantly honest, there is no luck in this game. Every decision comes back to bite you in the butt at some point because the wilderness in this game is despicable. And that is what is so unique about this game.
There are no exceptions.
There are no do-overs.
You will feel the full vengeance of Mother Nature whether you like it or not.
The world is beautiful looking and the sounds will truly make you feel like you are surviving in the unforgiving Canadian wilderness. The weather changes too (and affects how easy it is to survive). I remember there being a blizzard one night where you could barely see anything and barely tell time and then there being a clear day the next morning. The sound and visuals are truly 10/10.
You can play in the same areas over and over and get a different playing experience each time too since loot and your starting location are randomized. Also, you can still venture in a different direction than before and hope for the best.
By clicking spacebar you can see all of your items in your backpack and all of the items you are able to craft. Your backpack has some items in it to start, but they are given to you stringently. They are just enough to keep you going for a several days if you're lucky.
The crafting system is easy to learn since everything is laid out in such a way that in a few clicks you have what you need. This isn't to say that you can just craft whatever you want when you want. Of course you need the adequate supplies to craft something, but you need something more: energy.
Crafting, sleeping, walking, and basically everything else for that matter will cause you to burn calories as well as time. You have to be strategic in when you decide to do certain actions. From a game standpoint, this game nails realism as best as it can.
Even injuries will affect different game mechanics. Sprained wrist? You can't hold weapons. Sprained ankle? Walking sucks. And so on.
~~WHAT I WOULD CHANGE~~
If I were to change anything I would rather have the temperature and day/night hours always on the main playing screen (still having the question marks there when a blizzard occurs).
~~OVERALL~~
This game doesn't reinvent the survival genre. This game is reshaping the survival genre to meet different needs. This game isn't for people who want to come by resources easily and just enjoy the outdoors. This game is for people who want to feel like they are walking knee-deep in snow, avoiding a bear, struggling from a sprained wrist, and hoping to get warm...all at the same time.

Tropico 5 is an iteration in the series - and really only that. Very little will feel new, while many of the old annoyances still shine through along with a fresh batch of new ones. On its own I wouldn't say that it's a bad game, and in fact I'd recommend it if you're new to the series and it's on sale (especially if you're on linux/SteamOS and can't get the earlier ones), but if you played Tropico 3 or 4 and are looking to try out the latest...I wouldn't waste your money. You mind as well stick with Tropico 4.
PROS
- New buildings are pretty cool. Good variety, nice set of upgrades.
- Technology and building unlocks stretched out over historical eras (colonial, world wars, cold war, etc)
- Can assign buildings managers which gives perks, such as +10 efficiency or +20 worker happiness, etc
- Decent trade system
CONS
- Combat and invasions make literally no sense. A handful of rebels can annihilate a fleet of TANKS. They'll pop off their rifles at tanks, taking returning explosive rounds right to the face, but one by one your tanks catch fire. Just in general there's an unfortunate lack of balance or common sense in the combat mechanics.
- Related to combat, the AI is pretty atrocious.  Your soldiers will run around to the nearest targeted buildings in the most scatterbrained fashion imaginable. For example, I was invaded by the axis powers from the south side of my island (sounds cool, I know - but wait for it) where, despite having AMPLE troops available to defend, proceeded to destroy the bulk of my city...I'm talking expensive factories, guard posts which served at best as easy target practice...and why? Because my battalion of heavily armed vegetables decided to chill out by some corn farm at the north end of the island. One unit of tanks spent about 3 minutes going back and forth on the same road kind of glitched out, or maybe they were just feeling indecisive, who knows. I mean I don't expect Tropico 5 to be the gold standard of combat or RTS battles or whatever you'd call it, but come on!
- Infrastructure still has bottleneck or "gridlock" problems, just like the other Tropicos. Whenever population gets to around 1000 the roads tend to get bogged down really bad. Usually most of my production takes a steep dive. I think using the metro stations (like the T4 Modern Times DLC) can help alleviate this to an extent, but I always felt like these games were missing the tools we need to make the city's traffic run more efficiently. Multiple lanes, traffic lights, traffic circles. This is also probably an AI issue once again because cars will take the shortest distance to the destination regardless of how backed up it is, so side roads get underutilized.
- Way too much content is DLC
- Happiness system seems fickle..you people get free food and healthcare, shut up!
Not trying to be super critical here, this is a really fun series. But very little effort has been put into improving certain mechanics, and it's to the point where each new Tropico is starting to look like just a rehash with new buildings, a few gimmicks and way more DLC than anyone needs.

A really good semi-realistic 'Battlefield like' World war 2 first person shooter game. If you like World War 2, good weapon feel and cooperation with your teammates give it a try.  Full review follows.
"The earth shakes by artillery shells, bullets whistle around your head. Where is your squad? Alone you're just a piece of dead meat. Eventually they will find you. And kill you."
Red Orchestra 2 Heroes of Stalingrad is set during the battle of Stalingrad in 1942 in conflict between the Third Reich and the Soviet Union. Red Orchestra 2 Rising Storm takes place in hot and wet jungles of Pacific where United States and Japaneese soldiers are struggling for their lifes.
The game offers three basic play styles: Realism (semi-simulation, but not as 'hardcore' as Arma series e.g.), Custom (with modified parameters) and Action (less realism, more action and shooting! It plays a little bit like Battlefield games), and three game modes: Territory (similar to Conquest in Battlefield), Firefight (basicly Team Deathmatch) and Countdown (this mode isn't played at all as much as I know).
It has fair variety of well known period weapons like K98k, M1891, MP4o, PPŠ-41, MG42 (RO2HoS) or M1 Garand, Arisaka type 38&99, Thompson, Type 1oo or B.A.R. (RO2RS). Weapons in RO2 have real kick - if not aimed or even proped by the wall, it's sometimes really hard to hit something. Especially when you're under fire and heavilly supressed.
The game offers also wide variety of maps. From destroyed city of Stalingrad and wide steppes of southeren Russia to dense tropical forrests of Pacific islands or barren black beaches of Iwo Jima.
Red Orchestra 2 puts a lot of emphasis on cooperation with your squad and whole team. You're useless alone.
There are also classes in the game: Rifleman (the backbone of the army, always in the first row, carries a bolt action or semi automatic rifle, holds and defends positions), Sapper (or Enigneer, know how to handle explosives, carries a submachinegun), Assault (storms enemy positions armed with grenades and submachinegun or automatic rifle), Marksman (armed with scoped rifle so that he can spot or pick out defending enemies), Anti-tank (armed with heavy and most of the times useless anti-tank rifle), Squad leader (commands a squad, armed with submachinegun or semi-automatic rifle, smokegranade and binoculars, he  can choose artillery bombardment spots) and Team leader (this gentleman commands whole team).
Every class have separated progression system which grants you some bonuses when playing as the class. The ultimate level is 'hero' level, which grants you unique appearance and special combat buffs for your teammates.
Weapons in RO2 have also their own progression system: this have three stages (worn - well used - new). When unlocked, the second and third stage grants slightly better handling of a weapon (less recoil, faster reloading speed) and different appereance too (Stage 3 - new - weapon looks better than stage 1 - worn-). These weapon stages (or levels) also unlock some features of the weapons such as bayonets, better optics or alternative firemode.
(I don't think this progression system for weapons is necessary in semi-simulation game, but some people likes to unlock new things. Howewer, I can't imagine playing a game just for unlocks.)
In RO2 are also vehicles - T34/76,  T60 and Panzer IV. Vehicles have very detailed interiers, you can see other members of your crew and the rest of the tank.
RO2 has also really good soundtrack - personally I like the original 'Heroes of Stalingrad' one. It has real punch, created by singing of army choir (similar to Alexander Ensamble). When this plays and you are loading your last clip to the rifle and the Germans are coming, it adds truly heroic feeling to the game
My overall rating of RO2 is 8/10 - really good game, but your gaming experience depends on people you're plaing with. If you're in a uncoordinated team and your enemy is just a bit more coordinated, it is frustrating as hell. You're still in the spawn queue and that's really not fun at all.
But if you play with your friends on teamspeak or skype or whatever you like to use, it's really great. And if you'd like to play in organized group and if you're interested in army stuff, find some of 'divisions' (or clans/guilds) and ask them if you can join. Try 29th Infantry division. They're tough guys and they demand obedience and discipline under fire, but playing in 'real army' like organised group is interesting expirience that I can only recommend.

The Beginner's Guide is a narrative video game, a walking simulator, from the creator of The Stanley Parable.
The player is guided by the narrator through a number of incomplete and abstract game creations made by a developer named "Coda". During the exploration of those levels the narrator tries to make the player understand what type of person Coda is.
The gameplay is pretty simple, in first-person perspective the player moves through the levels and explores the environment and interacts with some elements of it from time to time while listening to the narrator.
Like The Stanley Parable, The Beginner's Guide is not a typical game with much gameplay mechanics, it is more like an interactive story.
The story can be interpreted in different ways, so two people who play The Beginner's Guide could still have different perspectives of the ending.
The voice acting is well done, it is absolutely enjoyable to listen the narration.
For fans of walking simulators a must have, for others probably not satisfying at all.

Excellent tactical RPG with a surprising amount of depth.
It's a bit of a business management sim on top of the RPG side, but they mesh very well together.
The game play works well, with plenty of options in combat to choose how you want to approach things, and a wealth of customization in the pre episode/fight setup.
A silly and offbeat story line with enough genuine comedy to make you laugh occasionally helps to spruce up the quality game play as well.
It starts off simple, so it's not difficult to learn but gets progressively deeper, and I can tell there is more to come. I'm genuinely looking forward to each new "episode" of the TV show you play in.
Difficulty wise, I'm playing on hard and it's just right for me. Hard enough I have to pay attention to what I'm doing and think out my actions, and most episodes I'm barely scraping through. Can't comment on how that would fit for others of course, but as someone pretty accustomed to this style of game hard difficulty has works nicely for me.
I'm not finished the game so I can't comment on length, but I'm a long ways from finishing and have put in about 11hrs on this save so far. So I'm confident there is a surprisingly large amount of content to play through.
I've heard tons of love given to the sound track for the game but... honestly I don't see it. It's not bad by any means but it's more decent and fits the game well, then anything truly memorable.
The visuals I really appreciate however, it's simple retro pixel graphics but the combat animations, movement, and even the special attacks are all very well animated and look quite nice. Lots of extra frills like a fast forward effect reminiscent of an old VCR on a CRT TV fit perfectly with the atmosphere.
I can happily recommend this to anyone who wants a lighthearted RPG, or just looking for something unique and different. Not much else out there like this.

Syder Arcade is a pretty decent side scroller shoot em up that I was able to complete within about 2 hours. The player is set in an horizontal arena and will either need to destroy all the enemies, escort carrier ship, or defend other large ships. The ship moves at a set speed and will go faster if you continue in one direction, but you will often need to flip around to deal with enemies on either side. Some enemies drop speed upgrades, weapon upgrades, and refiles for your health and secondary shot, which vary depending on your ship choice. The different playable ships also have different speeds and armor ratings.
I appreciate the the optional graphic filters that makes the game look like various old computer systems, but the game's visual design wasn't built for it, so the reduced colors, pixelation filter, and clashing smoothness of the actual game make them terrible for actual gameplay are they are essentially useless other than giving players a nostalgia trip - the CGA filters reminded my childhood Tandy PC that only had 4 colors in games.
$10 feels a bit much for a 2 Hour shmup. You can get some replayability by playing again with a different ship or playing survival mode. I'm pretty sure I got this on sale and I suggest you do the same.

I had a lot of fun with this game. I was a big fan of the D&D Cooperative Board games like Castle Ravenloft and The Legend of Drizzt and so I was very interested in playing through a digital version. The game feels exactly like the real thing, except thing you're playing as all the characters (1-4) instead of playing with friends. an online co-op experience would be great, but this is just as good, only different ala the digital version of the Pathfinder Card Game (Which you can also find on Steam).
I found this incarnation to be exceptionally easy compared to the older board games. I don't think that's because it is an electronic version, but rather the heroes vs the quests. It's very hard to die in this game (except for the wizard and bard) and I never failed a quest or even ended one with any of my four character immobilized or killed. The DLC helps makes this even easier (and I recieved it via the Yogscast Humble Bundle, giving me a reason to finally pick up this game dfuring the Steam winter sale) because everyone gets a legendary weapon which takes many hours of grinding off the game. I don't want to image how much you'd have to replay various adventures in order to get some of these items. By the time I finished every quest in the game (6.1 hours), I all all of the Ranger's legendary items, all but one of Dragonbaits and one for my mage and bard. So you'd have to put about twenty hours into the game if you wanted to get everything in the game.
There are a few bugs, like the bards healing spell only working on her despite the text saying everyone within a tile of her, and the acid arrow causing poison despite the text stating it will cause stun. Those are minor quibbles at best though and I definitely got my money's worth with the six hours it took me to complete this game. This is one of the better  recent D&D games out there and I'd love to see BKOM tackle to the older D&D board games from 4-5E that Wizards was churning out.

There is a warm comfortable place in my heart for all SHMUPS. Syder Arcade isn't a great game, but it's fun to play. The devs put in a lot of work to give this game a retro/arcade/funny feel. The text had a very 90s style because of it's poor grammar which fit well with what they were going for. It's an odd mash up of retro and modern. The power ups were plentiful even though it felt random what power up you actually got.
What set this game apart from other SHMUPS is that is added in a way to turn around. No longer are we obligated to move from left to right, but we can TURN AROUND! It's a nice novelty, but it doesn't change much other than direction. There's almost no real reason to use it.
Now for some of the downsides... Syder Arcade is more of a proof of concept than an actual game. It's way too short. I played 40 mins and beat the campaign, and even that time was with intermittent pauses so I could grab another beer. With all the effort they put into the player and enemy models, you'd think they'd throw in a few more levels. Another downside is the ships acceleration/deceleration seemed sluggish. Almost like it was on ice, even though you're in a spaceship.
Pros:
- Multiple ships to select
- Assortment of power ups to collect
- Great graphics
- Fun Audio
- Responsive controls (other than funky feeling acceleration/deceleration)
Cons:
- WAY TOO SHORT! Seriously, there is no reason this game should be so short.
- Power ups seem random and you never know which will be replaced when you pick up a new one.
- No multiplayer
Overall Syder Arcade is a decent game but feels like the devs didn't care about it and just wanted to finish it. That's really the only reason not to have a longer game or have multiplayer, even local. This game is definitly not worth $10. It's fun, just don't buy it full price.

Having logged countless hours in the retail version back when retail was up-to-date, I was eager to play it again and replay an awesome RTS in the SW universe.  Now before the actual review, I would like to warn windows 8 users: MAKE SURE THAT YOU DO NOT BUY THE RETAIL VERSION!!! You will find this game super cheap on Amazon, E-Bay, etc, but they will not run correctly on win8 systems. There is an official patch to fix this, but it doesn't always fix the whole problem. However, you will not need to patch and/or modify the game on steam to work :)
Now for the review:
Yes EaW is old, but it can compete with most current RTS games pretty well. EaW brings cool ideas to the table like space battles, hero units, and a conquest mode in which you have to conquer the galaxy!!! While EaW wasn't the first to do some of those things, they sure did them right. Ok now time for the generic Pros and Cons section:
Pros:
Doesn't feel repetitive
Has a large map variety
Explores a part of the SW timeline from an interesting new perspective
It's in the SW universe!!!
Space Battles
Balancing is ok (Aside from the Rebels and their suprise armadas out of nowhere!)
Zann Consortium adds a fun new play style
Cons
Kinda pricy for an old game
Graphics (Expected from an old game)
Battles should be bigger (There's probably a mod for that)
MP is dead :( (There are programs for running MP on Gamespy dependent games though, look up Evolve or Gameranger)
Rebels are really OP and can do massive suprise invasions
Conclusion:
If you like Star Wars, RTS games, or both, then buy this game. If you are looking for stunning graphics and scripted events every minute, then this game is not for you. I really wanted to like this. Apparently they've been working on it for over a year and they've still got a long way to go.
What I like: on balance, very little. It's got crafting and there's a lot of stuff for you to find and play with. You can set up a base camp in pretty much any building you want, going so far as to scavenge bed sheets and curtains from other places in order to cover the windows at your hideout so the zombies won't see you inside. That's neat and makes sense. The "world" (sandbox) is apparently pretty damn large with a lot of it being covered in trees where it's not roads, rails, and structures. You can wander into the trees and forage for... whatever you happen to get randomly generated. Berries, branches, twigs. Pretty much what you'd expect of wandering into the woods in Kentucky and not knowing what you're doing.
There's a skill and XP system. The more you do stuff, the better you'll become at doing it - once you've leveled up enough to actually buy the point. So, it's not like Skyrim in that you "level up" a skill as soon as you cross a point threshold. You need to put the time in as well as pick and choose what to increase level to level. I don't care for that, particularly because you can't continue gaining XP in a skill until you've taken that next level. In other words, no matter how much you successfully sneak around you won't actually get better at it until you spend at least five points increasing it. Which necessarily means you won't also get better at combat, or crafting, or healing yourself.
Healing is a big, big deal. You can look at my played time and see where I threw my hands up and said the hell with it. I got one minor scratch (as defined by the game) on my left hand. I found some disinfectant and used it on the injury. Well, for reasons unknown to me and left unstated by the game, that was insufficient. The bottle of disinfectant was not consumed or noticeably affected, the scratch remained A Big Deal that I was constantly alerted to with popups, and within 24 hours that single scratch (that I tried to disinfect) had me bleeding out as I staggered from building to building looking for... whatever the ♥♥♥♥ I was supposed to know I needed to fix the problem. No hint given, no helpful raccoon mascot popping up to say "Hey there guy! You need X to deal with that problem!"
This is a significant flaw and/or oversight in a game that stresses crafting so heavily. It's great if you've got an encyclopedic understanding of what does what in the game; I'm new here, I don't have that, and it's really goddamn dumb that in a randomly generated world I don't start off with specific, comprehensive instructions on how to deal with inevitable problems - like minor injuries that apparently incubate into Ebola within a day.
This is all in addition to no map of any kind. There's also a fog of war mechanic that keeps everything out of perception range as unbroken black. And even after you've explored it, exiting and restarting the game means your memory gets wiped (I guess?) and you forget all that stuff you saw. This is breathtakingly stupid in a game that seems to want to behave as realistically as possible. Turn on the stove, cook the meat, add spices, fulfill your hunger needs and stave off despair a little longer; steal curtains and bedsheets, black out the windows so you can huddle on a stranger's sofa drinking orange soda and imagining there aren't zombies outside trying to eat you. So with all these specific, thought-out attempts at realism in a zombie apocalypse evidently you moved into town five minutes before the♥♥♥♥♥♥hit the fan. Because you've got no idea at all where the city center is, where the police or fire stations are, where the hospital or veterinarian or ♥♥♥♥ing corner Walgreen's are. This is even dumber when you realize you start the game off choosing what amount to perks and some of those perks come with a job description: Police Officer, Fire Fighter, Park Ranger. Again: you may as well get air dropped into the city and be informed you landed on your head, wiping out all prior knowledge. Same result.
All of this is after at least 18 months in development. If you insist on giving them your money, wait till it's at least 50% off.

Arx Fatalis is a stellar dark fantasy game by Arkane Studios, the same group that would later be responsible for Dark Messiah of Might and Magic and Dishonored. This game is a spiritual successor to the legendary Ultima Underworld and was originally meant to be titled Ultima Underworld 3 but licensing issues got in the way. Arkane continued development despite these licensing woes and the end product was a dungeon exploration role playing game now considered to be a classic of the early 2000s. Unfortunately, Arx Fatalis launched at one of the worst possible times and went up against Neverwinter Nights and Morrowind, both of which drew attention away from this great game.
The most notable aspect of this game is the magic system which requires the player to find runes, through either exploration, reward, or shopping, and then draw rune symbols on their screen using the mouse. Certain spells require certain combinations of runes, and the player has the option to store up to 3 pre-drawn spells which can be accessed at any time. This system of casting means that the player themselves must become skilled and proficient at recalling rules and casting them, adding a very real sense of tension to combat where you are directly responsible for how well your character does, instead of relying on character or skill level like in other games.
Arx Fatalis also expertly does two things:
The game world is so large and sprawling that it would be daunting to otherwise throw you in to it without any guidance, so the approach in Arx Fatalis is to provide the illusion that you are on embarking on a linear quest: guards block your path, doors require a key, or you may not possess the combat aptitute or magic needed to advance to a new area. The reality is that nearly all of the impasses you may encounter can be circumvented without advancing the plot if you are clever enough and do not take a barrier at face value. This is not breaking the game or getting out of bounds like it may sound, and going where you think you should not can end up changing quests in ways you would not expect.

If you like games like Amnesia or Penumbra then boy, this will be right up your alley. In Outlast you play reporter Miles Upshur, who is looking to break a story regarding strange goings-on at a formerly asylum re-opened by a multi-national Biotech corporation. There's a great mystery to be solved when you play Outlast. But in order to solve that mystery you're going to have to run, walk or hide your way through 8 chapters of creepy gameplay. You aren't armed and you can't fight back which adds to the intensity of being chased through a beautifully realized asylum. Outlast is dripping in creepy atmosphere helped by excellent sound design. There are also plenty of gotcha moments with jump scares for the masochist in you. I completed the game in about 4 and a half hours which was perfect to me. There wasn't many things I didn't enjoy about this game. Maybe just a couple of the spots where I was chased got a bit repetitive.  Overall, Outlast gets a easy recommendation from me. Creepy gameplay at just the right length with a story that makes you see it all out makes this game a winner. Also if you liked this game, then the Whistleblower DLC is an absolute MUST. It fleshes out the story even more and is about 2 and a half hours. 8/10 from me for the whole 7 hour experience.

LYNE is a wonderful surprise. What I thought was going to be yet another average, indistinguishable piece of mediocrity turned out to be an incredibly lovely and enchantingly minimalist puzzle game.
In fact, LYNE is a rare and wonderful breed of puzzler: the one that isn't as interested in killing your mind as it is in trying to make you think calmly and cleverly.
(I mean, I haven't beaten the later levels, which I assume are miles more challenging, but the game's calm atmosphere contributes a great deal to the smoothness of the entire expreience.)
The fluidity of the puzzle solving feels like a breath of fresh air. The game controls smoothly (although the game can sometimes confuse one line for another) and the puzzles are open-ended, allowing the player to branch at least a few different pathaways through the level, even if the puzzle requires you to go through a specific idea.
The game will last for quite a while: The base levels will keep you thinking for days, and the daily challenges will have you thinking for weeks. And the game is great for quickly calming down and relaxing for a few minutes (or an hour).
Overall, LYNE is a nice, calm, lovely game that you can just keep coming back and relaxing too.
9.0 / 10
(One other thing: The game is 100% worth it as $3, but I have seen it go for a lot cheaper. It went for under a dollar during the last summer sale, and I have seen coupons that discount the game for really, really low prices. If you can, get it while it's on sale, but just know that the game is absolutely worth it either way.)

I have never been a huge Power Rangers fan. I only watched the first 2 or 3 Power Rangers seasons as a kid and I have ignored all other super sentai shows. This game made me regret that I missed out on so much.
+ Solid turn based tactical combat (think XCOM / Banner Saga / Disgaea / etc.)
+ Tongue in cheek humor that will dig its way into your heart
+ Awesome music
+++ Supreme commitment to its theme
- Mecha fights are kind of dull
- Later stages of the game can make side objectives frustrating
It's wacky, it's silly, it's fun, it will remind you of your childhood, the value of friendship, playing around with cardboard and wood back when your imagination had no limit. It oozes so much personality and it manages to both pay tribute to and satirize the super sentai genre and all sorts of other aspects of pop culture. It's a product of deep love and understanding of an entire subculture that most of us are barely aware of but the passion placed behind it transcends the limit of your knowledge and even personal taste to the point where it is impossible not to appreciate what you're seeing before your eyes.
The only reason not to play this game is if you really dislike turn based tactical combat. It's a really good game and an amazing experience overall.

So, what to say about this game...I can't recommend it quite enough for those into strategy games. You can play as the Empire or the Rebellion (or the Zaan Consortium, in the expansion) and battle against each other in skirmishes, campaigns or a free-for-all in galactic conquest. You manage the buildings on your planets, generating armies and navies. The ground combat is a bit lacking, but the space battles totally make up for it. Don't let my hours fool you, I used to play this game obsessively years ago, and picked it up on sale recently.
The only problem I have with the game is the balancing, in that there is none. It's actually kind of overshadows proceedings. If you want to play as the Empire, I'd give a couple run throughs of the Rebellion or Consortium first, because the Empire is severely underpowered compared to those two (until you get the Super Star Destroyer and the Death Star, which takes quite some time. Even then, they can only be in one place at a time). The Rebellion is pretty much unbeatable on the ground, having artillery that might as well just automatically win every assault, and the expansion gave them fast-moving torpedo ships that make space combat a headache. The Consortium generates credits so quickly they can just effortlessly throw massive armies and navies at you over and over until you Phyrric Victory yourself into the grave. Not to mention they've got the Canderous Assault Tank, which is so OP that ten of them can take out pretty much anything you've got. The Empire really has nothing to compare.
Still, balancing aside, it's a great strategy game, and if you love strategy games, you should definitely pick this up.

It is nice to see a survival game that has a different premise than zombies. This game is about a geomagnetic disaster that caused your plane to go down in the Northern Canadian wilderness. A story mode is in the works about some aspects of the game (including the plane crash) as of this review being typed. That mode has been stated to be giving a backstory on the disaster occuring...and will hopefully be super awesome.
Even then, the sandbox mode itself is great. Before you start a game you decide what difficulty you want to play on and where you would like to start out. Then, you show up in the cold, desolate wilderness.
After that it is all about survival.
You can explore where you want and choose what you would like to do. Making decisions can leave you feeling lucky or completely out of luck.
For example, you can drink dirty water and feel fine, but the chance of suffering from dysentery may be too big of a risk to take.
And to be blatantly honest, there is no luck in this game. Every decision comes back to bite you in the butt at some point because the wilderness in this game is despicable. And that is what is so unique about this game.
There are no exceptions.
There are no do-overs.
You will feel the full vengeance of Mother Nature whether you like it or not.
The world is beautiful looking and the sounds will truly make you feel like you are surviving in the unforgiving Canadian wilderness. The weather changes too (and affects how easy it is to survive). I remember there being a blizzard one night where you could barely see anything and barely tell time and then there being a clear day the next morning. The sound and visuals are truly 10/10.
You can play in the same areas over and over and get a different playing experience each time too since loot and your starting location are randomized. Also, you can still venture in a different direction than before and hope for the best.
By clicking spacebar you can see all of your items in your backpack and all of the items you are able to craft. Your backpack has some items in it to start, but they are given to you stringently. They are just enough to keep you going for a several days if you're lucky.
The crafting system is easy to learn since everything is laid out in such a way that in a few clicks you have what you need. This isn't to say that you can just craft whatever you want when you want. Of course you need the adequate supplies to craft something, but you need something more: energy.
Crafting, sleeping, walking, and basically everything else for that matter will cause you to burn calories as well as time. You have to be strategic in when you decide to do certain actions. From a game standpoint, this game nails realism as best as it can.
Even injuries will affect different game mechanics. Sprained wrist? You can't hold weapons. Sprained ankle? Walking sucks. And so on.
~~WHAT I WOULD CHANGE~~
If I were to change anything I would rather have the temperature and day/night hours always on the main playing screen (still having the question marks there when a blizzard occurs).
~~OVERALL~~
This game doesn't reinvent the survival genre. This game is reshaping the survival genre to meet different needs. This game isn't for people who want to come by resources easily and just enjoy the outdoors. This game is for people who want to feel like they are walking knee-deep in snow, avoiding a bear, struggling from a sprained wrist, and hoping to get warm...all at the same time.

I have never been quite as satisfied with a small steam purchase as I was with Arx Fatalis. This is a gem of a game and a spectacular RPG. The roughly 15 hours I spent playing this game were sublime and were enough to cement it into my memory and my list of favorite video games of all time.  Make no mistake; the game has flaws. However, if you can overlook some pretty bad voice acting and a relatively cookie-cutter story, and if you like RPGs with a classic feel, I believe that you will love this game.
As others have said, it is important to note that this game will likely not work perfectly on modern systems without tracking down and installing the Arx Libertatis community patch/mod. For example, when I booted up the base game for the first time, I found that my character would move at virtually the speed of light, smacking instantaneously into walls on the other side of the room with barely a touch of the keyboard while all other graphics on the screen were slowed to a crawl. With that out of the way, let me talk about all of the things I loved about Arx Fatalis.
Arx Fatalis reminds me a lot of the time I once spent playing King's Quest: Mask of Eternity. It is a game that is somewhat sparce on spectacle but ridiculously dense in detail and atmosphere. As is revealed in the first moments of exposition, the world of Arx is one in which the sun has gone dark and all of the world's inhabitants have been forced underground to avoid freezing instantly to death. Almost literally all of this game takes place underground, and the world the player explores is a complex, deceptivlely large and multi-layered dungeon, with end-game content hidden organically in plain sight right from the very beginning. Tight spaces, fairly excellent lighting and sound design, terrifying enemies, extreme amounts of environmental interactivity, and quests that require the player to research lore, remember important details and hoard potentially useful and plot-important items all combine to make Arx Fatalis one of the most immersive [emotionally, if not visually] games I've ever played. All of the game's underground environments feel oppresive. They are full of characters, monsters, secrets, riddles, puzzles and supernatural phenomena that all want to hold you back, and this makes the player's steady success rewarding and cathartic and their areas of safety a treasure. I, for one, found a long trek through the game's crypt to be a prolonged anxiety attack with just a sprinkle of paranoia and would lock doors behind me just to keep what's left of my sanity intact. You will be forced to think creatively, to sometimes take a few steps backward before forward progress is possible. Furthermore, you will sometimes be forced to interact swiftly with the environment under the looming threat of monster interception. All of this is great, except for when it isn't. If you're like most players, you will probably want to keep a walkthrough handy. My recommendation is to do your best to figure things out yourself and introduce just a little bit of frustration into your experience, but don't be discouraged if you need to utilize community resources, especially during the last 1/3 of the main story. It might also be worthwhile to keep a set of your own handwritten notes around just in case you plan to take a couple days off from playing.
If you have checked out more mainstream video game reviewing sources, you will have undoubtedly heard of Arx Fatalis's unique appraoch to magic. To reiterate on what they've said, I have certainly never played a game with a similar magic and casting system. Casting a spell requires you to draw out symbols contained on small little blue runes found throughout the game world in real time and in specific combinations. Yes, this can be finnicky at times, but it never really bothered me all that much; in fact, It was one of my favorite aspects of the game. The developers knew that using magic in combat would be pretty much impossible, so they included the ability for your character to store any combination of three spells for immediate future use. If you choose to invest the time into raising your casting skills and stats and hunting down all of the runes for your spellbook, you will have about 40 different spells at your disposal by the end of the game, and those are just the ones that are explicitly recorded in your spellbook. I assure you - there's more. You see, the runes that are used to cast the spells are actually like a whole language in and of themselves, and the spells adhere to the logic of that language. Much like how learning the roots, prefixes and suffixes of Latin can help an anatomy student figure out the structure and location of a body part, learning the underlying meaning of the magic runes allows the player to experiment and come up with new spells. Some rune meanings are obvious, but not all of them. I'll give but one non-secret example so as not to spoil the fun. The very first spell the player learns is one that lights up flammable light sources in the area, and the runes used in this spell are Aam [create] and Yok [fire]. Finding and tacking one more rune, Taar [missile], onto the end of that sequence turns a spell only useful for lighting torches and campfires into an offensive fireball. Pretty neat. It's also worth mentioning that the leveling system facilitates using the magic system to its fullest potential along with one or two other straightfoward combat specializations in the form of close quarters combat and defense or stealth and projectile weaponry and maybe even a skill like lockpicking if you are so inclined. In essence, a player can be a competent spellcaster [with access to every spell] and an axe-wielding armored tank maniac all in the same playthrough.
Overall, I can't recommend this game highly enough. It seems like there was a lot of love put into it by the developers, and there are quite a lot of things that I neglected to discuss in this review. Arx Fatalis is the textbook definition of a hidden gem, a diamond in the rough and imperfect perfection. You won't be disappointed.

LYNE Review - Raymond K. Turcotte
The reason why I bought this game was because I was granted a coupon for it. I'm happy i did! Bcause this is a challenging puzzle game that's addicting. But unfortunatly you might need a guide to complete it. The Achivements are pretty straight forward. Complete level A, Level B. "Simple right?" The game also had Tradeing cards witch is never a Flaw when it come money wise! Unfortualty i got doubles.
It's a very simple puzzle game, with one concept: connect like-shaped/colored blocks. You click on the beginning block of a certain color, and drag a path to the finishing block. It's very basic and simple, but it gets more complex when more colors are added, as well as when conjunction blocks are added that can have multiple paths go through them. I only got a couple hours of fun out of it since it's incredibly redundant, but if you're bored or want to exercise your brain a little bit, LYNE isn't a bad place to start. It has a very simplistic and sleek design, which isn't hard on the eyes. Also, for an asking price of $2.99, I can't really complain much. I've paid more for games that are much worse. Very fairly priced, fun concept, a little repetitive, kind of gets boring quickly.
I really recommened this Straight forward puzzle game with a Twist!

If you are getting the following error:
"A DDraw object has a non-zero reference count (meaning it was not properly cleaned up). This Program will now exit"
Some suggest to download "Arx Libertatis" to make the game work again which is a bit frustrating considering some of us already had the disc version and were counting on the Steam version to be future proof so instead of downloading a third party patch (which might still be beneficial) you can actually setup the “arx.exe” file to run in Windows XP (Service Pack 3) compatibility mode which will result in the following error:
“The program can't start because Steam.dll is missing from your computer. Try reinstalling the program to fix this problem”
So all you have to do is recover the Steam.dll from the Steam program files to the installation folder of Arx Fatalis and it should run along with the compatibility mode!

Ok, I have mixed feelings about this game and I love psychological horror games. I have played lots of them. First of all I would like to say that the settings of this game are done quite well. The amusement park is spooky and eerie and reminded me of those classic childhood horror movies of abandoned haunted parks. It felt really good to explore and soak in the atmosphere and enjoy the rides.
But apart from that the story is told in a very ambiguous way dropping us with some vague clues on what happened with the main character but clearly not explaining enough to build an assumed explanation. I have played a similar psychedelic horror game like this, "Layers Of Fear" and even though it was also ambiguous it clearly dropped enough clues to form some explanations on what happened.  While the story of this game is quite engaging it would have done some more effort to explain on what exactly happened. Add to the fact that I got to know later that it was made  as a spin off and is set in the same universe as another game "The Secret World" made it more confusing. I can think of one or two things that may have happened but not enough to get a satisfying conclusion. It could have been so much more as the game definitely had the standards to be a good psychological horror game from the rest of the things it did.
The rides in the game offered a little insight into the mindset of the main character and they were unique in itself. Also, the graphics were really beautiful and creepy and the game performance was good. I just wish the story could have been a little more polished so that I could have enjoyed it more. I never complain about the length of a game because if i enjoyed it for the time i played it then its good enough for me. You can buy this game on a sale and play it to experience the game settings and atmosphere of the amusement park. Other than that, I am hopeful the developers will make a more engaging story driven title in the future for us horror fans.

text:
This game makes you feel rather like an insignificant infantryman. You run around, a shot cracks in the distance, and you fall over dead, often not even knowing where the shot came from.
Red Orchestra 2 and Rising Storm are terrifyingly realistic. Players must account for bullet drop and taking cover is a must. Playing this game "CoD style", or running around the map shooting things, is a surefire way to kill yourself.
The cover system is well implemented. Once in cover, a player can peek and fire, then duck back into hiding. Staying exposed for an extended period of time will draw the attention of a sniper you will be picked off from a distance. However, even when behind cover, there is always the fear of a stray grenade bouncing over to your location, or an artillery strike raining down over your position. You are almost never safe.
The sound design in particular is superb, completely immersing you into the WWII battlefield. The crackle of gunshots, the screeching of artillery, your screaming comrades, and the shock of explosions all contribute to a pretty frightening war game.
The game also has a relatively small but active multiplayer community. There are always some servers that have a few people. The rest of the spots are populated by bots. These AI are relatively decent. They do know to take cover and can usually shoot to some degree of accuracy.
Gameplay itself is usually objective-based, encouraging players to play for their team rather than themselves. Killing enemies from or in an objective will earn a player more points, further discouraging people from playing "CoD style" and putting emphasis on teamwork.
Overall, this game is not for the faint of heart, but people wanting a break from annually-photocopied generic FPS games will appreciate Red Orchestra 2/Rising Storm.
Rating: PTSD/10

, the fifth installment in Nintendo's
series, is a story-based third person action adventure game. Dropping the player into the midst of an epic battle for control of Middle-earth right from the start, Ragnarok focuses on delivering an individualised single-player experience comparable to that of the Dragon Age series. The player meets his/her love interest, the knight Hans Rapad, early on before he is taken prisoner by an evil sorceror and trapped in an ancient castle ruin. Without spoiling anything, the second act of the game focuses on Hans' rescue, and as an avid Hammerwatch player I know that other fans of that franchise will feel very at home here. As with previous
games, abilities and combat strength is determined by a vast, inclusive skill tree--think Path of Exile, but without an initial choice of class at the beginning of play. Instead, the main character and all unlockable party members (each available for purchase in-game for $3.99) each start with a simple choice of Focus (Strength, Dexterity, Intelligence, Wisdom, Constitution, Speed,  Charisma, Presence, Corruption, Agility, Fertility) and build outward on the skill tree from there. This makes play highly customizable, and gives huge replay value to the game. Combat is similar to that found in the かたわ 少女 series, with fast-paced and innovative combos being the bread-and-butter. The unique combo system allows players to create their own combos, offering even more customization and crazy action possibilities. Overall, I would rate this game a
; while it offers a lot of options, great gameplay, an amazing story, and awesome replayablity, purchasing additional party members forces the monsters to scale their difficulty, which means one cannot simply pay real money to succeed at the game more easily. I'm looking forward to Nintendo adding that feature in the next
installment. Here's hoping!

Empire at War is a stunning Real Time Strategy revolving around the 'Rise of the Empire era' Star Wars universe. The main game allows you to take the sides of both the Galactic Empire and the Rebel Alliance across varied planets and participate in epic space battles above said planets. Famous environments such as Hoth, Endor and Coruscant return as well as lesser known planets from spin offs and extended universe canon.
Ultimately you control either faction with the goal of controlling every location in the galaxy. Along the way you will participate in skirmishes with land forces and space fleets and combat your enemies in engaging and clever ways. Land battles see you build bases and call in ground troops from your fleet in space to wipe out the enemy presence while space battles see you attacking or defending a space station with a wide range of units such as fighters, frigates and capital ships.
The expansion pack, Forces of Corruption, adds a third faction and a wide array of new locations, units, and ways to play.  You can now play as the Zahn Consortium, a group of intergalactic space pirates who want their own share of the galaxy. The new setting takes place during the galactic war and sees you entering the fight between the Rebels and the Empire.
This is an amazing RTS that really captures the feeling of being a part of the Star Wars universe. If there's only one Star Wars game you should play, this is it.

This game just ticks all of the boxes for me.
Games like Outlast force you to experience all the jumpscares. This goes for most games that belong to the horror genre. The Forest, however, is different. You can go the whole game without encountering any of the mutants and cannibals if you play your cards right. It's only when you let your guard down that you get ♥♥♥♥ed over. Nothing makes you♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants quite like seeing the silhouette of a hunting party sprinting across a hill in the distance. I've woken up some mornings and really don't want to leave the safety of my tree house. No other game has given me that gut-wrenching feeling as to date.
I feel as if i'm ♥♥♥♥ing playing Minecraft PvP all of again; holding down "sneak" for dear life and as not to get spotted. The AI in this game is fantastic. The cannibals will leave you alone for the first few days, watching your every move. As the game progresses they get more and more ballsy. The AI will test you to see how you respond. If you act fearful and run away they will see you as prey and you'll end up with more raiding parties visiting you. However, If you act aggresive then they will retreat only to return with an army that, no matter how powerful you are, you just wont be able to match. Staying neutral with the tribesmen requires maintaining eye contact, holding your ground and showing your strength. Gaining respect from the natives is crucial to your survival. I do have to poke some fun at the audio though. Whilst the atmospheric sounds are ♥♥♥♥ing on point, certain noises are just all over the ♥♥♥♥ing place. For example, when fighting a single cannibal it can sound like there are 3 more behind you when in reality there's not.
Beating a native to a pulp is incredibly disorientating when screams from the same cannibal move from your left ear to your right ear even though the tribesman hasn't moved. Certain water sounds are also unbearably loud when compared to other ambient effects. Obviously the game is still in alpha and these issues will surely be resolved, but the game already feels incredibly polished already; I've yet to experience any sort of game-breaking bug.

As someone who isn't into pure city builders, I've really enjoyed Tropico 5. While efficiency of things like transportation and economy are certainly at the forefront of the gameplay, other aspects like research, dynasties, trading, eras, diplomacy, combat, and the country's constitution give this game a lot of breadth.
Most of the negative reviews seem to stem from what people view as a dumbing down from Tropico 4. I put some time into Tropico 4 to compare, and I would certainly recommend the earlier game for genre purists. There's more control to micromanage each nuance (couple more immigration choices, change wages by $1 incremenets rather than only having 5 options, etc). That control would have detered focus from everything else going on in Tropico 5 though so I'm fine seeing it out of the game.
If you've yet to test the waters of the Tropico series it will, in addition to the above, provide fantastic humor, Rodrigo y Gabriella inspired music, clean graphics, Steam workshop with a ton of maps, and a fairly intuitive menu interface to get down to the nuts of bolts of what's working and what's not. I find not everything is clearly explained in any Tropico game, but it's a big enough series that Google will assist you in those troubled times.
The bottom line is that those looking to mix some element of 4x decision making into their city builder will find Tropico 5 has no equal. Those looking for a pure city builder should go with Tropico 4 or maybe an Anno game.

The second is a delve into our protaganists spiral into depression and mental illness. This is another one of those games that I'm sure I'll give a thumbs up to, but only once the developers starts fixing the major issues. Don't get me wrong, this is a good game, but development is rather slow but the bigger problem is that the developers don't prioritise things that most players are complaining about. My major concerns are:
-The game is difficult to get into for new players. There is a small survival guide but really you will need to go to the online wiki and online map if you are to have any hope of surviving. There should be much more in game help and tooltips, especially with regard to crafting.
- There really should be an in-game map (or an option to turn it on). It makes no sense that your character who is living in the town has no idea what the layout of the town is. I mean there is already an online map and everybody seems to be using it so the only reason for the developers not to include it is because they can't be bothered.
This is not a bad game, I bought it and it is a nice experience for 15$. I just wish the developers would stop wasting their time on things like making the game map bigger while there are other more pressing issues to sort out.
Update:
It's been about a year and a half since I reviewed this game, so what has changed? I think the map is bigger, and you can play as more characters. Also there are more sandbox options which is nice.
Long story short the issues that were there before are still there, and the features requested by the community still haven't been implemented. I don't mind supporting early access games that take a long time to get to full release, but that isn't the case here. The reality is that the development of this game has slowed down to a crawl.

The game opens with you, the mother, driving up to this theme park, Atlantic Oak or something along those lines. Your son Callum is in the car while yoiu get out and just walk away. Apparently we left his
