During the "First Chapter" we are allowed to Sprint, Call for our son Callum, and examine clues that give us more information on the theme park. While calling for Callum a blur will appear on your screen indicating you to go whatever dirction and Callum will call out with a "THIS WAY MOMMY!" Which adds some creepiness to the story. The atmosphere of the Park is actually pretty chilling. I did play with the brightness up slightly higher than suggested which may have affected some of the more ominous and scary portions of the first chapter. At this point, Callum has us running to the Swan Ride, on the way there we learn that the Mascot for
"Steve/Chad the Squirrel" is not liked very much and people think the person is a creep. After going down this small hill ight inside of the park, we are greeted by Callum and watch him joyously jump onto a swan boat and take the dark ride into the tunnel. We then get on the next boat and venture into the cavern, where we are greeted with "Hanzel and Gretel" projected onto the cave walls. The story goes through how their parents hated them, to the point they were going to leave them in the forest to die. Hanzel is like "I'll go out and make a trail of rocks and breadcrumbs to the house!" But we all know it doesn't work and birds eat that
right up. Anyways, they find a house made of candy after being dropped off in the forest and let to die for three days. Hanzel, being the little tubby he is, ate the walls of the candy house. An older woman then comes out and offers them food. Little did they know she wanted to eat poor little tubby. Gretel being the smart gal she is, asks the witch how to clean the oven properly and then rightfully pushes her in. Then the kids eat the witch and are so filled and happy. During this story the boat is knocked around a couple of times and the Mascot, Chad, is seen inside watching us for a breif moment.
After this boat ride, we are allowed to venture over to the Ferris Wheel. The Ferris wheel portion of the game provides us with all the info we need to start to feel horrible for our character. We learn her husband died while she was pregnant with Callum. We also learn that all we wanted for Callum was to have a great life, but unfortunately his sister died a still born. So we filled the part of his sister and his mother. The ferris wheel starts to creek and turn as we get more and more depressed thinking over how our life was. Once we get off the ferris wheel we are led down another hill, where we learn that the park was built on old haunted land. We also learn that people died all the time while this park was being built.
After we learn this, we go to the Bumper Cars where we learn that our character was hospitalized and injected and tested on with something. Nothing much else is learned other than we're depressed. during the end of the chapter, a bumper car taes life and starts to drive wildly towards us, unfortunately this game does not come with audio sliders, so the music was so loud compared to the SFX. We head over to this lake with this weird carnival theme. There's a giant spinning ride in the center of a pier, with extremely loud, over used, carnival music. I just ran around the entier pier neglecting anything scary, looking for clues about the park and my character. Fortunately, this area is saved by the backstory of "Steve/Chad the Mascot." This is where we see an Eye-Witness report of a murder that Chad commited. A person waiting in line was watching Chad make an ice sculpture, as he was very good at it. Chad was seen taking his time, but whatever he was carv ing had so much detail people could not look away. The eye witness reports seeing a face popping out of the ice, with no eyes and no teeth. Just as the eye witness was looking at the sculptor, two teens walked over and laughed at Chad. Chad took the ice pick and stabbed the teenagers over and over, until he got an eyeball out and put it in the hole of the ice sculptor.
This was a pretty interesting eye-witness report and it got my hopes up that Chad would soon scare the poop outta me.
Soon after this report, we walk up a hill to an employees room, where we learn a fellow employee of Chad had died. This employee had a note written saying how Chad never took the suit off, and it stank like decaying flesh. The employee said they hated Chad and sometimes he would walk over and stare at her. As soon as we put the note down, the lights on the inside of the room flash and we can see Chad's siloutte standing over an employee, holding his ice pick.
We head over to the carnival section of the map, but this area provides us with little to no information. The only detail here is that a child was killed behind the cotton candy maker. then we go into this weird psychadelic world, which feels like an Oxy trip, where everything is slow motion and the devil's laughter echoes in the background. Nothing more than that... We pic kup a bottle of pills and a roller coaster ticket though

If you like games like Amnesia or Penumbra then boy, this will be right up your alley. In Outlast you play reporter Miles Upshur, who is looking to break a story regarding strange goings-on at a formerly asylum re-opened by a multi-national Biotech corporation. There's a great mystery to be solved when you play Outlast. But in order to solve that mystery you're going to have to run, walk or hide your way through 8 chapters of creepy gameplay. You aren't armed and you can't fight back which adds to the intensity of being chased through a beautifully realized asylum. Outlast is dripping in creepy atmosphere helped by excellent sound design. There are also plenty of gotcha moments with jump scares for the masochist in you. I completed the game in about 4 and a half hours which was perfect to me. There wasn't many things I didn't enjoy about this game. Maybe just a couple of the spots where I was chased got a bit repetitive.  Overall, Outlast gets a easy recommendation from me. Creepy gameplay at just the right length with a story that makes you see it all out makes this game a winner. Also if you liked this game, then the Whistleblower DLC is an absolute MUST. It fleshes out the story even more and is about 2 and a half hours. 8/10 from me for the whole 7 hour experience.

With all the controversy surroudning this game right now, it's kind of hard to get an ubiased opinion.  Don't let the DLC doomsayers scare you. Here are the facts.
What you get for buying the standard 59.99 edition is this, 12 very unique Hunters and 3 very unique Monsters.  Same as every other purchase option.
One of the first things you'll notice if you try the game is that the graphics are stunning.  The more you explore the maps as either Hunter or Hunted you'll see just how alive each unique map is.  Each with their own docile and hostile creatures to aid or endanger players.  This game is not without it's problems.  There are bugs, like any other first week title and only a few of them serious (though rare).
The price point: This game offers three ways to buy.  Standard, Digital Delux and PC Monster Race.  All of which are effectively the same.  They all have the same numbers of Hunters, Monsters, Maps and Game Modes.  The only difference being that the Digital Delux comes with a season pass and the Monster Race edition contains a YET UNRELEASED Monster and two UNRELEASED Hunters and some skins.  So in essence, the larger price tag is only a Pre-Purchase of unreleased content.  It is not free or exclusive.  Though according to their current price plan for the Monster and Hunters, it ends up being a little cheaper than pricing each out individually.
The matchmaking and Preference systems leave more than a little to be desired.  While it does give you a slightly better chance of being able to play what you want, the chances are pretty low to begin with and the only way to guarantee you'll play your top choice is to stick with a match and wait your turn.
Evolve also offers a fairly unique single player option.  While the game itself doesnt have a true story mode or any compelling backstory as of yet, the single player option allows you to continue to progress your characters and your account should you lose your internet (travel with your laptop, forget to pay your bills, whatever the reason).  So when you decide that you need a break from the online community, and being honest, who doesnt from time to time, you can drop the multiplayer action and trade it in for some single player and not lose out on your progression.  The bots that play the other hunters and monsters could still use some fine tuning, but they do a decent job.
TL:DR
10/10 Sound and Visuals
6/10 Replay Value for lone Hunters (make some friends)
Knowing what I know now, I would still purchase the game as is if offered when I bought it the first time.  Avoid the 'discussions' forum.  It's all rants.

While the gameplay itself is awesome and while the monster's strength and the hunters combined strength is nicely balanced the game has an unfortunate downside. The voting, maps, and modes are not. This review will focus on what I find to be the largest flaws with the game. However. I would still recommend you play it because it is truly a new experience in gaming.
To start off there are 2 ways to play in matchmaking. Skirmish, which is by far the best way to play online, is nothing but the Hunt game mode, which is the most balanced mode in the game. With the mode Defend coming in a close second, The other two, Nest and Rescue, are inherently tilted towards on sides favor but that will be explained later.
Then there is Evacuation, the second way to ruin other peoples day, which is essentially the story-mode of Evolve. Evacuation consists of 5 rounds, of which the first four rounds are voted on by the players with the fifth round always being Defend. Unfortunately this is the only way to play Defend outside of custom in competitive play and is a huge bummer because it is the 2nd best game mode to play and requires a 30 minute commitment to reach. For the first 4 rounds, 2 maps with different modes are offered. The possibilities for these rounds are Hunt, Rescue, and Nest.
The big problem with evacuation, which should be the best way to play, is Rescue favors the monster and Nest favors the hunter. The Monster almost always wins rescue, and in nest the Hunters almost always win. Here is why.
In rescue both sides compete over randomly spawned and located survivors of which spawn in 2 groups of 2 and 1 group of 5.  Whoever saves or kills 5 survivors first wins. The downside is that with leaping and movement skills the monster can typically get to and kill, if not, eat the survivors before the hunters show up. The best the hunters can do is punish him inside a trap if they can catch him in it before he runs off. However, if the hunters do manage to get the survivors up and moving, all the monster has to do is come in and focus on the survivors who can be killed easily. Then promptly run away and wait for the next group to snack on.
With Nest its a problem of AI and map size. The rules are that the game ends when 6 eggs or the monster are killed. The monster can hatch one egg, sacrificing it, at a time into a stage 1 goliath as a friendly minion. Which would be alright if its AI functioned the same as having a goliath minion in hunt; which follows you everywhere mimicing and assisting you. However, in Nest it has a mind of is own and runs off to do only god knows what rendering it useless. It typically rushes the hunters until its quickly killed like an idiot leaving its primary use as a short distraction or assistance with the take down of the hunters at the cost of a point. Or it stays in one general area never contributing to the match and atleast if it dies quick you can hatch another egg to shortly distract the hunters again. I repeat becuase of its reckless behavior the minion makes a poor distraction at best. However, it's effectiveness as a distraction/FinishHelper is the only chance you will have a slight chance of winning. The other major critical flaw is that the maps are not big enough to conceal the eggs for long. Even when the AI minion distracts the hunters they typically destroy all but one or 2 eggs and are on the verge of finding the last ones by the time you are stage 2 forcing you into a fight you dont want to be in with no armor. Because every mode can be played on every map nest just does not work. 4 fanned out hunters can locate and destroy the eggs before the hunter can even defend them. It's hardly bearable for the monster on the biggest maps and excruciating on the more common smaller maps. I havent even won this game mode against the bots its so hard. It is the most flawed out of the game modes so far.
Now that we know whats wrong with the unique game modes its time to delve into the problem with the matchmaking of evacuation as a whole. Now the game is 4 v 1 and is set up as a 5 round pick between 2 maps with 2 of the 3 game modes where everyone gets one vote when choosing maps. Sounds fair right? In actuallity the hunter team bullies the monster with majority rule controling what map is played constantly. Nest is always picked if given the chance and hunt always picked when not. This makes it an uphill battle for the monster to win the long term 5 round struggle because this gives the monster 3 fair attempts to win a round with 2 rounds of hunt, 2 rigged games of Nest, and the gauranteed final mode, Defend. Obviously, with the hunters having four votes and the monster one, they will pick the map and mode that favors them and hinders the monster even when the monster politely asks for the fairer Hunt mode for that round. An easy way to fix this critical unbalance is to allow the monster 3 votes that way the hunters are forced to be united in their map decisions to render the monsters vote moot and/or to allow the choice between all 3 game modes to split the hunters vote between advantageous pick, fair pick, and disadvantageous pick.
Sorry for the rant, I'm just sick of playing as the monster and always playing nest while never playing rescue. Of the last 10 matches ive played 4 were nest, 4 were hunt and 2 were defend. I won one defend and 2 hunts. Every map was picked 4 to 1 with my vote as the monster being the odd man out. It's just so frustrating to always have no control over the map.

The thing that I love most about Bioshock and why I'd rate it so highly is the mysterious nature of the story and the creepy world of Rapture. It's a place where science and art run free of the normal restrictions society places on them. The amoral inhabitants explore the other sides of life, or what we would call, the darker and sinister sides of it. In Rapture people become artistic materials and science experiments, and little girls pillage corpses for their inner juices. And you? Why are you there? That's the million dollar carrot you chase all game long.
Bioshock's gameplay is made up of open areas you can traverse back and forth through, exploration, innaccurate guns, melee, and survival horror, all taking place in a captivating and eery city that's built underwater. The inhabitants are mostly socios. You'll meet a few friends and good peeps along the way, but they're the exception, not the norm. Most beings in Rapture are out to kill you. Your reasons for being there are unknown and little by little become apparent.
You can play it like a narrative driven game if you turn on the arrows that show the direction to go, or you can play it so that you're exploring the world more and finding the way on your own via discovery. I always play with them off. It's much better that way and you'll find yourself backtracking and getting a better understanding of the world and its characters. On higher difficulties it's a challenging game and you need to sneak and be careful about how you approach enemies.
Just a really fun, relaxing game. Very enjoyable.

I really wish there was a neutral rating. There were certainly aspects of the game I enjoyed, but boy oh boy are there bugs. This game clearly needed 1 or 2 more pollishing passes to balance out things and fix annoying issues with it.
It was also VERY short. I've played 1.7 hours of the game, and I've already completed it. One sitting. I even sat through a few plays of the gauntlet forever mode, but alas, I've lost interest.
Here's my pros/cons list.
Needs work:
- Some textures were great. Others were very pixelated. Set a standard for your textures.
- Zero character development. I realize that character development in these types of games may be difficult to do. But I think it would help get the player connected and involved in the story.
- Level descriptions were too busy. Couldn't tell if I was supposed to read them, or just click go.
- Sound system problems. From too many sounds overlapping and overdriving, to the music cutting out in an obvious loop restart
- SFX were fairly generic
- Dialog is a bit childish. It tries to be funny, but just.. isn't.
- Campaign was too short
- Level difficulty went from omg easy mode to omg impossihard. Level progression needs to be steady, not in your face.
Was good:
- Defender style gameplay was refreshing. I liked keeping an eye on my tail to be sure its clear
- Responsive controls. I'm using an xbox controller on my pc
- Addons and upgrades accumulate through the game. I liked that
- Music was GREAT. I really dig it, and thought it was the best part of the game
- Retro filters. You could play the game as if it was using an Amiga video card. Neat
I am in the middle of developing my own shmup, so I'm 'researching' by other games out there. It's really a lot of work to finish a game, polish it, remove what doesn't work, etc. But in the end, you absolutely must do all of that because it sucks to go 90% through the development only to fall flat because the last 10% of the work wasn't done.
Pay more attention to the details, and people will flock to your game.

(This is my first review so feedback would be greatly appreciated! :) )
First of all, I'd like to say that this review is based on Build 30 fo the game.
Project Zomboid is an early access game that allows you to play as an average male/female caught in an outbreak. There's no real plot as of the current build, but it is planned in future builds.
You do not play the role of a special agent, or a super-badass type character who discovers where the virus came from, your only objective in this game is to survive for as long as possible.
That being said, you probably won't survive for very long. (At first anyways...)
As soon as you've chosen your character and customised their skills and traits, you're thrust into a random part of the game world with nothing other than a brief tutorial. That being said, though, it isn't a bad thing as part of the gaming experience is dying. A lot.
The game mechanics themselves are rather solid, and don't feel clunky at all. The isometric view that the game gives you works very well and allows for some moments of tension when entering houses or walking around sharp corners. Combat is fairly basic, although stable and very exciting, mostly due to the fact that most weapons produce noise, resulting in more zombies for you to deal with (The game follows the basic rule of 'guns are bad but good'). There is also a crafting system present, which (in my opinion) needs some work to become more user friendly, although there are plenty of mods to help you out with this should you need it. The game itself has very few bugs or glitches, which is a massive bonus considering it's an early access game.
This leads me onto my next topic of its development process. The dev's themselves are incredibly attentive, and provide weekly updates on their progress with the game as well as what features they're currently working on. The few bugs that do exist though, such as graphical errors and whatnot, are fixed very quickly which is good by any standard.
Overall, I'd rate this game 8/10, mostly due to its amazing style and solid gameplay. This, coupled with a huge amount of potential and hours and hours of replayable zombie slaying, makes this one of my favourite early access games.

It all feels very pleasant, and at first it’s disarmingly simple. Soon, though, the game bares its teeth. Shapes are positioned in a manner that makes successful pathways between them all far from immediately obvious, especially once you realize paths cannot cross. Junction boxes add to the task, demanding you enter them a specific number of times to illuminate all their lights. Failure merely results in a sadly pulsating red outline and the realization you must rethink, experiment, and iterate.
At this point, Lyne could have become a frustrating mess, but smart design eliminates any notion of such a problem. Paths between shapes can be partially created and temporarily abandoned while you fashion the route for another. There’s no limit on time or attempts, and levels are unlocked in sizable sets, meaning you can always try an alternative if you find yourself stuck. Conversely, if you become a Lyne guru in short order, there are procedurally generated daily levels available once you’ve worked your way through the first two sets of 25 apiece.

ARX LIBERTATIS WAS USED - Thus game time was not counted by steam. My playthrough was ~22hrs. Arx Libertatis gets the game running on nearly all systems, I suggest it if you can't run the game normally.
Arx Fatalis was created by ArKane Studios who would eventually bring the world titles such as Dark Messiah of Might & Magic (one of my favorite games) and more recently Dishonored 1 and 2 through Bethesda publishing.
The setting for the game is one of the most interesting I've seen in an RPG that is nearly untouched by the actual game. The premise is that the sun for the world has been extinguished and the surface is now uninhabitable. Anyone who goes to the surface would freeze instantly type of deal. The humans (with the help of naga-creatures) along with other races fled to the underground and through tunnels the population of the world continues to survive (Metro 2033 anyone?). Arx Fatalis takes place in Arx, one of what's considered to be 'safer' areas. This was disappointing since it was more tame setting than I wanted compared to the Travelers guild and how they're in a daily life or death struggle continuing through tunnels that are riddled with monsters.
The crux of the matter on this game is that it's hard for me to pick a side on recommending it. I'm half-heartedly going with a No Recommendation despite thinking the game isn't that bad. There just wasn't enough to push me over to wanting to replay the game or encourage someone else to go through it.
To explain, the combat (the main portion of what this game will consist of) is pretty garbage (TES style). You're forced into either building as a hybrid or into a mage only and while you can pull off the warrior build it's highly inefficient along with the worse builds of rogue or archer. The spellcasting in the game is an amazing concept that not even the game was able to do properly. You must create the runes in the air manually in a correct combination to cast the spell. Anyone who hasn't played would think it hard to do in combat BUT the player can have up to THREE precast spells. This means mages can play with the runes until they get the three spells they want and easily murder any opponent with probably only two of the spells used. Fighting with melee weapons is a chore in comparison, as swinging wildly does next to no damage. The player must 'hold' the weapon until the gauge is full and then release to deal impactful damage (~5s per swing). While this won't seem apparent initially, when the player reaches the Ylsids that run slightly faster and can swing 3 times as fast, it'll spell your doom.
As a new player this was especially annoying since the runes recieved early on were practically useless, and a useful spell isn't learned until later in the game which encouraged me to stay mostly melee instead of a focus on spellcraft which ends up the far better of the two.
Now to me what is the real dilemma I have with the game. MECHANICS.
This game is a perfect example of the once and done feature. They place mechanics that exist in the game for the sole purpose of one point and then abandon the feature forever. This is excrutiating as a new player and people who played this perviously looking back with fond memories need to understand what I'm talking about. Mostly this is due a lack of both not showing and not telling what the player should do.
Here are some examples, spoilers abound.
But it's not as though the game was entirely misdirected
Cooking food was neat, spellcasting (despite precast ruining everything) was a good concept, and the whole staking the vampire ghouls in the crypt was a nice inclusion you wouldn't see in most games. (Plus the setting)
For the time when the game came out I could see why most people would love this game.
Personally I don't think the game aged well, and new players would certainly have more than one problem with it.

Arx Fatalis was the first game to be released by Arcane Studios (now mostly known for Dishonored), and very few developers hit it out of the park with their first game as much as they did. The game takes place in a world that might have once been a traditional fantasy setting, but the death of the planet's sun led the various races of the world to move into various underground cave systems, with Arx being the one that the game takes place in. The open world is somewhat like a dungeon crawler, and while it may seem like a small world at first you may be surprised as you unravel it and unlock its various depths and passages. It makes up for its size by being very compact, without the filler that most modern RPGs have. There are also various civilizations to deal with, with the humans living on the top level and various other races living deeper in the caves. Arx is full of secrets and side quests, and for the most part you're free to look for them at any time. The story is fairly simple, but it never chains you to it, instead opting to just leave you to go through things at your own pace.
Gameplay-wise, things are pretty similar to Arcane's later games. You can specialize in stealth, combat, or magic, along with other skills like the ability to identify enchated weapons and armor. The magic system is one that you'll either love or hate; you learn spells by learning runes found on stones throughout the world and combining them into spells by drawing the runes on your screen with the mouse, and when it works it's a really cool system, but the rune detection sometimes refuses to cooperate, so you'll probably want to keep your three pre-casted spell slots full in case of combat. There are lots of item crafting mechanics you can use, and they're all presented in a more interactive way than most games' menus, like how cooking food requires you to light a fire with a spell and drop your food items into the fire until it finishes cooking, which is pretty fun in a way that's hard to describe.
It's hard to describe exactly what it is about Arx Fatalis that makes it so great, because it's a game that's made great by the various moments and sidequests that make up the game instead of by the actual core mechanics and if I listed all of my favorite parts of the game here it would just be spoiling things. But everything about it comes together so well that the only reason I wouldn't recommend it is if you aren't very good with older control schemes. Even though it's old, there's a fan patch called Arx Libertatis that fixes things up to run on modern machines, and with the game's current $5 price I think it's a steal. It's an immersive and unique game that has a kind of magic to it that even Arcane's own later games haven't quite managed to capture.

A group of stuntmen of a sentai series decide to go indie after they get too annoyed with their boss' arrogance: starting from a small warehouse and using cardboard costumes you''ll be following their story in this tactical RPG.
Chroma Squas is not only a love letter to the sentai genre but also a very fun game to play thanks to its humourous story and gameplay straight out from the series it took as a model.
-quirky pixel art
-spot-on sentai-inspired soundtrack
-amusing plot backed by dialogues filled with references and humour
-story offers three branching paths that'll change scenes, bosses and even who joins your team
-the tactical combat is fun and offers a decent challenge, same goes for boss fights
-studio management, crafting, a shop and a few unlockable skills all give a fair sense of progression
-nice length, took me 11 hours on Interesting difficulty
-the actual studio management options are pretty light on content
-gameplay stays basically the same and can get a bit trite
-mecha fights get dull after a bit
-could have used an "undo last move" button and an animation speed option
-randomness in crafting is annoying
The sentai genre is everywhere in the game..it's in the costumes, the moves you pull, the mecha fights against kaijus and the over the top dialogues: but Chroma Squad also breaks the fourth wall by letting you see the cameras and green screen or by chatting amicably with the extra in the boss costume before you fight them. Eventually you'll realize that maybe not everything is just a special effect but the game rarely abandons its humour and will keep throwing references your way. You'll also have to manage your studio by buying upgrades and deciding which contracts to sign for marketing: while studio upgrades are a straightforward "more is better" story ad agencies all provide different bonuses to fights/ audience/ money gained letting you customize your experience a bit.
Most fights feel fair and some can be easy as long as you upgrade your equipment and play decently but, at times, you might end up making a bad decision due to not being able to see whether an enemy'll be in range of your rifle or how far you'll be able to throw teammates before you actually move: this is where an undo button'd have worked wonders in case you misjudged a distance-which is not as hard as it sounds- or just misclick. Mecha fights are enjoyable at first but they get dull quite fast as you're basically just chaining a combo, doing the "click to defend" minigame on enemy turn, and unleashing a special move when needed: it's not bad per se but the number of fights and the repetitive gameplay make the novelty value fade fast. Last but not least the crafting system is a bit of a chore as you'll be using materials dropped from fights or bought to build new costume pieces and weapons, sadly they come with random properties so it's mostly luck based whether you'll be getting something decent or useless: in the end you can either reload your save and try again or just buy some all around decent stuff from the shop directly.
Chroma Squad offers a good amout of fun, if limited in variety, gameplay enriched by an amusing story and narrative: it's good entertainment made even better if you have even just a passing knowledge of the sentai genre.

If you allow me, I'd like to just paste here a note that I made right after I finished the game. It has no spoilers, and I wrote it while being influenced by the game. After several months, I still believe what I've written. "The Beginners Guide" is short and can be easily finished in one sitting. It's definetly for people who like to think.
Forgive my English, I'm not native. I might have made up some words, I don't even know. I hope it's still understandable.
No one will ever tell me, that video games cannot be art. And if anyone does, I’ll never believe them.
I just played “The Beginners Guide”. From the guy that made “The Stanley Parable”…? So, sitting down to it, I expected it to be good, mind-twisting and meta – metaliterary, overstepping itself. And I expected something odd. New. Fantastic in its own, unique way.
But what I got was a handful of emotions. No, not a handful, a mountain of emotions. It made me hurt. It made me think. It made me restless, made me feel like I understand things when I didn’t; made me feel like I don’t understand a thing when I understood perfectly. It made me back away, it made me let go, it made me want to keep going, to reach conclusion that could never be reached outside of myself. It made me long for an essence, for a material object so solid, that I could touch it, feel its hardness under my fingers just to forget the emotionally-philosophical mess I had in my brain. While writing this all of it is still bouncing inside my mind and I cry and beg to forget it for now – because it made me feel. It painfully reminded me that I’m real, that I exist.
It made me feel. It made me think. It’s Art. And if that’s not art, then what on earth is…?
I love the game, though it's more of an interactive story than an actual game. If you liked "The Stanley Parable" - this is the next level.

Chroma Squad is a tactical RPG, which has quite the fast download baud. But there is more, because the thing about it that earned my immediate apllause, is that it is parodying sentai with several references throughout, which made me glad, but I have sadly found a lot of accidental hentai.
Super sentai, or to the duper americans power rangers, are shows about various dangerous threatening the world with a shower of monsters. So it is up to three to six teammates, to bring an end to the evils killing spree. The difference between sentai, and the ignorance of power rangers are huge, mostly in terms of violence because lord knows how hard mothers bother, they somehow still seek something that will make them take the offense and write angry letters.
The basic of the plot that quickly forms a blood clot, is five stunt actors are getting the brunt end of the stick from the director, mostly because the real actors are mostly spectators now. They get sick of this repetitive shtick, so they decide that instead they shouldn't bide their time, they quit on the spot leaving the old studio to rot, to start their own, though they bring their former director down by stealing the suits.
Earth is under threat, but like a stoners baguette the heroes take a long time to learn, and until then they are quite stern about this all being special effects, or defects. They use the footage of them fighting aliens, to get their show more lighting. I won't go further, because this does go deeper but is actually simple to follow, which is a nice dimple of quirks that I love.

You have a variety of not only weapons, you have a small soceity of actors to pick from, obviously some fit better into each role of the five, it is up to you to put down that tea cup and to decide which loon becomes a front line goon or a back line maroon. Items are dropped, as long as you aren't stopped from murdering aliens. Which can be used to upgrade your zord, or create weapons and armor out of cardboard.

Upgrading health care, so that your squad will fair better when taking hits, or upgrade the workshop to get more tiny bits to craft with. One thing I do enjoy, which was quite a clever ploy. That aside this game is grand, and all of the humor and references make it far from bland. Out of all the sentai references, the one that more so instantly hit my preferences, was a statue greater than sweet bubblegum, that was dedicated to big 1, from Jack-Q the second super sentai.

I really enjoyed the Park for being a really interesting game about how you go completely insane in under 90 minutes of just being there. The graphics are good, the spook's were ok and the storyline felt like there could have been more. I'll list a few things that could really improve this to be a 10/10 game:
What is good:
- The graphics are on point.
- The Park rides felt like they could have been real.
- The Music was good to set a creepy tone.
- Character design for Chad was great.
- The effects of Lorraine going more and more insane is creepy.
What could have been worked on:
- A longer game: they could have made more rides and make the story way more scary as you go from one ride to the next.
- More reading: this is the only way to set the scene is by reading little pages all around the park, super easy to miss and could be the down fall of the player not knowing whats going on.
- Shorter rides: The starting ride, tunnel of tales is the longest of the 6 rides (including the house of horrors, but not counting the part where you walk though the clown door.) so you sit there for a good amount of time waiting for the ride to end which is boring, but it turns out you can skip half of the rides and end up just riding the roller coaster, getting the flash light, and beating the game by entering the house of horrors! You just skipped half of the whole story to speed run the game! More rides could have gone in deeper of the true meaning behind the park and could have entered the world a little deeper of Lorriane.
- More Scares could have improved the game for being a walking simulator, to a real horror game with not just scares in pieces but all around you, feeling your heart pounding!
What needs to be fixed:
- so there is a glitch I was having where at the very beginning I had to hold right click to look around and I couldnt get out of the first object I was looking at, so to easily fix this I went into the parks menu and messed around with the mouse settings and fixed it right away. Great first impressions.
- I also noticed in some of the cut scenes that my character Lorriane would like flicker a little bit before looking in the direction of the event, this was notice at the scene of the bumper cars with shock Therapy. I guess she was still staring in the direction of what I was looking at before I  clicked the object that triggered the cut scene.
- The Story: OK... this one is really messed up but I thought they could have improved on it by a lot and could have built up a little bit more of why was the park haunted in the first place or was it really the whole time. I said I liked the ending but now I go back and think about it, it didn't really make a whole  lot of since to me. You could have missed the whole story line and saw all these random events and be thinking to yourself why is all this happening? I'll tell you something, make sure you read all the pieces of paper found around the park, it will help you understand a little more of what is going on.
SO, did I like the game after all I said? Yes, it was a fun game to play for myself. I would give it a 7/10 for graphics and having a really good concept that could have gone futher than  they did. Is it worth the $15? Not really, I bought it for $15's but I would wait till it's on sale just so you dont have to speed run it just for your money back because im stuck with it going almost to 3 hours just to get the whole story. I would say they could of done better with this topic, but we got this... it could have been so much better. But you can see me play it and get my reactions out of it here:
See for yourself with some real gameplay if you want to pay for it or just watch me get all the hidden things about this game. I hope this review was helpful for you!

For the most part, the reaction to this game is unnecessarily complicated for both sides. Yes, there is a crazy, borderline criminal DLC system. You WILL have to pay money to have more fun as the hunters. You WILL have to pay money to have more fun as the monsters. It's sad, yes. It's sad that the 2K felt the need to leach money out of those who already supported and defended this game. However, one must realize that DLC is DLC and for the most part, the DLC is purely cosmetic. Although frustrating, the DLC available in the store upon release is purely cosmetic/isn't implimented in the game yet. Yes, you can obtain skins in game rather than buying them. Yes, more skins are available if you purchase them. Coming from someone who has spent an embarrassing amount on DotA 2 cosmetics and still sucks♥♥♥♥♥at the game, I can confirm that cosmetics do not win games. However, it is fair to mention that all DLC maps and modes will be free and you will be able to play with those who have other DLCs such as monsters are hunters. Also, rumor has it that you will be able to play as the DLC hunters in custom matches with friends who own said hunters via the quick switch option between hunters. In other words, DLC will be strictly multiplayer.
Now, aside from the incredibly contreversial DLC plan already in place, this game is fantastic. The gameplay is repetitive, yes. However, the repitition can be the most fun aspect at times. The desire to master your favorite hunter/class/monster provides a lot of replayability in and within itself. The mastery system forces you to change your game play to level up. Granted, it can cause you to inadvertantly grief your team; however, it does provide a dynamic way to change your play style on a regular basis.
On evacuation: evacuation is honestly the pride and joy of this game. In retrospect, it's just a continuous string of multiple, singular games. In reality, it's an immersive game mode that yields different results depending on game outcome. You win a game, you get a map effect on the next game. You lose, you get a slight buff that helps even it out. In my opinion, evacuation mode counteracts the whole "wow there is like 16 maps HOW BORING I NEED 100 RIGHT NOW BECAUSE I NEED TO SEE A NEW PLANT OR ROCK TYPE OR ELSE I'LL GET BORED." Each map effect changes how games are played. Some map effects even change a map as a whole (the man eating eels, for example, transform any standard map into a the-ground-is-lava-type map that effectively rules out standard navigation of said map) or changes the gameplay of a game mode drastically (extra minions/extra colonists/extra food/ FLYING SNAKE THINGS/ FLYING ROBOT THINGS)
Touching more on repitition, I find the game to be largely unsatisfactory unless you're playing evacuation (which will have its own section) or playing with a group of friends. The game requires teamwork to win as the hunters. That being said, a lot of randoms you encounter in games aren't exactly keen on providing communication or teamwork. Adversely, the monsters require knowledge on the enemy hunters and their strengths and weaknesses. The monster requires mastery and repitition and practice against hunters to win. Although, it is repetitive, it is in no way stale.
On gameplay. Hunt is a cat and mouse game. Sometimes the cat is lazy and is really slacking on the whole chase part. Sometimes the mouse is feeling ballsy and will attack the mouse before it's eaten any cheese. Gameplay varies greatly based on playstyle/hunter comp/monster choice. I understand the argument that hunt mode is 70% chasing a ghost and 30% busting that ghost; however, one must understand that boring hunt gameplay is largely due to the experience (or lack thereof) the hunters. A bad trapper will never find the monster and create boring gameplay. A bad assault will never damage a monster enough to make late game fights fair and create boring gameplay. A bad support will think they're a secondary assault and won't do their job and thus create boring game play. A bad medic won't keep your teem alive giving the monster an advantage thus-- you guessed it-- creating boring game play.
Play. With. Friends. Really. This game is infinitely better with friends who can laugh about how bad they are or communicate how great ther are. Goes from like a 6.5/10 to a 10/10 with friends. No joke.
That being said, I enjoy the other games mode much more. Nest gives the monster the option to fight while weak but with minions or fight while strong without minions. Similarly, rescue is quite literally a confrontation between hunters and monsters every few minutes. It's different than the ever so popular Hunt mode and in my opinion, is more fun. However, people only seem to take hunt mode into consideration when judging gameplay.
All in all, Evolve is a GREAT, FUN game with a HORRIBLE, GREEDY DLC plan. Pick your poison. Me, like the other 90% of the people who bought evolve at full price, would advise you to wait for a sale. I don't say this because the game is unfinished or not worth the full price; I say this because by that time, more content will be released and it's more likely your friends will buy it with you. It is a great game that, in my opinion, is worth the $60. It's a gaming experienced unparalleled by any game I've ever played. It's refreshing, inventive, competitive, intense, and an all around rewarding and fun experience. The only reason I could understand someone not wanting to buy this game, currently, is because of their strong convictions against DLC.
PROS:
+fun, inventive gameplay different from anything you've ever played before.
+hours of arcade style gameplay
+fast paced. action packed (unless abe is your trapper. lol that monster might as well be invisible)
+rewarding mastery system
+great way to pass time with some friends and laugh at how the kraken looks like the lobster from futurama
CONS:
-DLC is kind of a stab in the back for a game that would be a literal 10/10 if it released it all for free
-inexperience can sometimes make the game frustrating and unfun
-solo can be a bit bland if you dont have someone to share the experience with
-a lot of content (other the DLC ones) has yet to be released
-a little buggy, but as to be expected
TLDR; It's honestly a fun and different game. Most opinions on DLC are uninformed/something they read on reddit. Still, DLC implimentations is kind of a douchey thing 2K did. Buy if you have friends who have it and want to mindlessly shoot a monster. Don't buy if you think spending money on a game is satanic ritual/ dont have any friends/ needs 100 different maps and 40 playable characters

I really want to love this game, but it's pretty simple and tedious to be honest. Great idea's here, the game needs more polishing. For a week now I've barely played more than an hour each sitting since it really doesn't grab me and becomes boring fast.
Most of the thumbs up reviews I see calling this an "Amazing Game" are from someone with barely an hour of total play time. They obviously didn't play it very far to realize the repetive simplicity. Or the frusterations with encounter management.
I don't understand why the "encounters" mechanic is so frequent. I did not play the board game so maybe that's a part of it, but I did DM D&D for decades. In D&D each individual character can take their move and action, then the round ends and there would be an encounter role. This would provide the feeling to the players that everything is happening simultaneously.
In this game, there's an encounter role after each character takes their move/action. So the feeling is more that three of the adventuring players are just standing there watching one of them fight/move/disarm a trap, ect. And then after that character is finished, the next one finally decides to move around and do something. wth lol?
The enemies you run across are rather more of a nuisance than a threat, as you'll spend most of your game time trying to manage encounters instead. Didn't make it to the edge of a map tile? Have an automatic encounter. You did make it to the edge of a map tile to explore, well here's an encounter anyway!
The encounters are so constant that the whole game is basically just trying to not die to them. If they would scale this encounter nonsense down it would make the game so much more entertaining. Why not at the end of each turn, instead of each player action? Then we could actually explore, adventure, and have fun. Instead of trying to race to the objections so encounters don't kill you ...

REVIEW MAY CONTAIN PLOT SPOILERS
The Park is a tragic horror game with a very complex, open to interpretation story.
In my own interpretation, it shows the struggle of a single, abusive mother with a child after being left by her partner (whom she describes as "dead" throughout the game, and might have possibly even killed him in a fit of rage). As her life falls apart, she resorts to prescribed psychotic drugs to cure her depression (to which she becomes addicted), trying to contact one of her very old partners for help and alcohol. Her struggle against self-guilt and trying to justify herself as a good mother and blaming her son and everyone around her for her problems. She eventually breaks down and murders her son (and possibly ex-boyfriend).
While this whole video game seems very deep and is a trip showing her life, I think it specifically focuses on an episode of her denying the murder of her son and pretending it never happened, her delusions grow more and more as she tries to wall-off the events of her life on bizarre reasons and fictional things.
The ending shows her being questioned by a police man asking her questions about the where-abouts of her missing child.
This is my opinion and interpretation of this game's deep and beautifully written story. 10/10.

I've played the WoC D&D board games (like Ravenloft) and this is a really faithful adaptation. It's a hell of a lot of fun and something you can play for 10 minutes at a time or as long as you'd like (being that the levels are randomly generated).
They put a lot of time and effort into making this feel like a board game. The tiles slamming down, the dice rolling. While I enjoy the board games, there are a lot of very complex rules, significant setup time, lots of pieces, cards, dice, and counters to keep track of, and depending on how you explore the dungeons, you need lots of space. Tales of Candlekeep automates all of those rules and makes it a joy to quickly fire up and play. You just need to decide where to move, which actions to take, and which edge of the tile you'd like to explore next. Everything else is handled for you, which is really nice.
The biggest drawback by far is the lack of multiplayer. This game would be about 100 times better if I could play with my family, on the same or different computers. They don't advertise it as a multiplayer game, though, so I don't feel cheated. I'd just really love to be able to play with friends.

You do not play the role of a special agent, or a super-badass type character who discovers where the virus came from, your only objective in this game is to survive for as long as possible.
That being said, you probably won't survive for very long. (At first anyways...)
As soon as you've chosen your character and customised their skills and traits, you're thrust into a random part of the game world with nothing other than a brief tutorial. That being said, though, it isn't a bad thing as part of the gaming experience is dying. A lot.
The game mechanics themselves are rather solid, and don't feel clunky at all. The isometric view that the game gives you works very well and allows for some moments of tension when entering houses or walking around sharp corners. Combat is fairly basic, although stable and very exciting, mostly due to the fact that most weapons produce noise, resulting in more zombies for you to deal with (The game follows the basic rule of 'guns are bad but good'). There is also a crafting system present, which (in my opinion) needs some work to become more user friendly, although there are plenty of mods to help you out with this should you need it. The game itself has very few bugs or glitches, which is a massive bonus considering it's an early access game.
This leads me onto my next topic of its development process. The dev's themselves are incredibly attentive, and provide weekly updates on their progress with the game as well as what features they're currently working on. The few bugs that do exist though, such as graphical errors and whatnot, are fixed very quickly which is good by any standard.
Overall, I'd rate this game 8/10, mostly due to its amazing style and solid gameplay. This, coupled with a huge amount of potential and hours and hours of replayable zombie slaying, makes this one of my favourite early access games.

This game is an absolute blast. It's hard to effectively convey how much fun this game is, because it doesn't seem like it would be fun and the trailers and screenshots do not do it justice, at all. But believe me when I say; if you're looking for a truely intense zombie apocalypse survival experience that is as realistic as it gets, where almost every moment incites true butterfly-inducing terror that resonates with your innermost being, while giving you all of this glistening, pant-soiling brilliance in a slightly retro, top-down, isometric view. This is your game.
I mean, for pete's sakes, you have to change your bandages at least twice a day or you run the risk of making your wounds infected, which will slowly kill you, unless you disinfect them with alcohol and a sterilized bandage. You have to cover up windows with blankets, otherwise zombies will see you/lights inside houses and they absolutely, definitely, positively will check and break a window. When you get bitten? It slowly gets worse as you succumb to the zombie virus, you don't die instantly. You get paranoid of anything, you become fatigued and, after about a day, you die. Slowly, but surely. This game is cool as all hell.
The controls are easy to grasp and the game runs smoothly, even if you're running the server software the game comes with and hosting at the same time, which is something I do frequently, to play with friends. It's also very easy to set up and comes with it's own server options.
Speaking of options. Holy hell, the custom options for starting a new game are phenominal. You get to customize what your character is like, down to their personality as well as how often weapons spawn, how often things decay and what type of zombies you're dealing with. You could opt for a 28 Days Later feel, making them fast, strong and generally a massive pain in the backside, or if you're more into your Romero lore, you could set them up to be classic, brittle shamblers that seem to spot you from 700 lightyears away.
Oh yeah, it's hard as hell as well. Don't expect to live forever, like other zombie games seem to allow you to do. This game is very realistic and eventually, you'll most likely run out of food and water. If you do manage to ensure your indefinite survival, then congratulations. You'd probably end up surviving a real zombie apocalypse.

Limbo is the posterchild for the arthouse indiegame, utilizing its low budget to full effect and creating a game more beautifully crafted and captivating than most triple-A games. It presents a dark and lonely world, where a young boy travels through a hostile enviroment where everybody seems intent on causing his imminent demise. There is a lingering sense of uneasiness here, with hidden traps and monstrosities suddenly seeping out of the shadows to attack. Even worse are the other humans - with groups of older kids throwing spears and having captured other children. What motivates them to such behaviour? It is never properly elaborated upon, with an ending that leave room for interpretation. Never the less its is a highly engaging experience well worth your time!

Bought the game after getting a coupon for it, I thought "what the heck, looks challenging."
Oh man, I was more right than I initially believed. The game is quite challenging, but that didn't matter to me, I was determined to figure out how to beat each level I played. Does my blue route need shifting? Is my green route default? These were questions that kept popping into my head, and in the end, I always found the answer.
Some puzzles you'll have one attempt and get it right, while others you'll have 30 attempts and say "this level has no answer, it's broken", but then you realize "nah, I'm dumb" when you figure it out. And then you'll play the next level and repeat this cycle.
Overall, like the description of the game says, it is "deceptively simple" and "infinitely complex", but don't let that detour you, it is a challenging and quite fun game if you're into puzzle games. Would definitely recommend to a pal wanting a challenge.

This game is awful.
I was legitimately dissappointed with this game. I wanted it to be as scary as everyone said, and I really wanted to love it as much as everyone else. Unfortunately, it's one of the most overrated games of the decade in my opinion. I've tried to finish this game 4 times, and I've only now brought myself to finish it. I've owned it on 3 separate systems (Xbox, PS4, and now PC). I've tried on all 3 difficulties. I still hated it.
The entire game isn't bad. The opening of the game presents itself very well. I even jumped when I opened that god forsaken door, but I was only startled, not scared.
I was hoping that this, given the reviews, would actually be scary. Unfortunately, I spent more time being annoyed by terrible game mechanics and being yanked out of any semblance of immersion by constant bad design choices.
First off, the enemies are incredibly stupid. On hard, you can literally sprint through the entire game and noone will ever kill you. I remember that one section with the doctor that I literally completed by alerting him, running around in circles for a while so he'd get lost in the room, and then progressing through the rest of the area. Because he couldn't follow me through the crack, I was perfectly safe.
This also showcases another annoyance I have with the game. There is very little punishment for being detected for the majority of the game, which ruins any fear of making a mistake, and since checkpoints are either frequent or too scarce, I'm either immediately back doing what I was doing before or trudging my way through 15 minutes of lost progress.
This game relies far too heavily on trial and error, and when you die enough times in a game, the fear of dying eventually fades away. And given the ridiculous difficulty spikes that happen randomly throughout the game (I'm looking at you Chris and shadowman) it quickly descends into tedium.
The gameplay is repetitive, with multiple sections telling you to go turn on X amount of Y so you can progress to Z, but be careful because W is chasing you. In between that, it's nothing but sprinting away and hiding under beds, or looking for meaningless collectibles to get some idea of what the mediocre plot is. I have rarely seen such a lackluster attempt at presenting a story in a game. It seemed to have tried to go the Dark Souls route of letting you learn as much as you want to about what's going on, but if you don't read it, you're completely lost, and the documents are so long that stopping to read all of them breaks the flow of the game.
And trust me, this game doesn't need any more help with breaking flow. Whenever the game would finally pick up momentum, a slow, tedious section would apper (e.g. immediately after the chapel) and all forward momentum would slow to a crawl.
All of these things could be forgiven though, if I could have become immersed in the world, but unfortunately, my immersion was broken at nearly every opportunity the game had to do so. The main character has literally no survival skills, with heavy footsteps, extremely heavy breathing (and freaking smacking), and slamming the door when there are enemies around. Worst of all, these enemies don't react to ANY of these. Helen Keller could hear this guy breathing in another room. I assume it was meant to be scary, but really, all it did was annoy me. By the end of the game, I WANTED my character to die. I literally hated him. You have failed as a storyteller if by the end, the character your audience was meant to sympathize with is hated. And man, oh man, was that ending something.
I have never before been so enraged by a game as I was with this game. This is coming from a Dark Souls veteran that isn't normally phased by death. Normally, I'll take the blame for my deaths as a misjudgement, but at the end, every death was due to bad game design. On hard mode, the difficuly I had played the entire game on, mind you, the enemy chasing you at the very end will kill you in a single hit, is faster than you so you can't get away, and can only be seen AFTER he has detected you. WTF were they thinking??? It wasn't scary, it wasn't spooky. It was absolutely rage inducing and left such a bad taste in my mouth that everything that the brilliant second act did was immediately undone.
The sections are so vastly different in quality that I feel the need to rate each act on its own:
Act 1: 4/10
Act 2: 8/10 (starting with the doctor)
Act 3: 1/10 (starting after the chapel)
Game: 4/10
Pros:
-Short (only a pro because I hate this game)

-Some memorable characters (i.e. the twins, the doctor, the priest)
-The camera is an interesting game mechanic

Cons:
-Ugly graphics
-Terrible optimization (walking through sewers shouldn't drop me from a locked 60 to 28 FPS)
-Stupid AI
-Not scary
-Tedious gameplay
-Annoying controls
-Unlikeable and unbelievable main character
-Horrible ending
-Lackluster and scatterbrained plot
-Random difficulty spikes
-Too much trial and error
-Did I mention the ending was bad?
-The ending sucked
-No option for surround sound so there's no way to tell what direction an enemy is in or how far away he is.
-No options for sound at all (the music can be obnoxious at times)

Outlast is a fast paced horror game where the character can't fight back so he must either run or hide.
Sneaking into an insane assylum where the nuts have taken over, you have to survive the blood soaked horror house and its inmates.  The gameplay is simple but the variety of enviroments and enemies make for enough variety to keep things interesting.  As well, there is an added weight to the game as story events that hurt your character can be felt as you play which really adds a sense of danger.

I've played plenty of horror games, and while many try to emulate others, FNAF takes a step away from the generic formulas presented by other games to introduce a unique concept. Rather than being out and about avoiding creatures of the night, you're firmly planted in one place, being your own office, and you must avoid the animatronic attackers by keeping track of them and using the lights and doors to detect them and shut them out, which brings a huge sense of suspense. The game can get quite hard in later nights, and can actually get tactical in some situations. While I think it is an entertaining game with a unique concept, it doesn't have very good longevity, and gets old after a while of playing it. It is fun to come back to every once in a while despite its low longevity, and I would say it succeeds as an above average horror game.

I didn't think I would like this game, but the developers at evil studio have done a fairly decent job. 6 levels on campaign (story mode) with 4 difficulty levels accompanied with 3 extra survival levels which just spawns a constant wave of enemies at you and you have to see how long you can survive overall. There are also various retro filters you can play with, so that you can see how the game would have looked if you still had a c64, amiga or spectrum. The game is fairly fast paced, the story was script up by crayon, it basically consists of here's the enemy go blow things up. Relatively bug free, though I have myself experienced some comical glitches in the game, like the storm on the last level sometimes has a mind of its own and can even go through the warp gate with you.
Music decent and groovy, the weapons and ships are cool and versatile, my personal favorite is the wasp with machine gun and special weapon activated. Basically it says 'get out of my way i'm coming through!'
The game was actually suppose to be a prequel to a upcoming game called 'Syder Universe' which the developers never really got off the ground. Even though this is their first game they have kind of lost interest for some reason and are trying to make a name for themselves with other projects. But by shifting their attention so quickly and not giving the customers things that they desire, they inadverty do make a name for themselves, but maybe one that is not so flattering. Because this is a really decent product, but short with content, throngs of gamers have expressed a desire for more levels both in campaign and survival and I myself would love to see that.
Achievement hunters may be somewhat perplexed with this game as several achievements require high score leaderboard requirements. Leaderboards more often than not showcase the results of numerous cheaters who often have scores demonstrating 100 million above everyone else. Biggest problem is that the developers every blue moon reset the leaderboard tallies. So gaining these achievements maybe taxing on serious achievment hunters. While some of these achievements seem more to be governed by the submitting of your score to the global score than the actual score itself being that important, it must be noted that this is only an expressed view of a handful gamers and no one really knows for sure how these achievements work as developers seem to largely ignore the fan base and ignore many queeries in the Steam forums.
Final thoughts is that the developers have used this game to showcase their talents and have also sadly at the same time displayed a barrage of false promises, inconsistencies with feedback and a lack of overall dedication to their first product. Still enjoyed it, but sad that the developers carelessness left many frustrated with the lack of content and with infuriating unrealistic leaderboards.

I'm gonna keep this relatively short and start off with the main con.
This game is a cash grab. The in game shop is completely unnecessary but it is completely neglectable.
Now with the good.
There are 12 hunters to play. 3 for each role. To unlock the new hunters you have to actually level up the other hunters. The four extra hunters in the bundle aren't even out yet. Each hunter has their own unique abilities and one ability that is shared for all in that class. (the trapper's arena, for example) This means that there are many different ways to play the game, regardless of what people seem to believe. Following Daisy is one way to find the monster, but you will never catch up if you stay behind her the whole time. Learning ways to cut the monster off and track it without daisy makes it a much more enjoyable experience.
Right now there are 3 monsters. Again you must unlock the rest. Unlike what a previous reviewer said, There are more ways to play the monster than just hiding until you get to your third evolution. You can take on a full group of hunters in the first stage and wipe them all out. This is harder than waiting for the last evolution but it is more fun. Each monster is completely different from the others and each has their own playstyle. Goliath is a melee bruiser while kraken is more of a ranged mage. Try learning the correct way to stealth if you feel that you're getting caught too often. Stealthing does not leave tracks so it is wise to start off the game that way.
There is no actual story mode for this game, but what they do have instead is a short 5 mission pvp "campaign" that puts a group of hunters against a player controlled monster. The unique thing about this campaign is that depending on who wins which mission, the next one is altered drastically. Having the monster win and egg hunt mission will reward him with minions or even environmental advantages. There are over 800,000 combinations of missions and outcomes which more than makes up for the lack of story mode. Only playing hunt will make the game boring after a while.
This is not a pve game. While it probably isnt worth the 60 bucks if they're going to add an in-game shop, it is still a fun game. I give it a 4/10 for price but a solid 8/10 for gameplay.

As shmups go, Syder Arcade is mediocre at best. The good things about it are elements of every shmup ever, but the things that aren't so good are its own additions.
There are multiple ships, none of which can possibly hope to match the power of the forward-shooting laser gun ship. Each ship has its own special weapon, none of which can possibly hope to match the power of the same ship's big♥♥♥♥♥laser. Level 3 has some very questionable design where part of the background is the exact same color as most enemy bullets, effectively making their shots invisible if they pass over it. The dialogue is so short, uninformative, cliched and referential that it actually detracts from the gameplay and would be better off being removed. There's a "hyperspeed" mechanic where if you keep going forward for a few seconds you get a speed boost, but it's not used very often - mostly on the last level, where you risk instant death from collision damage as a result. You can also turn around, unlike most shmups, but like the hyperspeed it's very under-utilized as 2/3rds of the levels go in one direction only and on the others you mostly just flip back and forth to face different waves.
It's not BAD, but it's not good either. Which brings me to the opening line: mediocre at best.

I have played a lot of survival games. For the most part, they all either start off great and end up stinking, or they stink from the onset.
This game is different. For the very first time I can say that a survival game has nailed survival. It is doing so in the most elegant and streamlined fashion, which I can't even believe I'm typing.
Years of games like Dayz have lead me to believe that survival games are supposed to be clumsy, sloppily designed, and painful to learn.
Thankfully The Long Dark handles cooking, crafting and inventory with an ease and simplicity that throws a middle finger to almost any survival game I've tried.
It's single player. I think, as of now, that is the only downside I would have for the game - but it isn't a downside.
This game instills a very tangible fear in you for mother nature. You feel alone, but you are surrounded by beauty. Gorgeous forests, mountain trails, and of course snow capped mountains and icy lakes.
The play area is massive, loot and spawn locations are randomized each new game, and the threat of harsh snow storms is only bested by the sight of a wolf, or worse, wolves... or even worse - a bear.
Discovering books allows you to read up on certain things, like ice fishing, firearms, or building campfires. Finishing these books enhances those abilities.
Finding your first rifle is empowering, and shooting a charging bear in the face 2 times before it mauls you is soul crushing.
That was me; Just over two hours into my first playthrough, feeling confident, I wandered into the dawn. Outside of my vision, a bear had spotted me. By the time I turned to fire, it was too late.
When the bear finished mauling me, I was shocked to find I was left hanging on to my life. I stumbled between some large rocks, built a campfire, and used almost all of the first aid I had. Still hopeful, I ate a meal and laid down in my sleeping bag to rest and regain my vitality.
Little did I know that my injuries would claim me as I drifted into dreams.
The game is complex, and yet every mechanic is intuitive and easy to learn. Exploration is exciting, whether it is a small lakeside cabin, an expansive network of caves, or an abandoned hydro dam. Often times the game evokes a sense of wonder, excitement and fear that I don't recall having since I first played Fallout 3.
Get this game. It's the best single player survival game I've ever ♥♥♥♥ing played, and I knew it within the first hour. If it wasn't, then why would I have stopped playing just to tell you all of this?
I am hopeful that one day a multiplayer survival title will take notes from this game. It would be amazing to play a game as silky smooth and devoid of zombies alongside friends and strangers. This is a title that would actually cause players to work together, because as threatening as the wolves and bears are - the world you must explore to survive is even more hostile.

This game is an absolute blast. It's hard to effectively convey how much fun this game is, because it doesn't seem like it would be fun and the trailers and screenshots do not do it justice, at all. But believe me when I say; if you're looking for a truely intense zombie apocalypse survival experience that is as realistic as it gets, where almost every moment incites true butterfly-inducing terror that resonates with your innermost being, while giving you all of this glistening, pant-soiling brilliance in a slightly retro, top-down, isometric view. This is your game.
I mean, for pete's sakes, you have to change your bandages at least twice a day or you run the risk of making your wounds infected, which will slowly kill you, unless you disinfect them with alcohol and a sterilized bandage. You have to cover up windows with blankets, otherwise zombies will see you/lights inside houses and they absolutely, definitely, positively will check and break a window. When you get bitten? It slowly gets worse as you succumb to the zombie virus, you don't die instantly. You get paranoid of anything, you become fatigued and, after about a day, you die. Slowly, but surely. This game is cool as all hell.
The controls are easy to grasp and the game runs smoothly, even if you're running the server software the game comes with and hosting at the same time, which is something I do frequently, to play with friends. It's also very easy to set up and comes with it's own server options.
Speaking of options. Holy hell, the custom options for starting a new game are phenominal. You get to customize what your character is like, down to their personality as well as how often weapons spawn, how often things decay and what type of zombies you're dealing with. You could opt for a 28 Days Later feel, making them fast, strong and generally a massive pain in the backside, or if you're more into your Romero lore, you could set them up to be classic, brittle shamblers that seem to spot you from 700 lightyears away.
Oh yeah, it's hard as hell as well. Don't expect to live forever, like other zombie games seem to allow you to do. This game is very realistic and eventually, you'll most likely run out of food and water. If you do manage to ensure your indefinite survival, then congratulations. You'd probably end up surviving a real zombie apocalypse.

There's a difference between a game being good, and a game being broadly-appealing. Cuphead is, unfortunately, only the former. It's got fantastic art style and sound. It's the kind of game I really really really want to like, but it's brutally difficult. Maybe with enough practice it's something I could conquer. Heck, it probably is. I spent about an hour with it, and what turned me off was two things: the controls being somewhat unpredictable, especially with a co-op partner in the mix, and the vertical difficulty curve straight off the bat. This is the type of game that "doesn't hold your hand," by which I mean it introduces you to the barest possible game mechanics and then immediately throws you headlong into the deep end. I prefer to get a chance to practice and build each mechanic on the one before it as the game ramps up in complexity and difficulty. This is not that type of game. Unfortunately I can't elaborate much beyond this, because in my hour of playing I didn't even clear the first level. I think having a co-op partner exacerbated the early difficulty because it messes with the camera progresses. If you're at all hesitant about it, just don't. Only buy this if you are prepared for an extreme challenge.
TL;DR Controls and co-op are funky, vertical difficulty curve, only pick it up if you're fully prepared for a challenge.

Pro's;
- Variety of buildings
- The Dynasty system
- Differences in eras
- Mod support
- Visuals
Con's;
- The happiness system
- Invasions/rebels
- The un-necessary decisions you are forced to make, why do I have to insult the King?
- Artificial intelligence
- Amount of content sold as DLC
- Combat system, why can a guard tower not kill a single enemy unit?
I find it hard to recommend Tropico 5. Its not a step up from its predecessor and is frustrating to play, especially when you are being invaded.
If you are looking for a superior Tropico experience, play the fourth instalment and avoid this title.

This game undeniably proves that it doesn't take nine figure budgets and an army of coders to produce a high quality, incredibly satisfying, and dangerously addictive game. As someone who is a veteran of many different zombie titles across multiple platforms, this one comes the closest to what I've always a wanted. They have a way of truly making up for the limited resources of being independant, by really compensating in the overall gameplay experience.
To start what I've always wanted was a game where I could test myself against the world. I always wanted to know how long would I last or what Mcguyver type device could I make out of random items in order to survive. How would I chose to hunker down and what would my defenses look like? I love the ability to customize almost everything. And the fact that the game forces you to become a better survivor by the simple fact that, unlike some other games where you can become a God like zombie slayer after only a short time, you must slowly build yourself up, find replacement parts or tools/materials to repair your current equipment, and if something breaks beyond repair and you can't find a replacement well tough cookies...this level of forced improvement is an incredible break from the all too typical "look at me I'm smashing zombies in the face with an unbreakable crowbar" type of games becoming common place these days.
Overall I can't recommend this game HIGHLY enough for someone looking for an exciting, addictive, and survival based sandbox game. It's a blast and a half to say the least.
