Good old open world RPG dungeon crawling that feels like Ultima Underworld. The locales and story reflect this sort of atmosphere. There's a lot of stuff to do, some cool abilities to fool around with, and quests that will make the player explore almost every nook and cranny in the game. The sidequests are fun, and don't feel overly compulsory. There are a lot of interesting little puzzles peppered throughout as well, which excellently showcase the model and texture creativity allowed with the game's engine.
Three complaints:
1 - It's very buggy. The game crashes when I wander into the path of an NPC, which happens at least every 10 minutes. Transparent textures render as pitch-black voids. Quests can be broken. Objects and characters can get pushed through objects. Enemies can get stuck on thin air, and this was usually how I ended up beating bosses.
2 - Artificial difficulty. This is not a term I typically use, but I'll make an exception here, because this game undeniably has it. The magic system is an example. I understand the need to have some kind of complex output for magic, given just how useful it is, but drawing out signs with the mouse is like doing so in Microsoft Paint. Even when I know how to do it, it takes, like, 5 tries before I create perfect shapes with the exact angles and straight lines. Meanwhile, the enemies can pinch 'em out in a matter of one or two seconds, but the enemies themselves are a different story. This is one of those games where "difficult enemy" means, that guy hits hard and has a lot of health. There's nothing wrong with strong bad guys, but making this the basis of difficulty for every boss and upper-level enemy in the game is just lazy. There is no strategy, just run in a circle until I manage to draw a perfect spell, turn around, fire it, rinse and repeat. Or, I suppose another option is to quickload until my opponent spawns in stuck and I can take my sweet time.
3 - A lack of explanation. This partially works to the game's benefit, making for quests that actually feel rewarding and puzzles that feel challenging, unlike certain games (coughSkyrimcough), but this stops being fun when the game takes too many liberties with this approach. I can deal with a spell in my quest log instead of my spellbook. What I can't deal with is having certain dialogues and cutscenes postponed simply, say,  because I haven't talked to a specific NPC, despite the fact that I already had the information I needed from reading a book, but no, I have to talk this person and hear what I already know, because it will trigger the next dialogue sequence with another character I had already gone to visit in an unfruitful attempt to advance the quest! This sort of situation is where the discrepancy happens, where the player is caught between the limited information provided by the quest log, and what action needs to be taken to progress. It results in a lot of pointless running around and wasted time.
Overall, I have somewhat positive feelings for the game. It's by no means perfect, but may have both the gameplay and atmosphere to appeal to more seasoned RPG players, specifically those who don't mind a few hiccups.

TL; DR: If you like X-COM style tactical RPGs, this is a pretty fun and light spin on it.  The game has some rough edges, but is a solid all around tactical RPG.
Long Version:
If you're into tactical RPGs like X-COM, then this is a fun 10-15 'light' experience.  The angle (you're stuntmen from a Power Rangers-esque TV show that get in a fued with the director and decided to start a new show) is original and can be pretty amusing.  For better or worse, you can fast forward through most the story.  I wish there was an in between, where you could read the cupious amount of story text quickly without reverting to warp speed, but it's either painfully slow or hyper speed.  The other thing holding the game back is a bit of UI/tutorial polish.  The game, especially in the beginning, rapidly unlocks new features, but never really even tells you they're there, let alone what everything means.  It's not a deal breaker, but I could imagine going through significant chunks of the game without realizing some suped up ability or item was available.
The other drawback of the game is the QTE Mecha mini-game that ends many of the episodes.  You basically are given a % chance to hit on a punch, to continure your combo, and have the option to switch to defense or lay a power move on.  Needless to say, you will feel the burn of the RNG when you miss 3 or 4 consecutive ~75% swings, each time taking massive damage because you can't properly defend when you miss.  You thene have a little bar that you have to click when it's in the right zone to deflect as much damage as possible.  I only 'lost' 3 or 4 times playing through the game, and every time it was in the mecha game.  Kudos for trying to mix it up with a different paced bit, but it's too rough around the edges, especially compared to the relatively tight tactical RPG play.
Speaking of the 'RPG' aspect, they are definitely on the lite side.  No XP, you just unlock the next level of the skill tree when you complete each season.  No mana points either, everything is done on a x-com style cool down system (also, there is no ammo, everything can be used as many times as it cools down).  There is crafting, though it's not very well explained.  The advantage of crafting is that the gear has a few set attributes, plus a few random attributes to it that MAY make it better than the items you just buy outright.  But you never know until you craft it, and you can't compare a craft item to your current gear until you actually make it.  You also have to combine lower craftable items into better items, and then better items again, to be able to craft the good stuff.  This, again, is never really explained and buried on a submenu - I didn't know I could do it until Season 5 (of 6), and until then, I was confused on what the point of a crafting system was when you never got the materials you needed to craft.  Turns out, I had plenty, but I had to combine my 75 rolls of regular tape into 15 rolls of silver tape, and then those 15 rolls into 5 rolls of gold tape...which I could then use to buy the pimp stuff.
If tactical RPGs are your thing, this is a nice light experience.  I imagine it has pretty low system specs, so it would probably be good on a laptop, though the Unity engine chugs occassionally, especially during the mecha scenes.  Definitely worth picking up for a few bucks or in a Humble Bundle.

I primarily bought this because it was on sale and due to the percentage of positive reviews.  Otherwise, before trying out this game I had very little exposure.
After having played it though, I'm not just disappointed but frustrated.  The game is essentially a walking simulator and not a great one at that.  You play an individual that can barely jog 100 feet, stay awake for 12 hours, not go into hypothermia after being outside for 30 seconds, or fall more than 2 feet into a pile of snow without breaking/spraining all sorts of bones.  Your sandbox is a barren, uninteresting place with no goals.  I've played a lot of survival games and there is often short term goals of getting camp setup or obtaining valuable supplies where, after having completed these goals, survival becomes easier -- there isn't anything like that (sure there are some items that help but nothing, even collectivelly, that really makes a difference).  Nor is there a long-term goal of saving survivors, contacting civiliation, or escaping the wilderness.  Put short, for a game about surviving, there isn't any point in surviving.  Beyond that there really isn't anything else in the game.
Therefore, in it's current state, I can't recommend the purchase, even at a sale price of $7.00.  Yes, it is early access but as is, it's not worth playing.
Misc Notes:
-The graphics are stylized but come off bland in-game.  The effects are also obnoxious as wind will flow out of rock faces and flow in impossible directions.  It can give the impression that you should seek shelter from the elements but what actually protects you is indiscernable beyond "go inside a building".  Perhaps the trailer might peak your interest but keep in mind other games who's trailers made their game seem better than they ultimately ended up being.
-The crafting system is tiny at the time of this writing.
-The best part of the game is the difficulty it sets forth, but without a reward or endgame, surviving the challenges feels flat and pointless.
-Development began in June of 2012.  It was released on Steam September 2014.  As of this publishing, it's still in alpha.
-"The first part of Story Mode’s Season One launches in Spring 2016, with the entirety of Season One being released episodically over the remainder of 2016."  Nothing have been release as of yet.  Additionally, your purchase will have only gotten you one episode.
-Even with the game's gamma set to max, the logo the player is supposed to compare it to isn't visable whatsoever.  This did make the game seem more realistic at night as without light pollution the world can be pitch black.  However it felt more like a badly implemented setting.

This game... is awesome. I love the concept. Created by Behold Studios, Chroma Squad is essentially a Power Rangers management sim. You get to make your own squad and customize your team to fit your desires of having one of the best or lamest Sentai teams ever!
The story is that a bunch of stuntmen quit their old job because they believe their director lacks creativity and want more creative freedom. The plot really goes off the rails later on but it's fun to watch. The dialogue of your team is super corny but I loved it however if that's not your thing then it might be something to consider if you're planning on getting Chroma Squad. The dialogue is filled with puns, references and enough fourth wall jokes to make Deadpool blush.
Visually it looks nice, it's some nice pixel graphics. I don't think they use it as a lazy excuse since it's nice good to look at and there is detail in the game. Not the heaviest but enough to distinguish everything easily. The music is personally one of the best parts of the game. This is some really good chiptune music, it has some great soundtracks that get you pumped up for a boss battle and my personal favourite "This is Cerebro" is so campy and so catchy.
The gameplay itself, when fighting is a tactical RPG. A pretty fun one, the game has an emphasis on team attacks which is pretty cool and works with the theme. You got abilities and cool weapons for the different classes to play around with and a cool chunk of bosses. You also get finishing moves for them which is pretty sweet as well. One thing that does bother me a bit is that a lot of the time the game can be too easy but then there is a huge difficulty spike in the last level. What is that all about?
When not in normal combat you're doing one of two things. The first is managing your studio, it's fun as you have to upgrade the studio, buy or craft new gear, hire agencies to promote your show, check emails and all that managment sim stuff. The other is the mech combat. It wouldn't be Power Rangers without a giant mech battle in almost every episode. It can be fun but really it just comes down to chance whether attack or block attacks. It looks cool but it's pretty shallow.
To conclude my mad ramblings I of course like this game a lot! It's one of those games I wished I played earlier when it came out last year. If you understand the basic core material you'll have a lot of fun with it.  If you've never heard of Power Rangers AT ALL or know exactly ziltch about it then I wouldn't reccommend this to you. Otherwise you should definitely get it! It's a game that's about having fun rather than being amazingly unique or difficult (for the most part). I give this an 8.5/10

Disclaimer: If you want to be scared constantly and have a fear of character death, this game is not for you.
Proclaimer: If you want to enjoy a fantastic, haunting, deeply emotional story, this game is for you.
I'll do my best not to drop any spoilers in this review. If you enjoyed What Remains of Edith Fitch, or The Secret World, or both; you will certainly love this game. It is a NARRATIVE game which is clearly said by the devs in the very first video on Steam. This should express to you that this game is about the story, and not a challenge. I feel that many of the negative reviews are based upon the fact that the buyers expected a jump-scare, chase-escape ridden Horror game. This is not that kind of game, and should not be advertised as such. This is like watching a scary cartoon only the subject matters are very real and haunting.
The plot? Well, lets just say they leave a lot open to interpretation and it's a good thing. You should be free to draw whichever conclussion you think best fits from this game and it's ending.
Play: Its point and click. However I do appreciate that the devs allow a run function while in the park. I do not enjoy a constant pace game which drags. This game allows you to follow what is an EXTREMELY linear path, but at your own pace. The prompted narratives are well placed and reminded me a lot of Edith Finch, which is an absolutely amazing game. Do not expect to play this game, just let it play and help it along yourself by reading the extra little notes along the way.
The Ugly: This game is not designed to be re-playable immediately. It's like a Movie, you watch it, you forget it, you think about it, you watch it again.
Personal: Without spoiling too much, this game does deal with concepts of psychological disorders in a very in-your-face manner. As a veteran with severe PTSD which causes depression and anxiety I greatly appreciated the fact that they do their best to show people how terrible of an experience it is to go into recovery.
8/10

"The Park" is presented as a psychological horror adventure, but it's actually a game about a common mental disorder. Horror elements are present (darkness, the occasional mild jump scare, a few hints about a "cursed" place, etc.), but rarely take focus.
The game is divided into two parts. In the first half, you explore a dilapidated former amusement park in search of your son. There is, however, not much actual exploration possible, as the park is rather small - it consists of only six attractions, which are arranged on a linear path. On four of those you can take a ride, which is usually a graphically unimpressive sequence where no interaction is possible while the main character may share some memories. One of the rides is a long, drawn-out, and frankly pretty boring rendition of the "Hänsel and Gretel" story. Apart from these rides, the only thing that you can actually _do_ in this park, is reading some notes that provide information about its background. Due to the linearity of the layout and the lack of more opportunities for interaction, I found this part fairly dull. The design of the park also felt very cookie-cutter and unimaginative, and its backstory did not seem particularly interesting to me.
The second part of the game is where the actual story kicks into gear. You walk through a run-down apartment and read more notes that detail the protagonist's condition, situation, and history. The game uses a clever technique of revisiting the apartment several times to demonstrate how the protagonist's disorder, combined with a very difficult emotional and economical situation, successively spirals out of control. This part
have formed a very serious story with considerable impact on the player, but at least for me, it just didn't work. After the slow and boring first part in the park, this second part of the game felt very rushed, the information just gets flung into your face with little opportunity to feel any emotional impact. I never found a way to empathize with the main character or her situation. On a cognitive level it was clear to me that "this is tragic and terrible", but the game failed to make me actually
that, it just never drew me in. Which is quite sad, because the latter probably
the goal of the writer, he just did not achieve it.
Other than the story, there is little to talk about. The game has no puzzles or action sequences. Graphics are okay thanks to the Unreal engine - they are a bit bland, but that fits the game's theme. The voice acting is a bit of a double-edged sword: on one hand, it often repulsed me rather than drawing me into the narrative, but on the other hand, the inadequate emotions and rigid negative judgments are absolutely fitting for the main character's condition.
The game is very short, I saw everything it had to offer in less than 3 hours (and I played very slowly). I feel that the game is a bit too expensive for the little content it has to offer. It's also not very polished, basic features such as key rebinding are missing, and right at the start I hit a common and still unresolved bug that prevented me from moving at all until I went back to the menu.
Let's get back to the story for a few final thoughts. I commend the authors of The Park for choosing a serious and important real-world topic for their game. The depicted condition - in the very severe sub-form that appears in the game - causes a lot of suffering, and games can actually help us unaffected people to understand how they feel for someone who's affected. However, this condition is very difficult to write a game about. I feel that the authors have succeeded in keeping their writing realistic and authentic - they showed the associated emotions accurately, they did not shield the player from the very disturbing thoughts that this condition can evoke, they did their research (as some of the in-game books demonstrate), and they handled their difficult subject matter carefully and responsibly.
At the same time, though, I feel that they have failed in turning this serious subject into an engaging game. For the game's narrative to work, it would have been imperative to address the player's emotions, and to let us form an emotional bond to the main character - and this unfortunately never happens, or at least did not happen in my case, although I'm usually very open in that regard. It would have helped to include some scenes about happier times, to give players more opportunities to resonate with the character they play. It might also have helped to let the player actually live through crucial situations of increasing severity, instead of just shooting a barrage of in-your-face texts our way in the second part.
In the end, I think that the game design and the level of the writing, sadly, just weren't up to the quality that the ambitious subject required. As such, the game straddles an uncomfortable position of having trouble to bring its psychological elements across, while not being scary enough to be a good horror game either.

TLD is a harsh, unforgiving first-person survial game that somehow reminds me of Dark Souls and Demon's souls. One single slip up, one idiotic mistake, one badly aimed bullet and you're dead. Weeks of time and effort, the life you have managed to build for yourself, all wiped out in an instant.
It is recommended to play at least one round either in a forgiving location or on a easier mode, just to get a feel for the game. From there, ramp the difficulty up to Stalker and never look back. The true feeling of triumph of Stalker comes from overcoming wolf hunting packs and ravenous bears, blizzards so cold they freeze you the moment you venture outside and a scarcity of any and all supplies.
As with all good steam games, the experience is constantly evolving. Challenge modes and skill levels were the recent additions, with plans for seasonal change and story mode to be released within the next few months. That being said, it is still very much an alpha, and i am greatly looking forward to what Hinterland comes up with in the coming months, hopefully aditional Challenge Modes being among them them.

decide what's important to your survival. You're fragile in this game and you will be beaten and battered to hell if you don't stay vigilant and aware to your surroundings and stats.
In my experience, I never really felt like I had everything I would need to be well off, which I really enjoy in a survival game. Makes you feel like you're actually

Travelling was always a big gamble, was I going to find shelter before nightfall? Was a blizzard, bear, or wolf going to catch me off guard? Simple tasks like hunting and scavenging became treacherous, but to stay indoors would bring on the threat of dehydration and starvation.
I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys immersive survival experiences, because that's exactly what you'll find in the sandbox survival mode. The game will be so much more when story mode is released, but I'm content with the current sandbox and challenge modes, well worth the cost.

So, I'm not one of the people that played this game when I was younger. I played a large portion of PS2 games, but I was never able to find a copy of these.
I plan on updating my review as time goes on, as this review would have to cover what this product is in it's entirety, and that spans four games.
Currently I'm 5 hours into the first game, and I have to admit, I'm horribly bored. I bought it because I've always heard a ton of great things about the game, but thus far it's been 90% cutscenes, and I feel like after five hours the story is moving, but I just haven't done anything. I can't even do any side quests yet until I progress further, aside from the first one. I'm sticking with it in the hopes that it picks up, by the second game at the very least.
As it currently stands thus far into the game, I have no problem with the visuals, as I feel they have been updated very nicely. Gameplay is pretty standard for what I'd expect and the game runs fabulously. However, as I have yet to be able to enjoy myself, I'll have to give the game a thumbs down at this point in time. If there was a neutral button, I would definitely choose that option, but I cannot give it a thumbs up at this point in time. Really hoping it picks up, though. I enjoy the cutscenes, for what they're worth.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
So, as of now I have about 24 hours into the game and have completed the first of the four games bundled. I still hold onto what was stated above, and the first 5-6 hours of the game felt dragged out and awfully slow. In about that time I think I actually played the game a total of ten minutes. Having never played this game before, and not having the nostalgia many others are basing their reviews off of, it was pretty difficult to force myself through the beginning of the first game. however, shortly after that 6 hour mark you get thrusted into the Arena and the game finally lets you free and I had an absolute blast.
The game mechanics, though outdated, were still fun and engaging regardless of how many times I repeated the same thing (in perfect MMO fashion). The whole "online aspect" of the game was a wonderful experience, and seeing how modern the game is despite coming out over a decade ago really shows the vision that went into this. They basically predicted current online play to a T. Building relationships and watching the characters grow and bond was a great experience, I just wish they could have blend the combat and cutscenes together better to make it more enjoyable.
Another negative thing I found about the first game is how frustratingly easy it was. Before I was even halfway through the game I was already capped at 50 basically one-shotting everything. To a degree it was my fault, but I didn't realize how quickly I would level up or how quick the level cap would approach.
I've just begun the second game and I have to admit, I am thoroughly excited to see where this goes. I would now definitely recommend this bundle of .Hack//G.U. games, especially if the rest of the games continue to improve at this rate as well.

Good old open world RPG dungeon crawling that feels like Ultima Underworld. The locales and story reflect this sort of atmosphere. There's a lot of stuff to do, some cool abilities to fool around with, and quests that will make the player explore almost every nook and cranny in the game. The sidequests are fun, and don't feel overly compulsory. There are a lot of interesting little puzzles peppered throughout as well, which excellently showcase the model and texture creativity allowed with the game's engine.
Three complaints:
1 - It's very buggy. The game crashes when I wander into the path of an NPC, which happens at least every 10 minutes. Transparent textures render as pitch-black voids. Quests can be broken. Objects and characters can get pushed through objects. Enemies can get stuck on thin air, and this was usually how I ended up beating bosses.
2 - Artificial difficulty. This is not a term I typically use, but I'll make an exception here, because this game undeniably has it. The magic system is an example. I understand the need to have some kind of complex output for magic, given just how useful it is, but drawing out signs with the mouse is like doing so in Microsoft Paint. Even when I know how to do it, it takes, like, 5 tries before I create perfect shapes with the exact angles and straight lines. Meanwhile, the enemies can pinch 'em out in a matter of one or two seconds, but the enemies themselves are a different story. This is one of those games where "difficult enemy" means, that guy hits hard and has a lot of health. There's nothing wrong with strong bad guys, but making this the basis of difficulty for every boss and upper-level enemy in the game is just lazy. There is no strategy, just run in a circle until I manage to draw a perfect spell, turn around, fire it, rinse and repeat. Or, I suppose another option is to quickload until my opponent spawns in stuck and I can take my sweet time.
3 - A lack of explanation. This partially works to the game's benefit, making for quests that actually feel rewarding and puzzles that feel challenging, unlike certain games (coughSkyrimcough), but this stops being fun when the game takes too many liberties with this approach. I can deal with a spell in my quest log instead of my spellbook. What I can't deal with is having certain dialogues and cutscenes postponed simply, say,  because I haven't talked to a specific NPC, despite the fact that I already had the information I needed from reading a book, but no, I have to talk this person and hear what I already know, because it will trigger the next dialogue sequence with another character I had already gone to visit in an unfruitful attempt to advance the quest! This sort of situation is where the discrepancy happens, where the player is caught between the limited information provided by the quest log, and what action needs to be taken to progress. It results in a lot of pointless running around and wasted time.
Overall, I have somewhat positive feelings for the game. It's by no means perfect, but may have both the gameplay and atmosphere to appeal to more seasoned RPG players, specifically those who don't mind a few hiccups.

FNAF puts you in the position of a nightguard at a local pizzeria, Freddy Fazbear's Pizza. Loved by children through the day, the pizzeria hosts animatronics to make their experience more enjoyable and memorable, a shame they don't know that in the night time, these animatronics become flesh-seeking psychopaths designed to jumpscare you right out of your chair.
The gameplay is simple. You are a night guard with a control panel that can switch between camera shots. You must rapidly switch between which camera you are viewing to constantly keep an eye on these pesky animatronics. If you lose them, the chances are, when you drop your control panel; you'll be greeted by a screen full of spooks and screaming. This isn't one for those who have a worry of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ themselves while gaming.
If you're searching for the next best soundtrack of the year, you're not going to find it here. But in terms of creating a mood and atmosphere, the FNAF grungy graphics style allows for the perfect ambience along with the creepy and straight-up spine tingling sounds effects. The tone is set, people.
There is a storyline in FNAF, believe it or not. There's a history to the establishment you find yourself working at for pay that isn't worth paying for a new pair of trousers every single night. Of course, this history stretches on into the next 3 installations of the game; but as far as actual quality of narrative goes, the history is there, and it's believable to an extent. No doubt, you'll be inclined to believe the history a hell of a lot more once you're in the room.
The game runs for 5 nights, obviously, but following this, there's a custom game mode at the end which will allow you to select the difficulty of each animatronic for the night. You can replay this game to your hearts content, until you memorise the whole pattern of the animatronics movement; which seldom occurs.
This game offers no multiplayer features.
Thanks for reading,

Despite the clunkiness of the old-school controls, the premise of Arx Fatalis had me fairly interested: the sun has died and the various races have somewhat put aside old grudges in a mutual effort to convert the old dwarven mines into a habitable  environment. As such the entire game (as far as I know at least) takes place in winding tunnels between subterranian fortresses.
The first few hours were also interesting in that outside of fighting your way out of the goblin prison you start in, the game was remarkably murder-free for a fantasy RPG, with most of your efforts being aimed at trading favors for favors in the hopes of unconvering your lost memories, the only combat being defending yourself from rats and oversized spiders in the tunnels between settlements.
However, shortly after you find out who you are and by extention the main plot of the game, this changes and for me ruined my interest in continuing to play. Not because of the murder, mind - I'm used to the notion that walking down the street in a videogame without ending a dozen thinking feeling lives is nigh impossible, and I would hope AF still keeps a nice middle ground - but because the game's combat controls are just that terrible.
Arx Fatalis, as mentioned earlier, takes place almost entirely in claustrophobic cave tunnels, and your melee controls are essentially limited to light attack or holding the button down for a heavy attack. No blocking, and no dodging to speak of besides walking briskly backwards in the hopes you don't back into a wall (and you will, because the entire game is tight winding tunnels).
And the magic controls are even worse, going for the admittedly fairly unique method of casting spells by tracing runes in the air, the sort of idea that would be tailor made for motion controls if they existed when this game was published, but since they don't you're forced to try drawing them with only a rough visual guide using your mouse. Good luck trying to scribble out a three- or four-rune spell while holding down the Ctrl key while being attacked by two or three goons. In all likelihood you'll be punched to death while desperately trying to get "Yok" to register.
Arkane Studios, the team behind Dishonored, were also responsible for this game and it kind of shows with the intriguing worldbuilding, but it also shows how much they've grown with practice since this. If you somehow can handle the awful controls I'm sure the story is interesting, but personally I can't recommend such a nearly-unplayable mess.

LYNE has been described as "deceptively simple", and it is just that. It encourages the player to sharpen and expand their minds as they struggle to work his/her way through a series of puzzles, varying in difficulty. LYNE combines soft tones, and pastel colours to make even the most perplexing maze a relaxing experience. I would recommend this game to new and experienced puzzle-lovers alike, as I cannot imagine a world where one would leave LYNE feeling less than satisfied.
LYNE is lacking in story, or rather, there is none - But this does not take away from the enjoyable experience that it provides.
The feature that stands out the most is the games progression. LYNE rewards its players through achievements, and not just the Steam kind. The puzzles are divided into sets of 25, in categories A-Z. As each set of 25 puzzles is completed, the player will be awarded a set of points (which eventually unlock different colour schemes and skins), and occasionally unlock another set. There is no rule for beating the puzzles in order, which prevents the player getting stuck on a difficult puzzle, and quitting the game. In the event that a player runs into one of these complex obstacles, they can simply move onto the next piece in the set, and return to the difficult one later with a fresh mind.
The fact that many puzzle games stick follow the concept of offering only one solution to each problem makes LYNE even more refreshing. There is always more than one way to reach completion through the labyrinth consisting of dots, colours and shapes. Furthermore, LYNE provides a fresh set of Daily puzzles to everyone, which keeps interest alive even after it has been finished. It is a game that can be picked up, and put down without the fear of having to restart it after a break.
While LYNE is not the most complicated puzzle-game on record, I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys the feeling of well-deserved gratification after an intellectual pursuit. LYNE will make you think, encourage you to challenge yourself, and potentially rekindle ones love for problem solving.
Amazingly simple. I absolutely adore the controls of LYNE, for the purposes of casual gaming. All you have to do is click and drag, and sometimes that is actually a good thing. =)
The interface is heavily geometric, and filled with pastels. Of course, you can unlock various customization options that will permit you to change the appearance of your LYNE to your liking. The graphics are pleasant, but I would not go as far as to call them godly.
LYNE's soundrack is simplistic, and not it's best point. While the sounds are soothing and dynamic, I was not particularly impressed by LYNE's audio appeal.
I will definitely be playing LYNE again, and can say that it won't lose its appeal after one playthrough. You might not want to play it everyday of your entire life, but sometimes, you might find yourself venturing back to it.

I'm into turn-based, tactical, strategy games. I'm into swords & sorcery, high fantasy settings. Things I like about this game: it is all of these things. It doesn't always feel like it wants to be turn-based though. For example, some text boxes seem to disappear on a timer, whether or not I've had time to read them. During a busy Villain phase, the camera will follow the action around the board, leaving me to look around afterwards, instead of taking my time to read the name, dice roll, and effects of each action as it happens, before moving onto the next one.
My biggest complaint is the lack of explanation. The tutorial doesn't cover much. It's one board, which does show you some tactical elements: how to move characters, explore, and attack. It touches on concepts like turn order and traps, but doesn't fully explain them. A lot of strategy goes into choosing how many and which heroes to use on any particular board, and also choosing which abilities they'll have. Nevermind explaining the strategy, the tutorial doesn't even touch on the mechanics of this part of the game. You could easily play for a while, while overlooking the fact that you can change your heroes' prepared abilities.
At times, the terminology is confusing and confused. A "tile" is 16 "squares" (arranged 4x4), and remembering which is which is important for understanding how your abilities work. The explanation for Birdsong's Bardic Lore mentions "treasure chests"; it actually applies to defeated monsters, not to either kind of treasure chest (those found within a level, or those awarded for the completion of a level). Melf's Acid Arrow claims to inflict "Stunned" status; it actually inflicts "Poisoned".
If there is integrated help (e.g. tooltips), I haven't found it. On the Steam forum, a link to a rulebook was posted several weeks ago. That helps, but it's definitely "version #1". It's got typos, it still doesn't explain everything, and it's not necessarily easy to reference or search while you're playing. I still don't know exactly what benefit I'll get out of crafting better bracers for Dragonbait, but I guess I'll just try it to find out. As a boardgame player, I really expected more clarity and explanations from this videogame which is adapted from a boardgame.
I got this game at a discount (~$10), and it's ok for me at that price. I probably wouldn't recommend it to anyone who isn't already into turn-based, tactical, strategy games with swords & sorcery, high fantasy settings. I probably wouldn't recommend it at full price to anyone. I definitely wouldn't recommend it to anyone who isn't prepared to poke around and click everything just to figure out what exactly it is that you do in this game.

Seriously, grab this game. It's the Power Rangers video game the world never knew it needed.

The FOV problem has been discussed in this game's Steam forum for many months, and the devs are absolutely aware of that. But they ... don't give a flying intercourse. Why is beyond me. Increasing that little number only costs a few minutes, and postponing this (It's an Early Access game.) only means that discovering and then fixing potential issues is postponed, too, meaning that since FOV is idiotically seen as something optional, it might not happen at all. This game provides a buffer of solitude within the maelstrom of everyday life.
Immersion in the stark beauty of the landscape is inevitable.  Realistic choices and penalties force reliance upon preparation and real-life survival analysis of every moment of play.  Every triumph over the environment, every advance, feels earned by persistence and wit.
The Long Dark did not hold my hand.  Poor survival decisions are easy to make and often unrecoverable.  My first death was caused by harvesting a deer, a committment of an hour or two, without checking my calorie reserves.  In-game, the consequences of overcommitting resources, energy, and willpower--of relying on luck or hidden strength to carry you--are devastatingly real.
But the world isn't dark.  It is beautiful, and if exploration holds danger it also holds reward.  Nature is both enemy and ally.
The Long Dark carries deeply satisfying echoes; reminders of our evolution as a cunning beast--the basic struggle to survive, and the triumph of overcoming obstacles with a mixture of forethought, persistance, and inspiration.
For the individual who finds peace and affirmation in the struggle for balance, I truly cannot recommend a game more wholeheartedly.
Edit 1:  I genuinely cannot thank the game creators enough for the option to play as both a female protagonist, and a female protagonist who isn't wearing a fur bikini.
Edit 2:   The new challenge mode is amazing.  This may actually be the best game I've ever played, and it's not even finished.

An innovative sci-fi FPS with a focus on storytelling.
+ Compelling plot
+ Customisation
+ Variety of weapons
+ Ambience
+ Graphics
+ Soundtrack
- Randomness in hacking (sometimes one cannot hack something manually due to the RNG)
- Hacking can be quite tedious at times
- Consolised gunplay
Bioshock is a unique sci-fi FPS. It tells the story of Jack, sole survivor of a plane crash in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean.
The action takes place in 1960 in the underwater city of Rapture. It was founded in 1946 by a businessman named Andrew Ryan, for he wanted to escape the political, religious, and social restrictions of the post-WWII world. Everything is privately owned, even the police. The result is a capitalist dystopia full of citizens addicted to a genetic-altering substance called ADAM. In 1958, a civil war outbreaks and leaves the city in disarray. The game begins with Jack finding his way to the city of Rapture via a lighthouse. The player has to make their way through the city. What is interesting, there are tons of voice recordings scattered all over the place, giving the story another layer.
The gameplay is centred on completing various tasks and harvesting or rescuing Little Sisters while eliminating Splicers, the insane citizens. Apart from rich weaponry (firearms, explosives, and even a crossbow), one can upgrade their character with plasmids and tonics. Plasmids are active powers (i.e. Electro Bolt, Winter Blast) and tonics are passive upgrades (i.e. more health given by bandages and snacks, easier hacking). There are limited slots for both but, as the game progresses, the player can buy more slots using the ADAM gained by either harvesting or rescuing Little Sisters. These young girls have been conditioned to gather the substance from corpses. They are protected by Big Daddies, genetically enhanced human beings transplanted into diving suits. Daddies are a force to be reckoned with, for they can take a lot of punishment.
The options provided by plasmids, tonics, and weapons are virtually limitless which is one of the greatest qualities of the game. Next, the compelling plot which is enhances the experience by the audiologs found throughout the game. The graphics and ambience are also important factors adding to the immersion.
However, Bioshock comes with minor flaws. First, the hacking mini-game may get boring really quick. Moreover, it is not uncommon for the manual hacking to be impossible due to the luck of the draw. Another nuisance is the consolised gunplay.
In conclusion, Bioshock is an astounding title. It provides an immersive experience and it stands the test of time. I strongly recommend playing the game even if you are not a fan of FPS games.

Let's face it, the only appeal for this game is its omage to golden era of hand drawn cartoons and animations; it is visually stunning and the music is superb; the gameplay however, is a very different story.
If this game didn't feature this visual style and music, it wouldn't be as positively reviewed as it is; it is a very flawed game from a gameplay standpoint.
This game isn't difficult by nature, it's RNG based, which makes the game more difficult than it needs to be.
You will often land in a situation where if you didn't move quickly enough through a section, you can get stuck between a rock and a hard place, somewhere where you inevitably have to take a hit in order to progress.
The game comes with a "co-op design", however, in many levels, especially the "run and gun" ones, you end up realizing that the levels were not designed with 2 players in mind:
- if one player makes a mistake, you both pay (which can be a good mechanic, but its executed very poorly here)
- it gets harder to distinguish your placement on the screen (and to tell yourself apart from your partner) since everything is pretty flat and in a state of chaos.
- you will more often than not be halting progress from your team mate since you hold the camera back (or vice-versa).

Whether you should buy this game or not begs one question: Is the pain of enduring poor game mechanics worth the treat for you?

Arx Fatalis is the 2002 brainchild of Arkane Studios, a studio that went on to make Dark Messiah of Might and Magic, and Dishonoured. Notably, the game was intended to be Ultima: Underworld III, but the studio was unable to obtain the license. Even without it, this has been hailed as the spiritual successor to Ultima: Underworld, and rightfully so.
It's "inspirations" are as evident as they are positive. The right-click menu overlay, popular in its early 2000s peers, once again makes it return and proving that it never gets old. Arx Fatalis handles it a tad differently to others, keeping the overlay mostly bereft except for inventory and controlling the bulk through separate windows brought up via the journal.
While manipulating the environment never gets old, the overlay itself does get clunky compared System Shock 2 or Morrowind. From inventories that give you separate windows when upgraded, instead of just making the existing window bigger, to useless, nigh unreadable maps, to the journal system that is Morrowind's, without all those pesky "search" functions.
Arx Fatalis boasts an "intelligent story", which is laughable. You start as the amnesiac named Am Shaegar, find out your purpose is to save the world, and then save the world. Along the way you bear witness to some incredibly hammy voice-acting, which falls directly into "so bad it's good" tier.
The worldbuilding itself is less hilariously trite. While the generic fantasy races stay generic fantasy races, the premise of being forced to live inside one big cavern system lends itself to some interesting towns and details - the giant pumps that flood the levels with air, for example. But Arx Fatalis hails to an era where the story wasn't the focal point of RPGs, pre-Infinity Engine.
King Lunshire's one-dimensional antics and cults that just evil cults only provide the background for the real draw: dungeon delving.
The game boasts being able to take care of enemies in a variety of ways. This is a lie. The game is based around a single playstyle - spellsword.
You may be able to fireball or stealth a goblin to death, but try pulling that on a Ylside warrior and watch your dangly bits get plastered to the ceiling. Your magic will always play second fiddle to your sword, and DEX doesn't get a fiddle at all.
It's therefore a shame that the swordplay is so limited. Arx Fatalis falls into the traditional aRPG trap of having the majority of the combat be incredibly simple and boring. You take out your weapon. You charge up your weapon. You hit things with your weapon. There's several different animations but they change nothing. Footsies that amount to kiting. No real movesets, no real variety, and even the speed of combat is deplorably slow.
It fails basic decisions/time game design, a common problem with these games. Buffs aside, you will largely be doing the same exact 3-step sequence from beginning to end.
Thankfully the incredibly hard-hitting enemies combined with limited resources in the midst of battle, especially when up against a Ylside or a Lich, keeps these battles engaging to the end. They never become a chore. The payoff of lobbed limbs and exploding enemies is a bonus.
The dungeons themselves are fantastic. Far from open-world, these areas are distinctly level based and are flooded with hidden secrets - which unlike the barren and uninteresting landscapes of open world games, have withstood the test of time.
The rest of the game's elements are particularly notable. There's some sidequests, but the triggers are arbitrary and you'll most likely just luck into them. The puzzles you encounter within the dungeons themselves can quickly get tedious, and rely on searching the area for items or buttons which are hidden in annoying locations. Occasionally with physics, and Fatalis' physics system isn't as great as its item manipulation system.
But it wouldn't be a true dungeon delver without puzzles, would it?
Arx Fatalis is a relic, and its a relic in the best possible way. Hailing back to the best of Looking Glass' work and Ultima Underworld itself, for every clunky mechanic there's another aspect that counters it to make it work.
If you're looking for an oppressive dungeon-delving game with brilliantly designed levels and inventory mechanics which don't treat you liked a fool, then I couldn't recommend Arx Fatalis more.

Please ignore the 6min game time. I Have completed the game. The time is due to using the arx libertatis patch without which the game is unplayable. But steam does not count time when using it ... I have spent about 20 hours on it.
I cannot recommend it to others despite its many good points such as,
- Excellent atmosphere
- Interesting setting
- Good basic game play
The problem is, that even with the well made fan patch Arts Libertatis it suffers from an amazing amount of annoyances and half-broken/half-working mechanics, examples,
- The magic system is drawing of runes on the screen. The problem is that the game has miserable recognition of what you draw and even after your 20th spell cast, you'll often have to retry 2, 3, 4 or 10 times.
- You can lose or sell quest objects and they have no tags, yep, sell or drop items, discover 2 mins before that you needed them for final door to last boss (not a joke, keep your akbaa stones).
- You have to suffer through an amazing amount of half messed up content, including Poor maps,  Bad quest log (going to need a walkthrough), Endless corridors for no reason, Bad as in really bad stealth
--- Aaaand in quick order, stuck mobs, stuck bosses (including the end boss), puzzles that decide to ignore you (ooh mithril goes into that 1cm area and everywhere else it results in a throw, funny...) or simply bug out (invulnerable, one-hit kills you, mandatory quest mob please met mr. stomper, uuuuh, mr. stomper? .... stomper? ... damn ... where is my closest save)
Add to this, that builds are badly unbalanced too and are to a large degree defined at start, leaving limited options to adapt them later on,
- Melee build? Can work. But Melee is near suicide at end of game, where out of nowhere the  gameplay become utterly anti-melee. There is a decent chance you cant complete last 20% of the game unless very comitted melee build.
- Ranged build? One weapon for ranged, yep, one, and you dont start with it nor necessarily pick it up. Does not make sense as a build.
- Mage build? Amazing overpowered magic (hello fireball on anything) except when it is totally underpowered (want to cast a non-prepared, max 3 prepared spells possible) spells in combat? ooh we are sorry, please redraw your runes while getting wailed at.
- Balanced build? Dont be stubborn and try it, odds are you cant complete the game.
It's not that the various build puts you at a disadvantage, but that they simply dont work and you likely cant do anything to fix it once you find out. So starting with a guide in hand is more or less mandatory and so is a mage build for big majority of players.
All in all, unbalanced and a general mess.
Essentially it is, for all nostalgi people have for it, a game that sort of never made it out of a late beta and frankly it shows. If you are fanatical, slogging through it might be worth it. But though I am a pretty hard core RPG fan, it came up short when I had completed it and thought if it had been worth it.
Grab something else on your wanted list instead of this.

Outlast isn't a bad game, it's just a bad horror game. Please don't judge my Steam playtime. I have unlocked ALL achievements on another platform, including one for beating the game on Insane without reloading the camera battery, so it's safe to say I know the game quite well.
The game initially starts off well and makes you anxious, but after the first level you will realise that the enemies are dumber than a sack of hammers and that the scares are merely cheap jumpscares the entire time. Chris Walker (big tough guy) is used too frequently as an enemy and his spawns begin to become a frustration rather than scare. Furthermore, the constant chase sequences are boring as hell and very uninspired. Not to mention that the enemies themselves aren't even scary. In addition to this, I dislike the constant crawl through vents/squeeze through barrier sequences. It becomes annoying and seems to be merely an opportunity to help the game load the next area. Not to mention that the game is exceptionally linear. There's something about having so many locked doors that irritates me. I respect that the budget for the game wasn't massive, but it still makes the experience less memorable.
On the other hand, there were some (but few) areas where I was actually terrified and I think this was mainly due to how dark the level was and not being able to see the dangers that lurked nearby. Sadly these moments are rare as the game relies on cheap jumpscares and extreme gore to startle the player.
Outlast is a relatively short game and will most likely take you 2-3 hours to beat on the first go. After that, it can be finished in a little over an hour. The higher difficulties and achievements do add replayability. The INSANE difficulty achievements were especially fun to achieve and I am quite proud to own them.
I'd say that the game is more scary and disturbing in regards to its story. I must say that the story told within Outlast is excellent and the prime reason why I recommend the game. After finishing the story, I became very interested in the lore and immediately downloaded the DLC, which also tells a good story and has strong ties to the main game. I also admired the graphics and attention to detail within the game's world and how such small details operate on the story's bigger picture.
The game is very similar to Layers of Fear. Short, linear, full of jumpscares, but tells an excellent story. I recommend this game to horror fans but I personally don't think it deserves to hold the crown for the horror genre.

Tropico 5. Good game but it has a few problems. Some of the mechanics don't seem to work sometimes such as:
-You can have plenty of food sources and have them evenly distributed around your population and have a distribution network (grocery stores) but citizens often still die of starvation.
-Even if you have built tenements and apartments, people won't move into them even if they can afford it. This makes the Hosuing Happiness to become stuck at loe even though it should increase
-The Teamsters system could use some tweking; often times they just don't seem to do their jobs transporting goods around the island
-The overlay system isn't always accurate or it seems to change; sometimes after placing a building down in a green space, the space will suddenly change to a lesser green or yellow reducing the buildings effectiveness
Note that these problems only seem to happen sometimes with a certain game mechanic just seeming to stop working but it happens often enough for me to notice it.
Aside from that, there are a couple other things that could use some improvement:
-Fishing is an unreliable source of food as the fish populations get depleted very quickly even with only one Fishing Wharf. This is also with Fishing Wharf upgrades that replenish fish populations
-If you place Oyster Farms out on Fishing Deposits, they suddenly become useless for gathering food through Fishing Wharfs
-Soldiers often ignore the most immediate threat/threat closest to them and go after another one far away
-It could use an actual day/night cycle
Having said all of that, this is still a very good game that is a lot of fun and a good time. I would definitely recommend it. It just seems like it is overdue for a new patch or update from the people who made it to fix some balance issues, bugs and improve basic mechanics.

Outlast, outlast, OUTLAST....
When I got this game (from a friend as a gift) I did not really knew what I was letting myself into... I didn't know anything about this game, whatsoever!
Everyone was like "OMG! it is so scary!" or "Goodluck, rather you than me" and I couldn't understand why. I kid you not, every single time I launched this game someone (sometimes more than one at the time) on Steam would either message me "Boo" or something related to me being scared or asking me what the fxck I am thinking.
My answer was always "I'm no poussey!" hence me being a professional kitty and all *wink wink*. But the truth is, I did get scared halfway through the game - not only did the game test out fears that I have IRL, but also I was not alone when I played it... I played it with someone who is very dear to me, and who basically used me as bait, most of the game XD
I didn't mind though, it was the most fun I have EVER had on a singleplayer game. Not only did we play it together - but we created a new way of co-op via imagination, which made the plot thicken so much more! We pumped each other up, so the scares were, techniacally, even worse than it should be!
I remember one night just after 2 having a major scare - it was the worst yet, I think I even woke up my neighbours with my squeel - the dog was crying in the other room.. I almost couldn't play t for a few days - trying to look for excuses like a "poussey". He felt so bad, but I didn't mind - it was the best game ever so far for me - and it was all because I could experience it with him.
And listen, scary games don't usually phase me at all, I am the type of person who laughs at horror movies - it's like a comedy to me, and I went into this game with the same mindset and I came out with a whole different point of view.. Maybe, I could be scared... But only if the ones I care about are involved - because not only do I carry my own emotions, but I was looking out for someone else.
Moral of the story - to have the "ultimate" experience, get the game - get teamspeak, and get someone to play it with... create your own imaginary co-op and experience this WITH someone who is awesome as he is. Don't think "Oh, it won't be scary because I won't be alone" because trust me - IT IS NOT LESS SCARY!!!!!!!! So try it, or are you too big of a "poussey"? ;)
All in all I rate this game a 9/10 :)

This release should be treated as both a beloved franchise and a potential fundraiser for future titles from the same developer. Is it debateable whether the original 4 dotHack games were more deserving of a remaster (I personally believed them to be the better games, but to each their own), regardless this titles success and early adoption by consumers will help fund its port and further new titles.
In short I fully recommend this game. Its aged like a fine wine, sure its a little grindy, but most JRPGs are, and with potential mod support....well the future looks bright for this game. Its funny we now live in a time where I have a VR headset and am playing the dotHack franchise on PC...were some argue it should have been from the get go.

Syder Arcade is a wonderful title that has brought all of the good components from the 90s arcade side-scrolling shooters into the modern-day era. Developed by Studio Evil, you are a singular ship thrown against innumerable amounts of enemy crafts to accomplish different missions, ranging from protecting a friendly but immense warship through an asteroid field, to simply destroying every ship that you aren’t piloting. These six missions are delivered to you in sequence in the form of a simple yet endearing storyline, and after a good ten minutes of flying around space with a level of skill that you can look back and be proud of, you can compare your scores to all the other pilots out there.
Immediately upon launching the game, you will notice the graphics, which can only be described as stunning. Even the menu screen is pleasing to look at and simple to navigate. The game also offers a “GFX” setting on this menu where you can select from between 20 different graphics filters. These filters are great fun to play around with, and some will certainly bring back memories of days gone by for older gamers while the more modern filters are very impressive for gamers who are perhaps not old enough for the nostalgia to extend to them. The graphics really shine through during the fighting; if you can manage to tear your eyes off of the seemingly unavoidable shots being fired at you for even a second, you will be able to appreciate the asteroid belts in the background and even the amount of effort and detail that has gone into the mines – which will only be on your screen for a few seconds before they violently explode.

Sadly, this game is plagued with bugs and questionable decisions regarding the achievement conditions. Regarding achievements in arcade games in general: They give you (or at least me) a purpose to push yourself further, that's why it's really unfortunate if there's a problem with them and that's why I adress issues with them specifically.
One of the very distressing bugs can occur in the last of the six campaign levels and prevents you from finishing the level/campaign (there are moving rings you have to fly through which sometimes simply don't move). Another one affects one of the three Survival levels, Ice Canyon, which prevents you from finishing it as well.
Many achievements aren't doing the game any good as well. For example, you have four achievements for completing the campaign on various difficulty settings. You might think it would be logical to unlock achievements of the lower difficulty levels automatically when you beat the campaign, but that's not the case here. Even if you beat the campaign the first time directly on Hard (“Arcade”), you still have to play the campaign again on Young Gun (“Normal”) and Tourist (“Easy”). Combine this with level-stopping bug and you're in for a time of frustration, and that's why I didn't even bother trying Pure (“Very Hard”).
Also, there are four leaderboard achievements which are simply dreadful. You have to be in the top 15% in the corresponding leaderboard (campaign and each of the three survival levels). Did I also mention that the achievements are bugged and sometimes get shown way later? One of the survival level leaderboard achievements is genuinely bugged and you can't get it, but you won't immediately know except if you look it up.
It is a shame. If there were less bugs, no leaderboard achievements and if it simply were more polished, it could have been really, really good. I actually even had some fun while playing it, but with the campaign-stopping bug present I simply cannot recommend it.

Decent sound and visuals wasted on a subpar by the numbers shmup.
If you are just getting into shmups there are countless better and cheaper alternatives to Syder Arcade. If you are a fan of shoot-em-ups, horizontal scrolling or not, you will find nothing unique or exceptional here.
The controls do their job alright, the ability to change directions will come as a unique selling point to anyone who hasn't played G-Darius in the last 18 or Defender in the last 35 years since they were released. The retro throw-back music does its job well, not interesting enough to be listenable on its own, but not bad enough to be a distraction. The same cannot be said for the visuals, that look appealing and crisp for the most part but seriously lack variety. The backgrounds also quite often get in the way of the gameplay when bloom hides enemy bullets. There's a wide selection of pseudo-retro Computer graphic filters you can add, that exacerbate this problem. It's a fun little gag for a short while but renders the game almost unplayable in parts. Enemy designs are dull and you've seen them in basically every shmup ever created. Whether that is an intentional nod to the greats or not is irrelevant. Being ironically uncreative is still being uncreative.
As a whole Syder Arcade has no substance and lacks anything unique. It's short, generic and wholly unremarkable, especially for the price. I understand that the developers may have a genuine love for the genre but they obviously did not have a single thing to add to the mix. Indie developers can do so much better and so much more creative, especially in 2013.
Don't waste your money on this one. I got it on sale for 1€ and I still feel ripped off.

Before skyrim, before oblivion... around the time of morrowind, there was a great little rpg game that came out called Arx Fatalis. Unfortunately, Morrowind cast such a huge shadow that this game was only seen and played by a few.
At the time however, it was just as immersive, in depth, and advanced as any elder scrolls game. This game doesnt hold your hand. It requires you to think, and be intuitive. The spell casting was some of the most unique of its kind during those days (you draw the spell symbols in the air with the mouse).
Anyway, this is a great, old school, first person, elder scrolls like rpg. Its slow paced and very detailed. If you have little to no patience, dont get this game.
One last thing. You REALLY need the free open source mod called Arx Libertatis to play this. Yes, it will run on steam, but expect REALLY long load times, framerate issues, and many other buggy things due to trying to run such an old game on modern machines. The ARx Libertatis mod basically fixes these thing, allowing it to run smooth and fast, as well as fixing tons of bug and improving the visuals. Dont play far without this mod, because it doesnt seem to work with non-mod game saves (at least from what I can tell). Best to just get it and play with it from the start. It doesnt change content, its just a fan made patch and improvement to the game that is A+ quality.

I recommend this game against my better judgement because the bugs make it unfinishable (and to many people probably unplayable) I actually cannot finish the game because if I try to cast 'enchant object' the game crashes with a fatal error! And you have to be able to do that to finish the game. Bumping in to people 30% of the time doees the same, or going up stairs... despite the crash worthyness of it I got a number of hours enjoyment from it and it is a very many layered game experience. Most of the puzzles are fun and interesting... a few are just pointless where it's overly laborious lever puzzles or click every pixel on an area until you get the thing you can't see and wouldn't know was there without a walkthrough. Mostly I didn't need to resort to them but when I did it was pretty much always a... you what?!!! how would you find that??!! There are a lot of different endings/options and side quests and the play is varied. The magic was an interesting idea but badly executed, you draw the magic symbols, however the character recognition is APPALLING combat casting even if you are really practiced is a joke. Additionally many of the damage spells are just a bit rubbish, however the range of options are good and you can use them in a lot of ways. Another way the game suffers is it's rules on stealth, I played a high stealth 80+ and magic. Despite having invisibility cast on myself and high stealth AND being hid in the shadows (and stationary) I still get a 'look it's him!' followed by being chopped to gobbets... Not very well done, which is a shame because the game has a lot of scope for it. I spent many happy hours creeping around casting extinguish spells on torches so I could terrorise monsters from the shadows but it only tended to work well on one hit kill monsters because despite hitting someone at range from a dark shadow in the back they automatically know exactly where you are and home in! Ducking behind a wall while your arrow was in flight would 'sometimes' allow you to avoid detection... Anyway, in a nutshell lots of interesting things to do and things to kill, quite a few frustrating gameplay things and buggy as anything but still very playable to the point where I'd be tempted to try again with a straightforward choppy character and see if the 'enchant' bug was just for this character which suggests it's a fun enough game to overlook the flaws. However as an aside I'd look up how to do some of the basics as the game provides sod all help on how to do even basic things i.e. how to pick a lock, how to combine items, how to move a stack of objects etc. etc. it's lack of instruction was apparently a 'gameplay' thing including rules on hunger... or rather no rules or indication you just have to eat food every so often or it's 'bad' but no food meter or indicator if you're keeping up with it or not... aaaaanyway yeah, but still fun. So hence 'against my better judgement recommends this game'

Arx Fatalis is a pretty difficult and hardcore experience.  The game relies heavily on puzzle and problem solving, which I found refreshing over its action oriented counterparts.  Not only that, some encounters are downright difficult, but the feeling of conquering these challenges is reward enough.  Additionally there is a fun rune drawing system to spell casting that puts an interesting spin on spell combat.
Arx hearkens back to the old days of first person dungeon crawlers which I found to be a blast of nostalgia.  Back in the ol' days (Read early 90's PC play), a lot of first person RPGs took place entirely either in a dungeon or underground complex, or indoors in some way (probably due to the fact you didn't have to render much). Arx also has it's share of secret doors and buttons hidden in the underground walls not dissimilar to what you'd expect during that era.
If you're going to play it on a modern PC system, you should probably download Arx Liberatis, a fan made mod that adapts the game to modern systems.  I had found that the game was almost unplayable for me until I installed the mod.

Wonderful little tactical RPG game where you control a team of actors with their own show where they fight monsters, which starts coming true as time goes on.
The meat of the game is the tactical turn based combat, and as someone who really enjoys this type of gameplay this is right up my alley. There are also some RPG elements outside of combat, such as allocating skill points, crafting and buying upgrades.
After completing most maps you join together and go into a giant mecha to fight the boss of the map again, with a different combat style which is focused on timing the hits and using a limited number of different abilities. This is a nice addition for the first few times, however it is not nearly as fleshed out and feels like an after thought. And seeing as how you have to do a bunch of these fights I'm quite sure everyone will get tired of them before the end of the game.
The story is reasonably entertaining, although it can become tiresome to follow since it is delivered solely through text boxes of the main characaters, and you have to wait for each one to finish scrolling in order to move on to the next one. So if you read much faster than the game scrolls then you're going to have to do a lot of waiting. There is an option to fast forward through everything, however it is not really useful if you still want to follow the story since the fast forward skips everything.
And the game does go a little overboard with the pixel artstyle, I certainly would have liked more definition and fluid animations. Also the overall design starts to become stale with time, especially since this is quite a long game.
I would easily recommend Chroma Squad to any fan of the tactical turn based combat style.

Chroma Squad is a Tactical RPG game made by Behold Studios, creators of the mobile game, Knights of Pen and Paper, an RPG that is more pressing buttons that movement. Now you'd think that this would make it hard for them, seeing as they're pretty much doing nothing the same. If you do, get out. This game is packed with humor, references, and breaking of the fourth wall. And while most people hate breaking the fourth wall, it's done in a way where if you literally are paying no attention, you will not see it. And if you're going into this game using the internet for the first time, the references to pop culture and video games will definitely fly over your head, but if you know the internet like the back of your hand, every reference will make you laugh, and there are a lot. The game play is simple, you have two actions you can do with every character every turn, and you can switch between who you're using by clicking their box, or using both of the above player's actions. Each "class" has their own unique set of skills, with customization diverse enough so that there is very little repetition. A lot of this game's achievements can be accomplished on the first run, but to get them all you will have to play the game at least three times. And if you get stuck, the community has already figured them out. After you beat the game, I reccomend sticking around after the credits for each run, and you will be pleased by what comes after, but stick around until you get forced out of them to get information that will complete the story more and more. Now buy the game and get to playing. #FrendshipIsForever

I think everything has been said about Outlast, so I'll keep my review short. This is by far the best and scariest horror game that I played in a very long long time.  It is technically very well made. Fantastic graphics and sounds, stable frame rates, found no bugs, responsive controls. The gameplay can best be compared to Amnesia, but in my opinion Outlast is doing everything better, in all aspects. This feeling of doom and helplessness is just fantstic. You never know what awaits you behind the next corner and horror and insanity are ever present. And yet Outlast is surprisingly fair at all times. I've never come across any frustrating moments where frustration kills horror. So yet I've died a few times but that's been my fault as there have always been realistic chances for me to escape or hide. Only the story is a bit thin and weak, especially the ending, which is why I definitely recommend playing the DLC "Whistleblower" as well. There, a lot of questions are being answered, and it provides a satisfying ending as well. It took me almost 13 hours to finish main game and DLC. It's probably possible to rush through the game much faster, but those 13 hours felt perfect for me - not one minute too long, not one minute too short. It's an intense game, a brilliant game, and definitely worth each cent!

This is a PC adaptation of the D&D boardgame 'Tomb of Annihilation'.  So far I've beaten the game on normal and am playing through Expert.  There are three difficulty levels and you get to craft new equipment with 5 improvement levels for each of your champions as you progress through the story.  As someone who has played the boardgames this is based on, I think it's a great adaptation.
Some people don't like the 'punishing' feel of getting forced encounters for not exploring.  That's probably because they're playing the game wrong.  Part of the enjoyment of the tactics is understanding how to be exploring every turn possible while clearing the monsters out for loot and experience points.  Also there are multiple ways to cancel bad encounters through equipment, skills, and adrenaline which is earned through defeating monsters.
Know when to cancel encounters and when to accept them.  Some are far far worse than others.  Happy adventuring!

Outlast isn't a bad game, it's just a bad horror game. Please don't judge my Steam playtime. I have unlocked ALL achievements on another platform, including one for beating the game on Insane without reloading the camera battery, so it's safe to say I know the game quite well.
The game initially starts off well and makes you anxious, but after the first level you will realise that the enemies are dumber than a sack of hammers and that the scares are merely cheap jumpscares the entire time. Chris Walker (big tough guy) is used too frequently as an enemy and his spawns begin to become a frustration rather than scare. Furthermore, the constant chase sequences are boring as hell and very uninspired. Not to mention that the enemies themselves aren't even scary. In addition to this, I dislike the constant crawl through vents/squeeze through barrier sequences. It becomes annoying and seems to be merely an opportunity to help the game load the next area. Not to mention that the game is exceptionally linear. There's something about having so many locked doors that irritates me. I respect that the budget for the game wasn't massive, but it still makes the experience less memorable.
On the other hand, there were some (but few) areas where I was actually terrified and I think this was mainly due to how dark the level was and not being able to see the dangers that lurked nearby. Sadly these moments are rare as the game relies on cheap jumpscares and extreme gore to startle the player.
Outlast is a relatively short game and will most likely take you 2-3 hours to beat on the first go. After that, it can be finished in a little over an hour. The higher difficulties and achievements do add replayability. The INSANE difficulty achievements were especially fun to achieve and I am quite proud to own them.
I'd say that the game is more scary and disturbing in regards to its story. I must say that the story told within Outlast is excellent and the prime reason why I recommend the game. After finishing the story, I became very interested in the lore and immediately downloaded the DLC, which also tells a good story and has strong ties to the main game. I also admired the graphics and attention to detail within the game's world and how such small details operate on the story's bigger picture.
The game is very similar to Layers of Fear. Short, linear, full of jumpscares, but tells an excellent story. I recommend this game to horror fans but I personally don't think it deserves to hold the crown for the horror genre.
