I'm a longtime fan of the .hack series to the point where you could call me a fanboy. I have criticisms of the first four games (.hack Infection, Mutation, Outbreak and Quarantine) mostly for being so stale and grindy. That being said, this is a detail-oriented review that seeks to answer questions like "Do I need to play the original series to understand this one?" So if you don't enjoy walls of text or you just want a direct review of THIS game ONLY, skip it.
The game has a complex story, so I'll try to simplify it.
Mild story spoilers ahead.
-----------------------------------------
If you haven't played a .hack game before, this is a great place to start. The game includes an "OS Terminal" that has a bunch of videos which will catch new players up with what they missed in the first four PS2 games, and while they're a bit slow and tedious to sit through, it sure as hell beats buying the original games for about $400 collectively and spending 2 weeks grinding through the story.
.hack//G.U. is an offline, single-player game that emulates the atmosphere and features of an actual MMORPG. It was designed back in 2006 for players that wanted an online game but couldn't justify paying $15 a month to play. It emulates a lot of the aesthetic of early Everquest stylings while also adding more modern sci-fi/hacking themes. If you like anything cyberpunk or futuristic mixed with high-fantasy medieval tones, you'll love .hack//G.U.
For clarification, the G.U. series on PS2 had 3 parts: Volume 1: Rebirth, Volume 2: Reminisce, and Volume 3: Redemption, which is a sequel to the IMOQ series mentioned above. This version, Last Recode, not only remastered the original PS2 series, it actually ADDED Volume 4 that included cut content from the original final game, complete with returning voice actors, new abilities/story quests and so on. It's kind of mind-blowing that a publisher would ADD NEW CONTENT to an old niche PS2 game and remaster it for current-gen consoles and PCs. That fact alone is worth the price of admission.
The story is very enigmatic and dramatic. I love cheesy anime drama stories, but this game takes it to the next level. There's a lot of screaming, death, romance, revenge, and everything else you might expect from a typical shounen anime. As a 16-year-old back in the day, this was really cool to me. As an adult, I acknowledge all the cliche's but I still love it.
In the original .hack PS2 series, the protagonist player named Kite logged in to play an MMO known plainly as "The World" (this was before all the cancerous Jojo memes, for the record) with his friend Yasuhiko who controls his character named Orca, a high-level and famous player. After a basic tutorial and a run-through of the combat and dungeon, Kite and Orca suddenly get teleported to an area where a mysterious white-haired, angelic-looking girl named Aura hands him an item called the Book of Twilight. She vanishes and a monster appears known as "Skeith," whom uses an ability on Orca known as "Data Drain," which kills him and puts Yasuhiko into a coma. Kite gets teleported out of the battleground thanks to the help of a hacker known as Helba, and he remarks that he doesn't know what happened to his friend, as he vows to explore the mysteries hidden within the world.
As he searches deeply for clues as to why a game can put a real life person into a coma, he looks to the forums for help, as he poses the question of whether or not anyone else heard of this coma phenomenon. When he goes back later to check, he finds his post deleted. The game progresses and it becomes clear that the system administrators of the game are aware of the problem but are trying to cover up the truth by censoring any of the discussion about the issue. If you want to find out the rest of the story, there are plenty of story cutscenes available on YouTube as well as within .hack//G.U. Last Recode's files, but if you like murder mystery or psychological horror, you've come to the right place.
Within the context of the first four games, the fear of that sort of thing happening once again is due to an event known as "Pluto's Kiss," in which a hacker shut down every computer in the world, arming the US's missile defense retaliation system and nearly ending the world before it was stopped at the last second. This is a fictional world in which fear of AI and network security is a very real thing that mirror's our own world's politics. There are news apps that update you on events going on in the real world within the game and multiple parallel stories (such as a documentary series known as "Online Jack" that takes place concurrently to the game's events) to give the illusion that this online game is both alive and impactful. In the first 4 games in the series, the games came with a DVD OVA known as
that also used a concurrent real-life story to supplement the in-game plot; the idea that everything happening in the game is making an impact on the real world in real time - a super interesting concept.
.hack//G.U. takes place after the initial four games, and it's a massive improvement. There's more action, better graphics, more polished voice acting and gameplay. If you feel the need to replay the original series in order to enjoy this one, don't. Aside from some narrative caveats, this is a fully-functioning standalone game that has nods and returning characters from the original series, but you won't miss much if you just watch a recap.
-----------------------------------------
.hack//G.U. stars a player known as Haseo who starts off as an idealistic youth engulfed with angst and vengeance, and I'll be honest, he's a huge d-bag that most players will find brash, unlikeable, and incredibly toxic. He thinks he's the best, he talks down to people who try to help him, and he's just plain rude. As the game progresses, however, he becomes completely redeemable as he matures in response to the tribulations he faces in The World. His primary motivation is, much like the last game, to unearth the mystery behind his friend Shino being killed by a hacker and put into a coma in real-life, but this time there's romance involved between the two. If you're interested in exploring the preceding events of G.U., check out the anime .hack//Roots, which is a prequel that takes place in the same universe with most of the same characters.
Haseo, like Kite before him, inherits a character with hacking skills. Within the context of the story, you're a hacker playing in a world full of normal, law-abiding players. You're basically a Gary Stu (aka male Mary Sue) who's stronger than everyone and the story revolves around you. Along the way you'll encounter a wide variety of interesting characters, like Sakubo, a player character shared by a timid little brother and a tsundere little sister, Saku and Bo, respectively. When you invite her to your party, there's a 50/50 chance of getting either one. You'll meet Piros the Third, who's actually based on the president of the publishing/developer company CyberConnect2, an eccentric roleplayer who never breaks character and acts incredibly cheesy and overly heroic. You'll meet a large beastman-character named Gabi, who, in real life, is a novelist and retired professor of cultural anthropology, who's so busy that he makes it a habit to respond to questions with only a one-line, several-word response usually accompanied by a smiley face. :) You'll also meet familiar faces from the first game, some of which have gone rogue and become the central antagonists.
I could go on and on and on about this series and why I adore it. The artists and composers are responsible for Ghost in the Shell and Evangelion among other things. If you like this game, watch the anime series. Read the wiki. It's a deep, never-ending mysterious series that treats the player like an intelligent adult. It's my #1 RPG series of all time and if you like these kinds of games, you'll love Last Recode!

Okay... I'm gonna cut to the chase here.  GET THIS F*CKING GAME, BROS!  For real -- it's free.  You can't beat that in the first place.  But beyond that, it's also INCREDIBLY fun!
It'd be a real challenge to beat this one in single player, despite the checkpoints and infinite continues -- but this is a game that's really MEANT to be played with some bros anyway.  The gameplay reminds me quite a bit of "Metal Slug" more than anything else, but the rag-doll physics, explosions, and destructible stage and background elements take it to a whole new level of insanity.
Literally... when my little brother and I played through this game, we were laughing like little kids to the point of tears.  ESPECIALLY at the ending "interrogation".
While it is a bit short, that is totally okay for such an amazingly fun (and challenging!) free game such as this.  Even so, there's quite a bit of replay value due to all of the different characters.  At first it irked me being randomly assigned characters, but I really think it's a strength after playing the game more.  It really adds to keeping everything feeling fresh and absolutely insane the entire way through the game -- and you will unlock plenty more "bros" as you make progress.
Based on the strength of this freeware game, I've just now picked up "Broforce" as well -- and truly cannot WAIT to play it with some bros!  If you're into old-school platformers, run-and-gun games, or anything fun in general, do yourself a favor and get this one.

This is the journal of Amy Williams.
It has been ten days since this whole thing started. When chaos broke out and the police finally gave up, many packed their cars and decided to leave the town. I was able to see a big fire for days near the highway, so I decided to hole up at my place. It was not long until I realized that I would not be able to survive for long. Food was running out and if someone decided to come in I would not be able to stop them. So I grabbed a frying pan and made my way around the block. Only a few houses down was my doctor's clinic. On the way I had to fight off quite a number of dead ones. To say that I was scared to death would be an understatement. I secured the clinic and holed up at the first story, the late doctor's appartement. In the following days I was able to loot the grocery store down the street and the houses of my former neighbors. I thanked god for Alex still having his two pistols. Poor guy.
Sometimes I hear screams in the distance and gunshots going off. But these beasts begin clumping up in packs and I was not able to find other survivers. I am all alone up here.

Fast, Fun... but short. This is a true arcade game in the most classic sense. This games feels like a coin-up in this regard because there are only 6 zones (levels) to play with increasing difficulty settings. The global scoreboard helps cement the whole "get the highest score" just like in the classic arcade.
I finished the campaign on normal difficulty with only 2 hours played. This isn't to say i'm "done" with the game forever, but like most arcade games it has the charm of being something you play once in a while for just a few minutes to scratch an itch. If you try to play the game more.. it feels somewhat lacking. This is how it should be, though. If the developers atempted something like a 25 level campaign with a deep storyline and so on i would probably hold it against them. The game doesn't need anything of that nature, so it's short play time and burst of fun style gaming is simply a retro throw-back that everyone can really enjoy. It is a refined modern coin-up distilled into a truely pure form.
Is it worth the full price? Sure, but maybe not worth knocking people over to get to. Should you definitely get it on sale? You'd be an idiot not to.

Must own for Shoot 'Em Up fans old and new (and if you are old enough, you are i for a treat). This is the free-scrolling shooter that plays much like the old Williams Arcade game Defender. The Shoot and Flip buttons will have you realize that real quick, as well as the radar, so if you have played Defender, you will feel right at home with the controls.
This game is also Bullet Hell for those of you who think you can dodge colored dots for days, you will enjoy trying your luck in this.
So what is Syder Arcade? It's a Shoot 'Em Up game that plays like the days of old-school shooters, where there is no grinding, no upgrades, no unlockable, ...none of that. You start the game, and you start shooting and trying to survive. You will hopefully be doing both equally as much. It will take all of your skills to reach the top-ranks of the leaderboard because the points do matter, and killing and surviving is just not enough. You will need to earn in-game score achievements like Chain Combos to get the bonus points needed to move up on the leaderboards, and there are enough of them to keep you occupied with improving your skills.
Campaign is your basic story mode and each stage will have it's own high score as well as a campaign highscore if you manage to finish it entirely. When you are done there (or want to take a break from it), jump into Survival mode. This is the true arcade feeling and a test of your skills to truly see if you are worthy of the SHMUP genre.
Also, if you've been playing games since the Amiga or Commodore days, listen the to music. You can tell this was an idea pulled from the mid-to-late 80's, and it was a good idea that is worth every penny.

Most of the reviews as of late is nerd rage over the pricing.  Not really helpful when it comes to actual game play.  Here's the skinny:
The game itself is "repetitious" by nature, JUST LIKE L4D, yet people STILL play L4D.  Why?  Because each game ISN'T like the last.  So please, find a better excuse to rage.  The game does play similarly to L4D, but goes further by adding class specialties and monster variation.
Hunters:
There are 4 basic class types with (currently) 3 different character for each: Support, Medic, Assault, Trapper.  The brilliant part of this game is the need for all of them.  There isn't a single class you wouldn't be hurting without.  And in that way, it makes it fun to play as any of the classes.  Bad assault-ers means you're likely going to be killed before you can kill the monster.   Bad Support-ers means no damage boost and lower utility overall (class abilities for support includes a UAV, tracking AOE dust, and a damage dealing missile barrage).  Bad Medics mean you die (and in the case of Lazarus, have to wait for an air drop).  Bad Trappers are scary, they can easily segment your team or keep you from getting to the monster.
The flip side to all of this is, when you have a cohesive team, you can really tell and it's very rewarding.  2K made tracking the monster a challenge and the low lighting mixed with tangled and rough terrain make the hunt more exciting.
Monsters:
They're still balancing things, but the monsters are also fun to play as.  As long as you are staying competitive in building yourself up while balancing that with the whittling the hunters down, the fights are very fair.  Because the hunters don't level up or grow more powerful as the round progresses, there's a very tangible sense of urgency as the monster grows.  This feeds greatly into the need for feeding and hiding until the opportune moment (which may not necessarily be at level 3).
TL;DR
The game is super fun (assuming you don't get a team full of Rambos).  Is it worth the money?  The base game, yes.  The DLC is ALWAYS UP TO YOU STOP RAGING </rage>.  As 2K announced, you won't be kept from playing in matches against/with people who have the DLC.  Considering this isn't pay2win and ALL the hunters AND monsters are being constantly balanced, this isn't going to hit a wall.  You want the monsters and hunters?  PAY FOR IT.  They didn't lie to you and tell you the season pass was for everything.  If you bought it, you knew what you were getting.  I think the game is a great piece of work and INCREDIBLY fun.
Edit:
It was requested I give more detail on the actual play out of the game.
You select your job class based on preference.  The system checks everyone elses preferences and assigns classes based on that (conflicts result in switching on each round).  Once you pick you class, you pick your perk (which you gain on leveling) and you get dropped from an airship after some witty banter and possible sexual innuendo.
Upon hitting the surface, you have to use the environment around you to track the monster.  Monsters running along will leave tracks (which are lit up to help you follow them) and monsters who kill and eat other animals leave behind carcasses and disturb wild life (which also show up to the hunters to track).
Lest you think being the monster is all about running away, you'd be wrong.  Aside from hiding and waiting for an ambush, you can also mess with the hunters by crawling around (not leaving any tracks) and then setting off indicators far away (to confuse the ever living daylights out of them).  Some of the monsters have the ability to grab a hunter and carry them away to be chased by the team.  Other monsters are simple brute force, squish your opponents type, and still others are a combination.  Being a monster requires you to be clever.  You may be a brute, but you can still die easily if you just charge in.  Monsters have 4 skills that you can choose to level as you eat other animals and evolve.  So eat heartily and stalk your prey.

), but all in all, the teams are fairly balanced. One of it's major flaws is that it has a matchmaking system out of hell. The networking needs to be improved dramatically.

Finished Outlast and its DLC Whistleblower. Phuuu! Played fully on Linux. (ref:
Outlast is a nice first-person survival horror game. You are an investigator researching the rumors about the Mount Massive Asylum. You arrive with your car, park the car just at the gate and from this point on you are on your feet, walking around the manor. No one is seen, doors shut tight. Then you find an opened window and you crawl into the building… starting the horror.
Pretty soon you find remnants of brutal massacres. Entrails, heads, limbs, and blood – gallons of blood – everywhere. This is the “good” old school of American horror: gore, gore, GORE! There is no time for a subtle inkling of some ‘thing’ which causes you goosebumps. Mhm, nope. It’s pretty expressive, direct. Brutal. And as if it isn’t enough, the DLC masters to even add to this already very high level of gore. Whistleblower introduces yet two other lunatics with a very unhealthy sense of body fixation. Along with several pretty hefty cutscenes.
And, oh – btw – the graphics are excellent. Light, shadow, smoke, all are very good placed. Some light bulbs are blinking, some lights are shaking. More than once you need your camera with some night vision capabilities to view your path in more or less absolute darkness. These all add to the atmosphere.
From time to time you find documents revealing what has happened to the asylum. The story which started off been rather some sort of cliche turns out to be quite interesting.
Then the gameplay: rather soon you discover to be not the only survivor in this pretty large building. Some inmates are afraid of you, some ignore you, and some … try to kill you. Namely, one big super strong guy, Chris Walker, is very keen and eager to get a “grip” on you. Pretty explicit when he succeeds…
Sadly you are not able to interact with the environment in any other manner than open doors, pick up batteries, jump over obstacles or crouch under them, pressing some buttons, moving some boards and pickup up keys to unlock doors. There is no inventory. You may not combine anything on your way through the manor. No nothing you can use as a weapon to defend yourself. Oh, and no health bar too: run for your life! … or hide under beds or in lockers and pray not to be discovered.
This is also the critic on the game: as a player, you have virtually no agency. There is always exactly one single way the developer wanted you to go. Sometimes faster under stress as been chased to death, sometimes with some leisure. However, you do not have any real choice. As such, Outlast is likely more a horror “movie” than a horror “game”. There is nothing for the player to do as to exactly do what the developers wanted to. Point. No (or at least a very, very limited) interaction with the environment. You can’t even turn the lights on (or off, if you really wanted to be it even darker than in the first place).
If you are interested in good stories, riddles, interesting places look elsewhere. If you are into the most extreme American teenager horror money can get you: welcome.
Still, the enacting, the presentation of the game is really engaging.
7/10

There's a difference between a game being good, and a game being broadly-appealing. Cuphead is, unfortunately, only the former. It's got fantastic art style and sound. It's the kind of game I really really really want to like, but it's brutally difficult. Maybe with enough practice it's something I could conquer. Heck, it probably is. I spent about an hour with it, and what turned me off was two things: the controls being somewhat unpredictable, especially with a co-op partner in the mix, and the vertical difficulty curve straight off the bat. This is the type of game that "doesn't hold your hand," by which I mean it introduces you to the barest possible game mechanics and then immediately throws you headlong into the deep end. I prefer to get a chance to practice and build each mechanic on the one before it as the game ramps up in complexity and difficulty. This is not that type of game. Unfortunately I can't elaborate much beyond this, because in my hour of playing I didn't even clear the first level. I think having a co-op partner exacerbated the early difficulty because it messes with the camera progresses. If you're at all hesitant about it, just don't. Only buy this if you are prepared for an extreme challenge.
TL;DR Controls and co-op are funky, vertical difficulty curve, only pick it up if you're fully prepared for a challenge.

Time moves only when you move. It’s a simple idea, all things considered, but oddly enough its taken until the arrival of Superhot before it has truly come to see the light of day. The basic premise here couldn’t be simpler; use this power to the fullest, kill everything that is trying to kill you, and don't die in the process. Sounds like a relatively easy affair, right?
Not quite. You see, it doesn’t take long with the game to realise that this isn’t an FPS in the traditional sense; one where you can immediately blast everything in sight without ever breaking a sweat. Instead, it takes on the shape or something closely resembling a puzzle... One that requires time and concentration, as well as dying a fair few times, before you can finally wrench victory from amidst the hail of bullets heading your direction. Yet this isn’t a bad thing – in fact, it’s quite the opposite. There’s great satisfaction in slowly breaking down a level piece by piece, then finally succeeding in putting it all into action, that honestly makes you feel something that resembles being the ultimate architect of death
Superhot knows its strength lies in this careful plotting and preparation, and in a sense its basic art style feels like a response to this. There are very few colours in play here, each serving their own purpose – black things are items you can use, red denotes enemies, and practically everything else is white or grey. With the rules clearly defined, it becomes a simple and pure battle of skill – you against the game, with nothing left to distract you or get in your way. When later levels see almost absurd amounts of enemies being thrown at you, it honestly feels like you’re fighting against the odds, with only your skills and time freezing abilities ever giving you a chance. Naturally, this makes succeeding in a situation where your back is against the wall all the sweeter – an actual accomplishment, instead of something you could have stormed through in under two minutes. It’s a good feeling.
It’s also a benefit in Superhot’s favour that everything that you’re getting up to just feels really damn cool. For example, some basic strategy here might see you toss your gun at an enemy, swipe the gun he drops as it flies through the air, and then spin around in an instant to slay the dude sneaking up behind you... And heck, I think it sounds cool when I write that, never mind when you actually do it. You that's not the limit of what you can pull off here, and the more you play, the more daring you will become. In the end, it becomes a challenge of squeezing out the best from every passing second and tiny movement, just to try and achieve something that essentially adds up to a few extra cool points. As the icing on the cake, once a level is complete you also get to see your antics at a normal speed, and that just ends up making everything you did look even more impressive. Thank goodness there’s the ability to save clips and upload them for all to see here, because some of the things you’re destined to pull off will be stuff you’ll be desperate to show off to the world.
Completing the story also grants you additional endless and challenge modes, which not only adds a thoroughly healthy chunk of gameplay to a title that would otherwise end up feeling slightly too brief, but also cranks the craziness up to the next level. Endless mode in particular is a treat, with wave upon wave of bad dudes pushing your abilities to the limit, as you desperately look for any solution or escape route as your margin for error gets smaller and smaller. It’s exciting stuff.
Enjoy feeling like the king of cool while you can, though, because Superhot’s got another goal in mind for you; it wants to mess with your head. Big time.
This is something that the game makes readily apparent it wants to do to you from approximately five minutes after you've started the game. This is because as a player of taking the first steps into the world of Superhot, you play the role of someone... Taking their first steps into the world of Superhot. Yeah, wrap your head around that. It creates a situation where every twist and turn may technically be aimed at the character you control, but instead feels like it’s directly aimed at messing with you, and it does so perfectly.
There’s a lot going on that's setting out to confuse and disorientate you, you see. Giant messages suddenly flicker and flash in front of your eyes (Photosensitive players beware, because this kind of started to give me a headache after a while), and the retro computer screens that form up the navigation and background to the game flicker and distort to ever greater extents as you descend further into madness. I won’t spoil anything in particular, but there’s a genius moment in particular where you’re compelled into doing something that you’d never expect, but becomes memorable simply because of the fact you weren't expecting it. It's clever stuff.
A special shout out also has to go out for the sound design. There’s literally no music in the game besides one track that only ever appears in the credits. Instead it’s down to a series of hums and beeps, constant buzzing static, and much more besides to create an incredible sense of unease. All things considered, I feel it honestly what's on display here unsettled me more than any soundtrack sound ever have hoped to do. Heck, even the word “Superhot” gets in the action, getting repeated endlessly at the end of each level; it becomes almost a sort of madness mantra, one that I guarantee you is almost impossible to resist repeating yourself. It's all so pleasingly disturbing.
Overall, then, I can find very little to actually fault with Superhot. There perhaps should be a little more to the story, all things considered, and especially considering the game’s relatively high price point. Additionally, there were perhaps a few scattered moments where the gameplay and difficulty slipped slightly too far into the infuriating category, but hey, maybe I’m just rubbish. In the end there’s nothing I can truly pick apart when it comes to what’s on offer here. When all is said and done... It’s the most innovative shooter I’ve played in years.

Admittedly, I Like the game and do reccommend it however it should be noted that this is after purchasing all the DLC. After all the DLC is installed only then does it feel fleshed out and new compared the Tropico 4 which is a shame to say as its blatant money grabbing.
Whats good? Well there are new gameplay mechanics involed like Espionage but nothing out of this world. There appears to be a large focus on more realistic populations in this game compared to Tropico 4, so instead of sitting around several hundred people you can reach 500 to 1k with ease adding to the challenge. It looks nice, plays quite well but you dont really feel in control ALL the time.
Where it falls short is customisation of your country. Most things have to be bought as upgrades or permanent addons to your buildings. Edicts feel a lot less useful than before as the risk for reward has escalated. Conscription is usually the only way to make an army otherwise no one joins. and changing it half way throughout your reign is a terrible idea. They are all gameplay issues that just feel off. However the combat system is greatly improved and now invasions can occur and defend your land, you can send troops abroad, have tanks and APC's, train special forces and even have drone strikes automatically conducted against your own people.
Early game is extremely difficult and slowly becomes easier and easier towards modern day. But whatever happened to the focus on that Cuba, Bay of pigs, Romanian, African style dictatorship silliness that was the cold war that was in turn tropicos great focus? It just feels like a period now. Nothing important even happens in that period. For the most part you finish the cold war by in game 1974 making it feel so under done. Why not have more impact? Maybe your country is what saves the soviet union? or maybe its involved in taking it down? Modern day is by far the most content heavy era as it has all the upgrades and buildings. The game from there onwards becomes dull. Little to no challenges to your monstrous economy and no serious international drama that would threaten your nuclear powered nation.
Its all nice additions but the game makes it difficult for you to try new things. I still enjoy the game, but I wish it had a little more variety. It has some cool story-like objectives that get you involved that can be funny but not enough diversity of events, something that plagues these style of strategy games.
I will still recommend it for the sake of launching airstrikes on rebel forces.

LYNE is a seemingly simple puzzle game with basic objectives, a multitude of levels, and an euphoric atmosphere.
The objectives are simple enough: connect the lines and fill up all of the spaces as you go. As the puzzles progress, different variations in the puzzles create new scenarios, and thus increase the complexity of each puzzle. By completing the puzzle, you progress onward to the next, and so on and so forth. There is no losing in LYNE. There is no time limit, either. You can take as long as you would like to solve each puzzle, and there is no penalty for simply coming back to that puzzle later.
In the game, there are 26 levels, ranging from letters A to Z. Each level has sub-levels of 25. This equivalates to 650 puzzles just in the regular game mode alone. However! After completing set A and B (I believe), the player is then allowed access to daily sets. These daily puzzles consist of a version A and B, both having 25 sublevels in them. That's another 50 new puzzles per day. These puzzles range in difficulty and are completely random. With a staggering number of 700+ puzzles in just a week, there is plenty to do on LYNE.
Not only is there no pressure for you to whiz by the game, but there is also a very calming and entracing soundtrack that accompanies you as you play. With each movement of the puzzle pieces, there are tones that mix together and with the soundtrack to create some really beautiful, relaxing music. Not only is this music a nice stress-reliever, but there is an actual science behind it. The ambient noises actually promote brainwave activity, thus amplifying a better mood, problem-solving, cognition, and much more. But, hey, who doesn't like to just hear something nice playing in the background?
All in all, LYNE is a fantastic game that can be played by any one of any age. Not too mention it is affordable at only $2.99 (about $0.75 with a coupon). It's a great way to relax after a long day at work, decompress after some stressful online match, or just to simply pass the time. If you haven't played it already, I strongly recommend that you do. It is really a gem that will have you hooked!

Puzzle: Here's some blocks with rules associated with them. Draw lines connecting the blocks such that all rules are satisfied.
You know how playing Tetris just feels intuitive, even if you've never seen it before? You just understand, on a fundamental level of existence, that those blocks should be packed in the most efficient way possible. LYNE has that kind of intuition. You look at one of the puzzles, and you just know those blocks have to connect in a particular way, even if you don't immediately recognize how that is.
But LYNE truly shines in its difficulty pacing. The puzzles get steadily more complicated, but it never feels like you ever hit a brick wall. It gets your brain rolling, but it never stresses you out. Speaking of which, the ambience is super calming.
In short, it's a good puzzler for when you need to unwind for a few minutes.

Challenging and highly atmospheric, if also heavily flawed, dungeon crawler/immersive sim that is in many ways highly reminiscent of Looking Glass Studios classics. You'll journey trough decaying underground world filled with dark ritual, bloodthirsty enemies and eldritch horrors.
Patience, experimentation and careful exploration are often rewarded, and also quite often -required- in a way that is rarely seen in modern games: Arx offers little to no hand holding to players during their journey through its sprawling, interconnected dungeons - thorough exploration and paying attention to clues and readables are keys to making any sort of progress!
Game isn't without flaws tho: magic system, while original and also quite impressive in a sheer number of offered spells and their possible effects, is also somewhat clunky, and spellcasting is often unresponsive. Controls & interface in general will take some time to get used to.
While game offers to player a freedom to develop his character in many possible directions, some skills are definitely far more useful than others, and some playstyles are far less developed than others. Stealth system for example is quite unrefined, and while it is sometimes useful and at some points borderline required to sneak (say early encounters with dreaded Ylside warriors), stealth tends to be rather useless and unsatisfying.
There is quite a bit of different types of fun-to-use melee weapons, each with their own pros and cons. Ranged combat on the other hand, while quite useful at times, is made unnecessarily monotonous by the fact that the player is offered all of -two- bows, second one being pretty much unreachable on first playthrough without any outside help.
Still, I'd say this game's assorted shortcomings are -very much- worth dealing with, and are far, FAR outweighed by its many qualities.
Pretty much recommended to anyone with some patience and willingness to deal with game's flaws and idiosyncrasies.
Also, i highly recommend using Arx Libertatis: it offers additional bug fixes and eliminates issues with modern hardware.

Most of the reviews as of late is nerd rage over the pricing.  Not really helpful when it comes to actual game play.  Here's the skinny:
The game itself is "repetitious" by nature, JUST LIKE L4D, yet people STILL play L4D.  Why?  Because each game ISN'T like the last.  So please, find a better excuse to rage.  The game does play similarly to L4D, but goes further by adding class specialties and monster variation.
Hunters:
There are 4 basic class types with (currently) 3 different character for each: Support, Medic, Assault, Trapper.  The brilliant part of this game is the need for all of them.  There isn't a single class you wouldn't be hurting without.  And in that way, it makes it fun to play as any of the classes.  Bad assault-ers means you're likely going to be killed before you can kill the monster.   Bad Support-ers means no damage boost and lower utility overall (class abilities for support includes a UAV, tracking AOE dust, and a damage dealing missile barrage).  Bad Medics mean you die (and in the case of Lazarus, have to wait for an air drop).  Bad Trappers are scary, they can easily segment your team or keep you from getting to the monster.
The flip side to all of this is, when you have a cohesive team, you can really tell and it's very rewarding.  2K made tracking the monster a challenge and the low lighting mixed with tangled and rough terrain make the hunt more exciting.
Monsters:
They're still balancing things, but the monsters are also fun to play as.  As long as you are staying competitive in building yourself up while balancing that with the whittling the hunters down, the fights are very fair.  Because the hunters don't level up or grow more powerful as the round progresses, there's a very tangible sense of urgency as the monster grows.  This feeds greatly into the need for feeding and hiding until the opportune moment (which may not necessarily be at level 3).
TL;DR
The game is super fun (assuming you don't get a team full of Rambos).  Is it worth the money?  The base game, yes.  The DLC is ALWAYS UP TO YOU STOP RAGING </rage>.  As 2K announced, you won't be kept from playing in matches against/with people who have the DLC.  Considering this isn't pay2win and ALL the hunters AND monsters are being constantly balanced, this isn't going to hit a wall.  You want the monsters and hunters?  PAY FOR IT.  They didn't lie to you and tell you the season pass was for everything.  If you bought it, you knew what you were getting.  I think the game is a great piece of work and INCREDIBLY fun.
Edit:
It was requested I give more detail on the actual play out of the game.
You select your job class based on preference.  The system checks everyone elses preferences and assigns classes based on that (conflicts result in switching on each round).  Once you pick you class, you pick your perk (which you gain on leveling) and you get dropped from an airship after some witty banter and possible sexual innuendo.
Upon hitting the surface, you have to use the environment around you to track the monster.  Monsters running along will leave tracks (which are lit up to help you follow them) and monsters who kill and eat other animals leave behind carcasses and disturb wild life (which also show up to the hunters to track).
Lest you think being the monster is all about running away, you'd be wrong.  Aside from hiding and waiting for an ambush, you can also mess with the hunters by crawling around (not leaving any tracks) and then setting off indicators far away (to confuse the ever living daylights out of them).  Some of the monsters have the ability to grab a hunter and carry them away to be chased by the team.  Other monsters are simple brute force, squish your opponents type, and still others are a combination.  Being a monster requires you to be clever.  You may be a brute, but you can still die easily if you just charge in.  Monsters have 4 skills that you can choose to level as you eat other animals and evolve.  So eat heartily and stalk your prey.

+ Smooth transition of animations and UI, creating an incredibly comfortable gameplay
+ Interesting setup
+ Great Camera Intro on Objective Monsters
Downsides to the game
- Lack of guiding information
- Repetitive Gameplay
- Non-intense combat
- Little personalization
- Grindy
- Insubstantial reward system
Gameplay experience
Initial start of the game, I felt bombarded with information and win with the difference in stats of the monsters and simplicity of the mission. The lack of a quality guide to new players would result in confused and irritable experience not knowing who to exactly invest in as the game progresses; in the beginning.
However, as the game progresses, one would have a better grasp of the situation and understanding of the game and attributes one should froster. The difficulty rises too as monsters health, defence and types varies more and more; with mini bosses being added into the new spawn of monsters. This causes however an attrition rate of discovery causing a huge drawout fight in finding what the mission seeks, a.k.a a timebomb against the huge amount of encounters one would soon face. In addition, the lack of variation in types of equipment and discovery or gain of new powers renders the game in colors of extreme unhappiness to progress further into the game generating further disengagement from the player.
Detailed Breakdown
Things to look at / Key Cons. (Optionals Add- Ons/Improvements)
1) Repetitive Gameplay.
After my 3rd - 4th mission, I felt like things were repetitive. I could not feel like I am progressing in the game. The lack of progression comes largely from the lack exploration feeling and rewards that make me feels satisfied.
1.1) Rewards
The rewards in this game is mainly just materials to craft better equipments. But there is a lack of variations in the equipments.
Items were some nice rewards too but feels meagre in compared to permanent reward,
1.2) Character skill / Progression (Levelling)
WIth no skills to level up or discover(learn), I personally feel like there is not much going on. Repeating the way in how i combat. True you give players the option to choose from a huge selection of skills but what i felt at start was being bombarded by just an overwhelming things that i do not know how to use or what's the purpose.
1.3) Equipments
As mentioned above, the lack of equipments which generates different effects render the game dull. The characters all have different equipment(names) but the effect are all the same makes it incredibly turn off for me. I would have a mindset of why can't i just rotate the equipment around if the effect is the same. It feels like a lie that i actually have different things going on where they are actually the same. If there is a visual change in the character (aesthetics) it would put less of a turn off for me since there is a cosmetic reward feeling.
1.4) Combat / Missions
The exploration phase, choosing of where to render them ineffective is great but feels personally easy and same throughout, they don't have enough posing on threat or reward, maybe the RNG. Most of the time I have more than enough adrenaline to render the criticals ambush and damaging ones away.
1.5) Monsters
So far, i have not encounter any really new monster other than the velociraptor which feels different since it pounch from a distance but mostly are just melee. The introduction of boss, boss of the Skeleton Warrior(can't remember the actual name) and the Great Ape is not bad. But other than the bosses I feel most monsters are just the same with difference in the health.
1.6) Map Design
Great artwork and exploration of tiles in the map design, but the lack of environment strategy makes the exploration less intense as its just moving from tiles to tiles and completeing / defeating whatever is there, traps, chest, monsters, etc. If would be great if the environment impacts the overall mission and combat.
Example maybe there are vines that obstruct movements? Then the Bird Character could fly across and deal with the range monster if not the vines would require an action to clear or skills (design thinking) rendering the melee character an extra turn to reach the monster would means damage or even certain death to other characters. VInes could also block range such as chance, etc..
2) Lack of Guiding Information
With a huge amount of strategy involve should the game improves @Dev, the lack of guiding information to players especially new ones would feel lost and demoralized as they have no idea what is going on. It would feel like solving a language barrier(puzzle) before even embarking on the game. Right now it really requires an explanation. I am still lost on certain attributes and do not know what to work on.
Reference: Darkest Dungeon Glossary
Note: General public don't D&D due to setup and time consumption.
3) Storage space
Would be great if I can keep certain equipments or items.
3.1) Item & Equipment Variation & Progression (Crafting)
Best if they can be upgraded or used to craft better ones in the future. Keeps the player in suspense where they do not know if the item is valuable now, to cash in for current equipment upgrades/ item crafting or keep for future upgrade as it might be required as a material involved.
4) Transition of UI
Great UI but one such improvement that could be made is the viewing of characters powers and skills which is currently separated where only after accepting a mission then can a character's skills be seen and edited which feels like a double job after editing equipment of character in their crafting screen though there is not much.
Note:
1) Take note increase variations and customization means a transition to more micromanagement gameplay as well as adding more information guide later on.
2) Variation would definitely help in displacing attention more towards repetition and grinding but take caution in grinding (time & reward, intertwine with quality and quantity).
Conclusion
Definitely a great job on digitizing a board game. the core is definitely there. If you're looking for action and more immersion from TBS games, it's definitely not like XCOM, XCOM 2... etc,
However, as a personal preference would like to see more variation and customization in most of your design if possible(loads of work as usual, up to devs).

All in all, personally for me, this game lacks a huge amount of progression and variation. The strategy feels simple for me and there is not enough element to sustain my interest in the role-playing. With a final critical blow to the game with the lack for guiding information to new players.
Some constraints would be the framework is from D & D but you can always have certain core elements from there and branch out further. It depends on who you want to attract.
Would definitely follow up the game and if improvements is made with more dlc to purchase, I would glad to support it.
Amazing job and thanks for the games @Dev.

I've never played this particular D&D Adventure System board game, but I've played a few of the older ones (Wrath of Ashardalon, Castle Ravenloft). This seems to be an extremely well made adaptation of the D&D Adventure System board games. The graphics and art direction is good, they look smashing at 4K, scaling is on point which is something I look out for having a 4K panel.
The game play is pretty simple. Your turn is broken into phases. You can take two actions, typically, on your turn. Move and attack. In the hero phase you do those two actions in any order. Then the turn moves to the encounter phase. If  you're on the edge of a tile where a new tile can be discovered, you explore a new tile. Any mosters that appear on that tile are now "controlled" by the hero that discovered them. If you are NOT on the edge of the tile so you can explore, a random encounter happens that is most likely bad it seems, but a positive event can happen sometimes, or perhaps nothing happens. Seems the higher percentage of encounters are potentially negative. I do like this since it forces players to keep exploring the board on their turn if they can. The other phase is the Villian phase, where a monster will attack a hero.
There's a ton of nuance to the game, you can find loot such as: components to use in crafting items, items you can add to your inventory and use immediately to give bonuses, etc..
There seems to be a decent variety of missions and quests to go on to kill monsters, find items, etc.. I've only scratched the surface so far so I would imagine there's some decent variety in these quests to fulfill various tasks. We shall see.
I've only sunk about an hour or two into it so far, but I'm extemely please with what I see so far.
If you're a fan of tabletop board games and/or adaptations of those digitally, this game seems like a no-brainer. Especially if it's on sale.

The game is probably one of the most fun gaming experiences I've ever had. A lot of people compare it to Left 4 Dead, but I think it's way better. Gameplay is fast and fun. Controls are decent for the most part, a few glitches here and there, but those will most likely be fixed. I guess there's a story in it, but it doesn't need one, 'There's a monster in the woods, go kill it' is good enough for me. The characters are actually well devoloped for the most part, in terms of personality and gameplay. The graphics look great, but not so great that you can't stay focused on the objective, which is neat. The monsters are also well designed, despite a few over-powered abilities that SOME monster has (
), but all in all, the teams are fairly balanced. One of it's major flaws is that it has a matchmaking system out of hell. The networking needs to be improved dramatically.
The biggest issue with this game is the price. While the game is fun as all hell, it does not have the necessary amount of content to be worth $60. The characters are fun and interesting, but there are so few of them, and putting a pricetag on the rest of them is a bit low. There are three Star Wars games that should really set the bar for any that follow them: Star Wars: Jedi Knight III: Jedi Academy, Star Wars: Battlefront II, and the one you are looking at right now, Star Wars: Empire at War.
Essentially a Total War game in the Star Wars universe, albeit with a realtime campaign map as opposed to turn-based, this game offers a deeply enjoyable RTS and Grand Strategy experience, all set in the wonderful world of Star Wars. Play the Empire and crush the rebellion with your lumbering fleets of Star Destroyers and the legendary planet-destroying planetoid, the Death Star. Alternatively, shatter the tyranny of the Empire as a fledgeling Rebel Alliance, utilizing fast and agile ships to run circles around your foe.
Ultimately, of the three gameplay modes, Space Battles are where the game design shines the most, followed closely by the campaign map, both of which overshadow, by a large degree, the lackluster ground battles. But this is not an issue. The Space Battles and Campaign map are so engrossing that you will likely get more fun and replayability out of those two modes alone, than a version of this game where more time were diverted to making better ground battles.
Ultimately, I highly recommend this classic gem of a game to Star Wars and strategy gaming fans alike!
P.S. I have probably over 200 hours in this game on the CD version, which I had since barely a month after its release!

Time moves only when you move. It’s a simple idea, all things considered, but oddly enough its taken until the arrival of Superhot before it has truly come to see the light of day. The basic premise here couldn’t be simpler; use this power to the fullest, kill everything that is trying to kill you, and don't die in the process. Sounds like a relatively easy affair, right?
Not quite. You see, it doesn’t take long with the game to realise that this isn’t an FPS in the traditional sense; one where you can immediately blast everything in sight without ever breaking a sweat. Instead, it takes on the shape or something closely resembling a puzzle... One that requires time and concentration, as well as dying a fair few times, before you can finally wrench victory from amidst the hail of bullets heading your direction. Yet this isn’t a bad thing – in fact, it’s quite the opposite. There’s great satisfaction in slowly breaking down a level piece by piece, then finally succeeding in putting it all into action, that honestly makes you feel something that resembles being the ultimate architect of death
Superhot knows its strength lies in this careful plotting and preparation, and in a sense its basic art style feels like a response to this. There are very few colours in play here, each serving their own purpose – black things are items you can use, red denotes enemies, and practically everything else is white or grey. With the rules clearly defined, it becomes a simple and pure battle of skill – you against the game, with nothing left to distract you or get in your way. When later levels see almost absurd amounts of enemies being thrown at you, it honestly feels like you’re fighting against the odds, with only your skills and time freezing abilities ever giving you a chance. Naturally, this makes succeeding in a situation where your back is against the wall all the sweeter – an actual accomplishment, instead of something you could have stormed through in under two minutes. It’s a good feeling.
It’s also a benefit in Superhot’s favour that everything that you’re getting up to just feels really damn cool. For example, some basic strategy here might see you toss your gun at an enemy, swipe the gun he drops as it flies through the air, and then spin around in an instant to slay the dude sneaking up behind you... And heck, I think it sounds cool when I write that, never mind when you actually do it. You that's not the limit of what you can pull off here, and the more you play, the more daring you will become. In the end, it becomes a challenge of squeezing out the best from every passing second and tiny movement, just to try and achieve something that essentially adds up to a few extra cool points. As the icing on the cake, once a level is complete you also get to see your antics at a normal speed, and that just ends up making everything you did look even more impressive. Thank goodness there’s the ability to save clips and upload them for all to see here, because some of the things you’re destined to pull off will be stuff you’ll be desperate to show off to the world.
Completing the story also grants you additional endless and challenge modes, which not only adds a thoroughly healthy chunk of gameplay to a title that would otherwise end up feeling slightly too brief, but also cranks the craziness up to the next level. Endless mode in particular is a treat, with wave upon wave of bad dudes pushing your abilities to the limit, as you desperately look for any solution or escape route as your margin for error gets smaller and smaller. It’s exciting stuff.
Enjoy feeling like the king of cool while you can, though, because Superhot’s got another goal in mind for you; it wants to mess with your head. Big time.
This is something that the game makes readily apparent it wants to do to you from approximately five minutes after you've started the game. This is because as a player of taking the first steps into the world of Superhot, you play the role of someone... Taking their first steps into the world of Superhot. Yeah, wrap your head around that. It creates a situation where every twist and turn may technically be aimed at the character you control, but instead feels like it’s directly aimed at messing with you, and it does so perfectly.
There’s a lot going on that's setting out to confuse and disorientate you, you see. Giant messages suddenly flicker and flash in front of your eyes (Photosensitive players beware, because this kind of started to give me a headache after a while), and the retro computer screens that form up the navigation and background to the game flicker and distort to ever greater extents as you descend further into madness. I won’t spoil anything in particular, but there’s a genius moment in particular where you’re compelled into doing something that you’d never expect, but becomes memorable simply because of the fact you weren't expecting it. It's clever stuff.
A special shout out also has to go out for the sound design. There’s literally no music in the game besides one track that only ever appears in the credits. Instead it’s down to a series of hums and beeps, constant buzzing static, and much more besides to create an incredible sense of unease. All things considered, I feel it honestly what's on display here unsettled me more than any soundtrack sound ever have hoped to do. Heck, even the word “Superhot” gets in the action, getting repeated endlessly at the end of each level; it becomes almost a sort of madness mantra, one that I guarantee you is almost impossible to resist repeating yourself. It's all so pleasingly disturbing.
Overall, then, I can find very little to actually fault with Superhot. There perhaps should be a little more to the story, all things considered, and especially considering the game’s relatively high price point. Additionally, there were perhaps a few scattered moments where the gameplay and difficulty slipped slightly too far into the infuriating category, but hey, maybe I’m just rubbish. In the end there’s nothing I can truly pick apart when it comes to what’s on offer here. When all is said and done... It’s the most innovative shooter I’ve played in years.

If you enjoyed Tropico 4 , you will likely enjoy Tropico 5. However, as someone who plays a lot of this genre of games, I will say Tropic 5 was the first Tropico where I actually had to become a dictator to survive. Note I only play on hard mode since I do have a lot of experience with Tropico games.
In every other Tropico game, all you had to do was give the people what they want (housing, food, religion, etc.) and they would vote for you. I almost never had to issue Martial Law or assassinate someone, unless I just wanted to do it for kicks. In Tropico 5, the factions have so much more power. You can have an overall happiness of 80% and an approval rating of 35%, so if you don’t rig the election, you’re going to lose. For example, if the majority of your population are environmentalists and you build a factory, you will take a huge hit in popularity.
It’s a pleasant surprise because no longer can you easily make huge island decisions and not be punished for it. If you’ve done mostly communist things for ten years and then all of a sudden become best friends with the USA and make the plebs pay for their own food and medicine, your population will resent you and rebel, even if their overall happiness keeps improving. And hope that those in your military aren’t part of those unhappy factions because even high wages won’t always save you from a coup d’etat.
Wages as they were in Tropico 3 and 4 are gone and have been replaced by something a little different. I’m not a fan of it because when I’m rolling in the rum and oil dough, I’d like to be able to raise everyone’s wage at the same time and now that can only be done on a per building type basis—and each type of farm is considered a different building, so you can’t even raise all farmers’ wages at the same time, you must go into each type of farm and change it. They also replaced Penultimo’s voice actor with someone much less annoying, and it bothers me.
Awesome music, good graphics, tuned mechanics, lots of humour, interesting campaign/story mode -- Tropico 5 has it all. Sometimes the interface is a bit lacking, especially finding existing building and issues with them, but otherwise this is the best game in Tropico series I've played.
Overall, it is definitely a buy if you can get it on sale. It’s quite different from previous versions but has the same feel-you definitely know you're playing a Tropico game. As I’ ve said though, if you’ve historically been a loving, graceful, democratic leader who would never really use the Secret Police to aid you, this game might force you to change your ways.

Puzzle: Here's some blocks with rules associated with them. Draw lines connecting the blocks such that all rules are satisfied.
You know how playing Tetris just feels intuitive, even if you've never seen it before? You just understand, on a fundamental level of existence, that those blocks should be packed in the most efficient way possible. LYNE has that kind of intuition. You look at one of the puzzles, and you just know those blocks have to connect in a particular way, even if you don't immediately recognize how that is.
But LYNE truly shines in its difficulty pacing. The puzzles get steadily more complicated, but it never feels like you ever hit a brick wall. It gets your brain rolling, but it never stresses you out. Speaking of which, the ambience is super calming.
In short, it's a good puzzler for when you need to unwind for a few minutes.

This is a free-scrolling 2D shooter. Unlike most shmups, you're free to turn around to destroy your enemies behind you as well as terminate anything that would dare attempt a frontal assault. It's kinda like Defender, except levels don't wrap-around. In fact if you hit either end of the level you'll bounce away like you were hit by a galactic tennis racquet.
The story is about aliens or pirates or hot babes or I can't remember. Basically it's an excuse to have six stages of blastemup action. You're given a choice between four ships, each with their strengths and weaknesses. Each ships has its own special weapon that does great damage while putting up a temporary shield. Unlike most other shooters, the federation gave you an actual armored ship. In short, you don't die in a single hit, unless you crash into something, or play on the "pure" difficulty which all but removes armor.
The campaign has a decent amount of variety to it. First stage is the bog-standard destroy everything, second is an escort mission (ewww), third you're expected to survive for several minutes. By the 4th stage you're fighting off a pirate armada, 5th has you taking on alien battleships, and finally the last stage you're trying to outrun a storm to destroy a...thing. I think this thing is dangerous to the human race so yeah, definitely blow it up.
There are three survival stages as well. First one can get pretty difficult, you're most likely going to die in 6 to 10 minutes. The second one you have to race through a passage of ice to destroy another thing. I don't get along well with 3D walls in shmups, I tend to do a lot of crashing. I don't know what the deal is with the third survival stage. It's wave-based, but nothing happens after I blow up the juggernaut, no more enemies appear or anything.
The score is mostly influenced by the difficulty. The harder the setting, the better the score. There are a bunch of medals that are awarded for performing certain tasks (dodging a lot of bullets, getting combos, etc) so look out for those as well.
There's not much else to say about this game really. It's not bad, though I think the player weapons are a little underpowered. This is especially apparent in survival stage 1, where it can get overwhelming simply because it takes too long to destroy the boss ships. Evolve is a first person shooter and a third person action game. What do I mean by that? Well if you play as the "Hunters" (humans) you play as a team of four people selected from a pool of twelve people (as you unlock them) each with their designated class (Medic, Support, Trapper, Assault), and you four play in the first person shooter perspective. When you play as the "Monster" you play in the third person action perspective, and you select one monster out of a pool of three (soon to be four, also as you unlock them). Now while the monster plays solo, it is not as weak as one might imagine, no, it is quite strong with four selectable abilities, each with three upgrade slots as you evolve ingame, so a total of nine upgrade points to use, but a potential of twelve upgrade slots. The Hunters themselves each have abilties themselves but most are different from each other (whether it's weapons or buffs and whatnot).
The actual gameplay is Monster has to eat prey on the map, evolve, then kill the Hunters for most, and conversly Hunters have to kill the Monster (the sooner, the better) for most game modes. There are four game modes and one campaign mode (which includes all game modes).
Hunt is where the Hunters look for the monster and kill it or survive until the 20-25 minute marker (which when the final timer begins can be stalled by the monster attacking the hunters) or the monster kills them all or destroys a power relay at Stage 3.
Egg Hunt is where the hunters have to look and destroy monster eggs/minions that spawn from them or kill the monster, while the monster has to defend them, kill the hunters, or keep the eggs alive until 8ish minutes to win.
Rescue is where the hunter save five downed survivors and take them to a dropship, and the monster has to kill five  survivors or all the hunters.
Defense is where the hunters must defend three generators for 5-6 minutes or until they kill the monster, the monster MUST destroy all the generators with the assistance of two monster minions (AI) that respawn, hunter kills are not necessary.
All the maps are pretty good, with minor clipping bugs with both the hunters and the monster, no character will fall through the map and into the abyss.
And last but not least the community is 75% okay/friendly and the other 25% is the usual salt/bitterness (At the moment).

Chroma Squad is a turn-based action RPG game that revolves around a group of
stunt actors, who are acting Power Rangers. They are unhappy with their director and with the studio where they are taking the show, so they make their own, Chroma Squad! The story might have few surprises for you but the main thing are the references and jokes, you'll find many of those.
Gameplay is classic for turn-based action games, with exception of acrobatics - a character can hold a position so another character can ricochet himself farther (closer to your target enemy). You can expect about 30 levels (split into 5 "seasons"), with repeating basic enemies but original bosses, which will make you laugh and, some later ones, might make you a little angry. You have to try hard.
But I don't want to scare you, I've played on "Interesting" difficulty (take it as normal) and I think it was perfectly balanced experience. I had times where I've almost didn't beat the level (last
Power Ranger standing!) and I've never felt the game was too easy, so I always felt motivated to do my best.
Anyway, Chroma Squad would totally suck if they weren't able to form into a huge mech. And guess what, you will have a mech action too! But don't get too excited for that, mech fights have completely different fight rules, there is no positioning strategy and your attacks are based on your luck.
Visuals are presented in neat pixelart style, combined with nice sound effect and soundtrack, which contains even a Japanese theme song! Everything gets you to the right mood pretty fast, so you can enjoy everything developers made - and there's a lot of content to see.
Chroma Squad is definitely worth recommending, I've enjoyed it for more than 10 hours and might even try to play it later again on higher difficulty for another endings. If you are looking for  turn-based RPG, pixelart and want many pop culture references, you'll love it!

*************** THIS REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS, IF YOU DON'T WNAT SPOILERS, DON'T READ THIS ***************
I'm going to start by saying that the beginning of this game is fun. Not a triple A industry release or anything, but it's fun.
But as you get closer to the end, it becomes less fun. A the same time, it becomes more engaging. And that engagement is what makes this game great. It's about one man trying to find meaning in a friend's work. And trying to understand himself through it. And trying to get validation for himself through someone else's work.
This man, this narrator, telling us about his "friend", is simply a narcisistic man who thrives on the attention of others, and can't understand the simple pleasure of creating to create.
You play through the levels as this narrator begins to have his breakdown, begging for forgivness through the same actions that got him ostrasized to begin with. There actually came a point in the game where he admits that he showed these games, Coda's games, to other people without Coda's permission. This journal of games that was shared with one other person that he trusted. I almost couldn't continue playing....
But, as the narrator says that he was compelled to try to reap the recognition for work that was not his, I was compelled to keep playing. Part of it was to watch this man suffer, trying to find meaning where there was none. Another reason, was to see how this ended. To try to see if this man was truly remorseful of his actions, or if he was simply trying to keep himself sane.
Well... His actions were all in his own interest. He wanted forgiveness for his own validation, and not through any sense of remorse.
This game isn't fun. But it tells an amazing narrative about selfishness and finding meaning where there is none. Throughout the game there is a simple door puzzle. You open a door, then close it while you're inside the other room. Then pull a newly revealed lever to exit.
But at the end of the game, there is no lever. There's just a guilty man, alone with his thoughts.
This game isn't fun. But it's engaging. It's an artistic piece on guilt and validation. And what is left when validation is taken away, and all that is left is guilt.
It's not fun, but it's a great experience.
I would highly reccomend this game to anyone who enjoys an unreliable narrator, and a masterful use of mechanics as metaphor.

I've played quite a few rounds on this now, I find it to be fun but it can also become a bit boring after a while because it does follow the same pattern, each match especially playing as the monster, though I have only played hunt mode, so maybe that's why.
I tend to play as the monster and recently I do really well(5 wins in a row, people just quitting, blowing the core) there's some tips I myself worked out that I will share that no one else seems to be sharing on the many guides I've watched....
Your success in this game is a bit like a game of cards, some of it is knowing the game, some of it is skill(timing) and then some of it is just down to plain luck(right place, right time).
As the monster the worse thing you can do is alert the players to your direction right at the start, if you get into a fight and suddenly they have your armor down with 30%-40% of your life, it's going to be a pretty crappy drawn out game for you, so simply don't do it, be very very careful at the start.
Got trapped in the dome? most monster players impulsively just run at the hunters to try and kill them because they can not flee because of the shield(fight or flee?), these are not the only options available; there is a very effective other option, HIDE behind geometry not in the firing line of hunters. They can't shoot you, they can't destory your armor right? and that dome has a timer.. Think about survival even whilst trapped.
They will have to decide who goes first, and most times there will be hesitation, which is a couple of more seconds off that clock. Most of the time they group up and come at you all at once and if you have hid right, it'll be in a tight space where you can blow most of your cool downs on them all in one spot and then run to the other side and do it again...it might not work like last time but they'll be slow to come at you again and by then the dome might be down and you'll have a lot of armor to quickly flee.
Once your armor is down, do not stick around, don't get greedy, the longer you live with lots of health, the higher the probability is that you are going to win.
I found the games environment is full of nasty zones playing as a hunter;  there are bits in the level that are mostly water which makes it incredibly hard for hunters to move(I consider this be a free debuff)...use them, if you are going to launch an all out assault do it in one of these areas. There's even one area that have a massive monster swimming in some pools(yeah, in this situation they pretty much have no chance), it's very satifying to watch them struggle to move whilst getting heavily injured when then you leap in for the killing blow to finish them off.
Try not leave a a fallen player until he is dead, do not let him revive, just sit on him.

The Long Dark is a fresh take on survival without the typical installment of having either zombies or bandits being the main antagonists of the story. Instead, TLD focuses on actual survival with the elements against you such as hunger, thirst, temperature, and most importantly, hungry, vicious animals.
You start off the game in a random area located in 1 of the 5 current starting zones. Project Zomboid is NOT a game for everyone. If you want a fast paced, not too challenging romp through the zombie apocalypse... This is not the game for you and there are friendlier, better-looking alternatives.
But if you want to play the game that comes closest to simulating what an actual zombie apocalypse would be like, this is for you. This game is TOUGh; the intro states that "there was no hope of survival" and that "this is how you die", and it's spot on. You WILL die, over and over, until you start to learn how the game works, how to take things slowly and steadily, and how to pick your fights.
The game itself is full of content. It has a deep medical/injury/mood system, a large map (unfinished but still full of buildings to loot and zombies to kill), a working crafting system for everything from a hammer to a wooden house, farming, and a dynamic world which will evolve and change as time passes, with seasons, water and power shutouts, etc. etc., forcing you to change your strategy as you survive longer and longer. But no worries, it will take you multiple attempts to even reach that point.
Also worth mentioning are the character creation system, where you need to pick negative traits (such as being grumpy, overweight, a coward, etc.) and positive traits (athletic, brave, eagle-eyed...) whose point values even each other out; and the multiplayer which allows you to do everything I've listed with a friend, and which I've found is very playable, even in alpha.
On top of all of this, the devs are present on the forums and community pages and consistently pump out new content for us to enjoy, which in this world of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t "grab the money and run" or "promise some stuff and then never deliver" or even "straight up lie to customers about the plans you have for the game" early access projects is really something to value. In fact, the devs love the game too, and have even pumped up the difficulty in recent patches, by making zombies more aware of movement and sound around them and tightening up zombie hordes instead of having them all spaced out. They want to make a true zombie survival experience, not some easy, popular but short-lived zombie killing action game, and I think they deserve praise for that.
In short, the game in its current state is already very playable and full of hours of content, both in single and multiplayer. And at 10 pounds or 15 USD, it's a steal imho.

This puzzle game is a surprising joy to play. Its really interesting and feels fresh from other games that I've played. What does it involve? Drawing lines... yep that easy. You have colored shapes, each set of colored shapes has 2 'cap' shapes, where you can either start or end the colored line. So you start on a green box / triangle, then click and drag your mouse between the matching color shapes making lines. All shapes need to be connected and can only be connected to once. The lines can only go in eight directions from each shape. Its super easy. Then the game adds different colored shapes, so you've got green lines and red lines. So what's the catch? You can't cross the lines. So where's the challenge? Eventually directional octagonal shapes get added, these are neutral blocks that you're able to attach multiple lines on in 8 directions, no matter what color the line is, just as long as you don't cross the lines. It starts with simple octagon blocks that need you to connect to them twice.... then three times and so on.
Can you lose? Nope. You have as much time as you want. You can't fail, if you do the puzzle inaccurately it just has a little red line around the box you forgot. Then you keep going. If you screw up, just click one of the cap shapes to delete the lines or back track your lines by clicking and dragging backward to remove the line you just made. If you ever get truly stumped, you can back out of that puzzle and go to any one of the 25 other puzzles in the group. You'll unlock a few groups at a time, so you'll always have 75 puzzles to chose from. The game goes in succession, once you complete one puzzle its immediately to the next. There is a legitimate sense of satisfaction when I complete a puzzle that I was stumped on. Not just that, but eventually I found myself thinking of the dynamics of these puzzles and realizing where I should start first.
The game has 25 puzzles per group and groups A - Z. 25 * 26 levels = 650 levels. Is that not enough for you? Well then there are daily levels with 25 levels of A B C making for 75 daily levels. The daily levels are considerably more difficult than the default puzzles. Its a nice way to keep fresh content and keep people in the game.
If you don't like puzzle games, avoid this. The first 50 levels are understandably easy, but they do get more challenging. It is a soothing game and the puzzles get complex, but still easy and simple.

All for the low, low price of... what was that again? Oh yeah: FREE.

One of my favorite games of all time. It seemed like it would be a typical FPS game, and in many respects it is, but I haven't had a game draw me in like this in years. The environment, backstory, and characters are so vividly imagined that this world feels quite real. I'm usually not big on story but it was hard not to appreciate the characters with their own uniquely depraved motives clashing together in a laissez-faire aquatropolis.
There are lots of fun weapon and plasmid (special power) upgrades. The optional "big daddies" that show up periodically put an interesting twist on the basic FPS formula, rewarding players who have stockpiled powerful ammunition by learning to be effective with lesser weapons - all the more so on harder difficulties.
I have since learned that this whole game is intended to be a critique of the novel Atlas Shrugged and Ayn Rand's Objectivism philosophy. In fact, you can think of each BioShock game as a sort of Petri dish that gives you a pessimistic view of how a particular political philosophy might play out. It gives your mind something to gnaw on while you're mowing people down.
