Highly recommended for those that have played and liked games like Ultima Underworld or Dungeon Master (Legend of Grimrock).
The developers wanted to created Ultima Underworld 3 but were unable to get the license from you know who, which is a shame. With stronger resources this game could have been very special indeed. For an old game (2002), the graphics are pretty good and sound in some instances quite amazing, the game engine has aged well. I played the game of Steam and in Windows 7 and it was more or less playable apart from some memory crashes - I learned to save often using all the save slots - you need to do this too, especially when you move between levels. It is best to play the game without any background noise such as the TV/ music or radio - believe that. Not only will you get immersed in the game world, beautifully crafted by the designers, you won't miss key information said aloud by your character and then never repeated!
It's a first person RPG/adventure set in a world where the sun has died so all races of the world live in a huge underground complex - the city is called Arx.
Arx Fatalis = fatal fortress (Latin)
The game does involve combat, magic and sneaking options. But most of the game requires exploring, adventuring, some puzzles (simple and fiendish) to solve, a lot of traversing to and fro.
You begin the game in a prison cell and yep, you guessed right, no memory of who you are! Wow, not seen that in a video game before. There follows an escape from prison and a gradual understanding of where you are and of your destiny. You escape the prison and then move onwards to different levels of the underground world, such as mining caves, spooky crypts, ice cavern (dragon) and a strange snake level!  It takes a while to learn the mechanics of the game but you give it a chance as the rewards will be many! Above all read and print off the manual so you have it with you. Yes ladies and gentlemen, this game was produced in the days where manuals actually were required reading and gave hints on how to traverse the game. Believe me it will answer about 75% of your questions.
Your character has the normal ST,INT,DEX etc stats as well as skills to develop such as magic, technical skill, intuition. Every time you level up these can be increased. Combat is similar to that found in Morrowind where I often found myself moving in and out of combat and swinging whatever weapon I was using at the time. Not great but ok. The magic system is something else, it is rune based and you need to draw patterns on screen with your mouse. This is pretty amazing and at the beginning you learn a new PC gaming skill - let's face it - that is pretty unique. Runes can be found or purchased and your journal will update to show the new spells you can cast. Oh - you reckon it would be pretty damn impossible to cast a fireball as a giant evil looking spider is looking to bite your head off? READ IMPORTANT - you can pre-save three magic spells! Read the manual properly for goodness sake - just do it.
Your journal shows your character stats, armour, inventory, magic book of spells and runes, map and some key information about the game interface and quests you need to complete. I stress "some". As an assistant in following the game story - the journal is next to useless. Exploration is encouraged and the game engine allows you to do some innovative stuff. The map is pretty useless too. Use a fishing rod to catch raw fish and then cook them next to a flame. Combine water with flour to create dough and then bake to create bread. I think you can combine it with apple to make apple pie. Oh - you need to eat and your character will moan when he is hungry. Apparently hunger was pretty common in earlier versions of this game but I think the latter patches made this less acute. Saying that, I did go through a stage where I was baking and cooking stuff a lot! Later in the game I stopped hoarding food and just munched down anything I found.
Your inventory is grid based and cannot be sorted, despite what some have said. You can stack some items and expand the size later in the game. This could be better as you spend too much time on inventory management. On the first play through you end up hoarding. As you learn all the tricks and want to do another play through, it will be less problematic.
The storyline is quite interesting, you have no say on what needs to be done and there are no dialogue options. At certain points in the story a cut scene will update you. There a lot of hidden items and locations in the game and exploration is encouraged. The world is beautifully put together and there are some real unique places and characters to interact with. It is quite complex and therefore some things are not explained properly and you will need to do some internet research to help you progress. Some tips:
Buy the key ring and combine all found keys with it.
Learn how to pre cast spells - especially fireball.
Read the manual and print it off.
Learn how to make potions - especially heal. Learn it. The castle in the human city has an alchemist which allows you to distil potions.
Don't worry about cash - I ended up with about £35k.
Some magic rings will disappear from your inventory after a while, these have a 12/20 or something. Ring of Regeneration.
Read the 'Races of Arx' book before going to find the dragon.
Find the activate portal spell in game or online and write it down in the manual - for some reason this spell does not show in your spell book.
Your character needs decent magic to progress end game due to very difficult melee warriors that will polish you off in two whacks.
Don't worry about hoarding food - just eat stuff as and when you find it.
Save often.
Shops are not always open, progress the story line and come back.
Check the keyboard control options to ensure you don't waste all your healing potions when trying to crawl or sneak!
There are some negatives. If you don't READ THE MANUAL, expect some frustrations with the game engine. The great magic system is limited as not all the spells are equally useful and I tended to play the whole game with fireball. However, you need to have decent magic to complete the game, do not go all out as a fighter or thief. Not everything is spoon fed to you, ultimately you can get where you need to go just by adventuring but sometimes a specific "go there" would be appreciated. There are only about 10 levels which you seem to traverse back and forward a lot, learn how to use the portals or this can be frustrating. The game world is complex and many things can be interacted with - this is also a downfall as often you need to make assumptions about how things work together.
Summary - really is a great and unique game if you like RPG or first person dungeon adventure. World is quite amazing. Some difficulty with the game engine which most can be sorted by READING THE MANUAL. 40 hours+ on first play through and a few side quests not completed. Repetitive towards the end as it suffers from lack of additional quests and locations which would allow greater use of spells and your character.

Decided to grab this game since I liked Tactics RPGs, and wanted something bright and colorful. Came into the game with pretty "meh" expectations and was blown out of the water.
As someone who watched Power Rangers when I was little, this game is an absolute nostalgia trip, while at the same time parodying a lot of the tropes of the sentai genre. The game starts with the protagonists getting a tutorial from their overbearing boss before quitting to form their own sentai studio. You get to name all your rangers, choose their colors (Even if the palette is rather limited), their mecha, their catchphrases, etc. Though this has no impact on gameplay whatsoever, it adds nicely to the fantasy of running your own show.
Gameplay is a relatively simple TRPG where you can only have one of each class, Assist, Tech, Assault, Scout, and Lead. This prevents a lot of the cheese strategies that are common in TRPGs like Fire Emblem and Final Fantasy Tactics. This game's difficulty in actual fights is usually pretty low. Instead the difficulty comes from getting your Audience meter filled up and then keeping it filled. The best way to fill it up is by doing flips, team moves, special attacks, and Director's Instructions, which are special submissions that can range from "Don't lose any of your team members" to "win in 5 turns" to "Defeat the boss before defeating any minions." The gameplay, despite being turnbased, really does a great job of showing how a sentai show usually plays out, and its very easy to see how cool everything would look to the eyes of a child watching the show at home. The only major gameplay flaw is that my scout always felt useless. Next to the rapid-fire skills of the Tech, the massive healing from the Assist, the raw damage and acrobatics bonus of the Assault, and the tankiness of the Lead, the Scout... moves an extra space every turn. This would be alright if his damage were anything special, but either my choice of actor or gear for my scout meant that he was consistently doing less damage than the healer. Though the scout does get several crowd control abilties, they all require him to be in the midst of battle, and the Scout's frailty means that these are very risky to use past Season 3.
Graphics are psuedo 16-bit, bright colorful and cheery graphics with some great sprite art. Not quite on the same level as Undertale's sprite art, but its all still very appealing. Boss designers are all unique and, with a few exceptions, creative. Though you'll be fighting in th same 7 or so locals a lot, I'm willing to write that up as part of the parody. Besides, the locations are all great looking and have enough functional differences from one another to keep you on your toes.
That's not to say the game is perfect. While the game is generally humorous, there are more than a few spots where I felt as though the game was expecting me to laugh and I didn't. Mecha fighting is pretty boring and one dimensional, and is usually the worst part of any mission its included in, which is a shame since a lot of its moves and parts are references to Mecha anime like Gurren Lagann and NGE, references I would appreciate a lot more if it wasn't part of the most boring part of the game. There's crafting, which is already a very played out mechanic that seems to pop up in every game nowadays, but at least here it fits the fantasy of everything on a sentai show being handmade and crappy looking. There's also multiple things that seem to ride the line between satire and unironic crapiness. When you reach Season 3, most of that season's plot revolves around your Lead growing an ego, which is a trite and boring plot line used in every sentai show ever. Are you trying to make fun of these trite and boring plots, Chrome Squad, or was your plot for Season 3 just trite and boring? Or did I just answer my own question?
Despite those flaws, I'd be wrong if I said this game was bad. The game just has so much heart and dedication put into it, the gameplay is fun, the visuals were colorful and the plot is meta-tastic goofiness. While the game didn't make me burst out laughing or bawl my eyes out, it was just so delightful I can't help but recommend it. If you love Tactics RPGs or Sentai shows, consider it a double recommendation.

Hello everybody, End World Gaming here to share an excerpt from my review for Tales From Candlekeep: Tomb of Annihilation by BKOM Studios.
Tales From Candlekeep is a board game style tactical RPG that’s actually based on a board game of the same name. It’s part of the Dungeons and Dragons adventure series so it uses a very different set of rules from the many other Dungeons and Dragons RPG’s out there.
The game puts you in the role of a 4 person party, each of a unique class and race. The characters include a Ranger, Wizard, Paladin and Bard. The characters races are Human, Aarakocra, Saurial, and Tabaxi, respectively. In the hero selection screen you can add the characters to the party, change their skills and view their stats.
On the world map you can choose the missions you wish to take part in. You must complete each mission in order but there are some side missions that you can complete to earn bonus XP, Gold and Items. Each mission has 3 difficulty levels as well and the rewards are greater the harder the difficulty.
The world map also allows you to use materials gathered during a mission to craft equipment for your characters. There are 4 different areas to craft equipment including Armor, Main Weapon, Secondary Weapon, and Accessories. Each piece of equipment has 5 different levels from common all the way to legendary. It’ll require a lot of materials to craft all of the equipment for each character so it’s a good idea to loot chests whenever possible.
It’s worth mentioning that from the very start of the game, it works against you in ever possible way. Not only do the enemies want you dead but so too does the world you’re exploring.
During the game there are 3 different phases for each character. The hero phase allows you to move around the active hero and perform actions. Next comes the exploration phase which can have positive or negative effects.
If your character is near the edge of the tile, the exploration phase will load a new tile for you to explore. If you aren’t the game will give you a negative effect based on the roll of the dice. Negative effects can not only stun your characters but also damage them. This is what I meant when I said the game actively works against you.
The third, and final, phase is the villain phase. Any enemies that are visible will perform their turns, usually to attack your characters.
I have to admit, I’ve been enjoying the game quite a lot. The game is pretty challenging, especially if your characters don’t have very good equipment but it’s also really addicting as well. It’s definitely one of the better board game inspired video games that I’ve played and if you’re a fan of Dungeons and Dragons or even the board game itself, you’ll likely find this game to be quite enjoyable. I will say that it might take a little bit to get used to the unique rules but once you understand it it’s really quite simple to get into.

[To preface this review, I'd like to start off by saying I've never reviewed a game on Steam nor ever really had the inclination to do so. And I've been playing games on steam (and PC games in general) for a long time. So this game had quite an effect on me for me to write this review in the first place. I should also note that I'm extremely inclined to love anything zombie related, so of course a game like this is going to stand out to me]
As much as I absolutely love this game, it isn't for everybody, so I'm going to get the "bad" out of the way before my glowing praise, because like most other games it does have it's flaws.
THE BAD
--------------------------
-It's still being developed, so it comes with it's own share of bugs and incomplete content. With that being said, none of the bugs that I've run into are really gamebreaking by any means, just minor annoyances or visual stuff. The missing content is also fairly negligable, because it's usually small things. Most of the major content is pretty fleshed out.
-A little bit clunky (at first). It will probably feel a little awkward at first, and combat will take a lot of getting used to. But as long as you don't ragequit, and take some time to figure out what works and what doesn't, what used to feel clunky will actually begin to feel fairly smooth.
-Lack of a real "objective" (other than simply surviving of course, which I suppose in a zombie apocalypse is as good an objective as any. But you know what I mean). As it stands right now, the game is completely sandbox mode, so you have to make your own fun. But the tools provided to you are top notch, so most of the time fun will end up finding you.
THE GOOD
----------------------
Simply put, this game will make you feel like you're in an episode of the Walking Dead, or playing out your own version of a Romero Movie (you do have the option to customize the zombies' speed and power in sandbox mode). I've been hosting a LAN Hamachi server for my friend and I to play together, and it may possibly be the most fun we've had in any LAN game. The atmosphere is top notch.
This is a game that is filled with incredible moments; say for example, your friend accidently leaving the oven on with salmon cooking inside it and burning down your safehouse, or; huddling in a dark kitchen with only the glow of a lighter to see and sheets covering the windows hoping zombies don't see you♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥yourself inside, then the sound of shattering glass and seeing them pour through a window across the room.
The combat is fun and nerve wracking once you get used to the controls, and looting your way through buildings has never been more satisfying. Managing your character's "moodles" (think "The Sims", little icons that let you know when your character needs something) allows lots of levels of realism, and the unforgiving and brutal combat/medical system makes stealth and zombie avoidance a neccesity; trust me, you do not want to get bitten or scratched. The RPG elements are fairly simple and straightforward, but work well within the game's design. Levelling up your skills is fluid and intuitive.
There's too much to go into, really, you might as well read the wiki page at this point. But let me just say, if you want to play the best Zombie Apocolypse simulator, than look no further than Project Zomboid.

This is a fantastic puzzle game about connecting all the same color dots together in lines as well as filling in the non-color specific blocks.  It's a nice little bit of brain training with both fixed levels to work through and daily levels.   The base levels unlock in sets as you complete them as well as do the first two days of daily puzzles.  There are 25 puzzles per set, with 650 puzzles total in the fixed puzzles.   That may sound like a lot, but some puzzles will take seconds to complete while others could take a minute or more so it won't take more than a couple days of regular play to get through them all.  But the daily puzzles tend to add up to another 350 puzzles per week if you play them all.   So even if you blow through the main puzzles in a couple days, there's plenty to come back to.  In addition to all of this there's a sort of meta game of collecting triangles as you play.  Each set is ranked by difficulty with 1 to 5 triangles and if you complete all the puzzles in the set you get those number of triangles added to a master score.   It's not a big thing, but I'm curious to find out what happens at 999 triangles earned out of 999.  I'm about a 120 away from there on the iOS version (so maybe a week and a half more worth of daily puzzles).  It'll take a lot longer on this version since I started it only recently.
In any event this game is excellent.  Not many puzzle games get me coming back to them... which makes this a pretty special game.  Plus I don't review games if I don't feel they are worth my time.  This one was more than worth making the effort to post a review.

Despite the whole 'Zombie Genre' being widely considered as run down and stale, Project Zomboid seems to really add a fresh twist. Since it's all about the survival aspects, Surviving against the zombies isn't always priority. The Zombies themselves aren't the run of the mill AI you see in a lot of games. They group together from noises, and potentially each other's groans. More urban areas, or places that normally rank high on a looter's list will normally have much higher concentrations of zombies to deal with too.
In a nutshell, if the idea of being under pressure to survive from the get go is a turn off, then this game may not be for you. However, for all you players who love a challenge, and love fighting for survival, then this game is for you.

I wanted to love this game, I really did. The game is absolutely beautiful, and it perfectly reminisces of 1930s cartoons with every detail in every frame being perfectly stylized. The amount of personality they manage to pack into each frame of animations is marvelous in itself. Simple things such as a boss’s head turning into a trash can in order to attack you by throwing up contribute to the style in a very satisfying way.
Every single boss is unique as well. There is literally a level where you fight a crossover of Pearl from Steven Universe and Betty Boop who turns into the MOON. Even the attacks that the bosses use are different throughout the whole game. How many other games are there where you can witness a giant carrot use mind control to launch other carrots at you to act as missiles? And you can be assured that every attack is as unique as this one, you never feel like you’re getting the same boss twice.
The bosses and levels are also very difficult, but the difficulty feels legitimate. You will get frustrated, but you can be sure that the failure was your own, rather than something like a BS hitbox or unavoidable attack.
So why do I hate this game? Well dear reader, I am here today to expose this game for the plagiarizer it is. You see, in Inkwell Isle One, the boss in Floral Fury is clearly a rip off of Flowey from Undertale.
Now I hear you saying, “but that’s preposterous, if Cuphead is such a great game surely it wouldn’t stoop to stealing from another, fellow great game?” Well, think about it. Not only is he a flower, but when you first see the boss, his face looks all innocent and happy, as you can see here:
Remind you of anyone?
Then when he gets angry, a sinister maniacal smile appears on his face, which you can see here:
Once again, doesn’t that ring a bell?
As you can see, this game is blatantly ripping off Undertale.
I give Cuphead a 0/10, you should try Undertale instead.

This game is absolutely remarkable, In terms of the emotions you will experience, the plots twists you go through and the bold characters you encounter. It is essentially a morality game and so it forces you to make crucial decisions of which both effect you, the outcome of the game, characters around you and most importantly the power you will possess. Everything in Rapture is destroyed with mere intentions that just go wrong, leaving a dystopian world of chaos and greed. Ever character appears to be what they are because of rapture and their involvement with it, therefore, no one is technically 'evil' just flawed on different levels.
Probably the standout element of Bioshock is the ability to modify your genetic make-up to develop new weapons and abilities - for instance, early on you gain the ability to fire lightning bolts from your hands, which can then be used on a simple level to stun enemies, rendering them more vulnerable to a solid whack with the wrench, or on a more strategic level to electrify water and take out multiple enemies, fry electrical devices, or enrage the Big Daddies and goad them into attacking other bad guys. Later on you can adopt more macabre plasmids, like the ability to fire swarms of bees, and passive skills like the power to tap into electronic devices.

After reading the reviews of this game i felt like writing one myself.
So, when first saw this game I was instantly happy to see a game like this. I bought it and started playing. The first thing that came to my mind was "Nice music!". When I started actually playing I noticed that the controlls are slippery. But I thought (and still think) it is something unique from this game and I wanted to get better. I only wanted to play a couple minutes but then I had so much fun that I played for 2 hours straight. I tested every map and although I didn't finish every map I found ways to "finish" the first half of some maps very fast. I am normally a very angry player and I scream really loud and annoying but this game didn't make me scream or punch something in my room. It made me calm down with its music and minimalistic / simple style after I got really angry at LoL. I died like 300 times on the first map and it didn't make me angry, not even a little bit. As I played, my "skills" improved and I could control the character better, even though it was still slippery. After these 2 hours I completely forgot the game and I got angry more often. After it got a patch today I noticed it and played again. It had the same effects on me like the first time.
The game has been patched several times and it is less slippery, has controller support, bugs were fixed, I think one map was removed or got moved (one from the experimental ones), etc. Although I understand negative reviews that have clear pros and cons, I don't understand people who just play it for 5 minutes and then return it. If these people that were complaining about the slippery controlls, no controller support or other things would have just waited a bit, they may be happy with the game it is today and/or will be. There are reviews about the game one day (ONE DAY) after the release of the Early Access version, that are complaining about these things and refunded the game. But it's their decision and I don't think that they will change their mind because of a review :)
tl;dr I think this game is much fun and you should just take your time to get better or at least play it some time before refunding it or write a review on it. The dev is also a pretty nice guy :). The only things I think are missing, are the soundtracks available for purchase and the Steam Workshop but I think this is either in progress or will be in the final version :D .

It's great fun and I will say to pick it up buuuuut...
Buy it on a sale or wait until they release more content. Currently there are only 4 game modes, which everybody plays pretty much the same. Rescue? Hunt the monster. Nest? Hunt the monster. Defend? Hunt the monster. Hunt? Hunt the monster.
Monsters are very unbalanced, Goliath is so weak and uninteresting to play that I haven't bothered to unlock the others yet just because I don't want to play Goliath. Kraken and the monsters beyond are vastly better to the point that if you get matchmade against somebody who has managed to unlock them you may are well leave and hope to get a Goliath in the next match.
The campaign mode has an "auto-balance" feature that buffs the losing team's damage output while the winning team gets some sort of map-based buff like opening teleporters or making the wildlife more hostile to the hunters. As implemented however it results in most smart monster throwing the first three rounds, then winning the final two rounds by virtue of doing 2x damage.
As with all 4 player co-op shooters, there is a "downed" mechanic that is made virtually useless by the fact that the monsters (even the goliath) have so much area dominance that they can deny revives by running around in circles and mashing the left mouse button. The only medic worth playing is Lazarus, since his gimmick is being able to revive people even when they are fully dead. Unless the monster immeadiately eats the hunter's corpse... There is no way to prevent revive denial other than hoping the monster is dumb and starts chasing another teammate instead of denying.
Technically the game is solid, a fact that is astounding in this era of half-unfinished unoptimized frankentitles, it mostly stays upwards from 60 FPS even on my computer with somewhat out of date parts and still looks pretty (and no I am not staring at wall textures a finer eye could probably find flaws but I'm too busy being pounded to death by monster fists). The netcode, the greatest flaw in most multiplayer shooters, has not shown any cracks yet.
I am honestly surprised how well this game has turned out looking back on the other recent releases this year. It's been good enough that I had to write a serious review of it rather than making some snide remark and leaving it at that.
I definitely recommend this game. It gives me my D&D fix while staying entertaining and challenging. The turn based combat could be a little better but you win some, you lose some.

Arx Fatalis is a fairly decent dungeon crawler RPG. Not the best, but still very solid. It can be compared to Morrowind in the fact that it is first person fantasy roll playing game, however, it differs from the Elder Scrolls classic in its gameplay machanics and its setting. It is set mostly in confined dungeon areas. I like this approach especially since most games like this are set in an open world anymore. Unfortunately this approach tends to cause most of the game's areas look the same and not stand out. This game also has a unique set of controlls, but you will probalby want to reset most of them, especially if you are used to playing games like Morrowind. Overall, this game is a solid RPG that you are sure to have fun playing, assuming you don't mind the outdated graphics. I give it a 7/10.

This Review of
is the first in, what i hope to achieve, a line of reviews giving detailed information about the game from not only my perspective, but i'll even try to stay close to the facts and just add my personal opinion in through small doses. I'll also try to steer clear of spoilers and not ruin the fun for anybody, but if you aim to play the game without any information on story or gameplay whatsoever, try it out yourself and don't read on. I'm a german native, so excuse any and all shortcomings when it comes to the english language.
is a single-player, first person horror game, currently sold in a price range of under 15 bucks. It is sarcastically labeled as a walking simulator and, while i don't support the mockery that comes with it, not entirely unjustified. The Park aims to deliver you a story. It does not want to show off crazy mechanics, breathtaking graphics or intriguing gameplay. It is just a story. Seeing that the Developer of the game is
, you can expect a good story though. The best way to describe this game is not as a game, but as a movie. You pay for the narrative, but this time it's you being in the drivers seat and exploring the story yourself instead of being told the narrative by movie characters. If you are looking for a game with great replayability or casual gameplay,
is not for you.
The game puts you into the perspective of Lorraine, a seemingly single mother, who took her son, Callum, to an amusement park called
. The game does not give you many explanations or an introduction, it just lets you jump right in. You find yourself in the parking lot with your son in the backseat of your car. Shortly after, you are being told that your son has run back into the park after it has closed, and you, being a good mother, run after him. From there, it all goes to worse. The goal of the game, as you are told, is to find your son, Callum.
The game delivers it's story to you via clever monologue of Lorraine while you steer her through the park and let her ride the various rides and attractions. The narrative just adds to the creepy and weird atmosphere at the park, and while seeming spooky, but not scary in the beginning, as you progress, more and more jumpscares are woven into the gameplay as the narration takes dark and twisty turns. The lore of the game, especially the location being the Atlantic Island Park, is a nod to Funcoms popular MMORPG „The Secret World“, the park being a location there and some characters from the MMORPG appearing in „The Park“ as well. Furthermore, the game has one or two missable side-stories tied in, and delivers some background through notes and letters scattered throughout the park. The gameplay is described pretty easy: You walk and interact with things in the park. There are just two buttons outside of your movement, one to interact with highlighted objects, one to shout for Callum. Everything that happens at the park has an effect on Lorraine, not only through her voice in the narrative and how she yells after her son, but through visual and aubile effects on screen, the vision becoming blurry and your heart rate becoming louder as Lorraine gets scared.
The story is on point with this game. If you love games with a good narrative, you will absolutely dig „The Park“. The atmosphere is beautiful, the imagery, even though simply designed, can let you stop in your tracks and just wonder, if you really want to go there. Lorraines monologues are perfectly tied in to your exploration of the park and herself, triggered as you walk over certain points in the map. The haunting scenery makes for an adventure, and while linear, it forces you to reflect on some things you've heard or seen.  For what „The Park“ wants to deliver, it does so with ease and to a certain point even perfect. Players who already enjoyed „The Secret World“ will have a bonus coming into this game, not only because of the already known locations and characters, but because it is just pure amazement, what funcom did with the seemingly small venue like Atlantic Island Park and also with the extension of the story already teasered in „The Secret World“.
There are a couple things that could act as a road block. Casual players may find many aspects of the game unenjoyable. The lack of literally any gameplay other than walking through the park and exploring it's locations makes for a dull experience for people who want to kill and shoot things. Although being a horror game with minimal survival aspects – heart rate, blurred vision, smaller view – you will never truely feel threatened or fear for your survival. Everything is just atmosphere, and there is no killer stalking you or moments where you have to take immediate action to save yourself. Some may find that a lackluster experience. For it's price, the game also does not offer a very long experience, even with full exploration and all secrets the game just takes 2 hours to complete – and with very little arguments for replayability, that is of course not very much.
For me, The Park was a fun experience and a good investment. I've played The Secret World, i'm a sucker for lore and story and i love the setting, so the game just strikes 10 with me. Even without former knowledge, you can enjoy The Park if you are into story driven experiences and if you really have the time to enjoy this game. What i mean by that is: Don't try to rush through the story. Don't try to play this game in an achievement hunt. If you don't give the narrative and the atmosphere a chance to grasp you, The Park won't be a good experience for you. Don't make the mistake of buying this game and expect something like Outlast or Amnesia, because The Park doesn't even want to be that type of game. Buy it expecting a movie, that focuses on introspective, creepy scenery and an increasingly disturbing tale of personal shortcomings, and you will have your fun with this game. I am biased towards The Park because of The Secret World and Funcom in general, so it has proven to be a good buy, even though i recommend waiting on a sale or holiday special to pick it up at a discount. Anyway: Give it a try if you're into it. It will give you little, but with that, won't disappoint you.

Overview:
The Long Dark is a game developed by Hinterland Studios. You play as a pilot, Will Mackenzie, who crash landed in the middle of the Canadian wilderness during a geomagnetic storm and must survive the unrelenting forces of mother nature.
Pros:
-Gameplay is refreshing and without monsters or zombies, you must survive on your wits alone
-Balancing hunger, thirst, fatigue and warmth makes the game riveting
-Permadeath system that means every choice you make can be your last
-A learning system that makes your character better as the game progresses and "Feats" that are a collective of all your played games which give you small bonus afterward
-Challenges which task you with doing something within a certain amount of time or with parameters
-Updates every month that add amazing features to the game
-Amazingly beautiful enviroments
Cons:
-Animal AI can be buggy
-Lack of other survivors
-Story mode still isn't out yet, but will hopefully be soon.
Conclusion:
This game is lovingly created by Hinterland and shows no signs of stopping anytime soon. The game says it's version 0.349 as of now, and could easily be passed off as the complete game. I would highly reccommend this game for anyone who wants a new take on the survival genre.

If you're looking for a casual, minimalistic puzzle game to click at, LYNE will certainly deliver.
With 26 sets of puzzles this game can definitely keep you busy, this isn't something you're going to breeze right through (unless you look at guides, I guess). Things start out simply enough; but with each set you unlock, the puzzles slowly and steadily become more complex. The puzzles themselves aren't terribly "big" per se, but you do run into some head-scratchers here and there that might take you longer than some of the others in the same set to figure out. Luckily each set has plenty of puzzles, so if you get stuck on one you can just leave it be, try another and come back to it later.
All I can say is, the way they've come up with so many combinations of lines connecting panels to color-coded diamonds, squares and triangles is somewhat baffling and maddening. I will recommend LYNE because I do enjoy it, but I'll also recommend you play it in small doses. I do a set or two at a time and then I need to move on to something else. Because although the puzzles are well done, after playing for so long it can start to feel quite repetitive and you may strain your patience muscle. The puzzles are very uniform but therefore also predictable and doing too many will make the game feel monotonous, which is really not fair to it, because again, it can be very enjoyable.
What else to say? It's peaceful, it's relaxing, it's simple and visually-pleasing and even comes with multiple unlockable color palettes... and with over 600 individual puzzles - not including the daily puzzles - LYNE is not exactly in any rush to be finished (so don't peek at solutions!). Grabbed this on sale but I think I'd pay the full three bucks for it. I'm not sure what the replay value will be like after I've completed everything, but for now I'm having a lot of fun with it.

The short of it:
The Park is replete with "horror game" clichés.  Cheap jumpscares, a creepy setting, flashbacks, disturbing imagery, and a flair for messing with reality all make their appearances.  There's also no compelling characters, combat, choices, gameplay, dialogue interaction, or payoff.  The obtusely-simplistic story is entirely unable to stand on its own, and has an ending that's so dull and predictable that my friends and I called it within the first 5 minutes.  The only thing about the game that's scary is it implies that Zoloft turns you into a pyschopath...
The long of it:
Set within the universe of
, "The Park" is meant to be a spin-off game.  Now, a spin-off needs something to stand on its own, such as expanding upon a small element of a larger story arc that ends up having its own dramatis personae.  Otherwise, it's not a spin-off, but rather just an episode of a long-arc TV show where if you haven't seen everything leading up to it makes absolutely no sense.  Playing "The Park" as an outsider of the MMORPG is like being the one person in the room with a bunch of die-hard
fans that has never seen a single epsiode or read any of the books.  You tilt your head at the screen and ask "So, what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on?"  While it might speak to those who play the MMORPG, it's an atrocious ambassador to that larger world for the rest of us, because if "The Secret World" is anything like "The Park" in terms of story or gameplay, you couldn't
me to play it.
While walking through the eponymous setting, your point of view is as the narrator and candidate for "worst mother on the planet."  Note that I don't say you "play" this character.  This is because you're merely looking through her eyes as you walk around the environment and things happen.  The entire thing is effectively (and often literally) on rails, and you have no ability to affect the story based on your actions.  There's no way to "win" or "lose," nor can you have any impact on the events unfolding whatsoever.  Sure, some of the imagery can be demented and weird, but it falls flat at being scary since nothing ever threatens you as the player and there are no tasks to be punished for failing.  You have literally nothing to do except visit various different places, and sit down to ride something while listening to faceless voices talk.
The only other "character" you encounter looks so visually out-of-place that his appearance is far more comical than disturbing, and he never grabs your attention long enough for you to want to know anything else about him.  The mystery of whether he's a hallucination, demon, or other such entity isn't compelling at all since he has absolutely no effect upon the main character in the end.  Just like the protagonist's aggravatingly disobedient child, he's flat and forgettable.  (There's another character you see at the end, but he's so forgettable that I actually
, and had to place this note here after the fact.)
But here's the absolute worst thing of all for me about "The Park":  Its astoundly ignorant and offensive treatment of depression and mental health.  Any and all remaining respect for the game I might otherwise have had is vaporized by the inflammatory and damaging portrayal of the effects of real-world medications that the game presents.
Perhaps there is some alternate supernatural explanation which one would need to have played "The Secret World" in order to know about, but based purely upon the context of what "The Park" tells us, the possible side-effects of being medicated for depression include hallucinations and murdering your children.  It relegates depression to the realm of "insanity" where mild seratonin imbalance medications (they riff on Zoloft with "Zolift") are the colloquial "crazy pills."
As someone who is close to multiple people who medicate against depression and who has suffered from depression himself, this is unforgiveable, and drops "The Park" to the absolute bottom of my list of games to recommend to anyone.  If I could, I'd rank it below "Dead Mountaineer's Hotel."

Игру заприметил еще на старте разработки. Подкупающей была тематика (ещё не заезженная на тот момент), пиксель-арт и, конечно же – изометрия. На данный момент это стильный и действительно интересный симулятор выживания на фоне зомби-апокалипсиса. И вовсе не только лишь потому, что изометрия и пиксельная графика. Игра обладает определенным шармом и без этого. Хотя бы на уровне своих возможностей. Будучи небольшой по размерам и миниатюрной в исполнении, игра оставляет за собой многие новинки из Early Access (далее по тексту EA).
В большинстве игр подобной тематики вы оказываетесь в декорациях, которые служат подстилкой для массированного PVP, где, в общем и целом, кроме него заниматься нечем. Мало кто прорабатывает «изнанку мира» (англ. background). В PZ подноготная рядом. Есть два небольших городка где-то в американской глубинке, фермы, поселки и леса. Существует даже карта на манер Google-карт созданная каким-то умельцем. Она позволят оценить размах умирающего мира. Здесь умирает всё, в том числе и вы. Это история где рано или поздно будет поставлена трагическая точка.
За регулярными вылазками в город в поисках медикаментов, продуктов и необходимых для выживания вещей (да-да, даже медицинскому пинцету найдется здесь дело) вы краем глаза замечаете, что и город меняется. Происходит отключение от глобальной системы энергоснабжения, постепенно прекращает свою работу трубопровод, подававший в населенные пункты воду. Еда в холодильниках портиться, и вы уже вряд ли сможете порадоваться хорошо прожаренной отбивной. Города подвергаются армейской зачистке, не сулящей вам ничего хорошего, да и ходячих с каждым днем становится всё больше.
Если совместить естественное умирание города с набегами других выживших, то картинка порой становится и вовсе унылой. Вместо богатства, ожидающего мародера посетившего брошенное место, вам часто приходиться довольствоваться каким-то мелочами. Нож для масла в качестве оружия, женская блузка вместо свитера, мусорный пакет или школьный ранец вместо хорошей сумки. собранный вручную топор, что развалится после нескольких ударов. Аутентичность на этом не заканчивается - забудете выключить газ на кухне (пока он еще остался в баллонах) и ваш дом превратиться в пепелище.
С тех пор как появился мультиплеер игра ещё больше расцвела. Помимо PVP серверов существуют PVE сервера и даже «ролевые». Попав туда, вы придерживаетесь канвы повествования. Вы больше не Ваня или Джон зашедшие покрошить других игроков. Теперь вы вполне реальный персонаж, переговаривающийся с другими выжившими по радио, помогающий другим выжить. Отыгрыш сбивает людей в группы, чтобы противостоять ходячим вместе. Богатство игровых ситуаций описать трудно. Ровно как и богатство способов умереть.
Разбил окно, полез в закрытый дом, разодрался в кровь влезая в него, впоследствии умер от заражения. Отравился плохой едой, отлеживался в каком-то доме, оказался в осаде - умер, будучи съеденным, заживо. Попал в засаду, был ранен, убежал, нашел какой-то дом полный алкоголя. Долго пил и радовался жизни. Выздоровел. Вышел наружу и столкнулся с ордой. Долго удирал от нее, забаррикадировался в каком-то отеле, затем спрыгнул с крыши второго этажа, сломал бедро, отполз в местный туалет и там умер. Всё это проза PZ дня. А ведь есть романы, поэзия. Всё это у вас будет, и каждый ваш опыт от игровой сессии будет разным.

Based on my experiences of playing this game for about 20hrs (the Steam timestamps are somewhat screwed up here) I'd like to warn fellow sympathisers of Ragnarok Online who are rushing into its successor with high expectations:
I expected Ragnarok 2 to have something to do with the original Ragnarok Online. I installed the game full of anticipation it would be a Ragnarok Online in 3D ! With a beautiful and diversive world to explore ! With new skills and a better fighting system ! I'll be able to make a completely individual char, a wholly black knight and♥♥♥♥♥♥like that ! This will be awesome !
After starting the game I figured that I would be disappointed in even my lowest expectations.
- The gameplay is a simple WoW copy and utmost boring. Why would you limit the fights to auto-attack rounds in a game like this? Let me fight myself.
- The "open world" is more of a path you follow - from village to village - doing your repetitive 'kill 20 of these', 'get 10 of those' quests. Always the same type of quests with no emotionally involving content behind. Couldn't they think of anything to evoke the player's passion about playing this game?
- Using the exact same job class system as in its predecessor I was very surprised to see that Monks now can't use the Acolyte skills they acquired before. I am sure there are similar rip-offs with other job classes. I am not against inventions, improvements and new stuff but there is nothing positive about this.
- Everything is very colourful and cute but the game fails to surround me with spectacular, astonishing or inspiring environments - Ragnarok Online does that even in 2D.
- I don't know why but I had difficulties crafting items, using items, buying items, trading items, ... maybe it's just me but it felt very complicated and not as conveniently accessible as it should be.
- Almost all usable items are timed, which makes you lose interest in getting or using those in the first place.
- Do you remember the feeling that you got in Payon Dungeon? Orc Dungeon? When entering Prontera? The Geffen fields? The Comodo Beach? You won't get even close here...
- "Ragnarök" is an event in the old Germanic and Viking mythology. The meaning behind all terrains, quests, names and monsters in Ragnarok Online is a combination of different culture's mythologies (i.e. Munak and Bongun referring to Chinese Jiangshi, you also find Korean, Taiwanese and other references).
Now in Ragnarok 2 I am told to obtain the crown of the Sunflower King. wtf?
I wished it was a Ragnarok Online turned into 3D graphics, with an active fighting system, some cool character individualizing stuff and maybe even some open world building elements (I'd love to build my own in-game house with my own obedient Kafra servant) but what we got is all annoying stuff about WoW put together in pretentious Anime style, claiming to be the successor of Ragnarok Online. I am sorry but I couldn't think of anything positive to say about this game. I guess the in-game music is not as disturbing as it possibly could've been. A few musical references to its predecessor would have been nice, though.

I wanted Final Fantasy Tactics in Sentai suits and was not disappointed!
No seriously, I'm calling
a must-buy in terms of tactical RPGs. At worst, the scenarios get kinda samey, the mecha battles are more luck-based than anything, Scout class needs work in terms of role within the team and the meme-based humour might get under some delicate skins. Never mind the details; as a tactical RPG, Chroma Squad gets everything right and even dares some neat ideas concerning character statistics, combat and the money/audience system.
What I'm saying is there's a deepness to the game despite the apparent simplicity of the setting, with clear character roles and a certain leeway in how you want them optimized. The love for the genre is genuine and goes a long way in enhancing your experience; it's more than just shooting aliens as in X-Com. Building an audience to gain money and better toys is a welcome change from XP grinding. The grid movement can be unforgiving what with the inability to take back a move but I feel as this just adds to the challenge factor.
In short: the core of the gameplay is great and the further you get from the tactical RPG, the worse it gets. I can't fault a game for false notes when it's just being overly ambitious. An original backdrop for an RPG, multiple story paths, clever insertion of Kickstarter backers into the story and the fact I've encountered no game-breaking bugs despite a Report button makes me want to heavily endorse this product. An example for other Kickstarter-funded game developers.

BugZy's Review: SinaRun - The best game you'll fail hundreds of times at!
The following is my opinion.
Retry, retry, retry, retry...
SinaRun is a great 3D platformer racing game, where you try to get to the end of the levels in the fastest possible time by using your extroardinarily fast cybernetic legs. The whole game is basically a time trial that is so relentless that if you make a mistake - and trust me, you will make several hundred before completing each level - you'll have to start from the beginning of the level. No checkpoints, no excuses.
The game currently has 17 levels including the tutorial, with the dev's best score displayed for you to try to beat and a leaderboard for your best score to be displayed publicly too. 17 levels may not seem like much for a game, but when you add the time between your fails and the amount of fails you have accrued, it quickly adds up, especially when you are trying to beat everyone's best times!
You will gain some very useful skills whilst playing SinaRun, such as the natural instinct to swiftly reach for the 'R' key if you get stopped or slowed down when missing a jump, or the ability to get used to the control of your character which can be somewhat awkward to get used to, seeming slippery in a sense. This can have a big impact on your experience, but once you get comfortable with it it becomes second nature.
Despite the game's visual theme being minimalism, it has a high level of beauty with the different map colours and particle effects flying fast towards you as you attempt to make it to the end. This, accompanied by the relaxing music that tries to keep you calm every time you fail, creates a very unique atmosphere (in a good way.)
All things considered, the game is a great play if you would like something to play every now and then and don't mind failing a few hundred times and in all fairness, for $3, it's a bargain!
I rate SinaRun 8/10 extremely quick wombats.

I'm going to open with this: There's a lot of negative reviews of this game on Steam, and almost all of them are talking about the DLC structure being really ♥♥♥♥♥♥. They are not incorrect. However, as of now, all of the DLC is cosmetic only - weapon and character skins, for instance. They're outrageously priced, but we don't need them, and not having them doesn't detract from the fun of the game. There is other DLC planned - a new monster, 4 new hunters. This will be priced at $7.49 per hunter, and $14.99 per monster (according to the publisher). This is extremely high. I feel sorry for the Xbone and PS4 players, I really do. But lucky for us, we're glorious PC gamers and we don't have to put up with that♥♥♥♥♥♥ Wait for a Steam sale, get the DLC for pennies on the dollar. Don't let the unnecessarily expensive DLC detract from the main point here: the game.
On that note, the game is a lot of fun. If you enjoyed L4D's asymetrical multiplayer, Evolve takes it to a whole new level of fun.
As of now, there are 3 monsters and 12 hunters (3 each of 4 archetypes) to choose from, and 9 perks each (9 for hunters, 9 for monsters) of which you can choose one per match that give pretty substantial but specialized bonuses. The hunters all have specific gimmicks within their archetype - for example, all Support hunters have a Cloaking ability that makes themself and other hunters near them invisible for a short time, and all Assault hunters have a personal shield, granting a short period of invulnerability. Additionally, they all have 3 other weapons or abilities that vary wildly, and the combination of hunters on the team create very different feeling matches. Further, the three monsters play completely differently, and the tactics required to hunt them are vastly different.
This is important, because it keeps the gameplay interesting. You never know going into a match what you're going to be dealing with (the hunters can coordinate their planning, but they can't see which monster they'll be fighting, and the monster can't see which hunters they'll be up against until they've locked in their choices), so the game does a good job of promoting on-the-spot tactical decisions. As the monster, do you try and fake out the hunters with some tactically placed tracks leading in one direction, then double back in another to buy some time at the beginning of the match? Do you try and use stealth to stay ahead of the hunters, or do you make a run for it? Do you engage them at stage 2, or do you bide your time until it's safer at stage 3? As the hunters, do you split up to maximize map coverage and find the monster early, or stick together to minimize the chance of an ambush? When you're hurting and have lost a team member or two, do you run and wait for them to respawn, or do you try and engage the monster with a skeleton crew?
How long the game will stay fun is hard to say at this point, but my educated guess right now is that if you're the type of person who didn't get bored with L4D, you'll find this fun for a long time to come.
There's a number of game modes currently in the game, with varying level of balance. Hunt, the flagship gamemode wherein the hunters have to kill the monster before it kills them, is very well balanced, and incredibly fun to play. The others, however, aren't.
'Nest' adds 6 monster eggs to the map, which the monster has to prevent the hunters from destroying for 10 minutes (or kill all of the hunters). This mode is heavily imbalanced in favor of the hunters, large because of the large amount of more or less autonomous damage the hunters have at their disposal. A number of characters have equipment that can do damage without their constant attention (airstrikes, combat drones, etc.) that can be used to destroy the eggs even when the monster is right there trying to defend them, and the hunters' damage output on some characters is such that they can get through all six eggs in very short order.
'Rescue' adds 9 incapacitated civilians to the map. The hunters need to revive them and escort them to a dropship, while the monster needs to kill them. First side to 5 wins. This is heavily imbalanced in favor of the monster. With a bit of armor, a monster can run up to a downed civilian, beat on it for long enough to kill it, and get away even with all four hunters actively shooting it.
'Defend' features three generators (with automated sentry turrets defending them), and the monster starts at stage 3 and has constantly spawning minions to attack the generators with. If the monster destroys all 3 generators, it wins. If the hunters defend for a set amount of time (5 minutes + 5 minutes per destroyed generator) or kills the monster, they win. I haven't personally played this enough to say for certain, but it feels very skewed in favor of the hunters. One of the monsters is far stronger than the other two for this mode, but I still have yet to see the monster win, even when the monster has a strong advantage from the start.
'Evaculation' mode is a series of 5 matches in a variety of modes, and whichever side wins a match gets an advantage in the next. It's great in theory, but the imbalance issues noted above detract from the experience. Each round, two map / game mode options are offered and the players vote on which one they want to play, but this almost always results in Nest over Rescue, because the monster gets a single vote to the hunters' 4 (1 per player).
There's a lot of rage over one particular monster (Wraith), and a lot of players seem to think it's overpowered, but I suspect this is more a matter of players not yet being familiar with how to combat it. I think we'll see it winning less games as the community's tactics evolve (pun intended).
Overall, the question boils down to this: "Is the game fun?" And I'm going to go on the record with a resounding 'yes'. Evolve is one of the most fun competitive multiplayer experiences I've had in a long time, and of the characters I've played (all 3 monsters, and 8 of the 12 hunters), there aren't any I did not enjoy, or who felt unimportant or unnecessary in a match. As with any similar game, some matches are over very quickly and feel like one side just got destroyed without a chance, but most are extremely tense, and really get your heart racing.
So, would I recommend this game? Yes, I would, even with the DLC issues plaguing it. Just remember what platform we're playing on, and don't get sucked into the outrageous DLC prices... buy the game now with confidence, but wait for a steam sale for the DLC (or just skip it entirely).

I remember seeing the preview build for it and being hyped as hell, thinking about how good the game could be with a decent bit of variety in gunplay and level design. Unfortunately, the release build of SUPERHOT is noticeably lacking in those exact areas.
The levels are ultimately uninteresting and samey, there's like 3 guns in the whole game and barely any new mechanics added by the end of it all.
Then there's the fact that the story is less than 2 hours and it honestly felt like half of that was "typing" in this heavy-handed "taking control away from the player" meta-narrative that just left me feeling so... meh. At first blush Evolve may seem a bit overpriced. $60 for a few multiplayer arenas and a couple handfuls of playable characters and monsters?  But then I played a few games and realized how well detailed the characters are, and how rich the sci-fi jungle setting is, and how darn pretty everything is.  And I realized the time and money that went into this game wasn’t squandered away like so many angry reviewers claim. This game clearly had a lot of love and sweat and attention-to-detail-and-flavor poured into it.
I would LOVE to see a single player campaign with scripted events, in-engine cut scenes, and a little more world building. In my last solo play, when a moment of quiet came in the hunt, some of the characters started talking to each other; one apologized for dragging the other off to this dangerous planet when she was all settled in and happy elsewhere. I wanted to know more about that back story, but even getting a hint of it helped me feel like the world Evolve takes place in is bigger than meets the eye. It was a good start.
I don’t mean to contradict the eSports/hardcore players who complain about balance. I just mean to show that this game can be appreciated as a title deserving of a normal, full AAA price. Yes, release-day DLC is lamentable and should be discouraged by us consumers. And maybe I’m being too hopeful that the publisher will provide some free or cheap updates in the near future to add more depth and balance to the game. But we still have a GOOD game on our hands here, regardless of some overpriced (mostly cosmetic) DLC hanging over our heads.

Tales from Candlekeep: Tomb of Annihilation is a bit of a hit or miss for me, yes I can appreciate the design of the game itself but there are a few mechanics that make the game less appealing for me. That in turn doesn't exactly make me want to go back into the game and play it more, it's a very slow placed, strategy, turn-based board game that doesn't really incline me to play more than about 3 hours of it.
The game itself obviously has it's problems, now whether these problems are balanced out by the positives of the game I couldn't really tell you. I am very much on the mixed side of things on this game, now the game sells itself like a Dungeons & Dragons game and therefore I was expecting there to be at least SOME form of customization on the characters that I would be playing as throughout. Unfortunately this isn't the case, you are forced to choose from the 4 pre-made characters to fight as. Not that this decision matters all that much, you will be able to recruit all of them on your team eventually so really it doesn't matter all that much. The lack of customization is almost like a back stab to this so called 'Dungeons & Dragons' game, at least a small amount of customization would be nice.
Now onto the core mechanics, if you were expecting some procedurally generated levels with some random D&D elements thrown in then your going to be disappointed. The way that the game plays out is that you have a main objective, and you start on one tile. If you end your turn by standing on the edge of the tile then another tile will appear in whatever direction you were standing in, this tile will be somewhat randomly drawn and then placed for you to move forward. But there isn't enough variation of these tiles to make each run of the same level feel different enough that it makes you want to go back and do the level on a harder difficulty. It lacks variety, as do the characters that you play as.
At this point I am struggling to find positives about this game that I actually enjoyed, I mean there must've been something that made me continue to play the game for around 3 hours right? Well I suppose that the fighting mechanics of the game are balanced well, there is that board game element that there is always a chance that you will miss your attack making you have to be more strategic with your moves. Some of these board game elements that they add make the game a bit more challenging, but more sometimes this turns more into frustration and a element that you can't really control.
For example a more frustrating mechanic is an encounter that will occur after you've used both actions on a character. 9 times out of 10 it will be bad and you can either 1. let the encounter happen to you and face the consequences (usually this will deal damage to certain heroes or stun them etc.) or you can use your adrenaline rush to avoid the encounter. In order to gain this adrenaline rush you have to defeat monsters, but you'll soon find that you won't be able to avoid all of these encounters that you will come across because there aren't enough monsters to defeat to gain enough adrenaline. Later on in the game, you will have no choice but to face these encounters and will probably die to them more often than not. This to me is more of a frustration than a challenging mechanic, it forces the player to rush through and complete the objective otherwise you will have to face these encounters and more than likely lose.
Furthermore, there is also a very basic crafting system in the game that makes it feel a little grindy in order to gain materials and resources. In order to get these materials you can either find chests throughout each level, or you gain a few when levelling up. With these materials you are able to craft better gear for your Heroes to give them more damage, more defence and so on. Of course as you progress you will have to find more rare resources in order to make equipment better, and that will probably make you grind more in previous levels. Now whether this is a good or bad element to this game I am unsure and I think it really depends on the person, it defiantly makes the game a bit more grindy and as the game is already quite slow paced I wouldn't think that it's a good element. But take this point into your own opinion, maybe you enjoy the grind on this game, but I for one didn't.
I really was hoping that the graphics on this game would make up for the cons of the main mechanics, but unfortunately there really isn't much to rave about. Considering the game was released on 2017, I was expecting there to be a little bit more done with the graphics, more the tile sets and the scenery that were being used. It all seems just very dull and boring, each area basically looking the same as the last with little to no variety. I think this is another reason why the game doesn't feel entirely procedurally generated, because everything looks the same. That being said, some of the attack graphics of the game do look nice, more the spell ones with vibrant colours that really stand out most from anything else.
+ Strategic board game
+ Some nice fighting graphics
- Lack of customization for characters
- Little to no variety on the tiles that are used to create 'procedurally generated' levels
- Encounter phase is more frustrating than it is challenging
- Basic crafting system makes you grind for more rarer materials to increase your stats, making you grind on previous levels
- Tile graphics all look the same and make the game suffer not feeling entirely procedurally generated
All in all I wouldn't recommend getting this game, especially at full price. The game seems to suffer a lot from customization to frustrating mechanics, I for one didn't enjoy the game as much as I thought I would. Maybe this game would be more appealing to the right type of person, but for me it didn't really live up to what I expected and didn't incline for me to go back to the game to play it more. If you are still considering purchasing this game then at least wait for a discount or for the game to be in a bundle.

LYNE is something I haven't found in a while; a simple puzzle game with a casual element to it. I've always loved casual puzzle games but I've never been able to find many, especially in recent times. I love the concept for being such a simple yet malleable one. All you do is connect lines. That's it, but, adding more simple ideas, such as different colors and looping lines through themselves, gives this game a great variety and suprising difficulty.
And it's not short either. There's 26 sets with 25 puzzles for each one and a steady increase in difficulty, introducing harder mechanics throughout every 1 or 2 sets. But what happens when you get through all of those? Where do I go now? Well, there's a wonderful daily system in place that randomly generates 1-3 sets, each with a varying degree of difficulty. Each day, you can come back and play a new daily set of sets, giving this simple game a huge replayability.
However, there are some minor, minor problems. One of which is the difficulty spikes. One puzzle in a set usually has me there for at least 5 minutes whereas the rest of them are around a minute or less. Now that's too bad, as getting stuck helps me get better at thinking in different ways; looking at things in a different perspective. Although, it is slightly annoying to be stuck on a puzzle for so long. Also, some people may complain about the "lack of tutorial" when introducing new things, but that's what makes this game unique and stylized. That's what makes it so rewarding to solve a puzzle that you've been on for 5 minutes or longer.
But the best thing by far in the game is the atmosphere. The sounds and the ability to change palette really sold me on this game. I thoroughly enjoy just clicking on the shapes and listening to the sounds ping off, and then connecting makes shapes gives me a little reward. When you complete a puzzle, a simple ambient sound resonates through into the next level and the screen goes white, knowing that I solved the puzzle and that this is my reward. When I don't complete a puzzle, it tells me what things I need to connect and flashes at me in red to help me guide my way into solving the puzzle.
All in all, this game is great at what it does and took a very simple concept and expanded it greatly. With it's wonderful sound and level design, it did great to suck me and it seems like a game I would play for years. Basically, purchase it now. It's cheap enough to not pick up. Buy it now!

Swanky Paint is for fixed palette pixel art with keyboard controls and a UI heavily inspired by the legendary Deluxe Paint that some of us wrinkly old puffins remember from the 16 bit era when pixel art was called "graphics."
I love creating art with Swanky Paint. I used it to make the art for a bunch of ludum dare games, and was very happy with the result and the workflow. Take a moment to familiarise yourself with the keyboard shortcuts and working in Swanky becomes fast and intuitive.
My favourite feature of Swanky Paint are the filters though. Scanlines and bloom, alternative pixel shapes... these allow you to export your pixel art looking beautiful and distinctive. Swanky Paint art has a very specific and attractive look that I find very appealing.
Pros:
- Fast, intutitive workflow (once you know the keyboard shortcuts)
- Heaven for people who used to use DPaint back in the day
- Great for working with paletted pixel art
- Support for animations
- Support for previewing 3d models (so you can swanky up the textures!)
- Every feature is actually useful
- Truly gorgeous export functionality
- Runs on just about any device/platform imaginable
- The developers are absolutely relentless when it comes to bugfixing, adding new features and supporting feature requests from the community.
- No, really, the developers are absolutely amazing
Cons:
- Would benefit from photoshop style layers
- UI might take a little getting used to for people who haven't used DPaint before
- Animation support is pretty rudimentary and would benefit from preview windows and onion skinning
Basically yes, I totally recommend this software.

To start with I came to T5 having played T4, Banished and Cities Skylines and I have to confess there is a lot to dislike in this game. Obviously the Tropico series is a light hearted and more fluffy city builder than Skylines which is fine, and T5 does some really interesting and novel things that T4 doesn't do/have - a ruling family dynasty, epochs which unlock buildings, tech and policies, building managers to give various bonuses, trade ships/routes, auto demolish building when resources are depleted etc. But....
T5 is overall presented in a somewhat 'half-baked' way - the game looks great visually and runs smoothly as well as being very stable, but trying to get detailed info about your settlement(s) is a real chore. Which buildings have been upgraded and which haven't - you must click them one by one to check, office blocks make money on people living in their vicinity - how big an area is the vicinity, it doesn't tell you. Same with manager bonuses which work in the vicinity - where does the vicinity end? Rebels are attacking !!! A zoom to button would be useful - no you must locate them manually. If you don't they may destroy a building that will remain a ruin for years until you accidentally notice it. Activating an edict closes the edicts box, you have to reopen it to select the next edict rather than a go back option to see all edicts available. Are you producing enough food to feed the population? You can't tell until you get the 'XX number of citizens starved to death last year' message.Quests that offer to improve relations between eg USA or USSR don't give opportunity to check current relations before picking which one to improve. Placing buildings, especially plantations is painful at times as the jungle hides for example how much of their fields are lost to uneven terrain. How large an area must I leave forested around my logging camp to maintain 100% efficiency - it doesn't tell you. Inexplicably, unlike in T4, you will end up with annoying empty little spaces in your city where no garden fits as you can no longer place 'trees' only square/rectangular 'gardens'.
Also annoying are the quirky history facts about the worlds zaniest dictators over the years - these pop up on various loading screens - I love to read them, the problem is the game loads so quickly (a great thing) you can't read the whole sentence about Gaddaffi's stairs phobia or Duvalier hunting black dogs in Haiti.
This may seem like a long list of negatives and a brief gloss over of the positives (which it is) that make T5 sound like it is not so good, Not true, it is a great fun, easy to pick up and hard to master middle complexity city builder, you just have to be aware that the games systems to keep you informed and provide gameplay functionality are....uhm.....about as well developed as the bureaucratic structures on any carribean island run by a tin-pot dictator. This translates to the fact that by the time you have developed a large part of your island the work involved in staying informed about what the hell is going on becomes very tedious very quickly.

It's been almost 2 years since I reviewed this game and I think an update is in order.
First lets talk about what the game has!
It works! It works well! I've ran into NO game breaking bugs and there is plenty of content even in vanilla. The game is playable and replayable. The more you play, the better you get. The more you survive, the better your character gets. Your skills upgrade, your abilities grow, and you can read books to gain new knowlege on how to make all sorts useful things.
So what cons are there? It can be very difficult to aim a weapon. You rarely know if you are shooting at a Zed or not. And when you do, it seems to attract Zeds for miles and miles, even using a quiet nail gun attracts Zeds from blocks away it seems. DON'T USE A FIREARM IN A CONFINED SPACE!!
Barricades seem to be easily broken down to me. I like to find large buildings with an upstairs or even roof access (for safe farming once I'm set up). I often find myself building log walls around outside doors to double up the defenses because a door and windows that are barricaded seem to fall too quickly to go to sleep at night. And if there is a mob, forget it, barricades just dn't last long enough. There needs to be a new option, like upgrading a door to be more durable, maybe replacing the door with a metal sliding bay door. But that's for another update.
The music and sounds get repetative but it's not horrible or annoying, but it does make you sleepy after an hour or two.
What to do? Everything. Play it, mod it, enjoy it! There is workshop access now and while there are some things there that don't blend well with the game, it still adds a lot while the updates come from the official dev team (small, keep that in mind when waiting for updates).
The dev team does keep constant communication and gives weekly updates. They are in love with their game and they are determined to make a complete product.

BUY WTH CONFIDENCE

The company didn't even care, in their now publically regocnized mistake, to allow preorders to upgrade to the packages that were later released. Gave them money when they were griping about delays? Not only will they treat you as second-rate to second-comers, that extra time was used to make DLC. They are and will only ever be interested in minimum input to maximum profit. I'm still in shock that they delayed this game just for the purposes of shoving additional day one DLC down our throats. It's unbelievable that they would ever think it was acceptable to take our money, and use it to delay the game just to charge us more!
In the abstract the idea of the game is great, but purchasing the game and its current content just can't be rationalized. In fact, I would have canceled my preorder, but the option to do so was removed for whatever reason by either Steam or Turtle Rock in my purchase history prior to release. Turtlerock is now as blacklisted for me as EA, never again.
Since I couldn't save myself the money I wasted on their inordinate greed, I hope that I can save you. I also hope that if you do buy it and feel as I do that you similarly contribute a negative review. And lastly I finally hope that the large numbers of negative reviews can teach the developer that it's the quality of the user experience that will make them money, not releasing half of a half-decent game to sell us rest at $5-10 piecemeal.

Pay attention, marketing people. THIS is how you do a movie tie-in. The Team America attitude and "ludicrous gibs" 8-bit gore of Broforce are a perfect match for The Expendables 3, and Lion's Gate funding a free demo of Free Lives' hit early access game on Steam is great for both studios.
I remain skeptical of Early Access for digital distribution because you basically give money up front to be a beta tester with a ticket for a final product that may or may not materialize. (Looking at you, DayZ.) This is the opposite, a callback to the old shareware days where you could get an entire self-contained episode of a game as a proof of concept, not a fifteen-minute demo that ends right before the first boss fight.
-Refined AI? Nope. You'll miss the slight difference between a kamikaze and standard soldier unit at least once, and it'll be hilarious.
-Story? Well, kind of. It's more like someone drank an entire quart of Red Bull and translated something from English to Japanese and back.
-Ten levels? Well, it *is* a demo. Don't get greedy.
+Crack team of Stallone, Statham, Snipes, Crews, Lundgren, Couture, and Schwarzenegger, each with their own weapons and special attacks, trying to kill Mel Gibson? Yup.
+Breaking out of ropes and chains by mashing Fire to flex? Uh-huh.
+Hypermasculine announcer, explosions, bald eagle screeches, and electric guitar meedlies as you exit each level on a rope ladder hanging from a helicopter? All of the above.
Just... go. It's free until the end of the month and it supports four-player couch-op. Get your friends together so you can punch them in the arm when they accidentally the whole level and send you plummeting to your doom.
