I really do like this game.  It does have a very pen and paper d&d feel to it.  The graphics are clear and defined, and the camera angles work well most of the time.  The turn-based element is fun, though it does limit which characters you have access to at certain times.  There have been many circumstances where I wish I could choose another character to act rather than being forced to choose the next one in the turn order.
There is a lot of randomness to the game.  Yes, you can upgrade your characters in a limited way to alleviate this, but there isn't much you can do planning wise when you uncover a tile and three baddies are revealed.  The way it works is that no matter what, the monsters get to act first.  There appears to be no initiative rolls in the game, so you have to hope that the lightly armored characters can survive long enough to move up the more armored ones.  There are also random events that occur every turn, and while they can be interruped with skills or "adrenaline", sometimes you just have to take it, which can mean a character takes damage or a status effect and there is nothing you can do.  I have survived to near the end of a mission to find I have to restart because of a random rock-fall or poison effect that there was no way to predict or get out of the way.  The missions aren't very long but it still feels like the tactical element of the game is superceded by the rng.
If you like d&d and turn-based games, and don't mind having luck play a significant role in your strategy games then this game is worth a look.  I just imagine I'm playing against a somewhat sadistic DM and roll with the punches.

I had a lot of money on me, right? I was like "Imma pick two visual novels". I'm glad Oblivious Garden was one of them.
I'll make this a short review by saying JUST GET IT.
It was worth my time. The 4 routes are all unique and have different and fun experiences in each one, and the overall design and style just felt right. Also, the narration and dialogue? On point. But, as you know me well, I must do a thorough and lengthy review so... Read if you want ^^
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
For a visual novel, story is everything. It has to be immersive and get you to draw opinions about the characters. This VN does just that: it made me feel emotions, as if I was Irell (main protagonist). The story, in short, focuses on Irell, a former-general who killed countless people in a war long ago. Stripped of his status, he is spared life by the Emperor who tells him to go to the Oblivious Garden and train the 7 princesses for the annual Miracle Play. Only 3 princesses have routes, however all 7 are in the game in various ways. Each route explains a different story that all revolves in the same universe, one princess being vastly different than the rest. Since it is a VN, there are also good and bad endings. All the good endings are logical and are not really confusing (minus Dyanna's ending). Overall, it has a simple yet large amount of lore you can derive from it, and I just eat that stuff up! Other than this, the endings all have a trend, usually. It kind of bothers me that it can be done easily, but
Characters... VITAL to a VN. Characters HAVE to be likable and serve a purpose. Oblivious Garden does this well. The only complaint I have is that there are a few characters I would've loved to know more about, but sadly did not get the joy of seeing much. However, the main route characters (Dyanna, Lin, Leira and Finn) are each very unique and have rather long routes, Finn's being the shortest. I really like how the dev team made each character have a unique issue with Irell or themselves, and the unique features/traits that everyone had (I want to explain but it would spoil a lot). But overall, excellent character design and personalities. I loved them!
VNs don't generally have much gameplay, however this is not a kinetic visual novel: there are choices. The choices in this game are generally challenging as well (especially with Leira), so you have to actually pay attention and try to pick the best thing to do. Choices go from 2 to 4 choices, and are not THAT frequent BUT they are at the beginning and middle of the route. Ending choices get very crucial to your ending status.
A unique feature this game has in an in-game mini-game called "Finn's Teatime" where you use your ingredients you have gotten to make new recipes and get the correct amount of everything to make the best tea. It sounds very simple, and it is, but it's also quite fun to get the achievements associated with it. Tea makes a frequent appearance in the routes (as this is a formal atmosphere).
The writing in this game, hands down is GORGEOUS. Storytelling at it's finest, ladies and gents. While there are a few flaws (from translation) overall it is very well-written. I didn't notice any sort of plot holes within the writing, and the dialogue for each character was pretty good. Their inner-thoughts and such fit very well with their personalities. The only awkward thing was when the dialogue box switched over to one of the princesses, and it was difficult to tell who was talking until they said "I, Leira, think...". I knew Irell was not talking, but when multiple princesses were involved, things got a little confusing. But this is no reason to dis the game, and this is only a small flaw that occurs maybe 3 times in the entire game so I would not worry about it.
If I was to score it, solid 8/10. There were not that many flaws, and the ones that were weren't huge and contributed to any gameplay. I cannot wait until the sequel comes out, and I will absolutely purchase it! Thanks for reading, and consider buying this game if you are into VNs!

If I were to ask what PC dungeon crawler First Person RPG you played way back in the mid 2000s you'd probably say to me Morrowind. And with good reason, it's one of the best.
But at the same time, another game came out by Arcane Studios that was shadowed by the success of Morrowind, a cult gem if you will of classic 3D PC gaming now all but virtuall forgotten save for a few souls who sought this title. What is Arx Fatalis? Is it good? Pros and Cons? Here's the run down.
Arx Fatalis is a first person semi-linear dungeon crawler where you play the role of Am Shaegar, a fantasy John Doe who wakes to find himself naked in a goblin prison in a world where the sun has died and the surviving peoples habitate in underground fortress cities and mines. The story follows Am Shaegar as he seeks to reclaim his memory, but along the way gets tossed into a series of events that could mean the end of the peoples of Arx and even the world.
While the story is strong in the beginning, by the middle act the it becomes predictable and there aren't any big plot twists or holy hell I didn't see that coming moments, but many of the characters and races of creatures of encounter and/or fight make that journey from start to finish interesting.
Because this game is well over 10 years old, it hasn't aged well in terms of graphics. Even Morrowind, however, suffers the same issue, so don't take this as a con persay. However, I've found that the Steam version is a tad glitchy with its sounds or even graphics, whether that is an error on my end or not I can't be sure.
Combat in this game is fun but takes a bit of time to get used to since depth in this world is a bit strange feeling when compared to modern first person games. There are dozens of weapons to find, enchant and utilize to bring death to the menagerie of baddies laid before you.
Puzzles in this game are much like classic D&D puzzles or even old PC adventure games, which means they range from no♥♥♥♥♥♥easy to what the ♥♥♥♥ hard on the first playthrough. The magic system is also unique and I wished that Arcane had taken the time to re-explore that in later titles because the concept of drawing magic spells to cast them on the screen is quite fun, though a nightmare in the heat of combat.
Difficulty can be...well, all over the board. Some enemies are unfairly overpowered even when you are higher level and certain spells and items that make fighting them easier aren't made clear in the game itself and are discovered through trial and error or game FAQs.
Pros: There are some horror elements and classic RPG elements that make this game feel like a classic. It's not difficult to pick up and get into, the characters and world is quite interesting, and the sound design is haunting (I seriously made a recording years ago of just background sounds in this game to use for Table Top role playing). The magic system takes getting used to along with combat, but once is mastered can make it hard to go back to other games of that time.
Cons: The game is sadly glitchy, the graphics did not age well and can lead to some headaches and eye strain during the first few minutes of play. Combat ranges from easy to unbeatable, puzzles aren't really spelled out, the map system needs work, and the story gets weak by the middle of the game.
All in all I rank this a 3 out of 5, its a game from my youth that I loved that nostalgia draws me back to for fond memories and aggrivating flashbacks of unkillable bosses. Its well worth the price here on steam and there are patches and mods all over the internet that fix some of these complaints. I'd like to see an HD revamp or even remake of this game, so fingers crossed.
GG

Playing
is a beautiful and romantic experience. Set in a far-off magical land, you step into the shoes of Irell Reis, who has been ordered to help tutor seven princesses. Each story route brings with it new adventures and dangers, this simple garden isn’t all that it seems. Become immersed in the lives of the princesses and the rich history of the Magical Empire of Latoy, learn about gods and war as you romance the lady of your choice.
Each route gives you different parts of the story, but all you know at the start is that you are Irell, a disgraced general defeated in an important battle that cost the lives of thousands of soldiers. The Emperor sees fit to give Irell another chance and he is sent to the Oblivious Garden to be a fencing instructor. The garden is so named as its residents are oblivious to the outside world, and with good reason: The garden is protected by a magical barrier making it more of a prison. On the surface the game might seem like it’s simply about romance but there is a lot of magic in this world and a complicated backstory that is touched on in pieces in each different route. Despite being in the garden with seven princesses you can only romance three of them as well as a maid.

Since this is a visual novel, the interface is exclusively point-and-click. You read through the story and at times make choices to help move the story in a certain direction. The game has the standard features for this genre; an auto text option, a skip previously seen text option and the ability to scroll back and see past text. You can save, load, remove text from the screen to see pictures fully and the game also auto saves. A nice feature I liked was the dictionary, which is available once you finish any route. It contains facts about Latoy and all of the characters. Another neat feature is the tea-making mini game. Since this game is about refined young ladies, tea takes a high priority, especially in Leira’s route. Through the mini game you can brew different types of tea with ingredients you gain through the story and also through raising your tea-brewing level. The only downside is that the game gives you little or no help on how to figure out how to brew good tea, without a guide you’re probably going to be lost.
Artwise there is nothing negative that can be said, the art in this game is beyond gorgeous. Every princess looks beautiful, the backgrounds are lovely and the menus and user interfaces are very elegant. The music is also amazing, every melody is beautifully orchestrated and I highly recommend picking up the soundtrack as well. Where the game falters is the voice acting. The main game has voices for the entire female cast while the DLC also adds male voice acting. I found the acting to be fine but the audio quality was inconsistent. At times some voices were loud, some very muffled and no one was at the same level or quality. What was worse was that at times there was no audio where there should be. Lin was apart of Finn’s story route but had no voice acting through most of it, she also missed lines in her own route. There were also times when what the actress said didn’t match with the text on the screen, though not many that I noticed with my very limited knowledge of Chinese.
Despite some flaws I personally loved playing this game. It was quite lengthy, easily offering 10-20 hours of gameplay to complete everything. There are many Steam achievements to get and also trading cards as well. While at times the story may feel contrived or confusing, I fell in love with the princesses as much as Irell did. My least-favorite princess, Leira, became one of my favorites. The game also has a side story that is free DLC about Leira though her personality is a bit different from the main story and there is added fan service but also more achievements. If you enjoy visual novels then I highly recommend adding
to your library.

Star Wars Empire at War combines a great combination of ground and space combat which not only looks great but also plays well.
The game works around the idea of a galactic map with planets that you control. these create a general map that you have to conquer, each planet can change control to whoever conquers it and has two levels of defence that you can have.
Ground defence allows you to have fight in traditional RTS ways where you have to eliminate the hostile forces to capture the planet  or stop an invasion force.
Space combat allows you to bring large or small ships into combat using RTS gameplay, this creates great combat and gives you the oportunity to play as you want. there can also be a space station and defences that you can build / destroy making space combat vary in each fight.
the game in general is good fun for anyone who likes RTS games with a unique take on the genre. i find that it is enjoyable and the game has its own fan made expansion which completely overhauls the game and changes the empire and rebels to republic and federation. This allows for an entirely new type of gameplay as the new units have far more weapon spots and units which makes your screen light up with turbo lasers.
the expansion however can run a bit slugish if you go insane and spam battledroids as the game tanks and doesnt run too well.
in general i would say if you like RTS conquest games then give this a shot, its pretty cheap now and the free expansion Republic at War allows for a near whole new game.

I was a fan of Tropico 3, and then a fan of Tropico 4. I was wary about Tropico 5, but the allure of some kind of multiplayer roped me in.
Now to preface this, don't get me wrong. This game is fun. But Tropico 4 is better all round.
The multiplayer is a gimmick and near pointless. It's slow, laggy, loves to desync, lacks host controls... It's not even worth talking about, it's utter trash.
The gameplay is, unlike every other Tropico, surprisingly linear. You're basically forced to build in a particular way if you want to stand any chance.
The economy is so turbulent it's insane. One moment you can be sitting on a nice stable income shooting you into the £100,000s, the next you're -£50,000 and unable to get out of the rut. Why?

Overall, not recommended. Go get Tropico 4, which is effectively "Tropico 3 Remastered".

This is definitely a title I'd say is "underrated". It's a relatively obscure RPG title that gives a fairly interesting setting and good mechanics.
The game is good overall, but it's definitely rough around the edges.
PROS:
The game is pretty immersive, with full first person and complete view of limbs and equipment. There are plenty of things to loot, plenty of things to kill. The game is also very atmospheric: lots of dank caves with dark ambience playing. The RPG elements are mostly good, but there's not much character interaction, no real dialogue trees. I have a lot of fun exploring dungeons in the game, they can go pretty deep and pretty wide. There are lots of immersive touches, like having to drag things manually into the inventory, to manually drawing runes to cast spells, to even staking zombies to make sure they stay dead. It helps make the game feel alive.
_____
CONS:
The game barely conveys any information to the player; I've had to rely on walkthroughs extensively. The journal is worthless, it tells nothing about current tasks or reminders of where to go. If important details from dialogue are missed, they can't be found again. Navigation is nightmarish as there are no clear paths to get to locations, everything is located on separate underground levels. The game also is unbalanced in terms of combat and specialization. Playing as a thief or as just a warrior is suicidal, as a certain kind of enemy late-game cannot be easily killed with brute force. I had to restart my game to play as a sort of battlemage build, and now everything is easier.
_____
It's a pretty mixed bag overall. If one likes RPGs with somewhat original settings, compelling mechanics, plenty of immersion, and plenty of loot, then this game is good if one can look past the glaring flaws.

I try to love this game. I really do. But all I get is an abusive relationship. While it looks great and has some great new features - building managers being one of them - it also has a lot of problems that make gameplay frustrating.
The Almanac isn't as informative as in Tropico 4. It's a mess trying to figure out faction relations and leaders. I also miss faction related tasks given by the NPCs. Faction leaders are now random people with a sign above their head (though, the sign is an improvement) and it's pretty random if/when you get a task to address a faction's happiness.
International relations don't list cause and effect. One moment, you have warm relations with the Axis, the next you want to start a trade route and nope, relations not high enough. Again, the game lost a lot charm by removing the leaders of other powers.
The new radio voice, Lulu or what her name is, is infuriating and annoying and makes me genuinely miss Sunny Flowers, of all people. Sunny at least had redeeming qualities and was funny. Lulu is a edgelord (edgelady?)  with no apparent agenda or faction and comes across as a bratty rebellious teenager at best. I turned the radio off when she made electric saw sounds.
I also miss giving election speeches. Elections just happen, and you can drop 20 % in approval by just having another wave of unstoppable immigrants who arrive poor and homeless. Even with your constitution set to "wealthy citizens vote". My borders are a figment of my imagination. No matter what option I take, I get waves and waves of uneducated schmucks. At least it doesn't seem to bother the nationalists, if they exist. I have not seen any tasks relating to their happiness and I finished the campaign and played a bunch of sandbox games.
Foreign powers constantly ask for stupid things, be it researching techs years away from what I can reasonably research or wanting me to export things I don't have, i.e. 10.000 milk when my entire island is at best 'yellow' efficiency for ranches.
The trade routes aren't the worst thing ever, but they are often not as flexible as they need to be. If I start importing the milk an ignorant foreign power demanded, I may sometimes only have an import offer lasting 15 years. So I either take it and block my ship for 15 years, or I assign it to a new route halfway through and get spammed with reminders that a trade route has no active ships.
The military, while having a good variety of new buildings, is uncontrollable. All I can do is litter my island with military buildings and hope the idiots dance in the right direction if I'm being attacked. The only unit I can tell where to go are scouting troops. Out of combat. It is a real improvement to have the Conscription option that allows uneducated people to become soldiers, which can help greatly in later eras. Most jobs will be High School and the neverending floods of immigrants are at least useful for a mass over class strategy of defense.
The most infuriating thing is wealth levels. Citizens will be broke, poor, well-off, rich or filthy rich. And anything below their level - which is entirely tied to their job - will be 'beneath' them. If you lower rent on a 'rich' category mansion to make it affordable for 'well-off' citizens, the rich will rather sit in a shack next to it than move into an unoccupied spot. If you 'upgrade' (downgrade) your Opera House to allow non-wealthy citizens in, the wealthy will shun it and whine about lacking entertainment.
Especially in the early eras, the options for entertainment are limited to three buildings only. And speaking of limited options, the entertainment category isn't the only one suffering from it. There are new Raw Materials (i.e. ranches have cattle, llamas, pigs and goats), as mentioned above new military buildings and a variety of new tourism buildings (mainly hotel types). Residental, on the other hand, all looks the same. Building the same tenements and apartments over and over again makes for pretty boring islands.
Mechanically, it is certainly interesting to have a Constitution (if the options worked as described) and to continue on the same island through all game eras (or better, 2 islands, as you switch between them in the campaign). As interesting as the idea is, as poor is the execution. If you made a mistake in the previous mission, there is no way to fix it. Events like disasters are apparently scripted and you can find yourself in no way out scenarios. There is no ability to 'restart', unless you make a new save file at the start of every mission. Even then, you're stuck with the old progress and the current status might be beyond repair.
I haven't tried multiplayer, but after reading it puts both players on the same island, I have no desire to try it either. What is the point of building on the same island, with the same resources? I was hoping for the option to have another player take a second island, to trade resources, maybe ship citizens or troops over in times of need, navigating diplomacy when each allied with a different superpower, competing for tourists, something like that. But nope, just trying to fit 2 cities on the same island for no reason.
It pains me to not recommend, but just looking prettier and having a few useful new features doesn't change the fact that Tropico 4 is the better game. Tropico 5 can feel like a chore rather than a challenge at times; a feeling I never had when playing Tropico 4.

There's a difference between a game being good, and a game being broadly-appealing. Cuphead is, unfortunately, only the former. It's got fantastic art style and sound. It's the kind of game I really really really want to like, but it's brutally difficult. Maybe with enough practice it's something I could conquer. Heck, it probably is. I spent about an hour with it, and what turned me off was two things: the controls being somewhat unpredictable, especially with a co-op partner in the mix, and the vertical difficulty curve straight off the bat. This is the type of game that "doesn't hold your hand," by which I mean it introduces you to the barest possible game mechanics and then immediately throws you headlong into the deep end. I prefer to get a chance to practice and build each mechanic on the one before it as the game ramps up in complexity and difficulty. This is not that type of game. Unfortunately I can't elaborate much beyond this, because in my hour of playing I didn't even clear the first level. I think having a co-op partner exacerbated the early difficulty because it messes with the camera progresses. If you're at all hesitant about it, just don't. Only buy this if you are prepared for an extreme challenge.
TL;DR Controls and co-op are funky, vertical difficulty curve, only pick it up if you're fully prepared for a challenge.

This game is a throwback to all the R-Type wannabe games from the 80's and 90's.  The music had that perfect "Amiga 500" feel to it, and the game's style in general made me think of some of the old shooters from that era as well.
You get 4 different types of ships to choose from with different movement, fire, armor, and special weapon capabilities.  Each one gives the levels its own particular flavor of challenge to it.  Instead of being a straight up "Fly to the right infinitely while destroying bad guys who attack in predictable patterns" style of shooter, they offer you the chance to flip between left and right so you can turn around and shoot those♥♥♥♥♥holes that come at you from behind.
Much like R-Type there's a multitude of in-game powerups you can pick up which you find after destroying enemies or waves of enemies, and there's also a plain looking white box style powerup that apparently adds to your special weapon charge. (though I'm not sure how that works exactly because it seemed like I was able to fire my special pretty often).
Also if that's not enough nostalgia for you, there's a variety of in-game graphic filters so you can pretend you're playing it on a 4 bit greyscale screen, 8 bit greyscale, Vic-20, C-64, ZX Spectrum, Amiga HAM (Hold And Modify mode), EGA, CGA, and modern graphics (I may have left something out though).
It's challenging without being too frustrating, it's got just enough bullet hell without forcing you to become the zen master at dodging everything, and the graphics and music complete the experience.

I wanted to like this game. The concept of former stuntmen making their own TV studio that you control mixed in with strategy RPG combat was a fresh idea in a landscape full of zombie survival games and minecraft clones. But having just finished the game, it failed to deliver on so many levels.
PROS:
- Great overall concept.  Run a TV studio while having your stuntment meet certain criteria in strategy RPG battles.
- The art style is interesting and has character.  The costumes pay homage to the various costumes seen in shows like Power Rangers.
- The music works well enough for what it is.
CONS:
- The studio management aspect of the game is very under developed.  Most of the choices, from the type of camera you use to the marketing agency that you hire, are shallow and don't offer more than slight bonuses here and there.  For example, you can have your marketing agency put up your actors for an award, but all that will do is increase your fan power, which is used to activate marketing agency policies.
- Objectives in battle could have been more varied.  As it is, there are 3 primary objectives that you'll see:  1. Kill X amount of enemies, maybe with Y time; 2. Kill the boss with a team member/team attack/finishing move; 3.  Keep everyone alive/above 50% health.   This is disappointing because, being a TV show that you make, you could have gone with more interesting objectives, especially if you the player could set them.
- The writing is not very good.  The story seems to be unsure on whether it wants to play a particular scene straight or comically, and so flip flops between the two extremes awkwardly.  In addition, the story progression is very clunky and poorly executed.
- The game is unfunny.  Most of the "humor" comes from blatant references to pop culture outside of the genre (such as a Robocop/Tiger hybrid.  That's it, that's the joke), with a smattering of poorly constructed puns to tie it all together.
- The localization is not very good.  The game was clearly translated by somebody that does not have very good command of the English language, as much of the text and dialogue just reads wrong to a native English speaker.  Getting a decent writer would fix this and some of the previous issue.

Graphic and effects look great and better than in most indie games, also backrounds of various planets and vast spaces are gorgeous, I even made a few desktop wallpapers. Sound is generally good and won`t dissapoint. Controls work great and responsive with gamepad.

+Cool Design

+Unique Jump momentum & Gameplay mechanics

If there was a "I am between yes and no" choice for the thumbs voting system that would be it. This game as a LOT of pentential. It could be one of my favorite games...
But sadly, the level design is way to hard. I played Mirror's edge to death getting every achievement for it (on Xbox), I SpeedRun DeadCore all the time, I even got in the top 10 fastest runs on the game, but this game...
When you try to do a level fast, there's only one path you can take and there's only one way to take it. Everything from the speed at wich you get there, the number of milliseconds you pressed spacebar, to the orientation of your cursor has to be perfect to do the jump. The levels aren't open enough and the platforms are way to tiny. I don't mind dying a thousand time over a level, but I want to feel that I genuinly made a mistake and not that the game is punishing me for no reasons.
There's an achievement about beating dev times on the levels... These dev times are not Mario Kart dev times or DeadCore dev times in the style of "Our best time was 12.345 seconds... Let's make a 15 seconds dev time, so that way people have a chance to beat it." Nope! I mean they could put their real time in I wouldn't mind, if the levels were open ended. Exemple: if a dev made the best run possible on road A and uploaded his time, that's good and pretty much unbeatable, but if you jump between road A, B and C to create road D, you can do it in 9.843 seconds! That's good design.
My point is: So far, the game has an incredible core, but lacks polish. Keep the mechanics the same, but build better levels. Keep the insanity levels you have there, but build some more accecible levels too. That way, people won't finish tutorial saying: The control scheme looks kinda hard to get, but with the first level the game should let me experim- oh my god what the hell is this.
Maybe after a couple of updates this review will change for a thumbs up. I can only hope for the best.

Absolutely loving this game and even have it running as I type out this review.
If any of you reading this have a love for Quake jumping or surfing/bhopping in CS then you will feel right at home with this game, and I would consider this to be the main demographic of the buyers, but would also serve as a great introduction to this sub-genre for first-timers.
The soundtrack for this game is absolutely fantastic. It soothes your soul as you approach the 200 deaths mark and allows you to keep on going trying to beat that time!
Another great thing about this game is that you can see the dev's time for each of the levels, which shows you that the dev cares about this game and is pretty damn good at their own game! I can assure you as a new player it will be taking you quite a while before you can beat the dev's time let alone the #1 spot time!
A couple of suggestions I would like to address to the dev:
The game likes to switch from fullscreen back to windowed (an easy way to replicate this is to have it and then press "Escape" to bring up the options menu which will put it into a windowed state).
Some keybinding options are not possible for instance binding "Jump" to "Mouse 2". I would love this due to all of the time I've put into KZ in CS where I either long jump with right click or regular jump with scroll down (I appreciate that jump cannot really be bound to scroll down as jumping in this game has a "height on hold" mechanic - although it would be an interesting addition if you did allow jump to be bound to Space/Mouse 2 and also have the possibility for scroll up/down to also be bound for minimum height jumps! Just an idea!)
I've noticed that "crosshair" is a toggleable option in this game. I think it would be fantastic if it is possible to customise this crosshair. Resize/re-shape etc similar to the sort of crosshair customisation you can find in CS:GO.
Another thing I would like to see added is the option for jumping sounds (probably footstep/landing sounds also) and I'm sure any Quake or CS player would also love this to be added. I understand if you wouldn't want to add this to the minimalistic theme of the game, however jumping sounds is just so iconic to these games it would be difficult to not suggest.
Now for something you absolutely should NOT add - a replay/ghost replay mechanic of the top times on the leaderboard. It would absolutely destroy the magic of this game, figuring out for yourself the most efficient way to set the fastest times with what you have at your disposal.
I would also like to thank Princesseuh for making a serious product and not making this one of those cheap "rage games" that you find a lot of famous YouTubers playing just to overreact and scream at in order to attract views. Thanks for keeping this classy.
Now with all that said and done it's time to try and beat my 13.214 record on Wandered Hideout (watchout Princesseuh I'm coming for you!)
Update: 12.201 record now :) Princesseuh you got some catching up to do :)
P.S. I've already recommended this game to one of my friends :)

I want to like this game, has a great deal of fun in the Beta/Alpha and love teh story and art direction of the game. The world is interesting with a good amount of lore displayed to the players through character dialogue as well as interesting looking characters themselves. However, the Elephant in the Room matter with this game is clearly the questionable DLC practices that Turtle Rock Studios have used in the production of this game. There is currently over £60 worth of DLC not covered by the Season Pass of the game. The game has only been out for a few short days and this is ridiculous. One may argue that they are simply reskins and offer no affect on gameplay whatsoever, and while this is true, it represents the sad state that the gaming industry is in today. AAA games are practicing this as if it were the norm, when only a few years ago the term "DLC" would often refer to a £15 expansion pack offering hours upon hours of new and unique content unto a game, not a simple reskin of a character or weapon model. As I previously said, this game is fun. However, out of principle, it should be made clear that the general public should NOT accept these questionable practices which most big name gaming companies seem to be so fond of today. If you truly want to stand against this, don't buy this game. At least, not for the full £40/$60 asking entry price.

Arx Fatalis is an amazing role playing game from the former half of the last decade. It features a very original world premise, it eternally snows so everyone lives underground in massive tunnel systems. it has a traditional rpg plot, but it feels immersive. Characters are seen as listless and antisocial, dreading their exile from the snowy abyss above.
The game has a very intriguing magic system that allows you to draw glyphs to cast spells. It feels very intuiative and as such if you play a mage character you get used to certain glyph formations.
Very recently Arkane released the source code for Arx and a source port named "Arx Libertatis" has been created, which finally allows players to play the game at a consistant framerate the way it was meant to be played when it first released.

Star Wars: Empire at War is a real-time strategy game from Petroglyph and published by LucasArts, the best strategy game in Star Wars franchise. Gold Pack also include the expansion pack Star Wars: Empire at War - Forces of Corruption in one package.
Star Wars: Empire at War takes place before and to the event of Episode IV, to the Battle of Yavin, while the expansion pack, Star Wars: Empire at War - Forces of Corruption follows the underworld faction Tyber Zann with the Zann Consortium.
Star Wars: Empire at War gameplay is more like map conquest called galaxy conquest since this is the Star Wars galaxy, you start on a galactic map, establishes bases on planets like Coruscant, Tatooine or Naboo, build up armies and galactic fleet, then engage in space or ground battles on map in real epic battles. You get to command the Star Destroyer fleet with the Galactic Empire or squadrons of X-wing with the Rebel Alliance. This game can entertain you for many hours.
While Star Wars: Empire at War has great gameplay, the graphics are somewhat, inadequate for me. Kind of like, ugly, but at least has some detail. The effect are not that great too, except for the Death Star. The performance are great nevertheless.
The one of many greatest thing about this game is that there are many mods out there making this game even more interesting and fun, like Republic at War or Thrawn Revenge, try them.
The downside of this game is with the expansion pack, Star Wars: Empire at War - Forces of Corruption, it still have many minor bugs that left unfixed. Although the bugs won't hinder your gameplay at all, but it is somewhat annoying.
Very addicting game Star Wars: Empire at War is for strategy fans, you get to fight twice to capture a planet, a space battle and planetary battle. I recommend this.

What a gem i discovered. Really loved this game, great indie FPS game. This game relies solely on gameplay and doesn't have realistic high tech visuals, nor any particular interesting storyline. It's just you in different white environments with red dudes as villain. Weapons are shotgun, pistol, rifle, katana, bat.
Time moves only when you moves. You can jump, stun enemies by throwing weapons or objects against them.
The story mode is short, like 2 hours or so and if it was only that it would certainly be overpriced. Endless mode is a bit grindy and the goal is to get a certain kills on a map before you unlock the next map. Fun is trying to get as many kills as possible before getting overwhelmed and killed.
Now the best stuff are the challenges, which make you complete all levels on certain criteria, like with katana or throwables only, time based, or completing all levels in one go without dying. Had real fun going for those. There's one specific level that is hard, called Elevator and that one really gave me some irritation when going for the norestart challenge. Just buy it on a sale, the game is a lot of fun and a bit like a shooter puzzle. Recommended.

Just you, your backpack, and an icy wasteland, where weather, wolves, and your own skills are what can continue your existence, or end it.
It's really enjoyable, exploring the rather large maps, that are all interconnected. After trudging through the bitter cold snow, you can cosy up next to a stove and cook some delicious rabbit stew, which is very satisfying to do.
I can't wait for the game to be updated with seasons that change, getting to explore the regions in their spring or summer forms after surviving the bitter icy winter would be very nice~
If you like survival games that are massively atmospheric and cosy, but at the same time bitter and hopeless, you'll love this game.

Are you familiar with Ultima Underworld? Because this is the closest we're ever going to get to an Ultima Underworld 3. It was originally designed to be a sequel, but the dev's couldn't get hold of the official license from EA, so they just filed off all the serial numbers and called it Arx Fatalis. Make no mistake, though - this is Ultima Underworld in all but name.
The story of Arx Fatalis sets you in a dungeon world where no one lives on the surface since the Sun was snuffed out some years ago. From there you begin as the classic prisoner arc type with no memory, set to escape from your goblin captors, for game-play It has physics similar to Morrowind but superior combat and graphics and an interesting spellcasting system.
Overall, this game is worth buying if you like games like Morrowind and Gothic. However. If you played Morrowind and want more of that, play Arx Fatalis. After that, you may want to look at Deus Ex.
IMO Arx Fatalis is up there with Deus Ex and System Shock 2 as one of the best FPS-RPG hybrids ever made.
Its a good game, mods make it infinite, I highly recommend this game, not just for Star Wars Fans, for everyone that likes strategy games like X-Com.

The Stanley Parable was a game where the player character expresses control over the game at the expense of the narrator, and subverts the idea of the narrator.  In other games, the narrator is an omnipotent demigod who directs the story; in The Stanley Parable, the player directs the story and the narrator struggles to keep up.
This isn't that game.
The Beginner's Guide is - 'game' is perhaps the wrong word - a piece of interactive art where the player character and the narrator are two facets of the same being - the player is the 'eyes' and 'hands', while the narrator is the 'mind' that interprets what you are seeing and doing.  Even though the narrator is by necessity scripted, and the piece allows for very little in the terms of player agency, both determine the pace at which the story proceeds.  The player and the narrator both take on different aspects of the narrator's role, and the 'game' itself is the player.  The narrator explains what is going on, the player executes it, and the 'game' attempts to use those limits to convey ideas, to explore the nature of games and 'games', and the odd sort of disconnection one suffers in an increasingly connected world.
It's a game about relating to people, and how so many of the ways we relate to people are really just attempts to fold their identities, expressions, and achievements into our own.  It holds a light up to the shallow connections we form, and how that makes us ever thirstier for meaningful connection.
I'm going to go hug my wife now.

Awesome little RPG. Feels a lot like a smaller-scale TES:Morrowind. There are only a few problems with it, one being the fact that overall, the game is pretty small (at least as far as I can tell, having not yet beat it; they elude to the possibility that there are more large areas you can go to, but I don't yet know if you can or not), and another being that the game feels somewhat linear, though you're free to go wherever you want, so long as you've come far enough along in the main quest. It has some cool features with it, most notably that you cast spells by writing the gestures onto the screen with the mouse. It's pretty nifty, I really like it. The setting is also pretty unique. Basically, you've got a standard fantasy world. However, the sun dies and the surface is plunged into eternal winter. The sentient races unite and spend the five years leading up to the loss of the sun moving their civilizations underground. It turns the whole thing into a subterranean dungeon crawl RPG, which I really respect in a game. I'd recommend anyone play it who like first person RPGs. However, do note that some newer systems will have problems playing it. I personally have found the game playable only through the Arx Libertatis fan mod. If it doesn't work for you or there are general issues with it, try the aforementioned mod, it might get the game working for you.

I don’t like walking simulators.  They’re boring, they have nothing for you to do, no puzzles, no fights, and for the most part, nothing to find.  You just walk.  If I wanted to do that, I’ll go for a real walk.
Before I purchased The Park, I had three other walking simulators… didn’t like any of them.  “So buy another one?”, you may ask.  Simple, I screwed up.  I thought there were some puzzles to solve.  “Why did you think that?” is the obvious follow up question.  Steam had their winter sale and I purchased several games and The Park was accidentally thrown into the mix, my own fault.  I had been reading several game summaries, (almost a dozen in all) and confused it with a different game which actually was a puzzle game.
When I started The Park, I noticed that one of the tags was “walking simulator”.  CRAP.  I wanted to request a refund but something in the back of my mind said, “Just give it a chance.”  So I did… and I was pleasantly surprised.
Pros:
-Descent graphics.
-A mystery unfolds as you play the game.
-Creepy as hell.
-All of the achievements are very easy to obtain.
-When you enter the park, you can only go one way.  Eventually, you’ll come full circle and find that you’re at the entrance again.  If you look closely as you go down the path again, a couple of things are changed, adding to the creepiness.
Cons:
-Much to short.
-A bit over priced because of how short the game is.
The first walking simulator that I really enjoyed and it was over in 2 hours, and that’s me trying to explore every nook and cranny.
All in all, I like this game.  I only wish it was longer.

is a first-person game of exploration and discovery... one which starts off as a walking sim, and which turns into a true psychological horror.
Initially the game consists walking around (you CAN run), getting on the rides, and discovering the story via paper clippings that you'll find as you explore.  Some of these are really hard to read (print too small!), whilst others I had no problem with.  You'll have one item added to your inventory, which will be used automatically when the time comes.
I was disappointed during these early parts of the game.  It was mildly interesting, and getting on the rides was different and enjoyable, but I did consider quitting.  I'm glad that I decided to finish it, as things really picked up later.
The second half of the game is where you turn the corner to something much more interesting.  Dark and disturbing and full of discoveries.  I can't say much without giving spoilers, but I will say that you need to examine items carefully, and sometimes more than once.
There are a couple of jump-scares in there, but the horror element relies heavily on the psychological side of the scale.   There are a few F-bombs in there, so be aware of that.
Items for you to interact with are sometimes fiddly, though that may be because I was using a controller.
14 achievements (I missed three, so they're not just "play the game normally to get all of the achievements")
Recommended for those whom are interested by what I've described above, though I would wait for a sale... $12+ is a bit steep for 2.5 hours of play.  Absolutely NOT for children!

It's made even better by the fact that because it's still in Alpha, there are few websites with detailed walk-throughs or player guides, so you really are left to find out most things in game by simply playing.

I'm in the minority with my views of this game but quite frankly, this game wasn't very much fun. Often billed as a horror game, the narrative kinda blows it's load early. After a scant few jump scares, you pretty much see everything coming. Either that or you hear it coming. Every enemy in this game constantly makes sounds so I can hear the people talking from down the hallway and around the corner. I know well ahead of time whether or not I'm going to encounter more splicers or a big daddy. That kinda takes away the fear and anticipation. Add that to the issue that dying has functionally no consequences and the whole game felt like a boring slog as opposed to a compelling adventure.
My second issue with it is the atrocious character development. Characters appear and disappear with little more than a, "Hi my name is..." This is a pretty big issue when major plot twists ask you to give a fluff about the secret identities of these bland, boring facades. In fact, *SPOILER* one major plot point involves a character telling you, the nameless, faceless protagonist that no one cares about, are in fact a nameless, faceless protagonist that no one cares about. Shocker.
Thirdly, we have the gameplay. It's so generic. There's a hefty armory of fairly uninspired guns plus the less than thrilling plasmids, few of which are interesting or useful. Towards the end of the game, after having come to terms with the meaninglessness of death in this game, I abandoned all pretext of strategy and just ran around in circles with a wrench. It was faster.
The game isn't all bad. It certainly looks really nice and probably was even better when it came out (by comparison). But over all, it was just uninteresting and unfun.

My 27.3 hours on record doesn't actually represent my playing time, since I've had this on Desura way, way before it ever reached Steam.
It's actually quite difficult to recommend Zomboid. I've got friends who own this and don't play it simply because the game is just not 'ready' yet. And that is true.
The game has been receiving overwhelming positivity from the community, and there is a LOT of new players, with a different perspective to myself. Since I've played this game way before the new graphics came into it, way before the new map, and all that jazz, I have a good idea on the development pace of this game and how it has progressed from then to now.
Project Zomboid development has crawled along at a slow steady pace, that has gradually picked up, but is still crawling along. The builds that are released, are on average, every 2 months, alhtough now and again there has been a build that was released the month after. You just need to look at all the past changelogs to see that it is mostly every 2 months or so, which isn't great but it's not bad either. Most of the changes are numerous. Majority of them are balances, small fixes and optimisation, with some features like farming and erosion thrown in.
However from my own perspective, not as a new player but an old player, I grew fatigued with Zomboid. Despite the changes brought in and despite the new features, Zomboid felt lifeless. There was nothing truly new that could add to the experience. That hardcore experience that I crave. Zomboid's tension was long gone for me. It felt more like a take on I Am Legend than anything else.
I came to the conclusion that this Zomboid fatigue that I was feeling towards one of my favorite zombie survival games was due to the lack of NPCs. My very first experience in playing Zomboid was playing with NPCs and even then, in their most basic form of rudimentary AI, they added so much to the game, that when they disappeared from the game for good, it felt like someone had ripped out Zomboid's heart.
With the continued promises of introducing the long-awaited well overdue NPCs from the rather emotinally sensitive politically correct developer, Lemmy, (who doesn't like constructive criticism, as is apparent to his twitter history and forum history - Sorry, developers who censor consumers is a pet hate of mine, had to get that slight in) one has to wonder if it will ever arrive, and when it does, if the very hyped up blog posts of old concerning NPC behavior will live up to their bold claims, or if those blog posts that promised so much, will somehow become 'deleted'...
The lack of NPCs is also the main reason why this game went multiplayer - People craved for tension, drama, anything to add to the game. Multiplayer does that in a way, but doesn't quite get it right. It's odd - DayZ is the sort of game that I will just not play on my own. I need to hop into a packed server just to get that tension from playing. With Zomboid, I will stay absoloutely away from strangers. I find myself enjoyign Zomboid multiplayer more from a co-op perspective, and I crave for the NPCs to add to the tension of that, rather than other players.
But most of all I just crave for the lost glory of what Zomboid used to be - A game about building tension, a game about your last days and a game about surviving. Now, now it feels empty. Whether or not Zomboid will live to its full potential has yet to be seen, but as of now I can recommend Zomboid, but I would suggest waiting for the full experience, less you become fatigued and tired from it like myself, waiting for something 'new' to inject itself into the game.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Tales from Candlekeep: Tomb of Annihilation (Candlekeep, for short) is the second Steam game from indie developers, BKOM Studios.
The game is a licensed Dungeons & Dragons title, set in the familiar Forgotten Realms game world. It is based on the D&D board game, Tomb of Annihilation, but I'm not familiar enough with that game to say whether Candlekeep is a straightforward PC implementation of it. Given some of the odd game mechanics, I'm going to guess that it is.
Candlekeep puts you in charge of four predefined heroes: Dragonbait, Asharra, Birdsong, and Artus. It's been a few years since I've immersed myself in Forgotten Realms lore, but I do remember Dragonbait at least. Unfortunately the characters don't speak, even in text boxes, and portray very little personality, so you may as well just be controlling unknowns.
Your mission is fairly typical D&D fare: something is causing magic in the area to become less powerful, or even reverse its normal effects, and you're contracted to find out who or what is doing it.
Graphics - First impressions are good, with the title screen showing an animated 3D lamia. The interface is good at first, too, but you'll quickly find the lack of tooltips on many elements to be frustrating. The mission map and character screens are pretty and functional, though the simplified RPG elements do leave it feeling a bit empty.
Mission graphics are bright and shiny full 3D, viewed from a 3/4 isometric-style view. There's a good zoom range and you can freely pan the game camera, but rotation is fixed at 90-degree camera increments. Levels mostly look the same as each other, following the tile-based appearance of the source game. There are nice lighting and spell effects.
Characters and enemies look good when stationary, but animations don't seem to be well blended and look a little out of place. Character close ups look pretty nice, too, though with the resource grinding required, the lack of character appearance changes is pretty disappointing.
There are some issues, such as crafting requirements not displaying the resources and unaligned status box text, but nothing major. A single graphical detail slider and resolution and full screen / windowed settings comprise the entirety of the graphics options.
Sound - Again, first impressions are good, with a gentle, haunting melody playing in the background of the title screen. This theme continues throughout, with similar sounding tracks on missions and when on the character management or map screens. It's a minimalist sort of sound, but well produced and really rather pleasant.
Sound effects are good, but nothing stands out as being particularly amazing. There are the usual fantasy game combat sounds, with weapon swings and clangs and whooshes: everything you'd expect. The characters and enemies are mostly silent when they fight, which is a bit disappointing; it's almost as though your characters are gagged until they die and manage to let out a final gasp or scream. There are no other voices; mission text is provided through text boxes and a portrait of the NPC who is speaking.
There are separately adjustable volume sliders for sound effects, music, and 'ambient', but I found the defaults worked well.
Gameplay - Candlekeep's gameplay is presumably very similar to the board game upon which it's based. The game is divided into missions that are selectable from the main map screen, each of which can be attempted as many times as you like at three different difficulty levels. When you start out you're only able to take one character on a mission, but very quickly you level up, and soon you can take the full party of four everywhere you go.
The missions themselves are turn based, with each turn divided into phases: hero, exploration, and villain, if I remember correctly. The hero phase is where you move and use your attacks and abilities. The mission area is divided into tiles, which are presumably physical pieces in the board game; if you finish next to an edge of one of these tiles, then in the exploration phase another random tile is placed next to it, otherwise you get a 'no exploration' event, which is usually bad. Finally in the villain phase, all of the bad guys have their turn.
Characters have a number of abilities assigned to different slots: at-will, utility, and daily. These determine how often you can use them, ranging from basic attacks to standard D&D spells (sleep!), to some cool, but usually fairly limited, in-game effects.
There's an optional tutorial that explains some of this as well as basic game terms, but it's pretty minimal; don't expect too much. The first few missions are frustrating as one learns the intricacies of the system through trial and error, but the game is very generous with failed missions -- you keep your inventory and you don't seem to suffer any ill effects.
Missions are divided into story and side quests, but there's not really any difference between them. Each can have different mission goals and rewards you with chests, gold, and experience points (XP). Chests give you weird resources for crafting equipment improvements for any of the PCs; gold is also required. XP is used to increase party level, unlocking extra character slots up to four and then providing more chests. Improvement is very shallow, like a 'RPG lite', but I assume it is taken straight from the source. Each character has four types of equipment with five levels providing boring bonuses. There are Steam Achievements for crafting the highest level item for each character, but be warned: there is a lot of grinding involved!
The game has very good writing with excellent grammar, but there are some issues that I found a frustrating. Character pathing is hidden, so characters can run through traps unintentionally; this is made worse with no undo feature and no split movement. The game also has only 13 story missions, but you'll actually find yourself having to grind a lot to become powerful enough to succeed at the story without good luck. There are also a few bugs that you'll have to overcome, like casting haste twice on the same character not working properly. But overall the game is stable with high production values.
Pros:
+ Nice graphics and sound
+ Satisfying once you get the hang of it
+ Steam Achievements and Trading Cards
Cons:
- Pay-to-Win DLC and lots of grinding
- Lack of interesting character progression or choice
Tales from Candlekeep: Tomb of Annihilation is a good game. It can get pretty repetitive and there's a general lack of progression and choice in your characters, but I think that's due to the source material. If you haven't played the board game then you'll probably find the game mechanics rather odd, but once you get the hang of it it can be quite satisfying.

Well, guess it's my time to put my thoughts into the fray.
The game itself is wonderful.  Gameplay is AMAZING, be it as either the hunter or the monster.  As the hunter, there is satisfaction in having achieved victory through teamwork and whatnot.  As the monster, the thrill is found as you flee in the hopes to find enough food to evolve, as well as when you get powerful enough to turn the tables.
Of course, the real issue (and the issue that has given this game a mixed rating) is the DLC.  While I'd normally say that having day one DLC is a bad practice, all the day one DLC is merely cosmetic in nature.  None of it will effect gameplay at all.  If you see one or a few sets that you do like, great!  You can buy the one DLC, not all of it at once.
"But if you want to play the upcoming monsters or hunters, you have to pay for them!"
While that is true, you're also getting new maps and possilbly game modes (don't know if they are going to release more) for free.  Plus, while other game prohibit you and your party from playing the new maps if you lack the pack, you can play with those who have acquired the new characters without prohibiting them from using them, even if you lack the DLC.
Ultimately, I'd recommend getting the game, especially if you're interested in co-op or finding a unique experience.  If you see DLC you like, be it a new character or cosmetics, get it.  Otherwise, remember that you won't be missing out if you don't want to get anything else aside from the game, and have fun!

Adapting a board game to a video game is not as simple as you might think. Systems designed to foster competition between players or add elements of randomness or risk often translate poorly into a different interactive medium. I can’t speak too much to Tales from Candlekeep’s authenticity to its source, but I can certainly criticize the result. As a game you’ll find this one far more punishing, repetitive, and imbalanced than whatever you might be expecting. I doubt it needed to be this way, but the design missteps are clear the whole way through.
The peninsula of Chult is suffering under a grim curse, which is basically catnip for Dungeons & Dragons heroes. Four adventurers have assembled to follow the trail of death deep into the steaming jungles, and eventually arrive at the Tomb of Annihilation. The path is not a clear one, though, so there will be more than a few favors to locals in exchange for information, the usual gathering mushrooms and destroying zombies and whatnot. While the main quest numbers a dozen quests or so, there’s a slew of smaller side tasks to take on for coin and treasure.
It’s a straight-forward pitch for an RPG, but don’t forget this is a board game. No matter what your quest is, the game plops you onto a field of tiles. Each tile is a 4×4 grid that you can move your heroes around on during their turn, but ending the turn on the edge of a tile adds a new one to the map. Starting from your two original tiles, you can expand the map in any direction by exploring the edges. New tiles can contain traps, treasures, monsters, or bosses, depending on the goal of your quest. This means you cannot progress directly towards whatever it is you need, but eventually the game will give you the necessary tiles to collect your mushrooms or battle your undead ape king.
The turn system is pretty obviously derived from the board game by its regimented phases. Every time one of your heroes gets to go, there are four phases starting with them moving and taking an action. If you end the turn on the edge of a tile, then during the exploration phase a new tiles is added. However, if you didn’t reveal a new tile (or the tile you revealed was unlucky), then during the challenge phase you face some dire event. These aren’t minor inconveniences either, these are your party getting attacked by man-eating insects or hit with meteors or ambushed by squads of skeletons. And immediately following that horror, the enemies that were activated by that hero get to take their turns.
In practice, this means that on a typical turn you can discover a new tile containing three enemies, all of whom get to immediately swarm your party with no recourse. Or you might be busy battling an enemy and not uncover a new tile, and instead your hero gets stunned and damaged by a challenge. Challenges can be dispelled by using adrenaline, a resource that builds slowly from combat and is used to provide important buffs, but you will never have enough to dodge every challenge or to use as a bonus. You also have healing surges to keep track of, which are revives if a party member is killed. They’re used automatically when the dead member’s turn comes around again, and if you come up on their turn with no surges left, you lose immediately.
After a few hours of these strictures, I was ready to call it quits. Everything you do in the game is fraught with penalties, too many to navigate without being worn down. If you explore, enemies get free hits. If you don’t challenges wear down your resources. Every quest becomes a rush to complete the objective before the mechanics grind your team to dust, and no amount of strategy or skill is going to make it less of an uphill battle. Parts of the design itself are incongruous, like the treasure tiles full of traps that take multiple turns (and thus challenges) to navigate safely. Some challenges are completely absurd as well, like the one that casts a random spell that instantly killed a full-health hero because it fired off one of the strongest spells, or the one that has a chance to eat one of your valuable healing surges. I also lost one side quest out of the blue because I was supposed to outrun a death curse, but despite exploring every turn and keeping all my healing surges I never found the exit and apparently died to some hidden turn timer.
There are loads of stats and equipment to keep track of on your characters, and plenty of D&D holdovers that make an appearance like rolling initiative, but very little you have control over. You can shuffle around inventory items (mostly consumables) and pick your skills from a small set, but equipment can only be upgraded using the mess of materials and gold you earn as you play. This design in particular is obviously lifted from mobile models, sticking you with multiple resource pools that overlap in painful ways. Here it’s gold, because even when you have the materials to upgrade everyone’s gear you’re only going to have enough gold for one. You can always grind more by replaying quests on higher difficulties, but it’s rather telling that one of the DLCs boosts the gold earnings by 50% throughout the entire game. If a balance element is that noticeably out of sync, it’s pretty unforgivable to put a price on the fix.
If you can somehow look beyond the needlessly punitive game mechanics, there’s just not much here to find. I’ve been playing for over three hours and still every single quest is on the same jungle tileset, with the same enemies and traps. There are no unique map features to look out for, and quests are merely “explore X tiles” or “kill Y enemies”. The text when you select a mission describes witch doctors and traders and secret dealings but you never get to see any of it, it’s all just fluff covering the same gameplay over and over and over again. The only way I can see anyone having the patience for that is if they’re absolutely obsessed with the board game, because for everyone else this is little more than a bland, repetitive, imbalanced mess.

I am most likely going to get downvotes and probably have my review marked as "funny" due to certain members of the community, but I'm here to say what I've been holding off on saying for the past few months.

I bought The Long Dark primarily for the Story Mode; back when it was seemingly right around the corner. On the fence about purchasing, I was persuaded by the 90%(!) approval rating and endless amounts of positive reviews, so I thought I'd buy the game. While waiting for the Story Mode, I thought I might as well give Sandbox a try, so I'll start there.
Sandbox mode started out fair enough - The visuals were amazing, the wolves felt like threats, and I was always on the edge of my seat, planning my next move. The atmosphere was great.
However, after some hours, it became obvious that there was no point to surviving - There is simply nothing much to live for. Even with these new "challenges," the game's sandbox lifetime is disappointingly short. Simply put: It gets rather boring. Surviving for months is a tedious chore, not a fun adventure. There's no reason to live. If the game had been marketed as yet another sandbox survival, I wouldn't have bought it. There's a multitude of those already, most of which are better than this game.
Moving on to the mess that was/is Story mode: 18 months and multiple failed release dates later, the devs have engaged in a rigorous "it's done when it's done" stance.  Waiting for months upon months for a story mode that was promised to be delivered months ago and may be at best only a few hours long is not my cup of tea. I have been holding off on writing this review, but as time passed I ended up feeling disappointed and angry as The Long Dark seemed to be traveling down a never-ending road of Early Access, sadly like so many other games.
This is the first Hinterland product I have purchased, and it will also be my last. I've uninstalled the game, and it will most likely remain uninstalled for the rest of eternity.

I hate how much I enjoyed this game in my initial playhrough. While I can't on good conscience recommend it becayse of the way that it depicts people with mental illnesses, it's difficult for me to deny that playing through was a satisfying experience.
"The Park" does have a lot of fantastic elements, and ableism aside, it does have an engaging narrative. While I hate to make excuses for Funcom, it's not like they're the first people to ever have a harmful portrayal of a character who struggles with depression and anxiety issues - in fact I would say that's an unfortunately common occurance in games of this genre.
You play as Lorraine, a woman who rushes into the park after hours to look for her son, Callum. As you follow him from one attraction to the next (all the while keeping your eyes peeled for the Park mascot, Chad) you can pick up clues that reveal bits and pieces of the location's dark past. This is exactly the sort of story-driven gameplay that I typically look for, and I have to admit that upon first playing the game I thoroughly enjoyed it. The simple gameplay combined with the intricately dark history makes for an all-encomposing experience.
What I enjoyed most was hands down the atmosphere. Visually, it's very appealing. There's something very eerie about the concept of creeping around an empty amusement park at night, and the design for this game harnesses that fear quite nicely. The slow build-up makes each and every off-putting thing all the more effective, and when combined with the occasional jumpscare, it's sure to keep players at the edge of their seats.
It's also worth mentioning that the achievements are all story-based, and can easily be obtained in a single playthrough. They're used to highlight certain aspects of the game and particularly potent parts of the story rather than to bribe players into spending longer than they'd like grinding for useless reasons - and I think this is a perfect example of how achievements can be used expertly to enhance a game, rather than distracting from it.
Aside from the strong issues I had with the writing and representation, there is one other serious drawback to consider before purchasing this title - and that would be the price. This is an incredibly short game, and it doesn't hold up well to multiple playthroughs. Considering that one can easily achieve 100% completion within an hour or two and be done with the game forever - $12.99 seems a little steep. If you are interested in playing (and unfortunately I can't blame you if you are) then I highly suggest waiting until it goes on sale.
Like with almost any game the park has both ups and downs - the downs in this case are just a bit more harmful.

Oblivious Garden ~Carmina Burana is a chinese visual novel which contains several different endings, making it a dating sim. Unlike other visual novels which are either a complete comedy, or a VN with a total tragic story, this VN contains both kinds endings, the bad and the good endings are completely opposing and are in 2 different extremities.
The story involves a man named Irell Reis as the protagonist, he had been fighting for his empire during several years and had always won, but lost an important war. After this, his title of duke was removed and he was expelled for a duration of 3 years before entering this 'oblivious garden'. There are in total 7 princesses, the story goes over 3 of the princesesses and a maid who is working in this garden.

Depending on your choices, these stories can go differently, every route has it's specialities, some of them contains both positive and negative endings,
there are also some extra bad endings that will occur if you change the choices of routes for each characters too many times. I won't go further in since you can find more details in the strategy guide.

遺忘庭園是一本中國式視覺小說, 其中包含著許多各種不同的結局。不同於其他以喜劇,鬧劇或是以悲劇收場的VN,這本小說不僅包含快樂和悲傷結局,比起另一本巨作’’刻痕’’以14種不同的結局所呈現的悲傷場面,遺忘庭園把好的和壞的結局以兩種不同的極端予以呈現。
故事裡敘述著一名叫做艾爾‧里斯的男子的生平經歷,從一名連戰皆捷的將軍,由於在一次重要的戰役中被敵方用巫術暗算而慘敗,轉變為一名不僅被剝奪了爵位,而且被放逐了四年的’’叛徒’’。三年後,經過皇帝的傳昭,進入了遺忘庭園並成為了七位公主的劍術導師兼神積劇主演。故事內容包含了其中的三位公主,以及另外一名在遺忘庭園服務的女僕主管。
視乎玩家的選擇而定,這些故事會分出多條故事內容,每一條線都有他們的特點和必玩之處,其中有些悲慘的結局,但大部分都是好的。玩家也可以在一直選不同角色線的情況下遇上一,兩個壞結局。就這樣,剩下的請玩家自行發掘,選擇的方法的話,攻略裡都有寫。
相較於像nekopara或sakura系列以鬧劇為主題的視覺小說,遺忘庭園比較正經,也比較動人。如果玩家想問出最會讓人笑的故事線的話,個人會回答萊拉線,其故事線不但描寫出了主角艾爾和萊拉在一開始所擁有的不愉快的回憶,同時也包含了許多惡搞人的笑話。個人最喜歡萊拉和琳的個性,也是從琳的故事線開始閱覽這本視覺小說的。
個人認為此小說的畫風,比起其他視覺小說品質稍微低下了一點點,不過這並不是大問題,視覺小說的重點是故事的內容而不是其畫風的素質(只要別太差就好)。此視覺小說擁有動聽的背景音樂,個人最喜歡所有背景音樂中兩首:’’開場’’和’’永恆衝突’’。不過,個人認為稍微缺少了點令人聽了毛骨悚然的恐怖音樂算是一處可惜的地方。個人推薦此小說的原聲大碟給所有的VN音樂粉絲,尤其是此遊戲的愛好者。

+每個角色都擁有著完全不同的個性

TL;DR for the review: possibly the best Steam game you'll ever buy for less than a buck.
I originally bought this because, well, I was buying all games that costed less than one eurobuck during summer sales. It's just the kind of person I am. Then, today, I saw the game had cards. "Yay", I thought, "I can get back a percentage of the money I wasted on this!". I fired it up, and the first thing I noticed was that the interface was quite polished. Easy on the eyes, ambient sounds in the background, minimalistic with clean, soft colours.
The game immediately starts you off with a tutorial, which flows naturally into the main game. The puzzles start off really easily, to let you get a feel for the mechanics. Then it introduces the hubs, as I've taken to calling them, and the game takes off. The main thing that makes the game so great is that almost every puzzle comes naturally, you're seldom stuck on something. That's not to say the puzzles are easy, no, but they're never frustrating. You try to solve one, you see it isn't working out, but you almost always have other methods to follow, there's never a point where you can't think of another way to solve a puzzle.
And oh boy is it calming. It's got really soft, ambient sound effects on everything you do, and the levels just flow into eachother. The UI almost never interferes with anything, and is only there when you call for it.
After you finish the second puzzle set, you unlock the possibility to play daily puzzles, which mean you'll never run out of content.
In conclusion, the reason I found out about this game was because it cost me less than 80 cents, but if I had known how good it was beforehand, I'd have gladly shelled out a fiver on it. It's just that good.

If you want the SHORT ANSWER,yes,this game is absolutely worth buying,if you like platformers. Hell, if you like good games, you should pick this up. It's fun and It's my favourite game of the year thus far. For the long and detailed answer,oh boy, dive in.
Cuphead,as I already assume you've heard it is a hard, 1930s looking 2d platformer,where you play as some guy with a cup for a head( actually thinking hard about it, who the ♥♥♥♥ put a straw in that size cup, whatever). Story is about as basic as it gets,only a couple of levels higher than "you have to shoot the thing". Cuphead and mugman(2p character in 2p mode) are in the devils casino and they made a deal with said devil. Unfortunately, they lost the bet and "their souls are to belong to him". However,they pleed for forgiveness and have collect soul contracts for the devil in exchange for their lives, which means that there are a lot of enemies to kill. The story is simple, but I think it doesn't need anything deep. Obvious goal for the killing of all the bosses and away we go...

Moving on to the visuals, I find hard to list anything major I dislike. I'm not sure how truly they recreated the 1930s look,since my furthest nostalgia is watching dubbed soviet cartoons, when I was 7, in 2003. But looking at the visuals, it's very good. Everything is clear, sharp, never looks muddy or too dark, my fear that the grain filter would be distracting were totally eradicated. The only gripe that I have with them is that the foreground can sometimes obstruct the view at the bottom when you don't want to. This was particularly annoing in the Dr. Khals Robot fight where in the last phase in expert mode, there were so many bullets I repeatedly had to be at the very bottom of the screen, but then I couldn't see the bullets, since the bottom of the screen is mostly filled with the moving foreground. That's was truly annoying.. Apart from that, nothing of note..
Now for the gameplay... I'm sure that by this point, all who are not platforming enthusiasts might be scared, since it's no secret that the game is hard, but I can assure you that it's not as hard as people claiming it to be. I like to think that all the great platformers are more like puzzle games, that don't really require mad reactions or skills to  win, but a calculated mind to figure out a solution for a problem. And Cuphead is exactlly that...  While yes, at first it might seem impossible to beat that boss, especially when after you die you see that you're barely into it(♥♥♥♥ you Dr. Kahls robot), but the high after you complete said boss is the best thing ever. It took me about 5-6 hours to complete the main game.. From what I've seen though, people usually beat it around 8-10 hours, depending on the skill level. 8-10 hours,in my mind, is worth  the 20 euro asking price. But I urge you, to not stop just with normal mode,I highly reccomend you try the expert mode,if you're up for one of the greatest challenges in this year, in terms of games. I'm in love at the moment with Cuphead, so after 18 hours that it took to unlock all Steam achievements,I'm gonna go dor S ranking all the bosses on Expert, which is probably the greatest challenge of my gaming life, because ♥♥♥♥ only being 0.4 % of people who only BEATING the game on expert, perfecting on expert is where it's at..
To sum up, Cuphead is the most fun I had in a video game for a long time. It might not be a massive game, but it will leave you more satisfied than any "Foaming at the mouth braindead shooting simmulators" which is pretty much all of Triple A gaming ever could
