FIRST and perhaps MOST important, TIS is a diamond in the rough and their game is truly a shining example of how early access development should be done. since introducing their project to the steam community they have been extremely productive and informative, posting a weekly devblog to the news feed and offering a public unstable branch that actually shows the progress of said devblogs. just go look for yourself.
this is an excellent zombie-survival game with a gritty, nostolgic feel to it. this isnt a heroic blockbuster where you wade through waves of starved zed, gleefully caving in skulls and emptying full mags of ammunition. death itself has an even more insatiable appetite than the undead and you will spend the beginning hours of every playthrough desperately clawing yourself away from its hungry jaws. even when you have become wise to the wasteland it will still easily find ways to commission you into the hordes. several large towns with fully exporable, fully lootable buildings spread out across a (still growing)country-side stuffed to the brim with true-to-the-name, proper zombies will keep you in an inevitably ending struggle to see another day.
every element of gameplay is creative, original and skillfully implemented. the inventory is governed by a weight system sprinkled with various containers for your items. zombies are lovingly coded and realized and are a constant danger whether alone in a public restroom or in a ravenous horde in the urban streets or forest. a "meta-game" system ensures they dont simply congregate in one area, instead following en-masse random sounds that keep the population shambling all ends of the map. as usual with survival games, essentials such as building, crafting, cooking and hunting/fishing are skills that can be mastered by gaining experience. to top it off, all of this can be done with friends with up to four players on one screen via drop-in/out style, as well as LAN and internet play. and yes, those up to four friends can drop-in/out during LAN and internet play.
as with any early access project, its still very much in progress. a few key promised features including NPC survivors and a story/campaign have yet to be realized but this small indie studio has shown they can deliver. it has taken them a long time to get PZ to where it is now and it will probably be quite some time before it will be called complete, but i wholeheartedly recommend you buy this game. keep it in your steam pocket. watch it become a classic.

Irrational Games’ (then 2K Boston) BioShock is the critically acclaimed 2007 first-person shooter. And I think the game is quite good, so why is my review saying “Not Recommended”, there are several reason, firstly the port isn’t that great but it is playable. But I’ll be completely honest I didn’t like the game past the first hours, let me explain why this is.
Let me start by saying that the story is fantastic and with exception of the way it ends, and of course the lead up to the end. The story explores the ideology of objectivism in a setting where it was allowed to thrive and how it was brought down by it’s own flaws, as well as a substance called ADAM. And if the game is worth going through it is for its story. BioShock is also known for having one of the best if not the best plot twist in a game ever, I won’t spoil it here in case you don’t know what the twist is (somehow). The setting and visual style is also made the most off, I really love Rapture, it is a wonderfully bleak reflection of its own Golden Age as learn throughout the game and Andrew Ryan, the founder of Rapture makes for a great antagonist and philosopher.
I also have quickly mention the fact of the horror aspect of the game, it is pretty much non-exsitant, as a rule I say that if a game cannot porperly scare or horrify me it should not be classified as a horror game, why me? Because I am extremly easily scared, the first few hours of the game are tense and suspenseful but the game never achieves being scary, if it was then I could forgive some of the clunkyness that is in gameplay in order add some more stress during the combat but now it doesn't and so it doesn't get any kind of free pass for that.
Now the gameplay of BioShock consists in 2 parts, first is combat and the second is looting and so each ties into and is important for the other, now the game features 7 weapons and 11 Plasmids, now Plasmids are genetic modifications that serve as “magic spells” created through the usage of ADAM. I don’t have anything against the usage of weapons and plasmids together in order create your own builds and tactics but the problem is that it wasn’t handled as well as it could have been. You the weapons and plasmids are separate, you hold all your weapons in your “inventory” at the same time while you have a limited amount of plasmid slots, of which you can buy up to a maximum of 8. The problem is that say you use your LMB (Left Mouse Button) to fire with say the Revolver and then you have to use the RMB (Right Mouse Button) to switch to your equipped plasmid, you can use the hotkeys though, and there is a hotkey for each weapon 1-8 and plasmid slot F1-F8 but the real problem is that they are separate meaning they can’t be used at the same time. The other problem is that the shooting is unsatisfying in pretty much every way and the aiming is not good at all. The shooting is also due to these reason prone to becoming ver repetative very early in the game.
Now the looting consists of searching for ammo, audio logs and other resources which helps you survive Rapture, there is something else you’ll need to survive Rapture and that is ADAM. And ADAM is something that can only be obtained 1 way and that is from Little Sister who are protected by Big Daddies who are the hardest enemies in the game, and then once you’ve defeated the Big Daddy you either get to rescue or harvest the Little Sister for the ADAM inside of her. Rescuing the Little Sister doesn’t give out as much ADAM as harvesting her but rescuing her lets the girl live while harvesting kills her, I’ll come back this a little later.
Now I said that the game had 7 weapons, those are the Wrench (of Death and Destruction) which is overpowered as hell, the Revolver, the Machine Gun (which is useless, don’t waste upgrades on it), the Shotgun, the Grenade Launcher, Chemical Thrower and the Crossbow. There are also weapon upgrades to find at Power to the People stations wherein you get to choose one upgrade for a weapon, which I find that I don’t like, I much prefer finding the upgrades hidden in the level which this sort of is but you get my point. Now those who were paying attention will have noticed that I mentioned that there are 8 weapon hotkeys but I’ve only mentioned 7 weapons.

Done? Good, the last one isn’t actually a weapon, it is a Camera which you use to take photos of enemies, alive and dead in order to increase your damage against that specific enemy type and well as learning their weaknesses and this serves as your way of  “leveling up”, just don’t forget to use it which is very possible, I do like it though.
Now previously I mentioned that the game has a really good plot twist (still won’t spoil it), but I will say that the game should have ended at that point instead of going on for 2 more levels and having the lead-up to the finale being equivalent of self-inflicted torture after which it has a anticlimactic boss fight and a horrible ending. Now the ending is horrible, or rather the endings are horrible, both of them. And the reason they’re horrible has to do with the morality system, you remember previously I mentioned the rescuing and harvesting of Little Sisters previously, and that is what determines which ending you get, if you rescue them all you get the good ending if you harvest them all you get the bad ending. Now the reason that they are horrible is that they go so far to show how good or evil you that it is ridiculous. it goes to the point that might as well have a halo or devil horns. Now technically there is a third ending, which you get by rescuing some Little Sister and harvesting some, but all you get is the bad ending but the character narrating it has a sad tone instead of an angry one.
Lastly there is the second to last sequence in the game, now I will completely spoil this sequence so if you don’t want to read it just jump down to the last paragraph.
Within this sequence you are put into a Big Daddy Suit and you are made to follow a cured Little Sister around as she leads you to the final boss, this sequence is horrible! The girl moves so slowly I could have ran back and forth to the room the boss is in three times over, could have but can’t since she stops all the time and is constantly attacked. The sequence is also so linear it is unnecessary to even have the girl there, now there are similar sequences in BioShock 2 wherein you carry around a Little Sister and protect her while she gathers ADAM for you, but you carry her around on your shoulder then, and BioShock 2 didn’t make me want to kill the Little Sister which I have the option to do in BioShock 2 but I can’t do it to this one and if I could have I would have.
After that there is the final boss which is anticlimactic as all hell, not fun and … the most I can say about it is that it isn’t the worst part of the game, that goes to the Big Daddy sequence, it is merely the third worst thing about the game, second being the ending. So here is my advice if you play BioShock and get as far as the plot twist but were already starting to get bored by the game then just stop there and let that be the ending.
And there is my opinion on BioShock, and while I didn’t like the majority of people out there do and it might just be so that I have no taste whatsoever, as I’m sure I will get told by someone out there. Anyway, I hope that this has at the very least been insightful and will help in your decision on whether or not to purchase this game, anyway ciao.

I didn't like sports already. However, with Frozen Cortex, someone has found a way to make a game about sports that's even less interesting to me than watching actual sports.  Running robots around a field with rectangular prisms cutting paths through it whilst two teams try to take a ball from one side to the other doesn't sound bad, really. However, actually playing the game comes off as a chore to me. Each action requires precision steps for every team member, going into excruciating detail of how long to wait before acting, how far to move in each direction, when to pass, when to remain still and block, etc. It's wildly complicated.
I've dodged watching a whole American football game all my life, but if someone forced me at gunpoint to either watch one or play Frozen Cortex for as long as that same real-life football game lasts, I am not exaggerating when I say that I would watch the live football game instead. I find this whole thing tedious. I might say that I don't like turn-based stuff, but that's not true, because I loved Shadowrun Dragonfall. Frozen Cortex takes a subject matter I wasn't into and makes it far, far more boring for me.

SUPERHOT... SUPERHOT... SUPERHOT... SUPERHOT...
You will hear this phrase approximately 400 times while playing SUPERHOT. You are a player in a first-person shooter (yes, that was meant to be meta) where time only moves when you move. You play the game at a speed somewhere between real-time and a complete stop. You are moved through a series of scenarios where the goal is to kill all the red guys. The way time moves means you are able to dodge bullets, line up shots and quickly asses the situation without getting riddled with bullets. It only takes one bullet to kill you, in the same way it only takes one bullet to kill the red guys. If you die, you start again.
SUPERHOT does try and add some uncessary Matrix-esque metagame to what is a fun shooter experience, and this could be considered appropriate given the bullet-time theme of the game. I wouldn't rate the metagame very highly, or not at least its delivery.
The reason why you play this game is for the "replay", the result of a successful run, played back to you in real-time.  Which means a 30 second replay is the culmination of about ten minutes of gameplay. This replay is somewhat marred by the words "SUPERHOT" flashing across the screen while being chanted with computerised montony, but is still satisfying to watch.
SUPERHOT does let you pull off some incredibly fun, action-movie style fight scenes. Like jumping over an incoming car in a car garage; punching someone, causing them to let go of their gun; grabbing their gun and shooting them in the head; doing a quick 360 spin around to take out a read guy approaching from behind; running forward towards two more red guys, weaving between bullets; shooting one of them, throwing your empty gun at the other; punching the guy who just appeared out of nowhere from between two parked cars; grabbing the gun from the man who received your old gun to the chest; shooting the out-of-nowhere man; and then- ah♥♥♥♥♥♥ just took a katana to the chest... start again.
SUPERHOT is a lot of fun and an interesting and unique concept for a game. It does come with some associated fluff that sometimes accompanies indie games, but is ignored easily enough for the experience.

Of the visual novels I've played, this is probably my favorite so far.
The artwork is lovely and the character design well done.  The music works well with the setting.  The character voices sound fine to me.  As with all translated VNs, there are some occasional clunks in the text, but I didn't feel it was bad.  I can't comment on the translation like I might with a Japanese VN as I don't speak any dialect of Chinese, but nothing in the text seemed overly hinky that would hint at a poor translation.
These are just basic good points you can find in a lot of VNs.
What really made this one stand out, in my opinion, is the vast difference in the stories for each path.  Most of the VNs I've read have had pretty much the same plot regardless of what path you're trying to follow, with unique scenes and dialogues inserted in based on your choices.  In this case, without spoiling anything, the entire progression of the plot is different.  Each girl's path is written individually so that if you finish, for example, Leila's path and then go back and play Dyanna's path, the story is brand new (and each plot is VERY different from the others).
Thanks to the real replayability of this sort of "four-stories-in-one" novel combined with the well-drawn graphics, I can't recommend it enough.  I picked it up on sale but would cheerfully have paid full price for the  amount of playtime and enjoyment I got out of it!

What this is: Connect the colorful, multi-polygonal "dots" on steroids.
If you find puzzle games extremely irritating to the point of (near) violence, you may want to pass.
But if you're one of the few looking for something that will pass the time and provide both amusement and brain-tingling exercise, then this is for you. The first time I played this, several hours passed somehow without notice. It's not overly cerebral, but it requires you to have some amount of spatial and pattern-detecting abilities. If you have none, just think of this as training.
New levels (and color palettes) are unlocked as you go, and get progressively harder to boot.
Additionally, there is also the option of daily puzzle challenges (with randomly generated difficulty levels). If you find yourself stuck on a particular puzzle/level, these are a great way to shift your focus and still feel like you accomplished something. But if you're reaaaaally stuck, at some point you unlock an area with content that looks like hints (or possibly solutions) to specific puzzles. I haven't really looked into it yet--but while I'm not quite mid-way through the LYNE, I can see where I might crack in the near future and start looking for assistance before I put a fist through my monitor. By the way, the individual puzzles within each level are independent of each other, making it easy to pick it back up for those times when you need a break.
The developer(s) are also pretty responsive--I had some issue with achievements acting funky and they responded to my forum post pretty quickly, so that was appreciated.
Disclaimer: I love anything puzzle-y, so I'm biased. That said, this is a well-done game that will give you many, many (possibly too many) hours of enjoyment.

First, I want to point out that a lot of people are complaining about poor translation. I have played the game thoroughly and, for the most part, it is properly translated. It starts to get iffy toward the end but it's bearable.
I think many players may be confusing translation with 1st and 3rd person writing. In this game, it switches between both and the only indication is the lack of a name for the speaker. This applies to Irell as well as the Princesses so it can get confusing rather quickly.
The writting format is pretty basic but enough to get descriptions and thoughts across. There's a heavy focus on how Irell Reis feels about every little thing. Some dialogue gets repeated despite already encountering it based on who you are following, ect. Probably about half of the dialogue boxes should be merged together or removed entirely to reduce redunancy.
The game would do a lot better overall just by enhancing the dialogue to make it more relevant. It would also be more believable and immersive if the vocabulary wasn't juvenile and overused; ex: "cute", "plebian" and nobility titles. I would like to see the game revised this way in the future, or have their next game written more eloquently.
Some of the voices sound like they were recorded at a low quality. Personally, I listen to the first few lines of a character and then turn it off. Most of them sound identical aside from tone. I enjoy imagining their voices on my own, with or without the tone implied by the creator.
It's very difficult to know who you've picked to follow or how to continue to properly follow them without a lot of trial-and-error, unless you use one of the player made guides. There's a few on Steam that work well. I recommend using the Story Line portions first. After that, you can replay the game to get any of the Achievements missed. Holding the space bar down will rush through all of the dialogue. It should only take a few minutes to get them this way so definitely enjoy the story line first.
Most of what you read is based on original lore and backstory for the characters. Once you've triggered an ending there is a -lot- of reading. You will need to get every ending to learn every characters story as only a few interact per play through. Also, keep in mind that not all of the character stories are updated at the same time.
Each ending varies in length. One of them was a good 3 hours of reading after the choices ran out. I didn't expect this as it was my first playthrough so it quickly became a case of "when is this going to end?" for 2 of those 3 hours. If you like plot twists, and the ones in this game can get ridiculous, as well as learning about characters then it will keep you playing until the end. Fair warning, it gets ridiculous.
The artwork, for some of the characters, was very well done. I would have liked to have seen more stills of events, especially during major scenes and Dyanna's finale. It would have made the bloated dialogue more bearable and the story more immersive overall.
The UI needs some work. All of the options in the menu takes a little bit longer than normal to load and usually feels like the game hasn't registered the request. By the time I move the mouse over and click the option a second time it loads. The Quick Save & Quick Load options are not explained. You can only manually save or load during dialogue where it is listed to the right.
[Having now completed the game, I will say that overall it has a low quality plotline from character to character. Personality preference will determine how much you enjoy the game. If you get bored with a character, I recommend either holding space bar and finishing to get the achievements or drop them entirely and move on to someone else.]
It's worth it at 50% off, plus free DLC.

So this game is pretty cool, pun intended. great concept for a game, I’m a 44-day survivor so far. I have almost died 4 times, 2 by bear mauling’s, freezing, and falling off a cliff. There are a few things I would like in the game, as I am from Montana and know a thing or two about winter and extended camping. 1. the ability to make jerky or pemmican so all the meat I get doesn't go to waste. 2. the ability to make a sled to haul things, i.e. wood, dead animals. so I don't have to harvest where it died...like real life. the ability to move the stoves you find in fishing huts to cabins or the fire barrels to better locations that make more sense. (you want to warm a small room vs a giant dam for example) Oh and some of the tasks take WAY too long.  even ones you think are ok I find annoying. 5 min to break down a branch into 3 sticks?? I can do the same task in about 10-15 seconds real world without a tool. 27 min to tear up a cardboard box?? really?? 1-2 min tops, with my hands, and more moveable/harvestable objects. I also think you get tired a bit to quickly...even when you do nothing but read them books you find. should have a better fatigue meter vs being actually tired. If a football player runs 100 yards he should not need to sleep for 3-4 hours to be rested again, it’s just fatigue. Also, why are we limited in rifle to an old .303 British rifle. the Canadians have better technology than that. bring in a .444 Marlin for them bears...heck even an old Winchester .22 long rifle would be sweet for the rabbits. maybe a pistol of some sorts....357 or a .44 mag. As far as the skills that get better with use. surprised there is a rifle skill but no bow skill. and how about Endurance? If I have to carry 50-60 lbs. on my back and person all the time I am going to get stronger and such. the Mountain men of old used to carry 100lbs of gear on them without breaking a sweat. strong as an ox and tough as a honey badger. With all this said, I am still enjoying the game
EDIT: Since the Release of the full game I notinced some hyper unrealistic things...ie.. getting hungry.....aaaannd needing to eat 7.7LBS OF MEAT to be full!?!? Are you kidding me?  If I cut up two trees for logs I shouldnt need 8 hours or more of sleep to recover Also 20-30 degrees fahrenheit is not that cold. at 15 degrees or lower I sometimes pull out a jacket when I go outside. below zero is when I actually wear a heavy coat. The body adapts quickly, it is a very resilient machine. its the little things that get to me. being that I live in Montana and see this weather ever year.

TL;DR:  if you're a shmupper, get this.  it's a worthy adversary!
===
this one promises old-school, kick-you-in-the-teeth shmup action, and by gosh, it delivers!
in doing so, looks great, sounds lovely, and plays like a sweet explosive dream.
there are four craft, each of which plays quite differently to the others,
as each has its distinct look, performance characteristics, differing armor levels,
and unique main and special weapons to go along with the in-game extra firepower that one can nab.
all of the ships fly a bit like the one from that old ballbreaker, DEFENDER:
the pilot has control over the ship's facing (left or right), but is able to fly any direction no matter what the facing.
moving in the same direction as the ship's nose works a lot better than trundling backwards,
and in fact leads to hyperspeed flight, which progressively becomes more terrifying
as the fighter edges closer and closer to the border of the game's viewport it's facing,
ever closer to smacking up against that mine that's glowing unnoticed on the radar,,.
things can become decidedly bullet-hellish at times on higher (Arcade and Pure) difficulty levels,
but one of the nice side effects of the player ships' special weapons is that they come with a short-lived but effective shield,
making the specials good for both ending lots of enemies at once and saving bacon at the same time.
with four ships, four difficulty levels, a six-level main campaign, and a handful of survival levels,
Syder Arcade offers a good bit of replayability for the money.

Cuphead is a great experience visually and aurally, but it leaves a little to be desired gameplay-wise. This game is often called "The Dark Souls of 2D Shooters," but I am not too keen on that comparison. There are many "cheap shots" that a boss will take at you that, your first time, are unpredictable and unavoidable. For Example, Dr Kahl's Robot shooting it's head at you at the phase change, or Grim Matchstick's 3rd phase shooting the flamethrower. The counterbalance to this is that, unlike Dark Souls, you do not lose anything upon your death except time. You have infinite lives and infinite attempts to repeat bosses. Overall, this game was well worth $20. It took me 18.8 Hours to beat this game on Normal, get A's on every boss, beat the game on Expert, and get all the achievements. If you were to just play this game on Normal and put it down, it would most likely take 6-8 hours , and with the incredible visuals and music in this game, it makes the price tag well worth it.

So this is one of the best shoot 'em ups I've ever played. Seriously. I'll give you my credentials, I've been playing since Gradius, Raiden, etc, I import Japanese shoot 'em ups like Ibara/Espgaluda/other Cave game, blah blah. I'm a huge fan of the genre. But this one is simply one of the best, because even after all these years, Syder Arcade took a classic genre and breathed new life into it.
Seriously, if you've ever played Gradius and wanted to just turn around and shoot that guy that
made it by you... do it! In Syder Arcade, you can literally turn your ship around in the other direction at will. Better yet, you can actually travel backwards through a level by doing this, in case you... missed a powerup, or an enemy, or whatever. There's even a defense level where you have to survive for a certain amount of time protecting a huge allied battleship (which doesn't need an egregious amount of protecting), and you will travel back and forth through the area quite a few times gunning down all the ships that appear. You can also stop moving altogether; the screen doesn't scroll without your permission. It's like... you're actually flying your own spacecraft. It's crazy.
Syder Arcade also does something else I haven't ever seen a shoot 'em up focus on: melee combat. I know, the idea is ridiculous. You're in a spacecraft, for crying out loud! But in Syder Arcade (like in many good shoot 'em ups), you have your primary weapon, and your secondary weapon (the latter of which needs to be charged in various ways). Though each of the four selectable ships have different secondary weapons, all of them put a shield around your ship for 2 or 3 seconds. During this time, you can literally just ram the hell out of enemy spacecraft. There are even bonuses for doing it! It is GREAT! You can also absorb bullets this way, for which there are also bonuses. And one of the best parts: you have a health bar. One mistake isn't necessarily the whole game!
Seriously, this game is worth playing, even for shoot 'em up fans that think they have seen it all. What I really like, too, is that it's not exactly a "bullet hell" game. I know those are really popular, like Cave games, Touhou, etc... and I like them, but every once in a while it's nice to focus more on blowing stuff up than memorizing bullet patterns and stuff. There are still plenty of bullets to dodge in Syder Arcade though, and the game won't go down without a fight on "Pure" difficulty.
The one thing I have to warn about: currently, Survival is quite buggy. None of the achievements for Survival unlock (at least, they didn't for me after 3 hours of trying and some top-80 scores). Also, the ice level is totally bugged and will freeze the game, and the juggernaut level also won't end and will just sit until you quit out. This kind of hurts Syder Arcade's replayability, because if it's anything I love about a shoot 'em up, it's a good Survival mode to improve my scores on. But even aside from this, it is so worth playing through this game and seeing what fun things you can do in the genre even after all this time.
Highly, highly recommended, a favorite of mine on all of Steam!

I've only finnished this game yesterday and since then I've wanted to write a short review of it. Bioshock is a singleplayer, fps that sells itself on an interesting combat system and unique and complex story. The game is set in the fictional, underwater city of Rapture where a new scientific descovery has caused the citys enhabitents to go mad and murderous and become what are called Splicers. These will be your main enemy for the game along with security bots and Big Daddys as you explore, back-track ( theres allot of that) and then explore some more of the huntingly atmospheric Rapture.
Now that i've mentioned the Big Daddys, they serve as optional bosses in the game. By killing them you can ether harvest or rescue the Little Sisters that they gard. If you rescue them then you get a small amout of adam (the currency for upgradeing your abilities) and the "good" ending. If you harvist them then you get lots of adam and the bad ending. But as i said you have to fight the Big Daddy to get these which serves as a nice risk and reward system.
The story (no spoilers past the first hour) starts with your un-named silet protagonist's play crashing into Rapture. He is then aided by a man named Atlas who tells your character that in order to escape he must kill the cities founder Andrew Ryan.  Audio tapes reveal bits about the more advanced story. The story grabs you imediately and serve as one of the best parts about Bioshock... until about 2/3s of the way through the game. After an epic plot twist that i wont spoil the game in general becomes a sudden chore.
After the twist the game throwes you into a long, boring fetch quest followed by one of the most hideous escort missions that ive ever played (if you hate this escort mission the you probably wont like Bioshock 2). Then there is an easy, anticlimactic boss fight followed by a TERRIBLE 30 second (if you get the good ending like me) cutscene. These missions, story choices acompanied by a huge difficulty spike make the last hour or so awful and boring.
The combat system is fun though. You will use a combanation of wepons and plasmids (basicly superpowers) to defeat your enemies. Useing different combos of wepons and plasmids you can find awsome ways to kill people , for example, an electric shock and then a blast from the crossbow is a good one to fight the spider Splicers. You can also hack droids to fight for you, but the hacking mini game is a dredful, anoying mess so unless you use all of your adam upgradeing your hacking abilities.
In the end i would definately recomend playing Bioshock as its a great, chilling experience with a cold (if a bit anti-climactic) story, but i would only buy if it was on offer as the game is diffinately without its flaws. Yet despite these flaws im looking farward to playing Bioshock Infinate (i tryed bioshock 2, but didnt enjoy it) to see a new story with some hopefuly improved gameplay.

I want to like this game, has a great deal of fun in the Beta/Alpha and love teh story and art direction of the game. The world is interesting with a good amount of lore displayed to the players through character dialogue as well as interesting looking characters themselves. However, the Elephant in the Room matter with this game is clearly the questionable DLC practices that Turtle Rock Studios have used in the production of this game. There is currently over £60 worth of DLC not covered by the Season Pass of the game. The game has only been out for a few short days and this is ridiculous. One may argue that they are simply reskins and offer no affect on gameplay whatsoever, and while this is true, it represents the sad state that the gaming industry is in today. AAA games are practicing this as if it were the norm, when only a few years ago the term "DLC" would often refer to a £15 expansion pack offering hours upon hours of new and unique content unto a game, not a simple reskin of a character or weapon model. As I previously said, this game is fun. However, out of principle, it should be made clear that the general public should NOT accept these questionable practices which most big name gaming companies seem to be so fond of today. If you truly want to stand against this, don't buy this game. At least, not for the full £40/$60 asking entry price.

It's a good game and I do recommend it, but I have one criticism: the online multiplayer.
The game is set up so you can take effectively as long as you want to plan your move. You can start several games, which can last days, and just enter your move in when you feel like it and go away while you wait for the opponent to make their move.
The problem with this is that inevitably people forget or get bored waiting, and I'd always start games with someone only to have them make one move and never be seen again. I get that the point of this game is that you can spend time carefully planning your move: but there needs to be a way to keep people online for the duration of the match because in my experience, once one player logs off, the game will never be finished.
At least, this is what the game was like when I first got it. Now there are only ever a couple of people online at a time and they never accept game requests. Probably people got frustrated and just stopped playing the online version.
Having said all that, the single player mode is good, there are options for single matches, tournaments and a career mode, and the AI is pretty good (at least compared to me). If I remember correctly, I got the game on sale, and I'm not sure its worth nearly £20, so maybe wait until its a little cheaper.

SHORT VERSION:
Slideshow with jumpscares.  Nobody over 30 would find this point-n-click scary. 2/10
LONG VERSION:
My six year old hates scary games.  To put this into perspective, she thought the Super Mutants in Fallout New Vegas were too scary. The SUPER MUTANTS, for crying out loud.
Anyway, I decided to see what all the hype was about, and I purchased this game during the Steam Monster Summer Sale for $1.  Booted it up one night about 10pm, beer in hand.
About 10:30pm my six year old knocks sleepily knocks on the door: "Daddy, can I watch you play?" She should be in bed but I let her watch me sometimes when it's not a school night.
"Sure, baby, come on in." She sits behind me on the couch, watching me through sleepy eyes at my desk.
I say to her, "I think the game is too scary for you, I'm going to change it."
"No, I like the bear and the duck" she says, soft and tired.  She's staring at the screen like she's waiting for a bus.
"Are you sure? I can change it."
"No," she says. I turn the sound down some, anyway.
And I go back to the game.  Frustrating gameplay: Start, wait, jumpscare, restart.
Five minutes later I look back at my kid:
She's sound asleep.
RECAP:
-10:30pm at night
-lights off
-6 year old and daddy unscared
-$1 steam sale, still feel a little jipped

Well, guess it's my time to put my thoughts into the fray.
The game itself is wonderful.  Gameplay is AMAZING, be it as either the hunter or the monster.  As the hunter, there is satisfaction in having achieved victory through teamwork and whatnot.  As the monster, the thrill is found as you flee in the hopes to find enough food to evolve, as well as when you get powerful enough to turn the tables.
Of course, the real issue (and the issue that has given this game a mixed rating) is the DLC.  While I'd normally say that having day one DLC is a bad practice, all the day one DLC is merely cosmetic in nature.  None of it will effect gameplay at all.  If you see one or a few sets that you do like, great!  You can buy the one DLC, not all of it at once.
"But if you want to play the upcoming monsters or hunters, you have to pay for them!"
While that is true, you're also getting new maps and possilbly game modes (don't know if they are going to release more) for free.  Plus, while other game prohibit you and your party from playing the new maps if you lack the pack, you can play with those who have acquired the new characters without prohibiting them from using them, even if you lack the DLC.

I actually bought Frozen Cortex on accident prior to Steam's newer return policies, and was stuck with it. I put off trying it for months (definitely DON'T consider me part of this game's target audience.)
I finally booted it up today, and enjoyed learning how to play the game. I actually was a fan of Frozen Synapse (despite not being particularly interested in a sports translation of that game) so the mechanics were a bit familiar.
I'm trying to stick with it despite throwing my hands up repeatedly. AI seems frequently to (A) run straight in to your guys, thus giving up the ball or (B) hurling the ball in to some far distance of the arena (even straight in to the end zone quite frequently). This kind of nonsensical lack of actual strategy heavily impacts the game as you really have to constantly think about what bizarre things the AI will do to try and take advantage of the sport's lax rules. It's not even really the AI's fault; this is simply what the rules of the game lead to as it's better to take a chance flinging the ball towards your goal line when things get tough.
In short, the sport they've invented here is missing some rules. Watching it isn't exciting, and playing it feels more like a test than a game as you're fighting to keep it from degrading in to just throwing the ball huge distances and seeing who picks it up first.
You could do worse it seems - I think the team behind it probably worked very hard - but an element of fun seems to be mostly missing. Just seems like the title they used to kill time until Frozen Synapse 2 is in full swing.

Even from just looking at its concept, you can tell The Beginner’s Guide is a rather surreal idea. In brief, it’s a narrated trip through the works of a game developer, whilst all the while the narrator is trying to pick apart the meaning of each game and how it could possibly reflect the personality of the person who made it. To say any more regarding the details of the plot would be to ruin the experience, as is often the case with these types of games – yet let it be known that the game is going to try damn hard to play with your emotions.
You see, there are moments scattered throughout The Beginner’s Guide that succeed in creating a sense of poignancy; little experiences that - just perhaps - might cause you to stop and think for a second. Many of these are fleeting, and none of them are really hard-hitting enough to leave a lasting impression… But they’re enough to as least make an impression, and that’s something that’s not easy by a wide margin. Again, these moments are hard to detail without ruining their effect, but look out for one in particular that sees you tidying up a house, which managed to instil a strange sense of calmness and serenity in me that I honestly wasn’t expecting.
Not everything the game tries to coax out of you ends up hitting the mark, however, and unfortunately I feel this is especially true of the ending. It has the effect of turning a lot of the things you’ve previously seen on their head - yet after the dust had settled and the credits started to roll, I realised that any impact this dramatic twist was meant to have on me had been rather lost in the mix. It’s a sound ending, don’t get me wrong, but the story always feels like it’s building up to something bigger. Additionally, the more I tried to work out its meaning in consideration with the rest of the plot, the more things ended up feeling muddled and confused. This, coupled with one or two other scenes which lack any real impact, creates the potential for you to walk away from the experience a little… Well, deflated. The Beginner’s Guide is made by the same guy who made The Stanley Parable, which shared similar issues when it came to the effectiveness of its narrative, so it’s a shame to see it carry over here also.
Despite this, if you take a step back from looking at the messages the game is trying to convey, you can recognise what is perhaps its greatest accomplishment - its visuals. There are scenes that are so striking they had me literally exclaiming out loud; huge labyrinthine structures spreading out every way you can imagine, a restaurant standing alone in a sea of white, and many others besides. It’s enough to make you fervently tap your screenshot key, just so you can print out the results and hang them on your wall. Coupled with some eerie sound effects and music, and there’s some areas that even create a deep sense of unease or concern that’s really hard to shake. There’s no stunning graphics here (a fact the narration itself alludes to) – just an intelligent use of light, shape and sound to create something that’s truly impressive to look at and listen to.
Considering that The Beginner’s Guide only lasts for approximately an hour and a half, then, is it worth your time? I’d be more inclined to say no if the game wasn’t being so transparent about what to expect in regards to content and length, but as it stands I have to say it’s worth a look. It might not leave the lasting impression on you that it perhaps wants to, but it’s got enough there (especially in regards to its visuals) to be worth paying attention to.

The world of Arx, has completely frozen over. The sun's gone, all sentient races have retreated underground and you wake up in a jail cell.
Arx Fatalis is an old RPG - Perhaps not counted as a classic - But it possesses an intriguing atmosphere, like a horror based RPG, not many of those come to mind. The closest thing you could relate it to is most likely Ultima Underworld.
The gameplay is simple, but open enough for you to have fun with. Design your character by adjusting his attributes and skills with a limited pool of points, advance in levels as you go on and invest futher into your skills. Despite this, you're mostly limited by the three stereotypical archetypes in RPGs - The Warrior, Rogue and Wizard yadda yadda.
Melee is a simple charge based system; hold down attack, gain more power, unleash more damage. Stealth is available, but to limited success, as there are only so many situations where you can use it, and eventually you are forced with a confrontation here and there. Magic is handled quite uniquely however, while you do cast spells like you would in any other title, how you cast them is different.
Magic is based around a couple dozen "runes" you can acquire, each one pertaining to a word, you mix and match them by making gestures in front of yourself, using your mouse to create them one by one in succession. The spells range from simple magic missles to impressive DnD spells later on. Eventually you are forced to use spells in certain situations to progress, but you typically are given scrolls to do so, just in case your magic isn't up to snuff.
The world of Arx itself is a lightweight version of being free roaming. After you finish up the introduction area of the game, it's really down to you on how and when you want to progress in the main storyline, though granted, there's only so many sidequests to do and there's not a large amount you can influence beyond that (the option of killing every inhabitant underground is always available however).
Overall, Arx Fatalis is a game most certainly worth a playthrough or two, it carries enough elements in it to make it an interesting one-time experience. A new playthrough will net you somewhere between 10-20 hours depending on your pace, and maybe a little more if you really push your exploration to the limit. Gameplay will be satisfying all the way through, beware of the
It's atmosphere is again, quite top notch, don't be surprised if you get spooked at any point of the game - It might've been justly warrented.

This game is scary. It doesn't cop out like so many others and rely purely on jumpscares. It puts you in a stressful situation, that often requires cat-like relfexes, and quick thinking. This is a great game, and I'll tell you why.
Graphics: The graphics in this game are outstanding. The gritty realism and disgusting amounts of detail only intensify an already off putting experience. Whether it be detailed, high-resolution blood mixed with chunks of flesh leading you to the next change of pants, or the disturbing scars of the deformed residents of the now abandoned Mount Massive Asylum. The graphics were mindblowingly great in 2013, and they still hold up today. 9/10
Sound: Good Lord, the sound in this game is good. Just the quality of every sound effect, the echos of water dripping onto the floor, the deranged mumbles and rantings of wonderfully voice acted mentally unstable scientific expirements, the heavy breathing and footsteps of the protagonist, Miles Upshur, as he runs from danger in the form of a madman. Just grab your favorite headphones and turn the volume up, and you're guaranteed to become immersed in the experience on a whole-new level. 10/10
Gameplay/Fun to be had: This game is so much fun to play. The controls are responsive and oddly satisfying, despite how simple they are. The stressful, high-speed, escapes from the ugly, terrifying former inmates will pump adrenaline and fear through your veins as you vault over overturned desks, scramble into air vents just your pursuer grabs you, and slowly inch your way along ledges as you gaze down to the horrors below you. 8.5/10
Story: This game has a great story on so many levels. It's obvious some serious thought, time, and effort was put into the writing of this game. The ending was a little disappointing, but I won't spoil anything. 8/10
Overall: You don't just play Outlast. You experience it, and you have a blast doing so.

A profoundly surprising and openly ambiguous game that clutches at the darker, more fundamental pillars of our most primal fears. Humans are never quite so afraid as when an offspring is lost or in peril and The Park is an excellent analysis of the impact that such loss can cause on a psyche. Set in The Secret World universe, The Park is richly voiced, well-written and possessed of lavish, creepy atmosphere, with truly dreadful imagery that bespeaks of unsettling evil that festers in the darkest corners of both our physical world and darkest recesses of our minds. The game is absolutely gorgeous and Unreal Engine 4 is used to great effect.
Everything from the hallucinatory episodes, to the imposing power of the ferris wheel, to the strangling darkness of the roller coaster all present a horrible playground of suffering and darker passions. The game is very short, averaging about 2 hours with careful exploration and, yes, the ending isn't conclusive or definitive. The game forces you to be mature, adaptable and careful with your analysis of concepts and events. The story must be carefully pieced together from logs, article clippings and journal snippets that you discover in your examination of the park grounds but thorough players will soon crack the nut of The Park's labyrinthine ending.
The game isn't scary, per se, but it does induce dread and it definitely has occasional jump scares, like those near the Octatron, and in the midway. What The Park does offer, is a clever, expansive world, more atmosphere than most games can ever hope to have in campaigns that are ten times as long, and a gorgeous aesthetic that is sure to please discerning gamers. The Park is an art piece advertising a game with far more inspiration/content but, sadly, far less style. Pick The Park up on a Steam sale, turn the lights off, dial up the volume and enjoy the experience.
In The Park, the ride may be short but it's certainly bittersweet.

To say Tropico 5 isn't worth picking up isn't to say it's a bad game. On the contrary, I've had quite a good deal of fun with the game, I've put 20+ hours into it in the last week or so and have had a decent amount of fun for almost all of it. However, a game needs to be reviewed in context. Many take the approach of wanting to appreciate a game in a vacuum, to take the game itself and judge it on its own merits. I don't necessarily think this way of thinking is *wrong*, but I don't think it is correct either, and it's not the way that I want to approach this game. Rather, I would like to take the approach of a die-hard, disapointed, Tropico fan. I take this approach for a few reasons. Firstly, to judge a game on its own merits, it needs to exist on its own merits. Tropico 5 does not do that, it instead builds on a decades old franchise and comes from an experienced studio. That studio's past experience should be taken into account when judging what they've accomplished. A game's merits can not exist in a vacuum, and should not be judged as such. Secondly, this review primarily serves as a buyer's guide. Tropico needs to be judged in comparison to its competition. This is how all reviews work, as comparison forms the basis for our understanding of quality, and reviews tend to score in relation to other products. As such, I would like to approach this game, as mentioned before, as a Tropico fan, and approach it in as full a context as I can.

The biggest critique I can raise against Tropico 5 is that, instead of feeling streamlined, it feels like content has been cut. Streamlining isn't necessarily a bad thing. Excess fat can exist in games, trimming it isn't at all bad and quite often is an improvement. The extended cuts of movies rarely are as good as the finished, "official" cut because what was cut is often boring and tedious. However, streamlining is only appreciated when what it cuts is truly needless or cumbersome. Sadly, what Tropico 5 cuts from 3 (the cutting may have begun in 4, 5 might even represent compilation over 4 for all I know, but it is cut in comparison to 3, the basis of my critique so) isn't at all needless. In fact, it's what I liked the most.

Tropico 5 cuts from micromanagement, which *sounds* like a good thing, but the result is that the player is disconnected, distant from their citizens. I never once felt particularly motivated to help my citizens out of empathy or desire to help, nor do I feel any joy when oppressing them for the fun of it. The people never amount to more than a number in the almanac. Tropico 3, on the other hand, gave very personal descriptions of each citizen's thoughts, one could easily bring the camera down onto one citizen and just watch their life. A detailed political background gives insight to how a citizen thinks, their thoughts clearly line up and reflect these views. One can easily and visibly see the material basis on which these views have been founded. A citizen isn't a citizen, they're a number. A person dislikes their house? You won't know except for the aggregate number in the almanac. This isn't to say that you can't figure out what a person thinks, you can, but it feels hollow. I never feel motivated to go beyond the almanac, even if the information exists. It's the difference between de facto and de jure. Yes, de jure, the information is there. It's in the game technically. But, de facto, it's not, because it doesn't matter. For a political equivalent, it's the difference between censorship in the USSR and lack of funding in the US. The USSR certainly appears more restrictive of its media, but in actuality the differences aren't terribly relevant. The degree to which this is true even prompted George Lucas to say he would have rather created Star Wars in the USSR, because there would have been less restrictions. This is the power of de facto vs de jure. Yes, citizen "character" is in the game, but every citizen lacks personality.

The game makes some advancements on the diplomacy and military fronts, however, these end up backfiring on the game as well. Tropico 3's military system was "buy guard towers, buy army bases, don't worry about it". Tropico 5 makes one keep placement and funding in mind, but combat is dry as a bone. Soldiers take minutes to die even in firefights and the player lacks any control. Yes, further involvement is there in comparison to 3, but it's nowhere near enough. In 3 it was a flaw, but it was so nonexistent that I could just forget it and overlook it. In 5, it's present enough to remind me that I wish it was better. International diplomacy is similar. In 3, all one needed to worry about was not getting invaded and, if one wanted to, send some diplomatic missions to the USSR or the US and receive free stuff after a few months. Again, far from the focus. A flaw, yes, but one easily forgotten. 5 makes foreign policy missions constant, but they still amount to little more than "avoid being invaded". It's hollow and terribly boring.

Not the result of streamlining, but econ management is absolutely horrendous in this game. I don't, and never will, expect to play a game and expect an accurate representation of how an economy would function. There are far too many variables, and the game would always reflect the ideology of the creators. A fan of Mises will create a different game economy than a fan of Krugman would who would create a different game than a fan of Anwar Shaikh would. While I would love to exercise my Paul ♥♥♥♥♥hott inspired techno-socialist ideology in a game, it isn't going to happen. However, that doesn't mean I can't enjoy being the all powerful dictator, controlling every aspect of the economy. Unrealistic as it may be, that's not what I play games for. One thing I do come to games for is entertainment, and Tropico 5 makes sure that I find that task a harder one to complete than is needed. Fundamentally, the economy is hard to manage in Tropico 5. Not from a gameplay standpoint, I've basically got the game figured out. No, it is hard because information is hard to actually find. Say, for example, you run out of coal. You won't know until you finally start looking around for reasons why your island is without power. Information is never relayed to the player effectively.
I have more to say on the matter, and will upload a full review to my blog [Link here when it is uploaded], but the gist is simply this: Tropico 5 is inferior to 3. That's all there is to it, really. Just buy 3. You won't regret your choice

A very good survival game, that is more suited to patient, thinking players than someone looking for lots of FPS action and zombies (not that there's anything wrong with that). The action is mostly slow - long trudges through the snow - punctuated by the occasional wolf attack (note that the recent builds allow you to turn this off so that animals run away).
There is survival and crafting, but you're not building split-level forts or suits of armour - instead it is patching clothes, making snares, boiling water so you don't get a bellyache and die, and building hasty snow shelters so you don't get hypothermia before you can reach a refuge  :)
It might sound too slow and boring but it's immersive as heck and very satisfying. It's a game in which you become very involved. It's also an "iron-man" type of game in that the only saves are the automatic ones that happen when you enter a safe area (ie a building), and they are just to let you save between gaming sessions. However if you die you can't load your save - you're dead. At first this may seem tedious, but once you get into the swing of things it makes the game quite challenging.
I'd definitely recommend The Long Dark, particularly because even though it is an early access game it is still very playable and getting better all the time. The devs are good guys, and worth supporting.

The Forest acomplishes everything it sets out to do. The wilderness survival aspects feel realistic unlike certain games where you need to eat 7 full meal to not starve during a single day. The added stats based off of what you eat and what you do add a nice extra layer to the gameplay. The building feels good even if sometimes it lacks a bit of precision and the buildings themselves look great. And the combat really gives the impression of struggling against very wild enemies. In addition, the end game enemies feel tough to fight but with good strategy and good base design, you can take the out easily.
The caves in the early game are amazing. When I went caving for the first time, it really felt like a well designed horror game. When a single aspect of a game causes more fear and stress than a fully develloped horror game, you know the rest of the game will be just as interesting. Walking slowly through dimly lit caves with a torch in hand, hearing dripping water and strange animalistic noises creates an amazing athmosphere. The enemies feel like they're part of some insane canniballistic cult and you can also run into some of the stranger enemies. Mutated babies, massive people with too many arms, when you turn a dimly lit corner and see something weird staring you down, it feels more like a horror game than most games that have come out in recent years.
The fact that this is early access is what amazes me the most. It's a full game with a ton of content and it's being kept in early access just so that the developpers can refine it to the point of perfection, which the have been steadily doing nearly every month for the past few years.
The forest is one of my favorite games thanks to, the beautiful world (that doesn't need an amazing computer to render properly), the survival and combat which feel gritty and real (even though end game survival is a bit easy), the building which is gorgeous and gives a great sense of accomplishement, the developpers who are constantly improving the game and finally the fact that it can be a horde survival game while being a building game while being a horror game while being a reaxing lumberjac game and so on. It is amazing thanks to all the well polished aspects of the game.

In Short - Buy it. this is a masterpiece you need to experience. 9.5/10
Long -
Usually i don't like to succumb to initial hype for a game, even if it is praised by many. After watching a couple of streamers play the first part of it, and a couple of YouTube videos, I've decided to give it a shot - and man, WHAT A RIDE.
I didn't expect i would get such a high value product from an inexperienced (by amount of titles released) team of ONLY 3 PEOPLE, PRICED ONLY 19.99$ on release. You don't see it a lot these days.
The Good:
- The art style is incredible, and even if you think the game looks weird, it plays fluently and catches you in the first moments you try it. The 1930's style complements the game's aesthetic and just feels right.
- The Music is INCREDIBLE. It will get into your head (wait until you get to King Dice's room).
- The controls are easy to learn, but hard to master. I've played on a controller, so i can't vouch for KB&M, but my experience was fluid.
- The originality of the world, level, enemies and bosses will surprise you with every encounter. Even if it is inspired by older games and cartoons, the sharp design just feels genuine and creative.
- The Story is pretty weird, but in a good way. You will smile often as many small details will uncover before your eyes. It's a really cool throwback to those obscure but funny old cartoons.
- There a few neat weapons and special attacks you can choose from, so try to find the way that feels the most comfortable for you to play and don't be afraid to test out  different methods for different boss and enemy encounters.
- Difficulty: Hard, but fair (can get overwhelming so take breaks if you feel like you had too much).
- Has it's own secrets so be sure to explore the world, and try to find creative ways to tackle every obstacle you meet.
- Has local COOP.
The Neutral:
- The default control scheme (on the controller) can be a bit uncomfortable, so if you feel it's not right just go ahead and change it. I have assigned the attack to RT, lock on to LT and the dash to B (XBOX controller) and it immediately felt better.
- Mostly a boss rush. Although there are a few Run n' Gun levels, it's mostly bosses. Can be a good or a bad thing, to each his own.
- The COOP can be funny, but it adds up more HP to your enemies, so in my opinion it's better to start alone, get used to the game, and then try the COOP.
The Bad:
- Currently it only has local COOP, and no multiplayer (maybe there are future plans, i don't know).
- Some special attacks leave you vulnerable after the execution, so be wary of that. I think it would be more fair to add slightly a bit more iFrames after the end of the special attack animation, because this is the only design choice that feels (for me at least) like artificial difficulty and not something you can overcome by getting better. It's not THAT bad, but can sometimes feel unfair and lead to unnecessary losses.
- Can sometimes get your eyes exhausted, it's like an acid trip with the animations, music and voices (maybe that's a good thing?). anyway, TAKE BREAKS!
In Conclusion - Surprisingly, this little game shines above many, and i'm still surprised it was made by a small team of people. The dedication and love that was put into it didn't let me rest until i sat down and wrote this review because Cuphead truly deserves the praise it gets. Bonus - it triggers gaming journalists :)

Now, before you decide to bash me for disapproving this game, please let me reflect some of my thoughts.
Syder Arcade is your typical spaceship shooter, that's ok to me, I like them a lot, even if they can get so generic. This game is sort of cheap 2.5D version of Defender, there is no doubt about that. 2.5D feels a little like unnecessary memory allocation and doesn't offer much gameplay-wise, other than giving you false impression of things you can touch and cannot, such as landscapes. Retro filters are nice idea, but in the end they are just video filters that make it harder to see what's going on, making some of the small enemy projectiles rather sneaky. I have seen games that do the same thing with changing whole tilesets and sprites while still giving the same feel to the game but offering fresh look at the game. Syder Arcade fails to impress here but I like the idea it is going for. There is no excuse. Just not fair enough.
You have four initial ships to choose from, but other than having different kind of weapons they don't make gameplay feel much different from each other. Variety is always a good thing tho, even when minimal. I like the way ships look. Enemy variety on the other hand is quite low profile and you'll be shooting through same masses over and over again. Luckily game has just handful of levels. There was a story mode too, but as an arcade man I couldn't care about anything that takes more than 2 lines. Tried reading it too, but it wasn't interesting or cheesy enough. But that could be just me. It is there though if you want it.
Controls are kinda stiff. Sometimes its very hard to dodge projectiles or enemies even with fastest ship. Hard to spot projectiles don't help much. I tried using arcade stick for maximum potential but it still felt kind of slow. Scoring system has nice idea to it with badges and such, but very often you get exactly the same ones. I chuckled at the easiest difficulty describing the player growing up with modern consoles because that is exactly what comes to my mind with this game.

Having a rather biased opinion of what I wanted/expected from this game due to having played it's prequel for years, I must say i was rather shocked. Patience is my weapon. It had taken me ten minutes but I had finally done it. The demolished building behind the advancing German line had long since been cleared out. A bloody mess of soviet and german bodies littered the ground and the steel boots of german footsoldeirs pounded the wooden floors of the buildings behing me. I crept amidst the bodies of these men and into the attic. My rifle only had one clip left following a prolonged seige in the schoolhouse, but this was enough for my goal. The floor was cold as the snowflakes swung back and forth through the blown roof and rested upon my back. In my scope I tracked german soldier after german soldier, imagining myself sqeezing the trigger, imagining the red puff that would emerge from their necks, imagining the red snow beneath their body. I held my fire. They're KAR98k rifles gave them away to be nothing more than footsoldiers. A worthless target for my five bullets. I swept my scope across the lines, seeing my comrades holding fast in the distance. I radioed in the opponents troop movements to my commander and held my fire. Then I saw it. The pinacle of german light weaponry. The MP40. The squad leader. His troops swarmed around him as they prepared to flank with the cover of smoke towards my allies. I lined upon his head and fired. The puff of red and the pool of blood was a welcomign sight. Panicked his men stormed through the smoke and were met with a volley of russian rifle fire. Without a moments hesitation I swung my scope to the left flank. An MG had setup in the nearby church and was completely covered from his front. It was a perfect firing line upon the russian reinforcements, and had claimed many a comrades life. His back however, small as it was in the distance, was wide open to my mosin. It was nothing more than a speck. I waited for him to fire, and watched the flash. I aimed slightly behind and above the flash and pulled. Another headshot. I waited, knowing that an MG of his calibre would have back up. Like clockwork his partner picked up the MG42 and began firing. I held my breath and let another shot fly. Footsteps! An enemy sniper had heard my shots and came running across the open street before me. Another shot and another body. My job was done here. I had a single bullet left. The MG squad was down, the First squad leader was dead, and their counter sniper had fallen. I snuck around in the shadows behind enemy lines until the last German had fallen, picking up any weapon I could find and always holding fire until I saw an officer. By the days end I had fired twenty shots and had confirmed twenty priority kills. The German offensive had been halted.

Overall, this game is superb in most aspects so there's no point in explaining them as they're quite self-explanatory, if you're looking to buy it I would definitely recommend it. It does have a couple flaws however, so I will quickly touch on them.
Firslty, the game isn't fully optimised and at some points fps can drop substantially causing lag spikes for everyone on a server, eg. in caves or running through the forest.
Secondly, if a player alt-tabs during the game in a server, the day/night cycle will rapidly increase meaning 6 days could have passed in a minutes time. This doesn't mean that much but as the number of days increase so does the difficulty so I would watch out for it.
Finally, (Spoilers) when defeating the end boss, if a player in the party dies just before the boss is defeated you will respawn at the plane whilst your friends are still in the lab, this means you cannot complete the game without having to spend 30 minutes trying to get back to your friends.
Hope this review helps, left a couple of minor details out as long reviews are boring, peace. -Oreon

Being a big fan of MMORPG's I had heard of the Ragnarok series beforehand, and therefore thought it would be a fun game to play. I had watched the trailer and loved the art, so I went ahead and downloaded it- only to be dissapointed to find out that the game didn't work. When entering the game for the first time I was welcomed with laggy, buggy characters, which eventually ended up freezing my pc. A broken, generic MMORPG which is pay2win.

Pros
- The general look of the game is top notch. It's very appealing to look at.
- The soundtrack is decent, albeit forgetable.
- Changes in armor and weaponry are actually shown on the sprites, which makes equipping new gear feel much better.
- The Teamwork function is pretty neat. It allows for some pretty interesting tactics in combat. Having one character toss another character in order to move them closer to an enemy is a cool way to move around the map. I just wish it was more fledged out. I feel like this would be a great feature if it was just developed a bit more.
Cons
- The game is very easy. I'm playing on the hardest difficulty and I'm having no trouble so far.
- Customization feels pointless. It doesn't matter what you call your crew, your show, your attack names, etc. It's just there for the sake of having it as a selling point.
- The writing is terrible. It actually has smileys - :) - written in speech bubbles. As though the characters are somehow able to pronounce ":)". Furthermore, not an hour in and the game blatantly tries to push an agenda down your throat by (poorly) criticizing the "damsel in distress" trope. A character mentions that his sister would like to appear on the show in respone to them needing someone to play the role of hostage, which another character immediately says they cannot allow, and they find a male person to play the role of hostage instead. It's never explained WHY having a woman in that role would be bad, they just say it's bad.
- You cannot influence the episodes in any way. How you take out enemies, how many of your crew members go down in battle, how long it takes, etc... All of that only influences how many fans your show gets, and it's all completely arbitrary. (A hero falling in battle for any reason will cause you to lose viewers, while something as simple as moving a hero around on the map can cause you to gain viewers.)
- Mecha battles are insultingly simple. You have the option to either attack or defend. You can attack as many times as you want, but your chance to hit decreases with each succesful strike. Defending ends your turn and gives you a bonus to defense, which increases the more times you've hit your opponent this turn. On your opponent's turn, you just click the mouse button at the right time to reduce damage. Eventually, you gain access to a finishin move, which deals high damage and ends your turn instantly. That's all.
I came into this expecting something like Agarest mixed with Game Maker Tycoon. I have to say, I'm very disappointed. Even if you're a huge fan of Sentai shows, I imagine the cringy dialogue, boring story, and shallow gameplay will start to rub you the wrong way eventually.
I cannot recommend this game to anyone, and it is certainly not worth the asking price. I doubt I'll ever finish the game, so I don't even consider it worth my time.

But fear not! Even if you know almost nothing about this sort of stuff, you'll still find something for yourself :).
Pros:
+ choose your own team - Want to have all female squad? Here you go! Or maybe men only (men dressed as panda by any chance...?). Why not! But how about... A robot? Or an alien? Or maybe even a beaver?
+ crafting, managing your own studio, buying upgrades, fan mails... Don't you have a feeling that sometimes game developers give us just "naked" game, without any substance besides main action? Well, you won't have this feeling here.
+ graphic - I cannot imagine better graphic style for this game.
+ music - simply awesome. I think Lord Gaga's theme will stay in my memory for pretty long time.
+ tons and tons of references!
+ funny, self-aware, full of intended cliches. If it won't make you laugh, it'll at least make you smile.
+ awesome, hilarious enemies.
+ challenging but not frustrating - I finished game on medium difficulty. It can be pretty challenging when you try to fulfill all goals, but still it's not that hard that you want to throw your PC out ;).
Sadly, there are also cons:
- too long fights. Not all of them, of course, some are very quickly, but there's tons of fights that just take too much damn time and it's not because player don't use proper strategy. No, no. It's because there are fights with tons of enemie's minions and each one of them need to make a move, EACH turn, and sometimes it really takes forever. And if you add mines/sprouts to that... It's just hell. And I don't think there's a way to skip it. There was a time, when I literally step away from my computer for a few minutes and when I get back, last enemies were still moving.
- mecha combat - it breaks my heart, but it may be one of the weakest points of this game. Of course you need to have huge robots and huge monsters with the game heavily inspired by Power Rangers. And don't get me wrong, crafting upgrades for your Mecha is pretty interesting, but fight itself... Boring and repetitive. If Mecha battles were reserved only for final episodes/bosses then maybe I wouldn't have this opinion, but they are a regular part o game. And they look exactly the same. You make combos, that ends with special move/defense or just because you didn't manage to do another attack. Then your opponent attacks - always three times (and sometimes there's a special move). You defend yourself by clicking in the right moment. And then the process continue. Regular fights are fun (if they don't take too long), because you have different enemies, with different skills, minions, attacks, goals etc. Here, no matter who your opponent is, fight ALWAYS looks the same. There's no much strategy involved.

The encounter system absolutely ruined this game.  To those of you saying "it's just like the board game..." It might be, I haven't played it.  But it sucks.
Essentially, EVERY turn that you DON'T explore an adjacent tile, you get penalized.  That can possibly damage you, stun you, spawn an extra monster, etc.  And this happens for EACH character at the end of each of their turn.  I hate, hate, hate it.  The game seems super interesting, but this one system caused me to quit after less than 2 hours, simply because it isn't fun and the extra "challenge factor" makes no sense at all.  It's designed to artifically introduce difficulty and encourage exploration, but every turn?  Really?  Forcing me to decide where to move, even if there are already enemies threatening me, just to "encourage" exploration is a crappy system.
Hey, there's a chest I want to open that's more than 1 tile away.  move there, open the chest, and then get penalized for not being near an unexplored tile.
Fighting an enemy that you don't kill in a single round?  Better run next to an unexplored tile in case you take extra damage or get stunned for a turn.
And I'll re-iderate: this happens for every character you control, every round.
Yes, I devoted this entire review to criticizing one gameplay mechanic.  Maybe that's saying something.  Play at your own risk.

Alright. Lets get this out of the way.
IT HAS EXPENSIVE DLC. Yeah, it does because everyone else does and why not. I bought the DLC, not because I will use the skins, but because I love this game and wanted to help it grow and fund it.
Lets talk abou the game itself now:
It's different. In the short time I've played, the hunter side is fun. Yeah it's a FPS catching up on the jetpack eveywhere space that games are going now, but the combat is class based, and I think it does it right. If you are a medic, your job is not too snipe the monster in battle. Its too not die and heal the other people, otherwise your team will lose.
If you're support, your job is too shield the group and support them. Trappers actually have to focus on keeping the monster from running away, which it can and will do. And if you're assult, deal damage like all hell is breaking loose.
I dont see many games now a days that actually follow the class rules theyre given, but every game I've played with Evolve has kept to their class.
And the monster class is EXTREMELY fun to play. If youre smart about it you can wipe out the entire hunter team without them even knowing. It's cool how they set this game up. Yeah their is one real game mode, but no game is the same, each battle is how the players make it.
In short, yes the game has a single mode right now thats fun, and yes the DLC is extremely expensive.
It is worth it to buy it, and if you want the DLC, you're helping fund the company to do more. So go for it.
If you hate the singlarity of the game modes, think about it this way. On League Of Legends, there is one map people play THOUSANDS of times. You dont get tired of that because people play it differently each time, so dont get tired of this. You have as much work as making this game as anyone else, it just gives you the tools to play a really awesome game.

Evolve is an incredibly fun game with strong mechanics and a ♥♥♥♥ing beautiful look and feel to the game. The matches are wide and varied with 3 monsters, 12 hunters, 4 modes and a dozen or so maps that each have their own environmental hazards and wildlife that serve different functions. It's satisfying and a joy to play and it's only going to get better as more and more content is released. (DLC strike and all aside, if they make maps into a necessary DLC thing and start limiting wider gameplay I'm going to immediately change the tone of this review.)
Of course, every game has its faults. The climbing is sometimes wonky on monsters and the matchmaking is mediocre at best. I've been thrown into a game as a monster I don't own at half health being tracked down by eager hunters not once, not twice, but three times. Coming into the middle of a game is jarring and confusing, and chances are the slot was open because some other guy saw that it was a losing game and dodged right the hell out. The punishment for leaving should be made a little more severe if it's going to be there at all. Godforbid you give them a minute to get a snack and a drink before they enter their next game.
As with all things online the people you get matched up with are going to decide the outcome of your experience. Pissy people will make for poor team play which makes for a crap game. I implore you not to judge the game based on its douchey minority.
Overall the game is excellent, the community has held up as solid despite a very visible minority of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Well worth the money I spent on it.
