The reviews Evolve has got on Steam are atrocious. The DLC-hating bandwagon is truly impressive, but I feel the game deserves a review that says something about the game itself.
Evolve is a FPS-game with a horror/survival/mayhem streak. You play either as one of the Hunters or as the Monster. Hunters are a bunch of colourful... space hunters, that are hired to solve the monster problem on Shear (the planet Evolve happens on). As ahunter, you basically zig-zag around the map, try to listen to monster footsteps, watch for birds and trust your trapper to find and trap the beast, so you can take it down.
Monster players plays one of the three (at launch) monsters. The goal of the monster is to feed, evolve and destroy the hunters. The Monster starts out weak and must try to feed in order to evolve (get more abilities and health). At this point it's cat and mouse and the hunters are trying to catch and trap the Monster as soon as possible. The monsters are very different from each other and provide each a very different kind of round based on which is picked.
Once the monster evolves, the tables are turned. The Monster is suddenly more powerful than a hunter group and at this point can start hunting them. The games last around 3-15 minutes each. If the hunters can catch the monster early (which is suuuuper frustrating for the monster) they can end the round in just a couple of minutes. Longest games take about 15 minutes, if the monster keeps evolving and picking off the hunters one at a time.
There's a bunch of different kind of gamemodes too and a mini-campaign, that I found quite fun. The DLC-business that everyone is so hilariously uproared about is mostly bogus. The DLC are reskinks and there's tons of content on the game already. At later point they will introduce more monsters as DLC though. Which I think is awesome, as even these three monsters are so unlike each other. If the next monster will be as fun as the three in the game right now, I can't wait to get it.
I have never enjoyed a PvP-FPS so much. All parts of the game are super-intense, as you either are scared of the hunters, scared of the huge flaming stage 3 King Kong or lying in a bush ready to pick apart a solitary hunter that strays a bit too far from the main group. Highly recommend!

First of all, this game is excellent.
The strategy is deep and addictive, with a nice little twist (the sports aspect).
My only real beef is that it could be SO MUCH MORE. And I'm not talking about the gameplay itself. The only real problem I've encountered with the actual matches themselves is that sometimes very close running/tackling situations do not play out like they're supposed to, but that happens so infrequently that it's not that big a deal.
It's the story/league, robot customization, etc. that could really stand to be fleshed out a lot.
For instance, during the season mode, you can earn money by winning and betting on games. But there's so little to actually buy with it that money doesn't even matter after the end of your first season.
You can buy a different robot model... but there's only one of them.
You can buy different stadiums... but they're the signature stadiums that the other teams in your league already use.
You can buy "holograms" that change the look of your robot... but they're extremely cheap and you can only use a few of them at a time.
I think it'd add a lot of replayability to the game to be able to do more with your robots and stadiums. Let me buy unique stadiums, customize the endzone, switch out the actual parts on my robots, etc. In short, give me stuff to spend money on and upgrade. It doesn't have to change the entire game. Just cosmetic items that make me want to keep playing.
Maybe even give small stat boosts for different items, so you can further cater your team to your playing style. For instance, legs that give your whole team +1 blocking but -1 speed.
More importantly, I think the actually roster management, etc. could stand to be fleshed out. It's extremely barebones compared to any actual sports game on the market.
Don't get me wrong... I wasn't expecting it to have the depth of franchises like NBA 2k or Madden, that have been around for decades.
But the entire roster management just boils down to releasing inferior/injured players and signing better players every week. As you win games, your salary cap goes up, meaning you can afford to put together a roster with better stats.
There's a "draft" but it makes absolutely no sense. It just shows you the players' college stats. You pick the guy with the best stats you can find, and he turns out to be terrible. And he's not just terrible... he's actually weakest in the areas his stats imply he should be good at. How did a player with -4 interception lead the college league in interceptions?
Going back to the salary cap... it goes up, but not down (at least not that I've seen). So basically your team just gets better and better and better as time goes on. And you can cut and sign new players every week without any consequence.
It's not like a traditional sports league where you're constantly having to manage the cap, resign players, and hope for a good draft. You could essentially change out your entire roster after every game. It takes away all of the weight from roster decisions.
Overall, it'd be awesome to see brief scouting reports/combine numbers for the draft, trades, a fixed salary cap for all teams, etc.
BUT don't misinterpret my suggestions as this being a bad game. It's a very good and unique game.
Just as someone who's a fan of both strategy and sports games, I think they could do more with the non-gameplay aspects. It would help the replayability a lot since the game doesn't have much of an online community at the moment.
I'm definitely glad I bought this game though and would recommend it 99.9%.

I was expecting something like the old Crush Deluxe game that used to be out on DOS, and Frozen Cortex is similar to that. I liked Frozen Cortex a lot at first, but now I'm in the 'it's OK' camp.
Pros:
1. The tactics are subtle and excellent. A situation on the field can be completely turned upside down by a slight difference in movement from a player.
2. The use of players in these tactics is also very good. It doesn't seem like there's too much difference between one player and another at first, but I start finding that I'll do something based on player matchups that I see. Again, the tactics are excellent. Just great, the way it's done.
Cons:
1. This sounds weird, but they used way more graphics than they needed to for this game. The 3-D field makes it hard sometimes to tell what kind of pass an opponent is capable of. Camera angles are awkward. Also there are a bunch of animations on and around the field that aren't needed at all other than for eye candy, and those things utterly destroy my framerate.
2. You can't improve your 'robot' players, so there isn't the sense of developing a talent that you'd get with other management sims. When you can afford a better robot, buy it immediately and drop whoever. It's not a strategic, long term thinking game. It's strictly about tactics in individual games.
* Edit - After a good deal of play, gotta add 3rd and 4th cons.
3. The other commenters complaining that the AI teams are too strong proved correct for me, too. I'm in my 4th season, I have a decent team, I've won about 60-70% of my games since the beginning, but I still can spend only half of the money that the AI teams do. One of the opposing teams has three players (out of 5) who are literally maxed out in every attribute. None of my players would even make their starting lineup. It's tough to even stay in the game against them; beating them is impossible. Even if you outstrategize the other manager, it doesn't matter because their players are so fast, so strong, so everything, that they'll still beat you. Very frustrating because even after all this time, I simply cannot buy anything better than a decent player. And while I know I can grind my way past that, I'm not sure I want to anymore. I've put in the time, won some games... let me buy some players already. The salary cap setup in single player is BS.
4. The college leagues look interesting but are really meaningless. You can't coach one. You can fill out a bracket, and bet on the games, but the winners are pretty much random. The money you win on betting isn't the same currency you actually use in-game. You use betting currency just to buy cosmetic crap... I don't get the point.
Anyway, there is a draft of college players, but drafted players are nearly always awful... like 'Never use them in a game under any circumstances' awful. You don't even know their attributes until after you pick them. So you have to build via free agency, and you can't do that as much as you'd like because of issue number 3.
I'm on the fence about this game now. I'm still recommending it, but it's a cautious 'recommend'. It's worth picking up in a sale but not for full price.

I've recently finished up a second playthrough of this game (the first being on the PlayStation 3), and unfortunately did not enjoy the game as much a second time around (more on this later).
After the first playthrough, I had the same feelings most people had after their initial encounter with Bioshock and the city of Rapture: awe, shock, and love. The story was gripping with one heck of a plot twist that was far from cliche. The city was fantastical and mesmerizing with it's old-world charm. I enjoyed roaming around corridors that led to who-knows-where and to who-knows-what: finding audio journals that gave glimpses into the history of the city or into the lives of the inhabitants that once roamed around.
However, after my second playthrough, now knowing the story, I had differing final opinions on the game from that of my first playthrough. I began to notice a few things that brought the game down a few notches in my mind.

The first of which being that the game's combat, although fun, is a little unpolished. The majority of the plasmids are completely useless (unless entertainment is what you seek), weapons aren't balanced (the crossbow is absolutely ridiculous), and you can honestly run through the entire game quite easily with just the shock plasmid and a wrench. Second, if  you're a fiend for audio journals and lore, be prepared to be constantly irritated by splicers interrupting your listening.
Finally, there were a few issues that I found occurred on the PC version (I never had these issues on the PlayStation 3). Audio tends to occasionally have hitches and stutters that, although not bad, were occasionally annoying. Also, if you decide to play with subtitles (dang near required if you want to know what audio journals are saying while being destroyed by splicers), they have a tendency to disappear onscreen midway through speaking.
Overall, it's a fantastic game and a must play. Don't let any of my qualms convince you out of playing - you will enjoy it.

Arx Fatalis is an RPG created by the same people who brought you the fun but somewhat flawed Dark Messiah: Might and Magic. Make no mistate though, Arx Fatalis is the game Arkane Studios was born to create. It's and classic RPG dungeon crawl in the vein of Ultima Underworld. You play and amnesiatic hero as he makes his way through the tunnels and dungeons of a vast underground system. What makes the game unique is it's magic system and subtle populating of this underground world. First, a dungeon crawler can sometimes seem rather lonely, with only the monster for company. Not so in Arx Fatalis, where entire city's exist and NPC are met frequently. Even more interesting is the magic system. Most game simply have you choose a spell and then CLICK, fire, done. In Arx Fatalis, the player has to use his mouse to draw a spell, making the act of casting a much more involved procedure.  However, a spell can be draw up, and then saved for later, to be launch with a mouseclick.

First off I demand to play Mugman in Singleplayer. He is awesome, so is Cuphead but I also love Mugman's design. ANYWHO. The style is flashy, cartoony and rememberable. The bosses are fun, and the soundtrack is gorgeous. The gameplay is challenging to say the least. It mostly operates on bosses guiding you to bosses that improve your actual skills while the run and gun segments are more for collecting coins to find specials, and new weapon types. The weapon types and effectiveness really depend on you as a player. While some people might find dodging and using a homing target gun good, others prefer the spread and charged shot. It reminds me of the original megaman, except instead of lives you take hits. The difficulty is akin to hitting your head against a wall, eventually breaking through and feeling like you achieved something. The 1930s Disney cartoon feel make me feel reinvigorated to try the boss again, and find more secrets on the map. The supers help, and everything has  a place. You can simply beat a boss, or try to get its soul contract at a higher difficulty. It pushes players to play better. If I had two gripes. They arent deal breakers just things that would have made bosses a million percent more fun is knowing how much damage you've done whether its cracks in a boss or a simple health bar it would make me feel like I can experiment with different weapons and see how I can knock a boss down easier. Second I want to play Mugman in Singleplayer. In any case having some cracks in a boss to show progress or a health bar would be nice but that said its a fantastic game and NEEDS to be in your library. Even with the difficulty I find the charm of the game overwhelming. 5/5

I don't really like the horror genre, in general, however I wanted to play through something short and atmospheric on Halloween night... alone... in the dark... with the surround sound speakers on. Atmospheric it was, and I certainly yelled profanity at the screen a few times, however the whole ride lasted 2.2 hours with a lot of pausing and getting-up to do stuff. I would say that 1.5 hours is about the total play-through if you check every nook and cranny.
The game is a walking simulator and there is only one ending. The story unravels through notes and documents you find around the park, and it was not hard finding everything. There is no replayability, and quite frankly, I would not want to go back to it, either. Despite what some reviewers stated, the game DOES make sense, however there are purposeful omissions as to what actually happened because this game is supposed to tie-in with the MMO "The Secret World" where this park is a location. If you really want the full scoop, there is at least one thread that makes sense of the loose ends also.
The game atmosphere and parts of the story feels a lot like Bioshock to me, however there is no real interaction with anything and the only goal is to go down a single linear path, which tricks you into thinking there are multiple paths until you walk in a direction you are not supposed to. Once the game is complete, it's done and you will have all achievements if you experimented with some things like I did, even without guides.
I would recommend this game to anybody who wants a short walking simulator with great graphics, really creepy atmosphere, and a few "oh sh!t!" moments... on sale. Full price seems a bit much due to your other gaming options available today. If you are expecting 1.5 hours of walking and reading at your pace followed by a short online search for the answers on the missing bits, the game delivers nicely.
A couple of notes I want to make is that I feel like my avatar was a bit more scared/confused than I was in 50% of the situations... I guess it would be scarier if I was actually there, though... the really confusing part to me, but which was not to my avatar, is why the heck am I riding on random rides when I'm looking for my lost child?! WHY?! It's pretty obvious that your kid is not on any of the rides... but yes, they were all creepy and unraveled bits of the story.

The Park is a first person walking simulator mixed with a quite amount of horror. You play as Lorraine, searching for your missing son who runs into Atlantic Island Park, a place that might seem normal at first, but is definitely a very unwelcoming location. Filled with stories of murderers and coincidentally uneventful accidents, Atlantic Island Park is not what the average park seems like, this is a much darker place to explore. While exploring as Lorraine, the desperate mom to find her son, you can shout for Callum in which you're given a visual tip of where to go or what to read around the park. It's an interesting mechanic to avoid the usual waypoints or mini maps with marked objectives. It is worth mentioning that this shout will change throughout the game, adapting itself to Lorraine's situation, making it creepier at times.
This is a nice looking game powered by the greatness of Unreal Engine 4. It ran mostly fine on the highest settings on my gaming laptop. The atmosphere is creepily haunting and darkly uncomfortable throughout the entirety the game, with off-putting sound effects and authentic-feeling voice acting that helps set up the feel of Lorraine's journey. While I haven't played the game in VR, I'm honestly interested in trying that out in the future. The atmosphere sucked me in well enough in a simple monitor, it must feel great with a VR headset.
Story-wise it's a confusing game. Obviously I'm not going to spoil anything crucial to the story, but the game has an abrupt ending that leaves you questioning what have you played for the last hour and a half. Of course there's theories, but nothing is a definitive explanation of what you've experienced. However, this park is actually part of The Secret World, another game. You can visit this same place on The Secret World and have some more input to this story and even do quests related to it, so it is possible this story will make a bit more sense in case you played TSW before.
I do have to write about the second but shorter section of The Park named the House of Horrors. This section of the game is absolutely phenomenally inspired by P.T., a demo I never got to play (I say that with a deep sadness of mine). Approaching the end of the game during this section, the rooms change each time you go by them, and these changes may be subtle, or noticeably severe. The House of Horrors is what made me realize this wasn't just another one of those walking simulators, or another one of those horror copycats that we see every day on Steam nowadays. The sudden shift in level design from open areas to closed spaces while still having the creepy atmosphere, concludes the game on a high note, which I personally prefer compared to walking around exploring the park and looking for Callum.
The first and most exploration focused "level" is good, don't get me wrong, but the second part is just miles better for me. Not to mention that dreadfully long section about Hansel and Gretel right at entrance of the park. I do know of it's importance for the game's story and how it unfolds, but that section is 7 minutes of doing absolutely nothing, just the story of Hansel and Gretel being narrated to you with voice recordings. While I was able to tolerate it in the end given it's importance, it's by far the least enjoyable part of the game.
Being a first person horror game and also a walking simulator, The Park is a wonderful experience. As I mentioned previously, the game's weakness is length. If you don't read anything and keep running through most of the game (which is not the way to play it), it takes about 30 minutes to complete. I did a playthrough in 2 hours if I recall correctly, because I read every note and explored everything there was to explore. With a price tag of 13€ at the moment, it is definitely a game to grab on a nice sale.
"In my heart and mind, I always return to Atlantic Island Park" 8/10

I have not played in three months and have only just come back to semi-serious playtime since interest has been piqued over this weekend's 40%-off sale.
Most of the criticism the game has received comprises accusations of a high price point and "day-one downloadable content", conveniently omitting the fact that the overwhelming majority of said price consists of cosmetic skins for the hunters and monsters.
Straight out of the box the vanilla game is playable and many meta teams - if that is your flavour of shooter - do not require additional hunters .Sure, you have to pay for a monster here and a hunter tier there but I haven't heard of anyone complain about non-essential content sold later in any other game either. And those are not day-one either, as anything after the first three tiers was released at least a month later and/or tied to pre-order bonuses and season pass.
I will not even give the point about the state of the playerbase, since most out there are impressionable and ignorant, and would have been influenced by equally ignorant and scathing reviews of a game they barely put any hours into.
What I will give is the state of the game: an extremely steep learning curve and a 100% mission-critical need for teamwork and decent level of skill. Good monsters will play by themselves and dunk on matchmade hunters; good hunters who inevitably have to solo queue will likely get a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ teammates and have to face off against aforementioned monster plus dunking. (This will demoralise anyone faint of heart, and to find these people you just have to look at every other negative review aside from those already mentioned who ignore the cosmetic nature of DLC.)
On that note, competitive play is still going strong, with a proper ESL showing and Go4Evolve every weekend. Tune in to those tourneys to get a look at what you're missing.

To be bluntly honest, I really hate this game. It's actually pretty difficult for me to explain my reasoning for why I dislike it to a person who hasn't actually played this game, but a lot of the problem is that the game ultimately came across as pretentious when I played it, which ruined any sort of emotional impact the narrative might have generated. It's not so much that the story being told is inherently bad (in fact, I might argue that the narrative was reasonably clever), but the delivery of the narritive quickly began to grate on my nerves. I felt that much of the moralistic story-telling in this narrative was clumsily implemented (or ham-fisted, if you will), and this meant that I could always tell what sort of emotions I was expected to feel, rather than actually feeling those emotions for myself. Essentially, I felt as though the game was telling me that I ought to feel specific ways about specific moments, rather than allowing me to experience my own emotions on the matter and develop my own opinions. Therefore, the game and its narrative struck me as very disingenuous, thereby ruining the experience.

9/12/2015
♥Five Nights at Freddy's is a simple horror game where you take up night shifts as a security guard for Freddy's resturant, strange and frightening things being to happen when the animatronics seem to develop a mind of their own after 12AM. You have a limited amount of power and thus, very limited visibility while you struggle to decide if you want to keep the cameras/lights on or the doors kept sealed.First of all, I am really glad that I took the time to play Five Nights at Freddy's, even though it's not the type of game or genre I would normally go for, it turned out to be a lot of fun and actually pretty scary, even though you know what's coming after a couple of play-throughs, the game still has an ability to keep you on the edge of your seat.For a game with a simple premise and simple controls (monitor the cameras, click the doors or lights when needed), the game is immensely terrifying. There's no background music, save for occasional moments where the Toreador March plays (which, trust me, is not a good thing), leaving players to deal only with the background noises: the hum of the desk fan, the buzz of the florescent lights, the clattering in the kitchen, the footsteps down a dark hall, the dum-dee-dum of the characters... the silence, truly, is disturbing. Combine the simple controls, the nerve-wracking environment, and the lack of music, and within moments (and it's actually happening to me just recalling it) your palms are sweaty, your heart races, and every noise causes a panicked twitch.It's too bad that the franchise is way too over hyped, but it's still a good game!♥

I can't figure out why I never got into this game earlier.  I love FPSs, but I had mostly been playing the likes of "Call of Duty" single-player campaigns, and I soon saw how boring they were getting. I liked how the old FPSs really got you immersed in the worlds they've made, at least until recently. After playing "Wolfenstein: The New Order" on my Xbox One, it reinvigorated my spirit and my joy at playing FPSs.
Then I decided to start playing games on my PC again, and I looked on this site, and there was "Bioshock" (and it's two sequels), and I decided to give it a try. And boy, do I not regret it. This game is very nice, and it really got me immersed in it. That, in my opinion, is a sign they're doing something right.
The graphics are pretty good for their time, the location is very nice, the gameplay is very easy to learn, and I like how this game gives you freedom.
Rapture itself is a unique kind of location, it's the kind of location you really want to learn about, and this game does just that when you collect the Audio Tapes. And I said, the detail is gorgeous, the sights really do evoke a feeling that Rapture was once a very classy and stylish city once upon a time. When I started playing this, I really felt like this was something that came out of a World's Fair of the 1930s-1940s. I really had fun exploring this city. Yes, this game is clearly old in terms of graphics and effects, but I'm cutting it some slack.
The gameplay is what you'd expect from an FPS, but, that's what makes it easy to learn, since I've played a lot of FPSs over the years, so it was easy to get into. The Plasmids were very creative, and some were what you'd expect, like Telekinesis, Pyrokinesis, etc., combined with the Tonics, you could make Jack (the player character) your own character, which brings me to my next point. I really love how this game avoids giving you greater rewards for using stealth. Most games try to shift you towards a stealth approach to get a greater reward, which is okay, but at times, it can feel restrictive, and limit your creativity. With this game, there is no real need for that, you can decide if you like to shoot your way through or not, hack turrets and cameras, or even sneak around, if that's your style. I didn't like having to switch from Plasmids to weapons all the time, but with my mouse, it really wasn't a big deal.
The morality part of the plot was black and white, which, although simple, actually works just fine. This game avoids letting the morality get too overcomplicated, or  make it feel like the wrong choice in the long run.
The plot itself was predictable, even if you don't pick up on some clues along the way, but even so, it evokes a response from you, and makes you want to keep going, despite the obvious twists. The antagonists really made me mad, and I wanted to get to them.
I didn't like the Hacking minigame either, especially later on in the game, when the bombs and alarms would be so numerous you might end up getting stuck because of how they're positioned. I was lucky to have enough med-kits on hand to survive failed attempts.
The enemy variety was okay, the Splicers weren't too challenging, except for Spider and Houdini Splicers, which were annoying as hell. But as I advanced, and took photos, it wasn't so bad. Oh, word of advice: when you get the camera: TAKE PHOTOS! You'll want the upgrades that come with 'em. Also, the Big Daddies, I like how they don't force you into a fight with them all the time. It gives you time to load up the proper weapons and plasmids to take 'em on.
Overall, this game, even if I played it eight years late, it still holds up very well for me. The setting is very nice and draws you in, the gameplay has a smooth learning curve, the game avoided overcomplicating the plot and morality, keeping it nice and simple. It has definitely earned it's spot as one of the best video games ever made. I intend to keep playing this series, and I will be playing this game again when I can.

I want to recommend this game, but I can't.  I want to LIKE this game, but I can't.
A deep, rich strategic experience in a novel format (i.e. future sportsball)?  Practically auto-sold on this game.  After playing through the tutorial, I get the basics of how to plan turns and such, so I move on to the Basic League.
Here's the thing, though:  this game does a terrible job of explaining itself.  I know how to move my bots, but not why I should.  It takes me a couple games before I realize that the goal of the game is less "get the ball in the end zone," and more "figure out what your opponent isn't going to expect or counter, and do that," but I STILL don't know how to reliably gauge what are good options or plays.  Half the time it feels like whatever I simulated during the Planning Phase doesn't work out -- bots don't block like I expect them to, or (more importantly) chase the ball carrier like I expect them to.   The bots have half a dozen stats that aren't even mentioned in the game tutorial/help (nor shown in the tabular Free Agent view).  I still don't know what the hell "Halt" does.
Undeterred, I move on to the regular League, hoping that will give me more options for managing my team between games.  But then I discover that I have the worst bots in the GCL, and my salary cap goes up by a paltry few hundred dollars per win while the free agents' "expected" salary shoots up by over a thousand dollars per game week.  So, I'm basically stuck with my starting lineup of losers and mostly-losers, facing off against teams with all green (positive) stats -- my bot tackled an enemy bot who literally shrugged it off and walked past because his RESIL was maxed.   I'm playing a game that appears to be about outmaneuvering/out-thinking an enemy when I am unable to estimate the outcome of a play and don't even really know which plays are good ones, AND my guys are the worst bots in the League?  The only way out appears to be to grind losses until I get better at understanding how to make the best plays possible with my awful lineup, and after 15 losses I don't think I want to play anymore.
I think part of this could be made better if there was a better strategy guide to the game, but I didn't see anything like it online.  There was a section of Mode7's forums devoted to Frozen Cortex, but there was nothing useful there.  It's a shame, the game seems like it has a great depth of strategy to it, but it's too obfuscated and inaccessible to new players.

Tales from Candlekeep: Tomb of Annihilation, a turn-based dungeon-crawling game based on the Dungeons & Dragons Adventure System board games.
I recommend Tales from Candlekeep for players who like board games or people who are patient. The game can be too slow for people who didn't know what it means. It's not like baldur's gate, dragon age 1 ...
I recommend you watch a gameplay video before buying it or not.
Pro :
- Niche game where you will discover a new gameplay experience, different from other video games
- The price is low for a game of this quality, especially if on sale.
- If you like board games, this one is faster/easier to play than irl board games and you can play it alone.
- 4 characters to play at same time (turn based) with different playstyles, gameplays, different looks. You can choose between different skills (not much choice but still some choices).
- I like the graphics, the game is stable too, actions are animated. Nothing crazy but it works well.
- Music is pleasant, ambiance overall too
- The craft : I enjoy to loot crafting materials in every mission to be able to improve the hero I want depending of the items I craft.
- You can choose the difficulty for each mission ; normal/difficult/hardcore which increase your rewards but make the game really harder. So the game can be challenging if you want (or grindy to craft beter items to improve your heroes). This is interesting to manage yourself the difficulty with risk/reward management
- Every "tile" is random, so even if you do the same mission, it will be different
Cons :
- Only 4 heroes : I wanted to choose/unlock more heroes
- The game lacks an option to be able to see beter the dices rolls if we want.
- You sometimes have to turn the camera to see beter a room
- The game is short. I finished the main campaign and almost all seconday missions in near 8 hours (in normal difficulty only) now I do the same missions with harder difficulties. So the game will be a lot longer but become more repetitive/grindy which explains the low price.
- Events are random and can be very unfair sometimes, especially in higher difficulties.
- Some things are not explained in the game. You can craft items which gives bonnus to a hero but you see the real effects of the crafted item, only after you crafted. And sometimes you will make bad choices because the difference will not be what you expected.
- If you are an hardcore board game fan, this one is limited with the choices, customisations
- Deluxe edition or dlc are bad :
I was very happy to see new dlc. But when I read the contents, it's just a save time dlc like in f2p mmorpg. You don't really have new content (characters, missions, skins...).
Starting the game with the deluxe edition, make the early game too easy and less challenging (because your heroes will be stronger quicker).
For players who want an easier game I would say : Prices of dlc are low and you can choose to just buy the gamebreaking OP one (+1 adrenaline per kill for Artus). This one is a real P2W

Usually in a case like The Beginner's Guide: the second game from the developer of a largely successful game (The Stanley Parable), I would avoid comparing it to the latter, as I feel it would be unfair. However, based on the steam description and one of the first lines in the game, I think it wants to be compared to The Stanley Parable, so I'll do as such.
The Stanley Parable featured two great characters, Stanley and the narrator; it featured a huge list of different choices the player could make, and had a great sense of humor. The Beginner's Guide also features two characters, the narrator and the friend, however neither character is likeable, and the game features no choices to keep the player invested. I was interested at th start, somewhat bored during 80% of the middle, and somewhat satisfied with the ending (which I feel went on for too long).
The Beginner's Guide is a walking simulator with heavy narration and it's all about game development. Everything within the previous sentence is something I would usually love, I enjoy relaxing games that can make me think; I'm also a game developer. I feel like I'm the perfect person to play this game, and yet I still don't like it. The narrator comes off as extremely pretentious, and neither him nor his friend are in any way believable human beings, which sucks due to the game trying to be a believable story.
Without going into any real spoilers, there's a little more to this game than just being something to play, and for those reasons I feel a little guilty being so critical, but it's those same reasons I'd feel guilty if I wasn't. I don't think it's an experience worth the full price, but I think there's something in the game that could have made it great. Due to state of mind, I understand why it is how it is, so I'll just end this by wishing the best for the developer.

Left 4 Dead, Avatar and Titanfall had a lovechild. Evolve is that lovechild. The game uses first person shooting as you hunt down an alien monster with your teammates or third person hacking and slashing as the alien itself. It is a cool concept, but that's where it ends.
It's too bad this feels more like a big budget early access title than it does a finished, triple A game. There is fun to be had here, but it is very limited and you will be spending a lot of time grinding to get the items and unlocks you want. Also, each match follows a similar pattern where you just run around following an NPC which leads you to the monster before it flees, then you repeat this over and over, fighting the monster occasionally until the match ends. Maps are huge and this can often go on for 30 or 40 minutes.
There are a few balancing issues which should be ironed out with updates and the performance is actually pretty good for a PC game. But I'm just not sure it's worth the price they're asking considering how limited the base game is.

Chroma Squad
There is alot going on with Chroma Squad but I'll keep it short...some areas of the game are very very very good...and some awful.
Let's start off with the good, Chroma Squad is a hybrid between simulation and turn based strategy. It sounds complicated, but they kept those two elements at the simplist form. So,  the developers pulled it off nicely.  I played on the easiest difficulty because I am atrocious at both genres, but this title kept me interested.  There are a few branching storyline choices to choose from, so that's a plus as well.
The storyline is hit or miss...so I'll try to keep the spoilers to a bare minimum. Note the word try:
If you read the description, if Chroma Squad, the player runs its own Super Sentai studio/show.  The actors who decide to start their own show are all best friends who got tired of their former show's director. So the player runs the studio, and the action(Turn based strategy) is the episode being filmed.
I wish it was that simple.  It begins to get confusing, because everyone begins breaking the 4th wall(from the show to their audience), sometimes the actors don't know if what's happening while on set is scripted or really happening, and then soon they begin to 'Morph'/Transform for real and fight real battles while its still being filmed.(In other words, the actors became real super heroes and saved the world). I sometimes got mixed up with what is real or what isn't real.  At one point, a developer comes on screen and tells the actors its all just a game and he made a glitch by mistake, is that the 5th wall being broken????
The gameplay was fantastic, and the retro style graphics were beautiful too.  I liked the idea of naming my studio and all the catch phrases, so the only thing I didn't like was the story, I pretty much hated it.  I wish it was either one or the other, either a Super Sentai game(Where I name the characters, catchphrases, customize colors/armor), or the same studio simulation/turn based strategy where it was kept JUST A TV SHOW without a confusing storyline.

Frozen Cortex is one simple patch from being an incredibly good, strategic, turn-based, futuristic sports sim. Bloodbowl meets Speedball; US Football meets XCOM. Poker meets electronic Chess! And this has no RNG - winning is all about second guessing your opponent.
There's a unique twist here as well, not only do you 'lock' in your own moves before your turn; you also get the opportunity to program in your opponent's too. And he / she is probably doing the same.
You both then get to see how the play might unfold based upon your own strategy and that which you've "anticipated" for your opponent. Then you COMMIT and watch the playback.
Well, there's an option to play games a turn at a time. So you can play one turn today, and come back tomorrow for the next. Kind of like play by mail. Put there I assume to compensate for the times when not many are online. Sounds like a good idea?
No.
With the multi-player PVP community what it is *cough*, you'll often find you take healthy lead, and the other player simply logs off. The next turn ... never comes.
I said there was no RNG. That's technically incorrect. Winning a match is just as much about your strategic brilliance as it is hoping you get lucky with an opponent who is willing to stick around for a full game.

This is a D&D game based on the board game. So first and foremost, don't expect a full fledge RPG experience with story and character progression. There are elements of it in there, some quite interesting, but it obviously cannot compare with other RPG games for the main reason that this is not what this game is.
The core of the gameplay is this: you attempt to complete a mission with 4 heroes with fixed sets of skills (you can select some options here but not many). You must make the most of what you're given. Turn by turn, you explore tiles and fight ennemis, looking to complete the mission's objectives. Random plays a big role, and the rules are stacked against you. Expect to die a lot. But that's ok, you're in for the quick fix adventure anyway. Dying is of no consequence.
So why should you play this digital version rather than the board game? The crafting system is interesting, even if furstrating at time when you fail to craft an item. It gives you a feeling of progression and purpose to any extra items you encounter. The various missions, the map, the level progression also contribute to the feeling of accomplishment for the lone adventurer.
That being said, the game does have problems. The first-time experience is dreadful: the gameplay is not well explained and you need to figure out a lot by yourself, including the WHY you're playing this. The interface in general needs polishing and the flow needs improvement.
All in all, not a bad game, it's an interesting port of the physical product. Just maybe not a purchase at full price.

Found an abandoned house in the forest after marching through the rain for what seemed like hours. The warmth of the fire from the stone helped me calm my nerves as the moans of the undead could be heard not far from where I was. I checked the cabinets for food. No luck. I checked the fridge. Nothing. There had to be something in this place. If the dead didn't get to me, starvation would. Finally, after searching the entire house, I found a bag of chips underneath the couch in the living room. They were the best stale chips I've had in what felt like days. For the very first time, I felt like everything was going to be alright, until I noticed the curtains in the living room window were still open, and the undead had spotted me. Their moans attracted more of them as they began to surround the house, smashing through the windows. Me, with my trust crowbar ran into the bathroom, fearing that this was the end. I closed the door behind me and frankly searched for a way out. Panic settled in as the realization that I had no way out with the undead banging at the bathroom door sank in.
I didn't survive 20 minutes after starting the game. 10 out of 10.

Long review, bear with me. Will update when I feel like it.
Thanks to Daniel my pocket buddy for introducing me to the game, and Rohan from 2K Games in Singapore for giving us the chance to play it at the office.
----
After preview testing, Big Alpha, Closed Beta, the Monster Race retail edition... this game has not let me down yet. The graphics are as magnificent as any CryEngine product tends to do, although three stages of testing still leaves a few bugs around.
The most intense shooter I've played, where every game is completely different and can go either way - monster technique and hunter cooperation are a must if you want to stand a chance. No playable class is inferior, everyone is equally important, and I say that to the greatest extent that words allow. Engaging the hunters as a stage one monster is no guarantee of a loss, and neither is a stage three a win.
Gameplay is brutal for newcomers and there is no notable tutorial for each class; videos are token effort at best and grossly misleading at worst. Strongly recommended to play with at least one friend, preferably with three others in a full party with voice comms. If you do not work together, I assure you that you will lose to a monster of your peer. (In that vein, there is in fact a solo mode but with an AI monster and absolutely atrocious AI teammates I hope you are prepared to play it just for the mastery.)
----
I have not played in three months and have only just come back to semi-serious playtime since interest has been piqued over this weekend's 40%-off sale.
Most of the criticism the game has received comprises accusations of a high price point and "day-one downloadable content", conveniently omitting the fact that the overwhelming majority of said price consists of cosmetic skins for the hunters and monsters.
Straight out of the box the vanilla game is playable and many meta teams - if that is your flavour of shooter - do not require additional hunters .Sure, you have to pay for a monster here and a hunter tier there but I haven't heard of anyone complain about non-essential content sold later in any other game either. And those are not day-one either, as anything after the first three tiers was released at least a month later and/or tied to pre-order bonuses and season pass.
I will not even give the point about the state of the playerbase, since most out there are impressionable and ignorant, and would have been influenced by equally ignorant and scathing reviews of a game they barely put any hours into.
What I will give is the state of the game: an extremely steep learning curve and a 100% mission-critical need for teamwork and decent level of skill. Good monsters will play by themselves and dunk on matchmade hunters; good hunters who inevitably have to solo queue will likely get a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ teammates and have to face off against aforementioned monster plus dunking. (This will demoralise anyone faint of heart, and to find these people you just have to look at every other negative review aside from those already mentioned who ignore the cosmetic nature of DLC.)
On that note, competitive play is still going strong, with a proper ESL showing and Go4Evolve every weekend. Tune in to those tourneys to get a look at what you're missing.

Horror is my favourite video game genre but unfortunately in recent years the genre has been saturated with low-effort indie garbage. Thankfully, small and simple Outlast makes an exception by being genuinely a good horror experience.
An independent reporter Miles Upshur receives a tip of ongoing illegal experiments happening in an asylum called Mount Massive. He goes to investigate with only the help of his camcorder and it doesn't take long for things to go terribly wrong for Miles. You'll have to survive many encounters with lunatics wandering about in the asylum, record everything and live to see the next day and tell the tale. Our protagonist can't fight back; he can only run or hide. Sneaking around the crazy and dangerous patients is the only way. And most of the times it's so dark that you'll have to use the camcorder's night vision mode to see your way through. This in turn will consume the batteries very fast, leaving you with the only option of scavenging more from the environment.
I have a love-hate type of an relationship with horror games in general. I hate how scared they make me but at the same time that feeling of being scared gives me an adrenaline rush. The first time I tried to play Outlast I had to stop just after 20 minutes because my nerves couldn't take it. It took a couple of years until I could finally continue. The game manages to make you feel isolated and terrified because of its unsettling atmosphere and disturbing characters. I'm sure there's a lot of us who can confess sweating profusely while being chased by these people. And in my opinion feelings like these are the best goal a horror game can ever reach.
And the characters, the occupants of the asylum, make Outlast great. At first look they might appear to be just crazy people who aren't fit to live with the rest of the society. But as you uncover more of the story you'll start to understand that they're merely tortured, pitiful human beings with traumatic pasts. Results of unethical human experiments. Some of them are more sinister than others and will go to any lengths to kill anyone in their path. Whether it is the calm, naked twins; a doctor who wants to cut a piece of you; or an ex-veteran with a fixation for military protocol. They are the ones who make the asylum feel alive even if most of the residents are already dead.
For an indie game, Outlast doesn't look half bad (granted there are some places so dark you can't see much of anything). The same goes for animations and I specifically like the way Miles moves. There is something natural in his movements; how he crawls with one hand when the camcorder is raised up, putting his hand on the wall when peeking around a corner or even trying to open a locked door. If there is one thing I don't like it's that there isn't much variety with the models of non-important characters. It's as if the asylum is full of Hitman's demented and mutilated clones.
The rest of the negative list isn't too long. Outlast is very linear and there isn't much change in the gameplay, if at all. Although in the game's store page it's said that the enemies are unpredictable, I can't see that being true. To me the enemies have very predictable patterns and they behave almost exactly the same way every time I play. Always doing the same thing and always going the same way. Any deviation from this was rare and surprising, but in a good way because it brought some excitement to the table.  I also didn't like the very last chapter. Up until that chapter everything was dark, spooky and full of murderous madmen. Basically a horror game in a nutshell. But then everything changes when you get to this lab and you feel like you transitioned from horror to sci-fi. The last 15 or so minutes is important for the story but at the same time I didn't enjoy those minutes as much as the rest.
If anything I wish the whole experience would have lasted longer. For a first timer it can take 4-5 hours and speeding through as less as 1,5 hours, cut scenes included. I actually really like this game which is odd because I normally have trouble getting into strategy games. Frozen Cortex however is a cool idea of taking a turn based strategy style game and giving it a sports theme, which to my knowledge hasn't been done since Bloodbowl.
It takes the notion of having many different ways to score ranging from super easy to complex, making you think out your moves even more than ever. Frozen Cortex also has a simulation mechanic that allows you to simulate plays before you commit your players moves.
And random generating maps create different matches everytime, unlike other strategy games where veteran players memorize the maps and know where to plant characters everytime on that particular map.
And it also has many Sports elements as well. You have team customization, individual player stats, season modes, even the ability to a create a pitch and play on it. and even better, it actually has a single player story. and its surprisingly good. I've never seen a story in a sports type game before.
but my favorite feature is the cinematic camera, that makes things look so cool to see individual plays. And it also has a "watch full replay" mechanic at the end of games that allows you to watch a whole match play out in the cinematic camera
If you're looking for something different from strategy games, give this game a try

Honestly, this game is one of the best frozen survival games that I have ever played, the time and effort that was put into this game to make it as accurate as possible is astonishing.
PROS
1. The gameplay is set in a frozen tundra with hundreds of km to explore.
2. The conditions that your character have to face for each region are super accurate for each landscape.
3. No matter which character you play as the stats are the same.
4. The weight for a lot of items is accurate to their real life counterparts.
5. This game makes you think about what is around you and how to use it to your advantage.
6. In-game temperature is accurate to what position the character is in, and the wind in this game is really really cold.
7. disease is present in the game and the character's stats are affected in certain ways because of them.
8. This game is one of the most beautiful games that I have ever played.   P.S. If you decide to buy this game that while your playing look at the sunrise or sunset once and a while, it's totally worth getting mauled by wolves while distracted
9. Wildlife in this game will respect their own space and your own space respectively depending on what difficulty you are playing in.

CONS
1. Some of the game is still a little glitchy, so if you see random rips in space and time...That's Natural...
2. Currently, the only forge in the game is in Riken (The shipwreck at desolation point) and the game has no other places than the Riken where you can forge materials.
That is honestly all the cons that I can think of, and both of them are quite small problems and can be fixed easily. Just don't mind the rips in time, they won't hurt you if you don't hurt them. And if you can't start at Desolation Point then start at a place close to desolation point and walk there.
I can firmly give this game a large 10/10 this is one of the most accurate, Beautiful, and unforgiving frozen survival horror games that I have ever played and if you like survival games then I strongly suggest that you pick this one up and give it a chance. Maybe you'll like it as much as I do.

This game has potential, but it requires work and polishing up, especially on net code. You will need a constant ping (constant meaning unchanging) to play this game without 'teleporting' all over the place. Other than the fun of using them, there also seems to be no advantage to using bolt action rifles and snipers. Every weapon seems to do the same amount of damage (and just as accurate) and getting sprayed and killed from 50+m seems to be the norm, and that is the engagement range of most maps I've played on.
Rushing in an clearing rooms by hip firing machine gun seems also to be the norm.
Apparently you just need to hear and be close to your enemy fire for you to get suppressed, the enemy does not really need to be shooting at you, or in your general direction. With every shot you hear, you twitch, thus making your character aim all over the place, so if you have a bolt action/semi automatic weapon, whoever is spraying can, and will most likely, also mow you down because you where too busy shaking and apparently your shots did not suppress at all.
Ideally, in my opinion, suppression should be changed to have gun sway while being suppressed as a whole, and not react to every shot, because this way, in my opinion does not promote accurate, but more spraying until only one guy remains. Having a jamming mechanism might also be a way to balance between weapons with different rates of fire.
Some other things: Sometimes the character enters a reload loop, wherein the reload animation just goes on and on. When respawning you have a 50-50 chance of respawning right infront of enemy units.

The long dark is a challenging survival game that will keep you on your toes. One moment you can be doing fine but the next you might be balancing on the verge of death.
In order to survive on the short term, you must traverse the icy landscapes and gather supplies that others left behind because they managed to escape the unforgiving climate…. or never had the chance to. If you plan on surviving on the long term, you can’t rely on these resources as they are bound to run out soon. You’ll have to craft, hunt and use your wits.
A strong feeling of isolation is created with the subtle use of music and sound. This game won’t hold your hand, there’s no contact with anyone, and every other living thing in the outdoors is likely a threat. For now I haven’t found a way to actually survive, your character is doomed from the start to succumb to the elements. Perhaps this will be added to the game later but on its own; it’s an interesting challenge.
One thing that’s not completely BALANCED about the game is how fast you run out of resources, the food can be somewhat explained due to the cold but tools break very quickly as well. Another thing I ran into (and heard other players about) is the fact that you are bound to run out of things to find on the different maps after playing for a few hours. Personally, I suspect the somewhat linear structure of the environments will serve a purpose in the upcoming ‘story mode’.
These are a few flaws in the current design, but keep in mind that this is not the finished product. I have high expectations of the end result due to the frequency of the updates and the beauty of the environments.

Basic game play: You find yourself in the middle of snowy wilderness and have to survive. You try to find shelter, food, equipment and other resources. Sometimes you will encounter wild life such as wolfs which you need to fight/avoid. Your main enemies are hunger, cold and dehydration.
The game is overall very well made and offers very realistic survival experience. I also loved the maps and the snowy enviroments which are quite beatiful.
Main problem I have with this game is the time scale. One day in this game is maybe 1-2 hours of gameplay. So in practice everything works accelerated: In order to visit nearby lake (few hundred meters away from my cabin), I basically need most of the day, whole lot of food and almost freeze to death instantly just by sticking my nose out of the door. You can also easily die of exhaustion if you do long tasks (such as extracting meat out of dead animal) and forget to check time requirement carefully.
Also the typical survival game problems apply here. Lots of work and micromanagement are needed to get by each day which can start to feel laborious at some point. Also dead means starting from the beginning and your going to be dying a lot. Typically unexpectedly and for stupid reasons.
But as far as survival games go, I think this game is a winner. If you like this sort of games you should definetly try it. Note that the game is still work in progress and it offers only sandbox mode currently.

First off, this is a video game adaptation of a board game...which is based on an adventure in Dungeons and Dragons. This video game is not an RPG, though it does have RPG elements, but I still found it very enjoyable. I am a fan of the board games that this game is based on (there are others based on Ravenloft and other settings) and I wouldn't mind seeing adaptations of those versions as well). This is a very good adaptation of that experience but I think if you're buying into this (at a relatively decent price) you should realize exactly what you're buying into.
There is a heavy dose of randomization in this game. While this video game adaptation doesn't visually represent aspects of the game (pulls random tiles from a pile, encounter cards, enemy cards, etc) you are basically pulling those from an unseen area. Combat is dictated by dice rolls but there is, again, no visual representation of this. I would enjoyed seeing the act of a dice being rolled but that's just the D&D player, and DM, in me.
Visually I think the game pulls off the aesthetic of both the setting (Chult, a tribal peninsula in Faerun of the Forgotten Realms setting) and the format (board game). Tiles being look great and enemies are easily identifiable. The sound design is nothing to complain about or praise; it is what it is.
The game's difficulty can ramp up tremendously, so much so I considered it cheap at first but its all just a bi-product of the randomization aspect. After over 2 hours with the game I got over it. If you fail a mission you can simply restart it if you like, there is no permanent game over.
The game is also single player so there is no same PC co-op or over the internet play. I would have enjoyed this option even if I didn't engage in it all the time.
All in all I really enjoy this game. I have been using it while I catch up on podcasts and streaming shows/movies. I actually hope this comes to console at some point as well. With my experience, the price point, and the D&D hooks I really recommend this game...just know that you're coming into a board game adaptation and not a true D&D or RPG experience.

This is a unique city building game that has a huge emphasis on diplomatic and political relations. This game does not require much micro-managing, but does require the player to be smart when it comes to building placement. Tropico 5 is an alright game when compared to the big city buildings games like Skylines.
The
in Tropico 5 is decent. The player is mostly responsible for placing buildings, deciding whether they produce local goods or international goods, what sort of goods to produce, hiring of foreign workers and policies and type of government. Additionally, the player has to build barracks in order to bring in a military presence (or hire one). There will be scenarios in the game which will ask the player some tough questions. The player can choose to support "the crown" for example or choose to support rebels. Other decisions can be around rigging the election or favoring one foreign government over the other. Every decision will impact the peoples opinion of you. If you don't have the popular vote - you lose the game and get booted from the government. There are certain workers that can offer benefits (+5% on produced goods for example) and even your dictator that you choose (you can make multiple) have their own personal benefits.
The
are okay for the most part. The camera scheme is very stiff and weird. If you have your controller plugged in at the start of the game, it will be near impossible to use your mouse and keyboard. Ensure you don't have a controller plugged in before booting the game to avoid this issue. The AI in the game can be seen fighting and working, but there is nothing really that stands out to make the visuals outstanding. The
and music are ok. Nothing incredibly outstanding in this realm either.
The game is okay. There are a few people I can see indulging in Tropico 5, but for the City Skyline types, it might be hard to get into. For this reason, I will not be recommending the game as its not my cup of tea.

People say Tropico 4 is better, and while I agree to an extent, Tropico 5 was a better sequel to 4 than 4 was a sequel to 3. If you played and love Tropico 4, you'll probably enjoy Tropcio 5 IF you don't go in expecting that its Tropico 4 but with more features and stuff. Tropico 5 is a different game, and knows its a different game, forcing the player to approach things from a different perspective. You have some concern with researching things and moving onto the next era, building a sense of progression, and causing old tactics to create less profit, but allowing for new tactics to reek in even more cash. It should be noted that there could be more content building wise, but if you buy the game with all the DLC in a sale it would kind of remedy that. As far as the content in the game itself, it works, but there isn't really anything too interesting except for maybe a few exceptions, but the DLC adds some fun stuff like the Ministry of Truth, which is actually a fairly intersting building to use, and the water pack adds some interesting stuff. By themselves however, the DLC isn't really worth it except for like two of them, so I would recommend getting the bundle on a sale. Online with a friend can also be fun, though it does crash sometimes. The concept of racing to resources and being a thorn in your friend's side is fun.
tl;dr: It's not the same as Tropico 4, but it isn't trying to be and benefits from that. It's differences give it an identity, but you might be better buying the game with the dlc bundled on a sale if you need more content. Either way, it's a decent game. Online is decent with friends.

This game will show you an infinitely possible world in an unforgiving way that makes everything you do dangerous regardless of how long you've been alive.
TL;DR: 9/10 - Best zombie survival sim out there today.
Zomboid is the type of game that might take a little bit of getting used to if you haven't played something like pokemon. IT will get even harder to get used to if you haven't thought about survival situations in your life. The day I realized I loved Zomboid is when I decided to try and craft something, without knowing the recipe, a molotov cocktail. I drank a bottle of whiskey, and ripped up a sheet, I then tried pouring a bottle of whiskey on the sheet, it didn't work. A couple of game days later I came across a gas can, I substituted the whiskey for gas, and 'lo and behold a molotov was created. These are the kind of possibilities that will keep you coming back forever. Everything makes sense.
There are no shortage of "oh ♥♥♥♥ I better drink some bleach because I'm about to turn in to a zombie" moments, or "The house is filled with zombies, I'm stuck in a second floor bedroom, I'm going to have to risk breaking my legs jumping out the 2nd story window". The zombies are dangerous, they can and will kill you in some of the most miserable ways. Sometimes it is as simple as looking through the window before you break in to a house to prevent a surprise attack from a hole filled friend. Shooting a gun is always dangerous and rarely can you take on a horde on your own, oh yeah this game is multiplayer too...
With so much content it is hard to believe a game beyond early access and with things like NPC's (really well done) and offline co-op on the way, there is an exciting future to zomboid.

text:
First things first guys. If you want a game with no bugs, or P2W, then pay a monthly fee. As you can see I like this game for many reasons, but I will be unbias in my review. Let's prove it by talking about the downfalls:
The three worse parts about RO2 are the leveling and the [lack of] PvP, and the release of new content. In my thousands of hours of WoW, it is fair to say, that a much better Quest line system from lvl 1 to max level is available in other games. The leveling is very, very grind-till-you-drop style. There are three kinds of Quests: 1. Kill this monster twenty times (some times for an item it drops to give to the quest giving npc) 2. Talk to this npc  3. Gather this item.
Poor planning of Patch release dates that bring new content to the game. There have been three, no wait, four new dungeons in six months added to the game. I have the best gear in the game (^^) but to be honest, a lot of people are either skipping new raid dungeons to go to the newest one, or moving to the most recent raid dungeons half geared from the one before it (my point is a "new" dungeon shouldn't become redundant after a month an a half). They would be better off releasing 4-8 dungeons a year all at once, or six months at a time, and letting players work through them tier by tier.
Pvp is entirely under developed, but they did add a new PvP map, which is actually pretty awesome, if you have a DPS cahracter. Healers are not really needed unless they are a hybrid (DPS mixed with Support). There are three maps: 1. Colo (it is a big open circle so not really a map) on this map you free for all with 30 other players for 5 rounds and people are eliminated each round 2. WOE (don't even get me started) this is a poorly designed map with too many choke points and you can only enter with your guild (fyi: I am in a very large, strong guild) and the big, strong guilds always win (my guild is PVE based) 3. Jehoon Training Site (nice map and game play) uses a lane and tower mechanic like DOTA or LoL with merchants to buy buff scrolls and monsters in the "jungle" which you kill for a quest to obtain items and points to win the match or buff your team (also debuffs other team).
PVE: The Good Stuff  : D
The best PVE content in my opinion is end-game. Like anything there are good and bad sides. Let's get one thing straight, I have done every raid a bunch of times on my own and in a guild, and they are all doable with Pugs (random people) aside from AoD (unless you are over-geared, but for review sake, let's assume you have gear from the tier below the raid you are doing). The bosses in the ten-man raids are all fun. They aren't too hard that you rage out and quit the game, but aren't too easy that you get bored and quit the game. There are two bosses though, that are extremely difficult to most people (Rat Master and Zoda). I did Rat Master with only pugged raids and killed it almost every time, but never the first try (Rat Master: two tries, four tries, nine tries.) in order to enter the Chaos Dungeon (newest raid dungeon). People say it is impossible and cry, and cry, and cry. Put simply, it takes chatting software, strategy, practice, and skill. Not every one is meant to make it to the furthest endgame content in any MMO, and those people, usually have trouble accepting it. For me, PVE is the best part of the game, and reason I have played so much.
Interesting Content: There are a lot of unique aspects of the game that I hadn't seen in others. 1. Costumes: these are either "grind your face off" or P2W items, but overall it is an interesting and "fun" aspect of the game. The amount of power you get from costumes depends on how many Runes you put in it to give you bonus stats. You can also combine costumes with a chance to get "rare" costumes. I have only gotten one "rare" from thirty combines total over a span of months of game play, but lucky people in my guild have gotten "rare" costumes with only one fusion.  2. Cards: cards are only dropped from monsters and bosses. They give you bonus stats, and you can combine them to get rare cards, with great stat bonuses. 3. Phantom Pyramid: this is a P2W mini-game that you play in order to win content. It is based on RNG and can provide great rewards, or waste money (in-game or real life money) and time.
Overall this is a great F2P *once you hit max level*. There are bugs, and the only real issue I have is the lack of attention put towards fixing those bugs faster. If you are a talented PVE player in any MMO game, be prepared to be surrounded by the most idiotic players you have ever seen (mainly Tier 1 raids and early game five man dungeons). You have to find people that are awesome players to raid with from the pugs you do, or join a great guild. There is a decent job system, and class system (with a nicely set up talent tree for each class). And even though I say to myself, "why would the developers do that?" more than I would like to, I ffind myself logging back in to play (way too often).
PS: Thanks for reading my book.

The staff regularly release new content and events but leave a lot of the game's problems to the side. If you check their Facebook page, people still complain about bugs and other problems with the game all the time.
The community is also pretty toxic since there are a lot of immature players who are super competitive about the silliest things, including sitting space in town. The only reason I stayed for as long as I did was because I had an awesome guild and really good friends who still played, so I was able to do endgame dungeons with a decent party. But when a majority of them moved to other MMOs, there was nothing left to do but leave as well.
Just... stay away.

I can't, in all honesty, recommend this game. Although the early game aspect is fun and exciting, that facade quickly slips. Despite easy and quick leveling in early game, late game content is still severely lacking, and heavily unbalanced. Constant gamebreaking bugs, pay-to-win events, poor server optimization, lag and latency issues, incredible graphical defects and compatibility issues with regional settings on your computer make the game nigh unplayable at times, especially after big patches.
The Pay-to-win model breaks balance between free to play players and paying players, and the gap between them is offputting to say the least.
The biggest problem I have with the game is the ridiculous amount of RNG uses in places where there shouldn't have to be random attribution. Random chances to get an item that once opened up, gives a random chance for an item, and combines with other items with a random chance to get a good item. So many recursive random chances that player advancement is purely luck based, rather than progression based on player activity is unbearable to say the least.
There are many good things about the game, but honestly, it's hard to talk about them, when the first thing you think of after a long session of raiding dungeons or grinding was: that was pointless.

Balancing is a horribly issue in this game. I got the PC Monster Race edition for half the cost, and I've been beating up monsters with my friends, or getting beaten up as the monster while running away crying frantically by people with their friends. This game is really solid all around.
The hunter classes are all great, and do a great job to contribute teamwork if played correctly. The three hunters for each class that the base game gives you are all pretty unique on how they work so changing up your technique with your team has options. The three monsters (Goliath, Kraken, and Wraith) you get are all very challenging, and that's one of the best features this game has.
If you can play the monster right, you can wreck face all the time, but if the team of hunters can cooperate effectively they can turn the tides easily at the start, or put up a fight towards the end. THIS GAME REQUIRES PLENTY OF COOPERATION BETWEEN HUNTERS TO TRULY ENJOY YOUR EXPERIENCE PLAYING THIS GAME AS A HUNTER. A lot of games say this, but this one really takes the cake. You just can't have two hunters on one side of the map, and the other two split up doing their own thing. You will get♥♥♥♥♥♥on. Do yourself a favor, and try to get some friends to play this game with. Playing solo can be underwhelming due to not having anyone to really communicate with if you're playing as a hunter, but of course you might just get into a lobby where people communicate. Try, and stick with 'em! If you like playing as the monster, by all mean, go solo.
Other nice stuff are the graphics, audio, and its tight gameplay. The graphics are pretty damn good, and they don't break my computer. I'd say you can get a smooth 60fps on high to very high settings on mid to high end computers. I'm not entirely sure on this, but I've heard this from others, and their rigs. The audio for this game is pretty spot on. Wildlife animals, monsters, and the atmosphere of Shear really bring this game to life. The hunters voice acting is also damn good. They did a good job making all of 'em unique with different accents, personality traits, and unique dialogue between one another. Gameplay controls are pretty standard for FPS players. You'll pick 'em up pretty easy like most FPS games, and the mechanics of the game very fitting.
Now why am I not recommending this game?! It's honestly because if I didn't get the PC Monster Race for half the cost, I would not have got this game. The direction 2K & TRS are taking this game in terms of DLC & pricing is absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing bonkers. They are gonna charge people 60 bucks for a game with two game modes, a handful of hunters and three monsters? They are gonna charge people a hunting season pass for 25 bucks that only has 4 of the 6 upcoming hunters you got planned out? So, wait a minute.
60 (base game) +25 (season pass) +15 (monster) +15 (monster) +7.50 (hunter) + 7.50 (hunter) = 130
There is already 70 bucks worth of content priced out as DLC right off the bat on release not adding the cosmetic shop. That's some kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥ I can really understand all the hate the game is getting due to this business practice. You just don't get anywhere near the amount of content for 60 bucks off the base game. If this game was around the 40 buck area it would be way more appealing to everyone, but it isn't. It's simple; buy the base game for 60, and you will be left out later on if you play this game a lot, or buy the PC Monster Race edition for 100, and be set for the current stated content. It's a super ♥♥♥♥♥♥ move that will hurt the future appeal of this game. But I guess since 2K did this with Borderlands 2 (not as extreme though), and games like PAYDAY 2 can get away with it without a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥brewing, they'll try it out.
It really is a great game, and I'm having a blast playing it, but what 2K & TRS are asking from its audience is too much. If the cost is ridiculous, and it's turning you away. It's understandable, but if you really wanna buy it & play it. Wait for a Steam sale, a definitive/complete/GOTY/whatever version with all the content, or search the internet for good deals like GMG,♥♥♥♥♥ or something. But if none of this bothers you, and you wanna pick it up. You'll have fun once you're in.

I really enjoyed the Stanley Parable. I milked that game for every last drop. It was cerebral, it was funny, it was intriguing. So, when I heard of this game, I was hoping for something good. I didn't expect something as magical as the Stanley Parable, but given the game's short run time, I was hoping to be at least interested, and perhaps satisfied in some way by the ending. Was I? Ehhhhhhh not really. For the first 45 minutes I was eagerly advancing, waiting for something engaging to happen. I was patient. I knew that all of this buildup was gonna amount to something, anything - but it didn't, really. There was kinda a twist, but not mind blowing or applaudingly clever, and the game milked it for too long. The fact that this very short game seemed to drag on beyond where it needed to should show you how few ideas this game is really built upon. Not worth the money I spent on it. If it's on sale, and you were a big fan of the Stanley Parable, and you also happen to like artsy crap a little bit, you can go ahead and get this game. But for me, this game missed whatever it was that made the Stanley Parable a good walking simulator. It wasn't intriguing, and the message it sent through its narrative didn't feel very poignant. 4.9/10: only if you really like walking sims.
And if you feel the need mark this review as "not helpful" not because of its content, but because you don't want to see dissenting opinions, maybe you didn't enjoy the game as much as you're telling yourself you did.
