Outlast caught my attention because I was looking for more first person survival horror games after playing Resident Evil 7. And not only is Outlast better than the afformentioned title, it's also more sick and twisted.
The gameplay puts you in a vulnerable situation where you'll have to run away from enemies while searching for batteries for your camera if you don't want to be left wandering blindly in the dark. The graphics are amazing for an indie game, and together with the soundtrack and sound design, it creates an immersive horror atmosphere.
A lot of people say this game relies heavily on jumpscares, however, they miss what the developers were actually aiming for: shock horror. Outlast is not a game about the cheap thrills that come with a loud noise, it's a game meant to disturb and gross out it's players. Multilation,♥♥♥♥♥♥ necrophilia and much more are shown in this game.
There's also a good bit of suspense. Scenes where you walk around deformed, tortured inmates of the asylum, that act like nothing out of the ordinary is happening, will stick in your head long after you played it.
There's also a stand out sequence where you're in a sewer, unable to run because of the water, and you just hear chain noises in the distance. It scared the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me, and it's one of the better moments I've seen in a survival horror so far.
It creates an atmosphere not with psychological horror, but with shock horror and suspense. (Even tought a psychological aspect to the horror would make the game so much more impacting. Hopefully Outlast 2 will fix this. Those school flashbacks are looking promising...)
So, if you're looking for a good horror experience that will shock you, go for it. But if you're the kind of "jumpscares-can't-be-done-right-and-♥♥♥♥-everything-that-uses-them-regardless-of-the-overall-quality-of-the-title" guy, just stay away.
(Also, am I the only one that noticed that Trager is an obvious tribute to Freddy Krueger?)

I can honestly say Bioshock is the most fun single player game I've ever played. It has a great story, moments of surprise and interesting twists. You have freedom to make your choices. You can decide whether to destroy or hack security bots, cameras and turrets. You can use weapons you like the most and you can upgrade them. You can choose active and passive abilities (combat, engineering and physical) according to your playstyle, preferences and situations. You can collect items and craft! You can buy items in vending machines and if you hack them you can even reduce the prices there! You can take pictures of enemies with your camera and yield rewards for it. You can also roam around, explore and possibly find valuable items.
So many choices!!! But can you really choose?

Make no mistake, this is a game. It has a compelling, cohesive story with a beginning, middle, and end. It allows player movement, allows player interaction, has an aspect of problem solving and innovative mechanics.
I understand the frustration people may have with it (though I have little sympathy--frankly, I don't know what people were expecting from tags like "walking sim" and "narration" in a game by one of the creators of The Stanley Parable). But to me, the best part of this game is that it shows what interactive media COULD be. What better way to tell the story of a game developer than to physically walk the player through the dev's games? What better way to give context than to, y'know, GIVE context? This was a strong, emotional story, and I can't concieve of a better way for it to be told. The game never claims to be more than it is, and what it IS is a wonderful, thought-provoking narrative experience.

I suspect this "game" was made to be disliked. It's in many ways the exact opposite of The Stanley Parable. It offers no choices, only a single linear maze like path for you to plod through while being talked at by the narrator. As a player you provide 0 input into the game. All puzzles are explained or bypassed by the narrator. Coda's "games" are sometimes architecturally interesting, but hardly qualify as games.
I'm not upset I purchased this because I knew basically what to expect, but it belongs more in the video rental section than in the games section of Steam.
But, there are some things I really enjoyed about the "experience." In roughly the time period this game takes place, and for a few years before, I would play experimental, student, and "indie" games every day after school. I would go to forums, blogs, anywhere where these games were being posted and download them and play through them. Many of them were quite similar to Coda's games. They were architectural, artistic, and spartan. On the other end of the spectrum were 2D pixel art platformers with a gimic. They offered new takes on established gameplay mechanics and twists on an understandable formula, but were overwhelmingly derivative. I've seen tons of that style continue on being made and released today, but very little of the architectural type. And I appreciated being reminded of that time in my life when I would play through other people's games and enjoy taking in whatever the maker wanted me to see.

I wasn't sure about this game. I thought it may be very slow, basic and simple. How wrong was I.
Basically, this is a game in which you are trying to get the ball to one side of the 'field' to the other, while your opponent is trying to stop you and get the ball to the opposite side. Sounds simple enough. The way you do this is quite unique. The game is split into turns. Every turn, you tell your robots (which look stunning, just like the rest of the game) to run or throw the ball. Your opponent does the same. When both are finished, you hit the 'play' button and see what happens. This is a great way to structure a game. Personally, I am a big fan of having a more chilled out, relaxed approach to the game.
But there is more to the game.
When it comes down to it, this is a strategy game. You need to work out where you think your opponent will move, try to intercept their throws, tackle them, and just generally get in their way. There is an extrordinary depth to the game, and is very easy to spend hours at a time trying to fine tune your tactic.

The rogue-like FTL: Faster Than Light was an uncompromisingly difficult game, where playing up to two hours at a time could be undone by one moment of chaos. So many times I ploughed through that game only to declare the universe as being intrinsically unfair as a simple mistake cost me a good hour of careful planning, only to have to start over again. The illusion is that next time I'd get it right. I'd shield the doors earlier, or make sure to stock up on extra missiles, or avoid saving the crew of a ship on fire.
The futility of the game combined with the (somewhat illusory) sense that I was in control kept me coming back. It was only when I could get through to the end of the game regularly that I finally lost interest.
Which brings me to Frozen Cortex.
Frozen Cortex is what you get when you cross American Football with Frozen Synapse - which is in turn what you get when you cross chess with guns. I really enjoyed the idea of Frozen Synapse, but I never could fully immerse myself in it (Hell is Internet multiplayer...) I haven't had that trouble with Frozen Cortex, already rocking up close to 30 hours of game time.
The funny thing is that there's really not a lot to Frozen Cortex. The entire game consists of short matches, with each player controlling 5 robots on rectangular arenas populated with various obstacles. It's simple enough to grasp, simple enough to control, and a tiny mistake can undo hours of meticulous planning. Any given match can be thrown away from incorrectly guessing what an opponent would do, and that makes knock-out mode all the more difficult.
Because the games are so short, minor mistakes have those major consequences. Screw up on your own offense, and it's virtually guaranteed to be game over. Misread your opponents and it can be similarly difficult to come back during your own. The game's annoying habit to "pause" the turn halfway through a touchdown pass can often be just rubbing it in that you didn't realise the opponent had that option open, and there's nothing to do but slam the PRIME button and hope there's still enough time to recover.
And there are many ways it can cost you. A slightly mistimed run means a key player is knocked out. Throwing to a player too close to an opponent gives them no time to act before they are tackled. Passes that get intercepted. Having your player slightly mistime an interception. Moving to the wrong side of an obstacle. And of course, all these are compounded with scoring pads littered throughout the arena. They are only worth 2 points (compared to a 7 point "touchdown"), but a good run can cross several pads at a time. One particularly bad example was a robot that could just sneak around an obstacle for an unguarded heavily-padded run to the end-zone.
It's that futility that like in FTL: Faster Than Light keeps me coming back. I didn't see that play. I'll be mindful of that next time. It's with that attitude I've been able to beat the game on season mode (and opened up interesting variations), but haven't quite gotten through a knockout comp yet. The game is cruel, uncompromising, punishing, and that's what makes it such a rewarding experience.

There are a number of obvious problems with Outlast. The story is fairly routine and inconsequential to gameplay. The game goes for excessive gore, which is probably exciting to kids but is pretty boring to me. The stealth system is pretty bad, and it’s often easier to just sprint through a level than to try to sneak around. The level art and enemy design is pretty repetitive. The encounters with one big brute enemy get old really fast.
But these are really just superficial problems. There are games with much worse stories, and much poorer stealth mechanics, that still manage to pull off some great gameplay. No, the real issue with Outlast is this:
It’s predictable.
Not just the story arc (although that’s also predictable), but the core level design. The levels follow such a routine, obvious pattern that everything from item placement, to pop-out scare pacing, to encounters with other characters is easy to read way in advance. In a game with very few interaction mechanics (you can move, hide in lockers, and look at things through night vision), predictable level design is a serious problem.
Comfort is the antithesis of horror. When the player feels comfortable, they aren’t feeling scared. In a game like Outlast, one of the primary ways that a player comforts himself is by anticipating what will come next. This is a mode of thinking that treats the game we are playing like a system. Every time you think, “oh, the obvious flashing light is to the left, so I’ll go right first,” or “this would be a good spot for a hidden item,” or “it’s been a while since the last pop-out scare, I bet one’s coming up,” you’re thinking about the game as a system that you are trying to solve. You’re not navigating the dark hallways of a corrupt insane asylum that’s been experimenting on its patients, you’re solving a Rubix Cube. Guess which one of those types of play is scarier.
Outlast’s main problem is that it has very little to work with to keep you uncomfortable. The levels are narrow and linear, and there’s only ever one right way to go (if there’s more than one way, there’s probably an item at the end of the alternate passage). The game mechanics are well implemented but extremely shallow, which makes the actual moment-to-moment gameplay very repetitive. The game dutifully saves before every major encounter (and immediately after) and helpfully alters the music to let you know exactly when you are in danger and when you are not. As a result, you know enough to see through the game content and treat it like a Rubix Cube.
The developers try to combat this with stealth sections. Sometimes they work; when you are hiding in a dark corner and can’t see your pursuer, it can be pretty tense. But the stealth sections quickly devolve into a repetitious, frustrating challenge, which feel unfair. After a few attempts, you realize it’s easier just to run for it. Now you’re treating it as a system again, and the power the game had over you is lost.
The only remaining trick the developers have up their sleeves is pop-out scares. But even those get old really fast. They are startling, and knowing that they could pop something out at you at any time is stressful, but they happen so often that the easiest solution is to just take yourself out of the game. Once you stop caring about your character the pop-out scares have no power, and their appearance becomes yet another thing to try to predict.
It’s a shame, too, because there are some great scenes in Outlast. My favorite is a bit late in the game when you finally exit the foreboding asylum into a rainy courtyard. It’s almost pitch black but the area is punctuated by lightning. This section only lasts a minute or two until you’re guided back into more strictly-linear passage crawling, but it’s a great scene.
There are some other nice touches as well. The night vision camera pretty much saves the day by giving you a very narrow cone of vision and forcing you to navigate unfamiliar territory with it. There’s a battery mechanic that creates some pressure between using the night vision to see your surroundings and trying to conserve your small supply of batteries for an emergency situation. The actual movement mechanics are good and the game isn’t buggy or broken (although the way the camera rocks made me feel like my character is wearing clown shoes). There’s some really nice automatic first-person body and hand animation that I haven’t seen done this well before.
But in the end, the thinness of the game mechanics and the predictability of the level design sucked all the scariness out of this game for me. The reliance on pop-out scares further removed me from the game, and by the end I was just Rubix Cubing my way to the finale.

Honestly, this game is one of the best frozen survival games that I have ever played, the time and effort that was put into this game to make it as accurate as possible is astonishing.
PROS
1. The gameplay is set in a frozen tundra with hundreds of km to explore.
2. The conditions that your character have to face for each region are super accurate for each landscape.
3. No matter which character you play as the stats are the same.
4. The weight for a lot of items is accurate to their real life counterparts.
5. This game makes you think about what is around you and how to use it to your advantage.
6. In-game temperature is accurate to what position the character is in, and the wind in this game is really really cold.

The long dark is a challenging survival game that will keep you on your toes. One moment you can be doing fine but the next you might be balancing on the verge of death.
In order to survive on the short term, you must traverse the icy landscapes and gather supplies that others left behind because they managed to escape the unforgiving climate…. or never had the chance to. If you plan on surviving on the long term, you can’t rely on these resources as they are bound to run out soon. You’ll have to craft, hunt and use your wits.
A strong feeling of isolation is created with the subtle use of music and sound. This game won’t hold your hand, there’s no contact with anyone, and every other living thing in the outdoors is likely a threat. For now I haven’t found a way to actually survive, your character is doomed from the start to succumb to the elements. Perhaps this will be added to the game later but on its own; it’s an interesting challenge.
One thing that’s not completely BALANCED about the game is how fast you run out of resources, the food can be somewhat explained due to the cold but tools break very quickly as well. Another thing I ran into (and heard other players about) is the fact that you are bound to run out of things to find on the different maps after playing for a few hours. Personally, I suspect the somewhat linear structure of the environments will serve a purpose in the upcoming ‘story mode’.
These are a few flaws in the current design, but keep in mind that this is not the finished product. I have high expectations of the end result due to the frequency of the updates and the beauty of the environments.

This game has potential, but it requires work and polishing up, especially on net code. Every weapon seems to do the same amount of damage (and just as accurate) and getting sprayed and killed from 50+m seems to be the norm, and that is the engagement range of most maps I've played on.
Rushing in an clearing rooms by hip firing machine gun seems also to be the norm.
Apparently you just need to hear and be close to your enemy fire for you to get suppressed, the enemy does not really need to be shooting at you, or in your general direction. With every shot you hear, you twitch, thus making your character aim all over the place, so if you have a bolt action/semi automatic weapon, whoever is spraying can, and will most likely, also mow you down because you where too busy shaking and apparently your shots did not suppress at all.
Ideally, in my opinion, suppression should be changed to have gun sway while being suppressed as a whole, and not react to every shot, because this way, in my opinion does not promote accurate, but more spraying until only one guy remains. Having a jamming mechanism might also be a way to balance between weapons with different rates of fire.
Some other things: Sometimes the character enters a reload loop, wherein the reload animation just goes on and on. When respawning you have a 50-50 chance of respawning right infront of enemy units.

I don't normally like sports games.  I got this game because I liked Frozen Synapse.  I've also really enjoyed the simultaneous turn-based strategy games ever since playing Laser Squad Nemesis back in the day and I wanted to throw more support behind the genre.  I was not disappointed.
It's challenging.  You can spend an hour trying to perfect your turn (much like Frozen Synapse) only to have your opponent drive through the smallest hole in your coverage and beat you.  Likewise, the feeling of realizing you positioned your players perfectly in an unstoppable formation is the best.
There are also great contectual clues baked in to the UI of moving your players around the map.  There are circles around the players to indicate at what point you'll block an opponent player.  The waypoints go hollow if it's possible to be blocked by an opponent before you get there.  Moving a waypoint around will show you your interception coverage.  When playing single player, the AI's chat will sometimes indicate if they're planning on passing or running; and if you're familiar with it enough, even where they're likely to do it.
They wanted the AI to be as similar as possible to playing multiplayer, so it can provide quite a challenge at times.  The nice thing about this is that if you're worried about playing multiplayer, you can work up your skill against the AI and be confident that you stand a chance against another real-life player.
While the tutorial teaches you the basics, I don't recall it going over some of the contextual information.  For example, I didn't know about what the waypoint going hollow indicated until someone else commented on it.  Not having all the information going into it definitely made learning the game more frustrating than it would have been otherwise.  It would also be nice if the interception coverage showed for a couple of seconds on setting a waypoint so you don't have to then wiggle it around to make sure it's good.
There can sometimes be some minor discrepencies in the preview vs what actually happens when you submit a turn (at least in the singleplayer). - Gameplay:
Very solid, very fun, easy to handle yet hard to master, i.e. the game handles and plays very well and smooth but challanges you hard at times.
The direction change is a neat addition to the mechanics, at first it seems "nice" but after playing the game for some more it really adds a lot - the levels sometimes fell a bit bigger and more important you don't have to wait for the "rear-shot" powerup to hit enemies that passed you, you just turn around and shoot them anyways :-D
- Graphics:
"2.5D" can - when done well - look amazing while not disturbing the pure 2D nature of the game.
And this one is done really well!
While the game and all it's environments / levels are sole 2D, the actual grahpic is rendered using 3D models.
Looks great, plays well.
- Music:
An amazing soundtrack that is a huge homage to "chip tunes" and really drills into your ears, you might catch yourself keeping the game running just to have the music playing.

Love this game, but seeing a lot of complaints.
>Evolve is repetitive.
That's the game style. Might as well complain about fighting games being repetitive. What is not repetitive is how each battle plays out. Sometimes the monster runs and hides, powering up while trying not to engage the hunters. Sometimes that's not an option, and it's a series of intense skirmishes. Sometimes the monster chases the hunters around, eliminating one or two at a time and toying with the rest. Playing through the Evacuation mode forces players into different scenario types, changing up which side is the aggressor. Eighty hours in, I haven't had two matches play the same way yet.
>You have to buy new monsters/characters.
No, you don't. The game comes standard with twelve hunters and three monster, giving you fifteen playable characters, all with vastly different play styles. This complaint also goes along with "day-one DLC" complaints, but that's simply not true for this game. The new characters and monster were not ready at time of release. Check the videoes online showing them being playtested by the devs after the initial game was released. Yea, we'd all love if everything was free, but having to pay for additional content is not really a big deal and completely optional.
>This monster/class is overpowered/underpowered.
I've seen these complaints in favor of and against the same characters. There are reviews saying Lazarus is the worst medic, and some that say he's the only one worth using. What it comes down to is knowing how to play your role in the team. Four people who all know what they're doing are going to work off each other, protect each other, and give the monster a very difficult time. The monster, in turn, should understand when it's time to stay and fight and when it's time to run. Choose your battles, know the maps, and you'll be very tough to kill. The game is constantly being tracked and tweaked by Turtle Rock who boasts a near 50/50 ratio in world-wide game win/loss. Neither side is overpowered. If you don't believe, check out the tournaments on youtube.
As always, it's up to your personal taste. The game gets compaired to Left 4 Dead, and I guess that's fair, but I think it plays a bit more like Team Fortress in that the classes matter. Oh, and if you have the game and you're feeling frustrated, check out the video gallery in the extras section. There are advanced play tips for every hunter and monster.

An amazing game with noticeable flaws that tarnish the gameplay depending on the player.
Pros:
Nostalgic soundtrack and gameplay, balanced difficulty, loads of content/replayability, and creativity. Many games this generation are essentially creatively bankrupt, but Chroma Squad realizes this and challenges the standard of games today. A tycoon game with rpg gameplay and tons of customization has been completely unheard of. Fun humor and fun character designs, the game doesn't take itself seriously at all and knows its limits. It is literally self-aware of the tropes and cliches it uses. For example, in one point of the game, a girl needs to be rescued. One of the squad members questions if it should be a guy just to avoid using sexist tropes. The game knows the stupidity of generic hero-saving-the-day tv shows and utilizes it to bring out the fun that is in them easily.
Also, if you are a fan of super sentai, you will laugh your♥♥♥♥♥off at these references. I promise you.
Subjective:
It's obvious just from the start of the game how much customization there is. You can customize everything- from your squad name, the names of your members, the attributes of the members, the weapons of the members, the abilities of the members, your mecha, your mecha's name, your transformation name, and way more. In theory, it sounds great, but when you get right down to it, it get's annoying. Have you ever felt the feeling of, "Ugh, I can't choose between these great abilities/weapons! I wish the game didn't even give me an option!" Well, half of the game is like that. It's so customizable to the point where it may ruin the enjoyment factor. Should I craft this? Should I buy this? Should I equip this? There's way too many choices. Me personally, I had only a few problems with this, considering how much I love customization in games. This is a pro or a con depending on the player.
Cons:
Repetitive. Incredibly repetitive, to the point where you say to yourself, "Really? This again?" The game is oozing with creativity but unfortunately the gameplay is designed so that almost all of the fights are entirely the same. Some enemies are different, the map layout is sometimes different (and other times copy pasted), but the game throws at you the same fights over and over again just to reach the conclusion. This is easily noticeable after getting through the start of the game.
No effect on overall plot. Nothing you really do changes where the game is going. Sure, occasionally you get fans praising you for doing x or shunning you for doing y, but it doesn't really do much in the long run from what I've seen.
Little strategy. Unless playing on the hardest difficulty, you only need a bit of strategy to complete the levels.
Dialogue. The dialogue is sometimes humorous and creative, but really? It can be written by 5 year olds and probably be the same. The writing is pretty awful and the characters have little depth. This I get it; that's the whole point of the game. It doesn't take itself seriously and is SUPPOSED to be immature. It isn't that big of a deal, but the game could easily be better with more engaging dialogues and more clever jokes.
Mecha fights. Fun the first time you launch it and the first time you use a new ability you got, but otherwise? Not engaging at all, and anti-climactic a lot of the time. Incredibly repetitive.
Overall though? Do I have to go through a bit of repetitiveness and subpar dialogue to enjoy a game with tons of replayability, nostalgic design/soundtrack and a unique experience? Definitely. This game is fun as hell.

This game is awesome. I don't understand people crying about the day one DLC because it's literally all skins and in no way affects the gameplay. Sure there will be more hunters and monsters in the future but they won't upset the balance of the game. TR has proven that they are pretty good at balancing the hunters and monsters. They posted the stats a day after launch and it was about a 51% win rate for hunters and 49% for monsters. That is pretty incredible.
Since the game is so balanced it's pretty fun playing on either side...if you know what you're doing. It can be frustrating if you are new to the game or just straight up don't play very well and you get matched up against a monster or hunter team that is profficient at the game. You'll get stomped by the monster if you don't coordinate with your team effectively and you'll get killed by the hunters if you don't adapt to the situation and pull some clever maneuvers.
Next thing is people complaing that the game is "repetitive" or "lacking content". This isn't the case. Evolve is worth the $60 price tag. The production value is great and the game is really detailed. The graphics look really good even on lower settings and I've only encountered about four bugs that are pretty minor. I only had one disconnect and other than that I haven't experienced any lag at all. There is a good combination of hunters and monsters to keep encounters fresh and different each time. There are also a few game modes you can play but Hunt will be the default for most people.
You can also play the game offline with bots if you want to practice without having other people yell at you for doing something wrong. Most of the time the bots do an ok job. Sometimes they can surprise you with how intelligent they can be but other times they will jump right into a tyrants mouth. Usually they are alright though and get the job done. Same goes for the monster bot. The neat thing is your progression from playing solo goes over into multiplayer as well so you don't have to worry about doing everything all over again.
Which leads me to my next topic. One of the only gripes I have with the game is the progression system. It feels a little too slow and not rewarding enough at times. I wish there was more to unlock besides the elite skins for the characters. The elite skins look awesome but the problem is they are only for your equipment and not your character (besides the monsters). This makes it hard for other players to see when someone has reached elite status with a hunter and it doesn't feel very rewarding. You can unlock emblems as well and customize them but I was hoping for a more robust customization system. Such as different suits for the hunters and such. It's not a big deal, just a missed opportunity in my opinion.
To sum it up Evolve is a great competitive game that can be very instense and fun. The progression system can feel like a drag sometimes but doesn't take away from the core gameplay. There are very few bugs and connection issues which as we all know is a rare thing these days when games launch. People saying that the game is too "repetitive" are some of the same people who play other multiplayer focused games where you basically do the same things over and over. Yet they only talk trash about Evolve and give the other games free passes. There are a lot of people being really hypocritical about it for whatever reason. It's worth the price tag and at least a second look from everyone hating on it for stupid reasons.
I'd give it an 8.5 / 10

Horror is my favourite video game genre but unfortunately in recent years the genre has been saturated with low-effort indie garbage. Thankfully, small and simple Outlast makes an exception by being genuinely a good horror experience.
An independent reporter Miles Upshur receives a tip of ongoing illegal experiments happening in an asylum called Mount Massive. He goes to investigate with only the help of his camcorder and it doesn't take long for things to go terribly wrong for Miles. You'll have to survive many encounters with lunatics wandering about in the asylum, record everything and live to see the next day and tell the tale. Our protagonist can't fight back; he can only run or hide. Sneaking around the crazy and dangerous patients is the only way. And most of the times it's so dark that you'll have to use the camcorder's night vision mode to see your way through. This in turn will consume the batteries very fast, leaving you with the only option of scavenging more from the environment.
I have a love-hate type of an relationship with horror games in general. I hate how scared they make me but at the same time that feeling of being scared gives me an adrenaline rush. The first time I tried to play Outlast I had to stop just after 20 minutes because my nerves couldn't take it. It took a couple of years until I could finally continue. The game manages to make you feel isolated and terrified because of its unsettling atmosphere and disturbing characters. I'm sure there's a lot of us who can confess sweating profusely while being chased by these people. And in my opinion feelings like these are the best goal a horror game can ever reach.
And the characters, the occupants of the asylum, make Outlast great. At first look they might appear to be just crazy people who aren't fit to live with the rest of the society. But as you uncover more of the story you'll start to understand that they're merely tortured, pitiful human beings with traumatic pasts. Results of unethical human experiments. Some of them are more sinister than others and will go to any lengths to kill anyone in their path. Whether it is the calm, naked twins; a doctor who wants to cut a piece of you; or an ex-veteran with a fixation for military protocol. They are the ones who make the asylum feel alive even if most of the residents are already dead.
For an indie game, Outlast doesn't look half bad (granted there are some places so dark you can't see much of anything). The same goes for animations and I specifically like the way Miles moves. There is something natural in his movements; how he crawls with one hand when the camcorder is raised up, putting his hand on the wall when peeking around a corner or even trying to open a locked door. If there is one thing I don't like it's that there isn't much variety with the models of non-important characters. It's as if the asylum is full of Hitman's demented and mutilated clones.
The rest of the negative list isn't too long. Outlast is very linear and there isn't much change in the gameplay, if at all. Although in the game's store page it's said that the enemies are unpredictable, I can't see that being true. To me the enemies have very predictable patterns and they behave almost exactly the same way every time I play. Always doing the same thing and always going the same way. Any deviation from this was rare and surprising, but in a good way because it brought some excitement to the table.  I also didn't like the very last chapter. Up until that chapter everything was dark, spooky and full of murderous madmen. Basically a horror game in a nutshell. But then everything changes when you get to this lab and you feel like you transitioned from horror to sci-fi. The last 15 or so minutes is important for the story but at the same time I didn't enjoy those minutes as much as the rest.
If anything I wish the whole experience would have lasted longer. For a first timer it can take 4-5 hours and speeding through as less as 1,5 hours, cut scenes included. I liked playing so much that I have completed the game over and over again, and will continue to do so in the future. Even the plot is unusually decent for a horror game. Outlast is definitely one of the best horror games to date.

Outlast caught my attention because I was looking for more first person survival horror games after playing Resident Evil 7. And not only is Outlast better than the afformentioned title, it's also more sick and twisted.
The gameplay puts you in a vulnerable situation where you'll have to run away from enemies while searching for batteries for your camera if you don't want to be left wandering blindly in the dark. The graphics are amazing for an indie game, and together with the soundtrack and sound design, it creates an immersive horror atmosphere.
A lot of people say this game relies heavily on jumpscares, however, they miss what the developers were actually aiming for: shock horror. Outlast is not a game about the cheap thrills that come with a loud noise, it's a game meant to disturb and gross out it's players. Multilation,♥♥♥♥♥♥ necrophilia and much more are shown in this game.
There's also a good bit of suspense. Scenes where you walk around deformed, tortured inmates of the asylum, that act like nothing out of the ordinary is happening, will stick in your head long after you played it.
There's also a stand out sequence where you're in a sewer, unable to run because of the water, and you just hear chain noises in the distance. It scared the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me, and it's one of the better moments I've seen in a survival horror so far.
It creates an atmosphere not with psychological horror, but with shock horror and suspense. (Even tought a psychological aspect to the horror would make the game so much more impacting. Hopefully Outlast 2 will fix this. Those school flashbacks are looking promising...)
So, if you're looking for a good horror experience that will shock you, go for it. But if you're the kind of "jumpscares-can't-be-done-right-and-♥♥♥♥-everything-that-uses-them-regardless-of-the-overall-quality-of-the-title" guy, just stay away.
(Also, am I the only one that noticed that Trager is an obvious tribute to Freddy Krueger?)

TLD is the definative survival game. Lightyears ahead of anything else.
Well I bought TLD sometime back in 2014, just after they added the Coastal Highway map. For the purposes of this review, i've only ever played on Stalker difficulty.
I still remember my first death.....I spawned, walked 20ft into a building and was mauled to death by a wolf that came running out of the darkness like some horror film whilst trying to work out how the inventory system worked 3 minutes into the game. I got better after that.
TL;DR
I'll say this and this only:
The Long Dark is the only game where I thought I should have bought it twice for the amount of effort and content the dev team have put into it over the two years since I bought it originally. I'd gladly pay for the whole game again. TLD is not your run of the mill survival game, If you like an atmospheric survival where you think and make your own descisions about what you do next, you will like TLD.
Full:
This is not your run of the mill multiplayer survival etc. It's more of a carefully crafted atmospheric story that drives itself as you play through the sandbox. There is no guide, no hand holding, no tutorial. TLD makes you think to overcome problems. If you think that is what you would do in real life, there is a good chance that is what you would do in TLD. You're bleeding and have no bandages? What would you do IRL? The more you do this, the better you get at the game.
The other thing is TLD can force you to make choices, There is a blizzard, you're slowly dieing of cold...do you hunker down?  or do you continue on? Will you make your safehouse?
It's nasty out and you're out of food. Do I stay and wait it out? or do I try and make a run for it? Do I know the way back? How far is it? Will I get lost? Will I make it back before the sun sets? Is it safer to stay here?
The above are all situations i've found myself in  within the game and made the right descisions to get out of them.
There is no game like TLD currently and it's one of the best games and personally highly rated games in my collection. It is the definitive survival game.
The devs are constantly updating the game and have added loads since bought it, including two new maps and mechanics changes and additions. The game has come a very long way.
Hinterland are very receptive to player input and feedback, more than any other developer i've come across. After playing for a long time I made several posts on the Hinterland forums about how to possibly improve the game (imho) and several of them appeared in later builds, most notably the addition of skill books.
A word on story mode. Yes it's been delayed several times but i've seen the changes that are being made and honestly, I had to pick my jaw up off the floor. I have every confidence in story mode being released and i'd rather it was delayed and highly polished than just released.
TLD really is a unique single player game, It has so so much more depth than anything out there. So, if you're in doubt, or teetering on the edge or comparing it with another survival title, just buy TLD, you won't regret it.

Syder Arcade takes me back to my old days of MSX gaming in the 80's, when  I used to play the Nemesis Saga games (Nemesis, Salamander, Gradius, and all of their sequels) with the MSX plugged to a color TV.
Syder Arcade does provide some of that feeling: the music is excellent, that sounds like the old 3-voices digitalized musics of the 80's arcades.
Another thing I liked is the default key controls: Z / X to shoot and arrow keys to move. For those who are unaware, the MSX keyboards had huge arrow keys, specially designed for games. I loved it!
However, there are some flaws.
1) It is not possible to leave the game in between phases, because the ESC key won't work until the game has started. So you are forced to go through the cut scenes between levels and wait until the game has started.
2) Unlike the games from the 80's, there are too many visual elements in the game and sometimes it is hard to tell between something that is "shootable" and something that isn't.
3) there are no hints or clues to what the difficulty levels are, since its names aren't very intuitive. Actually, there isn't a single hint in the menus!
4) There is too much story in the cut scenes. Sometimes I just want to get to business and start shooting. I don't care about the plot or the background story! I didn't care when I was 14, I won't care now!
Other than that and a few other minor flaws, it is a very nice game and I am very glad I got it. I've been acumulating hours on the game! I hightly recommend this game.

You don't see too many side-scrolling space shoot-em-ups anymore; their heyday came and went with the NES/SNES/Genesis era. However, the genre is not entirely forgotten, with the occasional title like Syder Arcade coming along.
The best that I can describe it for old-school gamers is to take an R-Type or Thunderforce IV, and give it controls akin to Defender where you can turn around and have a long range radar.
For those not familiar with the genre, you're a lone spaceship that has to kill lots and lots of enemies. You can move at any angle, but generally enemy attacks come from the left and right of you. There are lots of items to collect to power up your guns. There are several stages to complete, most of which are the get-to-the-end variety, but also an escort mission, and there are a few bosses to defeat as well.
First the good part - the graphics are bright and colorful, and even when the bullets come heavily you can usually tell where you are and what's going on. The controls are tight, and there are several types of ships that change gameplay quite significantly.  There are a variety of skill levels to insure that novices and experts alike can enjoy the game without too much frustration. The music is good, and it's a generally fun game.
It's not perfect, however. There are not a ton of stages to play, and they lack variety. The bosses are rather similar and unimaginative. The tacked on story is skip-worthy.
Overall, however, this is a fun little indie time-waster, and I am glad that I bought it. Definite thumbs-up.

The gameplay in Syder Arcade is a horizontal-scrolling shoot'em-up without forced scrolling and the orientation of the ship can be changed with the press of one button (like in Astro Tripper). The levels are essentially long rectangles (don't wrap around at the sides). The enemies and collectibles (powerups, bonus points, ...) are shown at the map, as well as the players position.
The graphics in the game look good and it also comes with a bunch of different filters to emulate various retro gaming platforms. These are fun for nostalgic values, but not so much in the main game.
The enemy bullets stand out well, which alone is enough to put this ahead of Ether Vapor Remaster, even if the story mode is far shorter.
The 'story mode' is a pretty short and simple affair - only a handful of levels with a plot that leaves huge gaps between levels. This mode is more or less a throwaway - the survival mode by comparison will take up most of the player's time.
The survival modes have endlessly spawning enemies in one single map. The ship always starts with the poorest weapons. The biggest problem here is that after dying, I haven't noticed a "Retry" option. Instead, the game throws the player to the main menu and the earlier selections I made are not stored, so just hammering the A button will just take me to the campaign, not the survival mode. Then the player has to choose the ship and the level again, which takes some time (loading and transition animations). This is a UI design problem.
As expected, the survival modes have online leaderboards.
There are a number of ships to choose from with different weapons and speed/armor values. There are also several difficulty levels to choose from.
I have encountered two things I'd call bugs. First, in the last campaign level, dying can result in the ship respawning inside rock. Cue an instant death. And the next respawn can also result in the very same thing. Second, again in the last campaign level, I must've missed something since I couldn't get the final enemy's first lock to revolve. Maybe the storm hadn't progressed far enough, but it wasn't moving anywhere either.

1. The gameplay is set in a frozen tundra with hundreds of km to explore.

If you grew up with games like R-Type, you're going to love Syder Arcade. It's the classic gameplay, simple yet challenging fast-forward shoot'em up action. Switchable add-ons, mega weapons that you need to charge before using them (and keeping you on the edge of your seat while loading - will the ship withstand the enemies' fire? Will - hell, yeah - take that -> whoosh!), it's all in here.
Side scrollers have always been titles that caught their audiences with great graphics. "Syder Arcade" is in no ways inferior to the classics. It really shines (not only) in this category. Be it the explosions, the 2.5 backgrounds, weapons, beams - this one really shines!
Fantastic extra: Of course you can play with contemporary graphics, but you can also choose from several old school modes like pixelated, greyscale, C64ish, Amiga style, CGA, EGA, VGA (320, 640) and many more.
The combination of old school- and modern styles continues. While the sound effects are rich and deep in sound itself, they're also classic for this genre. As for the music: I *LOVE* the score. Instead of using modern synths only, you'll get those awesome (and imho way more "organic") analog synthesizer sounds, too, which are genre defining not only in games, but movies as well.
@Evil Studio: Is there any possibility of getting the soundtrack? Would be a great addition to my 80ies Synth Collection).
Well, ok - what's to say about controls? You've got a classic 2D side scroller here featuring classic gameplay, so don't expect exczessive controller overkill. Studio Evil has done a very nice and also classic job on the controls here, so don't worry about getting entangeled in complicated keyboard layouts, just fire away. Just like the graphics: Thumbs up, guys!
One thing is for sure: The developers don't just *know* the genre, they obviously seem to *love* it. "Syder Arcade" is one of those rare titles nowadays, that really live up to the expecations of old school gamers (like myself) on the one hand, but can also bring good results in keeping things fresh and ready for a whole new generation of gamers.
Fantastic graphics combined with controls that are easily accessible with no troubles at all and a special treat for old school gamers, "Syder Arcade" grants a fantastic blast from the past done right, with either contemporary or classic graphis and a darn high replayability.

I've played a number of board games adapted to software, and a number of them make the transition well.  This one falls flat, although I don't think it was for lack of trying.  I think the character models, animations, and sounds are all quite nice.  It's just the underlying gameplay is so incredibly boring and unflexible.
-You control a group of heroes but you can't control in which order you use them.
-On your turn you can move and use a power, or double move.
-You have two options of at-will powers to use repeatedly, and some utility powers, and typically one power you can use just once.
-The bulk of every turn involving combat is to run up to a monster and click attack.  Hope your invisible dice roll is good.  Then do it again.
-But if you don't explore a new tile on your turn, you get punished with a typically bad event.
-If you do explore, you don't get punished, but then if one or more monsters spawn on the new tile, they get a free attack at you, as your character takes a quick break until their turn again.  Hope their invisible dice roll is bad.
I can see the appeal of maybe doing this with friends in physical space, but this as a solo experience is tedious.  There's no reward.  There's a thin story and a thin upgrade system and the (at least) the first five main missions take place in the same enviornment with the same starting tile with the same rocks and trees you see every time, with the same monsters and the same encounters and the same traps.
I appreciate that they patched in trading items between heroes, which shows that they care.  But that can't save an ultimately boring and repetitive product.  Save your money and buy a different D&D product.

I love Tropico games, as you can probably tell by my hours spent on Tropico 4.  I would actually advise purchasing this game even despite its deviation in gameplay for one reason:  it is fun.  However, every few hours I've experienced crashes for absolutely no reason.  Trust me when I say it's not my rig, though the haughtiest PC gamers out there simply say 'buy something better' (the monetary equivelent to 'get gud').  Telling you right now, it isn't a rig problem.  It's a windows problem.  If this rig can run Heart of the Swarm on high settings without hiccups then there's no way that Tropico 5 should be too much to handle on the lowest settings.
I've done just about everything I can to find fixes, work-arounds, and so forth, but every piece of advice I get is "update your graphics driver, play on lower settings, turn off this or that."  I've spent an entire week doing every single thing I can find to fix this; underclocking software, heat monitoring, forced updates to drives that didn't even need updates, screwing around in regedit, confirming it was in compatibility mode, always running it in admin, and even a factory reboot.  Still happens.  Still no clue why.  So, I say this to you:
It's a fun game, but you may well have to deal with random crashes and playtime loss with zero warning and pretty much zero logic.  This seems to be prevelent with specific graphic drives (AMD and Nvidia) and almost always on Win 8 or 10.  If you don't mind that type of frustration then go for it.  Have a blast.  Just don't say you weren't warned.

Chronicles of Mystery:  The Scorpio Ritual (City Interactive, 2008)
You know a game is good when the worst thing you can say about it is that it's the first entry in a series of five games and the other four aren't on Steam.  If anyone from City Interactive is reading this, please, make it happen, bring the rest of the series to Steam.  (Also consider putting the Art of Murder series on here as well.)
I'm not going to delve too deeply into the story, and the gameplay is standard adventure game fare.  There's a button to highlight interactive objects, which is good considering the highly detailed environments.  The voice acting is decent.  The screenplay contains several examples of broken English;  but that's no big surprise considering the game was made by non-native English speakers.  (And honestly, it's nowhere near as bad as some other Polish games.)  Sadly, this Steam version has no other language options.
I was tripped up early on and had to peak at a walkthrough -- not because the puzzle was hard but because the game makes use of a single tricky mechanic.  The latter entails you having to investigate items in your inventory by first right clicking on them and then left clicking on the enlarged viewing window.  Nowhere is this explained and nowhere is there any graphic indication that a left-click will do anything.  Most of the time you'll get no result from investigating items in this manner but some puzzles require it.
SCORES
Graphics:  65 %
The game looked fairly good when it came out back in 2008 and it looks fairly good now.  The visuals are effective at conveying the locations and, as previously mentioned, this is the first game in a series.  Having read up on the later entries it seems the technical qualities of the games have definitely improved with each entry.
Sound:  80 %
Good voice acting from the English-language version of any game is something of a pleasant surprise nowadays.  I prefer playing adventures in German (despite not being German), as the writing and voice acting tend to be several steps above the English version.  Here we unfortunately don't have the option of playing in German.  The voice acting is good though;  you'll note actors playing more than one character in-game, but that's clearly a result of budget restrictions as opposed to the developers thinking we wouldn't notice.  (And honestly, it doesn't detract much from the overall quality of the game.)
The musical score deserves special mention.  It's excellent throughout and, in my opinion, could easily stand in for any Hollywood blockbuster's score.  Superb.
Execution:  75 %
It's a well-executed lower-budget adventure game.  The Scorpio Ritual isn't going to compete with the much better funded Secret Files series or something like the truly amazing Perry Rhodan, released in the same year.  But perhaps it also isn't mean to.  The game gives the impression of real care having been taking with its development;  despite being on a strict budget the developers clearly still meant it to be the best it could be.
Addictiveness:  80 %
I enjoyed it, I wanted to see what happens next, I kept playing.
Overall:  70 %
I want to see more Chronicles of Mystery on Steam.  That is the best compliment I can give this game.  I don't hesitate in recommending it and hope that others will do the same.  Do note the playing time though.  The Scorpio Ritual isn't a game capable of standing on its own two feet;  it definitely feels like a first episode in a grander story;  and it has the length to go with it.  Meaning, you may not want to pay full price for it, but that's for you to decide.

This game is lovely! Very calming and peaceful. A delicately balanced ascending-difficulty pure puzzle game, Lyne immerses players in path-finding problems. The game is played in a window and is excellent to play while doing other things. As you make paths between shapes to form the lines which solve the puzzles, pleasant bell-like sounds follow your progress. Upon each level's successful completion, the presentation of the next level is rung in to satisfyingly calming tones of zen-like bells and gonging.
It's very interesting to find, when your brain tires of path-finding between sets of two similar shapes around the various set-piece board elements, you will grind up against a seemingly intractable level. Rather than imitate Zeno's arrow against this cognitive barrier, ignoring it for awhile tends to give the best results. Upon returning, parts of your subconscious mind which simply couldn't let go of the problem if you tried will have ceaselessly migrated requisite neurotransmitters to appropriate synapses. Just as in this careful shuffling of modulation chemicals, the solution will suddenly be found!
Additionally, Lyne is perfectly priced for the experience offered to players who enjoy these sorts of puzzle games. The nearest comparison to make is that Lyne is something like a form of arbitrarily complex visual Sudoku. Fantastic to play, especially while sipping herbal tea just before pranayama meditation. Just like meditation, playing Lyne is an ongoing practice rather than a discrete event, because players can design their own levels and publish them through Steam Workshop. Excellent!

Nice graphics, solid gameplay, cool gravitational mechanics, and different weapons to suit different playstyles. This is a good game missing a playerbase. You might find one or two servers sporadically at any given time throughout the day but don't expect much more than that until one of the steam sales.
There are two multiplayer modes: Deathmatch and Team Deathmatch which I'm not going to bother explaining. What I will make note of however is that in multiplayer, all players are given access to all weapons in the game, which you can switch out in between lives if you'd like which makes for a level playing field with the only deciding factor in matches being player skill.
There is also a very loose single player mode which is basically a time trial consisting of clearing a level of enemies as quickly as possible for up to 3 points (3 if you're quick, 2 is you're so-so, 1 if you're slow.) You start with the default weapon and progress through a set of different levels with progressively harder enemies. Once you've  accumulated enough points in a set you open up another weapon class and repeat. Though again this is meant more for getting a player accustomed to the mechanics of the game and becoming familar with the weapons, so it lacks the intensity and enjoyment that PVP matches have.
All and all I recommend this game, but not for $10 given it's lack of a playerbase despite the games heavy reliance on needing one to keep it's replayability since it's a PVP game first and forermost. Game is fantastic.  It's a breath of fresh air compared to what we've seen lately, and I hope to see more assymetrical style MP games in the future.
The nuances in the monster mechanics are impeccable.  There is a learning curve, but once you get it down, it's absolutely exhilarating to experience the back and forth interactions with a hunter team that just won't let up.  On the other side of the coin, playing as the hunter team against a monster that likes to stalk and strike at opportune moments to leverage the wildlife or terrain against your team is tense and really puts your team's ability to work together and coordinate abilities to the test.
Evacuation, the mode which you follow a 5 day (map) campaign offers an interesting take on how balancing a short series of MP games with the same teams can be done.  Each victory or loss impacts the next map in sometimes considerable ways.  For example, a win on one map for the hunters could mean the monster will have no ability to use its scent ability on the next map.  Or if the monster wins, a whole slew of tasty wildlife might be released on the next map so it has plenty of food to gain armor/evolve quickly.
Not to mention the different modes.  Specifically, the Rescue mode is really up my alley.  The hunters need to rescue downed survivors and deliver them to a dropship location, while the monster's goal is to take said survivors out.  This mode introduces a really cool dynamic where you're always looking over your shoulder to see if Wraith is waiting to abduct and destroy one of your survivors (or your medic...).  Since the hunters' priority is to escort the survivors, their attention is forcibly diverted from the monster and allows some insanely effective ambush opportunities for the monster.
There's plenty of information out there on the other modes in Evacuation, so I'll just say this, it's simply a lot of fun.  Since I started playing Evacuation, I can't stop.  Other games I've been playing have completely fallen off my radar for the moment.
This is a game I've been waiting for since I started PC gaming back in the 90's.  I haven't felt this kind of excitement for a multiplayer experience since the original Half-Life.  Very highly recommended.

Well that was a good game, but not all that long, on casual if you don't muck up, about a dozen hours. I just finished it as I type this review, their were very few things ultimately that bugged me however, nothing really that bad that I'd give it a negative recommendation, but still it bugged me.
First you don't have one of each pieces of armor and each weapons at 'Legendary' quality, you got a pistol & a sword, I guess so those can be wielded by everyone however if you got used to wield class specific weapons its a let down that you can't have a unique Legendary weapon for each classes, also while you got one armor and two helmets for your characers armor, I found it lacking that you couldn't have boots and make a full Legendary armor, which would have been nice for the finale, but from what I seen you can't sadly, it would have been really a great idea for the very last mission at least to be able to have all your team in full Legendary.
Next is New Game +, I saw the narrator after the credits mention that, it would have been great to finish your game on a level than be able to New Game + to the next difficulty level. Now the game has been out for a few months and still no  sign of that sadly. If not for a New Game + one thing that would have been great would have been to be able to replay any mission after the end or after having done them, so that you could fight again any battles, sure their might not be able to alter the storyline path you took, but just replaying the missions would have been a pretty good idea, give the game a bit more longevity. Right now the game feel limited in what you can do, since ou can't continue into a New Game + with your stuff or you can't continue in that game either , when its over its over, whatever you like it or not. I did see their is a mention of some sort of 'Episode Editor' program that would allow us to create custom episodes for endless gaming, I can't wait for it to come out.
Otherwise maybe the selection of potential characters is a bit limited too, I went for a all female team and I was just able to do it, you have barely enough characters of each genders to fill in a full team, without accounting I think for the backers special characters which are... peculiar... one is an weird animal thing, one is a robot, another looked like a lazy bum, and the last is some guy with a shop discount.... but it would have been nice to have a few more picks, if I want to play a new all female team I'd be forced to go with the exact same team and the only way to change things up would be to shift whom is what... so yea, a bit lacking on that part.

There are a number of obvious problems with Outlast. The story is fairly routine and inconsequential to gameplay. The game goes for excessive gore, which is probably exciting to kids but is pretty boring to me. The stealth system is pretty bad, and it’s often easier to just sprint through a level than to try to sneak around. The level art and enemy design is pretty repetitive. The encounters with one big brute enemy get old really fast.
But these are really just superficial problems. There are games with much worse stories, and much poorer stealth mechanics, that still manage to pull off some great gameplay. No, the real issue with Outlast is this:
It’s predictable.
Not just the story arc (although that’s also predictable), but the core level design. The levels follow such a routine, obvious pattern that everything from item placement, to pop-out scare pacing, to encounters with other characters is easy to read way in advance. In a game with very few interaction mechanics (you can move, hide in lockers, and look at things through night vision), predictable level design is a serious problem.
Comfort is the antithesis of horror. When the player feels comfortable, they aren’t feeling scared. In a game like Outlast, one of the primary ways that a player comforts himself is by anticipating what will come next. This is a mode of thinking that treats the game we are playing like a system. Every time you think, “oh, the obvious flashing light is to the left, so I’ll go right first,” or “this would be a good spot for a hidden item,” or “it’s been a while since the last pop-out scare, I bet one’s coming up,” you’re thinking about the game as a system that you are trying to solve. You’re not navigating the dark hallways of a corrupt insane asylum that’s been experimenting on its patients, you’re solving a Rubix Cube. Guess which one of those types of play is scarier.
Outlast’s main problem is that it has very little to work with to keep you uncomfortable. The levels are narrow and linear, and there’s only ever one right way to go (if there’s more than one way, there’s probably an item at the end of the alternate passage). The game mechanics are well implemented but extremely shallow, which makes the actual moment-to-moment gameplay very repetitive. The game dutifully saves before every major encounter (and immediately after) and helpfully alters the music to let you know exactly when you are in danger and when you are not. As a result, you know enough to see through the game content and treat it like a Rubix Cube.
The developers try to combat this with stealth sections. Sometimes they work; when you are hiding in a dark corner and can’t see your pursuer, it can be pretty tense. But the stealth sections quickly devolve into a repetitious, frustrating challenge, which feel unfair. After a few attempts, you realize it’s easier just to run for it. Now you’re treating it as a system again, and the power the game had over you is lost.
The only remaining trick the developers have up their sleeves is pop-out scares. But even those get old really fast. They are startling, and knowing that they could pop something out at you at any time is stressful, but they happen so often that the easiest solution is to just take yourself out of the game. Once you stop caring about your character the pop-out scares have no power, and their appearance becomes yet another thing to try to predict.
It’s a shame, too, because there are some great scenes in Outlast. My favorite is a bit late in the game when you finally exit the foreboding asylum into a rainy courtyard. It’s almost pitch black but the area is punctuated by lightning. This section only lasts a minute or two until you’re guided back into more strictly-linear passage crawling, but it’s a great scene.
There are some other nice touches as well. The night vision camera pretty much saves the day by giving you a very narrow cone of vision and forcing you to navigate unfamiliar territory with it. There’s a battery mechanic that creates some pressure between using the night vision to see your surroundings and trying to conserve your small supply of batteries for an emergency situation. The actual movement mechanics are good and the game isn’t buggy or broken (although the way the camera rocks made me feel like my character is wearing clown shoes). There’s some really nice automatic first-person body and hand animation that I haven’t seen done this well before.
But in the end, the thinness of the game mechanics and the predictability of the level design sucked all the scariness out of this game for me. The reliance on pop-out scares further removed me from the game, and by the end I was just Rubix Cubing my way to the finale.

So I wrote a quick review that was initially sardonically dismissive. And you know what? I still don't really like this game.  But it's important to flesh out exactly why. Because I'm thinking about the second half more and more and it's irritating me the more I dwell on it.
The first half is kind of a pleasant and witty excercise in dissecting the creative process of the game development equivalent of what people would call "outsider art".
In the second half though - even though the excercise continues, the game becomes sharply hostile towards its subject matter and towards the player. Even in some ways, towards its own existence. I've got no issue with playing emotionally manipulative games or games that break the 4th wall for such purposes, but this one is really uncomfortable, and maybe it's PTSD/post-isolation/depression triggering, but I felt some sentiments I wasn't exactly comfortable with. I don't why I'd give these feelings validation either since how am I to know that the narrator's/creator's subject even existed or whether this was all a construct to push buttons? I just know that I don't like these buttons being pushed. This is where my head's at on this one.

Syder Arcade is probably the best indie sidescrolling shooter out there or even the best one to come out in recente years considering not many have. Syder Arcade lets you choose from various ships and each one differs from the others by having more or less armour and more or less speed along with each one having a different attack and special attack. This game has also one really cool thing, which is, it lets you pick a different shader or filter (I don't know what to call it) which makes the game look modern with really good looking graphics or with graphics from the Commodore and Amiga era, I found this to be a really neat plus since you can play the game with various different "eyes" if you can call it that. Syder Arcade features a campaign of around 6 missions (can't exactly remember) and a survival mode which puts you against endless waves of enemies competing for the highest score. Syder Arcade has also one really special gameplay mechanic, which I believe is the first time used in a game like this, that is the ability to flip or ship to face the opposite side which lets you avoid projectiles and flee from enemies more easily and even getting better lines of "sight" to shoot the enemies. The gameplay relies on your basic attack which can be upgraded with different pickups and a special attack which takes time to charge or charges faster by picking up certain pickups and you also start each level with 3 lives. The campaign is easily beatable taking about 3 to four hours but I think that the incentive to keep people playing this title is the online leaderboard system which makes you compete for the highest place on the leaderboards according to your final score, this is probably more "intense" on the survival mode. Overall, Syder Arcade is an amazing sidescrolling shooter made by a small indie dev team from Italy and they totally deserve your time and money because they've made such an amazing game. Do recommend!

One of the most innovative shooters I've played recently. It's short, true, but it packs a lot within it's short runtime. You get to unfold a story of a nerd getting hooked into his game, becoming one with it at some point. Actually, you get to kill yourself, which is quite cool.

Enter the strange world of Dr Harmin and fight off his minons using nothing but your skull. While FrankNJohn may appear to be just another roguelike, it's also very much a twin stick shooter in disguise.
Starting with basic head attacks you progress through the world killing creatures, each level is multilayered and set around a 'tree of life' set in the center. You are able to clear them completely or just make a beeline for the next portal. Clearing levels is far more rewarding as you have the chance for more marbles (currency) and skull caps. Marbles gives you the ability to upgrade skill trees after your characters death which results in future playthroughs becoming much longer as you become more powerful. Skill trees included Damage, Defense and Utility and the  games 'hub world' seemed to contain secret areas to break open once becoming strong enough.
Skull caps are really the essence of the game, each having pros and cons while some had entirely unique powerups set on timers. During play I discovered all manner of caps, most being reference to great games from the past. Examples include Turtle Cap (TMNT) which provides a full body shield, Bomberman Cap which gave the ability to drop bombs as you moved and the Sonic Cap, which provided a great speed boost of course.
When first playing you will notice the art direction and level design, it's very distinct and beautiful, quite similar to the Trine series. Couple that with the music which was put together by Ben Prunty (FTL/Gravity Ghost/StarCrawlers) and you really do get drawn into a Tim Burton-esque world.
For Early Access this is a solid game that's addictive already (just one more turn!). At this stage it only includes the one area 'The Garden of Denial' and a boss fight with spider Queen Sheela but in future it will add many more zones, bosses, skullcaps and local co-op support. Would love to see online co-op added but I'm not sure if that's possible. Also I'm sure they are planned but achievements would be great. :)
If you enjoyed games like A Darker Purpose or The Binding of Isaac, FrankNJohn is basically a 3d third person version with similar dark twisted humour. Worth shortlisting and recommended. Cheers.

I bought this game because a review said it was like Defender meets bullet hell. On the surface that's true, but it is missing the best part of either.
Defender is a game of strategy, the player has lots of options (go left or go right, should I attempt to save a humanoid or take down those enemy's one screen over, when things get bad should I use a bomb or do I risk a warp). This game has none of that strategy: in the campaign you are either on offense and you go from left to right killing everything, or your on defense and you keep on ping-ponging between left and right killing everything. In survival you cannot just kill everything, but the enemy density is so uniform that whether you move left or right hardly matters, the entire playspace is equally full of enemies.
If you are looking for choices beyond what to kill next there is the decision or what power-ups to risk getting or not. Except it doesn't matter, all of the power-ups are incredibly weak and boring; for example: the side shot ability shots 2 bullets perpendicular to your ship's in-built machine gun. This gun could be incredibly powerful to keep enemies on your flanks from destroying you, except the gun is so weak it takes at minimum 3 seconds to kill the weakest enemy in the game with it, and this is a game where the screen is flooded with enemies. Why should I bother picking up a power-up that is so uselessly weak?
Clearly this game doesn't measure up to Defender, but it doesn't measure up to bullet hell shooters either. The best bullet hell shooters are about making the player incredibly powerful while simultaneously being incredibly weak, a hose of damage that can be destroyed at a moment. That isn't the choice the designers of this game went with; instead it is a battle of attrition where both you and your enemies have large health bars and take quite a bit of time to kill. And while you do need to constantly dodge dozens of bullets at a time, the game moves at a fairly slow pace for the genre so twitch skills are not required.
The game doesn't have strategy, its not very twitchy, its just a mediocre shooter. I suggest if you are looking for a game that has strategy like Defender and twitchy bullet hell just wait for Ikaruga to be released on Steam.
(note: I only played the game for an hour, but that was enough time to beat the campaign and play survival several times. There do not appear to be any additional unlocks so I have tried all of the content this game has on offer within that hour.)

Having now finished the main campaign (and one of the DLCs and half way through the 2nd DLC), I'll now consider this game finished, even though a game like this, its also very sandbox focus and in that regard, its never really finishable.
But anyway, having never played any of the previous Tropico games, I finally got around to jumping on board with the fifth instalment, so I can't compare do any previous games (though I have read from other reviews that maybe the fourth instalment is better).
But my review for this game, focused mainly on the campaign is actually pretty positive.
It starts off with you in charge of a colony island, where the overall goal is to gain independence from the crown, and then progress from different eras up to the present (think they are, Colony, World at War, Cold War and Modern Times).
In the campaign you have an...... interesting story, that progress you through these eras, while giving you objectives that make it feel like the goal isn’t necessarily just to speed through the time periods and as such works quite nicely, introducing the game mechanics, basically like one long tutorial but without the hand holding, your just told do this or build this and its up to you, how and where, so works brilliantly for newcomers like myself.
A neat little tactic that I liked to try, was holding off declaring my independence from the crown as long as possible to keep receiving money from the crown and avoid suffering rebel attacks, while I try and create an self sustaining island, that would hopefully keep the locals happy once we are an independent nation.
There is an occasional difficultly surge that threw me a curve ball, such as when you've got to research a specific technology within so many months, so I have built one of each research building and just ignored it while I concentrated on building my island to then only realised that I'm running out of time and I'm spamming research buildings as fast as I afford and build them to try and finish the goal. Which made me realise one nag with the game, you quite easily get lost in what you doing and then suddenly it goes wrong and you realise your last save was from ages ago, it does have an auto save but I would like it save more often.
Anyway, I've ranted on long enough now, so if you like your city builders with a bit of, maybe humour is the wrong word but doesn’t take itself too seriously, while still providing an enjoyably challenge……. then you've probably already played if not this game then another Tropic game already.
Oh, one thing that I did really like was, that your Islands save from campaign mission to campaign mission, as often with this sort of game, you have to build from scratch each time you start a new mission. With this your in charge of two Islands that you switch between but each one saves where you left off with that Island, so you don’t get sick of building from the ground up, while also making you think about the long term design of the Island. I literally restarted the campaign a couple of times until I got the hang of the game, as when I would return to an Island having learnt some new mechanics of the game, I was like, no, no, no, this won't do. One time I demolished all my island buildings, actually starting from scratch because of what I had learnt and how I was now leaning towards designs my Islands.

Welcome to your shift at Freddy Fazbear's Pizza, a pizza diner place built in the early 90s. At first the animatronics are creepy, but they're welcoming. You apply for the Night Shift, where Freddy & Friends aren't as welcoming.
From 12 to 6, you must fend off the animatronics from coming to your door and putting an end to your night. But how? Tactics in the games vary- This game has you shut doors and flick on lights to prevent them from coming in.
Shutting doors blindly will get you nowhere, and shutting the lights may be required to check for animatronics. And you may not like what happens if on the later nights you keep both doors closed...
You can also monitor the building, to check on the animatronics before they attack. Check out a guide I made on how to win.
With limited power, vision, and hope, can you survive till' dawn for five nights?
(get it if you love horror games. that's all i have to say.)
