LYNE is a simple game with simple visuals. It's tremendously relaxing but never to the point of putting you to sleep, which some other minimalism inspired puzzlers have been guilty of in the past. Instead, it launches new rules at you through obvious steps, expecting you to flow along with them and disregard the difficulty ramp which climbs higher after each 'set' of puzzles completed. Not to ruin the experience, but you won't notice the change in pace. You'll grow with the game and find your skill improving as the game evolves through mechanics.
With that said, it boasts a set of 25 levels for each letter of the alphabet and rewards you with new skins to play the game in... and it's enough. Finally a puzzle game that doesn't feel the need to bombard you with needless 'powerups' for completing level 57 in under a certain time. No, LYNE does something much better and allows you the freedom to explore the puzzles, learn the bits and pieces and relax all at the same time. If you like puzzle games, this is fantastic. If your interests lie with more expansive games that take a good 400+ hours to complete, then LYNE is certainly a great way to wind down at the end of the day.

Game is fantastic.  It's a breath of fresh air compared to what we've seen lately, and I hope to see more assymetrical style MP games in the future.
The nuances in the monster mechanics are impeccable.  There is a learning curve, but once you get it down, it's absolutely exhilarating to experience the back and forth interactions with a hunter team that just won't let up.  On the other side of the coin, playing as the hunter team against a monster that likes to stalk and strike at opportune moments to leverage the wildlife or terrain against your team is tense and really puts your team's ability to work together and coordinate abilities to the test.
Evacuation, the mode which you follow a 5 day (map) campaign offers an interesting take on how balancing a short series of MP games with the same teams can be done.  Each victory or loss impacts the next map in sometimes considerable ways.  For example, a win on one map for the hunters could mean the monster will have no ability to use its scent ability on the next map.  Or if the monster wins, a whole slew of tasty wildlife might be released on the next map so it has plenty of food to gain armor/evolve quickly.
Not to mention the different modes.  Specifically, the Rescue mode is really up my alley.  The hunters need to rescue downed survivors and deliver them to a dropship location, while the monster's goal is to take said survivors out.  This mode introduces a really cool dynamic where you're always looking over your shoulder to see if Wraith is waiting to abduct and destroy one of your survivors (or your medic...).  Since the hunters' priority is to escort the survivors, their attention is forcibly diverted from the monster and allows some insanely effective ambush opportunities for the monster.
There's plenty of information out there on the other modes in Evacuation, so I'll just say this, it's simply a lot of fun.  Since I started playing Evacuation, I can't stop.  Other games I've been playing have completely fallen off my radar for the moment.

Ragnarok online 2 I picked up by accident, clicking it while trying to get rid of an ad, and then downloading it out of curiosity. I am quite pleased I did.
The game itself is (from my limited experience), reminiscent of the playstyle of early WoW. Focused on the usual core classes and the first person MMO style I very much enjoy. The core classes are pretty varied, with option to diversify into two subsets when you get to a higher level.
Atop the core classes there is a Job system which is while second to your class, has its own leveling system and, through proper use of the job system will allow you to level much quicker. Simply put, you can make your own armor and weapons, make your own potions, or buff yourself even as a fighter before a match, depending on the job you pick.
The game is Free to play, so I would say it is at least worth a brief look at if nothing else. (As a note, the graphics start of fairly high end, nearly crippling my laptop on my first go. I would advise reducing the render distance to 2-3 to make sure it wont interfere with gameplay).
I would say that the game greatly benefits from having friends to play with, but it can be a fairly enjoyable solo adventure, with a surprisingly interesting story. I expected a simplistic, insulting reason to just go and murder several areas of color swapped creatures. Instead I got a large variety of creatures, many different NPC's and points of view. While not perfect there has been honest effort to make an interesting and involved story in which you participate, including an earlier section whereupon you end up fighting your own repressed memories.
I certainly would rate this worth a try, and possibly to keep.

Bought evolve.  It's a very good game. Pretty much all of the DLC packs in the game currently, are skins.  Whoopdidoo.  I've heard there's extra monsters for sale, as well as extra hunters, and therefore the game is incomplete for the retail cost, but honestly, this does actually feel like a complete game with 3 monsters, 4 hunter classes (12 total unique hunters), a leveling system for character classes and skills separately and a ton of thought put into the gameplay of a very welcome and refreshing take on vs.-only multiplayer.
I honestly don't see the problem, and am getting the feeling people are reacting much too strongly to the concept of Day 1 DLC for a triple-A game and a few unfortunate (and poorly chosen) phrases made by the games director and 2K's CEO.
It could be $10 cheaper (Listed on steam at $69.99 CAD), but considering the effort put into the game, that extra little bit is small price to pay in the bigger picture of things.

Linking similar shapes together without intersecting the link of the other shapes seems simple enough, and yes, it is THAT easy. However, it quickly becomes more challenging as you plough through the stages, with the introduction of 1 more shape and those blue points that requires more than 1 connection to complete the link. You'll have to fire up more neurons to clear through the puzzles in increasing complexity. With the aesthetic cool hues emitting a relaxing feeling, it is also great way to keep your mind sharp. A great combo at a well-worth price point. 10/10.

I really wanted to like this game. At first, I did. It seemed like a really good take on a survival game with good novel gameplay, but then as I got into it a bit deeper - it wasn't what it first appeared to be.
The first and most obvious - and mentioned by others, is the unrealistic wolves and bears. More the wolves than the bears. Wolves are not natural human hunters. Bears are a little more agressive in nature, but again not quite as the game makes them. I understand why. They wanted a difficulty ramp for 'hardcore'. Sadly though they have chosen an unrealistic mechanism for this. Yes, a game does not have to be realistic, but this one tries to, or looks like it's trying to be realistic.
But the real killer for me is that it is not a survival game at all in the end. It's a scrounge game. You must explore the remnants of civilisation to salvage odd bits and pieces to survive.
This is an ancient and worn out mechanism - you find it in all the old hack and slash games from decades past where you meander through town like some bandit lowlife and examine every house in the village, every shelf, drawer, desk, barrel and basket to pilfer what you can.
That is this games definition of how you survive in the long dark of a sub arctic wilderness. It just makes it boring as heck for me.
PS: The animal AI and pathfinding could use an overhaul. It's pretty weak.

I've never played a survival game before this, so when it hit me- it hit hard like a freight train. I fell in love with this game, its atmosphere, and the goddamn pianos. Also, pretty sure femshep's voice actress is in this game.

Fear
The psychology behind it. What makes us scared of certain things and not others? Childhood trauma? An innate instinct? Or just a lack of understanding of what exactly you're looking at? There are a lot of things that get my goat going in terror, but let me tell you: not one of them is being locked up in a mental asylum with a bunch of crazy freaks - yet it seems a common enough story setting in horror (In the Mouth of Madness) and even non horror (Arkham Asylum, Twelve Monkeys), but usually asylum movies are about testing a characters sanity (Shutter Island, Session 9) or the buildings are abandoned spook houses (Grave Encounters).
So what I'm saying is... it's kind of played out. Phony baloney sanitariums just don't scare me. So that means the game is bad, right? Well. Where the game actually succeeds is creating tense moments, flight or die situations - sitting in the dark, hoping for whatever it is to go away.
It's like playing a version of the Condemned where the main character is a
.
The game is jabs of intensity - when you think you got it down with its right, bam, it throws a left. The sound design is a big part of this, always trying to keep you off kilter with loud door slams, sweaty fearful breaths of the character and the whining violin strings that leave you on needles and pins as you're being chased - the music and sound deliver on all fronts - even to where just picking up a folder or a battery is something satisfying
The storytelling is decent-ish, partially relying on a heavy amount of backstory and lore, which is a pretty poor way to tell it. I mean, when you're on a rollercoaster, do you pause the ride and read flavor text about it?
Cause that's all it is - a ride - but even so, I found myself immersed in what I was doing. The first person, camera view point and NVG style that creates this eerie green glow is so enthralling that it was like finally playing [REC] - The Video Game, feeling more and more like an amateur videographer as it went along, even when I knew I wasn't actually recording anything. Although the character models aren't the greatest, reminding more of the aforementioned Arkham Asylum because it is UE3. The plastic toy model effect detracts mostly when you're seeing human characters in the Whistleblower DLC for example
Completing both the main campaign and DLC on hard netted me 6.6hrs worth of playtime according to Steam, which leads into Outlasts biggest problem -- that it's a "one and done" sort of game, in that there really aren't multiple ways to play the campaign outside of grinding achievements - but beating the game on Insane or collecting all the notes won't unlock you any new features or content. The Whistleblower DLC feels more like what you should earn after beating the game rather than paying for it, as it feels necessary to get both your story and game time worth.
But then Outlast might be a $40 game - or even a $60 game if we started piling on the extra content.
Outlast was a hard one to put down. Its first person style and tight controls will suck you in if you're not careful, but like real found footage films, if you're not willing to go with it, you won't enjoy it - but I did.

Let me start by saying I do believe this is worth buying but I caution you if you are a fan of RTS games that this may not be what you are used to. The modding community has also done wonders with this game and for the Republic at War mod alone is worth buying the game.
The game is split into 2 distinct parts. The galaxy overview where you build bases, move your troops and play in a Risk like format. The second part is the the RTS side of the game where you control your troops directly. This is further split into space combat and ground combat. I'm going to give each a review and then add the sum for my total review.
First with the ground combat it always involves protecting or destroying the buildings. The defending side get's units through deployed troops already built and gets further free troops from buildings designed to construct units. The offensive side I find often is at a disadvantage and it becomes of game of invading with totally overwhelming numbers or playing more tactically with stealth based units. This generally ends up being long winded and downright boring battles in the later parts of the game where the combat is meant to be more fast and furious to keep a game going. For the ground combat I'd give it a 2/5.
Second the space combat. This is where the game really shines and you can recreate some of the great moments from the movies. The Rebels and the Empire both play very differently and it keeps the fights fresh each time. The Imperials go for that ovewhelming numbers and get free Tie Fighters and bombers from the capitol ships. The Rebels why they need to buy Fighters and Bombers are generally more well rounded to deal with threats. Capitol ships on both sides play fairly the same with your standard Rebel Crusiers and Star Destroyers but what makes space combat so unique is that larger ships and space stations have hardpoints to target. To many Tie fighters take out the hangar. Mon Calamari Cruiser flanking around you take out its engines and leave it stranded. This adds a whole new dimension to and RTS that I've never played before and makes it a truly tactical experience. Space combat gets a 5/5.
Finally the Galaxy Overview portion. It's fairly straightforward and just involves moving units, building bases on planets, sabatoging enemy bases and upgrading the tech tree. For players who don't want to play the battles can actually play and entire match from this screen and let the computer simulate the battles for you. It's different, it's cool, it's noting totally special but does offer a new take at strategy games. The Galaxy overview gets a 4/5.
Don't expect much difficulty from the computer. The AI is somewhat dissapointing but fear not. One of the best parts of this game is what the modders have created for it. The Republic at War mod can take the place of the expansion and allows you to play out the Republic vs. Seperatist conflict. The AI in that is tough. I'm at the point where all I play is Republic at War and it offers the challenge that I was looking for from an AI in an RTS. AI gets a 4/5.
So when you add it up the game is a 15/20. That takes into accounts both the vanilla game and the modded game. The modded version is much better and totally free so it's absolutely worth getting. Vanilla version is more for people who want to learn the game or are big Star Wars fans. In all it's not super difficult and definately different from most RTS games on the market. I definately recommend this game!

Project Zombiod is a cool game.
I had looked at it a couple of times, but always veered away toward something else because of the graphics.
When I look at titles described as "rogue like" or "old school pixel graphics", I make a little tsk-tsk-tsk and think to myself, "c'mon it's 2015, make a great game AND give it modern, polished graphics".
I've never understood why a developer would create a game with retro graphics or why a gamer would choose a game like that.
So yeah, I never would have purchased Project Zomboid, and it would have been my utter and absolute loss.
The game really is great fun.  It's got depth, it's immersive, and when you are succeeding in your struggle to survive, it makes you feel like one man standing alone in the middle of the zombie apocalypse.
You can do all kinds of things in this game, fighting and avoiding zombies, obviously, but when you loot common-place items, you can use them in all kinds of ways.  Barricade yourself, create sheet rope to have an escape from a top storey window, cut down trees, create planks, build all kinds of defenses, structures and utility items. In short, this is an enjoyable game. However, if you're considering getting it because you really liked Tropico 4, I would say stick with Tropico 4. There are a couple of ways that T5 improves upon T4, which I will list below, but for the most part T5 has fewer options and is less interactive - in short, far oversimplified. T4 is an overall better game.
Pros:
-Research that opens up possibilities during a specific age, as opposed to everything of that age automatically becoming available.
-City planning made easier with a well-conceived grid that takes the guesswork out of building and road placement.
-Military made more useful/necessary by increased rebel attack-rate when citizens unhappy (could be seen as a con, but it's just more incentive to try and treat your people well!)
Cons:
-Fewer building options.
-Can't have multiple types of the same building with different specializations.
-Adjusting wages is a hassle that should have a fix-all option (it does, but in my experience it does nothing).
-Elections just happen, there's no chance to make a speech or anything.
-Interactivity lessened by only featuring dialogue/quest options from major political figures, no longer interacting with movement figureheads, like the environmentalists or nationalists and so forth.
There are other cons, but once again, they're all relative to Tropico 4, so if you haven't played Tropico 4 you'll think nothing of it. But I would just say that the pros of Tropico 5 can easily be sacrificed for the far superior Tropico 4.

If you like Turn Based Strategy games, and you liked Frozen Synapse, you will definitely like this game.
Frozen Cortex is a cross between football and chess.  It pits two teams, 5 players per team, against each other in an arena where there are "endzones" on the northern and southern part of the map, and the person who "starts" with the ball must pass or run it into the endzone, where the other team must keep them from doing so.  The defending team can intercept passes or tackle the ball carrier, which causes a turnover, resulting in the previously defending team to try to score in the northern endzone.  Each player on the team has different stats to aid them (or hurt them) in getting the ball into their endzone.
You get a "Planning Phase" where you can plan out what your team is going to do, and you can also plan out what the opponent could do.  You will get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you the first couple of games, but you will learn to do's and do not's after an hour or two.

tl;dr — Simultaneous-resolve turn-based sports game. If you like(d) either Blood Bowl or Frozen Synapse, check it out. If you're looking for a game that you can play with friends over long-distances that doesn't take a lot of time or emotional commitment, check it out. Mode 7 does great work, and nervous_testpilot's soundtracks are always top notch.
If you hated FTL or Binding of Isaac (or any of the games I mentioned above), you may want to pass. And if you're on the fence, check out Northernlion's preview of it. He gives a good idea as to what the game is like.
And now into the nitty gritty.
All in all,
. It's highly addicting, really fun, and the games are short enough that you can play one on a break or with minimum time commitment. Bonus, it runs on my toaster of a laptop. The controls are snappy and responsive with no noticeable input delay, and the interface is simplistic and clean. The background designs are gorgeous, in that whole cyberpunk future kind of way, and it's fun to see my old friends from Frozen Synapse making a return as coach icons.
That isn't to say I don't have my gripes with it, however. Overall, the game is not new player-friendly. That isn't to say it's not
, however. It has a learning curve that is relatively short, but steep, and hopefully players will go looking for assistance when they confront their frustrations rather than making smear posts on the forums.
Frozen Cortex can be absolutely rage-inducing at times. If you've ever watched (or played) sports, you should already be aware of the feeling of watching a good plan come crashing down. It'll happen. More than once. Get used to it.
Once a match starts, there is no RNG. Let me repeat that:
. People will complain that the enemy blocks you more than you block them, but it's a matter of using the tools you have available. If you know what you're looking for, you will never be blocked the entire match. Plain and simple.
However, there
RNG elements to the game. The pitch design is randomly-generated from a seed. Feasibly speaking, half of the map may be cut off from passing routes; corners may be entirely sectioned off and unavailable. End zones may have only two available avenues of ingress—and both of them may be blocked by the other team's defenders, with no way to pass them other than by risking them intercepting a pass.
The robots you have to choose from to upgrade your roster also appear to have randomly-generated stats; again, probably from a seed. In some modes, it appears that the opposing team's stats may also be randomly-generated, going from either junior varsity or the monsters from Space Jam.
My main gripe about the game is that the "standard" difficulty should not at all be considered "standard." It's really "hard" mode. You're given a team of tired, limping robots and expected to pull wins out with them—with better robots available based on your performance. So if you can't pull out a lucky win, by the time you get to Week 4-5 of a Knockout season, you're in hot water, especially if (again) you get a pitch that the more maneuverable opposing team can better take advantage of.
In a similar vein, why the developers consider Knockout mode to be the "primary game mode" puzzles me. The other teams in that mode are not single-elimination (they come up with some nonsense about how money's tight, so if you lose *at all* the season's over, GG no re).
Meanwhile, one click over, there's a much more "normal" season of 14 weeks, then a two-week single-elimination playoffs.
The teams are on a more even playing ground, you can manage your money and hire better robots in greater numbers if you know how to bet, and the game doesn't automatically send you back to square 1 if you make one mistake.
I find the match length rather short, furthering the "roguelike" moniker that if you make one single mistake (which may come down to a coin flip, even in the best of situations, if RNG just happens to stack that way), you will likely find yourself in an unrecoverable disadvantage. Furthermore, since we're human and the AI is not, one error often leads to another made in haste and frustration, while if the AI makes a mistake, it coolly carries on. This is why I said if you hated FTL or Binding of Isaac (or similar games), this one may not be for you. There *will* be times that you're put up against overwhelming opposition with no way to counter and a pitch that hampers your every move while the other team goes trolloping around. And you will lose. And if you're on Knockout mode, that's the end of your season.
But then there are the times you get it right. The times you land your blocker right in the runner's path and he kicks a robot in the gut, catches a pass, and lobs it back across the pitch to your runner on the far side, who squeaks out an easy and uncontested 11 points in a single run. There will be the times you'll punt it away only to run up and sucker punch the guy who claims it in the jaw. Those moments are priceless.
Last but not least, I feel like the tutorial is incomplete. This may be intended. There are parts of the interface that go unmentioned that can take a lot of the mystery out of the game, for better or worse. For example, the movement node is filled with color if the intended move can be completed without risk of any other players coming to block them. Nowhere is this mentioned in any of the tutorials I have seen as of the time of writing this review. It means that new players are going to get frustrated because they don't know all of the tools available to them, and that's not even factoring in the simulation mode that Frozen Synapse players are already familiar with.
But all that complaining aside,
It takes a bit of figuring out what modes you enjoy most, but once you've got some practice down, you'll be throwing long passes with the best of them. Moments of rage pillowed by hours of fun.

Game is fantastic.  It's a breath of fresh air compared to what we've seen lately, and I hope to see more assymetrical style MP games in the future.
The nuances in the monster mechanics are impeccable.  There is a learning curve, but once you get it down, it's absolutely exhilarating to experience the back and forth interactions with a hunter team that just won't let up.  On the other side of the coin, playing as the hunter team against a monster that likes to stalk and strike at opportune moments to leverage the wildlife or terrain against your team is tense and really puts your team's ability to work together and coordinate abilities to the test.
Evacuation, the mode which you follow a 5 day (map) campaign offers an interesting take on how balancing a short series of MP games with the same teams can be done.  Each victory or loss impacts the next map in sometimes considerable ways.  For example, a win on one map for the hunters could mean the monster will have no ability to use its scent ability on the next map.  Or if the monster wins, a whole slew of tasty wildlife might be released on the next map so it has plenty of food to gain armor/evolve quickly.
Not to mention the different modes.  Specifically, the Rescue mode is really up my alley.  The hunters need to rescue downed survivors and deliver them to a dropship location, while the monster's goal is to take said survivors out.  This mode introduces a really cool dynamic where you're always looking over your shoulder to see if Wraith is waiting to abduct and destroy one of your survivors (or your medic...).  Since the hunters' priority is to escort the survivors, their attention is forcibly diverted from the monster and allows some insanely effective ambush opportunities for the monster.
There's plenty of information out there on the other modes in Evacuation, so I'll just say this, it's simply a lot of fun.  Since I started playing Evacuation, I can't stop.  Other games I've been playing have completely fallen off my radar for the moment.
This is a game I've been waiting for since I started PC gaming back in the 90's.  I haven't felt this kind of excitement for a multiplayer experience since the original Half-Life.  Very highly recommended.

Occasionally, after finishing a certain film or book or piece of music or whatever for the first time, I'm forced to just sit there for a while to process what I've just experienced, and how deeply it affected me. In these rare experiences, I feel as though I've been struck dumb by just how extraordinarily brilliant and moving the piece of art is, so much so that all of a sudden it makes all of the other pieces I've previously seen from the same medium look like they were made by children, in comparison.
I've probably only had this experience less than 5 times in my life. And I had it at the end of the Beginner's Guide.
A lot of the power of the Beginner's Guide is in how different people interpret it in ways that are uniquely meaningful to them. This being the case, I won't give any specifics about it, because each word you read about it before you experience it for yourself will water down its power to speak to you uniquely.
So all I'll say is please, play this game, and before you do try to read as little about it as possible.

Don't be worried by the "early access" tag, this game is insanly well pollished. Hinterland is releasing more lands, more features, and tweaking the core gameplay, but everything is held to an excedingly high quality control standard before release. One that frankly puts many "AAA" titles to shame. The studio is extremly active in the community, both on their website and on steam. They release a major update every other month or so, ("major" being new tools, reworked gameplay, and often enough entirely new maps) and minor bug fixes and updates 2-3 times a month. They are beyond dedicated to this game.
The game primarily focuses on a hard-core survival experance, and has an admitedly steep learning curve. Surviving the first night took me two or three tries, and I played off and on for 6 months before I got the 100 days achevment. Your primary enemies are cold and hunger, but wildlife and sickness take their toll as well. The game has perma-death, and you can go from smooth sailing to dead with a single mistake. This is not a casual game, it is decidedly punishing, but it is also decidedly rewarding.
The world itself is beautiful, and only gets moreso as the game gets updated. Even after passing the 300 hour mark, I still find myself awed by the senic vistas you find by being in the right place at the right time. Sunrise and sunset are partiuarly inspiring.  The world is portraied in a rather unique style, the whole thing looks like a snow covered Bob Ross painting. This game is such a work of art I wouldn't be suprised to see a "let's Play" running in a gallery someday.
So far only the (debatably) secondary "survival mode" has been released, with a story mode still in development. But even unfinished this is a masterpiece of a game. I have far more hours invested in this saga than I do in most games I buy for 3-4 times the price, and gotten far mroe enjoyment to boot.
In short, the game is difficult, but like most difficult things, well worth the effort.

Frozen Cortex is a surprisingly engaging and complex strategy game. Based in a sort of future sport you have to work out a way out play your opponent. When your players are moving they are not able to attack other players but they can tackle the ball carrier for example. So you need to watch the lay out of the map to try an position key players to just block access. Set up points to intercept any potential passes and of course set up so get the ball to the goal area. Each turn starts in a planning phase you plan you move and keep adjusting it accordingly until you are happy then lock in your move. The game then shows this is nice action sequences until an event of import happens such as the ball being picked up. There's a lot to think about every turn which makes each plan critical. Trying to read the map to work out areas the ball cannot be thrown too because of obstacles or players, trying to control area on the map while also attacking and defending. It's pretty great and I'm really enjoying it!

Not a sports fan myself. Bought this on the back of Frozen Synapse, which was a diamond in the rough game in my honest opinion. Was apprehensive about the sports setting, but was very pleasantly surprised.

That said, there is full and in depth (albeit exclusively aesthetic) character and team customisation, which helps you become invested in your perfect team. A simple betting game runs behind the league progress, which you must use to your advantage (don't be afraid to bet against yourself once in a while :D) as well as swapping out players for better models with the funds you make through competition plus betting. The feeling of satisfaction as your bot scores a goal and does a victory dance in full cinematic glory, or the lesser fist pumping feeling you get from a succesful tackle or block are really something, and I am not a sports fan.
At the price of an indie title, you get 2 copies one for yourself and one to gift to a friend or trade. For an engaging and yet easily time adjusted strategy game that allows you to play as serious and intensive as you like or not, with multiplayer modes and tournaments in asynchronous turn based, you really could do a lot worse than give this a try.

Evolve is really fun for about two hours, but for a full price AAA title Evolve is so vastly lacking in content, diversity, strategic depth, and general charisma.
The game's biggest problem is its formulaic nature. There is one way every Hunt match plays out. The monster tries to avoid combat until it evolves to level 3. The hunters try to find the monster before it can evolve. This is the game. Unlike other games that allow for perhaps an early sneak attack (Zerg rush!) or unorthodox strategies, Evolve only allows for one way of play. You will conform or you will lose.
Apart from the signature Hunt mode, the "campaign" mode takes about a hour to finish. This mode could have been pretty interesting, with a real story and meaningful choices. Rather, it is just a string of 5 matches in a row with lip service to story. Think Titanfall's campaign but somehow worse.
The other game modes are very slight variations on Hunt that clearly were thrown together without much thought. Rescue in particular is so very poorly balanced with the Monster given competing goals of trying to evolve but also forced to immediately attack the Hunters.
This game could have been so much more. There is so much potential in the concept. It took Turtle Rock years just to come up with a barebones experience with formulaic matches. The unlock progression system is also of the extremely grindy variant that gives mathematical advantages to obsessive players and discourages new players.
Then there's the day one DLC and in-game DLC store despite asking full price up front. An abomination.
In conclusion, when Call of Duty has the decency to give us a full 10 hour SP campaign, a distinct Coop mode, and a full-fledged MP mode, Evolve's one gimmick game design just doesn't stand up to the competition. But hey, those first two hours were fun!

It took me a few hours of warming up to how the mechanics work, but the latest release has provided prompts for some of the unique rules that have been really helpful (such as "if you run here, you can't throw anymore"). Once you "get it", it's actually one of those games that really makes you think, and when a play does come off, it's pretty damn rewarding to watch (but equally frustrating when it doesn't). The simultaneous-turn-based gameplay is similar enough to Frozen Synapse, but the UI seems more streamlined and intuitive.
I will be playing this game for a while, and I listen to the soundtrack at work all the time. Keep up the good work!

I like this game. Don't let the sports facade fool you; if you like turn based strategy, this game has a lot more depth than first glance suggests.
Full disclosure: I was on the closed beta, so I've had more direct contact with the devs than your average player. My perspective may be biased.
As a fan of Frozen Synapse, I was expecting more of the same this time around. The first couple weeks of testing showed promise, but the sports theme turned me off, and the absolutely brutal AI made it difficult to enjoy. They've since tuned the AI and match settings to be more accessible at the beginning, and even more ridiculously difficult at the highest levels.
The real breakthrough for me came when I started to understand all the rules of combat. It IS a strategy game first and foremost, with a sports veneer. Winning is downright satisfying, since you know you'll never be handed a cakewalk. You start to accumulate tactics and tricks that give you little advantages here and there, and that depth is where it shines. The game becomes yours.
The waypoint system is polished and intuitive, the graphics are clean yet pretty, and the cameras and animations are very satisfying. The music is excellent. There is a story that pops in and out of the single player leagues; you can engage with it, or skip over it as you see fit. It's interesting flavor, and gives depth to the coaches, but not mandatory.
The multiplayer features are robust, and it's nice to be able to take as much time as you want to make your moves. Player-organized leagues. Multiple simultaneous games aren't unusual, so you'll never have to wait for a game. Email notifications of pending turns, YouTube auto-capture and upload... nice polish features.
It's a tight, aggressive strategy simulation that's easy to understand quickly, and has room for complex plans and tactics. I think it's worth taking a look, if that's your style of game.

Ragnarok Online 2: The Extremely Generic MMO Experience.
I remember the good old days of Ragnarok Online, with its cartoony top-down anime art style, cool spell/skill animations, and overall fun appeal. So naturally, when I heard there was to be a sequel, a 3D sequel at that, I was ecstatic.
-Insert several years of waiting here-
Then came the day when I heard Ragnarok Online 2 was available for play. I was stoked. What followed was roughly 45 hours of the most generic game I've ever played and refused to finish.
Where do I even start? I can safely say that I've played my fair share of MMO games, reaching into experiencing roughly 30+ different games. In the ones where I could make a character specific (Such as Mage, Warrior, etc), I would choose to make the healer. The most sought after, rarely played, and hardest to solo of them all. I also had a few other friends who were playing RO2 alongside myself. Well, over the internet of course.
The whole time we were playing, it just felt like a tedious run here, do this, run back kind of game. At first, I wanted to give RO2 the benefit of the doubt, but after hitting the 2 hour mark, I could see, and sadly admit to myself, that this game was just not that fun, even with other people!
During solo play, I found myself just mashing the 1 key to do my basic "Holy Light" attack, or whatever the skill was called. I barely gained another useful attacking skill for practically the entire time I played.
Playing with the group however was a more enjoyable experience. At least then, I was able to use my Heal, Revive, and Buff skill.
One of the cool things this game did have was the Card System. Almost every monster in the game would drop a card. These cards could be equipped; up to five. Certain sets would give you bonuses, and it gave the game a somewhat Pokemon-esque feel.
While the quests were generic, there was always a plentiful amount. Story, Side, Dungeon, Monster Hunters, and more. You never needed to worry about needing something to do.
Something Ragnarok Online 2 does that I absolutely LOATHE is having items, equipment, and mounts that had time-limits. Yep, you read correctly. Time-limits. The worst possible feature a game can have.

Oh, and the class change in this game is nowhere near as awesome as the first game. You finish the quest and the person just says: Congrats, you're now a X, whereas in the first one, you had a light beam down on you and your clothes would change.
Eventually I just got to a point where I said "I'm done." RO2 eventually becomes more of a chore than a game.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Quests: As basic as they can get; Split into the trio of: Go Kill X, Talk To X, Gather X.
Character Customization: Limited. Pretty much just Hair, Face, and Eyes.

To who I recommend this is at the end of this review.
(I have some experience with the game. As with beta so with full game. Also I should be placed around top15 with one character, so I can say that I've witnessed something so far.)
This is. A 4v1 game where the hunted one grows and then hunts.
Money! Almost every review states that there are tons of DLCs for ridiculous prices when the game is expensive itself enough. I can only agree with it.
Gameplay. Seriously, it really is a nice game to play. It has good graphics, full scale of unexpected moments during the gameplay, and progamers will find their place in this game too.
Lobby/Menu. Here you will spend a lot of time. Either wayting for players to be found, or just getting the class you really want to play will kill so much time as you would spend playing one match.
Classes. You got 4 classes made for cooperation to do this with monster: track it, trap it, kill it, survive it. In each class there are 3 characters with different abilities. You simply will find the specific character you want play and if not, playing as any character is satisfying enough.
Decision in menu. You got almost NONE! (Pointing at the previous two points.) You will make an order of characters you want play, and regardless of that the game will make the decision which character you will actually play.
Extensive explenation:
Technically it goes like this(from my personal experience): party is consisted of random players close to your level and close to you geographically, in lobby you will be assigned to a character which isn't already taken. You leave because you don't want to play that character. You're waiting 1m to be able to access the matchmaking again and this repeats. Eventually you get into an ongoing fight and a phrase like "my preference of characters" is taken as dirty there. Also, in a lot of times you being the highest level means you will most likely be the monster.
Of course, if there are players willing to listen to your whining, then I suppose you will get the class of yours.
Monsters. Right now you have 3 monsters to choose. One is tanky(Goliath), one ranged and middle armored(Kraken), and one fast with deadly abilities and quite weak armor(Wraith). When game starts you feel like you are the one being hunted, and when you hit stage 3 you are the one that hunts.
Bugs. I can't say that there are many, but those few are ridiculously annoying. The one with disapearing/still being visible mouse is the most common one. There are other of course. Not able to launch the game at all, ridiculous moments in the game (I bet that a lot of players could write essays about them, including me), and couple more. (See for yourself.)
Decision in game. So you've got 12 hunters, 3 monsters, 4 game modes(+2 modes that combine them) on 12 maps with 6 optional map dynamics. If it doesn't sound overwhelming then I can make sure it is.
Extensive explenation:
Each character means different gun with different abilites. Each monster has different approach. Each mode is different story (clasic hunt, defending ship, destroying eggs, and rescuing survivors). Each map means different environment(scale from canyon through forest to artificial nature). And map dynamics (known as map effects) may offer another monster in game, or teleports for either of teams, or just some spotting to make it easier to track down the monster.
Requirements. Weaker graphics cards will cry, unless you are willing to lower the resolution in order to get some FPS. I gotta say that it looks good, but there is a price for it.
Cooperation. The fact that each of the hunters plays major role in succes makes the game really fun and draging along a bunch of friends will make it a real memorable experience. Chat and voice chat are on the place, but spamming Q is much more fun (pointing at what is important, eg monster).
Balance. Fully balanced is only one monster; Goliath. No, really it is not fully balanced. Play a game against a decent player playing as Wraith and your keyboard will suddenly turn into your real enemy. When it comes to Kraken... well, he is at least killable. I would just say that he is the more challenging monster. He could stay as he is now actually.
But the experience that he wiped the whole team on first stage right when we dropped in still shocks me though (happened in beta).
Difference between alpha/beta and full game. Freakin' big. At least for those who were part of the testing phase. Those who are fresh have a lot of to look forward to, because their hopes may still lie ahead, but we, who witnessed the glory of the past testing phase, were literally knocked down by the bullsh... unreasonable things that decided the heads of theirs. (Just to make ..., huh, what? ...see the first negative point.)
Main story. There is none. Well, if you count that some monsters showed and began to be threat to all that lives, then ye, there is.
Character background. Characters chatter from time to time reavealing their lifes.
So I think that covers the major pros and cons.

Unlike many other horror games, Outlast has a very nice plot, along with good storytelling via collected documents within the gameplay. If you want to fully endulge in it, you can sit and read them, or ignore if you just wanna experience nothing but terrifying action. The gameplay itself works really well, where you've gotta depend upon your senses and smarts to get out of crazy situations, while having to think and choose your actions quickly. The only bone I have to pick with Outlast is that it doesn't last that long. I've beaten both the full game and the Whistleblower DLC in under ten hours on normal mode, reading any notes and documents I acquired. There is replayability within the varying difficulty levels and possible dedication to collect every document/note, but aside from that, you're prone to finish real fast, unless if you end up cowering in lockers half the time. Due to this factor, I would only recommend purchasing while it's on a substantial sale, as I have while it was 80% off in order to ensure that it'll be worth the cost.
All in all, it's an action packed, horryfying and gruesome experience that's fun for the whole family.

This is perhaps one of the most frustrating games I have played.
NOT because it sucks.
NOT because it has bad gunplay.
NOT because it looks bad.
NOT because it costs a lot
NOT because it has microtranscations
NOT because it has season pass
BUT...because it's  FFFF....BRUTAL
You can of course pick automatic weapons, but it's limited per team, and 90% of the times you WILL play as single shot riffleman. So expect to be good and fast, or enjoy those respawn screens.
The only game I remember dying more in was Insurgency, where I am excelling now and reaching top of the ranks, and a lot of MVP spots per each round. NOT RO2/Rising Storm. I still get my butt kicked, all up and down. Perhaps it's suppression that makes me miss, perhaps it's the fact that colors of the uniform blend into the environment, perhaps it's because it's single shot weapons that hate you if you miss, all in all game is unforgiving.
I have worked so many flanks and pulled all the way to the enemy lines, and was wiped off the face of the map, and forced to walk for another 5 minutes, but now unsuccessful, because enemy already reinforced the flank lines.
I do not remember the last FPS where I was in last place for 4 rounds in the row. Maybe it was being unlucky, but it was bad.
If you have a good team you will enjoy this game. If you have a bad game, you will want to tear nut hair out. Also, nothing like working the open field to be scoped by a sniper for last 7 spawns, while you still have no idea where he/she is. Essentially being bottlenecked on the battlefield, as everyone is falling into the same death trap, over and over.
If you don't have patience and easily frustrated...look SOMEWHERE ELSE for games.
Imo this is one of the most brutal shooters that take patience and mental composure of the Marine calmly pulling bullets out of his leg with a rusty knife around mortal fire. Speaking off...Artillery Strikes...will♥♥♥♥♥♥YOU....this perhaps is the most frustrating part of the game, you cannot predict where they land, and you really wish cancer on the commander that is spawning those strikes as you try to find cover to get a hold of the area while your silly teammates run around like chickens with their heads cut off and die right next to you.
Respawn-respawn-respawn-respawn...OOOO I'm ALMOST THERE....RESPAWN!
When do get a kill, it's so satisfying as enemy flops like a little fishy to the ground. Game also looks GREAT, very lifelike, minus player models.
Atmostphere is great, that is if you like clusterphobic experience with a sweet taste of artillery open air as you bleed through the jungle while getting burned with a flamethrower.
This is NOT a game for casual players that likes to relax. LOL...I woke up next day still frustrated after all that buttkicking. My hiney still hurts.
Still recommend, but beware of raw hardcore nature of this game, especially when it's filled with veterans with 600+ hours, while you are a noob.

Tropico - The original dictator simulator. Now in its fifth iteration, has enough changed to justify another purchase, after facing criticism of a lack of real progress between numbers 3 and 4? Well, yes and no.
I'd like to get this out of the way right now: Tropico 5 is a great game. In fact it's probably the second most fun, humourous and complete title in the series, and having played it through on the Xbox 360, Xbox One and PC, I can say without hesitation this is the version to have, right here on Steam.
Gameplay hasn't really changed much from the last title, but some alterations have been made which both enhance and detract from the experience. First of all, international trading is much more involved and satisfying. Instead of going into your almanac and simply checking off things you'd like to import and export, you click on your shipping dock and work to the supply and demand of each nation. You can assign more than one ship to a trade route, so if for example you're trying to get a nuclear power plant up and running early and China have a good price on uranium, you can stick three ships on that route to bring it in as quickly as possible. You'll also find limited time export deals, so you can send your excess stockpile of coal or canned goods to a country which will pay double the going rate for a contracted time of three years. Again, just an example.
Another big feature, especially when playing on randomised islands, is the RTS style 'fog of war'. In Tropico 5, you have to send out your palace soldiers to scout the land, uncovering the fog to reveal the landscape. You can see where mines and different are through the fog, but the types of mineral they hold will only be revealed by clearing the fog. You can't build in fogged territory either, so it's a balancing act between uncovering land to build, or making a bee line for the nearest mine to get your production up and running. Like any real time game, this is only really important during the opening stages, but if - like me - you're constantly in the red for the first year or so, paying $1000 per time to reroute your scouting party can prove a costly excercise.
A further decent addition is that of having a proper family dynasty. El Presidente will have children, and you can form a dynasty of up to five members. Each of these dynasty members has their own traits which affect the overall balance of the game, and you can select which one to play as before every mission, allowing you to preempt the needs of the people during that mission.
Also, you now unlock research, Civilization style, which allows you to gradually uncover more edicts to write and more buildings to construct. Edicts are plentiful and have a huge impact of gameplay, allowing you to do everything from banning tobacco to providing social security for your pensioners. Of course there are fascist ones as well, such as putting the entire island under military control or completely banning emigration.
When you first start a new island, you'll be running it under the command of the British Empire as a colony,and you have a limited number of months to achieve your goals and gain total independence. When this happens, you get to decide what kind of leader you'll be by signing a US style Constitution, setting out the terms of your leadership and controlling everything from who's allowed to vote, to how the media is run. If you decide to run your island as a democracy, you'll find yourself at the mercy of the voting factions every year, and as before you can make promises to sway the voters before each election. You can only ammend the constitution every four years though, so be very careful what you put in place!
Some of the micromanagement has been pared back, and to be honest it's not always for the better. The individual needs of your people are far less important than the groups as a whole. So, it doesn't
matter any more if a part of your community is outside the radius of a church or hospital - as long as the different factions on your island approve of you as a whole, you're not going to lose an election. Also, your happiness and approval rate are now separate stats, so again, as long as you are ok in the big picture you'll be fine. Direct control of your avatar has also been removed, so you can no longer visit your building sites and establishments to crack the whip.
Another simplified idea, which sounds good on paper, is the alteration of the island structure during the main campaign. Previously, you would manage a different island from scratch for every mission, allowing you to push yourself to meet the goals of that mission before moving on and starting afresh. Now, you have just two islands which you go back and forth between, with the idea being you play missions 1,3,5 etc on island one, and missions 2,4,6 etc on island 2. The mission goals change just as in previous titles, but your island is preserved as you left it. Again, it sounds like a good idea, as you have to think ahead about taking care of your people long term. But that's why it absolutely doesn't work: You have no idea what's coming next. Suddenly, you're out of space and you've built a carefully constructed military defence, only to have to tear it all down to meet the goals of the next task. The mission goals aren't structured to take advantage of the long term island system, so they may as well have left you island hopping as before. Half way through the campaign, you do get two fresh islands to start with, and it's a huge relief, but the same thing happens for the latter half of the game, moving between the two.
It's a good job then that the actual gameplay is still as robust as it ever was: Building and hiring workers is identical to previous releases, with a radial menu equally suited to mouse or controller. Yes, a city management game which arguably feels as at home using an Xbox controller as it does using a mouse, and it works straight out of the box, with the appropriate button commands displayed on the screens. The game still looks great, with fantastic detail on the buildings, allowing you to zoom right in and see the curtains in house windows, apartments with laundry hanging on the lines strung from wall to wall, and the gradual build up of goods in farms and factories waiting to be taken by your teamsters so the nearest dock. Individual garages have been removed, and people can now take their cars straight from any building with a garage to any other, and they've added a metro system, which you can place anywhere as a station entrance, essentially allowing pedestrians to teleport from any one to any other.
The disasters, complete with Penultimo's warnings, are back and are as destructive as ever. They have changed the voice actor for Penultimo, but when you get used to it he's just as funny and just as stupid as before. The great Latin soundtrack is back, and is as fitting and brilliant as ever.
Largely, the pros outweigh the cons in Tropico 5. Whilst I still consider 4 to be the peak of the series thus far, there's enough new, funny and outlandish content here to justify diving back in. With the whole collection being available for a good price, including extra missions and two extra campaigns full of new buildings and concepts, if you're a fan of the series you'll love it. If you're a city builder fanatic and have never played Tropico before, this is the perfect spot to jump right on in, but seriously consider picking up the marginally superior previous title as well.

The art is amazing, the themes and writing are really cool and well used, and you can tell the creators are huge fans of the Sentai series. Its just that the game is an exercise in incredible frustration.

: Behold Studios
: Behold Studios
: A key for this game was provided by the developer for the purpose of writing an unbiased informative review. No other compensation was given.
==========
Back in the old days there were a flood of Sentai TV series: Power Rangers, Sailor Moon, Beetle Borgs, Tattooed Teenage Alien Fighters from Beverly Hills, Samurai Cyber Squad, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, etc etc. The list goes on for quite a while. Sentai translates to "Task Force" or "Squadron" and is usually a team of heroes wearing color coded outfits or uniforms. Basically superheroes...Japanese style! Generally they come with a range of personalities/roles that usually follows some variation of the Five-Man Band. Known for their synchronized posing; also, a standard powerup pose is often used in many Sentai works during the transformation sequence. A key concept is that the collective team are more important than the individual, and that more can be achieved by working together. Chroma Squad is directly inspired by Saban's Power Rangers, and capitalizes on most of these concepts from the Sentai genre but takes it a bit further in that you are actually managing the studio shooting the TV series!
==========
Starting up the game you are introduced to your team of actors/heroes, as they are in the middle of a shoot for a TV show, taking a lot of crap from their director in the process. By the end of the shoot, the actors decide to ditch their jerk of a director and start their own TV studio and sentai hero show! One of the actor's has an uncle that lends you an old warehouse where you setup your new studio.
At the start of your new career, you get to customize your team of actors, choosing what color their suit will be, the actors themselves, and change their names. You are then able to choose your studio's name, and some various phrases that will you used throughout the game, such as when your actors "morph" into their hero suits ("Chromatize!"). As a studio manager, it's your job to choose which episodes get aired and in what order. At the main screen, you can choose to buy equipment/props for your actors that boost their stats in battle scenes. You can also check yoru fan mail, which you will recieve regularly and are able to choose differents responses to. Sometimes depending on your responses you will lose or gain money and/or items. Items can also be crafted using materials you find in combat, such as duct tape and cardboard.
The main draw of Chroma Squad is in the action scenes - combat. Chroma Squad utilizes a very simple tactical RPG system in which you can move your team across a grid on the battlefield. During your "Phase" you can direct any of your actors in any order you choose until they've all had an action, then it's the Enemy's "Phase". Each character has access to a limited set of skills, and the number of skills you can use increases as you shoot more episodes and as you wrap up more seasons of the show. Your team is able to use special "Teamwork" actions, which can be very, very useful in dealing damage or traversing the battlefield. For example, one actor can toss another one, enabling them to cover more distance. Another example is having 2 or more adjacent actors attack the same enemy in a team attack. Lastly, if all 5 of your actors are adjacent to an enemy, you can use a Finishing Move, dealing massive damage to your target! FEAR THE POWER OF TEAMWORK! Each scene also has special challenges in the form of Director's Instructions. These can range from reaching an objective within a specfied number of turns, or defeating a certain number of minions before attacking a boss. Completing these orders rewards you with extra points that are converted into fans and money at the end of every episode. Most sentai shows had giant mech suits...such as Power Rangers' MegaZord. Chroma Squad has a similar feature!
Perhaps one of the best things about Chroma Squad is the enemy designs. Early on you meet a fellow named Transitmancer -- a mage wield a staff with a traffic signal attached to the top of it. You will also meet enemies like "The Boxing Box"...which is literally a cardboard box with arms, wearing boxing gloves. There's way more creative ones and even some cameos, but I don't want to spoil too much of the fun!
==========
If you have played Behold Studio's previous game, Knights of Pen and Paper, you will be familiar with the art style used here. It's slightly more advanced than KoPaP, with even more details on each sprite. Combat animations, movement, and even the special attacks are very well animated and look really nice. Props look great, and like I said before character designs and enemies look amazing.
==========
This game has one of the most amazing soundtracks I have heard in quite a long time. The best tracks are the battle tunes by FAR. Just let a battle start and leave it there for a few to take it in. They really get you pumped up for any challenges you are faced with! I have added most of it to my YouTube playlist reserved specially for great game music! The soundtrack is available for purchase on the Store Page for $4.99. Well worth it! Seriously, just give this a listen:
The sound effects are pretty minimal, but they do their job. I can't fault the sound direction here, as it's pretty well done despite being fairly minimal. The soundtrack more than makes up for any shortcomings!
==========
Chroma Squad runs like a dream. No crashes, stuttering, framerate drops, or any weird glitches were encountered during my playtime so far, and I really don't expect to see any. Behold Studios is usually really good about the quality of their games, as we've seen so far. I didn't think to test the game with my controller, as mouse and keyboard worked extremely well. Probably best for this type of game anyway.
==========
If you are looking for a fun tactical RPG that's a bit different and has a ton of humor, Chroma Squad fits the bill perfectly. Such a great little title, and a complete joy to play. You should not hesitate at all in buying this, it's quite the gem! The soundtrack alone is enough to justify the purchase.

Based on 25 hours of gameplay (and counting).
Folks, I can't believe I'm saying this...but
Frozen Cortex is the greatest gaming purchase I've EVER made in my LIFE!
"Why is that", you ask?
* Sports - It's a sports sim...with transformer looking robots and dozens of skinng options. The game is *like* American football on an electronic pitch (procedurally generated high-tech circuitry on a gorgeously scuffed-up industrial-strength looking floor). Except this isn't just American football. It's that and Rugby, European Football, MMA, Roller Derby, Rollerball, and a throwback to Cyberball 2072! And THEN some!
* Strategy - Man, think grandmaster style Chess. Now think of something better, like Chess with Mechs. To say this game is a challenge would be an understatement. Just planning a move can be painstaking; let alone a series of them. Whether you're playing the AI or another human opponent, paying attention to every little detail can mean striking paydirt or get your bot's head ripped off (...that doesn't really happy but you get my gist).
* Tactical - People talk about games like Enemy Unknown and Shadowrun: Dragonfall's tactical gameplay. Not saying FC is any better or worse, but you would be hard-pressed even thinking about leaving FC out of the conversation. We're talking Wasteland 2 meets Fallout Tactics on the pitch. Your five versus my five. My brain versus yours. And there's no mashing buttons and constant clicking of the mouse or keyboard here DURING the play. You live with your choices! Once you map out your play, click the continue button and watch the carnage unfold.
You not only get to map out YOUR scenarios but you can map out YOUR OPPONENT's scenarios too. It's like Bobby Fisher playing  Boris Spassky in '72. What if while Bobby is planning his moves, he gets to MOVE his peices around WHILE moving Boris' peices around with unlimited access to see the counteractions of various strategies? He would've NEVER moved that damn Pawn!  Think about it! What if you can map out a "What If" in real-time, then rewind it back to do it again differently without retribution? Wargames anyone? I think I actually named one of my bots WOPR, btw. Furthermore, if you're anything like me, watch your opponent do the one thing you hadn't planned for and lay your best laid plans to waste!  >:(
Mode 7 should be commended for what they have bought to the gaming community.

Do you like Left For Dead 2? Do you like co-op, class based shooters? Having a hard day and you just want to thrash about in a big old jungle gym to blow off steam wearing a giant monster suit?  Evolve is for you then, whether if you're looking for a  good romp with some mates or just to drop in ramdomly. The base game is deep enough with lots of characters and a majority of the monsters you can unlock as you gain experience. And by the time you master all these characters, monsters and tactics, the DLC's will either be on discount or you'll have invested enough into the game to justify investing into more characters. Playing the Monster is great :D...but! freaking hard as hell to do well! Nothing more thrilling than to have a skilled human monster hunt you down or human hunters hunt a human monster down,  All my time has being playing online co-op randomly with strangers, and for the most part they're friendly and fun.
The only thing that needs addressing is the need for more game modes and more diverse "feeling" terrain (read the long for more details). Besides the odd server hick-up every once in a while, I've had a great time.
( 9  . 9) Totally nerve racking when this game is firing at all cylinders and better for it.
*note: I've not played the Alpha or Beta to this game nor followed the rabid fans/critics during that time.
And that's just the local creatures lurking in the environment.
As a class based four player team, working together is crucial and recognizing the environmental hazards keeps players on their toes and no two games are ever quite the same. The monster players have the most control of play and thus has the most tactical play to consider. This can be a problem because you need a skilled monster player to make the hunt fun, since the hunters have the advantage at the start of the round. In the absence of a skilled monster player, the Ai is pretty crafty can has some surprises in it's strategy tool kit and will take advantage of mistakes. Movement is fluid and very intuitive, makes for almost a track meet feel to the game.
There are 4 game modes to choose from and all are fun and requires different tactics for both hunters and monsters.
It's really easy to pick up on how to play all the hunter classes if you're use to co-op class based fps', and moderately difficult to become proficient at the various roles.
The monster is most rewarding of all. This comes at a cost though, the pressure is squarely on the monster to having decent familiarity with all the hunter's roles, the monster's powers, tactics to counter the hunters, and finally a strategy to win the round. This requires monster players to have many hours of game play before they can become effective at judging risk/rewards of the paths they take. Playing monster is very rewarding when your plan goes in order or when you must modify on the fly and/or exploit a situation.  Hunters may need to be on their toes according to their role, Monster players have to be on their toes about all the hunters and environmental hazards while finding a way to turn the tables on the hunters.  Oh and you do feel empowered like a bad♥♥♥♥♥monster when you Evolve and upgrade.

There isn't much of a narrative to look at and is really just stapled on for a premise and the world to exist. The four game modes are fun and highly replayable, but would like to see more mode types to construct a longer campaign mode. There is a custom game mode option which is a nice feature that offers a bit more variety. The terrain, though varied and complex, all looks very similar to the point where the stages are hard to tell apart besides lighting and snow conditions due to the palette and level design. Not a huge fan of collect "x" experience type to unlock other characters and monsters, but can understand why they did it to ease new players into the game.
Now for the 500 pound gorilla in the room. Class based co-op games are a favorite of mine, but recently my old favorite, COD MW 1, has had a franchise that's poisoned the well.  If you have read some of the negative reviews, a lot has been made about the DLC and pricing.
First the pricing. At $60 for the base game at launch, it's pricing as a AAA title and fans will pay that price. For me, the fair way to gauge value is how many hours of fun am I going to get.  And I found Evolve meeting those expectations so far. There still a lot I want to learn to play and people I want to challenge my skills and tactics against with the characters and monsters given in the base game. I was also able to get  Evolve at a 25% discount pre and post launch as of writing at other online retailers which also include a bonus monster type. $44 for a heavily community tested game seemed like a good gamble on a new iP. Plus the dedicated servers have worked really well with very few crashes or lags.
This dovetails to the second issue: the DLC. The base game is deep enough that I don't feel I need the additional content from the DLC. I still have many hours of exploration and experimentation with my existing characters and monster sets to master, nevermind the new tactics that players will learn to exploit and expand. DLC's are a bad idea when it unbalances the game so that the base game can't cope with, or worse yet: Maps as DLC (looking at you COD >:E). Given the descriptions of the DLC's, that doesn't seem to be the case. The DLC characters are just another take of an exisiting class, and the last monster isn't even ready yet. I personally think they did the right thing in making the extra characters and 1 other monster a premium, because it was priced for fans only from what I can tell. That way they can take their time to properly balance an expanded roster for those who are going to stick around for the long haul. Barking mad about the game over it's DLC/pricing seems like up the wrong tree and getting angry at a frighten cat for not jumping down, when the base game is pretty good already.
The thing the miffs me about the DLC/Pricing malarky boils down to one central thing. 2k's marketing departments needs a refresher at a communcations college and viral marketing training. The pricing descriptions were not well thought out and juvenile. They could have avoided igniting all this DLC flame warring if they just put the base version as "Evolve", the DLC as "Extras", and the rascist "Monster Race Edition" as "Evolve+Extras" edition. There, problem solved because that's what the DLC and reference to Nazi jingoism version really is from the current descriptions.

The roll of polyhedral dice, sound of paper being flipped as players turn over their character sheets, and sigh of displeasure at critical fails are what I expect from my typical Dungeons and Dragons adventures. Tales from the Candlekeep: Tomb of Annihilation is a D&D property game by BKOM Studios that captures a lot of those feelings in a digital format, but simplified (which is good). You follow the adventures of four adventurers. Artus Cimber the Human Ranger, Asharra the Aarakocra Wizard, Dragonbait the Saurian Paladin, and Birdsong the Tabaxi Bard. Your goal is to make journey to Chult and investigate the uproar of undead, which is of course caused by Acererak, one of Forgotten Realm’s most infamous necromancers and liches.
These are the only four adventurers you'll have throughout the game, with the game easing you into it by only giving you a limited amount of hero slots. By the third or fourth level, you should be rocking a full party.  There's 32 missions in the game, with plenty of main story missions and side quests. Although I played only six hours or so, I didn't feel like there was anything I had to force myself through and has a pleasant time doing all of the missions. They flowed smoothly and made my experience feel worthwhile.
Gameplay isn't anything to sneeze at, as it's played like an accessible board game. So if anyone was looking for the depth of Baldur's Gate or the pen and paper RPG, you'll have to look elsewhere. The classes feel as if you'd expect them to each play, the Bard being supportive, the Wizard being strong on AoE and magic mischief, the Ranger being overall decent at damage and mobility, and the Paladin at taking hits and killing undead (which Chult has plenty of).  All classes have interchangeable abilities, however, the game doesn't really encourage or force you to change abilities. Once you find movesets you're happy with on your adventurers, you don't really ever have to change.
Map and monsters feel varied, them being randomly generated and each tile being an "Uh oh, what's next" kind of experience. The way the game works, is that if you stand still, you're likely to incur a random event that'll be a monster spawning, environmental hazard, or something like a friendly chwinga (bunny with a unicorn horn) giving your hero advantage. This can be avoided with a resource called Adrenaline, which you can spend points of to skip detrimental events. Adrenaline can give your adventurers a stat increase if you spend two points of it, but I rarely did that, as the encounters can be truly devastating and made me starving for adrenaline as missions went bad. Your heroes can't explore forever, as the game is punishing the longer you stay in a dungeon, which puts a natural timer on each mission without actually doing so. None of the monsters feel too overwhelming, but  it can feel punishing if you explore a room and get punched for four damage by a Girallon (without any real true healing in the game) for following the pace of the game.
The loot is a touchy subject. You find items and gold in the missions by killing monsters and opening up treasure chests. Once your character gets an item, there's no way to trade them. So if Artus is dying and has no health potions you'll have to run someone over or he's going to die, while Birdsong is on the other side exploring tiles, you’re out of luck and there’s nothing you can do about it. A character death feels like the fall of a slippery slope, which is difficult to recover from, especially if monsters just have a tendency to attack lower AC targets. The trading of items that boost stats passively might help this, as I got a very good cloak that auto dodged an attack on Dragonbait early on, as well as some bonuses to hit rolls to hit and damage. Meanwhile Asharra had nothing the whole game and ended with an empty inventory. My Aarakocra Wizard felt like more of a burden than a boon most of the time.
With gold you can craft gear with various resources you find in treasure chests obtained in dungeons, through mission completion, or your player account leveling up. When the game first launched, you had a chance to fail that crafting, your gold and resources being consumed to the void. Now, the developers have made it an instant success, so no one feels cheated on a bad die roll. Good on them for that change, seriously! However, you can't obtain extra treasure chests, gold, or items by any means outside of the dungeon. Which means if you use a bunch of items and fail a dungeon, the next time going in, you'll feel naked and less prepared unfortunately.
Something worth mentioning, the developers did make the information available for all monsters by hovering over them, which was a new feature from when I first started the game. By the time I ended my campaign, I had a very clear idea of what each one did. (Even without looking at their stats, the game teaches you well, but their stat cards helped!) Some resources, such as surges I still haven't a clear idea of what they do, or if the monsters have any ability modifiers and how attack rolls are fully determined. There is a dice log, but if just tells you the initial roll on a 1-20, which isn't too helpful without knowing what it's being rolled against or for entirely. (I may be spoiled by Blood Bowl's dice log) The game would do well with an in-game dictionary for definitions and written explanations of rolls. As the only way to refresh your memory if by playing the tutorial, where an easy misclick skips over some vital information. (I ended up playing it twice, and I’m not unfamiliar with RPGs terms most of the time)
Overall, I like it a lot! The developers seem to be polishing it as time goes on, which is always refreshing to see. The MSRP $16 USD might be a little steep, but if it ever hits a Steam sale, I highly recommend this game to any RPG, strategy, or turn-based game enthusiast.
Pro's
-Unique adventurers
-Natural timer on missions
-Randomly generated tiles
-Monster variety
-DnD 'lite' feel
Con's
-Inability to trade items (This is huge and frustrating)
-Punishing spawns and encounter flips can lead to a serious tilt
-Not enough gold/resources to craft 1/4 the items by the end game, on normal difficulty
-No reference guide/book/wiki in-game for abilities/terms
While everything is randomly generated, I don't think I'll be too compelled for a second playthrough unless BKOM Studios adds in new adventurers or missions. Grinding out the rest of the gear to make my party into the Justice League doesn't seem too appealing without anything to look forward to. However, I will be keeping an eye out on this studio's future games, as this is one that earned its place on my shelf. Good job to the team and thank you for the great game!

Now this is something I haven't played before. You definitely need to play it with your friends, because playing alone just doesn't cut it. I mean yeah, it does have a campaign mode of some sort, but playing this game against bots just really doesn't feel right.
The game is pretty much jumping, flying and shooting. Well that could be any game, so let me go a bit more in depth.
When playing against friends, the 'levels' or, to be real, 'maps', are pretty much all the same structure, with minor changes regarding texture and placements of planets and other stuff that's floating around the level.
The base idea is, that there are planets/rocks or whatever that you jump off and on to the next one, while being under the influence of their gravity field. So you can also fling yourself to action by using these gravity fields, I hope you get what I'm saying.
Every time you die, you can change your loadout which consists of 3 parts; a skill or such (can't remember the real name but there are 4 options like mines, jetpack and such), a primary weapon and a secondary weapon, which can both be chosen from all the same guns, so there isn't a primary and a secondary category so to say.
Playing, at least with friends, is most of the time really fast paced and there can be a lot going on, depending on how many players you're playing with.
This game is some an ok shooter, at least for the price tag. They have tried something not so seen in shooter games, and I think this game pulls it off pretty well.
I'll give it a 5/10, for it isn't bad but it really isn't fun to play for a long time at once.
