If you are not familiar with the board game this is based on, here are some things you should know:
- While the story is inconsequential, the character abilities are varied and provide some interesting tactical descisions.
- The game plays more like a turn-based rogue-like than a normal RPG.  Each quest takes around 10 - 15 minutes and some feature larger monsters or bosses.
- While there isn't a lot of variety in the environments or enemies, it almost doesn't matter as each time you play floor tiles and encounters are randomized so that each play through of a quest feels unique.  Unfortunately, the best I can say for the graphics is that they aren't bad.
- If you are a fan of tactical games, adventure board games, or you just like D&D I recommend giving this a try.
If you are familiar with the board game, know that this is a very good recreation of that formula in video game form.  The game is also very well supported as they have already addressed some of my biggest gripes in just a few weeks.  I wish more developers would carefully  adapt board games this way, instead of just recreating the board game experience on a computer.

Evolve is a very interesting and unique experience, and one that I enjoyed quite a lot playing in both the Alpha and Beta tests that Turtle Rock and 2K invited numerous players into. Right away when you enter the game, you can see just how polished and well-created the game is, from the environments to the mechanics within - this alone speaks volumes to the heart and soul that these developers put into their game, not to mention the free Alpha and Beta releases to the public. This alone is a huge step in the right direction for this game.
The gameplay, on the other hand, has a lot of depth to it. While I won't go into detail on the specifics, each different monster and hunter respectively fills an entirely new twist on the role given to them - for example, my favorite class during the pre-release testing, Medic, had three different characters to play available - Lazarus, Val, and the third Caira. Each has their own unique kit, something different to their playstyle that makes them shine above the other, and while it does seem like the newer Medics (I'm looking at you, Lazarus) are more powerful then the standard, each does something completely different, and has a completely new playstyle attached to it. Each of the classes is this way, including the monster itself - depending on which character you choose, there's an entirely new playstyle and level of mastery attached to it. If you're one of those players who chases after such mastery, then this game can keep you occupied for quite a while - at launch, there will be 15 different characters to master, and more incoming as time goes on.
With that mastery, however, comes a level of difficulty that all hinges on the players - this can be exceedingly frustrating for new players put up against an experienced monster, or vice versa. The monster can be exceedingly hard to learn, and though there is an in-game tutorial, it does not begin to scratch the surface of what playing as the monster is like in a real game. The control scheme for monsters and hunters is very different, and can be difficult to figure out - this can turn off many players to the idea of playing as the monster. In comparison, the hunters require every player to know how to do their job correctly, or at the very least have an idea of how to play in order to have any chance at killing the monster. If you have a trapper that doesn't know how the Mobile Arena works, or how to navigate the terrain, you're going to be in major trouble. One of the biggest problems during the Beta was that because there were so many new players in the mix, experienced monster players from the Big Alpha could steamroll newbies over and over again, and most likely, this problem will occur once the game launches, frustrating everyone involved.
However, despite these small issues, the game itself has exceeding levels of care put into it, and a good balance to the characters. In addition, the developers aren't just releasing the game and raking in the cash as they work on another project - rest assured, the team behind Evolve has been listening to the playerbase during both test phases, and once the game releases, they will keep things in check, and provide us with more and more content as the year goes on.
So the final question is this: "Is Evolve worth the money and my time?" My answer is absolutely. While there might be problems in the playerbase, the game itself is beyond solid, and LOADS of fun, whether you're a solo player or able to play with your friends. If you are a solo player like myself, however, purchase with caution: while there is a solo mode, playing with others can be both tons of fun and exceedingly frustrating if people refuse to cooperate. If you truly want a challenge, go multiplayer. If you want to experience what this game is like first, go solo. There's plenty of things to try out, but at the end of the day, this game is a multiplayer, pvp game, and won't last long if you don't dive in.
I hope that this helps anybody on the fence about buying this game, as I have been the last few weeks. Regardless, bravo to Turtle Rock for creating such an amazing game for us all. I wish you success.

Some people have complained about the map sizes being too small but if some of them were any bigger then you would almost never find the monster. You should be nervous about running into the hunters and should play strategically until you're ready to fight them.

Again, if you play strategically and smart then you can win a game, even if the monster gets to stage 3 or if you run into the hunters at stage 1. There is a learning curve so you should play a few games with decent players before judging the game and saying that one side is overpowered.

For the record, I did play this game entirely with a Steam Controller, and I found navigation very clean with the Steam Controller and Steam Link, but that can not entirely change the quality of the game. The only other possitive that came out of this game was the fact that you move from game to game. In the first hour, I found this amusing. The potential is destroyed as you progress. I don't often write reviews, but for this I made an exception. I bought this game years ago in a sale when it was still early access (I think). At that time the game crashed every time I tried to load/start a map. I uninstalled it and figured I'd try it later.
2-3 years later I found it again in my library and gave it another shot, mainly because it didn't need much disk space. I found that the game now works but feels unpolished, unfinished and leaving in wanting. After a few hours I felt as if there wasn't much depth to it, a mile wide but an inch deep. F.e. you can assign your citizens a certain job (like a farmer or builder), but it is not possible to give them direct orders, so you are pretty much at the mercy of the sometimes illogical or unrelevant actions they commit to.
Another thing is when you find yourself stuck to get a certain building/job/whatever to work, the in game guide is not much of a help. Okay, so, although the game is very good, I would like to say one thing, I don't think this game is worth the £17.99 pricetag, I have completed the full (albeit short) story and nearly all of the challenges, played the endless mode constantly for a few hours, but I only have 17 hours on the game.
SUPERHOT is a game that reminds me of The Matrix, in that there are loads of awesome slowmo moments in which you glance over your shoulder and see that you just barely dodged a bullet. The gameplay is interesting and unique, but also engaging and exciting, you control a person playing videogames, and communicate to your friend through a chat box, he recommends that you play this new game called SUPERHOT.
The visuals, although not particularly detailed, are very nice, all characters are just crystalline polygons, rather than people, but this makes for some awesome looking kills.
The story lasted around 4-5 hours for me, which I have to say was dissapointing for me, as after that you just repeat the same missions over and over, which is still fun as you can find lots of ways of completing the levels, however it does make the game a little bit more boring after a while. The challenges add little twists on the game's original levels, and also add a few extra ones, but some of them are ridiculously frustrating and annoyingly difficult, like completing the whole game in real time or with just your fists.
Endless mode is fun and also adds some more levels, however, after a while, it becomes repetitive and quite boring.
Overall-
Pros -
-Interesting and original gameplay mechanics,
-Challenges add extra things to do
-Endless mode adds extra levels
-Thought provoking and almost creepy story
Cons -
-Endless mode is repetitive
-Challenges become increasingly frustrating
-Story is too short
Overall, IT'S THE MOST INNOVATIVE SHOOTER I'VE PLAYED IN YEARS

Day 7: Looting around the 2nd safehouse. Unfortunately, I got bitten by a bathroom zombie. I had an injury, wrapped it with Ripped Sheets and took painkillers. A few in-game hours later I started feeling nauseous
Day 8: We were looting around and found another horde of zombies. Killed it and looted some more. After getting back to the 2nd safehouse I started feeling Sick. Looked it up on Zomboid Wiki and we arrived to the conclusion that I'm infected.

This game doesn't seem to be finished.  They've added some cool concepts since the previous title, but seem to lack some of the previous things.  For example, there's a grade school education level, but there doesn't seem to be a grade school anywhere.  There's a huge lack of management screens as well.  There's no way to see the price of exports before exporting them or having a trade route established and it's not as simple to see factions' desires.
There's not enough character customizations.  I can't even customize the first one's name, but rather choose from a bunch of "Tropico names" where I just press left/right starting from A...  Also there's hardly any real customizations for like, clothing or hats and such.  They have the basics, maybe 4 or 5 that look somewhat decent, then a few more that I can't imagine using.  Like, who would use a pacifier or snorkel?  There's even Napoleon and steampunk - and don't get me wrong I love steampunk, but this isn't steampunk lol.
Possibly the worst part of this is it feels like it takes the customization out of everything.  The game randomly generates mini-quests which change everytime you play the campaign.  So you might start off with it telling you to make a couple meat ranches or sugar plantations, then the next time you come back to this map instead of going with something like a cannery quest or rum - it suggests planks.  Or you'll have a couple wharves already made and the quest now needs a couple more - I'm out of fish already.  And if you take initiative and try to make your population happy by building clinics and such, the next quests might be to build a new clinic or mission - wtf.  So I find myself more often just sitting back and following the quests instead of doing anything on my own.

I would really like to recommend Frozen Cortex (FC) to everyone, but sadly I cannot. The game still feels as if it's still in Early Access, or at the very least missing some main features. People who enjoy strategy games, don't really care about graphics. Frozen Synapse (FS) would be a prime example of that; the graphics are very simple, so Mode7 spent most of their resource on the gameplay and mechanics; which turned out great. However, for this one they spent more time on graphics, effect, and cinematic camera. The 3D view at the end of a turn is terrible; half the time it's facing some weird direction, and you'll end up watching the results again almost always, there is also no way to turn it off.
The gameplay is pretty decent, there aren't as many options as FS, so it's more newbie friendly; rules are few and straightforward, within few games you'll get them all. Although, it's missing basic options like, ability to wait a few secs and then throw, or ignore the ball so some other unit could pick it up. Which can be so annoying, because it can be so useful  deriving a better strategy and it would also deepen the complexity. Also if you are familiar with the FS's clocks feature, then you'll dislike FC's, it's very inaccurate, and basic. There are also some odd incidents where game doesn't play as expected. I’ve also had times where units would just let an other team’s player pass right through, or not do what I tell them to. Sometimes the turn wouldn’t end even if the ball carrier’s plan is finished, then he would just go straight to score, and get tackled. The procedurally generated maps can be faulty at times. I've had few times, where the offence would be closer to the ball, but they would have to go around some block as their path is blocked, so defence can easily get to the ball earlier and score.
Single player campaign is well done, and different AI do play differently, hence it's not repetitive. The good thing about the multiplayer system is that it's the same as in FS, but that's the bad thing too because it's lacking features it was in FS. Even though they may not be that important, but you would think that Mode7 would learn something from their previous games. Mode7 is quite famous for their terrible community involvement, so that was kinda expected and I won't hold that against them. I have never seen them actively respond on the forums.
Sound wise, nervous_testpilot did it again, it's fantastic. I'm sure you've heard in the trailer, and don't need any convincing. I do notice it breaking when I try out my turns, but that’s probably a bug and might not be the case for everyone.
To wrap it up in a pretty bow or whatever, it is a good game but it's not a complete game. You'll probably enjoy it, if you like the idea, or this genre. If you enjoyed Frozen Synapse, and can live with the bugs, then it’s your game. But if you cannot decide just yet, I'd wait it out and see how Mode7 responds. Hopefully, these issues are solved in the future, I wouldn't hold my breath though seeing Mode7's track record.

a great blend of strategy, cooperation, action, and fun.
playing as a monster is a blast, no two matches ever feel the same as you have to anticipate and strategize against 4 human hunters who each have a myriad ways of bringing the pain to you. you can stealth, choose to use hit and run tactics, flee for your life, and even use the environment (poisonous water, large hostile creatures) as a means to divide and conquer the humans
the hunter side can be just as rewarding, you play one role to benefit the entire team. when the team has good chemistry, their arsenal can be extremely devastating, you must know when to run, when to fight, and when to help your teammates who are downed or getting facesmashed by the monster.
each match takes anywhere from 5-20 minutes. do you choose to slug it out from the get-go? do you bide your time sneaking and evolving and finish the game with one climactic fight? i like that the arenas vary in size, some being enormous (very monster friendly) and some on the tiny side (human advantage).
there are, of course, a few downsides to the game. buying the base game is 60 dollars. all things considered, this is a AAA title through and through, so you have to expect the price tag. however, the DLC for 2 monsters, some hunters, a couple skins, and more maps makes the game quite expensive. for someone like me, this isnt an issue, i was actually happy to spend $100 for the PC monster race pack, i know i am going to keep playing this game for quite a while and i want to get the full experience the game has to offer as it comes out. i know the price tag has deterred a lot of people from enjoying the game and reviewing negatively but if this is a game you can get yourself immersed in, youll have an extremely enjoyable experience
tl;dr its expensive but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s of fun
edit: by writing a lot i hoped to emphasize the point of balance in the game. monsters and hunters alike have advantages and disadvantages. with some exceptions like a stage 3 wraith, a showdown between monsters and hunters can end with victory to either side, depending on how the cards are played

So for the most part the reviews of this game seem to be complaining and whining about the length of the gameplay.
Honestly the game is very very short, but the themes and psychological thrills the game is trying to accomplish can only go so far before they become tedious/uninteresting. The Park IS a short thriller, but it really delves into the workings of the subconscious and achieves a beautiful yet merciless atmosphere. I wouldn't recommend the title at full price, but it's one that goes on sale often. If you're really into narrative story-telling and thought-provoking materials, then this game is still worth the $12.
It does come with some replayability and the story is really envelloping, but I would have to agree that the game comes to close in a hurry. Just stop, enjoy the environments and all the themes and tropes the game deals with, don't rush through it to the end... Also if you are an achievement hunter, the achievements aren't too much of a challenge to acquire.
In my honest opinion, if you know what you like (this game is similar to Gone Home and games of that caliber), then this game is a gem, definitely worth even $10... If you want a game with an enemy you can combat, and with solid answers to the protaganist's experiences and questions, and a tangible reward that you can boast about, save your dollar. This game offers only logical treasures and thought-provoking build-up.

I will try to be brief.
Should you buy the game right now? No. Should you buy it when it's on sale? Yes, maybe.
Let's go over the pros first:
1. Visually the game looks decent.
2. The gameplay is more or less fun.  When you finally catch up to the monster it can get pretty frantic and fun. When you are searching for the monster, that's where it becomes dull and boring. After 4.9h over the past 2 days, I cought myself thinking "can I have some action please", when we were searching for the monster for 3 minutes streight yet again, and daisy was going back and forth in one sport without any indication whether she cought the tracks or the scent.
3. The character banter can get interesting.
Well, that's about it, pros-wise.
I am not a big fan of playing as the monster. Although I do admit that it is more thrilling, and some pople might enjoy that aspect of the game way more than playing as the hunter. Being a monster is a tenser experience. You're constantly on the move, constantly looking for food, and trying to figure out how much time to feed you have, before you have to run, and then where is the perfect spot to evolve.
Cons:
1. The content. The content in this game is minimalistic. There is a short "campaign", which is  basically 5-rounds of various modes. You can beat it in around 40ish minutes. And that's it. There's scarsly any story, and I just can hope that Turtle Rock will eventually release additional campaign chapters that will make it more interesting. Other than that you are getting 16 maps, 3 monster characters, 4 hunter classes with 3 characters per class. You can't customise your characters beying the perk that you select before the round begins, or the skins that you buy from the shop, but we'll get to that later. Evolve claims to be an AAA title, yet, given the content that is avaiable in this $60 game, I can't really agree with this claim. A stale series such as CoD usually offers you a full campaign (aka story mode), multiplayer with a dozen of maps, a fair ammount of customisation for your character. BF does the same. Alternatively, games like Wolfenstein: TNO, or Bioshock offer you an immersive world with a strong story and a overall a memorable experience. And I can't really say that Evolve offers any of that. What it does offer if, is a shop, to go and buy tons of DLCs
2. DLCs. There is a LOT of DAY ONE DLC content that 2K is trying to sell you for additional fee. In fact, the shop looks like something that belongs in a F2P game. Some people defend the game buy saying "well, you don't have to buy this content", "it doesn't affect the gameplay", and even "GW2, WoT and DOTA 2 have shops".
a) The fact that I don't have to buy all that content doesn't change the high probability that at some point this content was part of the base game .The sheer amount of it indicates that the customisation option is an innate part of the game, and at some point it was likely indluced in the game without the shop. Ripping contnet from the base game with intent to sell it on top for a $60 price tag, when the game on it's own is already a barebones product that doesn't shiny with an overwhelming ammount of conent to being with is just a poor sales practice.
b) A comparison with likes of GW2 is also innacurate, because GW2, albeit a beast from different genre, had tons of content in the base game, something that Evolve, with it's 16 samey-looking maps can't boast.
c) WoT and DOTA 2 and other F2P games don't  require you to ponny-out $60 just to get in to the game, so it's only natural that those games will have shop.
Finally, 2K's argument that allegeldy without that shop and ton of DLCs the game wouldn't be able to exist, is doubvious at best, when you see other AAA-titles brinning more content for the same $60.

When I have found LYNE on Steam, I instantly fall inlove with the graphics, simple and clean, but yet interesting. So I bought it (at the moment 1,99€ at Steam)
The gameplay is easy, you click & hold at the first main symbol (these with border & filling) and lead the way to the other main symbol of the same kind. Done. You can not cross a way twice. Thats the main idea, kind of like the old game most of you played in school "Dots & Boxes". As probably every game in this world, it get's harder and harder from level to level. After 25 Levels you gain a triangle and finished the sets just to unlock another one.
If you unlocked all sets, don't worry, after set B you unlock the ability to play daily sets. Every day you will get new sets with random difficulties to play and win.
:
I love the design. It is simple and clean, very interesting and smooth to watch. Sadly this game does not support HD/Full-HD on PC, so that some of the athmosphere gets lost. Also it's kind of unsharp in the fonts sometimes
:
The music theme of the game at all is awesome and relaxing. The sounds when you finish a level are great and make you happy, so you get addicted in unlocking more levels. The variety of the music is sadly pretty small and the sound of the symbols when you pass them sound like if someone is blowing into a bottle of Coca Cola and gets annoying after a while.
:
Clearly it is a very great gameplay if you love that kind of "strategy" games. It combines oldschool elements with some new interesting features. Also the veriety of levels and the daily feature is great. Sometimes the balance of the levels is pretty uneven, as example Level B18 was super hard while the next few levels where pretty easy. Fix the balance a little bit ande this would be amazing
:
If you plan to play this game on the computer I can just highly recommend you this game. But!: Be aware, if you look for some super sexy time killer, you will just get pleased in the time killer part, 'cause the fact that this game is not HD/Full-HD is very sad, 'cause the pretty design gets lost in unrendered and unsharp fonts. Still every little design element is perfectly planned through and don't hurt your eyes at all.

Unlike many other horror games, Outlast has a very nice plot, along with good storytelling via collected documents within the gameplay. If you want to fully endulge in it, you can sit and read them, or ignore if you just wanna experience nothing but terrifying action. The gameplay itself works really well, where you've gotta depend upon your senses and smarts to get out of crazy situations, while having to think and choose your actions quickly. The only bone I have to pick with Outlast is that it doesn't last that long. I've beaten both the full game and the Whistleblower DLC in under ten hours on normal mode, reading any notes and documents I acquired. There is replayability within the varying difficulty levels and possible dedication to collect every document/note, but aside from that, you're prone to finish real fast, unless if you end up cowering in lockers half the time. Due to this factor, I would only recommend purchasing while it's on a substantial sale, as I have while it was 80% off in order to ensure that it'll be worth the cost.
All in all, it's an action packed, horryfying and gruesome experience that's fun for the whole family.

Congratulations on your win nothing victory is what this game should have splashed across the final screen. Prior to purchasing, I read many reviews saying how deep or philosophical this game was. Bull, it's nothing more then walking from point A to point B and occasionally pointlessly interacting with something that the narrator tries to give meaning to but ultimately only serves to get you to point B. I wanted to like this 'game' as I really liked Stanley Parable and I will admit some of the areas were beautiful or at least intriguing. But whereas Stanley had the fun of thwarting the narrator and ultimately gave you the feeling that you do have some control over your destiny, Beginner's Guide is just dull and depressing with no humor and no control over how it unfolds. If I want to be depressed, I'll read the news. If I want to have a story with a lack of control over how things end up, I'll read a book. I play games to escape the dismal things in the world around me and hopefully through my actions leave the game world a better place when I'm done solving its riddles/killing the aliens/saving it from demon infestation. Maybe depressing pointlessness is the point of this game? I could have experienced that for free. Is it somehow deep or philisophical? Not really and I didn't give it a moments thought after I finished it other then to write this reveiw. Installed, played, beaten and deleted in 2 hours. What a waste of time and money. If I wanted to walk around while someone talked to me I would listen to an ebook and walk through the park and be ten dollars richer and better entertained.

Went in expecting a difficult action platformer with beautiful animation based on what I'd heard of the game. The beautiful animation part was right, this is some really top-notch work in that department. The gameplay, however, doesn't hold up.
This is mainly a boss rush game with a handful of small platforming levels sprinkled in here and there. Bosses are difficult, which is pretty great! However, they also have a TON of health and their random attack patterns can range from "walk in the park" to "this is really quite difficult." This leads to situations where you can either have a cakewalk without feeling like you've earned it if the boss hits all of their easy patterns or a highly challenging experience if they hit all of their hard patterns. Usually it's a weird mix in-between. You'll definitely have plenty of time to learn each boss' pattern as you die a few times, but the ohter issue I have is that the bosses have so. much. HP. After you've seen every pattern for a phase enough times you'll end up dying at a later phase and then it will take what feels like an eternity to reach the later phase of the fight again.
There are also rather lengthy transitions between most phases. I'm really on the fence regarding them; on one hand as a fan of animation they are really top notch stuff! However, as elements of a game it's an unskippable waste of time. You can shoot most bosses during the animations and they flash as if the hits are doing damage, but without any discernible HP bars I cannot tell whether this is doing anything worthwhile or I'm just wasting my time.

This a really cool, funny game. It's based on Power Rangers, so it's obviously already awesome just because of that, but the gameplay is what really makes me love it so much. This is a strategy game where your characters become more powerful by either (The long way...) crafting equipment you gain from various enemies, or (The easy capitalist way) paying for equipment at a shop. This game also has a few different possible endings, so that gives it some replay value, and since this game lets you choose different characters at the beginning as well as have your own play style, you shouldn't really be bored out of your mind replaying the game like I usually am with some other games. The price isn't really too much compared to what you get out of it, because there are a lot of ways you could customize your team to work with your play style (At least 3!.... Chroma Squad really gave me a lot of nostalgia, especially since I grew up watching Power Rangers, but I think I could really recommend this game to anyone who really likes any sort of strategy game or any sort of game where you can make important choices to decide what happens. The Park is sure to catch the eye of any horror fan, its setting and atmosphere excitedly screaming: Play me! Not being able to resist the seductive allure of its sinister facade, that is precisely what I did. After two hours it ended, and once again, a promising horror game has left me disgruntled. To be clear, the atmosphere is efficacious and a handful of the scares will leave you picking your fevered heart up off the floor, but the story, characters and themes drag the entire experience down. It would appear Funcom were entering the most unlikeable character of the year contest when they created Lorraine; a vacuous individual with no redeeming qualities whatsoever. She wanders around the park wallowing in self-pity, expressing her nihilistic views; which begs the constant question why she doesn't just turn back and leave, suddenly her loathing will be interrupted by a terrifying manifestation of some eldritch horror, which then prompts her to reminisce about bygone days with notes of ardour. I'm assuming this is meant to convey Lorraine's inner struggle, but it's a complete mess, it's all over the place and the story doesn't help matters at all with its stern intent of being vague. The child is nothing more than a plot device, and only has one line of dialogue if I recall correctly, which is probably a good thing.
If you're just looking for thrills and spills in a creepy environment, then the park is open. Anyone searching for something more, it may be wise to save your money.

Courier of the Crypts is a stellar throwback to golden age of SNES era gaming and is currently available in Steam early access. At present, the game offers roughly two hours’ worth of content and this could be stretched out a little if you plan on finding every secret. It looks great, sounds great and shows incredible promise – but at a fairly steep buy in price of £8.99, is it worth your time, and indeed cash in its current state? Let’s take a look.
Courier of the Crypts follows the journey of a nameless young courier as a routine delivery to the sacred crypts goes from bad to worse. Trapped in a living nightmare, surrounded by evil spirits with only a simple torch and his wits to keep them at bay, you must traverse the depths of the crypt and solve fiendish puzzles to discover the truth and return to the surface. Very little narrative is actually conveyed direct to the player, instead relying on hidden notes to flesh out the story and provide hints on where to find hidden treasures. There are occasional bouts of dialogue though these are few and far between – particularly as the story is still being implemented. While so far what little of the story I know of might not be groundbreaking, it’s enough to keep me interested and incentivises finding more hidden notes. One criticism however is the lack of interaction with the environment. With a solitary setting such as this, and very little dialogue, being able to inspect your surroundings and hear what the courier has to say about it would make exploration more engaging and enjoyable.
As far as gameplay is concerned, Courier of the Crypts would be best described as an exploration-puzzle game in a loosely similar vein to the Legend of Zelda (minus the combat). The game plays out in stages selected from a linear map like Super Mario World, this is slightly disappointing as I expected a sprawling interconnected over world with possible backtracking, but maybe I jumped the gun a little on that assumption. In any event, the level based design doesn’t detract from the game in any way, and I fully expect branching paths to make an appearance further into development.
The goal of each level is merely to reach the exit and proceed further into the crypts, and every step of the way you will be hounded by vicious spiders* , death-traps and puzzles. However, at all times you will require your torch to drive off enemies and find your way through the gloom. Darkness is a persistent threat and managing your light source is paramount, as when it runs out, it’s pretty much game over. The name of the game in COTC is conservation. Carefully managing your remaining ammo, torch levels and health is the key to success. By paying close attention to the environment, you can manipulate enemies into various traps, thus saving on precious ammo potentially needed to break down a wall leading to a secret area. Sadly, slain enemies don’t drop anything making fighting them all the less rewarding. For the most part they can be avoided altogether if you keep an eye on their path, of course this requires the torch to be kept on, and if you plan on exploring fully, you’ll run out of fuel before too long. There’s a careful balancing act involved in each level, but with all the secrets to find, and the fair challenge on offer, the game does a solid job of making each level fun and diverse.
Each level contains three hidden relics, as well as other gold and treasures – thus far there doesn’t seem to be a shop or merchant of any kind, nor do the acquired relics unlock anything. I don’t doubt that they will have interesting uses upon release, but at present, this is merely indicative of how little is actually there. Indeed, at the moment there isn’t even an inventory screen, and any acquired items are simply shown in the top right of the screen unable to be inspected. I would hope to see a proper inventory screen including item descriptions, as well as a running tally of discovered secrets and relics as the game proceeds through development.
Courier of the Crypt does a terrific job of establishing atmosphere, which is no easy feat in a retro styled game. It manages this through effective use of lighting and ambiance – both of which combine to create a genuinely eerie feel to some areas of the game. The retro pixel graphics are very nicely implemented and manage to remain, distinct and clear amidst the dark level design - the shading and lighting effects really make the crypts graphics shine through. The sound design is also incredibly competent featuring a number of fantastic compositions by Zdravko Djordjevic which were a joy to listen to. For the most part, levels have no music, instead featuring a cold ominous ambiance which highlights the sound effects of the courier’s footsteps and the creaking of old wooden doors. Again, the great sense of atmosphere really helps to realise the dark game world.
Overall, I greatly enjoyed the time I spent playing Courier of the Crypts, and was very disappointed that it ended as quickly as it did. With only six stages (as well as a fabled secret stage), there’s not a lot on offer, but while it may be in a semi-unrefined state, what little there is, remains incredibly promising, especially for the work on a single man. COTC has its share of problems such as some cheap deaths, infrequent checkpoints and poor English throughout much of the text, but those thirsting for a solid retro style adventure game need look no further. Upon release, COTC will be more than worth its asking price, and by buying in to early access, you have a chance to try it out early and provide feedback to help guide its future development. For all these reasons and more, Courier of the Crypts should stay firmly on your radar and is definitely worth a purchase in its current state.
*For the squeamish among you, there is an “arachnophobia filter” available in the settings menu which swaps the spiders for beetles…it’s not much better.

It's hard to believe that this game is developed by only one single person because the amount of effort and care that has been put into every single pixel, sprite and maze-like level is astounding. Each of the “crypts” feels like its own living micro-world that you have to navigate through in order to survive. The way each creature moves, attacks and flees is fascinating, and some puzzles can be a bit of a challenge if you aren't paying attention to the world around you. The main character, the Courier, is a young and lazy boy, who has stumbled upon an ancient torch that wards off evil forces. He must travel through the crypts in order to complete his courier job. Problem is every evil entity is after him and his magic torch capable of repelling the evil magic within these crypts.It is up to you to guide him through these mazes, outwit enemies, solve puzzles and complete his delivery.
There are multiple ways to travel within the crypts, and even someone who just likes destroying enemies will be satisfied with how this game plays. It is rewarding no matter how you play it, and there's no right or wrong way to get through each maze. While taking your time is encouraged to find everything but to discover the secondary story about the torches origins and the meaning of the small cutscenes requires more effort. The player will still understand the story, they just won't get the full lore and if that doesn't matter to them then it should be fine. The developer has ensured that players can play through this adventure using multiple methods, however the puzzles are subjected to one fixed solving pattern. But to get to the puzzle one could be stealthy, go in rocks blazing (Since rocks are your primary weapons), or you can always trigger the enemies to follow you and lead them into a clever trap. The sky's the limit for what you can do to finally reach your end goal.

Courier of the Crypts is like Goonies meets Evil Dead, with evil crawling around every corner and demons trying to chew your face off. A poor helpless child is thrust into an impossible situation and its to up you to guide him to safety and find out whats going on. The only protection you have is the light and your wits. Your only ally a torch which is slowly fading, and keeping the monsters at bay. You do not want to know what happens when it runs out. Time is of the  essence.  Courier is needless to say, a very difficult game. Courier doesn't do much hand holding and throws you neck deep into its puzzles, which you must carefully navigate as you face nightmares trying to kill you. While you can kill some of the creatures that chase you, your resources to do so are finite, you must use them wisely and at precise moments otherwise find yourself lacking in a key pivotal moment. Overall Courier accomplishes in its themes and aesthetic. The dungeon feels dark, evil, and mysterious. Cobwebs hang and treasure shines as you make your way slowly forward looking for traps. All the while watching your pitiful light fade ever slowly away. With bosses, shops, and more features to be added to this already fun and challenging adventure game. I personally cannot wait to see what is it that awaits for our Courier and the nightmares that will be unleashed.

Courier of the Crypts is a very atmospheric puzzle game with stunning lighting and beautiful 2D graphics. As you all can probably tell from the screenshots. I would highly recommend this to anyone who likes narrative game experiences combined with unique gameplay. The game is pretty much bug free, which is rare for an Early Access game. Some minor annoyances here and there, which will probably get fixed later (see cons).
This is not a hack 'n slash dungeon crawler so if you are expecting to massacre hordes of enemies and gather insurmountable amount of loot, this is probably not the kind of game you're looking for. You have projectile weapons and bombs (probably even more variety in later stages) but they are very limited and you're just best off trying to avoid enemies rather than waste bullets.
The main mechanic of the game is your magic torch, that keeps the enemies from charging towards you. They will still hurt you if you get too close to them but at least they won't run towards you from the other side of the room to eat you. You have a limited amount of power in the torch so there's a pressure to conserve the fire in order to make it through the level. Trust me, you don't want the torch to run out of juice..
Pros:
+ Graphics are gorgeous. Especially the lighting effects.
+ Great atmosphere.
+ Gameplay forces you to plan ahead, conserve your resources and to thread carefully.
+ Bosses are fun and challenging.
+ Sound effects and ambience works really well.
+ Interesting story and setting. Makes you want to find out what happened. Dialogues/monologues are also nice touch.
Cons (aka. minor nitpickings):
- The checkpoints only activate once. I went through a level where I finally beat the boss but still wasn't done with the level. I died after that and had to start from a checkpoint before the boss, even though I returned to the checkpoint after the boss fight. Would've liked a save after the fight too.
- Not too much variation in the gameplay for what I've played so far.
- Dialogues would benefit from professional editor's touch to make them less clunky. They are not bad by any means though.
All in all, I'm loving the game so far. It's very good for an Early Access game and the developer seems to be working hard on the game. It's definitely worth a buy even at it's current stage.

I bought this game a week ago, and before I even thought of writing a review I wanted to play this game extensively. Its been eight or nine years since Empire at War was released and it still holds up as a viable and entertaining game, even though the engine is a bit outdated.
Space Battles are superb and can mass into hundreds of ships locked in hull to hull engagements. The battles are so detailed to the point where you can order a squadron of TIE fighters or X-Wings to attack a starship using a unique hitpoint structure for the games time (We have seen it many times since). However, I have to say the space battles are the MOST impressive aspect of this game.
Unlike the space battles which is almost unlimited on your size of the seige, the land invasions are heavily restricted on how much is on the battlefield at one time.  You land at a command point with a set number of reinforcement slots and must wisely choose what unit you want on the field. The options are massive as the Galactic Conquest mode offers forty-three planets to dominate under the Galactic Empire or the Rebel Alliance. It is an amazing sight to see five to six AT-AT's roam Hoths frozen tundra in search of the elusive Rebel Base, and you actually command them!!
To tell you readers interested in this epic game the answer you were reading for, BUY THIS GAME!!! You will be blown away at the magnitude this game can throw at you making every unit and desicion you make a careful one! This game is easily worth the buy      9/10

This game is crazy.. in a good way. It is in essence a Diablo 1, without the weapons. Alone in the dark, without the really scary stuff. Call of Duty, without shooting, first person, weapons, vehicles, sheep.. Ok, it's not at all like Call of Duty.
You know, when I was a boy, we had a dog. It ate my homework, so I went to Mrs. Picklewood, and told her what happened. Do you know what she said? Me neither. I didn't even have a teacher called Mrs. Picklewood. But, that is nothing to do with the game, so back to the point.
Your main companion in the game is an everburning torch, that provides you with plenty of bright light, except for..
Well, it's not everburning, only if you always refill it. And, besides, 'plenty' and 'bright' are very subjective words. Let's just agree that it shines brighter that your dagger. Not that you have a dagger. But you have stones, plenty of them! (just remember, plenty is a subjective word)
Of course, you are not really in danger anyway. There are only spiders. And the thing that shoots you from far away. And traps. And lava. And the spirits that kill you if you run out of torch fuel. Aaaand... Anyway. At least you have puzzles. And funny jokes. And funny puzzles. And laughing spiders. And those machines that collect the corpses and make salami of them. (ok, maybe not the last two)
In short, buy the game and play it. And, when you are done, we look at each other with eyes shining with the inner knowledge. Then we look at 'them', the poor guys who never played the game, and we share a knowing smile.
Go and get it.

This feels like a true survival game.
You need to think as you would if actually left in the wilderness. From figuring out the most efficient way to satisfy your hunger, thirst and shelter needs, to the search for a way to protect yourself from the local creatures, everything is set towards using your brain to figure out how best to do it before you freeze to death.
The machanics are elegantly simple, yet true to reality (well as true as a game would allow). You need to build a fire? Sure, but that'll depend on you collecting a few things. You'll need tinder, a fuel source and a way to ignite it. Are you outside? It's probably going to be a little harder to build a fire. Are you outside in a blizzard? It's going to be impossible to make your fire without some accelerant, like perhaps that jerry can full of gas you picked up a few days ago.
The visuals on this game are just beautiful. The weather is a character of its own. You'll find youself walking in the sunshine, a pack full of food, thinking all is going to be fine. Then snow starts to fall. Just a little. Just enough for you to think; wow, that's really pretty. Then the snow comes in thicker, the wind starts to whistle the slightest bit and you realise that in maybe half an hour a blizzard is about to roll in. You need to find shelter. Now. Before your luck runs out.
And through it all, you are on your own. I cannot emphasis how much this game visually and environmentally forces you to realise how alone you are, and how vulnerable you can become in the blink of an eye.
And you will become vulnerable. You might venture into a ravine, and all of sudden a wolf takes a fancy to you. You grapple with each other. You stab him with your combat knife and he runs away to die. But now you're bleeding and you risk infection from the bite. You use your last bandage and pop some pills. Your clothes are torn, so you'll also need to repair them. You stumble on, following the wolf's blood spatters in the snow, and are fortunate to come across your foe's carcasse. You whip out your knife. Wolf meat for dinner tonight, once you find a place to settle and build a fire to cook it. And night is now closing in. Where to stay? What's that mound in the snow ahead? Is that a hatch? It is, and you spend the freezing night in a prepper's underground cache.
The next morning you rise, it is foggy. So foggy you are sure you'll get disoriented. But you can't afford to stay here. You need to find a gun. You need to find a more secure place to settle and start trapping rabbits and maybe doing a little ice fishing. You've heard of a valley and a farm where you can hunt deer and maybe settle down for a while away from the howling of these wolves. You repair your clothes. They're warm enough, but if that wind picks up again, their windchill protection isn't so great. Maybe you'll find a ski jacket somewhere along your journey.
You check your gear. Still some of that wolf meat from last night. Still some water. Enough materials for a few fires. Your bedroll, in case you're forced to sleep outside or in a cave. You take a step into the snow. About twenty metres away, you see a stump half rising from the fog. You scan left and right, and then you hear a gentle snuffling sound. That stump is actually a bear. The first one you've seen. You need to leave now, before he notices you. You back away, and the bear slowly ambles away from you and into the fog. You breathe a sigh of relief before setting off on your journey towards the farmhouse you hope to find.
A flake of snow drifts down from the sky.

You can find pieces of a few different genre's inside BioShock. But if I had to use one word to describe the game it would be "atmosphere". The visuals & sound effects really make you feel like your in another place, and time. The core gameplay is a first person shooter, but you acquire interesting abilities that really modify the combat. There's a leveling up system for your abilities similar to an RPG. All the story telling is done through audio logs you pick up along the way. The enemy’s come at you shouting crazy things before they attack. They come in a few varieties, and they have decent AI. There is no multiplayer, but the campaign gives you plenty of replay value. There are multiple endings depending on the choices you make further adding to the replay value. I really can't say anything more without giving you a spoiler or two. The graphics can be scaled back, and I find you can run this on practically any PC (not your grandmas Windows 95, but anything from 2012 and up should be fine). So if you've been on the fence about this one, and you like a single player FPS. Just do it! It's a fun playthrough.

After reading a handful of the negative reviews they all focus on the large upfront cost of the game with the pricy DLC planned. However I feel that punishing a very fun and unique game because their publisher wants to make extra money is not the right way to go about it.
The game itself is very fun, and it feels complete without DLC. 3 of each hunter and monster as well as 16 maps (and new maps are free), multiple games modes for when you get tired of playing cat-and-mouse in Hunt mode, and a reasonable matchmaking system. This does not feel like a cut down game to have pieces sold as DLC like Metro Last Light or any of EA's games. The $60 price tag is expensive but if you don't buy any of the cosmetic DLC and purchase the game on sale or from a reseller you can still get the game for a reasonable price.
Do I feel that 2k is making a mistake with the pricing and that they may ostracize a large amount of their potential gamers which can lead to a collapse in their own gaming community? Yes.
Do I feel the game itself should be punished for the pricing scheme that 2k has developed? No, it is not Turtle Rock's fault they got purchased by Take-Two when THQ went bankrupt.
Do I feel that the game is worth $60? Tentative yes. The game feels complete and if this is your cup of tea you will love this game, but if you are worried about the cost then purchase the game from a reseller (around $40) or when it goes on sale.
Are you going to pass up on a great game with very easy money-workarounds just to spite 2k and Turtle Rock? I hope not.

I certainly recommend this game to people who like casual abstract puzzle games. This isn't Rubik's Cube, but some of the levels can be downright diabolically devious to overcome. There's never a time limit, you can work on each level as long as you'd like. It's also one of those games that you can pick up, play five minutes, and put away. Unfortunately, it has a very strong "Just one more level" factor to counterbalance. The graphics are simple and elegant, very smooth, and very very effective at teaching the game to players without resorting to any language. Seriously, this game's look and feel teaches players how to play so effeciently that you find yourself automatically doing what it's asking without thinking about it. The learning curve isn't very steep, but the complexity mounts tremendously, moving from easy trial and error solutions to thought requirements then some trial and error. There's no scoring, just how many levels you've beaten. It's simple, beautiful, and a joy to work with. It's also available for Android, and I've already snapped it up for my phone and tablet. My five-year-old picked it up pretty quickly, too. Try it out!

As an avid horror game fan who's always craving for more, my expectations for Outlast weren't all too high - asylums, terrible secrets, yadda yadda yadda. Boring. Yawn. We've all seen it before. Actually, if it hadn't been for the 80 percent discount, I wouldn't have looked at Outlast twice. But I decided to give it a go.
Boy, was I wrong.
What Outlast loses in its boring premise, it gains back in gameplay. Run, hide, or die — love it! Not being able to fight back adds a whole new level of despair and horror ito the game. Knowing that the enemy could be lurking behind any corner at any time, and knowing that you have no way of defending yourself really makes the adrenaline kick in.
The typical "your flashlight might die" -scheme has been replaced by the camrecorder — and it works. At times, I truly did feel like an investigating journalist trying to capture the horrors of an asylum. At times I was more worried about my camcorder batteries than I was about the patients trying to take my life. And, at times — if not most of the time — I felt scared. Just like a horror game should make you feel.

I had never been lost before. It was not scary; it did not worry me. I just layed there on the hard ground thinking to myself, “I sure wish I had a blanket.” The ground below was comfortable due to the thick grass I had been lying on. When I finally did decide to open my eyes to this harsh world, I realized it was night time. I could see the outline of the leaves above me from the dim light of the crescent moon. I could not decipher what time it was because of the thick leaves above me. I propped myself up on my arms and looked around. I could only see maybe 15 feet in front of me. I looked back. The rock face I had fallen from earlier was still as tall as I remember. There were not any visual foot- or hand-holds that I could use to try to climb back up. The trees around me seemed to make a path that led straight forward. I got up.

This game manages to be worth playing while containing no fun whatsoever. My mood became significantly worse as a result of playing it, but it was also kind of beautiful. If you want some scary introspective stuff to chew on in your head for a while, play The Beginner's Guide. I'll be thinking about this game for a long time.

7. It Knows That Horror = Vulnerability
At no point in the course of Outlast are you able to get your hands on a weapon of any kind. In fact, you never even come close to wielding anything other than your trusty video camera. While Mount Massive Asylum isn’t exactly swarming with enemies, the sequences in which you are forced to contend with a patient – or something much, much worse – are spent playing the most demented game of hide in seek since the ending of The Silence of the Lambs, night vision and all.
Though thankfully sans this.
6. It Borrows Wisely
As mentioned earlier, Outlast owes a lot to Frictional Games’ Amnesia: The Dark Descent. Released in North America in 2011, the first-person horror game removed weapons from the equation and forced players to avoid its environment’s lumbering, unkillable monstrosities, often by hiding in cupboards (a method Outlast adapted by letting you wedge yourself in a locker or underneath a cot). It would be easy to say that Red Barrels simply copied Frictional’s central mechanic, but that would be simultaneously overstating and understating what the former pulled off.
While Outlast maintains Amnesia‘s run and hide nature, it’s a much leaner beast. Apart from eluding enemies, Amnesia had its players manage not only their health but their sanity as well; staring too long at one of the deformed freaks wandering the castle or spending too much time in the dark would gradually wear down on the protagonist’s psyche until the screen was crawling with hallucinatory bugs.
Though there’s definitely room for argument regarding which game has the scarier enemiesJESUS CHRIST
…touch?, Amnesia. Touch?.
5. Darkness Is Your Ally – and Your Enemy
Outlast is not a game for the nyctophobic. While it would be difficult to measure offhand exactly how much of the game’s environment is immersed in darkness, it would not be a wild guess to suggest at least half. Only one section of the asylum is well-lit – the last, risking a bit of a spoiler – but it stands in direct contrast to an entire sequence of the game spent in the hospital’s pitch-black open air courtyard. In these moments, the batteries for your camera and its oh so important night vision become the closest thing to ammunition in this whole bloody mess. If there is an upside, it’s that you’re the only person in the game who can see in the dark – but when a heavily scarred patient is standing ten feet away, brandishing a meat cleaver and listening for the slightest sound you might make, this isn’t much of a comfort.
And this isn’t even including the fairly brief but extra-tense portion of the game when you temporarily lose your camera, the device slipping out of your hand and through a crack in the floor as you shout “Nonononononono!” in true Shia LaBeouf fashion. The following five to ten minutes are spent creeping from one dim light source to the next, relying on sound rather than sight – and oh, the sounds you hear…
4. It Crafts Nemeses
Though you are semi-frequently stalked and chased by patients who lack a concrete identity other than Missing Half His Face Guy or Pretty Sure He Was Humping a Corpse Guy, a great deal of the enemies you face – or rather, try to elude – in Outlast appear several times throughout the narrative, have distinct personalities and motives, and consequently stoke your animosity much more than the average video game foe would. Calling them “nemeses” is especially fitting, giving that this element takes a few cues from Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, which saw you pursued by a particularly relentless (and heavily armed) biological weapon courtesy of Umbrella.
Besides being a twist on the usual formula, this antipathy by design keeps the game’s enemies from becoming forgettable.
3. Most of Your Enemies Are Victims
Though the mentally ill are far and away more likely to fall victim to violence and abuse than perpetrate it on others, they get a pretty bad rap in fiction, especially those who reside in mental hospitals. Outlast isn’t incredibly progressive in this regard – many of Mount Massive’s residents are more than willing to kill you – but through the documentation found in game it becomes clear that most if not all of these patients are victims of the hospital administration’s inhumane experiments. One such patient, self-proclaimed “Father” Martin, was finger-painting to his heart’s content until the administration took away his art supplies just to see how he’d react. You could almost forgive him for turning to blood as his medium.
PAINT IS CHEAPER THAN BLOOD, PEOPLE!
Actually, the basic setup of the game bears some striking similarities to a young Geraldo Rivera’s investigation of the Willowbrook State School for the intellectually disabled, where he exposed the staff’s horrifying neglect of their wards (snippets of the expos? can be seen in the excellent documentary Cropsey). Rivera’s piece went a lot more smoothly, however – much to the chagrin of those who can’t stand him today.
2. It’s Unnervingly Immersive
Outlast features full body awareness, which is a fancy way of saying you can look down and see most of your body – arms, legs and all. When peeking around a corner, your free hand grasps the edge of a doorframe to brace yourself as you get a better look; the other hand is can be seen holding the video camera when it’s not currently in use. Your torso and legs can appear pretty stiff, but compared to most first-person shooters, who treat the player like a floating head and pair of arms, it’s exceptionally immersive. And boy, do the developers ever turn that against you.
Roughly a quarter of the way through the game, the player is captured by Richard Trager, a Mount Massive Asylum executive who lost his mind during the phenomenon that triggered the initial incident and now mixes Josef Mengele-levels of medical depravity with a friendly bedside manner. In a largely non-interactive sequence, Trager uses a pair of massive shears to sever Miles’ right index and left ring fingers. After escaping your bonds – and being party to a brief, first-person vomiting sequence – you will spend the rest of the game occasionally glimpsing Miles’ bloody, mutilated hands, and it’s never not painful to look at. It’s rare for a developer to feature amputation of a player’s in-game body parts, but Red Barrels rubs your face in Miles’ vulnerability in a way that only serves to heighten the horror of the game.
1. It’s Pretty Much the Scariest Part of [REC]
Yeah, this reference was pretty much unavoidable.
The Spanish found footage horror movie [REC] – remade as the less than stellar Quarantine in the United States – features hands down one of the scariest scenes in movie history. At the climax, the last two survivors are cooped up in the attic apartment of a tenement that has become infested with swift, zombie-like Super Rabies victims over the course of the movie. Project Zomboid is an interesting experience.  It is probably the most "Realistic" zombie game I have played.  In terms of survival, this game takes the cake, but that cake will spoil once the power goes off in the fridge, so you'd better eat it first along with the other perishables, and make sure to only eat 1/4 of it at a time so it'll last.  If you don't get the idea, the survival aspect is taken quite seriously, so are other aspects like building.  If you want to build a wall, first you'll need an axe, then chop down a tree, that'll tire you out so bring some water, those logs will be heavy so make sure you dont have to carry them too far and don't plan on taking more than two or three at a time.  Once you reach you're base saw the logs with a hand saw, now that you have planks, make sure you have a hammer and plenty of nails to build your wall.  That wall will probably be pretty rickety so continue building until your carpentry skill improves.  the game rewards you for your efforts, but know that you will have to spend time embarking on looting nearby buildings and avoiding the undead.  It's very possible that you could die from not receiving medical treatment for a wound or for receiving a zombie bite in a swarm.  My only complaint about the game is that the standard (non-sandbox) mode is a tad easy once you get the hang of it, and the postgame becomes a bit repetetive.  But the game is receives updates rather regularly, so I can't genuinley complain.  Project Zomboid is probably the best Zombie game I have played.

I wanted to like this game. I spent a great deal of time searching for a game just like this one, read reviews, and finally decided that it was the one I wanted. Dropped $50 for the whole collection, and I will likely not play it again after the 150 or so hours I dropped into it.
Good
It is world-building, political gameplay that I was searching for in a sense. Much of the game allows you to control all of the little details that make the world your creating exactly what you want--for a while. The various constitution options were interesting, and it was one of the options that I found to be the most exciting, being able to control the type of people who come onto your island, controlling the state of the government, and setting up the professionalism of your military are all excellent options that I think really contribute to the overall feel of the game.
Bad
Execution of the above failed. The politics are largely one-way. You pick a side and can't really play the middle in any meaningful way if you want to complete a mission. In major-global conflicts, there is a political out if you are skilled enough. Not an option.
The game provides a limited and hilariously unsatisfactory tutorial that fails to explain most of the important aspects of the game that determine approval rating, military tactics, and government effects of a number of aspects. Moreover, most of the constitution is written to be funny rather than informative (along with quests, objectives, and so on), meaning that it is impossible to tell the exact effect most actions or changes will have until it is too late. And I say too late, because you can only alter the constitution once every five years. At one point, I altered mine and my approval rating dropped nearly 30% rapidly.
In regard to approval, it is almost a meaningless measure. Having an approval rating of 90+ is pretty safe, but as soon as you drop to 80 or so (keep in mind that U.S. Presidents largely have approval ratings of ~50%), rebellions happen constantly unless you are eliminating rebels (which is expensive). The further it falls, the more impossible it becomes to return the approval to the higher rating, largely because the constant threats result in rebellions, resulting in destroyed property, resulting in lacking the funds to rebuild the buildings that increase approval or eliminate the rebels that destroy them.
The military aspect of the game is useless. You can build a powerful military, but it ignores half of the threats that you come into contact with throughout the game. I lost several games because I had military units who refused to defend the palace. In other cases, the military units associate the battle with a specific location, that may not actually be associated with the battle, resulting in buildings (like guard towers) which get destroyed because your military is off defending a building and refuse to march to the actual location of the fight.
All and all, the game was goo for a couple of yucks, but ultimately is so frustrating to play, do to a lack of sufficient information from the game designer and buggy units that I cannot recommend it.

The most important part of this game is that it actually feels like a survival game i.e. the world is always trying to kill you (the damn blizzard, the damn wolf or the damn bear). Initially you might survive on looting the abandoned world, but sooner or later you will need to start crafting your own stuff. Although your character gets more skilled overtime, making it easier to start a fire or gather resources, sooner or later you won't be able to maintain real world gear (knife/hatchet and etc.) and will have to start using makeshift gear (improvised knife, animal skin clothing or even magnifiying glass to start fire). Nothing is permanent in this world of TLD, eventually everything runs out, until then, you try and survive for as long as possible.
TLDR:
If you enjoy survival games that sorts of parallel real life survival, or if you are sick of incomplete and broken survival game out there, you will definitely enjoy this game. My only hope is that the dev don't rush it and properly finish TLD.

If you look at this game and think "Oh, a sports game, sorry, not interested" then I have some fantastic news! You couldnt be further removed from reality. This is a strategy game, a balls to the wall, suspenseful strategy game with 2 incredibly rare and unique elements!
First and foremost is the fact that this game features exactly ZERO RNG. This game is about rules. And there arent many to learn, making it fast to pick up and play. Learn these rules, embrace them and victory will soon be yours.
The other unique feature is that this game is a simultaneous turn based strategy. That means you and your opponent plan what will happen during the next few seconds and once both of you have prepared your strategy, it plays out in real time.
If you were to combine the behavioural analysis of a game like Poker with the incredible forethought and planning of a game of Chess, then layer a visually stunning robo-handegg skin over the top combined with a robust and reliable netcode spine... well then you would have the glorious achievement that is Frozen Cortex. If you are a strategy fan and want to test the limits of your brainpower, this would be a fantastic place to start.
Oh, did I mention that the games do not require both opponents to be present at the same time? Turns can be planned at any time, which allows all of those with busy lifestyles to play a turn or 2 when they can, with no penalties for being unable to commit to longer timeframes.
All in all, this game is a triumphant follow up to the incredibly well received Frozen Synapse, and I could not recommend it more highly

Good game - the isometric combat is fun due to the characters having not just different abilities, but such different abilities that it feels good when you figure out a way they can co-operate to take down a monster. For example in one of the later levels I had to kill the boss with a certain character ("A") - 4 of the 6 team members were knocked out, the 2 survivors only had a few points of health left and were surrounded by powerful enemies - but the medic was *just* able to run inbetween A and the boss, so that A could leapfrog across the screen and give the boss one last punch, which was enough to win. The game is entirely set-piece scenarios, but the whole thing was like that: if someone scores a critical hit in a round all the tactics have to adapt. The other good thing is that the combat system rewards you for using sentai-hero logic, rather than X-Com logic. It's not about finding a weakness and exploting it, it's about trying and failing and returning again in a stronger form.
There are some downsides. Only 1 gamesave. There aren't any random levels which I think is quite a bold decision: the bosses and stage layouts are little works of art: I can see that just bashing randomly-placed waves of minions would get dull. But I'd still have liked to try it - some games have a horde mode where you survive as long as possible, even if it didn't work in practice it would have made me appreciate the scripting more, I think.
A side effect of everything being tightly scripted (except what actually happens in a battle) is that you can't build up or replenish resources (money and crafting materials) so if you wanted to go back and try a different character build then you couldn't (not that there are many, it isn't RPG-ish, just that you can select a couple of types of equipment for each of the 5-6 set characters). The writing is a bit odd: the overarching plot is somehow *even more* disjointed than Power Rangers, and they have tried to make *every* *single* *line* into a joke: but the layer of abstraction inbetween and the way they set each episode up to satirize the genre is ingenious - almost worthy of Charlie Kaufman at points. The stunt actors are on the way to film a scene, but monsters kidnap one of them, and when the others rescue her the first thing they ask is whether she has brought any food back (on the story's logic she was off the set).
The mecha battles are both disappointing and an excellent rendition of kaiju battles. Round 1: you win. Round 2: they win. Round 3: it's really close but you power attack charges up again just in the nick of time. The mecha's abilities upgrade, the monsters' abilities change, but the traditional pattern is honoured. They're only short, so it isn't annoying - but a tiny bit more mechanics wouldn't have gone amiss like choosing which weapons to take into which fights. In a real super-robot series they would have occasionally had the kindly scientist invent a jetpack so it could fight a flying monster, or something - just for variety.
Overall great fun though.

Although it does provide interesting gameplay through good and challenging puzzles, the greatness of this game is found in the haunting landscapes and cruel dangers your silent character must wander through in order to reach your unknown destination.

THE GOOD
- Really great atmosphere (albeit presumably of the "love it or hate it" kind). Enough so that despite of its problems, I still consider the price of admission money very well spent.
- Short. No, I'm not listing "short!" under "bad" -- for one thing, I was dead sure I'd played for 3½, maybe 4 hours when it was only two (very tense) hours. I'd argue the length is just about right; any longer than that would likely have taken away from the experience. At two hours, you can play it in one uninterrupted sitting, which I highly recommend. The length suited the story, and I consider it a boon to have a game with limited commitment (heck, I have a stack of 100+ unplayed games, and so, in all likelihood, do you). So in the end, it's a question of comparison -- at two hours, it was cheaper than a movie ticket, and a more satisfying experience than most movies I've seen in the theater in recent years. Can you get more play-time per dollar from other games? That's pretty much a given, and if that's your concern, fair play to you, buy this on sale, or take a pass altogether and buy Fallout 3 instead.
THE BAD
The game went out of its way to ruin the first impression, and I was yea close to returning it within the first fifteen minutes:
- Keys used for control are fixed. Yeah, in this day and age. I don't even.
- When first playing, sound would cut out unless graphics quality was set to Low. This on a (admittedly 4yo) box that runs The Secret World itself on high, and that I run X-plane on. In fact, it's the only game that I haven't run on 1080p high or ultra. That's a ridiculously poor show for a "walking simulator."
- For what it's worth, people look weird and wooden (the woodsmen, haha) in this game. Whether there being few of them means that it really doesn't matter so much, or whether it means that they should've gotten at least those few right, I'll leave for you to decide.
- In "Extras", they say some things that seem rather spoilery at the time.
THE REST
- If you look around a bit after playing the game, you'll see people discussing the ending, to the tune of, "10 posters, 20 opinions." Sorry, but if you're a storyteller, and after you're done, your audience isn't sure what story was told, you're not doing your job. Or at least, you're not doing it very well.
(And I'm saying that as someone whose favorite movie is Primer -- but while Primer makes you work for it, I feel you get a fairer shot at figuring things out.)
Moreover, people are likely to have very different takes on what happened depending on whether they've played The Secret World (whose universe The Park is set in). Whether the layers added by knowing The Secret World are neat in the same way it can be amusing to have jokes and references for the parents in a children's movie that will go over the latters' respective heads, or whether it's a dirty trick requiring you to buy The Secret World (a pretty good game in my opinion, but perhaps not your cup of tea, or more than you bargained for in terms of commitment) to fully understand The Park, I'll leave to your discretion.
Finally, this connection to the Secret World is exacerbated by the latter not only providing further context and lore about the setting (the Secret World universe in general, and the Park in particular). The Secret World also offers a "20 years later" type wrap-up mission which apparently is a SEASONAL mission, so if you play The Park any time other than Halloween, enjoy the wait for the wrap-up (or, you know, watch it on Youtube).
Much as I love The Park, and love The Secret World, I can't help but feeling that The Park would have been stronger standing alone. Conversely, as a TSW player it's hard not to think, "Wow, this is the atmosphere that TSW aims for, but often fails to create." (And TSW already does better than many; it's hard to get this right, and it's inherently unfair to compare spookiness of a game that you play alone, with a defenseless character, looking for the next item to examine, and examine again, versus one where a lot of your vocabulary for interacting with the world is violence, and you know the game gives you a fair chance at killing your problems. It's true that TSW pulls no punches when it comes to its riddles (Don't sight read sheet music? Don't have a baseline grasp of latin? Or morse code? Or Ivrit? Tough luck, this riddle is not for you, then!), but it's harder to ever fully engage with the atmosphere when you always have to be ready to fight at the drop of a head (and in a somewhat formulaic way at that).)

Banished is a colony building/micromangement/survival sim. Without mods, it was pretty challenging...for awhile. Played 30-40 hours and it became pretty easy to maintain a large city. Game is also lacking in minor things. There are no decorations for your town, very limited in the look of the buildings, limted crops, not many professions, etc. For only being made by one person, I was still impressed with the game overall.
Mods give this game a whole new feeling. There's a popular "mega mod" that pretty much adds everything that really should of been in the game to begin with and more.  Decorations, tons of professions, home options, tons of crops/animals, etc. Ramps up the difficulty and it's still regularly updated to this day. Adding a citizen "age slowing" mod makes it even harder and slows the games pace by quite a bit.
There's no endgame to this, other than seeing how huge you can get the town before it slows the heck out of your computer. Or seeing everyone starve to death in your town of 400+ because you didn't stock enough food lol.
I haven't played too many in this genre other than a bit of Sim City and Pharoah/Cleopatra. Banished is similar in some ways, but totally different in a lot of ways. Watch a video on it, don't think it's really everyone's cup of tea. It's a pretty simple game, but it's fun and mostly relaxing.
Pick it up cheap, play it unmodded to understand it's core, and check out the Workshop.
