The game took me 1.5 hours to complete and cost $10.  Having completed it, that’s certainly the most I would have paid for this game.  I guess I would liken it to the price of a used book or movie.
It's difficult to write anything about this game without spoiling it, or dampening the games intended message for potential players, so if you plan on picking it up you may want to stop reading at this point.
Otherwise...it's not so much a game in the generic sense of objectives and gameplay mechanics.  It's untraditional in that it is more of a graphical narrative in which I believe the creator attempts to express his views on the creative process and the isolation that can accompany it, in addition to success and the need for validation.  The game consists of smaller games and levels supposedly designed over a 4 year period by the narrator’s emotionally unstable friend.  As you and the narrator explore the levels, he discusses what he believes the author was feeling and expressing through his creativity at the time.  The co-exploration of the zones, guided by the narrator, is where the game really shines.  It was almost like participating in a short documentary, rather than watching passively.
Unfortunately, the message came off a bit heavy handed and slightly pretentious.  Anyone’s review that claims to have cried or been extremely touched by the message is either very naive in believing the narratives validity, or so simple minded that they succumb to any appearance of profundity.  There are a few different theories out there about the true meaning and intentions of the developer.  I lean towards the one that believes he intended the game to be an interactive journal or thought piece, recording his state of mind coming off of the work, release, and success of Stanley Parable.

You play as a security guard (i guess) who has to keep watch over Freddy Fazbear's Pizza place. now of course no horror game would be the same without moving things that shouldn't move and camera controlls.
The whole idea of the game is to make it through 5 (2 extra) nights right through from 0:00am to 6:00am (please be aware that the clock goes up per hour and does not show how many more minutes you have left.) Of course out new animatronic friends are unique and have never been seen in any other game before, i feel like the effect they have on you is a wear and tear kind of feel which links to what i said earlier, once you have already seen it many times, you become immune to such scares.

(new reveiw) Project zomboid is a isometric (means godseye/helicopter view) zombie sruvival game, same old same old right? dead genre, (pun not intended) nothing interesting here right? Wrong, this is is a game like no other, killing zombies is only a part of this, this is a game that requires you to ration materials, build a makeshift fortress, and most of all; always stay on your feet, as one mistake could put your character's life in jeprody. For example, here is my story: After the tradic loss of my first save due to hard drive corruption, I started a new save, this time in the more difficult town. I found myself a bat, medkit, food, and tools, what I was missing was a sledgehammer and an axe. Sledgehammer, the weapon that could get me into the gunshop, the holy grail of the game. And, an axe; the most effecient melee weapon in the game (the sledge does more damage but is very slow). I went to the south east of the town, using an online map. The area is highly populated with zombies, so i had to always stay on the move. It didnt help that half the house i went into had a burglar alarm (this atracts hordes of zombies from noise) my luck turned as i found vitimans to reduce my tiredness (I dont know how that works, either). by the time i made my way around the south of the town, i ran out of vitamans and started to get tired, the bat i was using broke, but i was lucky enough to find another in a wardrobe. i hastely crept into the first warehouse, but with little luck. the second warehouse, at the end, when i started to loose hope, i found a sledgehammer. but looking for an axe found no adavail. the last place i may find an axe was at the hardware store, in the middle of the town center. i tried to pass a horde in a feild, but some of them saw me, I was able to cross the feild but a small number of zombies were on my tail. I took them out, but I caused noise, this attracted a whole group of others, making this a cycle untill 15-25 bodies were strewn across the grass, the battle exausted me, as well as got me hungry and thirsty. I climbed through a window in the house, ate a snack, took a soda from the fridge, and got ready to sleep. This means I turned off all the lights in the house, closed all curtains, took a sheet from a closet to cover the bedroom window, and closed the door. I then took to bed, terrified that a wanderer would break the window and devour me in my sleep. I woke up, relieved, and prepared my journy out. By the time i woke back up, it was night. only steps away from the door, a massive, dense horde appeared in the corner of my screen. I paused the game to look for the best way through using the map. I found that there was a fire escape I could climb to get through a building, I would then use a stairway to get back to ground level. After breaking a window i would dash through a parking lot to a back door to the hardware store. the border of the horde was within spitting distance from the escape. although, if i was careful enough, I thought that I just may get through. Slowly, i crept my way to the stairway, it was only untill i got up was it that zombies started noticing me. they started to jog to the stairs and a hastely pressed e to open the door. Although, I misclicked, and instead vaulted over the railing and broke my leg. now, deprived of running, i was only inches away from the horde. I went as fast as i could to my last shelter, hoping to find a temporary haven. but then feet from my door i remembered, i loose health from a broken leg. the only way i might survive is to eat, which cancels out the health loss. I took chips from my bag, but berfore i could eat, i collapsed on the pavement, with the horde soon to envelope my already dead corpse. Text rolls up the screen, showing how long I survived, the ammount of zombies i killed, etc.. sitting on my chair, I lean back and sit in dumbstruck awe. as I watch the screen go dark.
TL;DR wow, that was longer than i expected, i was planning on saying more, but I will rap this up for your convience. so all in all, this game exceeds many standards and pushes the bondries of its genre. I would extremely recomend this game to any survival fans, or anybody else for that matter. One problem late game is too easy. Still, in the end, this game is worth every cent right now, with more on the way, as it is early access. 10/10 game of the year, this is finnal, as i am posting this on new years eve.

From all the zombie survival games I have ever played, this one hits most aspects I hoped for the genre. The goal of the game is simple, you must get from being a survivor to a rebuilder of a one-man society. You are on a time limit as the utilities will soon shut down within weeks, so you must quickly locate your pernament base and fortify it, then start building a garden and several rain catcher barrels to produce food and water. Melee weapons are more important than firearms, and fire can cause a little more destruction than necessary. The zombies, of course, can see, hear, and smell you, so cover up the windows and stick to the shadows and downwind to avoid detection. Remember that a single bite or scratch, even if it is disinfected and bandaged, will strike you ill and kill you no matter what, so don't be cocky and decide to take on an entire herd unless you have a stronghold to take shelter for your dramatic final stand.
The goal for me is always the same. Once the game is started, I quickly go out and search for a suitable shelter or stay in the one I have spawned in. Then I shelter-in-place, you know, cover up all the windows and such. I take inventory of my food, then one everything is situated, I go out into the industrial areas of the map to locate three things: An axe, a saw, a hammer, and lots of nails. The idea is to get an axe to chop down the many confiers that grow in the game world, then use the saw to turn them into wooden planks, then use those planks to build walls, doors, and all sorts of useful furniture to hold your important gear. Once the structure of the base is established, I started fixing up a garden. Sometimes I have to move dirt around, usually up on the roof where I don't have to worry about zombies trampling on my crops. I also build my kitchen outdoors, using a campfire as a stove. With the power and water lines being finite resources, it is imperative to get your self-sufficient base established as soon as possible.
If you are wondering there are vehicles in this game, then the answer is no, there is no planes, trains, and automobiles in Project Zomboid. Your own two feet is your way in moving around the map. Due to the nature of the game engine, I do not expect to find vehicles in this game anytime soon.

A creative tribute to the Tokusatsu genre that many have grown up to or still enjoy. The attendance machanic in general seemed a bit easy to abuse to an extent, should have a negative factor if either is overly used.
Having different characters to choose from at the beginning for each role is a really nice touch. It allowed to add in variety to characters with the abilities that affected the gameplay. This allows the player to choose how they would like to play their games, and not have a stagnant gameplay with fixed characters for the storyline only.
Storyline progressed at a decent pace and was well thought out in respect to what Tokusatsu's usually revolved around. But also adding in a bit of flare by blurring reality with fiction.

I just finished Chroma Squad and I loved it. I am gonna explain with a couple of keywords what kind of game this is (for those who are considering to buy Chroma Squad):
- Tactical RPG, the tactical form in this game is centered in how you skill your characters (more than positioning).
- Mech fights, YES MECHS.
- Game time, I completed the game in 20 hours.
- Difficulties, there is easy, interesting and challenging. Hardest difficulty is a real ♥♥♥♥♥!
- Managing, beside the tactical RPG side of the game, you need to manage your characters by crafting, teching their skills, upgrading your mech, marketing, responding to e-mail where choices matter (not heavily), upgrading your studio and buying items.
- Achievements, well done compared to most indie games.
- Comedy & awesomeness, this game gave me laughs and goosebumps. Comedy is based on parodies of modern memes, Power Rangers and other silly stuff. I got goosebumps in the final fight, where I just got blown away by the story and momentum of it.
- Story is well done and original.
TL:DR
Chroma squad is an original indie game which has two sides of gameplay: tactical RPG and managing your party. The story is wel done and takes around 15+ hours to complete. I had ALOT OF FUN completing this game and I am happy I bought it. You need to understand the mechanics, but the moment you do its fun as hell.
P.S. Don't craft anything until the later seasons, buying items is the way to go.

"Golly, what a mighty fine piece of art!" would be the proper thing to say about this game.
From the beginning on, everything is painstakingly created in a 1930s cartoon style (you might have noticed...) from the "graphics" to the soundtrack, even the speech and humor! Immersion is never broken, that you are in an old cartoon.
So far im 2,5h into the game, which says that im about 25% through (not getting the best rating everywhere etc), so i expect to get 10-12h out of it. I don't find it too difficult (for now), just the right amount. It's more of a trial & error kind of gameplay, as you mainly progress by learning the levels and bosses' patterns by trying again (and again...and again...and...) which can be frustrating for some people, but i don't mind.
The bosses each have unique (and funny!) ways to attack you, so there is something to see and learn everytime! Controls are easy to understand and learn (after all it says "run&gun"), though i would recommend a controller.
All in all i can just say: reward the developers for bringing us this gem of a game, don't wait to get the game in a sale, buy it now and support them this way! That's the only way for us to get such masterpieces in the future too!
PS: get the soundtrack too, it's an amazing testament to the music of the era and also worth listening to it without playing!

Gameplay is very well polished and I haven't encountered any game breakng bug (crashes and etc.). Also preferred the way they handle resource gathering (like chopping trees and transporting item), '7 days to die' and 'the forest' for e.g. has actual physics with the tree toppling and stuff but it usually ends up with really annoying physics game.
The most important part of this game is that it actually feels like a survival game i.e. the world is always trying to kill you (the damn blizzard, the damn wolf or the damn bear). Initially you might survive on looting the abandoned world, but sooner or later you will need to start crafting your own stuff. Although your character gets more skilled overtime, making it easier to start a fire or gather resources, sooner or later you won't be able to maintain real world gear (knife/hatchet and etc.) and will have to start using makeshift gear (improvised knife, animal skin clothing or even magnifiying glass to start fire). Nothing is permanent in this world of TLD, eventually everything runs out, until then, you try and survive for as long as possible.
TLDR:
If you enjoy survival games that sorts of parallel real life survival, or if you are sick of incomplete and broken survival game out there, you will definitely enjoy this game. My only hope is that the dev don't rush it and properly finish TLD.

StudioMDHR have done an excellent job in making this. Yes, I only have 5 hours in the game but do not let that put you off buying this. The boss design is excellent and any deaths are your fault and not the game's. When you die you are shown a progress bar indicating how far you got which gives you an incentive to try again and beat the boss.
There are also some short but fun 2D platforming levels known as "Run 'n' Gun". Each of these contain 5 coins which are used to buy items from the shop. Hidden throught the world are three Mausoleums where you can earn special moves called Supers. These range from a powerful energy beam to invincibility and a big ghost that damages enemies.
At the end of each level and boss you are given a grade depending on how quick you completed the level, how many hits you took, how many parries you executed and how often you used your super moves.
The graphics are amazing and unique. Everything is hand-drawn and resembles one of those 30s/early 40s Disney cartoons. The music is excellent and each track fits perfectly in every level.
Expect to die a lot as this game is brutally difficult!
After beating the game, you unlock expert difficulty which will make you want to go for those S grades!
Overall, I would definitely recommend picking up this!

Before writing anything I'd like to tell you that part of my favorite game genres are
fast paced hack n' slash (Like the Devil May Cry series), puzzle (Games that actually makes you think how to progress), story driven games (like RPGs and some others) among others...
With that in mind, there's something that's brutally important to me in games... And that's...
Both the controls and a tight movement.
Those two aspects are the weakest part of Limbo,
Movement feel way to clunky and the control mapping is not the best
Still if we manage to get past those aspects, Limbo is a nice platformer/puzzle game that will require you to use your brain quite often with some puzzles and how physics work in the game and you'll probably die a lot on your first run doing trial and error.
So... Pros:
-Ambience is very well done and the lack of colour boost that a lot! That's very well done
-Some puzzles are challenging and will demand a lot of your time to figure them out
-Although simple, the game often gives you new mechanics to work around
-The spider... You really feel weak if you don't know how to confront her/him/it(?)...
Cons:
-As I said earlier... CONTROLS AND MOVEMENT
-Although the ambience is well ejecuted, to add a bit more background music would have been great
-
-Ending could have been improved
So... Because movement and controls are a major thing for me...
I'll give it a 6.2/10.. I'd only recommend you to buy if it's on sale, or if you do like platformer/puzzle games a lot

Frozen Cortex is simple, clear, and yet infinitely complex. With the fantastic artificial intelligence system and randomized playing fields, even single player games are constantly keeping me on my toes and learning more and more about the game systems.
As someone who did not get very much into Frozen Synapse due to its complexity (facing / direction being vital elements), Cortex has instantly captured me by providing the same level of depth with simplified mechanics. As Ian Hardingham explained in a recent video, Cortex is based off a simple premise - "If you are standing still, you control the space around you. If you are moving, you are vulnerable." Mode 7 has done a fantastic job in creating a modern, fast-paced strategy game that keeps you guessing with every play.
In addition, the music is fantastic. But I'm pretty sure everyone on this page knew that already.
I would highly recommend this game to strategy lovers. It's an excellent take on the genre that provides a breath of  clarity many modern strategy games seem to lack. Frozen Cortex is clearly a labor of love from all involved, and in my opinion, surpasses and improves upon Frozen Synapse in every way.
The lore behind the game is very interesting.

When words are your only real avenue for creation, you tend to be a bit pickier with them than you would be otherwise. Or that's how it goes with me. A review, a window into my time with the game, should be just that; A window, to see what summary I can gleam from my experience and whether I think it translated into a satisfactory account for what I paid. It's an odd transmutation, I think; The actual of giving something tangible like currency for a product, whether physical or not, and then debating with yourself whether the quality of the experience that came with it was somehow satisfactory. For some, I guess, it's not hard. But I'm always left feeling like asking if my own personal account is what you really want to go with. Because it's hard to say to myself,"I paid X amount for this game, it needs to be good in some way, or I will be unhappy with my purchase." That's not why I play games. Or, it's not why I play games anymore.
More and more I find myself playing games less for entertainment and more for a chance to see the ways developers choose to express themselves, and when not themselves, then the story they want to tell. CoD still tells a story, same as any other game, even up to and including Undertale. Even games without a story still provide a focus, a discernable goal, and I suppose the real question is whether you thought the trip to achieving that goal was fun. Or maybe not fun, as it were, but at least evoked an experience that you thought was worthy of the money you paid for it.
So that brings us back to The Beginner's Guide. It's a short experience that not many would find enjoyable. There's little to no action, the story (what little there is) is a mess, and the entire narrative left myself with more questions than answers. With that said, I'm still going to recommend it. The obvious question then becomes, of course, why? Why would I recommend an experience that, for the most part, I did not seem to like? Because it's not always about liking things. It's not always about a positive experience. Sometimes it's about being reminded of parts of yourself that you don't like, and the effects they have on you as a whole. I don't think this is a stepping stone for a lot of people who might grapple with things like obsession, depression, or creative sterility. But for others...
It's The Beginner's Guide.

Simultaneous ("WEGO") turn-based games create a very specific kind of tension; you lock in a plan, and then have to sit back and watch the poop hit the fan, hoping that you guessed correctly about your opponent's moves. Frozen Cortex offers that tension in a digestible, clear-cut format without a lot of the fuzziness of more complex simulations.
Your available actions at any given point break down into just a few reasonable decisions, so there's less temptation to agonize forever than with something like Combat Mission, or mode7's own Frozen Synapse. The sports mileu makes for a good pretense to have a rigid set of comprehensible rules. (Ironically, while Synapse was much like a more modern and fatal take on the Maxis classic RoboSport, Frozen Cortex, which is ostensibly about robots playing sports, is a different beast with its lack of ordnance.)

Cuphead is a masterpiece. A mixture of Gunstar Heroes, MegaMan, Merrie Melodies and every good boss rush game since the early Genesis era, there's something for everyone to love, even non gamers, and that's considering how hard it is. You may not get far, but it's gameplay is tight and it oozes charm. I paid 15.50 by going through Humble but this game is fully worth it's ticket price and more for the golden soundtrack; you will listen to this forever, enthusiasts will want to grab the 4LP vinyl in a gold tinged case if they can pony up $100 (which I want to but likely never will be able to).
There are 6 Run n Gun levels in the vein of MegaMan and Gunstar Heroes and around 15-17 bosses. I have not finished the game but I have gotten decently far and have never used Simple Mode until right before I made this review. I don't like Simple Mode because it makes the fights shorter by removing stages. Removing the boss stages and only letting you fight the simple parts really detracts from the game even when you're not good. Only use Simple Mode as a training ground to get to the real part of the game unless you really physically cnnot handle Regular.) Anyway, every boss has 3-5 stages from what I've seen and they all have drastically different appearances, attacks, sounds and patterns. It's always interesting to see what twist on their own loose but charming formula they can make when they've already amazed you so much already.
The soundtrack is golden, the gameplay is tight and versatille, and it will not leave you wanting. It will be very short if you are good, but even if you speedrun platformers you will still have trouble with Cuphead, at least at first. Pick up this gem, it is a classic in it's own time.

This game is exactly what Kickstarter should be about: interesting idea, fantastic development team, and, most importantly, delivery of a finished product.
The game itself blends a business management simulation on the macro level and a tactical RPG for an episode of the TV series, played for greatest theatrical effect. The animation is simplistic and minimized, but that's okay. This game oozes nostalgia, and coming off as "Mario Brothers-esque" is not an insult. Music and graphical interface are smooth, but some small issues have arisen with different computers. The biggest selling point is by far the writing; snark and self-referential humor make reading the dialogue part of the experience rather than a chore. As an added bonus, there is a fast forward option via pressing the enter key. It's one of the many little details that says this studio cares about the fan experience.
The only real downside I can think of is the menu system: clunky and no real way to make transitions between the various sub menus easier, but perhaps that is just the nature of a game that puts you in charge of so many details. That being said, the positives outweigh the negatives by several orders of magnitude. Pick this little gem up; even at full price, it's a bargain.

A survival game done really really well- you can tell the developers put a lot of love into this!
I am more of the exploring-hoarder-of-stuff-maker-of-things-type player, so I have been playing this on the 'wolves don't attack you' mode. Which suits me fine because if I fancy a scrap I can provoke them anyway. If you are like me in those respects then you will have a great time playing this through, the world is huge and I've been playing for 26 hours and have explored most of almost 2 of them. So, yeah, lots to see and do.
Surviving has it's ups and downs- in that sometimes you will have times of plenty and sometimes you'll be numb and tired, with one arrow left in your quiver, desperately trying to take down a deer before you starve to death (only to then eat the raw meat and then die anyway from food poisoning). It all depends on where you go and what you do and how you ration out your supplies. I think it's pretty damn good, and everything seems to have been designed with realism in mind. Not saying it's all realism all the time, but they have obviously tried their best and it works with the game mechanic.
The crafting is very simplistic and functional, though I would like to see more options and more depth in later releases because once you make the bow and all the clothes then you're pretty much all set. Aside from lack of variety it takes a while to accquire the skills and materials neccessary to make good stuff without dying, which fleshes it out somewhat (but probably will get repetetive).
I for one love playing this game and am currently obsessed with it, even with the permadeath feature that caused me to rage like i have never raged before when my girl fell to her death on a misty day. On reflection I think it is a positive, as it forces you to think more carefully about your plan, and effectively manage your resources- even if it is a little bit soul destroying. Lesson learned- watch where the hell you are going! But I can't wait to see what more exciting new features the Developers will come up with in the future- maybe a jump feature? So I can jump out from between rocks I get stuck in? That would be nice.
So, if you like exploring, hunting, foraging, rationing, planning, starving, falling, breaking all your limbs, freezing to death and being torn to pieces by wolves- then this game is for you!
TL:DR Survival game is good at survival. Might get better as devs make more game. Also permadeath is a ♥♥♥♥♥.

Released last year by Funcom, The Park is one of those walking simulators where you do not have enemies who can kill you, you do not have levels to complete and you do not have a boss battle at the very end of your story. However, you do have an interesting storyline with psychological and supernatural elements.
You walk around in an amusement park controlling Lorraine who wishes to find her son. Callum has just run inside for no apparent reason - Lorraine is getting more and more desperate as night falls quickly and she begins experiencing one hallucination after the other. This creepy, dark and haunting environment is superbly brought to life thanks to the latest iteration of the Unreal engine. Lorraine's voice acting is also great and it accompanies the story very well.
Since this is a walking simulator you should not expect it to last longer than 2 hours. This is common and perhaps represents the only downside of the game. But then again this is common in this genre - you do not have many items you can interact with (mainly notes); they all help you understand the story (not just Lorraine's but that of the fun park).
If you like the genre you'll probably enjoy the ride - as for rides: Lorraine has the possibility to try almost all carnival rides. These are perhaps the most unsettling parts of the game and are there to shed light on the background of the story. Whilst a bit too short and pricey (even with 50% discount) The Park represents a great adventure that can certainly be very entertaining.

As a huge toku fanboy, I was excited to see a video game based on Super Sentai. One that kept in the spirit of sentai by parodying it, and at the same time, paying tribute to it. I've been following this game since Kickstarter, but only more recently got a chance to buy it with the Steam Sale.
As far as the gameplay goes, it actually managed to exceed my expectations. Everything is controlled by mouse and things like the the teamwork mechanic and skills you can switch out are things I've seen in other games, but this is one of the better ones in recent memory. Teamwork is more than just an extra person to help you attack, you can also use teamwork to get to spaces much farther on the field and pull off specials using it. This really helped me when trying to accomplish the special requirements. The game never felt imbalanced, too, which is awesome because it's the easiest trap to fall in with strategy RPGs.
When you start a new game, you're given the option of picking your team. While I wish there was more options for party members (DLC/Chroma Squad 2?), what characters they do have are very diverse and I think they have just a right amount of options for character selections. The plot itself is the exact same regardless of who you pick, so the main reason to do this is to decide your character's starting stats and which ones you would like to see for the rest of the game, which I really like a lot. The easy way out would have been to just always have them in the suit and choose their stats, or just have your five chosen for you. It even allows there to be a possible lesbian romance later on in the game depending on what gender you pick a certain ranger. Your main five are completely customizable.
As for the story itself, it's not like a mind blowing story or anything like that, but it does it's job of feeling like the power ranger/super sentai shows the game is based on. The end goal is defeating a big bad guy, and on the way, you defeat a ton of different monsters ranging from ridiculous to...well, more ridiculous. There's also trophies, multiple endings, storyline branches, and three difficulties to add some replay value.
There's one place this game falls flat for me, and I don't think it's major, because it only really started to bother me nearing the end. The humor in this game can be funny at times, and then at other times can get a little groan worthy with the memes. I don't mind a lot of the refernces. The non-comedic ones for sentai fans in the weapons/equipment/skills that referenced a bunch of different sentai series all made me smile when I realized the references, and certain jokes work really well. At one point, they reference the "What has science done" image with the Seagull with massive biceps, and jokes like that and the backstreet boys/lady gaga references work really well, but when it's just meme, after meme, after meme, it starts to get a little grating, not unlike being in the presence of an middle aged person who goes on Reddit.
Still, I would recommend this to anybody looking for a fun and quirky little RPG. It's definitely worth the price. I still have two more ending paths and minor storyline branches to get, so I may update this in the future, but having just completed my first playthrough, I just wanted to share my thoughts on it.

Puzzle games in my eyes need a few things to be entertaining, addicting tests of your wits. They should be easy to pick up, with basic rules that don’t require lengthy tutorials or wordy instructions to understand. They ought to be dynamic, built on a framework that can be easily reworked into a continual stream of interesting puzzles that don’t become repetitive despite being similar if not identical in design. And lastly I prefer them to be easy to pick up and put down, like a coffee table book that you can spend a few minutes or hours passing the time with, then set it back down for an unknown amount of time and still find it just as enjoyable the next time you look at it.
LYNE seems to have unknowingly looked into my head and designed itself around these ideals, forming into a simple but exemplary brain teaser that I fell in love with from the very first screen. It’s a relaxing yet engrossing experience that excels at putting you in a zen like state as you clear puzzles and feel especially clever each and every time you do.
In essence, LYNE can best be thought of as a nonlinear connect-the-dots. You’re given two points that you must connect, while going through all of the requisite points between them, but the order in which you do so is entirely up to you. There isn’t necessarily only one way to solve a puzzle, and this freedom is but one reason I find LYNE hugely refreshing compared to so many other puzzle games. As you progress you begin to deal with multiple colors, points you must repeatedly run through, and more complex designs that have you connecting lines like a mad cartographer, which from the outside looking on would seem highly complex and difficult.
But, it never feels that way when you’re playing. The fundamentals are so basic that it feels almost innate, like you’ve already been doing this for years. Something about LYNE clicked with me instantly, allowing me to breeze through level after level without an abundance of difficulty but leaving that satisfying feeling of accomplishment when you flex your frontal lobe and solve a problem. The soothing ambient sounds and mellow colors do well to elicit a calm mindset, making this an ideal way to let loose of your tension and unwind as you focus on the problem at hand.
In a similar way that many treat Sudoku and crossword puzzles, LYNE has something of a habitual quality; something you can go back to every day to help keep you sharp and relax after the more trying events of a day. The structure is tailor made for this style of play, with puzzles grouped into sets that are just long enough to be rewarding but not fatiguing. Random daily puzzles (though you’d never know that do to them being just as well designed as the base sets) provide consistent new content, at which point I can think of little more I could ask for.

I have a big problem with reviewing this so-called "game". This game, surprisingly, has complex structure of narrative so it's very difficult to describe what is actually wrong in simple words and without writing a few pages of boring text with notes and♥♥♥♥♥♥
But I'll try anyway.
First and the most important thing is emotional manipulation. Most of the time game is just showing you some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ games combined with narrator's interpretation. Narrator(and author, which, actually, may be two different characters, I'll talk about this below) is really, really-really trying to get some tears and sobbing out of you. And, as I can see by owerwhelmingly positive reviews, he did a good job. Narrator is constantly decieving you by saying how the games are good and creator is talanted, while they are certainly not.
Second thing is banality. I, personally, don't have anything against emotional stories about mental problems, depression and/or insanity - if the story can really say anything meaningful about the case. But this story cannot. In comparison to Stanley Parable, where an interesting topic with smart thoughts was presented, there is no such thing here.
Third thing is a little less important and a little more complex. As I was told by one of my friends, you can find some similarities with narrative composition, used by Borges. And knowing that, you can see one different level of narrative composition. Difference between narrator and author, which can give you understanding, that story, actually, is not about creator and his games, but about narrator's mistake of interpretation. And this understanding can really change everything. Now, in this perspective, author somehow shows as that narrator is a liar or simply wrong and this gives us different message. One little problem here. It's not simple to see this, cause a) emotional manipulation b) you need to have much more additional knowledge c) this may be just an assumption, cause author doesn't tell anything in actual game.
So, at the end, for me this is just a bad story, emotional manipulation and maybe, maybe, intended... let's call it joke, which is as funny, as if I could convince you, that your granny is actually an alien(considering, she is actually not). Funny, but only for a person, who knows it is a joke.
What else there is in this game? Nothing. No gamplay, just story. Of course, author's unique style is still present and his voice is still amazing. But style is definetely not enough in this case.
In conclusion, I'd like to put a quote - "I'm talking so much cause I have nothing to say".

I will review the game AND the fanbase seperately . Because this game blew up, of course it will get hate.
First game in the Series, 3rd setting in the lore.
FNAF 4 Fredbear and Freinds --> FNAF2 Freddy Fazbear's Pizza  --> FNAF 1 Freddy Fazbear's Pizza ---> FNAF 3 Fazbear's Fright: The Horror Attraction.
When you first install the game and play the first night, yeah if you listen carefully listen to the phone guy and explore the buttons, you will get the point of the game. You do not move, you do not walk around with a lantern and find demons, but you do have lights, doors and a camera. It's the fear of the unknown that's scary and this game delivers it well, and at a good pace too.
When the phone guy mentions moving children entertaining animatronics, you have a look and one is gone (Bonnie). Most people will panic, shut the doors and search frantically. The first jumpscares aswell will deliver fear and that is why this game blew up so much.
When they show up at your doors or disappear and reappear in a scary position you are urged to close both doors and check cameras but the power says otherwise and it's finding that balance that makes the game scary.
As the nights progress, it get's more complex than Bonnie and Chica moving around, the Phone Guy gives more details on the game mechanics and new animatronics and their patterns like Foxy and Freddy. As you get more used to the first jumpscares the newer animatronics will confuse you and re introduce that fear of the Unknown. That peaking out head and the running noise will surely give you a game you will remember.
BUT honestly the jumpscares are the most basic 'Scary' element to this game and it does wear off after a bit. You then try to strategise a pattern of beating the ever growing hardness of the game. Some people have beaten the impossible 20/20/20/20 mode. But the game goes from horror to spooky strategy.
This game was one of the most unique horror games of this time. After Scott's bad reviews on his holy games he took his negative reviews and adapted them to make this game. The game uses horror like never before mixing the moving animatronics with stopping them from getting in with power management.
The lore is long  and explained over multiple games.To get all the lore you need, you will have to dig in all 5 games of the FNAF series. here is the lore Wiki;
Basically one employee (Purple Guy) is a complete madman and lures in children and muders them and stuffs them into the suits. The spirits of the deceased children haunt the animatronics and with help of the Puppet (From FNAF2) they take their revenge by making the Purple guy become like them and get trapped in Golden Bonnie, SpringTrap, just like them by making him hide in the suit and then have it lock up and impale him. As seen in FNAF 3 good ending.
When FNAF2 launched it was secretely a prequal where you would see 'New' improved animatronics of these charicters. More lore before FNAF1 was revealed. Then onto FNAF 3 wich takes place after FNAF1. Then you get FNAF4 wich takes place from the chid of 'The bite of '87's perspective. As the games progresse more and more lore is revealed but there are still questions that need answering.

As a huge toku fanboy, I was excited to see a video game based on Super Sentai. One that kept in the spirit of sentai by parodying it, and at the same time, paying tribute to it. I've been following this game since Kickstarter, but only more recently got a chance to buy it with the Steam Sale.
As far as the gameplay goes, it actually managed to exceed my expectations. Everything is controlled by mouse and things like the the teamwork mechanic and skills you can switch out are things I've seen in other games, but this is one of the better ones in recent memory. Teamwork is more than just an extra person to help you attack, you can also use teamwork to get to spaces much farther on the field and pull off specials using it. This really helped me when trying to accomplish the special requirements. The game never felt imbalanced, too, which is awesome because it's the easiest trap to fall in with strategy RPGs.
When you start a new game, you're given the option of picking your team. While I wish there was more options for party members (DLC/Chroma Squad 2?), what characters they do have are very diverse and I think they have just a right amount of options for character selections. The plot itself is the exact same regardless of who you pick, so the main reason to do this is to decide your character's starting stats and which ones you would like to see for the rest of the game, which I really like a lot. The easy way out would have been to just always have them in the suit and choose their stats, or just have your five chosen for you. It even allows there to be a possible lesbian romance later on in the game depending on what gender you pick a certain ranger. Your main five are completely customizable.
As for the story itself, it's not like a mind blowing story or anything like that, but it does it's job of feeling like the power ranger/super sentai shows the game is based on. The end goal is defeating a big bad guy, and on the way, you defeat a ton of different monsters ranging from ridiculous to...well, more ridiculous. There's also trophies, multiple endings, storyline branches, and three difficulties to add some replay value.
There's one place this game falls flat for me, and I don't think it's major, because it only really started to bother me nearing the end. The humor in this game can be funny at times, and then at other times can get a little groan worthy with the memes. I don't mind a lot of the refernces. The non-comedic ones for sentai fans in the weapons/equipment/skills that referenced a bunch of different sentai series all made me smile when I realized the references, and certain jokes work really well. At one point, they reference the "What has science done" image with the Seagull with massive biceps, and jokes like that and the backstreet boys/lady gaga references work really well, but when it's just meme, after meme, after meme, it starts to get a little grating, not unlike being in the presence of an middle aged person who goes on Reddit.
Still, I would recommend this to anybody looking for a fun and quirky little RPG. It's definitely worth the price. I still have two more ending paths and minor storyline branches to get, so I may update this in the future, but having just completed my first playthrough, I just wanted to share my thoughts on it.

Frozen Endzone (possibly soon to be Frozen Cortex) is a brilliant new type of game from Mode7Games.  It mixes sports with the turn-based action of their previous entry into the market, Frozen Synapse.  Players plan their players moves, can plan opponent's moves to see what will happen, and then submit their turn.  Meanwhile, their opponent does the same planning process, and then after both players have submitted their turn, the game calculates and displays a result.  Best part is that you never have to be online at the same time as your opponent!
The game itself has simple rules.  You score points by running through bonus zones or getting into the endzone.  Players must advance the ball each turn.  Once you run the ball, you cannot pass it again, aside from a free turn at the beginning of a possession.
The blocking works well, with whoever is stopped first getting to block any moving player.  Players within a certain range will intercept a ball, and players within a certain range will chase after and tackle opponents.
I enjoy both major modes of play, Full Match and Duplicate.  Full Match involves 18 turns of play, with turnovers changing possession, and touchdowns causing the game to restart in the original position with the teams swapped.  Duplicate is almost an 'extra point' type situation, where the offense is trying to score and the defense just to stop them - possession changes count as ending the play and then the match restarts with the teams swapped, and whoever has the most points wins.
They're still improving it as we speak, and working on a single player campaign which sounds amazing.  This is a must have for anyone who has an interest in sports and loved Frozen Synapse, and is worth a try for someone who is a fan of either sports or Frozen Synapse.

I am an incredibly lazy and therefore never write reviews even though I play so many video games. I had to take some time out today to write a review for Chroma Squad, though, because this game is pure awesome. This game is a 75 on metacritic and thats a clear under-rating.
Yes, I'll acknowledge that Power Rangers/tokusatsu fanboyism is strong within my heart, but you do NOT have to love Power Rangers to love this game. If you can appreciate a creative tactical RPG with fun, geeky dialogue and story lines, you'll be happy with whatever they are charging for this nowadays. Oh, and choices matter!
Gameplay
The combat system is inventive and really lets the player decide how the battles will go. It's not very complicated, but its still satisfying. Think X-com. You can play with a very basic, methodical approach to the fights, or you can open up and fully utilize all the various weapons/skills in the game. Each of the characters has a particular specialty (like most RPGs) and sunergy is key. Between fights, you'll work on upgrading your characters, equipment, base; this aspect of the game isn't particularly deep, but the developer has adjusted to make it more interesting, in terms of viable options. I would say the Mecha fights are lame, however; good thing there isn't really many of them.
Graphics/Music
I'm not really a fan of pixel graphics and all that, but many people seem to love the pixel art. These are easy to judge for yourself. For this type of game, the graphics aren't important to me. But to be honest, if the game wasn't so much fun, I would probably complain about the character models. I think the environments looks pretty great, though.
The music is pure excellence if you are looking for a fully immersive experience. I tend to turn off music on games and listen to my own stuff, but this is one of the few games that I rolled through using the actual game music.
Story
If you are a Sentai/Power Rangers fan in search of nostalgia, you don't even need this section- it's epic.
If you are not as obsessed with sentai as myself, you will still enjoy the hilarious dialogue and story overall. There are some complaints in this aspect because of the imperfect English (dudes are Brazilian), and also because some of the jokes are dated internet-meme jokes, so if that would annoy you then I suppose you'll need to skip through some dialogue? People who complain about the dialogue have maybe forgotten what the dialogue was like in the shows this is modeled after. The plot will surprise you, even if you don't care about sentai at all.
TLDR
Simplified X-com + Power Rangers + loads of content + multiple storylines = FREAKING AMAZING

Let me preface this review by saying that I bought the game during BETA at the price of $99.99 for the PC Monster Race Edition and I am not defending the game, the devs and especially the publisher. I'm actually upset at how they presented this day 1 DLC cash shop, everything in the shop EXCEPT the monster (that they've said will be up for sale only) shouldve been unlockable for free.
Anyway, here are my thoughts and hopefully it will help someone who's thinking of buying the game.
1. Let's start with the DLC mayhem.
Weapon & Monster skins are forgivable, BUT $15 for a monster and $7.49 for Hunters is just deplorable. We have been told beforehand that ONLY 2 monsters will be available (or 3 if you bought early) to players and 8(?) hunters while the rest are DLC and that's fine and dandy to me BUT those prices are insane if you've already charged us full-price for this game. DLC rant, end. If you're charging that much, you're better off going the F2P model and I'll happily buy monsters @ 15$ a pop. God knows I've paid more for cash shop items that are worth even less.
Lastly, about the game and DLC pricing, here's a better breakdown:
2. Monsters! It may be just me BUT I actually prefer using Goliath in most games compared to Kraken or Wraith. Honestly, it is most fun when you play Goliath, taking the hunters head on. The thrill, the chills, nothing comes close to Goliath's up close and personal playstyle. So I tell you this, you don't need to buy that $15 monster because Goliath is the most enjoyable monster to play!
3. Game itself. I'll give it a 7/10 or 8/10.
The gameplan is almost always the same.
As a monster, you sneak around, eat fauna, evolve and then wreck the living hell out of the Hunters. Sometimes you'll square off with the hunters pre-stage 3 and that's fine but most games tend to be hide and seek.
As for the hunters, there's not much difference from the monster, it's just that this time around, you're the one looking for the missing Big Guy and holy freaking crap, you really have to look for it 90% of your games.
Yes, there are different game modes.
If you enjoy short bursts of 20min gameplays, you have the HUNT.
Then you have NEST (monster defends Eggs), RESCUE (Hunters rescue colonists while Monster tries to kill them), and DEFEND (Hunters defend their evacuation ship from the Monster and its goons).
Lastly, you have Evacuate which is a 5-part combination of the different game modes where the winner of the previous round gets a perk. this mode lasts somewhere between 50-60mins.
That being said, no 2 games are exactly the same.
They could've improved the game by letting the Power Relay available for attack 2 to 3 minutes into the game to add diverse tactics.
_______________________________________
Is the game enjoyable?
- Yes!
Is the price they're asking for too much?
- My feelings are mixed, graphics is certainly a $60 title, content is more of a $40 title and they added the ridiculous Cash-Shop to a full-priced game (again, if the went F2P and charged that in the cash shop, it would've fine too)!
Will I recommend the game to others?
- Hmm, for the base price of $60, I think you will get your money's worth of enjoyment.
- Wraith (Playable monster character DLC) is not worth the $15 so skip that. (But I'm biased towards playing the monster Goliath who is available at the base price of the game).
- DLCs are mostly monster and weapon recolors so skip those too.
- So ultimately, YES. I would recommend this game.

This is a tough one. If there was one game I thought would deserve the "mixed" rating, it would be Bioshock. It isn't a bad game and I would feel terrible giving it a negative review, but I don't think it's a good game either.
The Good:
- the opening - the whole sequence at the start of the game, along with Rayan's monologue, became a classic now.
- the look: steam punk mixed with art deco, vibrant colors, interesting design of a beautiful, but fallen utopian city; even 8 years after its release the game still looks beautiful.
- world building - although I didn't like how the game presented the backstory (mainly through audiologs), it was definietely interesting to hear about Rayan's and others' initial ambitions, how they tried to build the perfect city, and how eventually everything went downhill resulting in the distaster we can see in the game; there's also all the posters, writings on the wall, buildings, corpses everywhere, splicers' monologues etc.
- the game just oozes atmosphere.
- plasmoids - they were fun to use and along with toxics gave the game a pseudo-RPG element
- the story, at least for the first 2/3 of the game, along with an interesting twist.
The Bad:
- the story, for the remaining of the 1/3 of the game, along with a really rubbish, mustache-twirling villain.
- gameplay gets boring; you can see everything the game has to offer gameplay-wise withing the first half of the game and then, till the very end, you just fight on and on with the same (very limited) types of enemies and semi-bosses (Big Daddies), use the same plasmoids, use the same weapons, hack the same machines etc. The game tries to mix things up a little twice near the end, but it was too little, too late. By the end of the game I really wanted the game to just end.
- hacking mini-game; while it was a nice distraction at the beginning of the game, after a while it gets really tiresome. Every machine you want to get a discount in, every camera, every turret and bot - they all require you to play the same plumber mini-game. By the time you reach the final cut-scene, you will see it hundreds of times. A little diversity would be welcomed. It doesn't help that sometimes the mini-game is just unfairly hard, to the point it's impossible to solve (not enough required segments to solve the puzzle).
- fights design, or rather lack of it. Enemies usually just respawn whenever they want, sometimes even appearing in rooms without triggering traps you set up just outside the room. There are no interesting set pieces, no interesting boss fights, nothing.
- a really ♥♥♥♥♥♥, anticlimatic final boss fight. You know you fail when in a game that offers you semi-magic (plasmoids) it's easier and quicker to beat the final boss using convencional guns.
The Ugly:
- technical problems; fortunately I only encountered one - lack of sound - that I had to look up solution for online; for some reason the game requires you to set up a recording device, otherwise once you start the game, there's no sound at all.
Bioshock was fun to play... at least for the first couple of hours, until the novelty wore off. Then it just slowly started to become a monotonous fetch-quest with a very repetitive gameplay. I wouldn't bash the game, because I think it was still worth playing if only for the delightful city of Rapture.

I remember seeing Bioshock for the first time at E3 2006 before it was released later in 2007. It was by far the most interesting game trailer I saw at E3 that year. The underwater city setting, strange combat powers and gruesome violence were so unlike anything I had seen in a game before. When I eventually got my hands on the game it also played unlike anything I had experienced before, having at that time never played its spiritual predecessors, the System Shock games. Bioshock's combination of shooting mechanics, light RPG and puzzle solving elements, and high level of audiovisual presentation were unlike anything else around at that time. I remember being struck by how cinematic and directed the game felt. It felt like a movie. It felt like an amusement park ride where you're barraged by an overwhelming presentation of audiovisual effects that all spring to life as you pass by them. Bioshock's atmosphere was so unique and refreshing and it absolutely captivated me.
Bioshock takes place in the 1960s and follows the story of a man named Jack who, at the beginning of the game survives a plane crash that leaves him swimming in the middle of the ocean. You guide Jack away from the burning plane and to a lighthouse, the only structure visible in the vast ocean other than the flaming, sinking wreckage. Investigating the interior of the lighthouse reveals a bathysphere which takes you deep underwater and eventually reveals the massive underwater city of Rapture, where the remainder of the game takes place. The trip to Rapture is accompanied by a voiceover from a man named Andrew Ryan, who introduces himself as the creator of Rapture and conveys that he built the city as a haven free from external social, political or religious influences. But of course upon entering the city, it's immediately obvious that something has gone very wrong in Ryan's utopia and now masked and bandaged psychotic murderers known as splicers roam the remains of Rapture. You're contacted via radio by a man named Atlas who urges you to assist him in rescuing his family who he claims has been trapped in the bathysphere dock by Ryan. Atlas warns you to be wary of splicers who were previously Rapture's human residents, driven insane from abuse of a drug called ADAM.
When processed, ADAM becomes something called a plasmid, which when injected into a user's bloodstram can rewrite genetic code and grant its users dangerous and powerful new abilities. In addition to traditional firearms and melee weapons, pasmids serve as your main defense against splicers and Rapture's other many dangerous inhabitants. The use of plasmids also rewards players for their environmental awareness. For example, the electro-bolt plasmid is extra effective when targets are standing in water. Similarly, the incinerate plasmid is effective when used on oil spills that can be found throughout Rapture.
Experimentation with Bioshock's many plasmid powers is one of the most rewarding parts about the game. In fact, the game seems to reward experimentation and clever planning in general. For instance, when splicers are hurt, they often seek out a nearby health station to heal themselves. In addition to being used by the player to heal themselves, these health stations can be hacked to yield cheaper healing prices and to damage any enemies that tries to use it for themselves. Or the player can choose to simply destroy the station which yields several consumable first aid kits. Rapture's hostile security robots can be simply destroyed (they're weak vs. electro-bolt or armor-piercing rounds) or they can be hacked to aid the player in battle. There's a multitude of options available to the player on how to dispatch enemies and it's fun and rewarding to experiment with the game's many systems to find a playstyle and strategy that best suits you.
There's also a moral choice element to Bioshock. "Little Sisters" human girls who have been inplanted with a parasite and mentally conditioned to hunt for and gather ADAM are plentiful throughout Rapture. They and their powerful "Big Daddy" protectors are neutral to the player upon encounter, but Big Daddies will go hostile if they or the Little Sister are attacked. Dispatching a Big Daddy leaves the player with a choice: rescuing or harvesting the Little Sisters. Harvesting kills the Little Sister and grants the player a wealth of ADAM which can be used to purchase new plasmids and other useful upgrades. Rescuing the Little Sisters yields very little ADAM and gives few immediate bonuses, but rescuing multiple Little Sisters can unlock powerful plasmids later in the game.
Summary
Bioshock is a wonderful blend of an immersive and atmospheric environment, a memorable story, and well designed game systems that reward the player for experimentation. While Bioshock's sequels improved on some mechanics, I don't think they ever recaptured the brilliance of the original game and its great blend of atmosphere, story and game mechanics.

I always wondered what the charm was that drew so many people to BioShock. It's only been 8 years, and this game is heralded as one of the greatest of all time. So, I decided to pick up the trilogy on Steam and see just what all this praise was for. And I was not disappointed.
BioShock is one of the best FPS/RPG hybrids I've ever played. BioShock is also one of the best stories I've had the pleasure to play through. With the popular market for games revolving around dumb, pointless shooting- it's so fresh to see someone trying something new. BioShock uses a unique Western-RPG format, to make you play how you want. My style was to sneak around enemies, hack into the cameras and turrets, and let them do most of the work- conserving my ammo for the fights that mattered. And the game tailors to any specific style of play you want. But the combat flows smoothly enough, that it'll keep you on your toes and constantly moving around situations, using the resources you have to stop enemies. And the high framerates this amazing-looking game has is just amazing (And makes me all the more frustrated with the lack of cooperation from Assassin's Creed: Freedom Cry... but I want to think happy thoughts. Not bad ones.)
The game's story is very well-done. It pulls your emotions, and builds you up for a tremendous climax and then... one of the best plot twists I've ever seen ensues. It's one of the smart ones, like Knights of the Old Republic and Fight Club, where the clues were laid out before you ahead of time, but you never see it coming until it actually happens. And it's the story (especially enhanced by the plot twists) that bring up these heavy moral greys that come from a world heavily involved in science and logic, and the problems that that sort of society can cause- and even more so, on the freedom of a player's choice. Sure, it's no Stanley Parable, but it really makes you question just how free you are.
And, God, Rapture. Let me tell you about Rapture. The amount of effort to make this underwater achievement (and catastrophe) for humanity, look as alive (and dead) as possible... is just astounding. The game is incredibly atmospheric, and does the Fallout 3 style of subtle story telling, where you can assume a lot of details in the situations you uncover, and also can get video logs which tell you bits and peices of a larger story (Except these logs are read aloud, so that give BioShock a huge plus over Fallout 3!)- and, by the way, the voice acting is great. You hardly ever see the characters in person, and the protagonist is mostly silent but you really get to know characters like Tenenbaum, Fontaine, Ryan, and Cohen.
But... well, yes, there are flaws in this game. For one, the hacking game is completely stupid, and oftentimes broken. Sometimes you'll try to work your way around it, and you absolutely need one pipe, and not one other pipe will do, and there only happens to be one. Or sometimes broken pipes and alarms completely block your path to the ending pipe. Or SOMETIMES, the water flows so fast you accidentally found out that the way you let the water flow is not blocked by alarms and broken pipes, and you can turn the water around. And, the moral choice system makes no sense. I only harvested two Little Sisters. Two! And the game gives me the most evil of the three endings. I thought I would've gotten to the good or morally ambiguous ending, but because I wasn't sure whether to be good or evil at the start and stuck with good... I got the evil ending. For harvesting two of the thirty or so Little Sisters. Which is a massive load of B. S.
Despite these flaws, BioShock soars high above the video game market, and creates something truly amazing. If you've played this game already, I'm sure you like it. If you haven't played it... well, you've got to play it. Would you kindly?
Years later, I keep coming back to this game.

TL; DR: 4.5/10 Lots of good moments, overall not that spectacular.
Spoilers:
Honestly I’m trying to think of one good thing about this game to provide, it’s not terrible it’s just utterly forgettable. Think of it as a mixture of PT and Five Night’s at Freddy’s mixed with a dash of the incomprehensible twist building of M. Night Shyamalan. The problem is the twist they keep building seems like it’s going to go one way and have the game make sense, but then the game hightails it in a direction that doesn’t have anything to do with everything they just built.
There were moments when I was truly invested in the story with the main character trying desperately to find her child.
Sometimes, when the game played it right, my heart truly ached for the character and I found myself hoping that she would find her son alive and well. Even when I knew she wouldn’t and the events in this story were all in her head.
There were moments, like repeatedly beating you over the head with the story of Hansel and Gretel and the fact that the main character clearly needed medication, that you believed that in a fit of insanity and desperation she killed her son and cooked him. That would have been a truly terrifying experience to get to the end only to realize it’s just her trying to rationalize with herself what she had done to her child. Instead the “twist” ending we find out that she killed her kid at an abandoned amusement park.
I don’t know what this random a-hole in a chipmunk suit, or the freak in the top hat had to do with anything. They really didn’t add much to the story. Apparently they belong to another game, which shares the same connected universe as this one, and I’m sure if I played that one I would understand. But if you’re going to throw to random characters into a game to promote another one could you at least give us a little background on them first so we know what the bloody blue hell is going on?
In the meantime, we’re distracted by a walking simulator that goes from point A to point B, with a semi-coherent story with nothing else to add to it but the occasional jump scare. Other than this woman prattling on and on, that is.
Perhaps I am judging the game just a bit too harshly, but I love horror games and so when a friend recommended "The Park" I was very excited. Knowing that it wasn't a "AAA game" I didn't expect it to be overly long and complicated; what I did expect however was a thrilling and disturbing tale. Right off the bat the game lets you know that it will "mess with your sanity." However, all it “messed with” was whether or not I was fully invested in the story or cared. By the end the constant change of pace and tone only caused me to progressively hate the main character and her whiny attitude more and more.
Stock game is worth the price of admission.  DLC isn't necessary since fun levels are already 11/10.

I first played Empire at War when I was 9 and I have been hooked ever since. Now I'm 15 and I am still loving it. Although I personally never get tired of Story Mode and Galactic Conquest Mode, I occasionally look up mods (this game has some of the best mods of all time, even if you don't have the DLC expansion pack) and I love those too. I usually compare this game to Halo Wars on Xbox 360. The gameplay is very similar to upgrading buildings and telling troops where to go on the battlefield, and the space combat is exactly the same. There is an out of battle part of the gameplay (unless playing Skirmish Mode) where you send fleets and troops to other planets to attack, reinforce, or retreat. You also train troops and build ships and space stations for when you actually fight in this part of the game. There are heroes in the game you can play as (Darth Vader, Boba Fett, Han Solo, Chewbacca, Luke Skywalker (Red Squadron in base game only, Jedi Knight in DLC only), Yoda, and more). This game was a gateway drug to strategy games for me and I was obviously attracted to it as a Star Wars fanboy, but this really did get me into strategy games. The only thing I might be worried about is the fanboy level in this game. If you are not a fanboy, this game is still worth trying, but you might get bored way too early.

For an early access game The Forest is how it should be done, it's frequently updated, fun to play and I personally do not experiece any crashes. Of course some bugs here and there and sometimes a bit less than smooth gameplay with some FPS drops, but this is understandable and it's not exactly gamebreaking.
Hosting your own server is a bit of a hassle but once you figure it out it's easy to upkeep and play with your friends (which I really recommend)
The game allows you to be very creative in ways to dispatch of any Cannibals and building, it takes some work to build everything up and your first night may be a bit frightening but it'll be much worth it in the end.
The story in The Forest is also very enjoyable and well put-together, you'll need a variety of items found all over the island in order to even access the end-game area.
All in all I really recommend this game, and with over 120 hours of entertainment I am very statisfied with the amount I paid with this game.

Time goes by, I miss you, and so I decide since I am now a reasonably famous game maker because of a little title I made called the Stanley Parable, that I shall make a new game. Well, sort of.
It’s kind of a new game but actually completely filled with your work! I don’t even deny it! I openly admit I cannot get in contact with you thus ask for your consent to use your work!

This review is written for the alpha version .349 on 07/05/2016
This review is written from the viewpoint of the Long Dark being an alpha game in early development that will continue to see the addition of new features and content as well as upgrades to AI, crafting systems, cooking, etc. It assumes that such features will be added and thus the current cons only deal with problems I percieve in the way the game runs at it's current alpha level.
PROS:
Solid and Challenging Core-Gameplay
Fantastic Game Concept and Execution
High Replay Value
Beautiful Graphics
CONS:
Unexplained Gameplay Mechanics
Immortal Wolf Bug
Unrealistic Item Decay
EXPLAINATION:
I love this game and the core concept. Survival games have always been my thing and I'm a huge fan of the solo-sandbox experience. There is no thrill quite as great as starting out in the middle of nowhere in negative 20 ish degree weather with sneakers, a pair of jeans, and a microfiber sweater, and turning it into a 36 day survival streak. Knowing that your survival depends on this bowshot hitting that deer you've been stalking for the last hour in-game fills you with trepidation and adrenaline. It's wonderful.
There's also nothing more irritating than hitting a wolf with a bow only to have it turn and attack, then refuse to die as it continues to attack 2 more times, killing you and ending your longest streak.
All in all, the Long Dark is a wonderful game. The main idea and the core gamplay are enjoyable and almost worth purchasing the game for. The potential is fantastic, and I think that this alpha is definitely worth supporting.
The first two games will be weird and off-putting. The next two games will be interesting and engaging. Everything from there on is crack.

Aspects of what one would really expect from a zombie apocalypse is reflected in this game, from Sound/Sight attracting zombies (for fairly obvious reasons), to using almost everything you find as a potential weapon and even to storing of supplies (refridgeration of food etc).
Depending on what mode you play (I play mostly sandbox), your skill will be tested in a scenario where your likelihood of survival depends on your actions, sure you got a shotgun but do you really want to take that shot at a passing zombie knowing that the surrounding zombies from blocks away can hear it.

I highly recommend this game to anyone interested in survival gameplay. Set in a frozen Canadian wilderness, your first battles are against hypothermia and starvation, and you progress by finding better shelter, better clothes, and better tools. Pros:
- STEAM WORKSHOP. I can't wait for modders to dig in.
- Utterly immersive.
- Sometimes a little terrifying.
- Some tough challenges if you've already played it 239390259033783 times and are getting bored.
- They're developing a storymode!
- You will, at some point, have a brush with death. At first you'll probably succumb to The Long  Dark, but as you play it more, you'll learn how to pull through and believe me, it is satisfying
when you survive a major setback.
Con (more of a warning against hype/expectations):
- It's in early access; don't expect it to be how you thought it would, and expect changes in gameplay as it develops. Some things have only been partially implemented, while some things need some work/balancing before the game is ready to roll (such as some of the crafting recipes and resources/tools at the time of writing).
Don't expect the game to be totally like IRL survival. It's a fictional game, and still being developed at that; and as such the lore/story may change too. Games change plenty between the different versions. Think of early access as a chance for the devs to playtest as much as possible - some popular and highly acclaimed games/series such as the Half-Life series (as an example) went through some truly enormous changes to the mechanics and asethetics before becoming the games we know today.
My last advice is to wait until it's in a sale, and then buy it if you're still interested (as I did). Or you could wait until it's full release (there's no set date for this however, and will probably increase in price upon full release) and buy it then if it seems good.
If you do get it: May the best survivor- um - have this complimentary deer carcass.
Oh, I forgot to mention: Playable if you're a vegatarian. Probably. Well. Sort of. You're certainly hardcore if you survive in this game without meat for long periods of time.

I didn't fall for the hype of it being a classical platformer and i ignored all reviewes. Actually playing the game without giving a crap about reviews and drama surrounding the game, i enjoyed what it had to offer. The worlds, difficulty, animation, characters, sountrack, are all great.
Another big reason why i like it so much is that it fits within my standards of what a game should be. It comes in a complete package without no b.s dlc, microtransactions, and season passes. You can just enjoiy a game without feeling you missed something.
Looking into typical reviews right now, people have been comparing this game to dark souls because it's focus is difficulty and boss battles. I feel that comparing Dark Souls (which isnt even a platformer), is just wrong and meme worthy in my opinion.
The best i can say about this difficulty is that it's not easy. You have to memorize these boss patterns to proceed to the next boss stage. You have to watch your HP, doge at the right time, watch out for small enemies on your screen during a boss battle. This is not a simple 4 hours and you are done type of game. It's the game where it might take a ton of hours just trying to fight a single boss which might turn people off.
Pros:
Style/Animation- I'm in awe because of how well they were able to put this amount of detail into a 2D platformer
Solid gameplay- no bugs on my end
Excellent worlds- I like how each world is different and has different themes
Solid Soundtrack- The game provides some excellent soundtracks like the Kind of Dice theme and the Railroad Theme. The songs are appropriate and really fit what the game is going for.
Characters- Are cool and unique
Cons:
Keyboard controls are not great and i would advise to play with a controller
some bosses can be frustrating near the end- King of dice
Parry mechanic- I disliked it because at times it feels like an afterthought
Character- Even though i love the unique characters in the game, they feel lifeless and bland
Conclusion:
Is this game a masterpiece? In my opinion, i could say that this game is. Again it's just solid, great and unique compared to some of the modern games coming out. obviously this game ain't for everyone, but I would still recommend it if you are a fan of difficult games, or old animation. Even if you are a casual gamer, i would still try it out because you might like it in the end.

SUPERHOT is an interesting game. I remember watching videos of it back in 2013 when it was created for a challenge to develop a complete FPS demo in 7 days. While it was truly an interesting idea, (time moving at normal speed when the player moves or fires a gun, the minimalist art style, etc.), I didn't think much of it and moved on. However, upon its release on steam in 2016, I decided to give it a try. I was not disappointed.
It is a difficult game for those who can't adapt. Its something that requires you to think about what you are doing and be aware of what is going on around you. Trying to run-and-gun constantly will 99% of the time end with a bullet in your face. However, that does not mean you should be too cautious either. Allowing yourself to slow down for too long will most likely result in you getting boxed in by 3-4 enemies with pistols trained on you. You must remain alert or you'll end up staring at a bullet you could have dodged if you paid closer attention.
"But how is that fun?"
The key is, like I said above, to be adaptable. You must be able to change your strategy to meet new threats. You must think on the fly. Thats part of what makes SUPERHOT so unique. Making the player adapt to new enviroments, as well as giving them the tools to succeed (and look awesome while doing it). It brings to my mind Hotline Miami in a way. Both are games that require you to be alert and be able to react to threats as they appear. But while Hotline emphasizes speed in dealing with situations, SUPERHOT emphasizes precision.
I recommend SUPERHOT completely. The story is short and rather simple, but fits well in the style of game and original in a genre lacking in simple and original feeling stories. Plus, the numerous challenges and modes offered on completion of the story will keep you interested. The art style is unique and in combination with the gameplay, SUPERHOT demonstrates a game that has had true feeling and passion behind its creation. If $25 is too much, pick it up on sale. You will not be disappointed.
