Much as I would like to give this game a positive review, I simply find that I can't in good conscience.  The fact of the matter is that it did not scare me.  I won't lie and say that I am the world's fore-most authority on horror games, but I have played a few of them, and The Park is probably the least effective of the lot.  This may well stem from the fact that it is a walking simulator.  Now perhaps I should have realized this before I bought it, but I think the very fact that I did not, even after watching the video ad and reading the steam store text, is rather telling.
Unfortunately the story, which is very clearly the main focus of the game, is nothing terribly special.  It centers around a young (maybe, it's sort of hard to tell) mother, her child, and the amusement park which (rather indirectly) caused their lives to go to hell.  What's frustrating about it is that the bones of the narrative are pretty solid, it simply wasn't expanded enough.  It's clear almost from the get-go that the owner of the themepark was doing something not terribly nice, but they really never reveal what his intention was, or even what precisely it was that he was doing.  They bring up an incident from the past in which the park's mascot murdered at least one teenager (maybe more, it isn't very specific) but then his part of the narrative is never expanded on.
Speaking of the ice-pick wielding chipmunk mascot, there's a bit of a running theme with him showing up and attempting to scare the hell out of the player, but the fact is that this tactic simply doesn't work in a situation where one knows for a fact that he's not going to hurt the main character.  I suppose you could argue that I didn't properly "lose myself in the medium" or some such, but personally it seems like that's more the "game" failing to draw me in than me being unwilling to suspend my disbelief.  It's sort of like reading a book where, half way in, an extremely contrived situation shows up and threatens to kill off the protagonist.  No one will fall for it, because you're only halfway into the book, and it's exceptionally clear that the author isn't going to switch viewpoints after so much work developing their main character, so what is supposed to be a tense situation just feels like something you have to slog through in order to continue the story.
But I digress.  Probably the best feature of The Park is its atmosphere, and the quality of its visual design.  Easily the creepiest moments came not when I was paying attention to the story itself, reading notes or listening to the protagonist's internal monologue, but when I spent the time to inspect some well designed and indelibly disturbing thing that happened to be sitting around in the environment.  I remember one moment particularly well when I had to walk past a bizarre bird-like sculpture that was set along one of the paths in the park.  Not only was the character design interesting and unique in its eeriness, the game devs had textured in what I could swear were bullet holes in the thing, which made me almost certain it was going to spring to life the moment I turned my back, and start following me.  More's the pity when it didn't.
I suppose that's really the whole theme of why I can't recommend this as a game; more's the pity when it didn't.  There was a lot of potential for greatness here, but virtually all of it went unfulfilled.  I wouldn't say that there were no good moments in the game, otherwise it wouldn't have that tantalizing potential, it's more a matter of there not being enough.  All in all it's about like going through a haunted house, except you don't have any friends with you to make it more enjoyable, and there's only a couple of actors who are more or less content to just stand there and assume their costume is creepy enough.

It was pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥to be honest. I almost want to request a refund even though I've already completed it. It's obviously trying to emulate other great walking simulators like Layers of Fear and The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, but it fails completely in my opinion.
This game is ridicoulously short, completely linear, contains no scares or tense atmoshphere (apart from 2-3 cheap jump scares) and most of it just involves you riding theme park rides... not kidding. Where other walking simulators contain very little gameplay there is absolutely none in this game.

For example, I ran out of firewood because I built a building that took all the remainder of the wood I had. I added more people as foresters to catch back up my wood supply, and for years after that I had plenty of wood and not enough firewood despite adding 2 more woodcutters. Eventually nearly my entire population dropped dead. This thin ice, no-way-back type of gaming is more frustrating than fun.

Although I recommend Limbo, I still thought it was a pretty basic puzzle game.
The atmosphere is the most interesting part of the game. Although only white and black is used and most of the screen is black for almost all the game, the game still manages to draw you into the unique world that is Limbo.
Puzzles: Range from unique and satisfying to beat to just boring and tedious to complete. You will be dying a lot on your first play through and sometimes the game forces you to repeat tedious tasks. It seems the game missed an opportunity here for epic puzzles. Interesting game mechanics are introduced throughout the game but it never really seems to take off.
Game length: very short game (took me only 4 hrs). I rather have 4 hours of fairly interesting gameplay than a longer more repetitive game so I am ok with the length. Since it was such a short game however I would have expected more interesting puzzles.
Controls: you will be using 4 buttons. up, left, right, and ctrl. Sometimes the controls feel sluggish and the character seems to respond slightly slow to commands which can make percision and jumping tasks slightly difficult. Also, since up is both climb and jump, occasionally you will be jumping off of a ladder withtout wanting to. It's also a pet peeve of mine when you can't move left or right when you jump. You can press forward or back and jump to perform a jump in that direction, but you cannot press up and then move left or right. Small greivance, but that could have been helpful to have in game.
Story: There doesn't seem to be any. You're a boy stuck in some kind of horror world. Some people want to kill you but you're not really sure why. I suppose you're trying to escape the place but i am not sure why you're there anyway. I guess you're trying to get to your girlfriend? Really lacking here.
Visuals: that's really where this game shines. It manages to create a unique atmosphere and hold your attention for the few hours that you will play this game.
Verdict: 3.5/5
It is an average puzzle game with a few interesting puzzles and a great atmosphere. Give it a go if you have 3-4 hours to spare.

This game is a good combination of strategy and Star Wars.  If you are seasoned veteran with games like Rise of Nations and Age of Empires, then you'll understand the concepts of this game quickly.  The one thing which I find is that you cannot upgrade as much as other games (basically, you upgrade your space station for better vehicles and that's about it), yet it still requires some sort of challenge to keep the game moving along.  You do have the option to speed through battles, which can be handy if you have an overwhelming force, but that could cause more grinding moments instead of competition.  However, the game does offer some degree of difficulty, such as zones which disable commands, vision, etc, which adds to the challenge of might may not always help you in the match, but using it well.
Overall, an enjoyable play for strategy lovers that love a casual challenge or for Star Wars buffs to get involved in the strategy genre.  It's too bad that there was never really a sequel released to this game as it would have been nice to see exapnded mechanics built into later versions (such as Rise of Nations or Civilization) as this game would have been better, but it's like Civilization III.  You still play it because it's a fun game and enjoy the experience.

-The amount of detail is just astonishing. Like, when u fire a machine gun without ceasing fire it will overheat and u have to change the barell which is something unique in this game.

A surprisingly fun strategy game from Mode7 that takes a few steps to split from what one would normally expect in a strategy game.
The big draw is the simultaneous turns, which really builds a new metagame and there is a lot of satisfaction in correctly reading your opponents moves, or mis-directing them of your intentions. Being able to sim out possible scenarios, it's possible spend 2 minutes setting one turn up, only to be deliberating for an hour about the next; the best part being that either is fine thanks to the multiplayer system.
An elegant 'correspondence' style multiplayer means that you input your turns actions, commit and go check out any other active games you have and input turns for them whilst you wait. Notifications pop up to inform you when new turns are ready to be played and it's a very nice and relaxing approach to the format.
Beyond that, the visuals are nice, soundtrack top notch and is made by talented developers, so I am looking forward to seeing the future life cycle of the game. Lets hope more people pick up on this and really get the community booming!

This review was completed 4 hours into game and shortly after their first update.
Tales From Candle Keep: Tomb Of Annihilation is not a bad game.  With nearly 700 games in my library I don't have anything else like, and it has even managed to redirect a healthy amount of my time from another recent purchase Battle Chasers. However, unfortunately for the developers a lot of the great things about this title are subtle while its less attractive aspects are more glaring or simply cliche.
“All in all I'm realy digging this game...” a buy for fans
Pros
Excellent table top inspired game play
Graphically Pleasing
Cons
Limited Assets
Poorly Optimized
Mission Farming
Freemium Feel
Accessibility
limited training
As stated Tomb Of Annihilation has excellent table top game play.  Optimal outcomes will constantly require players to balance there offense, exploration, consumption, and risk in ways that produce very non typical results when compared to other similar titles.  The reason for this is the encounter phase.  It drives everything and will hands down the least palatable mechanic you've ever seen... for about an hour.
You see if a character does not discover a new tile or is simply unlucky enough to discover a challenge tile you'll be gifted, in most cases with a negative outcome.  Sounds horrible, right? YOUR WRONG! Its one of the more innovative table top mechanics I've seen and as a result Tomb Of Annihilation rarely devolves into your typical turn based scrum with your entire party huddled around one enemy at a time. Instead, TOA's tactics are much more versed.  You'll look for hit and run attacks on the regular.  Find optimum end turn positions to set up your next round.  Split up your team and carefully space them to mitigate risk and maximize opportunity.  Store interrupts for a large brawl or to by time to open a chest.  The only uninspired part of game play is the boss battle which I have almost always weathered by spamming my most powerful attacks and ignoring all else.  The game also has a pretty high skill cap early on and will feel punitive to most players for the first hour, but I highly suggest players considering a refund stick out that second hour so you might see whats great about this one.
Most of the titles cons are tell tale signs of a small studio. Environments feel repetitive b/c they are.  Though clean and beautiful, in larger quantities the repetitive look of environment numbs the senses.  While I rarely say this, a change of scenery would actually due wonders for the overall feel of this game. Its also a bit rough in the optimization department.  Frames are often dropped when exploring new tiles and even  traps/chest tend to pop in after a slight delay.
The least forgivable aspect of the TOA is its somewhat freemium feel.  Its Bright, colorful and the crafting feels a lot like a free to play storefront.  In addition Level difficulty has huge hills and valleys.  Your heroes also have no access to a consumables market. This will force most players to farm easier missions and horde items in order to press harder levels.  This always feels like an inauthentic way to extend game play and reduces some often excellent game play into a grind.
Lastly the crafting system feels uninspired but not shimmed in.  Each series of crafted upgrades offers linear buffs with very direct and measurable effects.  This is boring but useful for in reality the system is just designed to look like a crafting system but is instead another form of xp that allows you directly upgrade your characters.  Your never really short of materials, in game money is the gatekeeper here.  Clever players will identify and target hero short comings with this system and perhaps advance more quickly.
All in all I'm really digging this game.  Though the cons are more numerous I put a premium on game play and am loving it.  While I personally feel like the innovations here push them game into 7/10 territory I feel like the games limited accessibility and limited assets will deter many.
So in conclusion fans of great table top or RPG's seeking a unicorn should put down there miniatures and give Tomb of Annihilation a shot.  All others...wait for a sale.

Pros: Interesting setting, brilliant story, fantastic voice acting.
Cons: "Clunky" physics, repetitive combat, minor sound glitches, and infinitely-respawning enemies with little behavioural variation.
Moderately to highly recommended, even if mostly only for the unique ambience and captivating story. Combat mechanics are, unfortunately, less than fantastic, with clunky physics (even for 2007) and weapons which manage to "feel" insubstantial, even when upgraded to a devastating degree. The large variety of awesomely creative upgrades manage to carry the core gameplay, but ultimately even the excitement of casting fireballs and bees (yes, bees!) is dissipated by samey, copy-pasted enemies: if you've killed a dozen or so splicers and a big daddy, you've pretty much seen it all. This is further exacerbated by unwarranted and badly-disguised infinite respawning.
All in all, a fine game; the story starts off with a bang, gives a satisfying punch in the middle, but ultimately manages to just fizzle out adequately.

After platying for a while and beating most missions on Hard as well as a few on the hardest difficulty.. I feel like gear/difficulty progression from Normal to Hard was good but then you hit an upgrade brick wall and are unable to properly transition to the hardest difficulty...
Playing on the hardest difficulty is highly frustrating due to certain abilities that can one-shot your characters if they are not properly equiped (Better armor offers higher HP). For instance, when a spell casting skeletons die, they cast a random spell on death. There is no way to stop that spell or to influence which one will be cast or even who it will target. In a game where movement and position is super tactical, this is unacceptable. This spell can very well hit for 8 damage while your guys wearing green/blue gear only have 6-8 HP.
Being able to upgrade gear at a steady pace would help to somewhat counter the problem but the upgrade crafting materials are extremely hard to come by.... except if you buy their material DLCs...  Essentially, if you want to beat the game on its hardest difficulty, be ready to play for 400 hours of farming or to dish out extra cash on material DLC.
The other sad part is that when your characters die, they consume a Healing Surge. Your party has 2 and will always have 2 if you buy the base game. If a character is dead and cannot be revived by a Healing Surge because you ran out of charges, it's game over immediately. You can't even keep going with the remaining party members who are still alive.  I was OK with this mechanic playing on Normal and Hard but when abilities can one-shot your characters with no way to block or influence damage distribution on the hardest difficulty, it plainly sucks.
To make matters even worse, if you pay more real money for the Deluxe edition of this game, you get a extra Healing Surge. That's right, 3 resurects instead of 2. That's a 50% increase in survival right there and IMHO since this item is so important to being able to properly play on the hardest difficulty, it should be something purchasable in-game without needing to pay real $ for.
TLDR:
- If you want an experience sorta close to its board game counterpart and count to play on Normal or Hard, it's fun.
- If you want to beat this game on its hardest difficulty, get ready to grind crafting materials for a LONG time, or simply dish out real $ to get the said items immediately... You'll probably also need that extra Healing surge that is included in the Deluxe package (50% increase in survival rate).
I'm pretty disapointed that the end-game is pay to win.

Highly recommended. This is Mode7's second game. It continues along the same path as their previous game: Frozen Synapse. It's a simultaneous turn-based strategy game, both players take their turns, then the game plays out their turns simultaneously, and they see the result. The previous game, Frozen Synapse, took this idea to warfare. It was a somewhat difficult to grasp, rather complex game that was also incredibly tense and rewarding.
Frozen Endzone captializes on the lessons learned from Synapse and focuses. It doesn't quite dumb it down, though there are less options. It simplifies in the service of clarity, and provides players with a limited toolset that allows for a wide variety of strategems.
Forget the aesthetic of sports, it is just that, aesthetic. It's a reason to present the tactics available. This is absolutely not a sports game. This is a strategy game, in the vein of Chess, digitized for the modern era in a way that's not possible with physical board pieces.
Each player controls a team of robots, and each of those robots has a unique set of stats that govern how fast they can run, how widely from where they stand they can block, how widely they can intercept, etc. One team starts with the ball nearby, and must pick it up before the turn is over. A turn ending occurs at an event, such as picking up the ball, throwing the ball, catching the ball, turning the ball over, or when a specified length of time occurs. The rest of the offense (that didn't go for the ball), can wait in place, allowing their block radius to have meaning, or move as much or as little as desired (they can also wait, THEN move). The defense spreads out, or converges, or whatever they feel necessary. Their objective is to "block" the player with the ball, catch the ball instead of an intended receiver, or force the offense into "punting" by throwing it to the ground somewhere.
The player with the ball has two choices, he can immediately pass the ball, anywhere not blocked by a "high" block. He can try to get it where another player can catch it, or throw to the ground, hopefully at an adventageous position for his team (or at least not too advantageous for the other team). He cannot pass backwards. Alternately, he can run, and if he does so, he cannot pass again until a turnover occurs. If he runs, he must go forward at least (3?) blocks in a specified time period. The rest of his team can block, if standing still. He either makes it to the end zone, a period of time elapses without making it, or he is tackled, and loses the ball.
The period ends when a team moves the ball, held by their own player, into the opponent's endzone.
What's thrilling about this is how quickly the tables can turn. I was cautiously moving my offense up the field, passing the ball. I saw an opening to ground the ball near the endzone and pick it up with another player. Unfortunately, I miscalculated the distance, I realized that player was about to get blocked, and saw an opponent near my endzone, unguarded. I scrambled a player there, but it was too late, one endzone to endzone pass later, I lost.
This probably sounds complicated, it looks it, written out. But really, one 5 minute tutorial and it should all make sense.
I have not yet played much, but I'm already hooked. Highly recommended.

+SUPERHOT has a very unique style of gameplay: Time only moves when you move.
As a result, you can make projectiles travel very slowly and attempt to dodge them. It can be really intense when you're surrounded by a group of enemies all filling the air with scattering shotgun and machine gun rounds.
+In addition to dodging, timing the trajectories for your weapons and disarming nearby enemies are also vital skills. Using a Katana to slice apart bullets, and being able to transfer your consciousness into nearby enemies are some of this game’s other top thrills. All these mechanics come together and form some truly memorable gameplay. I enjoyed every encounter and would love to see more levels or future games attempt this concept.
+ I can imagine the game would be a blast to play in VR! It would also help a few story moments pack more punch and feel like something out of Inception.
- It can be a little hard to grasp your character’s hitbox, resulting in a few deaths that feel undeserved.
- Oftentimes the storytelling can feel more obtrusive and annoying than actually interesting. Upon finishing the game I guess the story is a good addition, but compared to the rest of the highly awesome game the story is definitely not a selling point.
-The final level is a very large difficulty spike vs. the rest of the game.
- Because some levels are a challenge and the AI is so reckless, the game can sometimes encourage the player to use “cheese” tactics rather than the special strategies intended for each level.
This game is short enough that you might want to wait until a sale, but you Definitely NEED to play it!

------------- Update 2015 Mar 26 ------------
With the new hunters coming in I wanted to see if the updates since launch had improved the game play at all. Sadly, they have not.
The game still feels like an extended game of tag where the hunters try to catch a monster, then immediately switch roles and try to avoid the monster or face getting chain stunned to death. It never feels like your hunting the monster, tracks and sign are easy for anyone to follow, most of the game is spent chasing the much faster monsters. There is the occasional chance to cut off a monster, but experienced players minimize these opportunities.
The thing I find most frustrating is that it NEVER feels like there's a balance, and the devs really don't know how to fix it. In the latest patch one of the characters I enjoyed playing, Cabot, received around a 50% nerf to his damage. He may have been slightly overpowered before, but a nerf that large screams lack of pre-testing or extreme over-reaction.
As much as I want to enjoy Evolve, I just find it an exercise in frustration. I've only been able to stand for a game or two during events, in order to unlock the rewards, before I want to play something else.
Still wish I passed on it at this point.
------------- Original Review -------------
I was looking forward to playing Evolve last night but was seriously frustrated by a lot of the functionality in game.
You cannot skip the initial tutorial, or any video. The character's are all introduced this way but their skills are simple for the most part, and could be introduced by a static graphic. Instead every player needs to sit around for 2 minutes while these videos play. I was so frustrated at one point I actually ALT-F4'd out of the game in frustration just so I could skip one of the lengthy videos.
In addition, you need to score your 'Favored' classes, there's no option to NOT play a class. I had no desire to play the monster or assault last night, but was stuck with them on multiple occasions. This included being selected for the monster in back to back games in a campaign, which caused me to drop out in frustration.
Evolve has been compared to L4D's asymmetric gameplay, but it's a poor comparison. L4D built tension with tight areas, harassed the survivors with NPCs, and provided the Infected interesting ways to disrupt. There's no tension here, the neutral mobs only exist to provide a temporary buffs, food for the monster, or a minor annoyance.
I think the most frustrating part is there's very little incentive for the monster to engage until it's ready. This might be interesting gameplay for the monster, but it means that all the hunters are doing is trying to catch up/cut off the monster for 1-2 big fights. That means in a 10 minute game all the hunters are doing for 7-8 minutes is running around the map.
I can't say the fights are particularly engaging either. Most of the monster attacks cause a fair amount of knockback, and most of the CC/Deployables the hunters have can be instantly broken by a basic attack. As a result, all the hunters are doing is trying to avoid drawing the monsters attention, with the primary target being thrown around and CC'd to death with very little chance of evading.
The game may grow on me, but it wasn't worth the cost IMO.
** Note ** The problem most people have is with the amount of DLC. Although I didn't have a problem when they announced the packages, since they were being upfront, I WAS disappointed to see a truck load of day 1 pay DLC not included. I stopped buying games from EA because of their practice of launching day 1, and microtransaction, DLC on full games. I will no longer be supporting 2K games after this.

Now I'd love to stay and write a big old review for this, but I'm far too tired. Anyway, the whole game is fantastic, and yes, like every game and especially indie games this game has bugs and things that need to be tweaked around with.  Because this game has an up and running mod community, most things that can be fixed, have been fixed by the modders. On to the actual game, it has a very interesting twist to it that I had never been exposed to before. The whole thing is you are already dead, the game's premise is that you have already died and the game you are playing is all just a flashback leading to your inevitable demise. No matter how well defended, how incredibly stealthy or how deaf, dumb and blind you made the zombie AI, you are dead. And that's the ideal feel of this game, you should never feel safe and really you never will, sitting at the computer watching your amassment of pixels as it struggles about fulfilling basic needs remains exciting as it induces constant paranoia, both in game and on the player themself. Best of all, once you are dead (again?) you stay dead, or undead, depending on whether or not you were devoured alive by the new populus and will have to make an entirely new character in a the world; the only way to retrieve your items is to defeat what horrendous monster your corpse rose to be, and this keeps the player on edge. And without being on constant alert and being incredibly paranoid, you're doomed, although you are already doomed. In summation, it's a very good game covering every last detail to making the most realistic zombie apocalypse survival game, I really would recommend anyone and everyone to try it.

In other words you might want to experience this because of how it relates to a small demographic of basically lonely male video game enthusiasts who have embarked upon the journey of creation, in order to see your emotional landscape and evaluate your own priorities in life and think mature thoughts reflecting upon those of the developer.
This narrative expresses both "I'm too shy to be a success" and "I'm too determined to be an artist." Duality. Paradox and perplexity. You knew what you were getting into if you'd played the Stanley Parable, even though ironically that game was full of pretense of being a game while this is completely empty. well anyway I don't recommend it as a game, but as art, it fits the mold.

I am not in the habit of writing reviews for games, so bear with me.
I did not expect to enjoy this game, as nice as it looked. Roguelike mechanics never really clicked for me in other games. For me, this has been the exception. While many complain about the negative effects of not exploring for more map pieces, the game seems to be about finding a rhythm between beating enemies, building up momentum without getting bogged down by too many enemies, and sometimes taking time to open a chest or two, all the while working towards the objective of the quest. When you get a big enough group of enemies or a boss that requires your full party to beat, you start using up your charges to avoid encounters, or use up utility/daily powers/items to avoid getting beat down. It honestly does come down to finding a rhythm, and fighting to keep it, managing all the aspects of the game.
The crafting system is simple and comfortable, which helps keep you focused more on the gameplay than the crafting itself, even as it complements the difficulty. Getting your first common At Will craft makes the game move a lot faster right at the beginning, without making it a cakerun even in the simplest difficulties.
I look forward to finding out what the development team has in store for us in the future.

Tropico 5 is broken. That's the bottomline. Have you played Tropico 4? Well imagine if they sawed Tropico 4 in half, and then improved the graphics. That's it. Half the content of 4, despite having tons of unneccessary and greedy DLCs in which you usually get about 1 building and maybe 1 outfit. You get hardly any variety in buildings, hardly ANY overlays, so you'd be hard pressed to understand what's going on at any given time. Okay food satisfaction is low, why is that? I have a ton of farms, I have places distributing food, WHAT IS THE PROBLEM? Do I need yet more farms, more workers, more markets? No idea, just guess work. In 4, and in fact in every previous itteration of the game EXCEPT FOR 5, you had overlays for pretty much everything, not so in 5. Oh and good look finding a building and seeing at a glance what buildings you've already built, what areas are serviced with what etc. Unless you're looking for one of the many gaudy eyesores that don't fit in anywhere on your island, like the circus tent, one of the extremely few available entertainment buildings.
Compared to 4, you get almost no chance of influencing the elections or the people in any way aside from what you build and the edicts. If you go into an election with less than 50-55% approval rating, you're going to lose. Penultimo as always asks if you want to "rig" the election, only in 5, he's hopelessly incompetent because he gives you so few extra votes that you won't win unless you were going to anyways or were balancing on a razorblade. Yeah, some dictator simulator.
In 4 you got the option of making a speech, giving promises, it was a great way to keep your head above water, you appealed to the largest group of voters and if you held your promise, great! In 5, you don't even have a faction overlay or anything resembling it anymore. There are factions, and they are discontent, but you don't know how many there are of each, what they want etc.
And there are no election speeches, basically it goes like this; Election time, have you satisfied most of all our needs beforehand despite struggling with money and gotten 50-55% Approval? Great, click election, keep improving and HOPE you´ll win. No? Okay, click no election, get instant mobs with 8000hp crushing your puny millitary and bringing down your palace. Or click yes for election and lose anyways.
Not even in the very first Tropico did this system function so very poorly!
So on islands with rebel threat and unrest, you stand no chance. No really, you don't. You need millitary buildings to fend off rebels, but those take up valuable highschool workers you could be using for factories and services. What's worse, despite having millitary, despite having all the upgrades and beefing up, the millitary doesn't stand a chance against a simple mob of people. A millitary unit has about 3500hp, a mob has 8000hp! You can build tanks in Tropico 5, the mobs kill them WITH EASE.
Oh and get this, thanks to the newest feature, the Dynasties (which is a useless feature much poorer than the ones in 4), you get to revisit your previous islands for each new time period during the campaign. Hey great, no longer do I need to start from scratch with every new mission! Yeaaaah, there is that, BUT you also need to make sure your island is tip-top, because when you re-visit with a harder mission, you're gonna have a much harder time. And that would sound fair, if it wasn't for everything I've already mentioned, so basically if you struggle early, your whole campaign might go down the toilet, and you won't know it until several missions later.
Tropico 5, is broken. Play Tropico 4 instead.

I pre-ordered this game at the time after a string of glowing reviews and actually never completed it. Why you ask? Surely this game's aesthetics are top notch? They aged rather well, too, and the sound and music are spot on. The setting is ingenious as well and yet ... yet I feel as if they wasted it on this game. This could have been a universe to rival Fallout yet it's always been the little brother hoping for the same kind of attention. Here's why:
- the story is told through brief communcations and logs. This is interesting but makes it rather a one-way street. You don't feel as connected to the world the way a proper RPG would make you feel.
- while the game has plenty of combat-centered elements (a handful of guns and a series plasmids/magic spells) combat doesn't feel that responsive. The mouse look is spongy and inaccurate, none of the guns are very satisfying to use and it all lacks oomph.
- speaking of combat, the game has too much of it. Enemies respawn constantly and while it increases suspense, the AI isn't all that great and combat isn't interesting enough to make it more than a chore. In Bioshock Infinity, the combat is far sharper and interesting
- the game is pretty linear despite some areas acting as hubs and it doesn't *quite* work. It's not bad but could have been done better - you never feel as if you're really exploring rather than going down one main paths with a few dead ends with a secret here and there.
- I don't like typical scripted events designed to scare you - it's why I don't rate Half Life 2 as highly as many others too - and this game is full of them. Pick up item X, and a bunch of enemies spawn to take you out. It's cheap scare tactics that were pioneered by Doom 22 years ago and by now, it just feels dated and harms immersion when it becomes a thing to expect.
- It's a very dumbed down RPG: no inventory, slots needed for plasmids, no experience, no levels, no true improvement of skills, etc. You got tonics, sure, but that's a very childish form of it.
- the game could seriously have used some proper characters to talk to as well, just to make the world seem more realistic.
In the end, it's a decent game but with quite a few flaws. It's a rather shallow RPG with mediocre combat, an AMAZING setting and a decent story but all of that combined does not equal an outstanding game sadly enough. It's a great EXPERIENCE but if you want to experience it but can't stand the combat and respawning, there's cheats available luckily.

Been playing this game since the first public beta back in December 2013. Being a big fan of Frozen Synapse I knew I had to give this a go. At first I thought "There is no way this is going to be better, it doesn't even have any guns! How is it going to be more intense?" I'm glad to say that I was immensely wrong. This game takes everything great from Frozen Synapse and takes it to the next level in every way. Don't let the slow pace fool you, this game is very intense. Loading the outcome of your turn to see if your opponent saw through your plan or not is a really intense.
Seeing your game plan work out and successfully fooling your opponent and running across the endzone line is one of the most satisfying moments that I've experienced in any game ever.
The fact that you always get two copies when you buy the game makes things even better, so grab a friend and get going. This is a game that I highly recommend! If you have never played Frozen Synapse or any other similar games, I encourage you to give this a try.

In early 2010, film critic Roger Ebert published an article regarding his position on video games as an artistic medium. Early in the article, Ebert firmly expresses his view on the matter: “Let me just say that no video gamer now living will survive long enough to experience the medium as an art form.” As much as I respect the late Roger Ebert, I have to disagree with this statement because gamers living today have survived to see at least one game rise above the rest as a work of art. The game in question is Bioshock, a first person shooter that combines exquisite storytelling, impressive presentation, and innovative gameplay into one cohesive unit that stands with any novel, painting, or movie as a piece of fine art.
Bioshock begins with the player’s character, a silent protagonist named Jack, surviving a plane crash in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. With nowhere else to go, Jack swims to a nearby islet occupied by a large lighthouse. Jack takes refuge inside the structure and discovers a small bathysphere that takes him to the game’s main setting, the massive underwater city of Rapture. According to a recording played in the bathysphere, Rapture was conceived by a business magnate named Andrew Ryan, who built the city with the vision of a utopian community where one could achieve greatness without any interference from outside forces, such as government or religion. However, upon arriving in Rapture, the player soon finds out that things did not go exactly as Ryan planned. The city now lies in ruin and all of its living residents have become murderous lunatics that lash out at anything that moves. Aided via radio by a mysterious man named Atlas, Jack must now explore rapture and escape with his life.
What makes this game stand out from others is that the player has full control of Jack during the entire experience. By immediately relinquishing control, Bioshock immerses the player in a captivating tale of freewill and madness that slowly reveals itself over the course of the game. In addition to scripted events, such as the masterfully executed opening, the player can listen to audio logs left behind by the once sane citizens of Rapture. These optional logs give the player deeper insight into the lives of Rapture’s residents and the events that led to the city’s downfall.
Ryan himself adds philosophical depth to the game’s already rich narrative. He exudes ambition and unrelenting determination to his beliefs with a charisma that makes him one of the most memorable characters in all of gaming. His attitude towards government and religious officials, which he refers to as “parasites,” heavily mirrors the objectivist beliefs Ayn Rand expressed in novels like Atlas Shrugged. The inclusion of these philosophical themes elevates Bioshock above the stereotype that games produce stories with little to no substance. 	Unfortunately, the story’s only flaw, and the main drawback of the game in general, is the ending, which feels abrupt and underwhelming compared to the rest of the game. Luckily, the rest of the story makes up for the lackluster ending with some amazing plot twists that will stick with the player long after their experience with the game has concluded.
If Bioshock’s mesmerizing plot doesn’t draw the player into its world, then its unparalleled presentation will. Every inch of Rapture is painstakingly rendered with borderline obsessive attention to the tiniest details. Water realistically drips from the walls and ceilings. Neon signs flicker and short out. Cheerful announcements fall on deaf ears over the intercom. These fully realized details add to the idea that Rapture was once a thriving metropolis where people lived happy and fulfilling lives, making its current state of disrepair all the more heart wrenching. Furthermore, Bioshock exudes a distinct art direction rarely seen in games. Rapture’s consistent Art Deco style will generate a sense of appreciation for the artistry required to bring these environments to life.
While Bioshock’s story and presentation already place it in a league of its own, the game truly shines in its innovations to traditional FPS gameplay. Throughout the game, the player gather’s a diverse arsenal of weapons, ranging from a pistol to a shotgun to a flamethrower. Aiming and firing each of these weapons feels natural and satisfying. Also, all of the weapons can be upgraded to increase their accuracy and damage among other traits.
However, Bioshock deviates from FPS norms with the addition of plasmids. These genetic modifications provide the player with a wide variety of powers, such as setting enemies on fire, picking up and throwing large objects, and possessing enemies to have them fight on the player’s side. In order to obtain these perks, the player must collect a gene altering substance called ADAM from small girls called Little Sisters that freely roam Rapture’s halls. However, the player must first defeat the Little Sisters’ guardians, huge diving suit wearing creatures simply known as Big Daddies. These intimidating monsters deal massive damage and will take a long time to defeat, but the satisfaction and rewards make it worth the effort. Once the Big Daddy falls, the player has the option to either harvest the Little Sister, which gives the player more ADAM but kills the girl, or rescue it, which yields less ADAM but promises the player a future reward. These decisions not only affect the player’s access to plasmids but also have moral ramifications that play into how the game’s story unfolds. This morality based choice system not only presents the player with an interesting dilemma with tangible consequences, but also perfectly ties into the game’s overall themes of personal growth and freedom.
When all of Bioshock’s elements come together into a singular piece, they form a thoroughly entertaining and thought provoking experience that only a work of art can provide. The story keeps players guessing and presents them with philosophical concepts that other games can only dream of expressing. The presentation engrosses players into a world so authentically realized that it becomes as deep and complex as any of the game’s characters. Finally, the multifaceted gameplay forces the players to make decisions that impact their individual endeavors in unexpected ways. If this is the only time gamers experience the medium as a true art form, I can easily say that Bioshock deserves that distinction. Whether you’re a seasoned gamer or a curious onlooker, you owe it to yourself to pick up this slice of gaming excellence.

"Golly, what a mighty fine piece of art!" would be the proper thing to say about this game.
From the beginning on, everything is painstakingly created in a 1930s cartoon style (you might have noticed...) from the "graphics" to the soundtrack, even the speech and humor! Immersion is never broken, that you are in an old cartoon.
So far im 2,5h into the game, which says that im about 25% through (not getting the best rating everywhere etc), so i expect to get 10-12h out of it. I don't find it too difficult (for now), just the right amount. It's more of a trial & error kind of gameplay, as you mainly progress by learning the levels and bosses' patterns by trying again (and again...and again...and...) which can be frustrating for some people, but i don't mind.
The bosses each have unique (and funny!) ways to attack you, so there is something to see and learn everytime! Controls are easy to understand and learn (after all it says "run&gun"), though i would recommend a controller.
All in all i can just say: reward the developers for bringing us this gem of a game, don't wait to get the game in a sale, buy it now and support them this way! That's the only way for us to get such masterpieces in the future too!
PS: get the soundtrack too, it's an amazing testament to the music of the era and also worth listening to it without playing!

Tropico 5 is broken. That's the bottomline. Have you played Tropico 4? Well imagine if they sawed Tropico 4 in half, and then improved the graphics. That's it. Half the content of 4, despite having tons of unneccessary and greedy DLCs in which you usually get about 1 building and maybe 1 outfit. You get hardly any variety in buildings, hardly ANY overlays, so you'd be hard pressed to understand what's going on at any given time. Okay food satisfaction is low, why is that? I have a ton of farms, I have places distributing food, WHAT IS THE PROBLEM? Do I need yet more farms, more workers, more markets? No idea, just guess work. In 4, and in fact in every previous itteration of the game EXCEPT FOR 5, you had overlays for pretty much everything, not so in 5. Oh and good look finding a building and seeing at a glance what buildings you've already built, what areas are serviced with what etc. Unless you're looking for one of the many gaudy eyesores that don't fit in anywhere on your island, like the circus tent, one of the extremely few available entertainment buildings.
Compared to 4, you get almost no chance of influencing the elections or the people in any way aside from what you build and the edicts. If you go into an election with less than 50-55% approval rating, you're going to lose. Penultimo as always asks if you want to "rig" the election, only in 5, he's hopelessly incompetent because he gives you so few extra votes that you won't win unless you were going to anyways or were balancing on a razorblade. Yeah, some dictator simulator.
In 4 you got the option of making a speech, giving promises, it was a great way to keep your head above water, you appealed to the largest group of voters and if you held your promise, great! In 5, you don't even have a faction overlay or anything resembling it anymore. There are factions, and they are discontent, but you don't know how many there are of each, what they want etc.
And there are no election speeches, basically it goes like this; Election time, have you satisfied most of all our needs beforehand despite struggling with money and gotten 50-55% Approval? Great, click election, keep improving and HOPE you´ll win. No? Okay, click no election, get instant mobs with 8000hp crushing your puny millitary and bringing down your palace. Or click yes for election and lose anyways.
Not even in the very first Tropico did this system function so very poorly!
So on islands with rebel threat and unrest, you stand no chance. No really, you don't. You need millitary buildings to fend off rebels, but those take up valuable highschool workers you could be using for factories and services. What's worse, despite having millitary, despite having all the upgrades and beefing up, the millitary doesn't stand a chance against a simple mob of people. A millitary unit has about 3500hp, a mob has 8000hp! You can build tanks in Tropico 5, the mobs kill them WITH EASE.
Oh and get this, thanks to the newest feature, the Dynasties (which is a useless feature much poorer than the ones in 4), you get to revisit your previous islands for each new time period during the campaign. Hey great, no longer do I need to start from scratch with every new mission! Yeaaaah, there is that, BUT you also need to make sure your island is tip-top, because when you re-visit with a harder mission, you're gonna have a much harder time. And that would sound fair, if it wasn't for everything I've already mentioned, so basically if you struggle early, your whole campaign might go down the toilet, and you won't know it until several missions later.
Tropico 5, is broken. Play Tropico 4 instead.

I can definitely say, I did not expect this.
The Beginner's Guide is a game, that felt nothing like a game while I was playing it. I was being told a story, and it slowly drew me in more and more; I was walking around virtual levels, but they felt real, not as if I was actually there, but as if they were more than just levels, and every bit of the narrative felt immensely important. When the game ended, I found myself frantically questioning it, my interpration of what I just experienced, and myself, in a state no other game has ever put me in. This, truly is, an experience.
One thing is absolutely essential for this game's impact though: you have to be able to become deeply ingrossed with the story, or you will not find much here. If you never really pay attention to stories in the games you play, then this one might not be for you, but, then again, if you are willing to try, this might be just the game to change that.
Overall, it was a superb experience, and I highly recommend it to anyone who thinks they might enjoy it--this game can take you somewhere maybe you have never been before, or maybe you have, and it will be all the more effective for it.
It lasts around an hour and thirty minutes for most people, and at its full price, you are basically paying a little more than what you would for a movie ticket, for an experience you will likely never forget. Of course, if the price still seems to high, make sure to pick it up when it goes on sale.

Build your own mega-fortress. Fill it with survivors and gear.
Build a community at the end of the world.
Drive armored vehicles through hordes of Zeds.
Farm for your homegrown food, after all the stores and supermarts have been picked clean. Forge your own weapons and ammo. Form raiding parties and go on Zombie hunts.

If you're looking for a terrifying game that can be run on a toaster and costs less than a fast food meal, this is it. One of the brilliant things about the game is that if you analyzed the game mechanics alone, it would actually be fairly easy; it's the perfect, intensely unsettling atmosphere that makes the game hard, because you'll be so shaky and jumpy you'll make constant mistakes. It doesn't hurt that the game also seems to be of the "learn by doing" school; while the phone guy will give you some tips that establish the basics of the game, the particulars of each animatronic are something you'll have to discover for yourself by playing, even as the phone guy gives you hints to their tricks.
The only downside of the game is that once you've worked out the patterns, you start to settle into a very simple and repetitive pattern of your own that will let you simply skate your way to victory barring unusually bad luck, but the same can be said for a lot of otherwise-great games, and even here the atmosphere and jumpscares are so well-executed that you'll never feel completely safe. This is a welcome addition to the library of any gamer who enjoys being scared out of their minds.

You can see all the jump scares a mile away and it becomes quickly apparent that your character is in no real danger, which takes away any feeling of fear the game could have illicited. Furthermore, it's a terrible exploitation of stereotypes of mental illness. Don't waste your money or time.

The Park is a psychological horror game that is set in the same universe as The Secret World, the latter of which I have never played; thus I'm unsure of any correlation between the two. After playing The Park, I can say that the game can be thoroughly enjoyed without having any knowledge whatsoever of The Secret World. While the developer and publisher, Funcom, have not brought us a plethora of releases, they are known for their quality work. The Park is their first true adventure into the genre of horror, and they take the leap very well.
You play as Lorraine, a mother who has gone back to the Atlantic Island Park to retrieve her son Callum's teddy bear. As you head to the information booth to see if Mr. Bear has been spotted, Callum takes off into the park and it's up to you to chase him down. It doesn't take long for things to take a disturbing twist, as a bright sunny day turns into a dark night where shadows are cast long and the rising mist is at its thickest. Your first of many rides will be taken through the Tunnel of Tales, where you ride in a swan boat and listen to the story of Hansel and Gretel; while this part is quite calm, the game quickly escalates into a full-on escapade of psychological terror driven by both narrative and visuals.
The dark secrets that Lorraine has lurking inside of her go from bad, to awful, to nightmarish as you progress through the story. Take special care to pick up and read any notes and documentation that you may come across, as these help fill in the blanks and enhance the story. The good thing about these notes is that they're never out of the way, and you will be hard pressed to miss any; they're always laid well within the beaten path. The Park itself is extremely linear, and as such there is no way for you to get lost. Even if you somehow cannot manage to find where to go next, you are able to press B (on an Xbox controller) to "shout" for Callum, and the game will then highlight your next point of interest.
The scenery is as creepy and disturbing as the story itself, and the further that you delve into both the more ghoulish it all becomes. During the latter part of the game, there is a very obvious ode-to-Silent Hills PT that is just astronomical. If The Park had implemented this sort of progression throughout the entire game, I feel as though it could've been even better than it already is; especially given the background and history of Lorraine. On the other hand, it's great that this title has its own unique spins to it, and the addition of actually being able to get on some of the amusement park rides is the icing on the cake.
Without a doubt, The Park is one of the better horror games to come out in the last couple of years; despite its short longevity of about two hours. The price is steep for a game with such a small amount of play time, with no replayability once its finishes, but the quality of the content is high. Even though the experience comes with many relied upon jumpscares, there is enough atmosphere, ambiance, and overall chilling backstory to push passed the cheapness of them. Highly recommended, especially on sale, I would not advise paying more than $10 CAD for this title, though it is a must play at some point, for all fans of the horror genre.

Enemy Mind is a classic wave-survival 2D space shooter with one twist: you can exchange your ship for an enemy ship. Ships are really unique and come in a variety of attack style/pattern, health, ammo count, maneuverability, and more. As waves become more challenging and the variety of viable strategies decreases, success comes from examining the weak points and attack patterns present in the enemy formation to select an effective tool.
Don't expect to go through a lengthy tutorial or have to memorize strategic details: All ships are stolen from enemies, so the details of each option are made known by showing how enemies behave rather than through a lengthy explanation. All you need to know is how to shoot and switch ships, from there it's intuitive.
It's clear to me they arranged waves purposefully, certainly in later levels. They are set up so that players are rewarded for finding the right ship and can plan ahead after screwing up the first time, while allowing for a degree of wiggle room in terms of viability. One example: a wave containing a ship that shoots up and down effectively was followed by two horizontal formations at the top and bottom of the screen which could only shoot ahead. Again, planning ahead and seeing the right ship makes things much easier to carry out.
The game's unique mechanic makes it way different from other 2D space shooters because your skill is in adapting to unique but simple battle formations in addition to the usual dexterity and execution.
I found it stimulating and fun. 10.99 seems appropriate and less seems like a good deal if what I've said sounds cool.

In Bannish you can screw stuff up and tank your small society. Typically in games you build population and use it to acquire resources. However in Bannished you are building in a harsh environment and if you increase population without having support for them and jobs ready so they contribute then they'll unbalance your economy and possibly collapse your small village.
One negative thing is that there isn't really an "end game". Achievements are really the only thing you're building towards. Which is fine but it does feel like there could have been just a little something more.
Anyway, this does enough differently from other builder games that I think it's worth playing.

People seem to say this is a difficult game.  I don't think that's necessarily true, as it's not hard once you figure out the right order in which to build and upgrade.  Which is to say, at first it's going to be tough, and after you restart a few times, it won't be as hard, but you start to feel like it's less open ended, as you don't (like the description claims you can) just get to build whatever you like whenever you want, so you're dragged along a slightly linear path if you want to not die of starvation and exposure.
That said, without going into what mods have to offer, it's a simple game.  Almost not really a "game", because there isn't really a final goal to tell you that you've "won".  You just continue not dying for longer and longer, and you're winninger and winninger.  It's really a lot like the first Sim City I played (the entire game was on a 3.5" floppy disk), where you just figure out the game mechanics and you play until you're tired of the game mechanics.  No deep story of intrigue or cataclysmic battle with whomever inexplicably kicked your people out of their castle, not even side quests to rebuild after earthquakes or try to survive a plague or invading army.  But it's pretty, and it's nice, and it's relaxing.  So don't play this expecting it to be something it's not; there's a lot of other games out there that are very not this.  If you want to manage a growing real-time civilization, this is a really fun one to occupy your time with.

To start off on a good note, this game is sui generis, kind of special treat for people in a particular mood - at least, that's what I gathered from reading other reviews.
On the less positive side, it might strike a chord with your heart if you're super depressed or in a state of soul searching, but on the whole, what springs to mind is a pedestrian performance - though, it is called the Beginner's Guide, after all. Might the case of caveat emptor.
Getting down to the actual gaming characteristics - it conjures up the image of a cross between an audiobook and a game walkthrough, where, instead of watching a video, you're actually guided through the game by a voice.
All the puzzles, well, in fact, the only puzzle, is an absolute cinch, but of course it is not supposed to be anything complex as you're being taken on an emotional journey down the gaming lane. You walk through a maze of feelings and moods and states represented by various structures and places. The graphics are nice, to pay the game its due, in their own style, some visual images are little short of breathtaking.
However, the whole experience feels like doing nothing but following the narrator's voice, who shows you, so to speak, the inner sanctum of a game maker through the world of his games - but it all feels like you've seen and read it before, like an attempt at going Freudian and then having an inevitable and rather expected psychological analysis volte face.
One could argue that there's good narration topped off with some epiphanies to this game - but it seemed just like one more story of this kind to me, I didn't feel involved - again, you can argue you're supposed to be  a spectator only.
Not something down my alley - and I generally love the alternative type of games.
Could be a 2-hour killer, a bit soothing, no strain involved but I honestly can't find the reason why.

After playing the game for nearly two hours, I realised that its slow paced start is not a start at all. It's the entire game. Throughout the entire game, there isn't much is going on. The answer for that was supposed to be the story mode, which was delayed again and again. Also, seeing David Gaider-esque tendency of pushing one's political agenda that the creator of the game has expressed, I do not think that the incoming story mode will be any good. The game about surviving in snowy wasteland is probably one of the last games I expected to use token character to please the politically correct community.
The pros:
+ The game is very atmospheric. The environment and the feeling of silence create a really great mood.
+ Game mechanics actually have depth, you have a couple ways of achieving the same results (using different tools to break the ice in order to fish, etc.)
+ The game is unique. In the sea of survival games with zombies, a game like this really stands out. Also, the graphic style is nice and it's not something you see in every game.
The cons:
- The game gets really repetative really quickly. Make fire, eat, sleep, repeat.
- There'll be plenty of times when you'll be just walking for a lot of time without anything happening. Some slow paced gameplay is fine, but this is too much.
- Everything depends on where you spawn. On my first game, I got stuck in blizzard with no visible way out and froze, on my second game I kept finding huts filled with food, clothes and tools.
- The game isn't optimised too well, as I can run Witcher 3 on Ultra-to-High, but with this game, High already causes stuttering.
- Your needs go down too fast. While it's rather obvious you'd get cold fast, I do not understand why I need to eat so often. Also, canned food goes bad rather quickly, you get tired very quickly and majority of actions such as crafting takes a lot of time.
- For understandable reasons, you're not gonna get much variety when it comes to maps. Don't expect to see a desert or the surface of the moon.
- The upcoming story mode most likely will not be good. It's just a theory, but nothing points out to it being decent (constant delay, creator's attempts to be PC).
Overall, you might try it out, it's not a horrible game, but it will get really boring really fast.

This game is ridiculously short, but to be fair they tell you that on the shop page so that didn't come as a surprise. Still I felt like it would have been better to perhaps do several separate short stories like this in one game, since they could have used many of the same assets for them. 1,5 hours for 12e is kind of steep even if you don't generally care about the price that much...
Otherwise this was pretty good, although the story is pretty predictable to anyone who has ever read horror. Also I'm not sure if setting this in the same world as The Secret World MMO was the best idea. This is supposed to be a psychological story, but in that game it's perfectly obvious all kinds of crazy monsters totally exist and the world is full of them. But I guess you can interpret this story in a few different ways.

The Long Dark is an amazing game. I have been playing it for a while and have seen most of what the game can offer. The combination of a realistic survival with an atmospheric horror (let's be honest we've all been jumpscared by a wolf or bear) is one i would like to see much more.
Difficulty:
In The Long Dark, once you start off on your first run, you will probably die, but once you get the hang of all of the aspects it is a bit easier to not die in the first hour. Yet still, it is a big challenge to even players that know all of the elements of the game. I have a run that has been going on for 21 days, and i have almost died 4-5 times. The difficulty in The Long Dark is challenging but not impossible.
Graphics:
I honestly can't say much about graphics because of my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ computer but for what i know, normal graphics is great. The snow doesn't look like white dots falling, it looks like actual snow flakes. The environment also looks amazing, the ice is very detailed, the trees look great and the houses look spooky on the inside and out. I could go on and on about how great the graphics are.
Survival:
Most of the survival games around today have hunger and thirst as main elements, but The Long Dark has much more. You must keep track of your warmth, your level of fatigue, time consumption, your hunger, thirst, calories and the quality of the food your eating. These elements isolate The Long Dark from other survival games. Another element of survival is sneaking past predators, this is one of the reasons i keep on getting wounded. It is very challenging to get past predators without a flare, rifle or emergency stim.
Horror:
The houses are terrifying. While you're inside you hear the creepiest creaking noises. I don't even care about getting spooked by a wolf or bear compared to the ambients of the houses. Honestly though, the wolves are pretty scary. Once you see one your like "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥i should avoid that," then in a split second its barking rapidly while mauling your face.
Crafting:
The crafting in The Long Dark is cool with how much time it will take to build certain things, but i don't like the way leather works. Once you get it off of a certain animal you need to keep it in a container inside for a week. This is very tedious and i think the time should be lowered. Besides that the crafting is great.
Concepts:
I have one thing i think would be cool for this game once it gets released. (even though it probably wont since it was said to release in 2014.) Multiplayer i think would be a really cool concept for this game. My friend and I have spoken about this and really want it to actually happen.
Conclusion:
The Long Dark is a great game. All of the elements of the game are well formed and i hope that the things i addressed are added in later updates. For those who are interested in getting addicted to a challenging spooky survival game, please purchase this game.
Great game.

Gory thrillseekers, jumpscare lunatics and those looking for mile a minute onslaughts of ghots and zombies probably won't get much out of The Park.  Much in the vein of Sylvio, The Park offers a bleak, desperate slow burn where you slowly explore your surroundings and deal with the mysteries at hand.  There's even less combat than Sylvio and despite The Park's slant towards a nail-gnawing walking simulator the game's formula works and have a way of digging its way under your skin thanks to some frightening flashback sequences, the main character's emotional breakdown and the fact that the deeper you go into the game the more helpless you feel.
The premise is simple.  Mother Lorraine and her son Callum are about to head for home after a long day at the park but Callum left his teddy bear inside.  Despite Lorraine's rocky emotional past with her son she agrees to be the hero and find the boy's missing bear.  Within instants of being let back in the park to begin your search, it's obvious that evil forces trap you inside and soon Lorraine is on a journey filled with taunting phantoms, malfunctional amusement park rides, narrow escapes, suspenseful chases and all sorts of danger.  The game plays out like a point n' click adventure with the player tasked with tracking down the son by exploring all of the park's lucid areas, reading notes that reveal the park's history as well as the darkness in Lorraine's past.  Though you can't die and none of the puzzles are extremely difficult, you'll find the grim atmosphere begins suffocating the senses like a blanket of despair.  The establishment's supernatural denizens will play constant tricks on you, proving that your presence is unwanted.
This game's got great atmosphere with rich graphics creating breathtaking environments, rich backgrounds, lush use of light and shadow and a design aesthetic that gives even The Park's rickety, rustic rides each a personality of their own.  Not only do the graphics create a noticeable feel of decay and isolation but the sound delivers as well with haunting drones, the sudden rumble of ressurected machinery, appropriately evil dialogue from the demons and Lorraine's mental/verbal battle with herself where she reveals some particularly disturbing revelations about motherhood.  This is the purest definition of a psychological horror game as it borrows influences from film including the works of David Lynch, Jacob's Ladder, The Machinist, Session 9, Tourist Trap, Funhouse and perhaps John Carpenter.  The experience really comes together in the dark on a good set of headphones.
As for gameplay, things aren't too deep and there's not alot of actions to perform but they all make sense in the context of this cinematic gaming experience.  You can run, walk, collect/read documents, pick up an item or two, use a flashlight, ride the park's rides and interact with switches/levers and do whatever it takes to progress.  Sometimes time will violently warp between past, present and sheer madness, maintaining an aura of a creeping unknown dogging you until the game's very end.  The story held me in for the long haul and a late game sequence inside of a funhouse gets increasingly hopeless as it progresses.
Though Steam can certainly cough up a few titles disguised as horror that end up being nothing more than incomplete garbage, The Park managed to captivate my attention from the beginning until the very end.  It took me roughly 4 hours to beat the game with all achievements and searching high and low for every single note to read and piece of the story.  Depending on how thorough you are it could take as little as 2 hrs to finish the game in a single sitting.  If anything, the game could have been longer because it really does grab you once you get into it but I got it on discount and was very pleased with my purchase.
Pros:
-Entrancing story well told through notes, collectibles, flashbacks and character monologue/dialogue.
-Excellent setting makes for intense feelings of isolation.
-Well-designed areas and nicely detailed graphics.
-Hair-rising sound design.
-Unfolds like an interactive movie with cool ride sequences.
-Some truly spooky sequences and set pieces.
-Fairly open set-up letting you progress somewhat how you want.
Cons:
-Pretty short even if you're an achievement hunter.
-Not alot of challenge.
-Minimal puzzle solving.
-Really only incentives to play through once (unless you really liked the story, which I did
Overall:  8/10
Despite the short length and some of The Park's flaws, the story was engrossing and the game was hard to put down once I got started.  It's not a typical horror game and wants to deliver a few righteous blows to the player's psyche before all I said and done.  This probably isn't an adventure for everybody but those that enjoy a twisty plot, pitch black atmosphere and a sense of mystery with their adventuring should really enjoy Funcom's admirable efforts!

Fantastic survival game!
No zombies, no enemy soldiers, no aliens or vampires. Your adversary here is the cold and scarcity of food.
A wonderful expansive environment awaits your exploration if you survive long enough to find/craft some decent clothing.
You'll feel the panic rise as you get totally disoriented in a heavy snow storm.
You'll feel elation as you snare your first rabbit.
You'll feel terror as a bear charges you.
You'll feel relief as you make it home to your warm cabin after a long day scavenging carcasses.
This game is so brilliantly balanced that you never feel cheated, but survival is tough. You need to plan your outings into the cold, and make the most of the daylight hours to attend to your immediate needs, when things work out it's hugely satisfying, and when they don't your situation can become dire, but there are plenty of resources to aid you if you're determined to live.
The UI works untuitively and quickly whilst leaving the screen uncluttered, I play with an xbox controller and everything is fast and easy. Mouse and keyboard works well too.
The Audio is worth special mention -   The distant cries of wolves, the howling wind, the creaking of your cabin and the crunching of the snow are wonderfully rendered and the immersion and atmosphere created by the soundscape is really something special.
The game is 'Early access' and things are being added, the devs seem to care very much about their product, are open to suggestions so I believe the game will only get better, but just as it is now is worth your pennies.
Buy this game, you'll love it.

Chica the Duck, Bonny the Bunnie, Foxy the Fox and Freddy the Bear become posessed by long dead children, and you must survive the night by any means necessary. 12 AM to 6 AM you are forced to act or be jumpscared in a game that is ready to scare your socks off and send chills down your spine. I wanted to like this game. The idea of being able to take over any ship in the game and use it? Awesome idea! It's just the every other aspect of the game is mediocre at best.
The waves are fine, not unfair, but not very much thought went into them. Just clusters of enemies put together because, well, it's a wave of enemies. The controls are *terrible*, at least for mouse and keyboard, and it limits what buttons you can bind to in such a way that there's no reason to even try, because the convenient buttons aren't allowed. And nowhere was I informed it was meant to be played with a controller until I loaded up the game, which was irritating sinceI don't own a controller and wouldn't have purchased the game had I known.
To add insult to injury, every time you run out of lives you have to restart the entire game. Each death puts you at the start of the wave, but every game over restarts the entire game. That sounds fine, and it's not the worst thing, but it means that after a couple game overs it's not even worth slogging through the same mediocre waves over and over to get back to new content.
The story is vaguely interesting, but not enough to keep me willing to slog through the levels over and over after a game over to try to get new story. It's 2 sentences of story per wave beaten, which doesn't motivate me to go through the same levels to get the next tiny clip.

The game is absolutely amazing and requires more teamwork, as a hunter, than any other game I've ever played. Meanwhile, being the monster is fairly basic unless you learn that you can utilize your environment to turn fights into your favor. If you manage to get a good team of hunters going, the Monster will either try to run (and inevitably get caught by a skilled Trapper), or it will realize it has no chance to run and will try to fight. The most adrenaline-filled moments in the game are when you're a medic trying to keep up a team by the hair of their teeth, or a trapper trying to stop the monster from getting CLOSE to your team, or a support when you go in with your team cloaked, ready to take out an unexpecting monster. Also the Assault, making sure to nail every weak point provided to you in order to ensure the monster's armor dropping like a brick. Lastly, when you're a skilled monster, and you've finally met your match in a team of hunters, trying anything to kill them to no avail, giving you the arenaline rush of a cornered animal.
The game is great, and people bash it because they are unhappy that there is DLC. However, the DLC is meant for expanding the lifespan of the game. The cost may seem great, but the amount of change that each DLC that is introduced will cause will be drastic. This will result in a greater experience for all those involved, and expand the strategies needed to take out the new monsters, or hunters even. Not only all that, but all the map DLC is absolutely FREE. It wont cost you a dime, and it takes TRS a long while to create new maps, new monsters, new hunters that it is JUSTIFIED that they do it this way. Also keep in mind, you do not require to buy ANY of the DLC to play with people that DO have the DLC.
Also, there is NOT DAY 1 DLC FFS, THEY ARE BONUSES FOR PAYING FOR THE FUTURE CONTENT EARLY.
Anti-DLC Liars within the reviews are everywhere, please do not give way to them.
In the end, this is what people have wanted for a long time. To play as the boss in a game. A game that requires extensive teamwork and communication. A game that is TRUELY Next-Gen. The optimization is great, the visuals are beautiful, and the gameplay is absurdly well-balanced (so long as your teammates know how to do their jobs properly).
