Despite all the controversy about the day one DLC, I'll give my input, as to if you should buy it or not.
First step, do you want to support these devs? And their business practice? (Day one dlc, free-to-play model inside a $60 game.)
If not, then don't buy it. Do not continue reading this.
If however you are amongst the people who really don't mind the microtransactions and you're looking to figure out if it's worth buying, here's my pointers.
I've had a lot of fun with it today, the solo campaign has its moments and to me served as an extended tutorial before I moved on to multiplayer games. The campaign hosts a large number of maps combined with certain events triggering if you win X map, or lose X map. Which makes every playthrough different than the last.
You can play as the hunters and the monster during the campaign. You can do it solo, or in multiplayer.
One playthrough takes roughly 50 minutes, which is not a lot of time for a campaign. Even if you count it twice as hunters & Monsters. Leaving us at just below 2 hours on 100minutes for two playthroughs.
This is bad, if you're going to implement a campaign of any sort, there should be at least a couple of hours worth of gameplay, despite if the game is focused on multiplayer.
What it lacks in campaign the game makes up for in multiplayer.
There are several modes in the multiplayer right now, it's the straight forward quickplay which is just 4v1 arenastyle battle. Monster wants to evolve, so it can kill the hunters, and the hunters wants to kill the monster.
Evacuation however (The campaign mode) offers a diverse experience, as it is objective-based multiplayer. You play for '5 days' during it. 5 Different maps, 5 different outcomes depending on who wins and who loses certain maps. Which makes it a lot more diverse than the quickplay. Also a heck of a lot fun. The changes made if you win a map are minor, but they add a lot to the game itself. Making it different each time.
Gameplay.
The gameplay is great, the guns work well and all are super fun to use, especially the trappers mobile arena which is core for the hunters.  I have yet to play the other classes since beta. But they all offer a different experience, if you like being the damage dealer, the trapper, the healer, or the support. Depending on which you play you will have a unique experience in that game. If however you do play the same class, the experience will likely be the same.
The monster is fun, dangerous, and pretty hard to play. It takes time to learn, and as of right now there are three monsters, all which have unique playstyles when it comes to how to battle the hunters.
You have to Goliath which is balls to the wall jump in and just deal MASSIVE damage.
The Kraken which is a ranged monster, which relies on keeping a distance, and seperating the hunters with its vortex ability and dealing massive damage with mines and lightning bolts.
Then there's the Wraith, which is more of a stealth-based monster in my experience, it relies on fooling the hunters with decoys, and abilities which will confuse them. In the sense of then seperating key targets with abduction to get an easy kill. The Wraith lacks a lot if it comes hand-to-hand against all of the hunters but excels at taking them apart one by one.
Overall the game is a great time-killer if you enjoy multiplayer, arenastyle games. The diversity of it only goes so far and after a while you are sure to repeat all that you have done. Which doesn't have to be a bad thing.
Out of all this I will recommend the game, because I myself enjoy it quite a lot, either be it playing solo just multiplayer or even against the bots, I'm having a blast. I have yet to invite friends to play with as hunters but I imagine that will be quite fun.
In short, if you don't mind the micro-transactions that are present in this game. Buy it, it's a blast moreso with friends. If you do not like the micro-transactions. Don't buy it.

I bought this game in Summer Sale 2017 and here is my review:
Im going to start with the biggest drawback:
Hardware / Tech
Im trying to run this game in 2560*1440 and its not supporting that resolution. There are a ton of reports about it but as far as im concerned the DEVs didnt state its not working nor did they provide a fix or workaround. So, i can assure the best you can do is 1920*1080.
With that resolution, the same does have some minor slowdowns (on my machine) in certain areas.
Im using a Xbox 1 wireless controler with stock MS wifi connector and its working alright.
All in all, i give this game a 06/10 when it comes to the tech because basicly i feel like selling a game that is 2 years old ? but doesnt support high end resolution is a major letdown.
In addition, i encountered a fatal bug. When i tried to control an enemy ship, my vessel went out of bounds (= the game was stuck in a loop and i was sliding along the ground, without and screen transisitions happening, ever).
I feel like this really sucks and i hope i dont lose another 30 minutes again.
Saving:
The game is divided into 8 big levels which are split into like 5 segments each, with a boss at the end. You cant save, but when you finish a level (LEVEL), you can start at that point in the future. There are checkpoints at the start of each SEGMENT. This is fine with me.
Graphics:
The game uses a very retro pixel art. While being kinda minimalistic, its a very great art style and fits the game good. Animations are decent. Also there is paralax scrolling when it comes to background and stuff (which are also pixel art and awesome). Personally, i like the visuals A LOT and im happy we dont have some crappy 2d renders but instead minimalistic, yet beautiful pixel art.
08/10
Gameplay:
The game is a shoot em up along the lines of Gradius and R-Type. There is no shop-system like in Raptor or Tyrian.
The game also plays left/right and not bottom/up.it has a very nice spin though in that instead of having different weaposn available, you are free to take control of any enemy ship you can see, permanently. So, instead of having one ship with 20 different guns, you basicly have 20 ships with one gun each, though they arent freely available (obviously they need to be on screen to take control of them). I find this really cool and it also offers a ton of strategic options because these ships move and attack differently. In addition, they have different Health.
You will be constantly change ships, because each ship only has a limited amount of Ammo. It feels good in that regard.
08/10
Music:
Like most Indis with retro (pixel) graphics, it also uses retro 16 bit (?) music. I think the mudis fits the game greatly.
08/10
Story:
Without spoilering, this game has a decent story. Depending on which ship control when finishing a level, you will get different "part" of the full story being told (3 factions, 3 stories which make sense when interwined).
Personally, i feel like the story could be expanded upon. Getting 2 or 3 sentences for each level feels like its being cut short.
7/10
Overall concensus:
All things considered i give this game a 7.2/10 and this is mostly because the whole resolution thingy is a major issue for me. I wish it would be fixed. Also, i think this game and the whole (mind control) thingy has a TON of potential. I kinda wish the Devs would expand the game either via an addon or a second part.
Without the tech hickups (and assuming there are no more out-of-bounds-bugs) i can fully suggest this game to anyone that likes shoot em ups and (easy) bullet hell games.
Its CURRENTLY down 80 % and i think its even a really solid buy for the full price.
IF the resolution-switching of windows doesnt bother you OR you run 1920 ether way.

As RTS games go, this title isn't going to redefine the genre in any way. But that doesn't stop it from being an enjoyable enough game, especially if you're a Star Wars nut. Personally i find the space battles to be the real highlight for me, they're just so much better than ground force battles. I also must admit to having NEVER played as the rebel alliance, i always play as the Empire... purely because their ships and vehicles look so much better! For this reason i'm not sure just how balanced the gameplay is in terms of unit strength or if the number of recruitable units varies to make up for the difference in strength... after all, sure an AT-AT is going to be pretty tough to beat, but i wouldn't fancy the rebels chances if the Empire could recruit as many AT-AT's as the rebels can recruit in soldiers!
Those of you who want to play as the rebels will be at least partially pleased to hear that the AT-AT doesn't appear until VERY late in the campaign. Same applies to the vast Executioner class Star Destroyers, although those ships seem to be lacking in firepower and are little more than enormous target practice sites. The bad news for the rebels though is if the Empire manage to finish constructing the Death Star and retrieve the stolen plans, they've already as good as won. If you're playing as the Empire then consider this good news, especially as you then get to destroy 4 or 5 planets and revel in genuine global destruction.
In terms of graphics and audio, this game is fine and has stood the test of time well. In terms of gameplay it's pretty simple, bringing in little in the way of new features to the RTS genre. So if you're a fan of Star Wars and like the established RTS style of game, you're going to really enjoy this. If you're looking for something new, this will be a very shallow game indeed.

Fantastic survival game!
No zombies, no enemy soldiers, no aliens or vampires. Your adversary here is the cold and scarcity of food.
A wonderful expansive environment awaits your exploration if you survive long enough to find/craft some decent clothing.
You'll feel the panic rise as you get totally disoriented in a heavy snow storm.
You'll feel elation as you snare your first rabbit.
You'll feel terror as a bear charges you.
You'll feel relief as you make it home to your warm cabin after a long day scavenging carcasses.
This game is so brilliantly balanced that you never feel cheated, but survival is tough. You need to plan your outings into the cold, and make the most of the daylight hours to attend to your immediate needs, when things work out it's hugely satisfying, and when they don't your situation can become dire, but there are plenty of resources to aid you if you're determined to live.
The UI works untuitively and quickly whilst leaving the screen uncluttered, I play with an xbox controller and everything is fast and easy. Mouse and keyboard works well too.
The Audio is worth special mention -   The distant cries of wolves, the howling wind, the creaking of your cabin and the crunching of the snow are wonderfully rendered and the immersion and atmosphere created by the soundscape is really something special.
The game is 'Early access' and things are being added, the devs seem to care very much about their product, are open to suggestions so I believe the game will only get better, but just as it is now is worth your pennies.
Buy this game, you'll love it.

How many hours have I put into this game? Steam says 50, but it feels like so much more. Every time I feel like stepping out into the Canadian wilderness, into that blinding, enigmatic white wasteland of ice and snow, this game fills that void. It's quiet, with only the game's deep, atmospheric music to comfort you, the sound of the weather to torment you, and the sounds of the animals to frighten you. I love this game.
In the time since I picked it up, it's undergone some massive changes to make it more robust, more than tripling the available play space with the number of zones. It's added features like new weapons, creatures, crafting, survival, and even weather. Every update is usually a few months apart, and every time I start anew, a new survivor.
The locations are largely static, with some buildings being randomized in certain locations, especially the Prepper's Cache. The materials you'll scavenge are always randomized, though certain items (the hunting rifle) have set spawn points that they can be in. That doesn't mean the game is in any way easy or simple to manipulate. Mostly, because each time you start in an area, you begin in a random location. With time and diligence and a willingness to explore, though, you'll become a master at surviving The Long Dark.
The animals are a nightmare. The wolves come after you and chase you, the bears are very tough to take down. The deer seem to sprint off at just the wrong moment. The rabbits are incredibly hard to capture or kill. At least the fish don't go anywhere...
Crafting in this game is quite satisfying. Things can take hours or days to craft. When you finally swap your down jacket for a wolf skin coat, you feel as if you've earned the benefit that your new clothing will give you.
But for all of this, the game is about exploration and isolation. This is the game to play when you need that moment to yourself where all you're facing is the elements in a gorgeous environment that's always trying to kill you. Seeing the new, beautiful vantage points is a real thrill. Waking up ready to go scavenging only to find a blizzard is torment. The moments come in equal measure, and they're always there, ready to surprise you.
I can't recommend this game enough.
Edit: After more time and more updates, I still have to recommend this game. It takes me hours and hours just to go through one "playthrough," and I start over every time there's a major patch. I love it.
Update:
After Episodes 1 and 2 released, I was pleasantly surprised to find that some of the areas I spent a lot of time in during sandbox mode in early access were also being used in the story mode, but with substantial updates and changes. This made a familiar area feel very new. And the story's pretty good, too, if not a bit linear. If you're used to survival mode, then story mode will be pretty easy, but it's rewarding, too. Pick it up!

Personally I haven't played a lot of survival games, (only DayZ and Minecraft) but I like this game a lot. It's mechanics are coherent; they encourage establishing a base and staying there for some time or living a nomadic lifestyle, depending on your objectives. Also the dificulty is really balanced and makes the game inmersive
The graphical style is kind of cartoonie with relatively simple textures and lightning, but the graphics fit the game really well and you get into this style in no time. Also, despite they not being as astonishing as the ones in "The Forest" (judging from trailers, in a technical way) they are really well made and the game is pleasant to the eye. Also the landscapes can be reallly beautiful, and sometimes you'll find yourself simply admiring them while exploring the map.
Talking about the map(s), In my 10 hours experience I only stayed in the first map of them 5 and I still haven't explored it all. Also there are some challenges that add a twist and some objectives to some of the main surviving experience. In conclusion the game offers a great amout of content despite being in alpha, honestly personally if they stopped adding anything new I'd be kind of staysfied with the current material, currently it has lots of hours to offer.
Let's talk about what could possibly push you from buying this title. I only got 10 hours (~16 in-game days) on my back and I'm already feel like I'm able to survive with relative confort (playing on normal) and having steady food and wood resources, which lessens the fun of the game. Despite all that I know that my gear most likely will start to deteriorate and I will not be able to repair it anymore so probably the experience will stop being that steady and easy.
Apart from that, once you memorize a map it can become predictable making the player lose interest. This realtes too with the challenges and the upcoming story mode, they may get less interesting when the player gains expercie (I don't know because I haven't played this parts yet and I'm still a noob). I wonder if the story mode will be afected by that too, I hope not. Just an annotation, this point depends on the type of player you are.
As I see it as a person who has not played lot's of survival games, this is a great game that has a lot to offer and makes you play seriously and puts you in your character's shoes. It's safe to buy it because you'll surely enjoy it.

But every game has it's flaws. A few things bugged me. One, which may or may not be a bug, was that whenever I came across a frozen deer carcass and tried harvesting it, it told me I couldn't touch it with my bare hands. So I put on gloves, and even then it told me I couldn't harvest it. This bugged me. Another thing is something that I mentioned above. There's very little starter items, just some bandages, food, water, clothes, and a few other odds and ins. In every type of plane, there's some sort of weapon, right? You start off with no weapons, and where exactly is the plane? Why aren't you able to search it, or hide in it? This also bugged me a little. The thing that poked at me most was the snowy climate. The world is full of climates, and I admit I absolutely adore the snow. But shouldn't there be other climates too? Deserts, evergreen forests and many more? I wouldn't really be mad at the game or anything if other climates were never added, but it'd be nice to have variety rather than playing the same snowy forest over and over again.
Sometimes it depends on your gameplay. This is NOT a game for screwing around. If they added a mode where you could, then yeah, it would be. Sandbox only means it lets you choose gamemode, region and gender. If you screw around, not focused on surviving, you won't last a day.
Overall, I highly reccomend this game, it's stunning how people are able to make a game so vivid and full of life. I'm appalled, and can't wait for the story to come out!

Hoo boy, I am LATE to this party. Right, let me get this way out of the way right now: I don't hate the horror genre in any form of media, it just mostly bores me because very few people seem to understand how to do it properly. Unfortunately, this is one of those instances where the "horror" is in substance only yet not in actual gameplay. >.>
Basically, while the backstory is fertile ground for a good horror film it's not brought up during gameplay but rather in the form of easter egg style newspaper clippings hanging in various rooms in Freddy Fazbear's. Notice I haven't gotten to the gameplay aspect yet; that's because this is the most boring part. You play as Mike Schmidt, the new security guard for a Freddy Fazbear's Entertainment location, and lucky for you you get to work the graveyard shift for five straight nights (no, really? XD) with the only slightly horrifying catch being that the animatronics that are the attraction's centerpiece are only allowed to wander at night rather than during the day after one of them bit the frontal lobe off of some anonymous customer in 1987 (the incident infamously named "The Bite of '87".) It's explained by the infamous "Phone Guy" that if you're spotted by the animatronics you'll be seen as a naked endoskeleton and since it's against the rules at Freddy Fazbear's to be outside of your suit, you'll be stuffed inside one of 'em, but this will spell out your death in bold letters, so the objective of the game is to keep the animatronics from getting into your office. Sounds exciting, but really it isn't. You start out every night with 100% power and it very quickly starts to drain to 0 and if it reaches 0 Freddy will appear right outside your door and you get an instant game over...unless you've made it to 5 AM. When the clock rolls to 6 AM, you win, so if you can preserve power 'til after 5 AM, you're pretty much guaranteed to win.
The main gimmicks are as follows: 1. watching the cameras to keep an eye on the animatronics' location (there are four animatronics to keep an eye on...Bonnie the rabbit, Chica the chicken, Foxy the fox, and Freddy the bear), 2. pressing the door light button for either door if you can't find Bonnie or Chica, and 3. pressing the door button when the animatronics get too close for comfort. As explained by Phone Guy, you only get a small window of opportunity to react; the only annoying thing is that you aren't given any indication on how quick you need to be (no timer, no nothing like that) before it's decided you were too slow and die via jumpscare. Also, it isn't advised to watch the cameras, use the lights, and keep the doors closed all the time as this drains your power to critical levels very VERY quickly no matter the night. The only cameras you really need to keep an eye on are the one trained on Pirate's Cove, the left hallway when Foxy leaves Pirate's Cove, the stage, and right outside your right door when Freddy leaves the stage. Really the only time you'll ever need to look at the cameras is when you hear footsteps indicating the animatronics have moved.
Now for the most annoying part: the jumpscares. Honestly, I did get jumped a few times myself, but only because I zoned out and wasn't expecting them to be so close (especially Freddy whose proximity is indicated by a slowed-down child's laugh that grows louder.) As such, the animatronics tend to play a wee bit unfairly. Here's the best part, though: break the game down to its basics and it's literally just you sitting around waiting to die.
Five Nights at Freddy's as a game fails to be fun and engaging while trying to sell itself as a cookie-cutter horror game. I'm sure that Scott Cawthon was trying his hardest to make something enjoyable and worthwhile, but as it stands it isn't a good game and isn't worth its pricetag. If you want a better idea on how the game plays out, go watch Markiplier's Let's Play of all four games. As for me? I beat the first four nights no problem and only died a total of four times on the fifth night...dead serious. Take it from me, Dead Space and Bioshock are far better horror games.

Talk about a hidden gem!
I wasn't sure of what exactly I was expecting when I purchased Chroma Squad, but I liked the combination of tactical RPG and Power Rangers references enough that I had to give it a shot.  I was impressed right out of the gate as the game incorporates several different genres very well and even adds several new elements that I have not seen before.
The tactical combat of the game is very enjoyable and there is much more to it than I had initially assumed.  Each episode begins with your heroes arriving on the scene and battling their enemies in their plain clothes.  While in this form you don't have access to your equipment and abilities, though you are formidable enough to go toe-to-toe with the villains all the same.  Once you transform, however, you get your costume and the previously stated abilities unlocked and you can really do some impressive things.
The aspect of combat that really caught my attention and made this game stand out, though, is that your goal is to make every fight as cinematic as possible.  For example, every battle has two Director's Objectives that give a massive boost to the points you earn for putting on an exciting fight, your Audience.  You also gain audience for performing special skills, defeating enemies, using teamwork to give a teammate a boost (the boosted character performs an acrobatic maneuver to move additional spaces that turn), and most of all for performing unified 'team attacks' where you set your squad up in such a manner that they all focus on and attack the targeted enemy at once,
The music is enjoyable, the battles challenging and fun.  Did I mention that you get to customize the look of your gear, colors of your outfits, specializations of your stats and skills, and actors who you use for your squad?  Oh right, and you get to customize and do battle with your own mech!
I can not put into words how highly I recommend this game.  Truly a hidden gem and one of the best games I've come across in awhile.

In my opinion, I got exceptionally lucky with this one.
I had never heard of its existence until E3, and when I saw it I was blown away. It was one of about three things at E3 that didn't make me want to completely abandon the Western games industry, in fact. I didn't really follow much else about it until release, so it was a hugely pleasant surprise in a variety of ways. I had not expected it to be as difficult as it was, the kind of rewarding difficulty you can really put yourself into a kind of glorious trance and submerse yourself in deeply, Marianas Trench style, until you emerge with forbidden treasures. I hadn't known it was so heavily inspired by Genesis/Mega Drive classic Gunstar Heroes from legendary developer Treasure, down to the weapons, style of the bullet hell sequences, and structure of the penultimate boss battle, and lastly I hadn't known how much glorious posterior pain it would inspire in the tight-jeaned hipster games journalists we all love to hate.
The game essentially consists of a strangely Commander Keen-esque overworld, boss battles made up of debtors to the devil on whom you must collect, a store for buying weapons and charms which alter the mechanics in various ways, run and gun sequences for earning coins to buy weapons and upgrades, and jumping/timing challenges to unlock powerful special moves. Some bosses and some run and gun levels are bullet hell sequences, which makes for a nice mix-up without altering the way the game works too severely.
I appreciate the overworld and the fact that it needs to be opened up by beating bosses or run and gun sequences, but I feel like very little thought went into how this could dictate the progression of boss fights or allow for choosing different paths or ways of reaching a goal, possibly accomodating different strategies and weapon/charm loadouts to favor one route and the accompanying boss fights over another. But then, the hipsters would be screaming even louder if the game required that kind of resource management and strategic choice.
The only thing that I really feel doesn't fit are the run and gun sequences. I like the themes and they look delightful, but they ultimately come off as less impressive boss fights, since apart from coins for the shop you really get nothing from them you don't get from bosses, and I would have taken one or two more of the incredible and bizarre characters who serve as bosses over these sequences any day. I should note the game isn't actually that challenging by any but our current standards, but it will keep you occupied. It took me 8 hours to make my way through all bosses on Regular, and I'm getting ready to run through again on Expert. Maybe it's just because it's all I ever used, but it seems to me like the Smoke Bomb charm, essentially allowing you to teleport horizontally instead of dash horizontally, is a bit too easy mode.
The visual style is the sort of thing I didn't know I wanted but needed badly. The design of Cuphead and Mugman is suitably reminiscent of the wide-eyed heroes in those 30s shorts, although I'm always mildly disturbed when Mugman drinks from himself. I was particularly fond of Porkrind, the traveling salesman, most likely because his vocal samples are distorted in a strangely nostalgic manner. There's a vast variety of bosses and monsters, mostly organized around a very solid visual concept; a mouse with a DIY tank, a mischievous genie, a goofy clown, or a haunted train. The only thing that bothered me visually was the CG used to make some of the backdrops rotate. While it's something that would have been technically possible in the 30s, the process would have been so expensive and protracted and prone to failing through human error I can't imagine it ever being done. It probably won't bother you unless you're into animation.
If you like the style, and I don't know what's wrong with you if you don't, were a fan of Gunstar Heroes, or enjoy a fun challenge, the asking price of $20 is more than generous. MDHR must have spent a lot of money on the animation, so they could use every penny. I think pretty much everyone on Earth has already bought it, but in case you were waiting for some anon to post another review, here you go.

It’s not often that one show can take control of an entire generation. For my childhood it was Power Rangers… This multi-cultural love-letter to nostalgia took over many homes in the 90s with force. Its flimsy morals and clunkily scripted acting were apparently exactly what most of the world was looking for, as we stumbled out of the cocaine-fueled haze that was the 80s. There are very few shows today that manage to galvanize fans in such massive numbers. Maybe Spongebob comes close, but he’s a crossdresser who lives inside of a fruit. Chroma Squad is a tactical RPG about a tokusatsu show similar to Power Rangers. Each character has a specialized role, but are able to be slightly customized to your liking depending on the actor/equipment you choose. Chroma Squad does have a few blemishes, but is an overall amazing experience. Will it hold up for those who aren’t wearing nostalgia goggles? Let’s find out as we look deeper at Chroma Squad.
Fantastic retro style coats Chroma Squad, from the graphics to the music. While the gameplay starts out feeling extremely simple, it quickly deepens as the odds are stacked ever-higher against you. After moving you can attack, move a second time, or prepare for teamwork. Teamwork is an awesome aspect that allows your characters to toss each other around in fantastic acrobatics, or prepare a combo attack on an adjacent enemy. Teamwork attacks are an absolute necessity, as later enemies take multiple attacks to defeat. Aside from fantastic agility and teamwork, the Chroma Squad doesn’t have much in the way of firepower when they’re in their 28-year-old-teenager form. However, once per fight though, you can Chromatize. Transformation not only fully heals all your characters, but also unlocks a variety of special abilities. Every season you will unlock a couple of new skills to pick from, and this extends the replayability of Chroma Squad greatly.
The fights take place in a variety of sets. Some are fantastic to look at, with a variety of hazards. Others are completely stark with nothing on display except for a couple lighting guys and key grips using their bellies to knock bowls of mac’n’cheese off of the craft service table. At least that’s what I like to imagine. The gameplay grows even deeper as you realize there are a variety of director actions you will need to follow during the combat in order to maximize your audience and gain new fans. Chroma Squad isn’t all about high-flying action though. Between episodes you will need to craft equipments and gear up your heroes, choose between a variety of marketing agents with tons of different boosts, and assemble your mecha to do battle when your enemies go super-size. The management aspect is extremely interesting, and while praying to RNGsus while crafting for a decent upgrade can become a bit frustrating, it again does wonders to extend the replayability.
I’ve sung so much praise for Chroma Squad that I am loathe to point out the low points, but it is about that time in the review. The majority of the controls are point and click, which can be a bit of a drain when sitting for extended play sessions. The less-inspired set designs seriously break my heart, as there is much more potential than a big empty room. The story does alright, aside from some pretty blatant SJW messaging in the beginning. It might be tongue in cheek. I can really only hope. Overall I think Chroma Squad is an experience worth having, especially if you were raised on Power Rangers or Big Bad Beetleborgs or VR Troopers. There really were just a plethora of these shows on in the 90s. This is why it’s pretty obvious to me why this game was so easily kickstarted, and I am positively overjoyed that Behold Studios was able to bring Chroma Squad very close to its full potential. I really do hope to see a sequel sometime in the future.

Anti-DLC Liars within the reviews are everywhere, please do not give way to them.

Despite all the controversy about the day one DLC, I'll give my input, as to if you should buy it or not.
First step, do you want to support these devs? And their business practice? (Day one dlc, free-to-play model inside a $60 game.)
If not, then don't buy it. Do not continue reading this.
If however you are amongst the people who really don't mind the microtransactions and you're looking to figure out if it's worth buying, here's my pointers.
I've had a lot of fun with it today, the solo campaign has its moments and to me served as an extended tutorial before I moved on to multiplayer games. The campaign hosts a large number of maps combined with certain events triggering if you win X map, or lose X map. Which makes every playthrough different than the last.
You can play as the hunters and the monster during the campaign. You can do it solo, or in multiplayer.
One playthrough takes roughly 50 minutes, which is not a lot of time for a campaign. Even if you count it twice as hunters & Monsters. Leaving us at just below 2 hours on 100minutes for two playthroughs.
This is bad, if you're going to implement a campaign of any sort, there should be at least a couple of hours worth of gameplay, despite if the game is focused on multiplayer.
What it lacks in campaign the game makes up for in multiplayer.
There are several modes in the multiplayer right now, it's the straight forward quickplay which is just 4v1 arenastyle battle. Monster wants to evolve, so it can kill the hunters, and the hunters wants to kill the monster.
Evacuation however (The campaign mode) offers a diverse experience, as it is objective-based multiplayer. You play for '5 days' during it. 5 Different maps, 5 different outcomes depending on who wins and who loses certain maps. Which makes it a lot more diverse than the quickplay. Also a heck of a lot fun. The changes made if you win a map are minor, but they add a lot to the game itself. Making it different each time.
Gameplay.
The gameplay is great, the guns work well and all are super fun to use, especially the trappers mobile arena which is core for the hunters.  I have yet to play the other classes since beta. But they all offer a different experience, if you like being the damage dealer, the trapper, the healer, or the support. Depending on which you play you will have a unique experience in that game. If however you do play the same class, the experience will likely be the same.
The monster is fun, dangerous, and pretty hard to play. It takes time to learn, and as of right now there are three monsters, all which have unique playstyles when it comes to how to battle the hunters.
You have to Goliath which is balls to the wall jump in and just deal MASSIVE damage.
The Kraken which is a ranged monster, which relies on keeping a distance, and seperating the hunters with its vortex ability and dealing massive damage with mines and lightning bolts.
Then there's the Wraith, which is more of a stealth-based monster in my experience, it relies on fooling the hunters with decoys, and abilities which will confuse them. In the sense of then seperating key targets with abduction to get an easy kill. The Wraith lacks a lot if it comes hand-to-hand against all of the hunters but excels at taking them apart one by one.
Overall the game is a great time-killer if you enjoy multiplayer, arenastyle games. The diversity of it only goes so far and after a while you are sure to repeat all that you have done. Which doesn't have to be a bad thing.
Out of all this I will recommend the game, because I myself enjoy it quite a lot, either be it playing solo just multiplayer or even against the bots, I'm having a blast. I have yet to invite friends to play with as hunters but I imagine that will be quite fun.
In short, if you don't mind the micro-transactions that are present in this game. Buy it, it's a blast moreso with friends. If you do not like the micro-transactions. Don't buy it.

If this game wasn't as hard as it was, it would be pretty boring.
Although that isn't a bad thing, it's definitely something to think about.
If you're looking for a visually appealing, charming run-and-gun type game, then you've probably already bought this game. However, if you're on the fence and aren't taken by the visuals... I'd say you should pass. Don't get me wrong, this game's good at what it does. It catches your eye, and you'll either get so frustrated that you'll stop playing, or you'll channel your anger and continue until the end. But... does that make this a good game?
Is this game's difficulty due to good, or bad design?
The game is fairly simple to understand. You move left to right, shooting everything you see. You dodge enemies, and their projectiles; and you can only get hit a certain number of times before you have to start all over again. No checkpoints, no continues, and I guarantee that you're going to die at the very end of a level quite a few times. It's difficult, even the first level can be seen as difficult to somebody who is fairly new to these kind of games. However, what causes the difficulty?
Oh no! Your screen is being filled by projectiles, being flung in a rythmic pattern...
You've encountered a boss, and he's throwing things out that you've never seen before. You die, because you're unable to adapt in time. You play again, and get past the first stage... but now he's throwing something else out that you've never seen before! Die again, and restart. Rinse and repeat, until you've memorized exactly what the boss will do. Now it's a piece of cake. You can dodge, parry, and get damage off perfectly. Now, is that good difficulty, or bad difficulty?
Personally, I find that difficulty that's based off memorization is pretty... lackluster.
It's definitely old-school, which is what this game is going for. Pick up a game like Castlevania, and Mega Man, and you'll be treated with the same recipe. It's not bad , but I certianly wouldn't call it good . I'd say it's... okay. It's fine to do that, but the game will become less satisfying once you've memorized everything. You'll be able to beat the game almost mindlessly. Unlike newer games, where the difficulty doesn't decrease because of memorization. Yes, you can become good at Cuphead... but will that be because you've become more skillful... or because you know when to press what button, and what each boss is going to do? Also, I'd like to add that sometimes you
Please don't take this the wrong way, as I don't think this game is a bad game.
If you're interested in the game, by all means get it. I don't regret getting the game, although I don't think I'm enjoying it as much as I thought I would. It's fun, but I don't exactly feel like I'm getting "better" at the game, and I feel like once I know exactly what the boss is going to do... it becomes boring. The visuals wear off, the gags don't have as much kick. The music that has been looping loses its touch. For me, I felt like I was left with playing an elaborate quicktime event.
Cuphead is not a bad game, but I honestly feel like it's pretty flawed... and I don't understand the praise.
This game feels like an experience. One that everyone should try, if they feel interested. However, I don't see myself playing this game again after I beat it. It's definitely fun to watch, and the developers should feel proud that they've put so much effort into this game, because it SHOWS and I can feel the love OOZING from the game.
However, charm and love don't make a game good. What does is entirely subjective, but Cuphead doesn't have much to offer.
The difficulty won't last once you memorize everything. The charm won't last once you're playing the game for long hours trying to beat it, tackling the same boss over, and over again.
This game's a good experience, but I don't know if I'd classify it as a good game.
In terms of gameplay, it's pretty average. It doesn't offer anything new, and what it does, it does decent enough. In terms of the experience, it's good! Definitely worth playing for the experience, if that interests you. I don't recommend the game, not because I don't think people will enjoy it... but because I can't see myself telling everyone to play this. If you're going to hate me for that, that's fair. I'm enjoying the game. But, in my opinion... I'm not enjoying it for the right reasons. In the short time I've played this game, I'm already tired of the charm... I really see this game's praise dying down in a few weeks...

I usually play games on Steam Offline during Summer, therefore play time is not accurate, especially not for this game which I've sunk a ton of hours into.
Although RimWorld is my current all-time favorite "survival city builder", this game is my current 2nd favorite.
Banished can be really tough if you're not too careful but it is super fun in the beginning and while maintaining your town(s).
Banished goes like this: You control a banished family (or families) and now you have to start from the ground up; building houses, doing some hunting, doing some gathering, all that while building more and more advanced buildings as you start being able to afford them. However, plagues, famine and accidents can make you lose your residents almost instantly. If you're unlucky it can happen as soon as you start the game.

I would, however, recommend the first playthrough to be vanilla to get familiar with the controls and how things work. Afterwards? I'd say go look through the Steam Workshop or check
and pick the mods that might interest you. I highly recommend Colonial Charter (aka CC), Smaller Vendor Buildings Compilation, and maybe some QOL mods.
There are no enemies or even dangerous wild animals. The game "ends" the moment you have built most advanced building... There's nothing exiting after the initial dangers. There are also no quests or anything to keep you entertained for more than 30~50 hours. There's also no story or background, no text other than the menus. So, really, it's pretty bare bones and not too deep.
HOWEVER, seeing as this game was made by 1 guy alone, I'd say this game is really neat and an impressive feat.
On Sale: Absolutely, but use mods too.
Not on Sale: Only when you want to use mods.
When you don't want to use mods: Nope.

It is truly extraordinary that four people can deliver a game this impressive and this content-filled for only 15 euro (or less depending on sale). You can easily spend 50-100 h just exploring and building. I have done so myself and I can tell you that I am far from reaching the endgame nor am I starting to get bored.
Now, before I get carried away with all the goodness that is this game, I can tell you that this game is indeed in an alpha-state, which may show sometimes. There are bugs here and there and the gameplay is not always perfected. However, looking back to when I bought it, there is no denying that this game is much better now than it was then. And that, of course, is to be expected. But that is also one of the reasons that makes this game so great: the developers. The Forest is consistently being updated and patched, something that is very important. Indeed, that is what keep gamers coming back to the title.
The good:
Graphics. The game may be quite demanding (I have the 1080 paired with i5 6600k and play ultra 70-80 fps in 1440p). That is not the best performance but certainly not the worst and The Forest looks very beautiful somtetimes (very subjective of course and my bar for "great" graphics these days is set quite high). For what it is though, your eyes will be satisfied.
Exploring. The map is just the right size to be packed with content for the player to find. There are mainly several caves that are inhabited by both useful gadgets and, well... cannibals.
Crafting...
wait...
no...
CRAFTING (that is better). Okay, so I love the crafting and I think that everyone that tries it will. There is not much else to say really. It is just really well made.
Ai (enemies). The enemies in The Forest are cannibal mutants(?) Anyway they are all (there are different kinds with strengths and weaknesses respectively) quite disturbing, especially at night. But it is their behaviour, the ai, that is truly impressive. I can easily compare it with an AAA title. I mean I am by no means an expert but it comes down to how authentic the gamer feels that the ai is. And I can only say that it feels as though I am facing "real" cannibal tribes (speaking from experience). They call (no not via cellphones) eachother, they carry wounded ones away, they help trapped ones get away but they can also face off against eachother. It is great.
Building (gameplay). This is what you stay for. Well, what can I say...? If you like building defences or treehouses instead of finding your beloved son(?) Timmy: this is the game for you.
Multiplayer. Oh, I failed to mention this feature? Let's just say that if you have nice friends to play this game with, you are going to have a great time.
The bad
Story. Okay, so I kind of feel bad for putting the story under "bad" but come on, I do not think that anyone bought the game for the story nor do I think that the developers put too much time focusing on it. It is there though and I might complete it one day.
Bugs. Yes there are some bugs. Game breaking ones? you ask. No, I have not encountered any at least.
Horror elements. Since the game calls itself "a survival horror simulator" I feel the need, not for speed but to review this in-game element. Oh boy it is a tough one though. I have played a few horror games in the past (outlast 1 & 2 and Amnesia etc.) and to those survival horror titles there is no contest, The Forest fails to deliver scares in the same proportion. That is not to say that this game lacks creepy moments. The thing is, though, that these moments are quite repetetive. The first time you find yourself being hunted through the forest at night it sure is creepy. But, alas, after a few hours in you get equally as used to punchy cannibals as new (mediocre at best) Marvel movies.
As a final note: This might just be the best 15 euro I have ever spent on a game (full price).

Simple but fun game, this is basically a village building sandbox sim. The only goal is keeping your people allive and expanding, there are a solid amount of resources to manage even without the mods which add even more.
One thing this game has going for it is there are not "right or wrong" ways to play many aspects of the game. For example for food you can hunt or gather, or farm your own crops and livestocks. Or later on you can trade excess food for various goods or trade extra goods for food. It takes a balance of different approaches to maintain a healthy village in this game, you can focus on individual methods but for example when the lakes start running low on fish you're going to have problems if you are just fishing for most of your food, or when the weather changes and crops won't grow any more.
There are a lot of crops to grow in this game but most have to be traded for and they are not cheap. You start with 1 random crop which is all you need at first but it's smart to trade for more as soon as you can. Same with livestocks, you can just keep expanding cattle farms but once you trade for some chickens or goats you can start mixing it up.
All in all this game is pretty solid, especially on sale. There are probably more "complete" city building games out now for around the same price but this one has a certain simplistic charm compared to more modern games that become very confusing with all the features

Players familiar with shmup will have to learn the parrying mechanic that will reward them for absorbing pink projectiles. Ikaruga anyone? Players can collect coins in non-boss stages which are used to purchase upgrades at stores. Upgrades consist of an extra lives or a new projectile type. The icing on this wonderful shmup cake would be the astounding music. The art direction and music combine into a well made package. Everybody should play and enjoy this deceiving 1930s cartoon turned into shmup hell.

The trailer barely does the gameplay justice. Even in the tutorial where everything is under control I was anxious to see how things would turn out. In an actual game, I have rarely found myself just sitting around, speeding the game up, and waiting for things to finish building.  However, you need patience and focus if you want to make it, as rushing with the development of your town could bring about it's downfall. The maps are proceduraly created, and even repeating the same seed with the same conditions won't yield the same starting location, so you can revisit a seed you liked, and see how you can build your town and advance your community differently.
Graphics are very pleasing, with the focus being on the sorroundings: nature and buildings, rather than actors. Even so, the humans and animals seem realistic enough considering you never see them from up close, with the help of sounds. There is no speech, but the animal and tool noises are distinct and clear. The soundtrack is...complex, but in a good way! The music provides an immersive experience, both settling you down into the gameplay and keeping you alert at all times, without elevating the tension. For me, it is good enough to listen even outside the game.
It is worth at full price, and a real bargain with any discount.

I've never played a tactical team play game that grants the flexibility, the complexity, and the amount of realism that Red Orchestra 2 brings. I can't think of any parallel that comes close. That alone should say a lot if you're looking to buy the game. In short, it's worth every dollar even at regular price, but for any game, I still say wait for the sale. This game hits sale price a lot.
Now, I'm not saying this game is perfect. It has a few negatives which I'll cover but take the negatives with a grain of salt. The positives within this game far outweigh the negatives.
I'll start with the negatives, the integrated "Cover system" is broken in some ways. It doesn't entirely keep you in cover. I find, players who use the Cover system easier to kill behind cover. This is because, the animation your character goes into when using integrated covering leaves your character's head and back exposed to fire at modest angles. And by modest, I mean an enemy won't have to move much to kill you in the integrated cover system. I turned my auto-cover button off by unbinding the key associated with it under Game Options. If I want to use cover, I do it myself without the integrated system.
That's honestly the only negative I give this game. The rest is good news in terms of how much I enjoyed this game for challenge and reward. You'll find after several hours or several dozen hours that this game has very extensive experience system. Guns gather experience, classes gather experience, and your character level gathers experience. The experience system is not just a number, higher levels grants suppression resistances, stamina buffs, and accuracy buffs. These buffs become quite helpful at higher levels. Guns that gather experience will gain tiers, each gun has a maximum level of 50 and there are 3 tiers associated with it. Each gun gets tier 1 by default, tier 2 is unlocked at level 25 and tier 3 is unlocked at level 50. Depending on what gun you have, tier 2 and tier 3 will have unlocked attachments for the gun like long-range sights and bayonets or extended magazines. This system is very grindy however, since there are so many guns to level. If you're a completionist like me, getting every gun to level 50 will take a very long time.
There are a wide variety of historical guns for all four nations. Each gun has better uses than others, it's up to the user to decide which gun you like most. Majority of players will say PPSH-41 is the weapon of choice, while others will counter that the MG42 and Mkb 42 are better. It's a constant daily argument. I personally like all the guns, even the bolt action rifles. In a full 64-player game, I was able to get MVP using only a rifleman class with a bolt action rifle. It depends on how well you want to perform.
There are vehicles, there are medium tanks, light tanks and troop transports. Medium tanks and light tanks get their own classes and are effective but not over-powered. An experienced tank driver can cause a lot of headache, but in contrast, an experienced anti-tank gunner can take out a tank with a single well placed shot at the tank's ammo rack.
Being Commander is a lot of fun but also actually requires a lot of hands-on command skills. Commander's job is basically to sit at the radio and call in artillery or recon. Commander can also force-respawn players waiting to respawn. Giving orders is important, not only are you telling your team where to go. Players within the area of your order get +1 points for each kill and capturing objectives as a result of your order. Additionally, AI actually follow Commander orders. Sending 30 or so AI into a single base is quite funny.
The AI is not the smartest nor the worst... It's difficult to describe the AI, they're amazing and terrible at the same time. Sometimes you can stand in front of an AI and it won't shoot you or it will miss you a dozen times. And on the other hand, AI are known to do 180 no-scope headshots. It's up to you to decide on this one.
It's almost nearly impossible to notice for new players so I will point it out now. There
bullet drop. But bullet drop is not noticeable until you are about 200m away from your target. But that is rare, majority of the time you will be shooting within 170m on average and a lot of close quarters right down to melee combat. In all my hours of playing this game, I have only had to change my sight range to 200m for only one kill.
Overall, I highly recommend this game. It took me away from Battlefield 4, haven't gone back since.

The Beginner's Guide is a short experience which details the interaction between two people. One, "Davey," explains how he met with a hobbyist developer, "Coda." He presents the player with a series of simple games the latter created and how he found them to be signals of unhealthy thought. He then relates the series of events that followed as he presents to the player the games chronologically and notes how they changed.
It's a provocative game, to be sure. If you've got some time on your hands and have a mind that thinks, you might want to look into this game. It introduces thoughts that anyone should be aware of and open to.

To elaborate, you basically have one hero who moves per turn. But the thing is monsters also move per turn. So if your hero activates a monster, that monster will move almost as much as the hero if not more. Then you have the penalties. Because you unlock the map by moving to the edge of tiles, if you DON'T unlock a map piece per turn you can get a challenge role. This could be something that boosts your stats like adrinaline, or cause fireballs to come literally out of nowhere to damage your hero. Forcing you to press forward to unlock tiles...or suffer possible random damage.
Between the akward feel of the game, the weird turn system, and the lack of making your own character...I just couldn't give the game the full hour and a half I planned to try it for. I couldn't even make it past the tutorial, which is pretty darn bad in my eyes.

This is a fun digital version of the board game of the same name which is about to come out, based on the earlier D&D board games.  Those were based on the 4th Edition ruleset, and this one isn't much different even though there some effect called Advantage and Disadvantage now.  The rule set doesn't really matter much other than the names of the abilities you have (At Will, Daily, Utility etc).
For as simple as it seems this game actually has a lot of strategy to it!  You can move and do an action each turn.  If you fail to explore (move to an edge tile to reveal a new tile) then Encounters happen.  These suck, a lot.  But there's a lot of different ways you can avoid them and picking those at the right time is a big challenge and kind of fun.  Do you take the few hits it's going to take for your tank to cross three tiles to get to you or do you burn a Crystal Ball to keep yourself out of trouble during the trek?
When you complete a map, especially by the skin of your teeth, you get a huge rush of satisfaction.  I'm really enjoying this game so far.
Inventory could use a second look from the devs (which they are going to do).
All in all, this is a really enjoyable light game with a lot of depth to it, a comfortable UI, pretty graphics, fantastic sound and music and an excited and responsive development team behind it.  Looking forward to more from them!
Also, it's a good price, especially at the launch discount!

Aaaah! After 10,000 years I'm free! Not only from the infernal hellfire of school, but from that god awful writer's block! Time to conq- write; write a review. Sorry. It's on Chroma Squad, so strap in.
REVIEW
Chroma Squad
GENRE
Tactical RPG
STORY
The year is 20XX probably. Five stunt actors with attitude are recording their parts in the most recent episode of the hit sentai show sensation: Super Rangers! The show stinks though, and so does its director: Dr. Mi Ah. [More like MAMAMiAh, amirite?] No cool monster fights, no struggles against the higher ups, and most of all; no giant mecha fights! Our heroes are fed up and, immediately after finishing the recording session, quit Super Rangers to start their own sentai show. The gang sets up their base of operations in Blue's uncle's warehouse; unsure of where to begin. However, in the center of the room stands a large object obscured with a large bedsheet. Pulling the sheet off, our actors find the start of their new journey,  and after signing a contract or two; they're ready to Lights, Camera, Chromatize!
GAMEPLAY
Chroma Squad is very unique in its gameplay, fairly simple, but unique nonetheless. You control your units on a grid, taking turns moving your units and allowing your enemies to move. Simple. You can utilize a teamwork mechanic to not only group up on an enemy, but launch your rangers to spaces they couldn't normally reach. Unique. Each of your units has specific passives and abilities tailored to their class. Simple. These abilities may come into play for completing 'director's instructions'; secondary objectives that will give a healthy boost to your audience. Unique. Every mission features a big boss monster that has its own special attacks and abilities. Simple. Just like in Power Rangers though, the monster becomes gigantic after you beat it; bringing you into a risk-vs-reward kaiju fight minigame. Unique. You get the jist.
Outside of combat you can upgrade your gear, improve your studio, answer e-mails, sign marketing agencies to your show, and upgrade your mecha. Upgrading your gear not only increases certain stats, but visually changes the look of your heroes for hire. Improving your studio provides you with an advantage while recording your episodes; though you really shouldn't think too hard about them. I'm not rally sure how upgrading your light fixtures makes enemies less likely to dodge attacks, but I also don't get how so many people burn their meals while watching my show. E-mails range from heartfelt to crazy and everything in-between Sometimesyou get fan-mail about aliens and tinfoil hats, and other times you get companies asking you to buy a 'sword enlargment kit.' Marketing agencies provide temporary bonuses in and outside of combat depending on which agencies you sign your brand to. Personally, I always chose Toys-R-Fans because I like money having money; lots and lots of money. Upgrading your mecha simply gives it small bonuses during the kaiju fights, such as increased hit chance or a chest beam. Y'know, little things.
VISUALS
The visuals are nice, not too complex, but very charming. The pixelated aesthetic compliments the game nicely; and this especially shows in the exemplary boss design. You'll start out fighting monsters like Boxing Box; a cardboard box with boxing gloves. [You're on a tight budget okay?] Eventually however, you'll be fighting intergalactic evildoers such as Tengu, a Japanese demon with cloning capabilities. Either way, the game was pleasin' to my eyeballs and I think it'll please yours too.
SOUNDTRACK
Hot diggity dog, this is a good soundtrack! Featuring 31 unique tracks composed by a variety of artists; you couldn't ask for anything better to accompany your multi-dimensional misadventures. Each track fits its respective scene beautifully, with the timing on some of them being downright god-tier. [That might be a bit of an exaggeration, but you get the point.] Personally, my favorite track has got to be the main theme. I can't tell you how much time I've wasted on the main menu listening to it. I probably need help.
FINAL THOUGHTS
It takes quite a bit to make me buy a game based off of impulse alone, and Chroma Squad happened to have that special something. It was charming, enjoyable, and just challenging enough from start to finish to keep me wanting more consistently. In a way, I got hooked on Chroma Squad the way you get hooked on a show. My first thought after beating an episode was 'Man, I can't wait to see what happens next!'. Being able to choose my actors and their names was a great touch, and the ability to modify the catchphrases and names of aspects of the show took it to the next level. I don't think I'll ever get tired of a wise, robed monk yelling 'Prepare for dank justice!' before turning into a spandex clad superhero. The gameplay is simple, but brings a unique twist to just about every aspect. The dialogue is... cringe-worthy at times to say the least. At the same time though, it reminded me of the horrible dialogue in my favorite shows as a kid. I love the look of it, and I don't think I'll ever quite get over how fantastic the music was. This game is by no means perfect, but for what it's worth; I'm willing to say that this is everything that I've ever looked for in a videogame. It panders to my inner-child, it indulges my unhealthy addiction to customization, it scratches that tactical gameplay itch, it gives me goosebumps when I listen to the music, and most of all; it makes me remember why I love video games. Thanks Behold Studios, I needed something to get me outta this rut.

Still excellent after all these years and makes me nostalgic for the System Shock games (that's a good thing, btw). Graphically it's showing it's age, but there's still enough novelty to be found in the nature of the environment to balance that out. Gameplay is challenging and dynamic, and you can easily find yourself regretting a choice one minute and loving it the next (depending on the challanges you face).
Story wise the game makes an excellent job of immersing you in your role from the very start - you don't ask why you're in the scenario you're in initially because there's so much to see and explore (you kind of assume you'll find the answer yourself anyway). The twists make it a fantastic game, and the subtle points being made throughout ("a slave obeys!") really do give it immense depth - without giving too much away Andrew Ryan's hope for his vision for humanity never ever wavers and that makes your role all the more complicated.
Performance is obviously superb on any gaming hardware from the last four or five years - even with the DX10 option enabled.

First things first, I love horror games...however I get scared pretty easily, so this game did freak me out a little. The atmosphere was on point, some jumpscares did get me (I admit a few times I had to pause the game to recover), whereas there were a few towards the end of the game that felt slightly cliched, no spoilers though.
Although this is essentially a walking simulator, I felt immersed and loved some of the horror mechanics introduced that weren't just trying to say boo!  Little touches which add to the suspense, things moving very slowly, noticing something out the corner of your eye.  Its small things like this which make the game much more interesting.
I was drawn in by the story, which is quite controversial, but I'll say no more.
One small issue I had was the drop in frame rate at the beginning of the game, which took away from the immersion.  Had to drop down to high settings which seemed to fix the issue, but felt that it shouldn't have had a problem running on ultra.
One thing which I think is important in horror games is the audio, again adding to the atmosphere, the devs got this right.  All the little sounds you hear, the whispering, the protagonists desperation in her voice to find her son, and her reminiscing, all added to the immersion.  Best played with headphones so you can hear everything going on around you.
Overall, I would recommend this game when on sale.  I completed the game in 80 minutes.  While it's all about quality and not quantity, some may be disappointed with the content for the price, but if you are after something that's got scares, and an explorative experience, this is great.

Honestly, the best thing I can say when recommending this game is to actually do your research and see if the game is for you. The worst thing you could do is listen to the vast majority of the negative reviews on steam, which are grossly misinformed.
FACTS:
-There is day 1 DLC. However this is only in the form of cosmetic skins, which there are alternatives of that you can unlock just by playing the game.
-There was a monster offered as a pre-order bonus. However, this was exactly what it was, a bonus. The monster is not near finished which is why it wasn't included in the release of the game.
-They will charge $15 for each additional monster and $7.50 for each additional hunter. However, not purchasing these does not separate you from participating in a game with someone who does own them, and you are able to control them if you happen to join a game and they are AI controlled.
-ALL MAP PACKS WILL BE FREE. This was the requirement Turtle Rock demanded, leading to the publisher (2K) demanding the potential money be made up elsewhere in DLC.
That being said the game is really fun. Each match is an engaging set of mind games as you try to either avoid the hunters or chase down the monster. The cat and mouse gameplay gives a sense of distinct tension as the round progresses as the Hunters rush to kill the monster before it evolves and they become the hunted instead. The closest analogy that can be applied has been said before but I'll say it again: it's like they took the tank battles from Left 4 Dead and extended/fleshed them out to a ludicrous degree.
However, while there is the ability to play offline with bots, the lack of actual single player content could most definitely be a deal breaker for some people. Also, being a multiplayer only game, there are a decent set of maps, however you will soon run into repeats. If those things bother you, I'd definitely recommend waiting to purchase the game on sale. If not, I'd for sure recommend this game, it's fantastic fun.

This game takes patience. Most of the bosses have attacks that are nearly impossible to dodge on your first try, so there's a lot of trial and error. I also think some of the difficulty is artificial. The decision to omit checkpoints and health pickups certainly makes the game harder, but I can't say that it makes it more fun. It's a shame because there is a lot of genuine challenge in the game and it seems the only reason to make the game so difficult was to make it last longer since it's pretty short. It reminds me of older games like Contra that were ridiculously hard just so they would give people their money's worth, but Cuphead is very reasonably priced so it doesn't really have that excuse either.
Ultimately, what kept me playing Cuphead was the truly unique presentation and creativity that often put a big smile on my face. I think that alone makes it worth playing, or at least watching a let's play if you're not the patient type. If they make a sequel, I would love to see more run & gun levels, difficulty that feels more fair, and online co-op. I love being summoned in Dark Souls to help random people beat bosses. If Cuphead could add the same feature, it would gain a ton of replay value.
In summary, it's a good game, but it can be frustrating at times and the difficulty might turn some people off. But if tough platformers are your thing, you'll probably love Cuphead.

This game looked to have a lot of promise and turns out it does.  I've been very happy with the game so far.  Combat seems balanced though if you have a weak link in your team, the monster can destroy you.  Same if you have a bad monster, you can kill it pretty quick.
I've gotten tired of the same ole deathmatch recipe and Evolve does a great job at changing things up.  Single player isn't bad either.  The AI does a good job on either side if you're looking to practice and hone your skills.
My only wish is if hunters could get upgrades during gameplay too.  Yes, you can kill certain beasts and get a small buff, but once the monster hits level 3, its rather easy for the monster to kill the hunters.  Perhaps reward the hunter with small boosts to damage, speed, jetpack fuel for how much damage they do, using all their abilities during a match, etc.  Don't buff so much that fighting a level 3 monster feels like a level 1 monster, but enough that it doesn't feel like you're shooting blanks.
I am not a fan of the shop page.  However, those are just cosmetic changes.  DLC when the game is released is shady.  However, DLC isn't required to play.  If it gives a person an advantage, its bad, but for now, its just cosmetic.  I do like that all future maps will be free and available to everyone.  Future characters and monsters will need to be purchased if you don't buy the season pass but you can still play the game with those expansion characters that other people are using if you didn't buy it.  I don't really mind this type of DLC model.  I used to be a COD fan and hated getting kicked from lobbies because I didn't own the expansion.
Would definitely recommend anyone that enjoys FPS games.  It is a fresh feeling game, you don't have to get involved for long periods of time to play.  Have 20 minutes, play a match or two and thats it.  Want to play for hours straight, go right ahead.  DLC is a part of gaming life and I don't feel DLC is as bad in this game as it has been in others.  Don't like DLC, don't buy the DLC.  In this game, you won't be left out of lobbies because of it.

"Great gameplay along with nostalgic references, couple of tweeks to mecha combat needed and more diverse storylines wouldnt hurt"
I picked this game up based on the theme and overall design and i am so glad i did! Brilliant references to 90's culture and an interesting tactical RPG combat system make this game very enjoyable. The scenario is you are stunt performers of a super sentai show who decide to make it on your own by kickstarting your own, the plot then twists from what is a tv show with stunt actors to then turn into something alot more real. The game gives you full control over your cast, studio and many other things which makes this game very interesting and different from the norm. With your team of 5 unique classes you can take down foes with a variety of unique moves or work together and form devastating combo attacks. The fact each character is a certain class is a great idea keeping you thinking about what form of attack you will make that will benefit the battle in the long run. Your characters strengths can also be upgraded with an interesting upgrade system, with a shop you can spend program revenue with to buy stronger equipment or a crafting system in which you can create equipment with drops or purchased materials to help make your characters or mecha stronger. As far as the mecha is concerned it is perhaps the weakest part of this brilliant title, although it feels incredible the first couple of times it happens the tactical tile RPG suddenly turns into a 2D fighting mechanic that feels as though it relies on luck far too often. Your accuracy ratio reduces the number of successful hits you make in the same turn, there were times however where i would hit once have an 85% hit chance and miss finishing my combo. i understand it can happen sometimes but it happened alot more than it probably should have. It made it more frustrating given the fact the enemy monster had the same attack pattern which never missed and then could also do a super attack every few turns made some of these duels long, repetitive and rather frustrating. I feel if the mecha combat was still a tile combat system where you fight in the city it could be made a lot more interesting, whats to say your viewer rating could go down based on the number of detroyed buildings via combat, or using the environment to your advantage. It would certainly make the currently bland mecha combat into something a bit more interesting. The story structure is set in a number of series in which the goal is to increase your fanbase and revenue by putting on an awesome show. You are also in charge of advertising and the studio which can be upgraded to help with the show. The idea of seperate series is great and makes the game into more bitesize chuncks that open up possibilities of extra content later on. With multiple endings the game does have replay value and the episodes in each season can be played in any order desired. The enemy designs are fantastic and some of the stories are great but perhaps more of a mixup with different scenarios would only benefit the game more, party members could be missing or sub objectives could be more diverse with perhaps saving civilians or dealing with environmental scenarios. This does happen sometimes but maybe not enough.
The soundtrack is a pleasure to listen to and keeps the tempo going. it plays very well along with the artistic style of the game.
Overall the game is a great experience, especially if you are a power rangers/super sentai fan with some great story and combat design and an interesting yet simple upgrade system and tle based RPG combat. More diverse storylines and some work on the mecha battles would only do this game good! If they bring out more content as well this game could be played long into the future.
