My experience with this game can be summed as thus: every update I found myself testing the changes, nodding in satisfaction, then quitting the game to await the next update.
Arkane knows how to make a good game. No question. But if you film an Oscar-worthy movie and the lens is smudged while filming, you can't judge what's underneath without acknowledging what's been marring your experience the entire time.
=============================
PERFORMANCE
Everyone is aware of the performance issues, and these still persist to this day. It runs much better than at launch, where it was literally unplayable, but that's because the game looks worse than before - the most noticeable change being the extremely aggressive LOD scaling. Out of the corner of your eye you notice the shapes of window frames and posters on distant buildings morphing in shape, or the furniture at the opposite end of a long hallway suddenly blinking into existence. FPS dropped to 15 when stabbing a gravehound, so they simply removed the inky visual effect that was causing the problem instead of optimizing it.
Also, Denuvo authentication is one of the longest "loading screens" of the game. Around half a minute to a full minute or more every startup.
=============================
GAMEPLAY
For the most part, gameplay is excellent and is Dishonored's strongest suit.
Dark Vision was changed to a blurry short range sonar so unlike Dishonored 1 you aren't constantly seeing blue and yellow because you had no reason not to
AI is much smarter
Nonlethal combat options are a blast
Bonecharm crafting system allows for player flexibility and "builds"
Each level feels lived-in while maintaining the duality of directive flow and open options that made the first game so good.
Emily and Corvo have distinct animations and final weapon upgrades. The animations are supremely cool.
Each level is fairly distinct, some with extremely interesting central "gimmicks." I do, however, wish the game relied less on them and had more "regular" areas.
However, under the hood lie other problems. Most of them are quality-of-life issues:
Gone are the hotkeys for journal, inventory, bonecharms, powers. Only one "journal" exists now, despite still having separate subsections.
It took months for the power wheel to be fixed. It took almost a full second after activating to pop up and be usable, breaking flow so badly I almost never used it in the first place. It's finally fixed now, but this issue was glaring and it took so long to be addressed most of us played through without it fixed.
Thrown objects don't always go exactly where your crosshair is. While this adds a layer of difficulty, it feels noticeably more clunky than in the first game.
Mana regen is pitifully slow. From using a power to fully regenerating, Dishonored 1's time is 4.7 seconds -> 3.1 seconds with Spiritual Pool. Dishonored 2's time with 4x Spiritual Pool is 6.3s -> 5.5s. The devs said they fixed this effect, but it was only made worse.
Bugs. Street speakers not playing. Dying after possessing gravehounds. An arc pylon never shutting down after pulling out its power, leaving it to either be dangerous to you to dangerous to your nonlethal playthrough. Some of these still aren't fixed.
=============================
STORY AND ATMOSPHERE
Reactivity
Great. My favorite part of Dishonored. You need to hide from a gang member to access a certain black market shop, and there are different scenarios and dialogue for if you hide, if you run into him outside, kill him outside, or kill him inside.
Emily and Corvo
Emily and Corvo are voiced. And... they don't talk enough. It's good that they're silent for most of the game, but there are times when you come across a portrait or photograph with an "Inspect" prompt. I'd love to hear Emily's thoughts on the High Overseer as see how that compares to Corvo's, or if it changes based on whether or not you accept the Outsider's Mark. Instead, all I get is the protagonist muttering the name of the person pictured. What's the point? Might as well keep them silent.
It made sense to me to play Emily first, but her story felt lackluster, like people at every turn were saying "check your royal privilege" despite my efforts to resolve everyone's problems without drawing blood. Corvo's is MUCH more interesting as a veteran of Dishonored 1.
The Outsider and The Void
I hate the new Outsider and his new voice. He felt threatening and malicious in the first game due to how calm and composed he was, and the Void felt like a strange and otherworldly place. The vignettes of Dunwall made it feel both unnatural and unnerving yet fundamentally woven into the universe. In Dishonored 2, it's just smoky blackness and sharp rocks. The Outsider is much jollier and moves around erratically, making grandiose hand gestures. They actually had a plot plot that could explain this change, but it was never addressed, so it just seems like a pointless retcon to me.
Main Plot
Dishonored's worldbuilding was always one of its appeals, and that remains true in Dishonored 2. However, the villains felt lackluster. Only the main villain has a real presence throughout the game, whereas everyone else feels introduced abruptly only to fall by your hand, all within the same mission. In Dishonored 1 everything felt personal and real. Perhaps it was because of the long intro where you interacted with most of them, or the Hound Pits's cast of characters all having different connections to your targets.
=============================
As you can see, I've played this game a LOT and have put a lot of thought into it. It was definitely worth all those hours and all that money, but the condition it was at launch and the sluggish drip-feed of support we barely get now is unacceptable. To set a precedent for future games, I can't recommend buying this unless they manage to fix all the performance issues and bugs, which doesn't seem to be happening anytime soon.

Star Wars: Empire at War Gold is the definition of a classic sci-fi 4x-strategy game where players explore, expand, exploit and exterminate their foes. It offers turn-based gameplay with real-time battles. One of the coolest parts of the game is that it allows for the ability to fight in space and on the surface of a planet, something no other game in this genre currently offers! Another cool aspect of the game is that the various space and land enviroments really come into play. For example, whlie battling in space players can use things like nebulas to cloak their ships from enemy sensors to launch a surpise attack just after the enemy flies by. On land, if the planet you are battling on is covered in lava then you will want to use mainly vehicles or find some serious cover like a bunker so your troops don't melt. Furthermore, players can also use their capital fleets and any orbiting bombers to aid them in their land battles using tactics such as oribital bombardments and bombing runs. Moreover, the ability to target specific systems of the enemy's larger ships and space stations for destruction as well as various special abilities for units really makes the game feel incredible. That, combined with the ability to acquire Star Wars hero or villain units, depending on your faction, really makes the game feel alive. Thus, Star Wars: Empire at War Gold is superbly polished from start to finish and any fan of the 4x-strategy genre or Star Wars will surely appreciate all that this game has to offer. Therefore, I most definitely recommend this game! It is the definition of a classic sci-fi 4x-strategy game and is a timeless masterpiece.

This particular ditty was released back in 2006 and at the time, I couldn’t have been more excited.  A game like this was a long time coming, as the last title to have a similar theme (“Star Wars: Rebellion”) was released back in 1998.  I won’t bother reviewing a game that is well over five years old, but I will say that it was an incredible feat and achievement.
Essentially, the player will control either the Rebels or the Imperials and attempt to wipe the other out.  Galactic Conquest mode will let you play a game similar to what you may have experienced in “Star Wars: Rebellion”.  You’ll attempt to grow your empire by capturing planets, which in turn gives you more money in which to expand further and build fleets.  Unlike “Rebellion”, you’ll be in complete control of both space and land battles, though you can automate them if you wish.  Skirmish modes are available for those who just want a quick fix, though it doesn’t do Galactic Conquest justice.

An expansion was released later that year (“Forces of Corruption”) that adds a third faction.  This faction resembles a pirate faction that acts very differently during Galactic Conquest mode. I honestly wasn’t very fond of this new faction, as spreading corruption around for the sake of earning credits was tedious and repetitive.  The expansion also forced all three to be played in Galactic Conquest mode, rather than allowing you to pick and choose which factions would be present.  Luckily, Steam lets me load the core game and not the expansion when I want to eliminate this faction.
Overall, still a great game after all these years.

Just plain and simple, this isn't a particularly fun game as far as I'm concerned.  The concept is great; mechs in some sort of 2D space-theme shoot-em-up with massive stellar bodies and varying gravity, but throwing in non-optional and timed "orbital trials" just to unlock weaponry is annoying...
The Best:
- High quality backgrounds, backdrops, and environments (sort of a must-have for any 2D platformer style games these days).  If the trials weren't timed, I'd probably appreciate these graphics even more...
- Sky is the limit (or space) as far as "how good you can get" is concerned; get comfortable with how the gravity works, how to move around, and be able to switch weapons when needed, but reaction-timing and coordination are serious game changers.
The Good:
- not terrible digital/techno style soundtracks
- challenging fast-paced gameplay
- rather challenging movement (in order to complete trials in a timely manner or be reasonably competitive in multiplayer, you'll have to be able to sling-shot around stellar bodies to get to some locations)
The Bad:
- TIMED TRIALS: you HAVE to follow the progression to be able to unlock each subsequent weapon, regardless of preferences in playstyle
- Hit boxes: time and again, thought you just hit that enemy?  Well, it sure as hell hit you.
- Lots of different "Gravitational Bodies," but none of them labeled or any inkling of the effect they will have on your or your weapons.
The Ugly:
- At least on PC/Mac, the keyboard controls are very difficult to get comfortable with; you can hold down the left or right arrow key and start running around a planetary body, but go to jump off or use a thruster and the arrow key held down still dictates your direction (even if you've run around to the opposite side)
- No apparent variation in the stats of the mechs to fit different playstyles (slow and tanky, bruiser, fast but weak, etc.)
- Timed trials are exactly the same each time; no variation in enemy behavior asside from scripts relating to player position means all you really have to do is get familiar with the layout and weapon characteristics and play a level over and over until earning 3 stars.
Overall:
As far as controls are concerned, I'd like to atleast have the option to keep the player "upright" constantly, and rotate the screen as you move; otherwise my personal opinion is that you HAVE to have a controller with an 8-direction pad for the movement to ever really feel natural, and a monitor refresh of at least 120hz.  Otherwise, as many would agree, if you're looking for a fast-paced, intense, and dynamic 2D game, Orbital Gear is probably for you.  If you get irritated easily when gameplay isn't particularly intuitive and you don't care for timed-trials (like myself) then Orbital Gear isn't.  If you can get past the timed trials, the multiplayer can be a lot of fun, as long as there are enough people online...

How many hours have I put into this game? Steam says 50, but it feels like so much more. Every time I feel like stepping out into the Canadian wilderness, into that blinding, enigmatic white wasteland of ice and snow, this game fills that void. It's quiet, with only the game's deep, atmospheric music to comfort you, the sound of the weather to torment you, and the sounds of the animals to frighten you. I love this game.
In the time since I picked it up, it's undergone some massive changes to make it more robust, more than tripling the available play space with the number of zones. It's added features like new weapons, creatures, crafting, survival, and even weather. Every update is usually a few months apart, and every time I start anew, a new survivor.
The locations are largely static, with some buildings being randomized in certain locations, especially the Prepper's Cache. The materials you'll scavenge are always randomized, though certain items (the hunting rifle) have set spawn points that they can be in. That doesn't mean the game is in any way easy or simple to manipulate. Mostly, because each time you start in an area, you begin in a random location. With time and diligence and a willingness to explore, though, you'll become a master at surviving The Long Dark.
The animals are a nightmare. The wolves come after you and chase you, the bears are very tough to take down. The deer seem to sprint off at just the wrong moment. The rabbits are incredibly hard to capture or kill. At least the fish don't go anywhere...
Crafting in this game is quite satisfying. Things can take hours or days to craft. When you finally swap your down jacket for a wolf skin coat, you feel as if you've earned the benefit that your new clothing will give you.
But for all of this, the game is about exploration and isolation. This is the game to play when you need that moment to yourself where all you're facing is the elements in a gorgeous environment that's always trying to kill you. Seeing the new, beautiful vantage points is a real thrill. Waking up ready to go scavenging only to find a blizzard is torment. The moments come in equal measure, and they're always there, ready to surprise you.
I can't recommend this game enough.
Edit: After more time and more updates, I still have to recommend this game. It takes me hours and hours just to go through one "playthrough," and I start over every time there's a major patch. I love it.
Update:
After Episodes 1 and 2 released, I was pleasantly surprised to find that some of the areas I spent a lot of time in during sandbox mode in early access were also being used in the story mode, but with substantial updates and changes. This made a familiar area feel very new. And the story's pretty good, too, if not a bit linear. If you're used to survival mode, then story mode will be pretty easy, but it's rewarding, too. Pick it up!

Personally I haven't played a lot of survival games, (only DayZ and Minecraft) but I like this game a lot. It's mechanics are coherent; they encourage establishing a base and staying there for some time or living a nomadic lifestyle, depending on your objectives. Also the dificulty is really balanced and makes the game inmersive
The graphical style is kind of cartoonie with relatively simple textures and lightning, but the graphics fit the game really well and you get into this style in no time. Also, despite they not being as astonishing as the ones in "The Forest" (judging from trailers, in a technical way) they are really well made and the game is pleasant to the eye. Also the landscapes can be reallly beautiful, and sometimes you'll find yourself simply admiring them while exploring the map.
Talking about the map(s), In my 10 hours experience I only stayed in the first map of them 5 and I still haven't explored it all. Also there are some challenges that add a twist and some objectives to some of the main surviving experience. In conclusion the game offers a great amout of content despite being in alpha, honestly personally if they stopped adding anything new I'd be kind of staysfied with the current material, currently it has lots of hours to offer.

I only got 10 hours (~16 in-game days) on my back and I'm already feel like I'm able to survive with relative confort (playing on normal) and having steady food and wood resources, which lessens the fun of the game. Despite all that I know that my gear most likely will start to deteriorate and I will not be able to repair it anymore so probably the experience will stop being that steady and easy.

I wonder if the story mode will be afected by that too, I hope not. Just an annotation, this point depends on the type of player you are.

I normally don't like survival games, nor am I very good at them. But this one caught me by surprise. Steam reccomended this game to me, so I thought, "What the heck?" and bought it. It is absolutely amazing.
The graphics are absolutely beautiful, every part of it. From the wildlife to the shelters, it's an incredibly stunning expirience. I haven't played much of it, but I needed to write a review to tell everyone how wonderful it is. When you walk around in the snow, you leave footprints behind, along with being able to see and hear your own breath. It's absolutely breathtaking, and I could've sworn I was in the wilderness myself. Being that this game is still in alpha is amazing too, I haven't met one bug nor have I crashed. Although I am not one to say, because I suck at survival games, I can't quite understand how anyone could last 50 days in the Sandbox, let alone 200. It's extremely hard to survive, faced with a ton of hostile wildlife and very little items to start off with. But it's stunning either way, even if you're getting mauled by a wolf, freezing to death or dying of starvation. Quick tip.. If you find shelter that is in good condition, like a house or a trailer, you're set on warmth and rest. Here you can rest and you automatically gain warmth. If it's a good shelter, that is.
But every game has it's flaws. A few things bugged me. One, which may or may not be a bug, was that whenever I came across a frozen deer carcass and tried harvesting it, it told me I couldn't touch it with my bare hands. So I put on gloves, and even then it told me I couldn't harvest it. This bugged me. Another thing is something that I mentioned above. There's very little starter items, just some bandages, food, water, clothes, and a few other odds and ins. In every type of plane, there's some sort of weapon, right? You start off with no weapons, and where exactly is the plane? Why aren't you able to search it, or hide in it? This also bugged me a little. The thing that poked at me most was the snowy climate. The world is full of climates, and I admit I absolutely adore the snow. But shouldn't there be other climates too? Deserts, evergreen forests and many more? I wouldn't really be mad at the game or anything if other climates were never added, but it'd be nice to have variety rather than playing the same snowy forest over and over again.
Sometimes it depends on your gameplay. This is NOT a game for screwing around. If they added a mode where you could, then yeah, it would be. Sandbox only means it lets you choose gamemode, region and gender. If you screw around, not focused on surviving, you won't last a day.
Overall, I highly reccomend this game, it's stunning how people are able to make a game so vivid and full of life. I'm appalled, and can't wait for the story to come out!

I recommend this game but I do so with a few reservations for all Old School D&D Players. So, I have not played this game for days on end obviously, but I played through the tutorial and the first several quests. I used normal difficulty and went with mostly default power selections for my hero. I thought the graphics were pretty nice and the animations were smooth. Sound/Music was exceptional. Unfortunately the game mechanics and overall gameplay are a bit obscure and because I expected a D&D RPG, it was sort of off-putting for me. Please bear in mind that what I see as shortcomings for this game are based mostly on opinion so your take on things could be quite different than mine.
As I said, I am an old school D&D player and I am talking nearly forty years of playing what I consider to be the greatest game environment/setting/backdrop/whatever. I believe it is safe to say that if you are lookng for an old school Dungeons & Dragons game, then TFC:ToA is not it.
PROS
- Graphics are very nice.
- Audio/Music is exceptional.
- World is procedurally generated.
- Excellent replayability.
- Quick and easy game flow.
- Good/Interesting crafting system
CONS
- Characters/Heros are pre-rolled with VERY little customization aside from a few powers.
- Game balance needs serious tweaking at least in first few quests.
- Gameplay uses turn based divided into phases that are nothing like any other D&D games I have played.
- Maps are seperated into tiles that are shown in the exploration phase which only reveals if you are on the edge
of your current tile, and if you do not reveal a new tile in each exploration phase you automatically generate an
encounter.
- Auto encounters generated from exploration phase fails are usually made up of bizarre magical attacks that seem
to appear from out of nowhere for no reason. Like a magic trap that spawns for no discernable reason.
Every hero must reveal a new tile on their exploraton phases or a random encounter/trap/event happens for

This game is more or less an expansion upon The Secret World, the Funcom horror MMO in which a player takes up the role of a magic-powered vigilante protecting the universe from that which goes bump in the night.  But this isn't The Secret World.  You don't get any guns, knives, or books to protect you.  And what lies in the dark will look into you.
Lorraine and her son Callum live in the in no way sleepy town of Kingsmouth, New England.  No matter how much they try to leave, they just can't bring themselves to part from The Park, where Lorraine met Donald, the father of Callum.  Unfortuately misfortune struck, and it's left Lorraine and Callum in dire straits.  As a nice afternoon of forgetfulness they go to The Park.  But Callum lost his toy, and so she decides to go inquire.  Unfortunately, Callum's rambunctiousness causes him to escape the car and enter into The Park as the sun sets.  Given permission by the park entrance staff, Lorraine enters The Park to look for her son, and this is where you begin your walk through the park.
I found the game to be very moody, very creepy, and quite intriguing.  The game does build on to the lore of The Secret World, but this game is definitely put together a lot better than the Secret World version of the park, and the park is pretty darn big. Hello everybody, End World Gaming here to share an excerpt from my review for The Journey Down: Chapter 1
The Journey Down is an episodic point and click adventure game series. It follows a Jamaican man named Bwana and his friend, Kito. Chapter 1 revolves around Bwana making repairs to his father, Kaonandodo’s airplane after he is hired to fly an important person somewhere for a job. The story is often pretty humorous and the characters you meet along the way are all great as well.
The game revolves around solving inventory/item based puzzles and none of them are too difficult to solve. If you’re a veteran of point and click adventure games like myself, you shouldn’t have any trouble solving them. New players to the genre may find some of the puzzles somewhat tough to figure out, though. Mostly because it only gives you small hints as to how to solve each puzzle.
I was also really impressed by the game’s custom engine. The mixture of gorgeous 2D backgrounds with impressive 3D character models was great. Also, the cutscene animation was equally impressive and was incredibly well done.
I also found the voice acting and music to be really good as well. I especially found the main menu music to be incredibly catchy and there were many times where it got stuck in my head after playing the game.
Overall, chapter 1 of The Journey Down was a great introduction to the series and it’s characters. It was very entertaining and it reminded me of why I enjoy point and click adventure games so much. While the story was limited to a single area, it’s characters were all unique and it’s world was beautifully designed. It’s a great, short adventure and I highly recommend checking it out.

If this game wasn't as hard as it was, it would be pretty boring.
Although that isn't a bad thing, it's definitely something to think about.
If you're looking for a visually appealing, charming run-and-gun type game, then you've probably already bought this game. However, if you're on the fence and aren't taken by the visuals... I'd say you should pass. Don't get me wrong, this game's good at what it does. It catches your eye, and you'll either get so frustrated that you'll stop playing, or you'll channel your anger and continue until the end. But... does that make this a good game?
Is this game's difficulty due to good, or bad design?
The game is fairly simple to understand. You move left to right, shooting everything you see. You dodge enemies, and their projectiles; and you can only get hit a certain number of times before you have to start all over again. No checkpoints, no continues, and I guarantee that you're going to die at the very end of a level quite a few times. It's difficult, even the first level can be seen as difficult to somebody who is fairly new to these kind of games. However, what causes the difficulty?
Oh no! Your screen is being filled by projectiles, being flung in a rythmic pattern...
You've encountered a boss, and he's throwing things out that you've never seen before. You die, because you're unable to adapt in time. You play again, and get past the first stage... but now he's throwing something else out that you've never seen before! Die again, and restart. Rinse and repeat, until you've memorized exactly what the boss will do. Now it's a piece of cake. You can dodge, parry, and get damage off perfectly. Now, is that good difficulty, or bad difficulty?
Personally, I find that difficulty that's based off memorization is pretty... lackluster.
It's definitely old-school, which is what this game is going for. Pick up a game like Castlevania, and Mega Man, and you'll be treated with the same recipe. It's not bad , but I certianly wouldn't call it good . I'd say it's... okay. It's fine to do that, but the game will become less satisfying once you've memorized everything. You'll be able to beat the game almost mindlessly. Unlike newer games, where the difficulty doesn't decrease because of memorization. Yes, you can become good at Cuphead... but will that be because you've become more skillful... or because you know when to press what button, and what each boss is going to do? Also, I'd like to add that sometimes you
Please don't take this the wrong way, as I don't think this game is a bad game.
If you're interested in the game, by all means get it. I don't regret getting the game, although I don't think I'm enjoying it as much as I thought I would. It's fun, but I don't exactly feel like I'm getting "better" at the game, and I feel like once I know exactly what the boss is going to do... it becomes boring. The visuals wear off, the gags don't have as much kick. The music that has been looping loses its touch. For me, I felt like I was left with playing an elaborate quicktime event.
Cuphead is not a bad game, but I honestly feel like it's pretty flawed... and I don't understand the praise.
This game feels like an experience. One that everyone should try, if they feel interested. However, I don't see myself playing this game again after I beat it. It's definitely fun to watch, and the developers should feel proud that they've put so much effort into this game, because it SHOWS and I can feel the love OOZING from the game.
However, charm and love don't make a game good. What does is entirely subjective, but Cuphead doesn't have much to offer.
The difficulty won't last once you memorize everything. The charm won't last once you're playing the game for long hours trying to beat it, tackling the same boss over, and over again.
This game's a good experience, but I don't know if I'd classify it as a good game.
In terms of gameplay, it's pretty average. It doesn't offer anything new, and what it does, it does decent enough. In terms of the experience, it's good! Definitely worth playing for the experience, if that interests you. I don't recommend the game, not because I don't think people will enjoy it... but because I can't see myself telling everyone to play this. If you're going to hate me for that, that's fair. I'm enjoying the game. But, in my opinion... I'm not enjoying it for the right reasons. In the short time I've played this game, I'm already tired of the charm... I really see this game's praise dying down in a few weeks...

This game looks good at first glance. The protagonist is sort of likable, and the quasi-cyberpunk setting, complete with what seems like an emerging megacorp, is interesting. But that's about it.
The writing is bad in all the wrong ways. It's empty filler, with no characterization, philosophy, or even humor. The characters are hardly memorable. Most just seem uncommitted, while others are mildly annoyed at the protagonist.
The plot so far can be summed up as "Miss McGuffin is on the run from BBEG. Protagonist needs to repair airplane to help her escape".
The art style is generally ok, although some bits feel massively unfinished (e.g. the woman cooking stew - seriously, look at the character model!). The music is repetitive and lackluster, and there is at least one blatantly obvious stock GarageBand reggae drum loop used in one of the cues.
The voice actors do okay, although there seems to be inconsistencies in their recording setups - some of them sound like they recorded their lines on a smartphone. Sadly, there's only so much you can do with paper-thin writing like that of The Journey Down.
And finally, the gameplay is... sorta okay, actually. There are no super-cryptic long puzzles resulting in epic aha-moments, but what's there is mostly agreeable. You'll be combining items, doing a few semi-fun environment interactions, and a few mechanical puzzle -type minigames that are small and easy enough to not detract from the actual game too much. Sure, a few bits feel a bit far-fetched or shoehorned, but nothing is overwhelmingly unfair, really.
Better writing, art, and music could have easily made this game get away with the mediocre gameplay. When everything is mediocre at best, however, I can't really say I want to check out the remaining episodes.

Limbo is a dark platform/puzzle game developed by Playdead, which mixes difficult platforming sections with interesting and sometimes mind-scratching puzzles. The game focuses on a small boy that runs linearly in a single direction trying to reach the end point of the game, whilst also solving a variety of puzzles and completing challenging platforming sections. The atmosphere in this game is very dark, with a black and white contrast colour style.

Although, I would recommend this game to gamers if they are fans of dark platformers with light puzzle elements, however some of the final problems were quite difficult to figure out for me personally.
The unique visual design aspects to this game are extremely good and pay off very well in its favour, the design quite minimalistic overall but seems to suit the game and atmosphere perfectly. The colours of the game actually support the game in its dark themed story. The unique 2D style of this game also work to its advantage, and can give some of the puzzles real interesting twists that 3D puzzle games can’t perform. The physics of the puzzles and platforming sections are also superb, although sometimes frustrating in some parts, such as when you miss a jump by millimetres and plummet to your death instantly.
The game performs extremely well on the PC and there will most likely be no problems while running the game at all, the game is even optimised for mobile devices.
The gameplay is overall pretty simplistic, mainly broken down into platforming and platforming/puzzle sections. There are a few enemies in the game which are trying to murder the protagonist, these include other dark figures, large insect creatures, and even some brain bugs!
The game is extremely unforgiving, often even the simplest of mistakes will be met with an instantaneous and gruesome death. Luckily, the checkpoint system is very well designed and normally you will not have to go back very far, usually to the beginning of the puzzle. The chapter system is also very good, especially for when going to collect all the hidden secrets in the game.
However, if you’re not a big fan of watching a child get killed over and over, this games is definitely no for you.
The sound design in this game also matches the atmosphere perfectly, and adds to the tension when performing some of the nail-biting platforming sections in the later chapters.
There is not really much of a story here in limbo at all, the protagonist is mainly just trying to keep himself alive from all the unimaginable horrors this world has to offer, as well as overcoming all the awful traps and mechanics in his path. Overall, the dark and dank atmosphere is great and keeps the play feeling a sense of terror at what horror is going to be lurking just out of the screen.
The ending sequence of the game is ok, but leaves the game on a kind of cliff-hanger, unsure if the boy’s goal has been reached or not is open to interpretation by the player, however this could be in the actual design of the game by the developers.

Overall, Limbo is a good platforming game with a few fun but challenging puzzles set in a very dark and oppressive world. This game takes patience. Most of the bosses have attacks that are nearly impossible to dodge on your first try, so there's a lot of trial and error. I also think some of the difficulty is artificial. The decision to omit checkpoints and health pickups certainly makes the game harder, but I can't say that it makes it more fun. It's a shame because there is a lot of genuine challenge in the game and it seems the only reason to make the game so difficult was to make it last longer since it's pretty short. It reminds me of older games like Contra that were ridiculously hard just so they would give people their money's worth, but Cuphead is very reasonably priced so it doesn't really have that excuse either.
Ultimately, what kept me playing Cuphead was the truly unique presentation and creativity that often put a big smile on my face. I think that alone makes it worth playing, or at least watching a let's play if you're not the patient type. If they make a sequel, I would love to see more run & gun levels, difficulty that feels more fair, and online co-op. I love being summoned in Dark Souls to help random people beat bosses. If Cuphead could add the same feature, it would gain a ton of replay value.
In summary, it's a good game, but it can be frustrating at times and the difficulty might turn some people off. But if tough platformers are your thing, you'll probably love Cuphead.

This review may contain spoilers.
set out to be an experiment in first-person horror survival , but ended up an exemplification of a perfect nightmare. A must-have for fans of the horror genre that might find themselves jaded by the medium.  This experience follows Miles Upshur, an idealistic journalist that sets out to investigate the horrifying mystery behind Mount Massive Asylum. One of the things
does so effectively is craft interesting, non-repetitive levels all inside one overarching location. Mount Massive Asylum's hellish level design will burrow under your skin like a bloodthirsty maggot. The puzzles are organic and challenging enough that in order to survive, the player will have to balance critical thinking skills with the fear of getting caught by these asylum's demented denizens. You travel through sewers, prison cells, hospital wings, administrative departments, morgues and more -- all unique levels with beautiful lighting, graphics, puzzles and terrifying antagonists. This title utilizes atmosphere, classic jump scares, a disturbing narrative and a continous descent into madness, both by the protagonist and everybody around him, to effectively terrify the player.
Another aspect I liked about
was how it effectively incorporates found footage elements into its gameplay. Aspiring directors of the genre (or just fans) should genuinely sit down and play this game if only for the cinematic and storyboard techniques reminiscent of found-footage classics like [REC], Grave Encounters, and Cloverfield. The crutch of the found footage genre is that it relies too much on saturated camera chromatics, unfocused close-ups, the infamous "shaky cam", low-quality video and/or audio recording, and a lack of clear vantage points (to name a few).
, on the other hand, manages to incorporate the success of some of these while also introducing new ways to visually tell a story in the found footage format. For example, this game continuously switches from found footage [the camera] to first-person POV [protagonist], adding a level of variety to the cinematography. Moreover, the lighting isn't always the camera's brightly lit flash, or a godforsaken useless source of lighting like a lighter or a phone screen. It introduces night vision, and “no vision” [when the camera runs out of batteries, yet you still have to progress to the level regardless of how dark it is] to keep the player’s suspension of disbelief on edge.
In this game, you are not a fighter, but instead of having a gas lantern like in
, you have a cam recorder. This adds a second layer of purpose and functionality to such an item because not only does it illuminate your way through the asylum you're investigating, but it also allows you to record the events that are unfolding. The first, a brightly lit exposure that while arguably allowing you to navigate clearer and quicker, might alert the monsters lurking around the corner by disclosing your location. The second, a dark mesh of black and green hues that barely allow you discern between dead bodies, monsters and the walls around you. Other game mechanics include: hiding under hospital beds, lockers, and air vents to avoid death. You play a lethal version of hide-and-seek with one particular mutant that is hell-bent on tearing you apart limb-from-limb. The story is also well-written and well executed. You unfold the asylum's mysteries either by collecting scattered records and files, or, by literally recording key events with your camera. The former method is done effectively, with the files providing enough information that progress the narrative forward and inform the player of important details while also introducing new questions that compel the player to want to find out more – and trust me when I say, you will not expect the ending.

difficult-- frustrating. If not moving, the game is essentially slowed to a near pause. Moving at all or taking action makes everything go full speed. You will die often and you will die fast. Honestly, the best thing I can say when recommending this game is to actually do your research and see if the game is for you. The worst thing you could do is listen to the vast majority of the negative reviews on steam, which are grossly misinformed.
FACTS:
-There is day 1 DLC. However this is only in the form of cosmetic skins, which there are alternatives of that you can unlock just by playing the game.
-There was a monster offered as a pre-order bonus. However, this was exactly what it was, a bonus. The monster is not near finished which is why it wasn't included in the release of the game.
-They will charge $15 for each additional monster and $7.50 for each additional hunter. However, not purchasing these does not separate you from participating in a game with someone who does own them, and you are able to control them if you happen to join a game and they are AI controlled.
-ALL MAP PACKS WILL BE FREE. This was the requirement Turtle Rock demanded, leading to the publisher (2K) demanding the potential money be made up elsewhere in DLC.
That being said the game is really fun. Each match is an engaging set of mind games as you try to either avoid the hunters or chase down the monster. The cat and mouse gameplay gives a sense of distinct tension as the round progresses as the Hunters rush to kill the monster before it evolves and they become the hunted instead. The closest analogy that can be applied has been said before but I'll say it again: it's like they took the tank battles from Left 4 Dead and extended/fleshed them out to a ludicrous degree.
However, while there is the ability to play offline with bots, the lack of actual single player content could most definitely be a deal breaker for some people. Also, being a multiplayer only game, there are a decent set of maps, however you will soon run into repeats. If those things bother you, I'd definitely recommend waiting to purchase the game on sale. If not, I'd for sure recommend this game, it's fantastic fun.

Hmmm...
Ok. It's a good concept. It's different, unusual, out there.
I played 56 minutes in total before requesting a refund.
But that's all it is. A good "concept". I requested a refund for this game because of the reasons below.
The way the story is written is very unrealistic. Let me explain below:
The start of the game finds you as Callum's mother, in the car park of the theme park, and he has left his teddybear in the park. The park has closed and the gates are locked, so you go to check at the ticket office to see if it's been handed in to lost property.
Fine. No issues there.
Next, the member of staff you are talking to says that Callum has just gone back inside the park. The gates are locked, and you can't get in, so how the hell can he? The ticket office man says he will unlock the gates and allow you back in to go and get him.
How can Callum get inside the park if the gates are locked? That's the first major flaw.
He could have been kidnapped by "something", or ventured through a hole in the fence, but he goes through the locked gates.
I tried to overlook that, and carried on playing. Next, you have to go up some escalators.
As you ascend, everything goes dark and the game "fades out". Suddenly you are back, and it's dark, and the park is in disarray. Broken lights, overgrown, untidy etc.
There's no explanation why this happens, and the character you're playing doesn't react to it, it's as if it's a normal event and supposed to happen. It doesn't make a lot of sense.
Another point is that you can ride all of the rides in the park, and this is part of the game (you have to ride them to hear more of the story).
Why would you venture into a theme park looking for your child, to start riding the rides? What makes it worse is that the rides are supposidly "dangerous", yet you still ride them. Why are you doing this when you're supposed to be looking for Callum?
The game is a little distrubing in places too. The mother, although she is in the park looking for Callum, starts calling him "little f***"" and saying she says she should just leave him there. Why would you do that if you've gone into the park in the first place?
When anything scary happens to make you jump, you get a Steam Achievement. This pops up on the right hand side in a box, ruining the effect and distracting you away from what has just happened.
And the "acheievements" aren't an achievement at all. They're things you have to do in the game to contiunue, but you still get rewarded for. I played for approx 56 minutes and unlocked 64% of them already!
Walking around the park, you find accident reports. Why would these just be left on top of a bumpercar or on the outside wall of the ferris wheel control box?
This is a story game. Far too much story and spoken audio, and not nearly enough game play. It just gets boring and repetitive.
The controls on this game didn't work properly for me. I'm using a keyboard and mouse, but when holding shift to run, it only did it half of the time.
This will eat away at your graphics card too! I can easily run Planet Coaster, which can be very graphic hungry, but I had to turn the graphics down to medium on this game, just to make it playable.
The lack of realism in this game, such as riding the rides (why?), events that don't make sense, long audio speeches and a story that's unbelieveable, really spoils the game in my opinion.
As I've said, it's a great idea, but it could be told and written so much better. Callum could have been kidnapped by someone or something and notes left to tell the mother he is in The Park. That could have been the reason why she had to go in there. Not because Callum ran through locked gates (!) and then she has to find him. Why would he keep ignoring his mothers calls and continue to go further into the park?
Maybe I'm missing something. It's a creepy, scary, dark idea, great for a horror/ thriller game, but the realism is severely lacking, making it unbelieveable, unrealistic, and just not half as scary :(

So I have decided that I might write a review for one of my favorite games ever (Make that my favorite game ever) and I must say, that if you haven't bought this yet, you really should.
So why should you buy it? What could a game like Project Zomboid offer to you? Well first, let's talk about that early access, and let me state that I would declare this game playable in its current state, and even in many of its previous states.  Something that the Indie Stone (The devs of PZ) have done is make it so that there are 2 seperate branches of the game, a much more stable branch that is the default for everyone, and the I-Will-Back-Up-My-Save branch, which is an open branch that anyone can access that acts as an experimental branch. What's also fine is that the game is regularly updated, often in the timeframe of a month or two.
Now off of the topic of early access, what about the actual game? Well as far as the game goes, it is wonderful. Currently the game has a number of features, including things such as a medical system, cooking, hunting (Not completed), infection (And zombification), weather, guns, and much more. I should also state that all of this works in multiplayer (Yes, it has a multiplayer) and also that it is quite moddable. The game also has one of the best music soundtracks I have heard. The map of the game is also quite huge, it will take you a good sitting to get from one side of the map to the other, and the map is not even finished yet. Also it has one of the greatest sandboxes I have ever seen, with a great number of options when it comes to customization. For those of you who don't like zombies, you can turn them off completely and make this into a survival game set in a world where everyone is gone (Sadly, NPC survivors have yet to be implemented, however they are close to release and by the looks of previews, be fairly complex in simulation) or even have it so that power and water is gone from the start, so you have to immediately get a source of water.
Now I should state again that the game is unfinished, and many features are still being developed (NPCs, vehicles, and such) however for what it's worth, anyone interested in a good zombie survival sandbox should buy this.
Oh but you might want to be warned, you will die, and die a lot in this game. You will break a foot and get swarmed by zombies for jumping out a 2 story window, you will burn yourself trying to cook some chicken, you will be bitten and fall to infection, you will be shot by some guy with a shotgun, you will accidentally drink bleach mistaking it for a water source, and most of all, you will die from your own stupidity.

More or less an in depth review
-Pros
~This game brings you back to your childhood (or lets you experience a childhood), bringing me back to the days where I proudly watched series like Power Rangers. Not many games that want me to feel nostalgic can do it like this game, the next best thing for nostalgia would be Shovel Knight, but this takes the cake
~Simple , yet extremely fun RPG mechanics. Ok lets get this down, 5 base classes, the lead, support, techie, assault, medic. Each class is equipped with each special ability of course, but then there becomes another layer, with the inclusion of different characters with each their own respective stats and weaknesses, this can dramatically effect the way you can fight a boss. An example would be, my lead, who i chose to be the Panda Guy (Forgot his name!) has reduced movement speed, because of this one of the episodes required me to kill the boss with my lead (This is also known as Director Instructions, although not required, it gives you a boost in "audience" which helps you use a few Studio options which will be explained later) My lead was way too far from the boss and there was no way to get to him before the boss dying from my techie's amazing counter-chance. Thus causing me to feel the want to restart the level and do it again to 100% it, and I did, I had to dramatically change the way I play by having the Lead always stay close to the boss while the others protect him. Now I would explain the skills to you, but they are fairly simple and standard RPG mechanics (Use them and then you have a cooldown, the usual)
~What it wants to introduce to you though is it's "teamwork" mechanic. This mechanic allows you to have one of your well....heroes...can sacrifice their turn to say instead of using a skill to kill an enemy they switch to teamwork mode so that another one of your team can go to them and be launched farther than they can usually move, you could also do a teamwork attack. Which consists one or maybe even all of your team to attack a single opponent, which does become very useful against harder minions.
~Music- Goddamn the music is so nostalgic, it literally brings the heart of 8-Bit RPGS and Super-Sentai series and puts them together to make just an amazing soundtrack
~Story - To me, the story is the important part of a game (If it offers a story, it better be damn good *cough cough Call of Duty Ghosts cough cough*. Now at first the story may seem pointless, but after maybe the 2nd season if i recall, it gets just a huge jump in drama and everything just starts to mold into place. Each character is given their own little "arc" or little segment focusing on them and their personal problems, and by the end of them season you feel satisfied and you just want more. Although I won't spoil much of the story, I can tell you that the dialouge includes many pokes and jabs toward internet memes and commonly uses smiley faces (Which too me is very refreshing) Now in terms of story itself, you start off as very ticked off actors that leave the studio they are hired at and buy/create their own. As you progress you are given "choices" through "fan mail" which people send you, although it may not seem significant, these fan mail choose the path you will be taken on and how your fans will react, also be warned there is no voice acting so get ready to read.
~Bosses- Each boss is super memorable and actually are pretty damn funny when intended, each skill set makes sense for each boss and are actually pretty fun to figure out how to fight against. Now after certain fights, you are allowed to what some people may call MECHA FIGHTSSSSS!.....now these are simple but are actually pretty fun and poke fun at the *ahem* Power Rangers mecha fights.
~Stuio/Crafting Etc. - In the studio you can buy stuff from the shop or look and change the skill sets of your characters. Inside the shops you are given the ability to buy Armor and Weapons. Now most of these items are basic and the best usually come from crafting (DUH) but are still useful. Now crafting, simple, yet not the best or even my favorite, so ill explain my dislikes of it later. You can also go to the "Studio" options which allow you to spend money generated from episodes to upgrade certain attributes (Health Care gives your actors +Health and HD Cameras give you better Audience Conversion Rate). Next up is the Mecha Screen, basiclly upgrading the parts of the mecha to make it better as the story progresses. Not too overly complicated, but could be a lot better.
-Cons
~Crafting- Because you cant replay episodes, you better hope you get those crafting items by luck OR you can spend considerable ( A LOT ) of money from episodes you did to buy Material Packs and because of this you may be out of luck for the first few seasons or you force yourself not to buy better Armor/Weapons/Studio Upgrades.
~Agency Buying- I held off talking about this because I'm more or less biased toward this, but as you progress thorugh the story you can hire agencies to promote your show, this gives you special boosts to a certain amount of episodes (1 or 3) and of course it tells you the boosts but it doesnt tell you how much fan power it costs (You earn fan power during episodes) which left me bummed out because although there were 4 boosts I liked on the agency, I could only get 1 of them for 3 episodes because I didnt know the fan power was so high. Leaving me a lot of money down the drain.
~All in all this is a great game, it achieves what it wants and does even better than certain rpg's. I would give this game the Indie Game of the Year if i could

You explore some randomly-generated maps that is revealed tile by tile, as the board game. 4 different classical characters from the D&D universe (knight, ranger, mage, bard).
The turn-based combat system is simple yet effective, with skills that can be used as much as you want, passive abilities and ultimates that can only be used once in a quest, so make it count!
The game is pretty demanding with a high skill cap, even on normal mode. Hand-holding is kept to a minimum after the tutorial, and even the first few mission can be challenging.
You should plan every action with great care in order to avoid being submerged by ennemies. Mobs and encounters (random events happening every turn) will make your HP melt away fairly quickly, and your recovery options are limited, so do not waste any time.
Overall I recommend this game, it is fun and challenging, even if sometimes RNG decides to really mess with you.

As the seeds of adventure are barely sprouting, our protagonists Bwana and Kito is having a normal day working at Gas ‘n Charter located in Kingsport Bay. With only having a small set back of their lights being turned off due to not paying their bills. Of course, they’re not smart as the box to turn them back on was only blocked by tape. Though this is only the start of their unusual day.
Right as the lights illuminated Gas ‘n Charter again, Lina comes on the scene asking for an old book. Not just any old book, but one that has information on a place that might exist over The Edge called The Underland. The reason many might not have traveled to see may be the fact that traveling down to see it was deemed illegal. And if the location of the book, The Journal of the Journey Down Under, has already been pinpointed, it’s no surprise that Bwana finds it for her. After this point, the bulk of the game starts.
Lina is not here for gas and not only here for a book, but also here to grab a ride on the plane that has not worked for 20 years. Bwana and Kito split up the work to get that old aircraft up and running based on their skills. Bwana tasked with getting the parts needed while Kito will repair the plane. We spend our time looking for these parts around the various areas located close to the docks. Not only being greeted by Bwana, Kito, and Lina, but also the various characters working and visiting.
The various puzzles that are presented in The Journey Down is very reasonable. They are not too difficult, I only had to peek at a guide once, as you can see the items you need before you will actually need them (other than the items placed within drawers or cupboards). The information to solve them will be referenced, with only you to figure out what is needed to be done or collected. Just be sure to look inside various compartments just in case an item you need is there.
At the same time, we get insight on a businessman looking for the same book. However, as he is so desperate to get his hands on the book, he hires a pair of mobsters to get it for him. You can’t have a seemingly important businessman looking for a book open to the public after all. While Bwana and Kito are working to service Lina, these mobsters are coming in hot to Gas ‘n Charter.
The art style is very interesting. All the backgrounds are gorgeous and the character designs are interesting. While we were given an overview look of the bright lights of the city, the little dock brings it’s charm. All of the characters give off a claymation-skeletal vibe as everyone looks different from their body shape, head shape, and even the markings on their face. Once you finish the game, you can look through some Behind the Scenes notes in which they mention that the characters are based on African tribal masks and you can definitely see this inspiration shine through.
I also love the voice acting. While there are some characters that the quality is not on par with the others, everyone has a Caribbean accent. Along these lines, the writing is amusing and filled with various jokes which gained some chuckles from me. The music tops everything off as it a jazzy feel to everything.
+ Great soundtrack
+ Interesting Visuals
+ Interesting and amusing characters
+ Puzzle solutions reasonable
+/- Some may be disappointed this is more of a prologue
- Sound quality spotty
- Possibility to crash
The Journey Down: Chapter One is essentially a prologue leading up to the main action. Setting everything up for the rest of the trilogy as we are left with a cliffhanger. If you had even a passing interest in Power Rangers as a kid, you'll get a kick out of this, even more so with the fact that you can tweak your team from the start by changing their names, appearances (or even, in some cases, race) and suit color to add your own personal flavor. I spent a good ten minutes trying to come up with my own team name and catch-phrases. The tactical RPG aspects are simple and enjoyable, and I like a more streamlined approach to gearing the squad. What I really love about the game, though, is its consistent charm; from my characters yelling my ridiculous catch-phrases, to the Assist character constantly using emoji's in dialogue, to some of the ridiculous bosses you face (shout-out to Transitmancer), I often had a wide grin on my face while playing.
As for gripes, well, the Kaiju battles got repetitive; spam Punch until you were at about 60% accuracy then pop Defense, Defend self against enemy's attacks, repeat. It'll probably be harder on higher difficulties, but I found myself getting somewhat bored during a battle between a GIANT ROBOT AND A GIANT MONSTER. Also, there were a couple bosses who kept doing knockback abilities that kept me from doing a Finishing Move, which happened to be a side-objective for that Episode, so I spent maybe twenty minutes trying to get into the correct position.
That said, though, this is perfectly viable nostalgia fuel that manages to be fun, engaging and lets you have a beaver on your superhero team. Sheer brilliance.

Hardcore D&D fans need to be aware that Tales from Candlekeep: Tomb of Annihilation is a casual take on the D&D Adventure Board Game, and you will not see the in-depth character creation or gameplay of the tabletop RPG here. Regardless, if you like well-made digital board games and check your expectations at the door, you can find a very enjoyable experience here.
(Watch a gameplay video before purchasing to see if it's for you)
*********************************************************************
I came into this game with zero expectations, and have been having a lot of fun with it. BKOM intended to make a D&D adventure board game and did so very well.
Play as a Human Ranger, Aarakocra Wizard, Saurial Paladin, Tabaxi Bard or combination of them to embark on adventure scenarios depicted on the world map beginning in the Mistcliff Mountains near the Bay Chult and continuing southward through the continent.
Scenarios take place on board game-style diorama maps which are made up of smaller square "puzzle piece" areas that the player will carefully explore to reveal their risks and rewards. These puzzle pieces can have traps to disarm or trigger, monsters to kill or avoid, quest items to collect, treasure chests, etc.
Progression through a scenario takes place in hero phases and enemy phases. Successfully completing the map objectives rewards you with gold, experience, and treasures and also unlocks new scenarios on the map. Heroes and Villains will gain strategic advantages in combat for meeting certain criteria. Use skills, utilities, interrupts, items, and potions to overcome each scenario's challenges.
In between adventures, players can craft better gear with item rewards, alternate between their heroes' skill sets, and select which character(s) they wish to bring on the next quest.
Quest modes come in a variety of difficulties: Normal, Hard, and Horrific.
+ Music is excellent and atmospheric. Mildly reminiscent of Diablo II.
+ Sound effects compliment the actions and style very well.
+ Graphics are very appropriate and aesthetically pleasing. A nice style for D&D environments & monsters.
+ I'm a sucker for the diorama maps.
+ You can zoom in close to the action.
+ The player characters are simple, interesting and fun to progress (You have options to play as a few different premade characters, who then give you options for various skills and abilities).
+ Options for various difficulty modes and rewards.
+ Multiplayer as an intended future feature.
- I really appreciate a short tutorial, as I have a very short attention span, although I can see where this can be fleshed out more for those who don't.
- Phases pause the flow of the game, and there are several phases. I did not have issue with this personally, as I enjoy drinking coffee while I relax and enjoy the adventure.
A fun, casual D&D adventure to spend some time in this autumn season under a warm blanket with a hot drink. Easy to pick up and play for short or long gaming sessions.

This is an amazing RTS game with three main areas. Ground Strike. Space Conflict. Planetary Management.
Ground Strike is both in the main conquest modes and skirmish. It is where you take your infantry, tanks, scouts, and heavy tanks to try to destroy the enemy base or otherwise win. No battle is the same.
Space Conflict is again main conquest modes and skirmish. You take your fleets against the opposing fleets and there is usually a massive space station for one side or both.
Planetary Management is for the conquest modes and is where you decide what structures are built on each world and which units you build.
This game is incredibly addictive and has many mods for it that take literally seconds to install with ease so even if you have beatne the campaign and Galactic Conquest a dozen times for each side, just put on a mod and try it all again.

As of June or some other month in 2015, or maybe 2014, whenever GameSpy shut down, this game NO LONGER has multiplayer. In order to play with your buddies you will have to download and install a program such as Evolve or Tunngle, in order to play online over LAN.
Star Wars Empire at War is a strategy game.
Unlike some strategies, Empire at War is very basic. With little micro management, and a small unit cap. This makes it great for those new to the genre, who are looking to get into it.
The gameplay is in real-time. Meaning it is actually fun, unlike turn-based titles. There are two types of battles: space, and land.
In space battles you have a space station, which you can upgrade. Through this station, you build new units and buy upgrades for them, unlocking more units and upgrades as you upgrade the station. You must destroy the enemy's station to win.
The land battles put you on a planet in the Star Wars universe. You have a base with multiple buildings, each one allowing you to buy different units/upgrades. As with the space station, you can upgrade your central command building to unlock more advanced technology. You must destroy the enemy's base to win.
With both battle types, you can change the win conditions. So instead of just having to destroy their base, you have to wipe them out completely, etc.
The Gold Pack comes with both the original Empire at War, and the Forces of Corruption expansion pack. Unfortunately Forces of Corruption has some balance issues, but the game is still extremely fun.
The original game allows you to play as either the Empire or the Rebellion. It has it's own campaign, which is around 5 hours or so in length. But as with most strategy games, the campaign is more of a slow tutorial to prepare you for multiplayer.
Forces of Corruption adds a new campaign, and also allows you to play as the Consortium. Which adds new units, upgrades, abilities, and requires you to change your strategy in certain ways.
The multiplayer still has a very active, but very small, community. If you do plan to get the game, be sure to switch your location to the US in the options, otherwise you will see few, if any, matches.
Empire at War is an excellent RTS, and definitely one to consider getting whether you are a veteran of the genre, or have never played one before.

story
The park takes place in the same universe as Funcoms MMORPG the secret world. In this reality all of Earths myths and legends turn out to be true the boogeman is real and his precense is felt in atlantic ilsand ammusement park.
You play as  Loraine a single mother who is leaving the park for the day with Her son Callum who realises he lost his teddy bear Mr. Bear. Loraine tells Callum to stay in the car while she checks with the information booth to see if anyone found the bear, Because Loraine does not use child locks on her car Callum runs off into the now deserted amusement park she chases after the little brat and you must explore the now seemingly deserted grounds uncovering its dark history while riding the rides and reading letters lying around.
you learn fun facts such as There is a history of children vanishing after dark and grown ups being unable to remember they ever existed. The Park being closed due to a number of unexplainable accidents killing patrons one of whom just so happens to be Callums father. If that was not bad enough their was also that one time the parks mascot Chad the chipmunk gouged out a childs eye with an icepick.
presentation
Visually the park is hit or miss the scenery of the park itself is very well done the rides look great the atmosphere is unerving and the transition from day to night reminds me of entering otherworld in silent hill. However the character design leaves something to be desired. Loraine looks like a robot and when you enter the haunted house she looks like a robot zombie I have never seen a robot zombie before, but that is what Loraine looks like.
The sound is spot on the developers recomend playing with a headset for good reason everything from the rattle of the rollercoaster to docks of the story time boat ride sound steller. The sound team deserves to be applauded.
The voicework is also on point the game uses a mechanic where you call out to Callum and he calls back leading you on your journey. I was able to feel Loraine grow more desperate as the night went on. this was a great touch and for a staff of only five voice actors they all gave a great effort.
I played the game using a wireless xbox one controller, but it also supports mouse and keyboard. The controls are tight, but limited you move slowly and even when Loraine runs it is as if she is out of breth. you may also interact with objects mainly letters that help to progress the story I should mention some of the letters gave me trouble seing them as the font seemed blurred and as stated earlier you may call for calum.
before moving on to the next section it is important that I mention at beginning of the game their is a strange bug that had me restart the game three times before I figured out a fix If you interact with one specific plaque you lose the ability to move This was extra frustrating because it is likely the first item you will interact with and the game tells you to. the fix is to hit escape on the keyboard.  This was the only bug I found on two complete playthroughs but it was annoying.
Dificulty
The park would best be described as an interactive movie it is not like a traditional survival horror game Loraine is not able to die and there are not really any puzzles to solve outside of slowing rides down so you can get onto them. The hardest part of the game might be finding all of the hidden notes, but due to the parks design being linear it is hard to get lost. When you ride the rides it is just that you are riding a ride you may look around and some creepy things might happen, but it is a passive viewing mode. This does not mean the game is not fun as the story is engaging and the atmosphere is top notch, but the game is about as difficult as drawing a circle as that is the path you take.
ending
thorughout the game you will see Chad the the killer chipmunk stalking Loraine as well as glimpses of a shadowy figure that is revealed to be the boogeyman. The player learns that Loraine has been on medication and seems to really hate children. In the haunted house she finds Callum on an alter  and with the guidance of the boogeyman kills Callum with an icepick. Earning her the mother of the year award
the screen fades into Loraine talking with a an investigator who just so happens to be the park attendent she spoke with at the beginning of the game.  she repeats her opening monologue as if she is reliving the horrible memories in her shattered mind. The moral of the story is if your mother tells you to stay in the car you better listen or she will hunt you down kill you with an ice pick.
bonus content
The park has a few unlockables. First there are 14 achievments that you may earn while playing. Most are unlocked just by simply riding the rides and exploring the park. Unfortiatly you will not get anything extra for earning all achievments there are also 6 steam trading cards based on the parks rides you can only get 3 for playing the game forcing you to trade with others to complete the set.
The final peice of bonus content I could not take advantage of because it requires that you have a seceret worlds account. If  you do  have an account  it unlocks a Chad the chipmunk costume as well as receiveing 3 legendary talismans 1 for healer, tank, . This is a neat nod to the players of the secret world, but since I do not play that game I have no idea if they are any good.
I do wish there was something extra to unlock for completing the game maybe the option to dress up loraine as Chad the chipmunk on your next playthrough as it stands outside of maybe earning a missed achievement there is very little reason to replay the game.
final verdict
The park is very short it took me under two hours to beat.The game is linear with little room for exploration best described as an interactive movie. The tension slowly ramps and the last thirty minutes is almost worth the price of admission alone the game has dropped from $20 dollars to $12.99 on steam if you own the secret world this game will unlock some extra perks so if you enjoy creepy games and don't mind jump scares I would say it is worth a play

Rising Storm/Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad is the sequel/expansion spinnoff to the original Red Orchestra.
The game is a World War 2 First Person Shooter designed to be multiplayer only, with a singleplayer "campaign" against bots.
If this sounds boring, it's only because this has been done SOOOO many times before.
So what makes this game stand out from the masses?
2 main things:
1) The painstakingly historical accuracy
2) FUN
Red Orchestra, while somewhat obscure, has always been reccognised by those who know about it for it's historicaly accurate portrayal of World War 2. Red Orchestra 2/Rising Storm continues this tradition to the (somewhat) extreame.
This is no Call of Duty, and this is no Battlefield. The only thing "Battlefieldly" in this is the hellhole of chaos that happens on the maps. While it doesn't have the Blockbuster-like fun of World At War, and without the characters and story of Brothers In Arms, Red Orchestra 2 is more of an interesting history discussion than a movie or book. If you are someone who enjoys history discussions, then you will like this a LOT.
Red Orchestra 2 is set in 1940-1942 on the Eastern Front, and portrays historical battles in it's multiplayer matches, where you play the grunts and soldiers sent into the meat grinder for the Russian/German war machine.
Don't worry: it's not like it's going to be a documentary with someone from the History channel commenting on your every action: it's more of a WW2 Simulator, and not one of the bad ones.
Let's get into the meat of what it has to offer: While there is the "Normal" style of play, which is very much like Call of Duty, the MAJORITY (94%) of the players are playing on the "Realism" mode (The way is was ment to, and should be, played)
The game uses a minimalist HUD, with UI only popping up when neccisary.
Seeing as this is so close to real life, there is no Health bar: You die in a SINGLE BULLET, to the head, chest, and groin. If hit in the arms and legs; you either use a bandage (which takes time to put on, and can only be done twice) or you bleed out to death as the screen goes dark, and everything goes quiet.
The weapons are awesome. In "Realism" there is not crosshair, meaning you have to use ironsights, and blind fire is about as effective as harsh language. All weapons have accurate recoil, modeling, sound effects, damage (Rifles kill in 1 shot anywhere, machine guns are similary powerful)and animation. Like how you not only have to reload machineguns; you have to change the barrel if they overheat. Or how you can toggle the Scope or Ironsights on a sniper weapon. Or how you can't ironsight a machinegun unless they are mounted on cover.
There are various classes in each team, each with different weapons and ablities, so how many weapons you have depends on your choice. Ultimatley you can carry a maximum of 2 primary weapons, 2 pistols, 2 grenades of 2 types (Smoke or Frag), and (depending on class) binoculars. You can't have every weapon in each class, so you have to find them on dead bodies.
The Movemnt is nothing short of amazing: you can sprint forever, but your soldier tires out after a few seconds, so your walking speed is faster then sprinting. You can stand, croutch, go prone, and lean. Your movement depends on your weapon that you are holding, so you don't feel, like in Halfe-Life, that you are a floating orb zooming around everywhere; instead you feel like a human snotling, lugging around a heavy firearm. The game also has a First Person Cover System, where you can latch onto walls. floors, and in trenches. You can blind fire around cover, or use Ironsights to peak out, but it makes you visable and you probably will get shot. Sounds like ARMA, but plays a lot differently.
The battlefield is a scary place, full of mines, barbwire, trenches, buildings, and corners for enemies to hide in. Smoke, dirt, and body parts fly up in the air, as a commander calls in an artillery strike from a radio. With this comes problems however, because the environments are ususally the same colour as the players, so it is VERY dificult to tell apart the Grey team from the Slightly Orangey-Brown team. Friendly fire is always on, so you will be seeing frequent use of "sorry" in the chats.
While the game is realistic, it also means you won't be killing many people. The game wants you to make a last stand against an enemy and preform a heroic sacrifice, like the real heroes of the war, but it doesn't realise that 90% of the time, you will be behind a wall/box/cover, crying for your momy, while you soil your pants.
And finally: TANKS. Not the normal tanks: FIRST PERSON TANKS.
All the tanks have a first person modeled interior, with the commander, gunner, driver, loader, and radio operator, all cramped inside this steel beast, with interactable pistol-ports, and parascopes all present. As you see the loader refill your tank gun with either High Explosive or Armour Piercing rounds, you feel like Steel Batalion, and that you are really driving around a sluggish piece of metal with death able to come in an eyeblink.
A very immersive and impressive experience then. Red Orchestra 2 might not be the same for veterans and purists of the original, but to newcomers, Red Orchestra 2 is a very profesional game with a high skill level and a ton of fun to play. and for $20USD, you are getting 300+ hours of experience (while I haven't reached that far myself)
At the other end of the spectrum there is Rising Strom; the standalone expansion to Red Orchestra 2, and a damn good one at that.
This time it's the Pacific front, with Uncle Sam going against Tojo in a head-on turkey shoot, with the Yanks and the Japs in the firing line (Americans VS Japanese)
The gameplay is basically the same as Red Orchestra 2's, with the only changes being American/Jap weapons, No tanks (sad face :( ) and MUCh less of asymetrical gameplay. The American side is VASTLY overpowered with Thompsons and Flamethrowers, and can steamroll the Japs, sometimes.
SOMETIMES.
The Japs are more specialised, and they are able to plant booby traps-
and they have Swords.
Yes you weeabo nitwits: THEY HAVE KATANAS, and they can do morale sapping BANZAI!! charges against the Yanks.
While not that effective, it is AWESOME when it pays off.
Rising Strom is also much easier than Red Orchestra 2 for newcomers, and it isn't as... "grimdark" as the Eastern Front
But Rising Storm is a VERY good EXPANSION PACK (not DLC) and you are getting an entire full game for half the price.
To conclude: Rising Storm/Red Orchestra 2 is a VERY intense and fun game, that sinks it's teeth into you, and never lets you go, if you let it. If you ever wanted to play a game that REALLY simulates World War 2 the RIGHT way, then you have found the Holy Grail.
Easily a 4.5/5
[And as a side note: one of the mods for this game: "Heroes of the West" simulates the Western Front with the Americans against the Germans. It's still in progress, so it's not ready yet. but deffinatley something to look forward to if you get this game]

(Seriously it's worth it) ]
