It's a great treat for The Secret World players, but probably not from the perspective of somebody that knows nothing about the park and the story behind it from the game.
-The rest of this is probably full of indirect spoilers. You were warned!
First of all, I've heard complains about how the game is just cheap jumpscares, but that is not true at all. The game provides a proper psychological-horror experience if you play by its rules and follow the instructions it provides instantly and linear path it clearly puts you into. I was wondering what's really going on during my trip in the park and why I am seeing what I see. It's mostly an interactive story, a walking simulator, but it's a well delivered story.
The problem with the story though is that even during the events and the rides, you get very little background as to what is really going on, mostly in the form of boring newspapper and general papper cutouts. That leaves those that know nothing about the park in TSW in the black. There are also monologues by the main character throughout the game that help provide a background, but while it helps understand the main character, it doesn't help understand the world you are in.
Graphically wise, the game looks great. It provides a "spooky" atmosphere and combining that with some weird events that happen gives you the feeling that you are not really safe even if you know you are. Funcom has never really failed to deliver on that department, so it doesn't surprise me!
There are a few issues though, like some events needing more... oomph so to speak. Some things appearing and disappearing in a very cheap way and the mouths having light in them for some reason, making it always look weird. Nothing too major though, just nitpicking.
Yeah, I do recommend this interactive story. It's good if you are into this sort of experiences. However, if you haven't played TSW and don't feel like going through some in-game reading then you probably can skip it. If you are really out of horror games to play and you are looking for anything, it's good enough!

Tales From Candlekeep: Tomb Of Annihilation is based on the upcoming D&D Adventure System Board Game Tomb Of Annihilation.
This is a true-to-form translation of the board game experience to a digital board game experience. If you have played any of the D&D Adventure Series board games, then you will feel right at home here, for sure. The same basic rules for the board games will apply here, there a few changes, to help the translation to a video game, mainly there is a new crafting system, and you can cancel encounters by using adrenaline that will you build up after you defeat monsters.
They managed to capture the feel of the board game, via a video game, right down to those nasty encounters that will pop up and might be a bad thing for you, Monsters spawn, ill effects. That’s part of the board game for those that did not know, and I’ve seen a few people talking about that, Keep in mind, you don’t get an encounter on every hero turn. You only get an encounter when your hero doesn’t explore a new tile or when the newly explored tile is of a special type that causes an encounter anyway. They are random, could be good, or bad, it’s the RNG that decided your fate!


The look of the game is great, the colors in the jungle are lush and green, the character models, and the monsters are well done, and detailed. As this is based on a tile laying game, I truly love the fact they chose to have the new tiles, “drop” from the sky. Another way you are immersed into the game. The characters move fluid and combat does not seem to stutter.
I’m a sucker for video game music, if you read some of my other reviews, you will know this. Let me say I love this soundtrack, I want it as a DLC. Just to play as I’m working or cleaning or something, it’s great. It sets the mood just right, wonderful use of instruments.

So far I’ve been pretty positive about the game, and overall I am. But, all’s not well in the jungles of Chult.

[2017/07/19 Update]
I'm leaving my original review below, but tl;dr:
This version of the game is broken on newer systems. Grab the Remaster instead.
Disclaimer: My playtime didn't register for reasons explained near the end of this review.
I actually completed the game twice (a Normal run with all audio logs and Little Sisters collected, and a Hard run with Vita Chambers disabled), so I know more than enough about this game to make a proper review of it.
Welcome to Rapture, a once thriving underwater city that fell to insanity and complete chaos after its inhabitants got addicted to ADAM, a substance granting super-powers and enhanced healing capabilities. You play as Jack, the token silent dood who's unlucky enough to plane crash in the middle of the sea and find himself in Rapture in the aftermath of the war confronting Andrew Ryan, the visionary leader of Rapture, to Atlas and his band of rebels, who are desperately struggling to stop Ryan's madness. From there, you'll embark on a grim journey in the depths of the ocean, fighting your way through underwater buildings and corridors infested with the deranged splicers, as well as the infamous Big Daddies, pedophiles in diving suits moaning like whales and stalking 8-year old little girls with giant syringes and glowing eyes.
Without spoiling anything, the story of the game is interesting and complex enough (for a FPS) to follow till the end, with its fair share of plot twists and excellent voice acting, although the endings were in my opinion slightly disappointing. Visually, the game aged quite well and the various steampunk environments of Rapture are a real treat to explore, which you'll have to do if you're interested in the background story of the city, distilled through audio logs scattered around the levels. The musical score is quite discreet but comes at the right moments, and the soundscape is well done. Atmosphere-wise, the game clearly takes inspirations from classics like System Shock 2 (the insane splicers from BioShock and the enraged infected from System Shock share some similarities) and the game certainly got its lots of creepy moments, from your first encounter with the splicers to your stroll through the medical ward, without forgetting your stay in Fort Frolic, the depraved home of the equally depraved Sander Cohen. Don't expect however visceral horror that will make you soil your pants as you would in games like Outlast or DreadOut. BioShock barely rely on jump scares or stuff of the sort, and while there's gory scenery here and there, the fear it tries to instill is more subtle, often mixing the awe-inspiring marvels of Rapture with a dose of creepiness to strike a chord of the uneasy kind.
Gameplay-wise, I'd hardly say the game has RPG elements, unless you count ADAM as experience points. However, it allows you to customize your experience in three different ways: Plasmids, Tonics, and weapons. Plasmids are kind of the equivalent of spells and come in many sorts (elemental attacks, ability to create a decoy or to mind control a Big Daddy to make it temporarily your ally...) - you use a "mana" bar (EVE) to use them, and you acquire most of them by spending the ADAM you will collect from the Little Sisters you encounter in the various levels. Tonics are passive abilities that you can equip on your character to give yourself various bonuses (see that as rings or amulets maybe?). You can find many hidden off the beaten trail in the levels, while others are bought with ADAM or offered as rewards for performing certain actions in the game. Finally, there is a variety of different weapons which all come with three types of different ammunitions whose effectiveness act on a rock-paper-scissors basis on ennemies depending on their weaknesses. You can also enhance permanently your weapons in different ways in specific stations scattered throughout the game which can be used only once for each. There are some other ways to customize your character, as ADAM also allows you to buy more Plasmid or Tonic slots to equip them, and to increase your Health or EVE bar. Later in the game is also introduced a crafting system were you can create your own ammo with materials you find on ennemies or in containers.
Now if we have to talk about the flaws, I'd say there are two main ones in this game. The first is that you're actually more limited than you think when it comes to customization. You'll quickly learn that some Plasmids and Tonics are must-haves, while others are completely useless (I'm looking at you, Natural Camouflage), which substantially reduces your options, as a lot of Plasmids and Tonics also have synergies between them. Same goes for the weapons: I found myself never using certain types of weapons or ammunitions because they proved utterly ineffective even when fully upgraded compared to other ones, and the weapon enhancing part with the previously mentioned stations also only gives you the illusion of choice, as you will eventually get all the upgrades anyways if you manage to find them all (which isn't that hard). It only comes down to which ones you take first. The second flaw for me is that the difficulty wasn't balanced very well. The game can be excessively hard and unfair during the first half of the game (this is especially true on Hard), with some ennemies being huge bullet sponges and hitting like trucks while your own options are very limited. But by the time you reach the second half of the game (around the end of Fort Frolic, beginning of Hephaestus) and have accumulated enough Plasmids, Tonics and research on ennemies, you'll often find yourself not being able to loot ammo or money because you have already plenty of them, to a point where I ended up just hacking everything I was coming across with money or auto-hack because hacking the regular way was getting too dull after the 150th time (one other small flaw I should have mentioned).
I would however say the pros of this game make up for the aforementioned cons. It was a very enjoyable ride that can still hold up to the current gen FPS, which I'm not sure is saying a lot considering today's low standards. If you have a taste for story-driven FPS with an interesting setting, great atmosphere and enjoyable gameplay, you should definitely play to BioShock.
Brotip: If you're going to do only one playthrough, try to save all the Little Sisters. I can assure you you'll find the ending much more satisfying than the other one.
Why a negative review then? More explanations below.
Should a "Neutral" review button had been available, I would have gone for that actually, but I just can't press "Yes" for the following reason.
This game is old, and isn't meant to be played on systems beyond Windows Vista. For those still running on Vista or older, then consider that review a definitive Yes. But if you're running on Windows 7 and above, the game crashes constantly (or doesn't launch, plain and simple), to the point you'll spend more time watching the opening logos than actually playing the game, and the ways to fix this can greatly vary for one system to another. As far as I'm concerned, I had to mess with the .exe file in the game folder and launch the game through it. Adding the .exe to my Steam library as a non-Steam game worked, but the Steam overlay had to be deactivated as it would also make the game crash. So my registered playtime is only the time I spent struggling to reach the end of the first area with a crash every 2 minutes.
If like me, you waited way too long to play this game and are considering whether you should buy it or not, I'm warmly encouraging you to give it a go. You won't regret it. But not on Steam. The Steam version doesn't have any extra feature you could possibly miss.
Do yourself a favor and buy it somewhere else.  Another version will most likely still have the same problem with crashes no matter where you get it, but at least it will be DRM-free.

Chroma Squad is, as it says, a tactical RPG that was inspired by the many Sentai series such as Power Rangers, Kamen Rider and many, many more. What is the story, you ask? Well, essentially, the story of the game goes like this: You have a bunch of stunt people who recently quit their jobs because of a director who was, shall we say, demanding and is overall being a complete♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and they all decide to start a studio of their own! From the beginning, they don't have much to work with, using cardboard, duct tape, and third-rate costumes to get by, eventually, they start having an audience to work with.
The gameplay is quite fun, you kit out your actors in the best gear that cardboard and duct tape can buy and record new 'episodes', essentially maps, for the season, each with their own bonus objectives that don't punish you much for failing them but the extra fans and cashflow you can get from maxing out your audience each episode is a nice incentive to do them. Every actor has their own special abilities that are accessible as soon as they suit up which can be sometimes impossible to do at the start of the episode as you need to build audience power first before chromatizing. The phrases said throughout the game such as "Chromatize" and "Mecha Power, Activate!" can be modified in the studio to your liking. Yes, this means you can be as silly or as creative as you like... or creatively silly.
The difficulty of the game is strange at times, some episodes are easy, others are pretty difficult, even with the best gear for the season's tier equipped, and others still are fairly difficult. You'll end up curbstomping half the time if you're playing on the normal difficulty if you know how to play tactical RPGs, well, tactically, and I'm fairly certain hard mode is pretty challenging but I can't quite say that for myself. I'm not going to say that this game is too easy but it feels too easy at times, especially when you have an assault one-shotting everything they touch that isn't a boss monster or a shielded enemy.
However, despite the odd difficulty curve, I absolutely adore the presence of the game and I absolutely love the feel and the gameplay of Chroma Squad, it kind of reminds me of XCOM, in a way, with all the aliens but minus the permadeath. Oh, and the music's damn good too, I will admit that the title theme may have dug deep into my brain and has implanted its melody into my brain and it won't get out. Although, there's not really much replayability in this game apart from the acheievements and, well, I can't say all that much without spoilers.
In short? Fun game, even if you're not very familiar with the subject of the game, although most references may fly over you since this is an homage game, after all. Worth a buy? Sure. It's a good game for its price although it tends to be lacking a bit in the replayability department, it's fun for what it's worth and that is what matters.

I decided to wait to review this game after I 100%ed it so I could get a good feel for the amount of content the game offered for its price. I wasn't disappointed.
Coming off of games like Furi, Bayonetta, Nex Machina and the Nier franchise, I found that games with tight controller gameplay and satisfyingly difficult bosses were right down my alley and so I decided to pick this one up as well. Let's get one thing straight, if you have a decent amount of experience with these types of games then Cuphead isn't going to be the punishingly difficult game it was hyped up to be. However, don't be quick to discredit its intensity and fast-paced gameplay that will leave even the most seasoned players challenged at least a few times during the first run of the story.
The visuals are fantastic and were the first selling point for me. It has wonderfully crafted animation style straight out of the 1930's with a great OST to boot. I was very surprised to see that even with hand-drawn graphics the hitboxes were really well done for this kind of game, which were a major concern for me going into it for the first time.
Attack telegraphing is on point 99% of the time, with very few attacks from the baddies feeling unfair and unprepared as attacks from the player feel and sound powerful with each projectile released. There were very few instances where hit detection was a problem and I only saw 2 skipped animations during my entire run of the game.
The game can take anywhere from 3-9 hours on the first playthrough, and about 10-20 hours for all the extras after the normal playthrough is completed. I completed all achievements in 19.2 hours and I have yet to get a perfect rank on most bosses, so the game is not lacking in things to do. Overall Cuphead is a delight to play and the $20 price tag is justified by the amount of content it provides.

I will review all my humble bundle games and see which is worth playing and which is not! Like a lot of people i buy H.B. games as a pack because i want some of the games, but not all. I will play for 5 minutes (or a little bit more) and give you my opinion on it. Sometimes the game will surprise me, sometimes it will be a total disappointment. Just keep in mind this is my opinion only and is not an objective view of the game. You might actually like it!
The review will be constructed into 5 parts:
1. Game description (from what I’ve seen in the time I’ve played).
2. Did i finish the game (YES/NO/Maybe in the future) and why.
3. Pros/Cons.
4. Final thoughts.
5. Rating
So let's begin...
1. Game description:
It’s hard to describe this “game”, if you can call it that. It falls into the walking simulator category, however, in my opinion  it’s not a good one. The athmosphere is decent, the music and sounds blend in OK with the game, but…there is no gameplay…it’s just that…an interactive story. It ends pretty quickly and the story itself is not so interesting. The only slightly interesting bits for me where the ones about video game programing, and that only because I am a programmer.
2. Did i finish the game? YES
I wanted too see where it was going with the story, however I was not impressed. Thank god it was short.
3. Pros/Cons.
PROS:
- Interesting insight into the world of video game programming
- The music, sounds and scenery blend in perfectly
- Short game
CONS:
- Boring story
- Nothing to do, only walk.
- Short game
4. Final thoughts:
This is one of the few games I actually regret finishing. It left me with nothing. No emotional bond with the narrator, it had a basic storyline and it had absolutely no action. I know a lot of people like it and say that this is art, but the same as I cannot understand paintings I cannot understand this game. Games should be fun, a way to escape reality and relax. This game is not that!
5. Rating

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I have had quite a hard time reviewing this game, as it is difficult to articulate exactly what it’s like to play without sounding like a 10 year old, but perhaps that’s the point. Put simply, this game is what happens if you take raw awesomeness, condense it into 2D, add as many explosions as will fit on the screen, and throw in a few jokes at America’s expense.
In this game, you play several different members of a team called “Bro Force” sent in to “Liberate” whole regions of what I can only assume is the 3rd world, and they do this by killing absolutely everybody there in a hail of bullets, bombs and deadly knife attacks.
With names like “Trent Broser”, “Bro Ceaser”, and “Broctor Death” this team of elite demolition experts chase down an evil villain by “liberating” any region they find him in. This had the potential to be a fun little game.  Unfortunately, most of the mechanics remove any tactical components from play.  Most of the game play is involved in migitating random events.  There are so many random events that they just become annoying.  After each time a character moves a random event is generated unless a tile is explored then it could generate a random event.  Most of the random events cause damage to one or more characters.
To avoid random events, you must move a character to an unexplored tile edge.  However, the tile is not exposed until the character's tun is over.  This usually leads to a wasted move as there isn't a mechanism to hold the action or even use if for an attack of opportunity.   It also generally generates another random event (monster, event, or both).
Items discovered cannot be transferred between characters, so they can never be distributed to those characters that could use them the most.
Because of this it is difficult to coordinate character abilites.  The game continually robs agency from the player.
Finally, the game only offers the four characters.  The bard character has little in the way of damage output.  Killing enemies it s major part of getting gear.  So the paladin usually has all of his gear slots full and constanly has to scrap gear, while the bard rarely gets any gear to fill its slots.  The ability to transfer gear between missions would greatly improve the game play.
Overally, the game feels like it still needs a lot of work to improve the balance.  Also a choice of more characters would definitely help.
If you are not interested in achievments, there is about 6.5 hours of content in this game that isn't repetative.  If you do the achievements, that involves replaying each scenario at least twice and possible more to get the necessary gold and components to improve all of the items.
At this point, the balance, especially on Horrific mode, is terrible.  So I would only reccomend this game if you like fighting a random number generator.

Summary: The game is great only hindered by some difficulty issues and minor bugs. The games story and graphics are fantastic. Upgrading is satisfying and also takes a lot of thinking. Combat takes strategy and is near flawless, for the most part aside from the Mech battles difficulty spike.
Lengthy-er Review: Combat is great, it takes a lot of strategy of what combinations of teamwork, and skills to boost your audience meter. The game lets you customize what your squads name is, transforming motto, and actor names. This makes the game feel way more your own and adds a lot of depth. The story is silly and over-the-top enough to feel very Sentai-like. The "hub" where you buy upgrades and items is another fantastic aspect of the game. Buying new items and mech parts, along with buying new marketers who can bring you special benefits depending on which person you sign a contract with. Replying to fan emails was also a joy to do. Now onto the cons. Mech fights are incredibly challenging even on normal mode, it took me NUMEROUS times to defeat most makes in the final 2 seasons. Mech fights also lack strategy and ends up mostly being dependent on luck. For example, for each punch you start off around 90% chance to hit, then goes down to around 80% for the next punch, and so on. Problem is healing skills require you to get around a 4x combo of punches to do any real healing, and so does the +Def move. It is nearly impossible to get consistent 4x combo, myself rarely even getting 3x combos. Even with that decent sized flaw it doesn't take away too much from the game, it is still fantastic and charming. All the pro's easily out weigh the cons.
Rating: 9/10

Bioshock is a hell of a game I'll give it that. A first person shooter with RPG elements and a knack for scaring you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
+The graphics look beautiful for a game that came out in 2007. Sure the textures aren't great, and the characters are a little cartoony, but everything about the aesthetic of this game helps to fully set the atmosphere. And take my word for it, this is one of the most immersive games I have played in a very long time when it comes to the atmosphere.
+The soundtrack is phenomenal. It fits every single scene. It helps draw you into the game. It can make even a bathroom that lacks jump scares the most terrifying place you've ever tip-toed your way into.
+The level design is fantastically done, if poorly translated onto a 2D map. The underwater city of rapture has a mild claustrophobic feeling to it, but it makes sense. It fits the setting quite well, and when you need space? You can usually find or make it.
+The story is fantastic, Ken Levine does wonders with stories. Draw dropping plot twists and endings that'll leave you speechless, i loved every second of it. There isn't a story in the world Ken Levine could write that I could forget.
+Decent-length. Got 21 hours out of the game after getting it for $1 in a bundle. Definitely worth the price. I was partially a completionist however, I explored almost every single room and shelf in Rapture. I also moved very slowly at points since I scare easy.
+Since the tags say it's horror, I can tell you it really does horror right. Jump-scares when you least expect them. And a very creepy atmosphere that doesn't rely on jump scares to begin with.
-Respawning enemies. Just...ugh. Bioshock as a series is infamous for throwing enemies, and bullet sponges at you. If it bothers you, play on a lower difficulty, you'll become a bullet sponge yourself.
-Bugs with Win7 or later. From random crashes (That lead to all of your settings resetting) to the sounds cutting out when too make sound sources are coming in at once. Most noticeable when guardians of rapture (Sounds better than dinky flying robots) are shooting. Especially noticeable towards the end of the game. Immersion-breaking to say the least...but not game-breaking.
All in all, this game holds up. I'm very glad I made my easy-to-scare♥♥♥♥♥finish the game, as it was totally worth it. Keeping its buggy state and flaws in mind, I give this game an 4/5. I think this is a game that everyone who enjoys a good immersive story should play. Were the bugs fixed, I'd give it a 9/10, so maybe a console version might fare better for you. Either way, I have to admit that it is an amazing game and it has defined the standards for the horror FPS genre. Now, would you kindly consider giving it a try? =)

LIMBO was a game I really wanted a few years back as I saw a lot of great things said about the game. Well, then it became free for a while, and as I played it, well. I was disappointed.
While I certanly didn't hate it and I would rather play this than many of the recent titles, I still did not manage to enjoy this to the fullest due to some simple things.
The puzzles in this game are made to be simple, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, as a matter of fact the puzzles were quite enjoyable. Instead of making the puzzles complex they made them simple, but still a little to think about. The puzzles are heavily reliant on timing for the most part and object placement, which I found to be great, but unfortunately there were a few flaws which made me really have an unenjoyable experience:
Learning from your mistakes as you die was clearly the focus of this game, but only effectively used this at the start of the game and midway trough, as in for example at the beginning they had put a hardly visible trap on the ground, which of course killed you, but also clearly was meant to aid you, and the game delivered this message to the player quite fast making you use the trap in a creative way.
But as I said, half the time this was not the case, and you would often find yourself dying in unfair circumstances, and all you will learn from them is to avoid them. This felt like a waste of time for me, and possibly many others.
The biggest problem with this game though was with the controls and movement:
First you get thrown into the game with no introduction, you just need to run and then drag a box under a platform. There is the first problem: I needed to spam my keyboards every single button until I found out the correct button to grab objects with. They did not bind this control to anything obvious like E or Shift, but instead to CTRL. A button rarely, possibly never used in any video game to do similar tasks. For many people it is very hard to move pinky to such location, and even for a person like me who uses this button to crouch in every game, it felt very slow compared to buttons they could have used, such as E.
-Another problem with this is the fact that the only way to change the key binds is to go trough the game files to find the correct file in which you'll be able to tamper with controls. The game should have had some keyboard customization options at least.
After this the game progresses nicely, but you'll encounter various places where you will have troubles with how the movement works.
The first problem being the CTRL bind for grabbing, as you will need to use it a lot while trying to go trough challenging areas where slightest error would cause a death, but the placement of the key makes it frustrating at times.
Secondly after climbing on top of a box you will not be able to jump for a brief amount, so you might end up spamming the jump key in a tight situation, and jump at a 0,2 second latency, making you unprepared for the late jump which leads to your death.
If you think you can get past these, then by all means have a go with this game. 2/5

Here we have a game that started an enormous trend amongst the internet, with mostly children around twelve and up playing the game, and despite it's horror factor (which is somewhat meager), it has spread as a strong internet phoenomena, and even since it's release date of August, 2014, exactly a year before creating this review, it has been extended in to a four-game franchise.
If I wasn't 100% honest with this review, I'd say that this game is the spawn of Satan, or something ludicrous, but that really isn't the case, while I admit that the general fanbase for the game is realtively annoying and most certainly an indicator that the game is overrated, even I have to say that from my meager, but still existent perosnal experience with this game, I found the jumpscares to be somewhat fulfilling, not hardly as much as I'd have hoped, but at least enough to encourage you to want to play the game with caution.
In all honesty, I do not regard the game as a perfect game, not even close, I would put it on the same level as casual game, but it has made itself a well-earned reputation, and it was clear that the devotion put in to it was strong, for instance, the 3D models rendered to make it were made with good care, and it was ensured that all of the materials rendered made the game look as spooky or ominous as possible, this was very effective, even to the point where seeing the animatronics up-close gave some sort of fear factor, to me at least.
One thing that seemed to be weak and light about the game were the jumpscares, the pitch and volume of the noises emitted when the jumpscares occur seemed to catch me off guard, and the animatronic models, while retaining a cartoonish style to some degree, had some kind of ominous appearance to them, but the way these elements were stitched together gave no core-shattering effect that put a constant fear in you, in most cases, you know exactly when the jumpscare is about to occur, making it even less terrifying than it could have been, not to mention the overall weakness of jumpscares' use repetitively.
Overall, I wouldn't recommend this game, not because it's a bad game, but because it just doesn't fulfill it's purpose, and that is to be a "scary" game, there's a fine line between something being sometimes shocking, and something being scary, and while this game tries to be a strongly scary, it still doesn't 100% fulfill the reputation given to it by the public, this doesn't by any means mean not to buy it, that is your choice, maybe it is that I'm strong-hearted in comparison to others, I don't know, but it's not a game I would recommend in all honesty.

There is a long list of things wrong with this game for me to tell you straight up that it is not worth downloading/playing this game from the start.
First of all, this game is pay2win, as there is a VIP item in their cash shop that gives +10 to all stats and something like 20% movement speed bonus.  This item is not permanent, and the shop seems to only currently sell it at one week increments.
Second of all, this game is bound to your steam account, so that means that if you were playing this before the steam version came out, or were unlucky to begin playing on the first day, you can't actually run this game through steam.
Third of all, this game plays like a generic MMO where your main source of experience is fetch quests, so either find x person or gather x items, as this game has level barriers, which means that if you encounter enemies 5 levels above you, it basically means it won't be worth trying to kill them as they will probably one-shot you or you will not deal enough damage to make the experience worth it.
Fourth of all, the steam cash shop is actually more expensive than if you were playing through the original game client.  This is because they made it so that steam users are bound through their steam account, so the cash shop transactions go through steam, and I guess steam wanted a cut of the profits or else this game wouldn't have gotten onto steam.
Fifth of all, the endgame of this game is only raiding with people.  This might not be a downside to a lot of people, but if you check youtube for any videos of raids in this game, it looks horrific with the horrible camera controls and boring combat.  There actually is zero reason to play this game, as there are better free MMO's out there such as Neverwinter or Path of Exile.
The final complaint that I have about this game is probably centric to only me, as other people seem to get by fine.  I cannot use mumble with this game, as it locks my voice in-place as soon as it launches, so if my mic is held down when the game launches, it will be stuck to the "on" position until I alt-tab and repress my push-to-talk key.  It's the same if it were "off" when it launches, which means that I can't talk to my mumble friends while playing this game.
It makes me really upset that I was looking forward to fooling around in this game for a small portion of the summer, because the main reason was to play with my friends, but this game apparently does not want to allow me to use the characters that I made because their release went horrible (although most MMOs/games in general have horrible week 1 releases).  Their reasoning for separating steam accounts with no option of logging into an already existing account is completely illogical, and boggles my  mind.  The bugs with mumble was the last straw, and I can't bring myself to play this game even if some of my friends are still willing to play this just because it is free.
I have not played the original Ragnarok Online and my only experience with the Ragnarok series is through the mangas and Ragnarok Offline, which is my disclaimer that maybe someone who enjoyed the first might like it;  On the other hand, I have seen countless forum posts complaining that this game is not an official sequel, as it's a different company and people who have played Ragnarok Online for years are absolutely heartbroken at what this game has become.  The posts I've seen have described this game as a generic WoW-clone rehash with the Ragnarok name.
Play at your own risk, but I would recommend against it!

As a horror game fan, I had high hopes for Outlast. Sadly I was let down.
The immersion just isn't there. The story is disjointed, and even buggy. (My character listed the name of a man I encountered, even though he had no way of knowing the name, and several other funky things with the journal)
The mechanics of the enemies are horribly transparent. The fact that if I hide in a locker, they will always check the locker immediately next to me made me audibly groan every time.
If that wasn't enough to take me out of my immersion, progression ended up as a series of trial-and-error grind fests to learn enemy AI and exploit it.  The element of fear was gone, I was playing against silly robot AI, and I was in a Comedy instead of a Horror.
Perhaps I could forgive it if the chase scenes or trial-and-error were fun or interesting, but they weren't.
So much potential wasted. Save yourself the time and play SOMA instead.

Old school space shooter with a really novel and interesting mechanic of being able to take over any ship. Gameplay and game design decisions ruin it. There's only 8 levels, and each 1 consists of like 9 waves of guys. The problems are with the switching. For some reason, each ship you take over has only like 5 shots before it runs out of ammo and is useless. It doesn't help that each shot is super tiny, and each ship moves all around, so its easy to miss most shots. Furthermore, each ship, no matter how big, can only take 2 hits to die. This means you can be this big ship and 1 little blaster shot from a tiny ship puts you near death. It doesn't help that each ship moves super slowly for some reason and dodging is all but impossible. There's no period of invulnerability after taking a ship, or after getting hit. I would sometimes take a ship and there would already be a bullter about to hit me so I'd start with almost dead. Or when the screen is filled up with shots, taking 1 hit of the wave will kill you bc 2 shots can be stacked almost on top of each other, counting as 2 hits that happen in 1 second that you can't react to. Insta dying from a wave of fire sucks, and it is worse bc u have to start the wave. Then if you die a total of 3 times, which is super easy bc each ship is made of glass, you have to start the entire level, all 10 waves,  over again. I understand the tiny ammo pool and no life of each ship encourages you to switch, but its annoying and artifically made by game design you have to switch ships every 5 seconds because you took a single hit or shot 5 times. I want to enjoy a cool ship. There is a large number of ships, but each level reuses the same group of 6-8 or so, so it can get repetitive. There's also no real story, just a few random sentences of nonsensical text that pop up after every wave and level.
In the end, the great idea is marred by failed execution. The arbitrary low ammo, tiny health, and lack of invulnerability after getting hit ruin the fun that could be had. If you like repeating levels though, due to poor design decisions, this is the game for you.

Evolve is a asymmetrical multiplayer based game for five players or AI counterparts.  The premise of Evolve is that four players play as the hunters who are dropped on to the planet Shear to remove a "wildlife threat" - The monster.
Currently, Evolve has three different playable monsters; The Goliath which is a large tank that can deal large amounts of damage with rock throws, fire and charges.  The Kraken is specialized in ranged combat while the Wraith is a master of Stealth. The Behemoth will be the fourth playable monster, which will be £10-£15 at launch.
There are four different classes of hunters to play; Medic, Trapper, Support and Assault. Each of these classes give the player three characters to unlock who all come with their own set of tools and weapons to help your comrades take down the monster before it inevitably leads you and your squad to your impending doom. If we take the medic for example, Val (The first playable Medic) has a medgun but Lazarus (Second playable medic) does not, instead he possesses a tool that can revive fallen allies.
The four classes having three playable characters each is a bonus - Of all of the characters I have played no two play the same.  Val is a more focused Team Fortress 2 style of medic while Lazarus can be on the offense more with the ability to revive allies who have perished.
Turtle Rock have set up the medic class in such a way that it will appeal to more players and that is fantastic - Human Medics are better than AI ones after all, right? Val has a sniper rifle that places weak points on the monster that your other team mates can shoot to deal bonus damage, a simple medgun to heal all of your teammates from a distance, a tranquilizer gun that slows down the monster considerably and a healing burst which heals you and your allies instantly. Having four different tools gives the medic a different dynamic compared to some other titles.  It is fun to lay waste to the Goliath with weakpoints while they are being shot at by your other team mates and slowing it down when it attempts to escape.
The trapper has two main jobs; track down the monster and trap him within a large dome.  Once the monster is trapped, they can not escape until the dome runs out or is taken down. If you have a good trapper on your team who does not miss when throwing the trap, you stand a good chance of winning the match.
Assault is exactly what you would think it is - A class to deal damage. The primary job of the assault is to deal mass amounts of damage to the monster while being supported by the other three classes.
The support class is the only class that I have not played much of, but what I can say from what I played is that the biggest selling point of the Support is to offer shields to your allies. The shield works in the same way the medgun does - Point and shoot at your allies to shield them from damage.
Overall the classes have a nice variety to them and each class has a important role to play during the match - Always play to the strengths of the character you have chosen.  When you play a class for the first time you will receive a brief introductory video before the match begins to give you a rough outline of what your primary job is and what your class specific tools do.  This is especially important in a game like Evolve when you need your teammates to pull their weight as the monster gets more powerful.
Outside of the traditional hunt game mode, Evacuation mode is available.  In here you will find a little back story to what is going on within the game world along with several different game types. The objective of Evacuation is to save as many survivors as possible over five matches of Evolve - This can take up to one hour of gameplay. Evacuation features different playable game modes including Nest in which the squad of hunters must hunt out and destroy the monster eggs before the monster has a chance to hatch them, Rescue is exactly what it says on the tin - find and rescue survivors and the final match on day five forces the hunters to defend generators from oncoming waves of enemies to allow the survivors to escape.  I have had varying experiences on this game mode - Playing in public lobbies I can get both team mates who play their role well and roughly have the jist of what to do and that can be a fantastic and rewarding experience for five straight games.  On the other hand, having players who are brand new to Evolve, haven't completed any of the tutorials or watched the videos will likely prove you with a frustrating experience.
I find Evolve entertaining enough to continuously go back and play "just one more game", even in public lobbies. However, during matches it can begin to feel slow or even sluggish when you have four hunters running around a empty map searching for the monster for minutes on end.  This is especially frustrating when a match of Evolve is generally 10 - 15 minutes in length. It is possible that when players have more experience with the game, those of us who play as the trapper will have a better idea of what is going allowing the monster to be tracked in a more efficient manner.
This title features a lot of downtime - There are loading screens when you start up the game, before a match and after a match.  Downtime can occur often during a match  if you are the type of player who will often go down in a fight, or even if your medic is not doing their job properly. When you die in Evolve you are forced to spectate your remaining team members while waiting for a drop-ship to throw you back in to the action after a few minutes.
I have found a issue with the PC version of Evolve, after I have played a couple of games my mouse cursor will vanish from the screen and menus and it makes it incredibly difficult to select anything.  This can be annoying to both you and your squad who are patiently waiting on you to select your character, class, perks and skin.
Speaking of skins - Evolve has A LOT of DLC, and I mean a lot. I believe every character has skins and/or a skin pack you can buy, the monsters have different skins to purchase, there is a monster DLC pack, Season Pass - In fact there is so much downloadable content for this game already, on day one, that the cost of it nearly surpasses that of the base game itself.  That is absolutely absurd and I completely understand why there are many, many unhappy customers out there who feel that all of this content (beside the monster pack and season pass) should be in the game.  Why cant we have unlockable skins within Evolve instead of paying around £5 for a skin?
It almost feels like Turtle Rock set out to create a premium game with a freemium monetization model and it has♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off a lot of customers.  If you do not want to put your money down for this type of transaction - I urge you to not do it if you feel like it will show developers that this type of DLC is not wanted by a lot of customers.  However, if you want to purchase the DLC you should obviously go right ahead with your purchase.
I own the Season Pass and even I was confused at what content I gain from it.  The Steam store page for the season pass states that I unlocked the tier three characters for each class which means that, these characters which are already in the game are hidden behind a paywall.  You can not play the final character of each class unless you fork out £19.99 for the season pass.
If you have watched gameplay of Evolve or you have read some articles and reviews and you think this game is for you, give it a go. Games of Evolve are fun and thrilling to play and can lead to some seriously intense moments.  I have enjoyed my time with the game so far and I am looking forward to jumping back in.

I would recommend this game to anyone looking for a zombie experience that is both enlightening and challenging. Set in a post-apocolyptic Kentucky, you find yourself thrust into a world filled with zeds and not but the clothes on your back (for the seasoned veterens looking for more challenge).
The game puts lots of emphasis on simulation over some zombie-slashing-shoot-em-up style of play, what with the market flooded with all too many (I'm talking to you, mobile developers). This game proves to you that you are not invulnerable but, in fact, another specimin waiting to be picked apart by hordes of undead at any moment you slip up. Fortunately, the game offers lots of options for you to customize your experience with the game. You can take it easy, or bathe in flames. Your choice. That's what it's all about. Choice. Every choice you make can either spell doom, or give you another day to mark off the virtual calendar that you've survived. Let me remind folks that this game is a huge work in progress (alphas, man) so please, DO NOT EXPECT PERFECTION. I can't stress it enough. There are bugs, things that don't work, and things yet to come. So far, at the time of this writing, there have been HUGE developements to the game. Just today, they changed the shaders to make the game less cartoony and add some gloom to the doom. Weapons have seen a lot of love as of late with a mechanics overhaul including weapon upgrades and skill tree improvements. No more gunning down ComicCon-sized hordes with a 9mil. Pistols can have red dots and custom optics to improve your ability to cherry pie some zeds from afar, and do it well. Shotguns can get an ammo sling to speed up zombie shredding glory with each shell. There's also a hunting rifle for those days you feel like keeping a distance, yet still have something to laugh about to yourself over a nice bowl of stew. Hunting, foraging, cooking, fire making, fort building; all part of the experience you'll get to see and be a part of with this game. It'll eat away at your free time like a hungry zed to a fresh corpse. If you're on the fence about this one, let me just say that you can feel confident in your decision to come on down and join the carnage. Welcome to the apocolypse. Please, enjoy your stay. Zomboid style.

I feel bad leaving a negative review, I really do, because a part of me wants to love this game and I burned many hours on Tropico 4. However, I haven't finished the campaign and do not feel the DLC merits spending because of glaring gameplay issues and I really hope the developers read this and there will be a new and improved Tropico 6. The short version is that you will probably be better off buying 4 if this interests or taking a pass if you are only tacitly interested in city simulators. On the off chance that a developer will read this though (or if you are really curious), there is a long version below.
I want to start with the positive. The new look of Tropico 5 compared to 4 is an improvement, the basics of running an economy is still there and I appreciate buildings like the office block which rewards you for building a large and dense city just when natural resources will start running out. I feel like if they expand ways for you to make money outside of pulling crops, metals and oil out of the ground then the sequel will give people the freedom to construct much more personalized cities that fit their own styles. I also like that a new level of complexity has been given to elections but that is where we quickly run into problems.
The fundemental problem of Tropico 5, which made it too frustrating for me to want to finish, is the dimension that requires you to keep control of island despite elections, coups and revolutions. People who move from Tropico 4 to 5 will be startled what a much larger role factions play in getting re-elected. Now you can largely ignore basic services and as long as you build a new church or start taxing the rich at election time you can make huge gains. Unfortunately, this is very poorly communicated. The most effective thing to do is to see which factions have the largest populations, see which ones you can make happy at the same time and then tailor your constitution and edicts accordingly. However, while you can guess who will like what changes (ten dollars for guessing the Religious will like a Theocratic State) there will often be people who dislike one change that you could not really have forseen and because there is also a penalty in relations from changing policies that people liked you are quickly trying to fix them all before all of a sudden you lose.
I get the feeling that the first couple levels were trying to familiarize you with this system but because I was able to beat them without going in-depth, and no text pointed me in the direction of the factions, this was a poor tutorial. I ended up having to look up why I was having so many popularity issues (strictly in the game I mean). A tooltip under edicts, buildings, and amendments that told you who liked what and by how much would have gone a long way. If that is too much handholding it would be fine if there was an option to disable it. However, it would allow one to more effectively build a coalition by avoiding decisions that will permanently and unforeseeably damage relations with one faction. Without being able to be that effecient, I feel like I am constantly trying to patch relations to please these factions so I do not suffer a game over. While some people may like this, I feel that these challenges should force a player to adapt their city, not completely rewrite. The way it is now, I feel that I do not have any substantial control over how I build on the map and then ruins the city builder fantasy for me.
Along similar lines, if we had more information on triggered revolts and coups then I feel like this game would be alot less frustrating. I saw other people calling attention to this in the comments and I feel like it would go a long way towards helping. I am not sure if the difficulty itself actually need to be reduced but I definitely feel that I do not have a way to address these fundemental obstacles in the game, lose, eventually get frustrated and just quit. I mostly play it on the offchance of a eureka moment that will finally let me finish the campaign, but I am not holding out much hope. I hope great strides are made in Tropico 6 but I will have to wait a while before I decide to buy it.

The spiritual successor to System Shock 2. Compared to System Shock 2 I think a lot of things got easier for player like we get the object arrow, no inventory management, easier resource management, no weapon degregation.
Yet a lot of things changed for the better in a lot of ways. This game is super fun to play. You get to use all kinds of different strategies for defeating the enemies, be it setting up traps, turning them against each other, spells to stop them or just straight up blowing them up with different weapons. You also aren't really forced to stay on a path when it comes to that. You can constantly change the way you play on the fly, there's not really a leveling system that would need to be rerolled.
I think the best thing about this game is in the atmosphere for sure. It feels like a real city. There's a lot variation too. Texture quality is good for the most part even for a game this old now. Not everything feels underwatery, but that is still the theme that repeats of course.
What I really liked was the old school level design, like in Doom or something. There's a lot of secrets! If you just look to loot the enemies and some easy to spot safes you are missing a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of stuff! You really have to search for hidden doors, under the stairs, on the ceiling, on the bookshelfs. The devs really got good at hiding items from the player and trying to find everything was great.
Sound design is excellent, you hear enemies talking behind corners all the time, saying really creepy♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's just awesome. Same with voice acting, excellent job by everyone. There's a LOT of audio recording in the world too so those who want to dig deeper about the issues in the city can do so. While those who just want to see gameplay and the major plot can skip all the recordings.
Story and pacing is great. I hate super long cut scenes and long talks, not really the case here. There's not really many cut scenes. Everything is usually shown in the game world, a character appearing and talking to you or through the radio and I liked that approach a lot.
If there's any negative about the game it's maybe the super simplified, black and white mechanics with little sisters. The game has 2 endings depending on your choice. The sort of grey area is missing, either you are a hero or you are not. I felt there should have been more choices throughout the game, like when you meet the citizens of the city- do you help them or destroy them? There could have been factions, side quests or something and multiple endings.
Now the replayability is basicly on if you wanna see the other ending or not, which you probably should just youtube, since the game is so linear in that sense and you don't see anything new besides the 30sec ending video. Rather the replayability comes from the great gameplay, try different approach and difficulty setting, take more time to find the secrets, look at the level design, listen to the tapes.
This game is easily 9/10 for me.
If you end up liking this game a lot give System Shock 2 a try too, read the steam forums, update the textures and models a bit and it should still be a great game even today, That's what I did and liked it even more than Bioshock!

Non-violent adventures with little interactivity, the so called “walking simulators”, are used more and more by the developers who want to make an interactive story. After Dear Esther, this subgenre gained a lot of popularity, but also a lot of criticism that “it’s not a real game” because there’s usually no real danger for the main character or no way to get stuck. Beside the story, another major attribute of this approach is the atmosphere, and it’s exactly what the Funcom studio made the most of with The Park.
Like a large number of horror movies, this adventure starts in a seemingly cheerful manner – playing as Loraine, you took your son Calum to the amusement park. Colorful, cheerful place where you can have a great time? Oh no, no way, because as soon as you step through the park gates, the true menacing face of this place is revealed, wrapped up in darkness and shadows within which nightmares lurk.
The Park is a game that only had enough ‘strength’ for one run. Not only because of the awkwardly written scenario or the lack of mystery and suspense throughout the run, but also because you’ll get to see everything there is to the game during its short duration. This is another adventure where the player is mostly a passive observer, with not enough interesting ideas that made me want to explore the universe it’s set in.

Here we have a game that started an enormous trend amongst the internet, with mostly children around twelve and up playing the game, and despite it's horror factor (which is somewhat meager), it has spread as a strong internet phoenomena, and even since it's release date of August, 2014, exactly a year before creating this review, it has been extended in to a four-game franchise.
If I wasn't 100% honest with this review, I'd say that this game is the spawn of Satan, or something ludicrous, but that really isn't the case, while I admit that the general fanbase for the game is realtively annoying and most certainly an indicator that the game is overrated, even I have to say that from my meager, but still existent perosnal experience with this game, I found the jumpscares to be somewhat fulfilling, not hardly as much as I'd have hoped, but at least enough to encourage you to want to play the game with caution.
In all honesty, I do not regard the game as a perfect game, not even close, I would put it on the same level as casual game, but it has made itself a well-earned reputation, and it was clear that the devotion put in to it was strong, for instance, the 3D models rendered to make it were made with good care, and it was ensured that all of the materials rendered made the game look as spooky or ominous as possible, this was very effective, even to the point where seeing the animatronics up-close gave some sort of fear factor, to me at least.
One thing that seemed to be weak and light about the game were the jumpscares, the pitch and volume of the noises emitted when the jumpscares occur seemed to catch me off guard, and the animatronic models, while retaining a cartoonish style to some degree, had some kind of ominous appearance to them, but the way these elements were stitched together gave no core-shattering effect that put a constant fear in you, in most cases, you know exactly when the jumpscare is about to occur, making it even less terrifying than it could have been, not to mention the overall weakness of jumpscares' use repetitively.
Overall, I wouldn't recommend this game, not because it's a bad game, but because it just doesn't fulfill it's purpose, and that is to be a "scary" game, there's a fine line between something being sometimes shocking, and something being scary, and while this game tries to be a strongly scary, it still doesn't 100% fulfill the reputation given to it by the public, this doesn't by any means mean not to buy it, that is your choice, maybe it is that I'm strong-hearted in comparison to others, I don't know, but it's not a game I would recommend in all honesty.

For 15 or even 30 bones, you really can't do much better than Chroma Squad. Even if Power Rangers (or Super Sentai if you INSIST) isn't necessarily your jam, it hits all the right notes for making a good gaming experience through that Triple-A seems to have forgotten; It's fun. Fun. You remember that? You know, when you get giggles or smile? When you get drawn into the experience not because of the spectacle, but because the game directly involves you and lets you make it your own, that's how you make games fun.
Throwing down on some details, here's some specifics of why it's already made my top ten for 2015 -
-Turn-Based strategy, not RPG. Think XCOM: EU, but with goddamn Power Rangers.
-Customisation and upgrades for pretty much EVERYTHING.
-Resource management that's more give-take than just your standard subtraction. It reminds me a lot of how the economy worked in Mechwarrior 2: Mercenaries, a type of economy system I feel got left by the wayside in favour of simpler/easier things that don't add any weight to your decisions.
-Crafting, a system that is notorious for earning my ire by basically being utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t roughly a million per-cent of the time, actually makes some sort of sense in how components are named/what goes into what. It's also not needlessly complicated, which is a gigantic tick in my "yes" box.
-It's got good moments of humour in it. It's not a comedy game, per se, but it knows not to take itself too seriously, and the humour it employs has a nice spectrum, from subtle pointing out of tropes, tongue-in-cheek, to bad puns, to breaking the fourth wall, and even some nice.... "meta" moments.
-The art is nicely done, and consistent. While I can't say I have any particular love for the "retro" style that just about every indie game is doing, this one has really nicely animated sprites with a lot of good character to them as well as fun and well-done environments.
In conclusion, if you're one of those indie-game wads that just can't get enough of retro-styled graphics, crafting and whatever, you should have already creamed your free-trade, locally sourced shorts just by looking at the game's trailer. But even if you're not, this is definitely a game worth playing if you just want to have some goddamn fun playing games for once.

An attempt to do something ambitious with the Secret World engine, ultimately crippled by technical hang-ups and a hum-drum horror experience.
Game has style, but its art and graphics will not woo anyone accustomed to current gen console specs.  Some haunting music will creep in from time to time, but is not memorable.  Expect the occasional orchaestra sting to shake you out of your seat briefly.
The story of the game is simple and quick to grasp, with character dialogue that's well voice acted to build up the tension.  The background of the protagonist is well explored and interesting, although relatively mundane compared to standard Secret World stories.
Game is very much a walking simulator.  No puzzles, simply an invitation to explore and spin random objects around in your hands.  Game never quite makes it to "scary" but does dance on the edge of creepy from time to time.  Sadly, one of the game's best horror moments was straight lifted from a rather popular and increasingly rare title that'll be immediately apparent to anyone who plays this game.
The technical problems ultimately ruin the experience.  Framerate drops will disrupt visual and audio noticably, dissolving all the tension the scene is attempting to build up.  This is especially aggravating during moments where the protagonist is monologuing to herself or when the game hitches up in a jump scare.
The experience will run you about 1-2 hours, and has nothing to offer after the first run.  At $5.00 or less, you could do worse, but at it's current retail price, it's not worth it unless you seriously need a chipmunk costume or 10.9 trinket in Secret World.  Layers of Fear is a more comprehensive and intense walking horror simulator.  Those looking for something with more game to it should consider Amnesia, the Dark Decent.  Fans of The Secret World would be better served with one of their episodes

Amidst a 4 day long house-sitting venture for a friend, I have been searching steam for games that I could play to pass the time and will run on my laptop. I stumbled upon this new release which also happened to be on sale. I was a huge fan of the D & D world in the late 1990's and early 2000's during my college years. Seeing how Candlekeep wishes to bring the world of D&D tabletop to me via a keyboard in a single player setting, I was peaked with excitement for a nostalgic experience at the very least.
I got much more! To me, D & D at its core is like creating your own story everytime you play. That is what I remembered most from my days playng the tabletop besides the swords, sorcery and mythical creatures. Playing D & D there is a luck/risk factor experience you find in very few forms of entertainment with the game being controlled via the roll of dice (Most commonly 7 dice total. A 4-sided dice, 6-sided dice, 8-sided dice, 10-sided dice, 12-sided dice, and 20-sided dice. Sometimes a second 10-sided dice is used when players are using their own house rules.) With the developers including this base mechanic into Candlekeep, they NAILED it with me for that experience I was hoping for. Sweet!
For those new to the D & D world, the game gives the option of starting you with a short tutorial mission which I recommend even seasoned D & D veterans to play so you know how the game flows in digital format. The game flows with alternating turns between the hero and villain characters with an encounter phase after each hero turn unless you don't move to a new tile with the hero or perform an action. (An encounter is where the game rolls the die creating a random event based on the tile your active hero is on) There are also other ways to avoid encounters which usually result in negative effects for the heroes. The game is set on a map with quest icons. Each quest icon having an objective for you to meet in the game world. The music, graphics, character models, and spell effects are all very well done. The game has a simple crafting system, where you can upgrade your heroes equipment from loot you get during the quests.
Overall, I have to highly recommend this game to fans of the D & D universe. I have played other digital transitions and Candlekeep is one of the most true to the tabletop while adding a little flair of its own. Those who are fans of RPG games but have never ventured into the D & D world I also recommend giving Candlekeep a go. In just the second quest the game captured that nostalgia and love of the D & D world I was hoping for. I was using Birdsong the bard (One of 4 currently available heroes) I had one HP left, and 2 more enemies remaining to defeat to achieve my quest objective so I figured I was going to fail this time. I had one potion that would restore 20% of my health. (Likely 1 HP) but figuring I would still fail, I decided to attack and rolled a ''20'' resulting in a critical that took out one of the 2 remaining baddies and also scoring a rare wand of fireballs as loot. Whooo-hooo! My, excitement was short lived, I have to now survive one encounter, and villain turn. Potions are a free turn so I drank up. The encounter was an attack which hit me for 1 HP damage...I was gripping my mouse  tightly at this point since likely with the villain move my quest was over. Here we go..villain turn! A swing and a....MISS! YES whoooooooooooo! My initial risk paid off and I got lucky! I busted out that new shiny wand of fireballs for a sure victory! So as you can see, for a D & D fan like me at least, the game captured the atmosphere of the tabletop perfectly, knowing one bad roll can meet in success or failure for me and all heroes. I will be going back to Candlekeep quite often, and I urge you to do the same. If there is any complaint I do have with the game it is a small one. I wish the developers actually showed the dice rolls via an animation. Playing with, kissing, and begging to our die rollers for a good roll is a big part of what a D & D geek like me also enjoys from tabletops. That is just a small gripe in an amazing game that I can tell BKOM put their full effort into. I had to slip in this little edit when I learned how attentive the developers are when listening to feedback from us and plan to implement patches for the biggest issues players have with the game. Not only that, but they are planning to add much more content (such as more heroes) plus upcoming DLC. YES! Please check Candlekeep out!

I first learned about The Journey Down while searching for freeware adventures many years ago. Among a list of amateur made games like The White Chamber and Out Of Order, there was the little pixelated prototype of The Journey Down. I played it and i loved and i wanted more of it. So here i am, finally having played the first 2 Acts of the commercial version. And i am more than satisfied.
The Journey Down is very reminiscent of Grim Fandango in the best possible way. Intriguing setting, funny dialogue, cartoony visuals, surprising amounts of world-building. It provides everything i am looking for in a Point'n'Click game.
Puzzles are pleasantly intuitive. There were only two times i had to resort to a walkthrough. First time because i overlooked an interactable spot. A hotspot indicator would have been a useful addition to avoid small annoyances like that. Second time was the very last puzzle of Act 2, which sadly is one of those abritrary idiotic pictogram reading and switch pushing puzzles. You know, like everything in the final area of Syberia 2. Ugh. Here's hoping there won't be any more of this nonsense in Act 3.
The music accentuates the reggae atmosphere nicely. The voice acting is unfortunately rather uneven. The main character's VA is perfect for the role, everyone else ranges from passable to terrible. The audio quality itself fluctuates quite heavily as well, i had a hard time understanding certain characters.
These are only the most minor of complaints though. All in all, i am super hyped for Act 3.

I decided to wait to review this game after I 100%ed it so I could get a good feel for the amount of content the game offered for its price. I wasn't disappointed.
Coming off of games like Furi, Bayonetta, Nex Machina and the Nier franchise, I found that games with tight controller gameplay and satisfyingly difficult bosses were right down my alley and so I decided to pick this one up as well. Let's get one thing straight, if you have a decent amount of experience with these types of games then Cuphead isn't going to be the punishingly difficult game it was hyped up to be. However, don't be quick to discredit its intensity and fast-paced gameplay that will leave even the most seasoned players challenged at least a few times during the first run of the story.
The visuals are fantastic and were the first selling point for me. It has wonderfully crafted animation style straight out of the 1930's with a great OST to boot. I was very surprised to see that even with hand-drawn graphics the hitboxes were really well done for this kind of game, which were a major concern for me going into it for the first time.
Attack telegraphing is on point 99% of the time, with very few attacks from the baddies feeling unfair and unprepared as attacks from the player feel and sound powerful with each projectile released. There were very few instances where hit detection was a problem and I only saw 2 skipped animations during my entire run of the game.
The game can take anywhere from 3-9 hours on the first playthrough, and about 10-20 hours for all the extras after the normal playthrough is completed. I completed all achievements in 19.2 hours and I have yet to get a perfect rank on most bosses, so the game is not lacking in things to do. Overall Cuphead is a delight to play and the $20 price tag is justified by the amount of content it provides.

You will die A LOT, and when you lose all your lives, you have to restart the entire chapter over again. The difficulty comes from the fact that each ship you possess can only take a few hits before it's destroyed, and only has a small amount of ammo, to encourage you to change ships. Most ships only have 2 hits, and with the large number of projectiles and objects being thrown at you after the first couple of levels, it makes it very easy to die. I myself have never made it past Level 4. Overall, it's a really fun game, but you need to go into it with the fact that this game cannot be beaten without a lot of concentration, quick reflexes, and a ton of patience and determination.

A Shmup (shoot ’em up) with a difference, you have to warp into enemy ships every 10 or 20 seconds cos your ship only has so much ammo and can only take so much damage. This is a cool gimmick when you first start playing, but I kinda wish you didn’t HAVE to warp into another ship all the time, but I guess if they didn’t force you then you wouldn’t bother switching once you found a favourite ship.
The alien ships you warp into are all different sizes and have a nice array of different shooting styles, so there’s a constant variety and evolution of core gameplay on offer.
However, I’m not particularly good at Shmups, and this one gets pretty hard pretty fast, I only managed to get to level 4 (of 8) without cheats. At the start you have 3 lives, if you score well and increase the multiplier you can get 2 more, but each level has 8 waves or sections to it, and if you use up all you lives at the last wave and or boss, you have to restart the entire level over again.
I don’t have the time or patience to play each level 50 times for 5 hours each level to beat it, so I don’t see myself coming back to it anytime soon. In the steam forums the developer said he might add an easy mode or a save point after each wave, but he didn’t want to because he thinks the game would be too easy then, so don’t hold your breath for that.
There’s a cheat code to get unlimited ammo, lives and health as well as some other stuff if you go into the options menu and press...
(on the analog stick) up x3 down x3, up, down, up, down, down, down and then press A (or I guess enter on the keyboard).
If you’ve done it right you should be on the screen settings menu before you press A. Like most games tho, if you have the cheats enabled the achievements don’t drop.
Another cheat code for a level select:
Go to the Level Select screen and enter the Konami Code.
(GamePad) Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, B, A, Start
(Keyboard) Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, X, Z, Enter
I’d only really recommend this game to people who are good at Shmups, the cheats are fun, but take away the challenge. If the game was more balanced (easier) I’d probably recommend it to everyone.

Outlast is a game developed and published by Red Barrel Games
This is one of the better horror games out there. First and foremost the sound of the game is probably the best I have ever seen in any game apart from Amnesia: The Dark Descent
The amount of detail that can be heard when wearing high quality headphones is impressive and it makes the experience very realistic, besides helping the player project where the enemies are in the darkness of the Asylum.
The graphics are incredible. The voice acting is another one of the strong spots of this game. The screams and speeches of the patients sound extremely convincing, making the player forget it is a game
That combined with the high sound quality and amazing graphics makes Mount Massive Asylum a very real place and makes playing the game a more than enjoyable experience
On the other hand, the game lacks a little in story. Not to say that the story is bad, but the dynamics of the game makes the player sometimes forget what he's doing since he's too worried in not dying or getting caught
In other words, it's easy to forget your current objective. The game ends just when it's about to become repetitive so the length feels perfect. Not too long and not too short
In summary, Outlast is one of the better horror games ever made and it is definitely worth your money if you're looking for something that will keep you up at nights for a while. It's not recommended, though, for those easily frightened and that don't know what they're getting themselves into
