Just an update: I have been playing Tropico 5 a bit more, and even though my issues with it remain, I have found some things that make the game better. MODS.
Google Tropico 5 mods and you will find a lot of useful mods. Be warned however that if the mods mess up your save Kalypso might not be able to help you. I personally recommend Road and Sea Rage to make vehicles and ships move faster and clip through each other reducing traffic congestion.
Compared to Tropico 4, Tropico 5 isn't as good, even though it has its strengths.
The Positive:
- For what it is, it is fun and challenging.
- The different eras add a bit of variety, and it also means that you won't be dealing with the USSR in 2025.
- The dynasty system is different, and allows you to use it in tendem with the manager system.
- Missions involving sending dynasty members away for a while and they come back with a perk and some experience
- Actual use for your Swiss Bank account, adding the ability to upgrade your dynasty member's abilities.
- Managers that add a perk to a building, examples include increasing the beauty of an area or increasing production.
- The constitution and edicts have been added and overhauled and I think for the better. The constitution especially allows you to customise what kind of government you are, adding more personality to your island. The edicts also unlock every era which means you have plenty to think about as time passes.
- Researching is now a thing in Tropico 5, unlocking manager slots, building upgrades and more buildings. Penultimo also says something funny in relation to the topic when you fully research it.
- The humour. Penultimo is the best sidekick a dictator could ever ask for (said no one ever)
However, there are several mixed and negatives.
Mixed:
- The shipping system is a change, but after a while becomes comes off a bit weak compared to Tropico 4. The import and export contracts are a nice addition, but overall you'll be overburdened with trade deals and the inability to make the transactions you need because you ran out of ships. I am fully aware that you can remove ships from a route, but it isn't good for the long term.
CORRECTION: I thought that if you add ships to a route you won't be able to export everything else. Turns out freighters and trade ships are different. I still don't feel like the shipping system is better in Tropico 5 than 4 though, so it stays as a neutral.
- Faction and foreign relations decay over time. It sounds like a fun challenge to some people but I personally dislike it, it means juggling between factions that will eventually hate you no matter what you do.
And now the negative:
- Elections are worse than in Tropico 4. Although you can appoint a dynasty member as a new candidate, allowing for several presidentes, there is NO feedback whatsoever of why you are losing. Also, you cannot give speeches. Which means you cannot legally swing votes in your favour more easily.
- The modern era is basically the same as the Cold War but with China, the EU and the Middle East added alongside the US and Russia. Which makes it like Tropico 4 Modern Times. Which I can get for cheaper with all the DLC.
- All the DLC are overpriced and I only recommend a small handful of them. Espionage and Waterborne are pretty good though.
- Penultimo's voice. I just don't like it compared to Tropico 4. Bit of a nitpick but yeah.
- And this one sounds even pettier, the lack of a god mode. In Tropico 4 I have two sandboxes. One with God Mode so I don't have to care about stuff and just build, and another with normal gameplay. (and a third one which is normal but with a lot of cheating).
- The multiplayer is forgettable.
- Traffic congestion is still AWFUL. However with the aforementioned Road Rage mod it'll be solved.
- People still live in shacks even if you have a lot of housing with no feedback as to why. Apparently they refuse to move out even if you've fixed it.
- Again, no real feedback.
- The budgeting is awful. No real way to see why people aren't taking the houses here or taking jobs. Budgeting also decreases the service quality of houses but makes it cheaper for Tropicans which does ♥♥♥♥ ALL.
It is a good game, and I would really recommend it if it hadn't been for one thing: the fact that Tropico 4 exists and is so much better than Tropico 5. I'll give Haemimont credit here; they innovated a lot more than they did with Tropico 4 so it wasn't just a more stable reskin. However the additions are just not as good of that as 4, which may not have innovated as much but they added a lot of stuff (behind a paywall, sure) that made it a very good game. It's because of this I'm mixed on Tropico 5. It's a lot of fun, however it's just not as good as it's older brother. On it's own, yeah sure, get it. If you want a cheaper Tropico game go for 4. You'll be less disappointed.

Pros:
-The atmosphere is probably the best of any game I've played, and that's not an exaggeration. Instead of going for an ultra-realistic look that they knew they wouldn't be able to achieve, the devs went for an art style that looks like a painting. The clouds, sunsets, and skyboxes are gorgeous.
-What really makes this game is the sound. The sound of the wind howling during a blizzard was enough to make me start shivering and grab a blanket in my 75 degree room. The voice acting is good, and the general sound effects sound like what you'd expect in real life. You really feel like you're freezing to death in the woods.
-Map design is intuitive. There is a serious risk involved in going out to try to find another location. Buildings are spread out and often times a building will lack a single ammenity (a fireplace, or a bed), and so you'll be forced to choose somewhere else. I died within hours the first time I played, but once you start planning your moves, it becomes a lot more rewarding. Currently I've stayed alive for 10 days on my best game, and have trecked between three of the different maps.
-Gameplay is intuitive and fun. There isn't an "easy" way to play this game. No matter what, you'll be forced to leave the cabin you'll find in order to find food. The UI is also good and makes sense. Some people dislike the fact that you don't actually see the crafting happen when you make things, but it doesn't bother me much.
Cons:
-You get tired WAAAAAYYYYY too easily. I'm pretty out of shape, but I can carry my ~20Kg backpack to school and back, whereas my character in the Long Dark requires a 3 hour nap afterwards, or they die. IMO the energy bar shouldn't tick down as fast as it does when you're doing nothing. A good night's sleep and maybe a short nap should be enough to stave off exhaustion.
-Tools wear down too fast. A knife, crowbar, or can opener can survive years of use in real life, and I understand that the devs decided to make them wear down more quickly for the sake of gameplay, but it's a little ridiculous. I shouldn't have to worry about losing my crowbar because it breaks for at least 50 days, but I've already worn mine about halfway down in my 10 day game just by prying open lockers. Also, clothes shouldn't be completely destroyed so quickley unless I get mauled by a bear, which brings me to my next point.
-♥♥♥♥ING BEARS. and wolves. They're wayyyyy too dangerous. I understand that the devs wanted them to be a challenge, but it's too much at this point. If a bear sees you, you're basically screwed, and there's nothing you can do. You'll lose your clothes, and if you don't have first aid, you'll die within the next hour. Wolves aren't as bad, but can still run you down, although they are easier to scare away. To fix this, I'd suggest making it so that I could use my hatchet, knife, or crowbar as a melee weapon instead of having to go through an animation.
Overall, I really like this game. It definitely needs some work, but it's a ton of fun, and it's surprisingly polished for an early access game.

The Walking Simulator genre is a loved & hated phenomenon in gaming. The haters claim they're not really games if for example you can't die, if there's no or limited interaction or puzzles, or if the game is short. But games comes in all shapes & sizes. If they're distributed on gaming platforms, we may as well call them games, and then put a fitting sub category to it. I mean I don't consider all films films just because they were shot on film, some are actually pure garbage, but hey.
I enjoyed this little game for it's story & atmosphere, which resonated strongly with me. But it won't with everyone. I still think it is an unusual story & themes seldom touched upon baked into a classic haunted house type of frame. I applaud the makers for being so brave, & I think stories like this needs to be told more.That is it's strong point. For me, this combined with the setting, designs which is very Tim Burton-esque, excellent sound design & focus on psycholocial horror more than cheap jump scares makes it worth while.
I have not played "The Secret World" which takes place in the same universe as this game, but doing so apparently enhances the story somewhat. They're still both completely self contained though.
On to the negative aspects then:
1.) It is overpriced for what it is. But the developers are totally upfront with both estimated length & price, which leaves it up for consumers to decide if it's worth it or not and if they wanna support it.
I've never understood the objection to short games myself. But the amount of work, or lack thereof, behind a game I can understand objection to. If someone slaps together a game of 1 hour without any innovations applied to mechanics, designs, storytelling etc, and made with only allready existing say music, textures and so on, then yeah, it should be really cheap or free.
But would you like something to drag on just to fill out time, or have it condensed & paced properly? To me the answer is clear. And how do we put a price on an experience, short or long? I know some who thought "Alien: Isolation" got too long, good game as it is. For many it may have been even better if shortened somewhat.
2.) There's also no replay value, except if you want possibly missed achievements. It took me 2 hours to complete, with pauses to fix with recording software, make tea, toilet breaks etc. and I missed 2 achievements.
3.) The story/twist isn't too hard to figure out, even early on, but the road to the revelation is still worth traveling in my opinion.
4.) It's also extremely dark, in more ways than one, but I mean literary so dark that I missed some scares. I doubt that was the intention so you may be advised to make the setting slightly brighter than you think when first presented with the brightness slider at the beginning.
You're also give a flashlight at one point, and I thought I could actually equip it. But you can't and it's auto selected for a certain section. This was unclear to me, but no major issue.
Some complained about not being active in a certain cutscene. But I think the point of the game is to observe a reveal of a mental breakdown and a realisation sort of, and to emulate the feeling of not being in control is great. That can be how it feels, you'e out of control, you can't stop yourself, just as at times you're frozen with fear and can't move. We may complain about people being idiots watching from the distance, but do we know how it is to be that person in that situation? This is what games can force us to do better than possibly any other media: Experience and see from other perspectives.
Also the complaints I've read about boring bits/fillers between the rides/scares, I'd call that build up in this case. Though for some it's probably boring, just like Kubricks "The Shining" is boring for some.
Important stories in games can be told with smart cues, like SPOILER FOR AMONG THE SLEEP! "Among the Sleep" being about the horrors for a toddler living with an alcoholic single parent. The clues among other things being the revelance of empty bottles that start appearing more and more frequently throughout levels that if knocked over will aggrevate the monster. SPOILER END! ”The Park” does the same with some early monolouges. This is what elevates some games beyond their mere base.
Many have pointed out similarities in visual design with "The Babadook", the excellent horror film by Jennifer Kent, but they share similiar subject matters as well.
Horror games has gone from simply being subjected to horrors from others or circumstances around you (basically playing the victim in a horror movie) to incorporate deep psychological meaning (such as with "Silent Hill 2", experiencing the manifested horrors of your own guilt) to even getting to feel the horrors of being or realising that you are "the bad guy". We've come so far in the way we can tell stories in games and it is fantastic!

This game may have been released too soon. Once it's fully bug tested and no longer freezes during the interminably long last mission (which I finished after 7 attempts and two weeks), this game is a 4/5. As it stands, with these glitches, it's a 2/5.
Positives:
- The idea is well thought out and utilized.
- The main RPG game is fun and entertaining, and fairly deep.
- The fourth wall breaks and overall sense of humor are fun.
- Customization- you can change your team's name and their various battle cries. These make the in game dialogue awesome at times. (No, Bill, of course you're as important as anyone else in Sakura and the Rest!) I'd like more costume choices, but what's there is fine.
Negatives:
- The mecha missions are incredibly dull, since it always comes down to the same exact fight (punch punch punch punch special. Click to lesson damage. Click to lessen damage. Click to lessen damage. Punch punch punch punch block.) A few of the enemies have very slow animation that makes the battles even MORE interminable, especially the Barney parody. I changed the mecha summoning catch phrase to "Let's Get This Over With!" I seriously dreaded them every time.
- Glitches. These are the game's current biggest issue. They seem to be clearing up, but they kept me from finishing the last mission for two weeks, which destroyed the game's momentum and my interest in pursuing the other alternate endings. Buyer beware.
- The last mission. There's a plot twist in that last mission that changes who the villain is that makes it less satisfying. I didn't get the final battle I REALLY wanted.
Overall, this game is a lot of fun and incredibly imaginative. Once it's fully polished, I recommend it. Just check out the community board before buying and make sure that things have been cleared up.

Who didn’t have at least some fascination for Power Rangers when they were a kid? Sure the effects were cheesy and the plots formulaic, but there was a special magic when you were younger to seeing a team of colourful heroes take down hordes of nameless aliens and monsters. Hell, Marvel Disney seems to know what’s up. With the help of Kickstarter, Behold Studios launched their tactical RPG based off Saban’s hit franchise with amazing results. Get your suit ready, it’s time to Chromatize.
For such a lighthearted tone, the storyline is legitimately captivating. In what almost seems like a metaphor for the formation of Behold Studios, the 5 stunt actors that do most of the work on their past Sentai show decide to quit out of frustration with their director’s lack of fresh ideas. While building a studio from scratch, our heroes need to shoot episodes quickly and establish a fanbase to turn some revenue so they can keep the lights on, the actors paid, and the new season contracts coming in. The entire game is framed around this television production point of view, with missions gradually blurring the lines of reality into the realms of fantasy and superpower for the characters. Setups for conflict are playful with these ideas; an episode may require multiple reshoots due to on-set power outages, and other times you could be joined by unexpected ally rangers with their own personal vendettas against the alien baddies. Each level ends with tweets from your followers either praising or criticizing your work, and a fun email system helps to make you feel like you’re actually interacting with your niche crowd. The brief tutorial on combat helps succinctly explain the flow of fighting without dragging down players with over-explanation, and it does a great job to tie into the introduction of the story. The whole game carries a consistently fun tone that’s easy to enjoy. It’s a cheerful and self-aware romp through the experiences of being an independent studio and crafting something meaningful to both the creators and fans.
For veterans of the genre it may feel slightly basic and on a smaller scale, but every element you’d want in a tactical RPG has been incorporated here fantastically. There are 5 separate roles for each party member to fill. There’s the lead that acts as a tank, support as a healer, a stealthy and mobile scout, an assault character as your heaviest damage unit, and a techie that specializes in ranged combat and item use. Each class has distinct capabilities and limitations for moving around boards and dispatching enemies, making your choice of team member just as important as what you want to do with them. Audience is gained by performing skillful moves and combos, and this metric dictates your overall fan count and income. Just like most Power Rangers episodes, the squad usually has to engage in some out of costume combat before having enough audience power to Chromatize and activate your powerful suits and abilities. Skilled players can be rewarded with bonus audience by following special director instructions in each episode shoot. Trying to setup tactics to fulfil every side goal can be challenging, but other times the objectives sort of complete themselves.
Players can employ a variety of tactics to clear levels; strategies don’t simply involve just hiding weaker units behind tanks. There are two phases to each character’s turn, allowing you to creatively set up attacks with special weapons, abilities, and a unique gameplay element called Teamwork. Activating this ability sets up the character to help gang-attack enemies with subsequent Rangers, or catapult teammates across the board to reach distant foes. Setting up a Teamwork attack with all 5 members results in a satisfying finishing move that deals massive damage, but players who aren’t careful to use this maneuver appropriately are punished with a loss of audience interest.
Of course many bosses take on a second life after defeat, becoming Kaiju beasts to destroy with your giant mecha robot. These sequences handle similarly to piloting a World of Warcraft vehicle, but unfortunately for how common these parts are they lack the same amount of strategy that can be found in the rest of the game.
Players that put in the time will find it easy to see the inspiration taken from the source material in a loving way, and the thoughtful game behind it. Your experience feels totally customizable from the start. You choose from a large variety of actors; characters with specific stats to fit into the game’s 5 main roles for your squad. You can set the colour for each member as well, fully immersing your interest in your team. If you want the pink ranger to steal the spotlight with the lead role you can totally do that here, or maybe you don’t want a red ranger at all, there really are no limits to team assembly. The unique T.V. production management system to your team’s growth is a wonderfully creative way to explain the game’s action and provide a narrative backbone to the accumulation of player wealth.

Rather than gaining experience and levels, characters boost their stats through buying and crafting new gear. Creating new items from dropped material makes outfitting your team to be a more involved endeavour than simply spending money at a shop, and it motivates you to defeat just a few more foes in each stage to get those extra drops. Quirky item descriptions help keep a smile on your face while you click through these menus. There’s a good emphasis on needing to understand how to get the most out of your cash and saved up materials in order to make your team the best it can be. There’s also an interesting balance between managing your budget to buy your team these upgrades and to also spend on studio expenses, such as better lighting and healthcare, each adding their own statistical advantages. A variety of marketing companies can be hired for different perks in order to gain a larger audience and more income, and just like the items more of these are unlocked as you progress through the story.

The game’s broken down into 5 seasons, with each stage acting as an episode shoot. Starting a new season unlocks the next tier on each character’s ability tree, giving exciting progression to each of the distinct classes. Players can set their team’s abilities to their preference and go back to tweak them later with no penalty, giving a level of freedom to experimentation on these trees that isn’t in most role playing games.
The level of detail in the presentation truly creates a vibrant world to take in, all accompanied by a soundtrack that’s honestly one of the most enjoyable we’ve ever found in an indie game. Little touches like the plucky upbeat signature jingle complements the rest of the perfect retro groove that the music carefully weaves with its effects and scales. Seriously, they’re some of the best bit-style tracks this side of Megaman. Art is so fine-tuned as to even include bent corners on menu screens to make you feel like you’re watching from your tube TV. The familiar pixel art style is done expertly; there’s a real level of character given to the sprites by the careful expressions and animations. The isometric perspective works extremely well for both the gameplay and the artwork.

Behold Studios really hit all the right notes, giving us a great tactical turn-based action title that’s a perfect game for fans of the genre or anyone looking to try it for the first time. You might spend some time wading through some new gameplay elements, but it quickly clicks and with enough skill you’ll soon be taking down monsters just like they do on TV. There’s no doubt that you should take up your offer to join the Chroma Squad.
SCORE: 9.0

A fun environmental survival sandbox that is plagued by terrible combat and lacks base-building mechanics.
To elaborate on the second bit; Once you get out of the inital "I'm going to die" phase, you'll need to find a nice home somewhere to start drying ingredients. Not being able to make a place your own, not even being able to craft a couch when you have five forests worth of logs, really hamstrings the mid to late game experience and not only makes it repetitive, but dull and unimaginative. The game sells itself (perhaps unknowingly to the devs) on exploration, and to make the best items in the game you need to remain in the same area for weeks on end; a complete bore.
The updates are overall quite good and add realism, and are not released as slowly as some others claim.
But I must emphasise, the "I'm going to freeze to death" early game is terrific, and I recommend the game on that alone. I've started several games and never "finished" them because it is quite fun to start in a new area with nothing at all and seeing how you manage to survive even when the RNG dooms you to only find a hachet five days into a blizzard.
TL;DR: Good early game, but terrible mid to late game due to some awkward design choices. Get it on special and periodically check on it for new areas and some good, fun, and tense time-killing.

DO NOT BUY THIS GAME!
It was released in an unfinished state and abandoned by the developer.  At some point, I'm sure Quantum Phoenix intended to release a real second chapter in the Butterfly Sign saga but for whatever reason they were unable to do so and instead, rushed out a slightly modified version of chapter one and then vanished from the internet.
Here are the main problems you will encounter with this game...
1 - You might not be able to play it at all due to a bug that freezes the game on the menu screen.  A version of this bug was in chapter one.  It was never fixed and it carried through to this game.
2 - 75% of the content is an exact repeat of chapter one.  Same areas, same interactions, same everything.
3 - The story is not advanced and there are no answers for questions from chapter one.  The few new story elements are wedged in chaotically and make absolutely no sense.
4 - Over a dozen of the achievements are broken.  Achievements from chapter one are repeated even if they were broken there too or if the actions required were cut from this release.
5 - The developers left the Steam forums the day the game was launched.  Within a month they had abandoned their website and social media accounts.  There is no help coming.
The first Butterfly Sign game showed a lot of promise and I always want to support small creative developers.  Unfortunately, Quantum Phoenix were unable to deliver a second chapter.  Instead, they pushed out a buggy unfinished director's cut of part one and faded into the darkness with whatever money they had grabbed.
At the end of the credits for the aptly named Chapter Two: Human Error, you are told to look for Chapter Three: Wreck of my Warship in the second quarter of 2017.  It's probably for the best that this didn't happen.
Very little content makes the game feel stagnant fresh out of the box.  You play one round, you've played pretty much everything the game has to offer.

That is not a mistake in the system requirements, this game does occupy 20 GB of disk space. And I do mean occupy, there isn’t 20 GB worth of game here.
If you take your time and look around in every room, watch every cutscene, read every document, listen to all the audio logs and ask every question the game is still only about 40 minutes long, give or take some walking speed. I did not play chapter one, but did watch a play through. Most of this chapter two is a copy and paste of chapter one.
There are no options to rebind controls and no option to save. If you quit and continue later you will be back at the start of the area you were in and may have to repeat some steps to make your way back to where you were.
After the opening cutscene you are asked if are you ready, it does not matter what you answer. You can set the difficulty, this only changes how many times you can select the wrong answer, unless you are deliberately selecting the wrong answer to see what happens it is unlikely to ever be an issue.
As you progress through the game you will find a total of four corpses each with three or four nearby items to investigate. Interact with the items and select the correct answer to solve the case, the correct answer is usually obvious.
There is one simple puzzle dragging and dropping some tiles onto a board.
There is a computer with a working web browser, presumably why anyone would bother putting that in a game is a mystery you will have to solve in chapter 3.
At the end you find a fifth corpse and have another choice to make. Once again your answer makes no difference to anything. The game ends abruptly telling you to wait for chapter three. Which no doubt you will be expected to pay for, should you want it.

It only took me 8 hours to beat the final boss on normal mode but even then I would say that Cuphead is worth the money. I should stress that the final product wasn't what I was initially expecting. I thought we were getting a traditional platformer but instead what we have as a very "boss fight" centred game with about 90% of the game being boss fights, as I didn't really follow the hype for this game save for a couple trailers. That being said the game did not leave me dissatisfied either way.
From the off the easiest thing to praise in this game is the visual style. The game looks amazing as it nails the classic 1930s cartoon look and paired with catchy as hell jazz music from the same period it makes for one of the best visually and audibly designed games in a very long time.
Keep in mind there are some platforming style levels but these are very few and far between with the big emphasis being on the boss fights. Like I said this doesn't bother me but this might be a turn off for some platforming veterans. Also this is such an unforgiving game. It isn't the hardest game I've ever played but is easily one of the hardest modern 2D games I have played. World 1 was fairly comfortable with a few rough patches here and there but once I got to world 2 I wanted to snap my controller in half. Despite this, the little line you get when you die saying how close you were to beating whatever boss is a great way of maintaining that "just one more try" kind of gameplay that this game excells at.
My only two problems with the game is 1. the hub world and 2. the shop system. This hub world was so unneeded. Sure it works and you could do worse but it just serves to break the pace of the game. Sure having hidden paths to skip parts of the game is a cool idea but you would want to try to beat every level anyway. It just felt like a forced addition to keep up with the plethera of modern games that use hub worlds these days, and once I had defeated the final boss it was a pain to constantly be going back and forth through the map to get to specific bosses I felt like retrying. Also the shop system is awful. You pay for new upgrades with coins you get from some levels which is fine but the bad part is that there are only ever four items to buy at one time. When you buy something it is replaced with something else and what it is replaced by is fixed for that item. So let's say there is an upgrade you don't want, but there may be a really good upgrade following it if you buy it so you take the gamble and buy it. It's a complete guessing game whether it was worth your hard earned cash. I get that's kind of a stratergy in gambling but it really made me relucant to buy anything in the shop without a guide so that I didn't miss something that could really help me.
Those really are my only problems with the game. As far as gameplay goes this is one of the best indie games I have played in years. A lot of the time some indie devs will intice you over with the promise of a great product, and they will get you to spend £15 on something that isn't even finished (I'm looking at you Derelict!). This isn't the case with Cuphead. Here you have an indie game with more love and passion put into it than most AAA games these days. Remember though the game is VERY hard so if that isn't for you then think twice before you buy this. If however you love a challenge then the game is selling for such a steal of a price so I would recommend it hugley.

By now you've probably heard about the highly renowned platformer Limbo. The game has won a bucket full of awards since its release, and rightfully so. Artistically, it was one of the pioneers of the black and white, minimalistic silhouette design; it went on to inspire a plethora of copycats. Though often duplicated, the experience that comes from playing Limbo is one that's unique, and it could never be duplicated even if one tried hard. Originally launching in 2010 for most platforms, the title found its way on to steam in the middle of 2011.
There's no real outward story to speak of, but rather a series of events that the developer, Playdead, have left gamers to interpret for themselves. A small boy wakes up in a new, unforgiving, and sometimes treacherous land, but it soon becomes apparent that he's chasing after someone. The landscape begins as a forest, laden in thick fog, but later turns into a crumbling city. You may think that at some point you'll come across even the tiniest spark of color, but alas all is gloom here. Be prepared to meet some characters that are like you, stuck in the void as they bombard you with obstacles, but most that you meet will be dead; ususally by apparent suicide.
The world of Limbo is filled with platforming puzzles and hazardous traps that will undoubtedly keep you on your toes. While taking in the haunting scenery, you may find yourself victim to stepping on a well hidden bear trap, or not quite making a precision jump that ends with you landing on a bed of spikes. Maybe you think you need to push a box further into the water, only to find out that you cannot swim, and subsequently you drown. Death will come many times over for you, though favorably the checkpoints in this sinister land are forgiving. Much like its aesthetic design, the controls are also simple; you can jump, walk, climb, and move some items.
Truly a haunting, gloomy, and at times depressive experience, Limbo is an amazing platformer. Even those like myself that may not be enthusiasts on the genre will find themselves enjoying this bleak adventure. There's no tutorial, given the simple design of the game. There's no text, the world and its events are left up to your perception and imagination. Despite the lack of narrated story, the game stands strong and immersive. It's one title that you won't forget for years to come. Highly recommended for platformer lovers, enjoyers of the bleak and depressive, and those seeking an unforgettable event.

If you're expecting a D&D roleplaying game (like Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights, etc), look elsewhere. That's not what this game is about.
This is a D&D Adventure system game, a digital adaptation of the "Tomb of Annihilation" board game. If you're familiar with this already, you may love it. Seems true to that style of challenging tile-based play.
For newbies like me, or even those who've never heard of ToA but thought, "Oooh, D&D-based game for a reasonable price? Let's check it out!", this review is for you. :) Please read on for basic info about this game:
+ + + PROS + + +
+ Seems like a faithful adaptation of the board game by the same name. Same default heroes, setting style, similar (but expanded) content, etc. If you liked the game IRL, or just read/watch something about that, you'll probably love this version too.
+ Crafting system. A feature not found in the board game, allowing you to boost heroes with better weapons/armor/etc. (essentially the only control you have over their build) at the cost of gold and materials found during missions. It's very linear, but the layout is clear and concise, showing all the possible options, with a symbol that appears to remind you that certain categories have something you can readily craft.
+ Graphics and audio are both great. Really enjoyed some of the "boss" music and general atmosphere.
+ Because you are constantly encouraged (if not forced) to keep moving and discover new tiles, it keeps the content fast-paced, so it never feels too boring (although it can become overwhelming for the same reason - see Cons)
- - - CONS - - -
- First disappointment: you are limited to four set characters, with no option to create your own. Human Ranger, Saurial (Lizardfolk?) Paladin, Aarakocra Wizard, and Tabaxi Bard. Each have set attacks (with an alternate option here of one other weapon/spell choice) and abilities that may be triggered under specific circumstances, but there's not much chance to even customize these guys. So already it feels like you're forced into certain styles of play, but then some of them, (at least early on) struggle to survive WAY more than others, which only further limits your choices for certain missions. If this game someday added Custom characters, I might be more inclined to replay.
- Encounter system. Random events trigger for every individual character turn if you do not "discover" a new chunk of the map (which can in itself lead to more enemy spawns, more negative effects, etc.) That means, when you're controlling 4 characters, you can end up with 4 negative effects. Because these effects often hurt multiple characters (attack all within an area, impose disadvantage, spawn more enemies, stun your character, etc), this can quickly become overwhelming. When you're already in combat, it can be downright ridiculous. Just walking around feels more dangerous than fighting enemies! This challenge walks a fine line, but encounters just feel more frustrating than fun.
- Crafting system. Even the earliest, easiest items only have a 70% chance to succeed, but even if you boost them up to 90% (by paying extra gold on top of the base price) you can still fail, which means you lose all the materials and gold invested. I think these odds (or the cost to aid them) need tweaking, because it really sucks to lose all your hard work. Permanent risk, not much reward.
- Combat. Mostly this was fine, but I found it frustrating that as soon as you discover an enemy on a new tile, that enemy takes a turn IMMEDIATELY after the discovering character's turn. There's no way to stop it or mitigate it, almost as if the enemies have permenent Surprise on you, but you never get that in return.
- Clunky non-combat turns. This would be an easy fix, but it was a pet peeve for me: even if there's no enemy in sight, the game still takes an unskippable "enemy turn" for every single character turn. May not sound like much, but it really drags to watch that annoying animation when there's no need to have it at all.
~~~
All in all, it's not a terrible game. Like I said before, if you're looking for D&D core rules with in-depth storyline and character development, this is definitely not for you. If you can forgive some of the aforementioned shortcomings, and already think you might like the D&D Adventure board game style, go for it. When taken for what it is, "Tales from Candlekeep: Tomb of Annihilation" feels like it has potential, but needs some changes before it can really feel like fun.

Anyway, it's basically a Star Wars Total War game. If that sounds appealing, grab it!

First off, The Beginner's Guid is not a game, for the most part. It is essentially a story spoken to you with the content on screen complementing the story in a more interactive way than a movie, but that is necessary because of the story itself. An experience like that is not a game, but I would still recommend it if I thought it was good. The Beginner's Guide, however, is not.
The Beginner's Guide tells a story about the human psyche. As a person suffering from PTSD and depression, that is a theme I struggle with every day. As a developer I can relate even more.
The story is open to interpretation, you may take it at face value or you may seek deeper meanings. Another option you can do is to take it as an experience (and I say experience rather than a game because it really isn't a game) and not attach any meaning to it. Whichever way you choose to go, I would not recommend this, not even at the currently discounted €4.49 price tag, let alone the full price. The reason is that, whichever way you slice the story, unless you're taking it just as an experience with no real meaning, it is pretentious and has a much great value to the person telling it than the person experiencing it, yet the person experiencing is the one paying for it and the person telling it is the one receiving money for it. If you look at it as just an experience, rather than an experience worth your while you can look past some of the issues mentioned earlier, but you still get a not so interesting experience that you had to pay money for.
The Stanley Parable was a great game, I love it and am really glad we got to experience it, however, this experience tarnished even The Stanley Parable for me. This is the kind of thing I would pay someone to experience, not expect someone to pay to experience it.

I recommend it if you enjoyed left 4 dead when it was first released. It's the same style of game, if you enjoyed, and put a lot of time into, left 4 dead I'd be willing to bet you'll do the same with this, I know I'm going to.
Pros
: So far I've only played as support and assualt(by choice) and can say those two are fun. I havent even played as the monster so I won't talk about that area much. Playing as the hunters is basically a more in depth left 4 dead. Each character brings something unique, other teammates need to save someone who's gotten attacked, need to stick together etc.
: I've enjoyed that characters personalities and banter so far.
: The maps are varied enough, and have changes that can make things easier for the monster or hunter (weather makes it harder to see/track the monster)
:Unlock hunters fairly quickly, so if you really want to try different characters it only takes a few games to get the next one in that class.
:Overall solid gameplay, a few bugs but I've had nothing game breaking
Cons
:Not the games fault, but since each class is important when you get a teamate who isn't very good it can be frustrating, even more so then in left 4 dead. Trying to track the monster when your assualt keeps getting caught by wildlife is difficult.
:Connection problems, I didn't get to play at midnight release but evidently it had some lag issues then, when I started playing (at around 4pm the day of release) I only had one game that had bad connection issues, every other match had no problems, for me at least.
So far these are the only problems I've had.
Now Ill move into the thing everyone else is reviewing the game about, the price/dlc.
First off I can't speak about the Australian price, I don't live there and also don't know who decides that price, steam or the supplier.
About the different game versions.
100$(The one I purchased second) This one gets you the season pass along with some monster skins. So all the hunters and monsters with some added goodies for 40$. The price of a monster is 15$ and a hunter is 7$ or 8$ evidently. What this boils down to is knowing where to buy the game. I bought this version (legally and everything) for 75$, so I basically payed the price for the monster to get the monster along with all those extra goodies. Im not even mentioning everything because Im lazy, but basically it's an ok deal for the full asking price, and it's quite easy to get for cheaper.
80$ I didn't purchase this one, so I'm going to keep my mouth shut about something I don't know.
60$(First version I bought) This is the base game, I first bought this one for 45$, about the price everyone is saying the game should be (for some reason). Again it's about knowing where to buy the game (again perfectly legally). If you don't know you can always wait till the inevitable steam sale when the game drops this low, or lower.
Overall I think everyone needs to do some research and find where to purchase the cheapest game. When I bought the base game the other two versions were out so I can't say to buying the base game and then having other versions with dlc included announced. What I can say is steam has a nifty feature that lets you gift a game (imagine that) so if you bought the base game and then for some reason decide to purchase one of the other versions for the dlc, you can give it to one of your friends. It's a simple process that can actually be done right through steam too.
While I do think 15$ for just a monster is quite a lot of money, why not just spend that to get two monsters and six hunters.
Overall good game, try to get it for cheaper then it is, recommend the 100$ version, even if you can't get it cheaper which is easy to do.

Evolve is a asymmetrical multiplayer based game for five players or AI counterparts.  The premise of Evolve is that four players play as the hunters who are dropped on to the planet Shear to remove a "wildlife threat" - The monster.
Currently, Evolve has three different playable monsters; The Goliath which is a large tank that can deal large amounts of damage with rock throws, fire and charges.  The Kraken is specialized in ranged combat while the Wraith is a master of Stealth. The Behemoth will be the fourth playable monster, which will be £10-£15 at launch.
There are four different classes of hunters to play; Medic, Trapper, Support and Assault. Each of these classes give the player three characters to unlock who all come with their own set of tools and weapons to help your comrades take down the monster before it inevitably leads you and your squad to your impending doom. If we take the medic for example, Val (The first playable Medic) has a medgun but Lazarus (Second playable medic) does not, instead he possesses a tool that can revive fallen allies.
The four classes having three playable characters each is a bonus - Of all of the characters I have played no two play the same.  Val is a more focused Team Fortress 2 style of medic while Lazarus can be on the offense more with the ability to revive allies who have perished.
Turtle Rock have set up the medic class in such a way that it will appeal to more players and that is fantastic - Human Medics are better than AI ones after all, right? Val has a sniper rifle that places weak points on the monster that your other team mates can shoot to deal bonus damage, a simple medgun to heal all of your teammates from a distance, a tranquilizer gun that slows down the monster considerably and a healing burst which heals you and your allies instantly. Having four different tools gives the medic a different dynamic compared to some other titles.  It is fun to lay waste to the Goliath with weakpoints while they are being shot at by your other team mates and slowing it down when it attempts to escape.
The trapper has two main jobs; track down the monster and trap him within a large dome.  Once the monster is trapped, they can not escape until the dome runs out or is taken down. If you have a good trapper on your team who does not miss when throwing the trap, you stand a good chance of winning the match.
Assault is exactly what you would think it is - A class to deal damage. The primary job of the assault is to deal mass amounts of damage to the monster while being supported by the other three classes.
The support class is the only class that I have not played much of, but what I can say from what I played is that the biggest selling point of the Support is to offer shields to your allies. The shield works in the same way the medgun does - Point and shoot at your allies to shield them from damage.
Overall the classes have a nice variety to them and each class has a important role to play during the match - Always play to the strengths of the character you have chosen.  When you play a class for the first time you will receive a brief introductory video before the match begins to give you a rough outline of what your primary job is and what your class specific tools do.  This is especially important in a game like Evolve when you need your teammates to pull their weight as the monster gets more powerful.
Outside of the traditional hunt game mode, Evacuation mode is available.  In here you will find a little back story to what is going on within the game world along with several different game types. The objective of Evacuation is to save as many survivors as possible over five matches of Evolve - This can take up to one hour of gameplay. Evacuation features different playable game modes including Nest in which the squad of hunters must hunt out and destroy the monster eggs before the monster has a chance to hatch them, Rescue is exactly what it says on the tin - find and rescue survivors and the final match on day five forces the hunters to defend generators from oncoming waves of enemies to allow the survivors to escape.  I have had varying experiences on this game mode - Playing in public lobbies I can get both team mates who play their role well and roughly have the jist of what to do and that can be a fantastic and rewarding experience for five straight games.  On the other hand, having players who are brand new to Evolve, haven't completed any of the tutorials or watched the videos will likely prove you with a frustrating experience.
I find Evolve entertaining enough to continuously go back and play "just one more game", even in public lobbies. However, during matches it can begin to feel slow or even sluggish when you have four hunters running around a empty map searching for the monster for minutes on end.  This is especially frustrating when a match of Evolve is generally 10 - 15 minutes in length. It is possible that when players have more experience with the game, those of us who play as the trapper will have a better idea of what is going allowing the monster to be tracked in a more efficient manner.
This title features a lot of downtime - There are loading screens when you start up the game, before a match and after a match.  Downtime can occur often during a match  if you are the type of player who will often go down in a fight, or even if your medic is not doing their job properly. When you die in Evolve you are forced to spectate your remaining team members while waiting for a drop-ship to throw you back in to the action after a few minutes.
I have found a issue with the PC version of Evolve, after I have played a couple of games my mouse cursor will vanish from the screen and menus and it makes it incredibly difficult to select anything.  This can be annoying to both you and your squad who are patiently waiting on you to select your character, class, perks and skin.
Speaking of skins - Evolve has A LOT of DLC, and I mean a lot. I believe every character has skins and/or a skin pack you can buy, the monsters have different skins to purchase, there is a monster DLC pack, Season Pass - In fact there is so much downloadable content for this game already, on day one, that the cost of it nearly surpasses that of the base game itself.  That is absolutely absurd and I completely understand why there are many, many unhappy customers out there who feel that all of this content (beside the monster pack and season pass) should be in the game.  Why cant we have unlockable skins within Evolve instead of paying around £5 for a skin?
It almost feels like Turtle Rock set out to create a premium game with a freemium monetization model and it has♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off a lot of customers.  If you do not want to put your money down for this type of transaction - I urge you to not do it if you feel like it will show developers that this type of DLC is not wanted by a lot of customers.  However, if you want to purchase the DLC you should obviously go right ahead with your purchase.
I own the Season Pass and even I was confused at what content I gain from it.  The Steam store page for the season pass states that I unlocked the tier three characters for each class which means that, these characters which are already in the game are hidden behind a paywall.  You can not play the final character of each class unless you fork out £19.99 for the season pass.
If you have watched gameplay of Evolve or you have read some articles and reviews and you think this game is for you, give it a go. Games of Evolve are fun and thrilling to play and can lead to some seriously intense moments.  I have enjoyed my time with the game so far and I am looking forward to jumping back in.

I really wanted to like this game. I kept seeing people praising it everytime it was mentioned, so I decided to pick it up during a sale. Unfortunately it turned out to be very disappointing.
The first major issue I ran into was the absolutely horrible performance. My modest rig can play Battlefield 4 on high settings at a rock solid 60fps. I've had to lower the settings in this game all the way to the absolutely lowest and it still has constant frame drops and graphical glitches like geometry spazzing out.
Secondly, while the pace of play and the realistic feel of the gunfights leads to some amazingly tense moments, these moments are few and far between. The problem is that the game heavily favours camping. If you move, you're a target. If you lie down in a corner somewhere and just wait for people to pass by you can be a killing machine. So in game modes where there is an attacking and defending team, the defenders are heavily favoured.
Also, there are no indicators showing if someone's a teammate or enemy. For hardcore fans this is a plus that adds to the tension. For me it got annoying fast. The different models and costumes aren't distinct enough to quickly see if you're facing an enemy. If you're in a game with Japanese vs US troops, good luck. The major difference between the two is that Japanese outfits are tan coloured (brown-greenish) while US costumes are olive coloured (green-brownish). Expect constant teamkilling and a chat filled with "sorry".
Then there is the upgrade system. Yes, this so called hardcore old school shooter has you gaining xp, leveling up classes and unlocking weapons and attachments. Expect not to even have a pistols for the first dozen or so matches you play, and expect to not touch any class but rifleman for a couple dozen hours. Also expect to be completely blown out by players with machine guns.
Even if you get past these hurdles. there are only a few active servers, the rest are mostly filled with bots. And for some reason everyone just seems to be playing Bridges of Druzhina. In all the matches I've played I've seen about 4 maps in total. The urban maps are fine and well designed, but the more open maps feel too open, with very little to cover your advance. This again leads to camping being the mostt efficient strategy. Also, lot's of servers have custom rules that you can only find out by visiting their websites, so it feels like playing blind a lot of the time.
I really want to like this game, and I'll keep trying at it, but I don't think all the praise is deserved. The good points are not strong enough to outweigh the issues. I'm sure experienced players will think I'm a casual who's too stupid to apreciate this game, but the fact is that as a new player this game just fails to be engaging enough.

I'll start things off by saying that I did have a hard time getting this game to work at first, which was a disappointment considering how much I was looking forward to playing it. The issue being that after installation, the application would get hung up on the "preparing to launch" dialogue box without actually launching the game.
That being said, after quite a bit of research I discovered that many others were having the same problem as I was and came to the unfortunate realization that there were no actual solutions to be found. I immediately headed over to Playdead to contact their support team and to my surprise, they responded very quickly. Just to give you an idea because frankly, I think it deserves mentioning; I sent out my initial e-mail at 3:41am, to which I received a response at 6:17am, less than three hours later. Needless to say, I was quite impressed.
The individual that contacted me seemed genuinely nice - as far as these things can be judged without speaking to the person directly - and found them to be friendly, concise and very helpful. I was provided a number of possible solutions and steps to take, along with clear instructions on how best to solve the problem.
I'm not sure if the issue is the same for everyone, but if I were to make an educated guess based on the system requirements and my own experience, it seems Limbo throws an error if the Shader Model hardware utilized by your GPU is outdated. In order for this to work properly, the easiest thing to do would simply be to download the latest drivers for your particular video card. I also updated DirectX and made sure there were no pending updates for my system whatsoever, just to be on the safe side. With that out of the way, the problem I had was a thing of the past and wasted no time in booting up the game to see what I had been missing out on.
My opinion may be a little biased given that I'm a sucker for these types of games but with that in mind, on to the actual gameplay...
You start off in the middle of a somber forest filled with various dangers, obstacles, and good old-fashioned film grain effects, which I have to say were an interesting design choice; one that was quite beneficial as it added to the overall feel of the game. Within the first couple of minutes, you quickly discover that the concept and control scheme are simple enough, which is what you want for a puzzle-platformer.
All you need are five buttons (four arrow keys and "Ctrl") on your keyboard: walk left, walk right, push/pull objects and climb ropes and ladders. That's all you get. Can't get much simpler than that, right? Well, I suppose you can, but that's beside the point. Don't let this fool you though because the game is quite challenging in certain areas as you brave the perils of various twisted environments as a young boy in search of his sister.
The story elements present in LIMBO are subtle and left up to the interpretation of the player, inciting a great deal of speculation among fans as to what the boy's treacherous journey actually means. If your curiosity was strong enough to warrant a search of the game's plot you would have found out right away that there aren't any definitive answers, yet there are some clues and a general understanding regarding certain aspects of the story.
There was no BGM to speak of like you would traditionally be expecting but rather just the subdued, ambient background noise that seems to fit the developer's intentions very well. The black and white tones and sparse lighting came together nicely and added a great deal to the experience. The effects seemed appropriate to the situation in which the player finds themselves and added to the atmosphere and immersion of the game to give it an eerie, haunting feel.
One thing of note that I don't see or rather hear in a lot of games are that certain areas actually employ the use of auditory cues in order to progress. This is most prominent in the secret level, where the player must traverse an entire stage - that is somewhat longer than prior chapters -  in complete darkness. Do yourself a favor and crank up the volume before attempting this. Having a good headset or even a pair of speakers here will make your life a lot easier.
The puzzles had an interesting curve and there was a definite, noticeable progression to the difficulty, which flowed exceptionally well and I felt kept things from getting tedious. At the same time, the puzzles weren't so easy as to induce a coma from mind-numbing boredom or hard enough that they would make you rage-quit or suffer for hours on end trying to solve them. LIMBO found the perfect balance between the two by providing enough challenge and stimulation that makes you want to play it again and again.
All in all the game was quite fun. I've played through 3 times already collecting all the achievements and it still hasn't gotten dull. It has 39 chapters, not including the secret area, which may seem like it's a bit longer but is honestly on the shorter side of that spectrum. Start to finish I'd say it's possible to complete the game in roughly forty-five to an hour, give or take a few minutes; after you get your bearings on the first play-through that is. Keep in mind, however, this doesn't account for speed-runners, who I can only assume are capable of finishing in much less time.
Bottom line is, Limbo is a simplistic, streamlined puzzle-platforming game that has a certain charm to it and I would definitely recommend it to anyone who is a fan of the genre or anyone else for that matter. It was well worth the effort it took to get the game working and after I had a chance to play it for myself, I have to say that all the hype surrounding it has not been exaggerated. LIMBO is a phenomenal piece of creativity, a credit to the indie community and the industry as a whole.

Chroma Squad is full of style with its fun writing, simple yet engaging gameplay, and so close to copyright infringement for all its references it's not even funny. In the game you control a group of people that run a live-action power rangers rip off show where they fight evil baddies and have huge mecha fights.
Before you start one of these levels though (referred to as episodes in game), you have to micromanage your money at your studio (It is a t.v. show after all), in this section you purchase upgrades for your studio and purchase equipment for characters and such and it is surprisingly engaging how much thought I personally put in to figure out where to put my resources, did I want to put more money towards purchasing materials to craft cardboard box equipment, or did I want to invest in marketing agencies to increase my fanbase and reap extra benefits for a few episodes? It gives you enough to manage without overwhelming you.
The combat is your typical tactical rpg with skills and classes and such,however there is a nice little temawork mechanic where if you set a character to teamwork mode you can assist other teammates in team attacks and acrobatics for more movement adding a little extra depth to the combat. Mecha fights play differently as when you're fighting bigger monsters you play a sort of risk-reward turn based game, you basically have hit chance and damage multiplier, whenever you attack and hit the monster you get to keep combo-ing them with attacks and other abilities and as long as you land hits, for every successful hit your damage for the next attack goes up, however it has a lower chance of hitting and when you miss it becomes the monsters turn, this also employs a decent amount of strategy but can ultimately feel like luck sometimes, its still enjoyable and doesn't detract from the main game
When it comes to customization this game handles that aspect very well allowing customization of not only characters, but even the customization of the company, you can name the super hero squad whatever you like as well as the mechas and what they shout when they suit up, heck if you wanted to you could even theme the whole thing around butts! Butt Squad! Mecha Butt! Butter up! There is a great amount of customization in the game!
Overall it comes down to this:
Do you like Power ranger esque tactical rpgs with funny parody writing, lots of customization, and fun gameplay, while micromanaging your own butt studio?
Then Chroma Squad is for you

Before letting the hate flow, my review is
for people that like the board game, but for people who've never heard of the board game who might be thinking "This looks like an interesting tactical RPG!" Naturally, my review will be criticizing the board game as well as the video game as this appears to be a faithful vidya remake.
Do not buy this if you're expecting a TRPG. It's not a system of "The player team acts and then the enemy team acts", or even "One character acts and then another acts". It's Villain phase > Hero phase > Exploration phase > Encounter phase.
Now, the hero phase and villain phase are to be expected, that's just TRPGs in general. The exploration phase is .. okay? You can only move once per turn (based on the little I've played), and when you end your turn, a new map block drops into its place, almost like a jigsaw puzzle, and you see the traps/enemies in that block. The problem is the villains on that block immediately get a turn after you discover them with basically no way to mitigate that. It would be like a cop kicking a door open and somehow the criminals get the drop on him every single time. I feel like that's stupid, but once again, I'm a TRPG player, not a board game player.
And then you have the "encounter phase", which pretty much seals the deal that it's not meant for TRPG players. I was playing one of the earliest quests on Horrific difficulty which I'm sure people will have a problem with, and just walking around without any enemies in sight, the "encounter" would result in poison darts, rocks falling on my head, etc that would deplete half of my HP against something I can't prevent. I don't like that system at all.
Also, this is one of those games that isn't at all D&D core rules, but rather D&D themed with the D&D logo slapped on it. Not unlike the Neverwinter MMO! Though that's really just nitpicking given the whole boardgame thing.
EDIT: I'd give this game a double thumbs-down if I could due to a person I've been arguing with here in the comments; I'm pretty sure it's a company shill. Whatever he's being paid, it's too much. If you're interested in seeing what a shill on Steam looks like, check the comments.

I have over 600 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #57 - Enemy Mind
I cracked a smile right off the bat as I started playing Enemy Mind as it reminded me of playing Gradius on the NES.  It's got the same side-scroller point of view, and the pixel art style has a similar feel to it as well.  I really enjoyed the sound effects as well, they mostly sounded like something you'd hear on an 8 bit machine, mixed with some sounds that I swear sounded like they came right from an Atari 2600.
But what's most interesting about Enemy Mind is the twist it adds to the typical shooter.  You've probably gotten use to the whole shoot enemies, dodge bullets, and pick up powerups that give you new weapons or other abilities.  In Enemy Mind, you don't pick up powerups, but instead you take over other ships, inheriting their abilities instead.
You basically have 2 weapons.  One is your offensive weapon, which varies based on what ship you are currently in.  The other is your psychic beam, or whatever you want to call it, that when it comes in contact with another ship, you take it over.  If the beam misses, then it just boomerangs back to you.
This changes up the gameplay because each ship has a limited amount of hull and ammo.  So you can only take a couple of hits (varying based on what ship you are in), and you have a limited number of shots.  So you're forced to continually bounce between different ships in order to stay alive.
Each ship type has a different weapon, and some of these are exactly what you'd expect in a shooter, varying from your average straight shooting bullets to lasers, to triple-fire shots.  But other ships add some unusual variety, such as the ship that launches itself forward like a missle.  You can even take over asteroids which don't have any offensive capability, but basically just house your consciousness until you can project yourself into something else.
The game is broken up into multiple levels, with each level being broken up into multiple stages, with the final stage being a boss battle.  If you die then you start over at the beginning of the stage you died on.  You do have a limited number of lives, but you can continue when the game is over.  Also once you progress past a level then anytime you start a new game you can skip levels you have already beaten.
I played with a gamepad, and didn't have any issues with the controls at all.  I also like the fact that it supports a second local player, but I didn't actually try it out with a second person.
I had fun with the game, but it also doesn't look like something that I would play for hours on end.  It seems more like the kind of game where I will get through all of the levels and beat the game, and move on to something else.  It's fun and all, but for me not necessarily a lot of replayability.  So with that in mind, you might be a bit wary of the $9.99 price if you don't think it's something you'll spend a lot of time with.  This might be a better game to pick up on sale or in a bundle.
But, unlike many shooters I've played, I genuinely feel like Enemy Mind has added something new to the genre and isn't just another generic shooter.  Between it's uniqueness and the well done implementation, this is certainly a game I can recommend checking out.

Pros:
+ The level of quailty and polish in this title, despite its graphical style, is astounding
+ The pixel graphics fit the game, as its an almsot perfect callback to the arcades.
+ Gameplay is fluid and tight. Each wave is a new challenge to surmount, and in later levels strategies can be formed to defeat each wave.
+ For a shoot'em-up style game, the story is exceptional. The story-telling in the game is both clever and well-written.
+ You can shoot the credits
+ The Aratus, the opposing force to the humans, are more interesting aliens than those in other games
+ Bosses were creative. They weren't just bullet sponges, and the mind-control mechanic is realy put to the test in these fights. There were all rewarding to defeat
+ For once, points were something I acutally cared about. I felt amazing to see those numbers go up.
Cons:
- The difficulty spike of the last level was unwarranted; the levels leading up to it should've matched this difficulty slope
- There was inexplicable fps drops at seemingly random* moments, despite my computer being more than capable of running the game
* "Random" meaing completely unpredictable. Happened about 3 times in 10 hours of play (No general interval of time between them)
Final thoughts:
A must-buy if on sale. Even if it isn't, I'd say its worth the $10 anyway. Gameplay is innovative in the best kind of way. It honestly just makes sense, rather than being some weird gimmick. Art syle is fantastic, even with its low resolution. Game is polished and has a level of quality other companies seem to forget when they go for a 16-bit art style.

Stop reading these reviews and give your money to these awesome developers!

I rarely write reviews, but I have enjoyed this game so much I felt the developers deserve it.
I started out in this game with little clothes, in a valley someplace in a fridgid environment, no idea of directions and starting to freeze immediately. It was frightening. Starving, no water, and not realizing how fast I could catch hypothermia and die were constant companions. The game does a great job of immersion and I must admit I was sucked into it for almost 40 hours within a few says before I realized how much I was playing it.
Early game the worst part was the freezing, getting caught in a blizzard or high winds with little protection, getting lost and not knowing where my basecamp was, even what a basecamp was. I got lost constantly, trying to remember landmarks but when a snowstorm comes up its so easy to get lost.
No water...dehydrated....weak...starving...calories burn faster the colder it is...didnt know that....so cold.
That moment when I spot a deer carcass..my heart jumps and I am so hopeful, only to find out it is frozen and I am unable to harvest it with my bare hands. I think I died from hypothermia that night.
Early game I died quite a bit, my first 5 games often dying within the first 48 hours.
Then figuring out how to balance my time, because originally I was pretty frantic and not knowing what to do to survive. One minute I would be gathering wood, next getting dehydrated because I ran out of drink and not knowing how to melt snow. Starving...getting attacked by wolves...really scary stuff.
I am now past day 50. I have figured out how to balance my time, and to plan my days out in advance. Have killed wolves, deer, have made clothing from their hides which allows me to manage the cold quite well, even in the worst storms. There is no longer constant terror as a companion, but there is no time to sit on my laurels, firewood, food, water, repairs to equipment does not allow a life of leisure.
Overall, I really recommend buying this game. It is worth every penny.
Last comment...screw bears in general. Getting mauled sucks.
Good luck out there.

Developed by SkyGoblin Studios, the Journey Down: Chapter One creates an urban world where the player takes control of Bwana, a cool, Caribbean "brudda," who works at a gas station on a pier.  The game begins when a young woman comes looking for a mysterious book that Bwana's long-lost adoptive father, Kaonandodo, once possessed.  This is only part one of a game trilogy.
Though the game is relatively short (if you speed-run it and skip all the dialogue, you can beat it within half an hour), exploring the game and taking the time to look at each detailed scene will give the player an hour or two worth of time. The art style is immediately reminiscent of Grim Fandango, though with a more African and Caribbean theme.  The characters resemble Moai statues or strunken heads in a pseudo-modern setting.
The puzzles are designed simply and the game is short enough that you won't have any problem remembering which character required which item or what item was needed to solve which puzzle.  The puzzles are very much like puzzles in the Monkey Island games, and it's clear the studio used LucasArts adventures as inspiration for style and presentation.  The cast is fully voiced and they will give enough hints to imply what they need.  There might be a time when you find yourself clicking everything on everything to  see what works, but the solutions are logical and with enough thought can be solved without ever needing a walkthrough.
Though some reviewers have criticised the voice acting (and at times it isn't perfect), the one character I've seen the most criticism from is the main character, Bwana.  He has a thick, stereo-typical Jamaican accent, and despite the criticism, I find him the most charming and funny character, closely followed by his adoptive brother, Kito.  The wit in the writing stands out with these characters and Bwana's delivery on lines is so funny, though many times the limited animation on his face detracts from the seriousness of certain parts so the character often fails to come across as sympathetic in a few instances.
The atmosphere created in the game is stunning.  With very little exposition and establishment of the setting, the player is brought into this cool, dark world run by an evil power company.  The painted backgrounds are gorgeous and accurately represent the urban setting cut off from the high-society.  The tone is eerie, with this goofy character, Bwana, juxtaposed by the governement corruption and dirty-dealings going on within the city.  Characters constantly drop hints about the evil power company, an embargo, and other political and corporate dealings that build up the city as a character in itself.  My favourite scene in the game is when Bwana talks with a man who works a newsstand under a bridge.  The man explains how the train doesn't stop at his location any more. That scene captures the setting completely with the ideas of corruption and not looking out for the little man.  It feels like a real city, even though the game only represents a minute fraction of the whole city.
Lastly, the most noticably brilliant part of this game is the music.  It is astounding.  The composer who worked for SkyGoblin sadly passed away during the development of Chapter Two, but his legacy lives on through the game's soundtrack.  The soundtrack is available on BandCamp and I fully suggest getting it for both Chapters One and Two.  The music adds so much depth to the setting, creating the final piece to really put the player in this game's world.  It's memorably catchy, and adds an appropriate amount of melancholy to a generally humourous game.
If the current price tag for the game is too much (given you are only getting one chapter), I suggest waiting for a sale (I bought it on sale as a Chapters One and Two Bundle).  However, if it's still too much for you on sale, the developer's website has a free, low-res version which makes the game pixelated, making it look much more like Monkey Island. A lot of love and care and research went into this game and I suggest supporting it.

The encounters are a bit frustrating, and I would like it better if they gave you more of an indication of what is happening rather than just text. I know there are sound effects and animations for some things, but maybe they could add some immersive art that pops up with the encounter text. This would really help give the encounters recognition and meaning. Right now they feel random and annoying. The same could be said for the trap effects. What is happening here? -Just some small text in the combat log. Adding a d20 that pops up and rolls would be a really beneficial addition to the text in the combat log. There are other things that could be fine-tuned too (how do I know where an ambush site is?) but I will wait until I finish the game to compile a full critique.
If you are looking for an expansive, in-depth, or open-world computer role-playing game experience, then this is not a good fit for you. However, if you are looking for a casual and good-looking adventure board game in the digital space, then I would recommend that you try out Tales from Candlekeep: Tomb of Annihilation!
