Bioshock was one of those games that initially passed me by in 2007 but I had always been curious to play it  so when I recently saw it in a sale I snapped it up and I really dont regret it.
it's is a very tightly driven fps/adventure game that for a 2007 game is stunning, tight controls married to gorgeous 50's modern/chic design it simply glistens with personality and can really offer a unique and entertaining experience...while it could be argued it does share a lot in common with Fallout 3 in regards to design and aesthetics I personally think it differenciates itself enough to stand on it's own two feet (Though some may disagree on that point) The range of Weapons in game is impressive with a nice difficulty curve to match, the ability to use plasmids (Essentially magic spell/lasers that fire from your hands) is also welcome for racking up decent hit combos (You will experience no greater in game pleasure than stunning an enemy with lightning fingers only to then beat them with a frozen wrench). The scripts as well are equally as sharp with enough Tape Diarys and main curios hanging around the establishments to give plenty of exploration opportunities.
While this game does offer tight controls and a generally quite impressive overview it does have its problems however. I personally found the endings a bit blunt (I played for the good ending and found it much of a much...the bad ending was about the same as well) with you also being just dropped back into the main menu after completion without so much as an end or credit screen in sight...which I would compare with someone just finishing the last page of a book only for someone to leap out of nowhere snatch the book from your hand and run off...it does somewhat dampen the overall experience and doesnt allow much in the way of reflection time...but thats a personal complaint.
it probably should also be mentioned that the game itself at this stage has been reported by many (Myself included) to have a number of small bugs from issues starting the game in the first place to sound and text issues (My playthrough was entirely silent for the first hour of play before I shut it down and re-opened the game at which point the sound came back but I was spammed with all the text options that hadnt appeared in that first hour of gameplay) though there are work arounds that can fix these issues so while it may not be an "out of the gate" experience it is playable on most modern systems which is a definate plus...
All in all I can wholeheatedly reccommend picking a copy of this up if you havent already it offers a lot of playthrough potential and the story is very engaging and overall enjoyable...if you are a fan of Borderlands or the Fallout series you'll definately feel most at home here. Give it a try sometime. :)

Although a very very old game, it provides an excellent blend of Galactic management, ground tactical battles, and space tactical battles.
The best parts:
Interactive galactic map that, while it appears overwhleming, it actually extremely simple. Planets have space stations, ground structures, and special effects based on the specific, such as planetary weather or tactical advantages such as production discounts for specific units.
Space battle mechanics. Frigates, Cruisers, Capital ships and Space Stations have "Hardpoints" that have different functions, like torpedo launchers, turbolaser cannons, shield generators, or engines.
The hardpoints are individually selectable as targets and can be destroyed in any order. As hardpoints are destroyed, the ship loses functions, for example destroying turbolaser cannons will silence them, destroying shield generators permanantly disables shields, and destroying engines reduce speed and manuverability.
The hardpoints also have limited firing zones. What his means, is that turrets can only engage targets in their cone of fire, so it's possible for skilled tacticians to ambush larger ships and hit them in their "Blind spots" to gain a tactical advantage.
Each factions has it's own unique line-ups of ground forces, starships, and heros. Each one is unique, and nearly all units have special abilities to exploit. All units also have carefully designed strengths and weaknesses, and using each one correctly is the key to success.  No point-and-click tank and plane wars where the bigger army wins. A small force of well-played units will trump a large force of point-and-click steamroller armies.
Of course, the game is a bit outdated. The graphics aren't up to date, and the game sacrifices intense, specific battles. It makes up by combining all 3 levels of command in a simpler way that caters to smart, creative tacticians rather than "Point-and-click steamrollers" who are used to just ordering a hundred tanks and craming them down the enemy's throat.

**The game is based on the D&D Adventure System Board Games**
Do Not go into this game expecting "Baulders Gate" or some type of ARPG, you Will Be Disappointed. If you are unfamiliar with the D&D Adventure System, my advice would be to watch a Twitch stream first, maybe a YouTube video, before you purchase this game. After that, if you think it may be for you, or if like me you enjoy the Adventure System, then this game will provide a very beautiful and challenging experience. A ton of work has obviously gone into this game and the Devs should really be proud of the accomplishment.

I'm sure the reason we have these four Heroes is due to them being the default heroes for the "Tomb of Annihilation" board game itself. I would like to see a better verity of Heroes come to this game and the Devs have said that they are not against the idea of adding Custom Characters as well, which would not only be amazing, but something the board game does not offer, giving the PC version an added feature.*

The idea of the game is why most people are going to be interested in it, if you dont move time doesnt move. Simple, right? At the start you can run around the map like in any other shooter just for the bants, but as you go further on the game becomes more challenging, and you begin to need more concentration. The maps also vary nicely as there are some on trains, subways and offices.
The story was very interesting in my opinion. [SPOILERS AHEAD ----- YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED _ If you dont want spoilers on the story skip down to where it says ending of spoilers]. Your friend invites you to play a game, you play the game, the game tries to get you to not play the game, the game takes over your life, the game destroys your friendship, and in the end the game tells you that you are worthless and has you kill yourself. Now I know that that is very basic, but I dont want to ruin the whole story.
In addition to this rather simple story, I believe that it has a deeper meaning. By attempting to kill the in-game you the red enemies were attemptint to protect you from having the game control your mind, through telling you that your body is holding you back. So are the red men your enemies in the game, or are you your own enemy. Its up to you to decide this, but I found this an interesting perspective to look at the game.

Okay, let me start off by saying I am a fan of these types of sandbox survival games. That being said, this is one of the better ones I've played since I first discovered How to Survive. The graphics are not out of this world, but for me that's a good thing, since my pc is not exactly up to date, so less requirements the better, and this requires very little and runs very well on even my junked up pc. The gameplay is what matters, and it's great, even with everything not fully implemented yet. That means is we have all that good stuff to look forward to. The game is pretty simple to learn, and has a built in tutorial to read if you choose, and it's pretty useful. There's enough guides out there to get you started too. It is a built difficult trying to figure some of the cooking recipies out, but the carpentry tells you exactly what you need for each task. I haven't really gotten to play around much with the fishing or trapping skills, so I can't really comment on them. The combat is difficult, and well it should be. This is a zombie survival, not zombie action. In a real life survival situation you would not go looking for fights, they would be difficult, time consuming, and potentially use a lot of resources or you could end up hurt or killed, the risk may not be worth it, just as it is in the game. There are some parts where you can pick off individual zombies easy enough, but if you attract the horde and stay to fight, you should plan to join them soon enough, cause they are going to overwhelm you quick. As far as downsides to the game... I don't think it's really fair to say anything yet, because it's not finished, they may change things that I don't like. For instance I would like for alcohol/pain pills/other drugs in the game to affect your character's performance, if you get drunk, your screen blurs and you stumble around, if you pop too many pain pills you move slower and might nod off, etc., as well as a chance to become addicted to them. It could still happen though. Would like to see some more map options too, or at least expand on the ones they have, but they might be, so we'll see I guess. I am looking forward to build 30 and the new systems being implemented, the first aid will be interesting...

I played this game a bit before it came to Steam while it was still in beta (I think).
I have spent countless hours in the original Ragnarok Online. I first started playing it many years ago and I absolutely fell in love with it, and it was my very first MMORPG experience. Since I stopped playing that time, I've kept coming back to it several times, and every time I get swallowed up by it. It's still the very best in the genre that I have ever played, and I've played quite a few.
When a sequel was first announced, I, like other fans, was really excited. Eventually they showed a very different game and the general opinion on it was luke warm. Gravity Interactive decided to scratch the whole thing. Later, this new sequel appeared. They have stated that they wanted to go back to the world of the original game. Finally, the game has reached the international player base. It is many years overdue.
So, how does it hold up? To be blunt; the game is a bland, average MMORPG. Some elements have been kept, but all in all completely changed. There's a new card system unlike anything I've seen in any other game, but that's pretty much it. The rest is nothing special, and not a lot of fun. I think they completely blew it. It's very little impressive.
If you are looking for a great MMORPG experience, this is probably not it. I suggest you try the original instead. It's free to try though.

If you like co-op gameplay with a team of four like in Left 4 Dead, you will like being a Hunter.
If you like being a lone wolf, proving you are better than 4 other human players combined, you will like being the Monster.
You have 12 Hunters to choose from, 3 for each class.
Medic: Heals / Revives the team.
Support: Gives the team buffs or strategic advantages.
Trapper: Hunts the Monster down using varying skills for each character, and uses the Dome to trap the Monster, forcing it to fight instead of constantly running away.
Assault: The damage dealer, he deals the most damage out of all the Hunters and should generally be in the Monster's face when under the Dome.
Currently there are 3 Monsters with a 4th being worked on as DLC.
Goliath: Ground based brawler, gets in the Hunter's faces.
Wraith: Ground based Assassin / Glass cannon. Sneaky, uses hit and run tactics.
Kraken: Aerial monster. Uses area of effect and ranged attacks.
Behemoth (DLC Monster): Ground based Tank Monster. Massive armor and Health, but slow moving.
Evolve has a team of four human controlled players against one human controlled Monster. The Hunters win by killing the Monster, the Monster wins by killing the Hunters or destroying the Power Relay in each map.
The Monster starts out at level 1, as he eats wildlife on the map, he gains energy to evolve to stage 2 and then to stage 3, when he can wreck the Power Relay. Each time he evolves, the Monster gets stronger, so it is in the Hunter's best interests to find and kill the Monster as quickly as possible. This is the basic game mode, Hunt.
There are other game modes as well.
Evacuation: Instead of a dedicated campaign, you have Evacuation. Where you play a series of game modes you vote on, and the outcome of each match affects the next. Comes with a narrative to guide the story along.
Rescue: Escort AI controlled soldiers to their evacuation point before the Monster kills them.
Defend: Defend generators and the ship refueling depot from non stop wave of level 1 Monster minions, and the enemy Monster at level 3. Win by holding out for enough time as the Hunters, or win by destroying the refueling depot as the Monster.
Nest: Egg hunt mode, find all the Monster eggs on the map and destroy them or kill the Monster to win as Hunters. Kill all the Hunters to win as Monster. The monster can hatch one of the eggs at a time for a Monster minion to help in killing the Hunters.
ALL FUTURE MAPS WILL BE FREE. ALL FUTURE GAME MODES WILL BE FREE.
There are more DLC Hunters and Monsters being worked on, which are not ready yet. If you buy them you can play as them, but if you do not buy them, you can still play with them as your allies in matches. Or setup solo matched where the Monster can be a DLC monster, and your allies are AI DLC characters. Not buying DLC will not separate the online community.
Turtle Rock Studios, the developers have said time and time again, the DLC characters will be balanced, this will not be pay to win. The studio aims for a 50/50 win/loss ratio for all Monsters and hunters. Meaning only skill sets you apart from the average Hunter to win.

Great game.  Unfortunately, it might die because it has become fashionable/meme-like to diss this game's DLC practices, and trash it at ever turn, even though I personally don't see what the hullaballoo is about.  Future publishers may want to take note, however--not necessarily because the haters are right, but because they are, at the very least, vocal.  I'll admit my opinion about the DLC/pricing set-up was skewed a bit, mostly because of the vocal hate.  Thankfully, I did some research on my own.  Here's what I've come up with:
This game's DLC is similar model to games such as League of Legends--cosmetic skins and future playable characters will need to be bought.  They have stated that new maps/game-modes will always be free (which will be great as it won't split the playerbase), and you will be able to play against others who own monsters and hunters you don't own.  Pretty much like League and other MOBAs.  The big difference, of course, is that Evolve is 60 USD for the base game, while most games that generate revenue from micro-trasnactions are free-to-play.
That said, Evolve has the graphics, gameplay, sounds, maps of a AAA title.  League, perhaps, is a great game, but it is not sylistically what we've come to expect from a AAA title.
As far as the gameplay, I have no complaints.  Every game has been different, exciting, and I look forward to putting in more hours this week on my medic.  There is a nice sense of progression through the tiers to unlock each hunter/monster.  If you like arena type gameplay, asymetical fighting, and strong group tactics, then you will probably really like this game.
I want to reiterate that NO ONE who purchased DLC day 1 has any advantage of someone picking up the game right now.  All they are getting is skins/monsters/hunters which are to be released in the future.  This is pay2customize, pay2playstyle, not pay2win.  If, perhaps, there is an overtuned monster/hunter that is released in the future that is a "must" own because it is overpowered or whatever, then hopefully the dev's will act quickly to rebalance it, as they seem to have done quite well with the monsters/hunters on release.

Back when the Power Rangers were a big deal in 1995, my parents wouldn't let me watch it. They deemed it too violent. Mind you, they're telling this to a guy who is chronically addicted to Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles and tuned in every Saturday to watch the Spiderman and Batman cartoons. Power Rangers were much too violent though. When my folks finally gave up on controlling my viewing habits Power Rangers quickly became a guilty pleasure and I watched it until Wild Force. Enter
, a retro style turn based tactics game that puts you in control of a squad of power rangers. It is every bit as fun as going round your parents' back to just watch cardboard robots beating up rubber monsters.
's premise is very catchy hook to begin with. A group of disgruntled stunt actors are fed up with their boss and quit their current Ranger season to start their own series. With buckets, old shirts and cardboard boxes your crew assembles a set of costumes and backdrops and the battle against evil can begin. Along the way you'll find that there is a little more to playing Power Rangers than just making cool poses.
The game's real kicker is the ability to create and assemble your own team. You can possibly recreate every Ranger team down to the letter with the game, or engineer a squad entirely your own. Did you like Mighty Morphing Power Rangers? Just pick the five colours, three boys, two girls and be on your way. Fed up with the patriarchy? Pick five girls, colour them all in shades of purple and kick some♥♥♥♥♥ Feeling grimdark and edgy? Pick five depressed kids, paint them black and act like Batman. Everything is up to you. Each Ranger has its own role. Lead is in charge and gets additional hitpoints, while the tech rangers does bonus damage with weapons. The colours are up to you, so you can make the Pink ranger be the boss this time round and let the snooty Red ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ be the butt of the Megazord this time.
After you tune your squad you record your episodes. This is a turn based tactics game where you fight minions and monsters on a grid. The real selling point here is positioning and teamwork. One ranger can kick a mook for sure, but positioning your squad in such a way will allow you to vault your rangers straight into the bosses face on the first turn to deliver a juicy team attack. It is key that master the acrobatics and abilities to chase down the shifty bosses, or that you weaken and wear out the brawlers without losing a Ranger, because no one likes it when the good guys lose.
You performance isn't measured in money, or experience; it is measured in audience. Since you're recording a TV show your audience is your life; and you cannot survive without loyal viewers and fans. Every episode gives you a hand full of objectives to clear to make your episode a bit better. More audience, means more fans, means more money, means better suits, means better TV, means more audience, etc. It is a simple, yet fun system, because it invites you to think of other ways to approach a problem, rather than to look for the one tactic.
The entire game is booming with references to the Power Rangers and its Japanese original: Super Sentai. Finishing moves, focus on Red, giant robots, believing in your friends, mystery helpers, talking jars, it's all part of the experience. During your downtime you have time to craft new weapons from arts and crafts materials as well as answer fanmail and hire marketing groups to propel your show to the next level of hype. You'll quickly fall in love with the familiar and sometimes cliché traits of the series that round out the experience.
All in all, the game presses so many right buttons, it's hard not to like. Though the sometimes lazy writing rips you out of the game, the desire to know what kind of crazy thing the devs have cooked up for the next episode will have you coming back soon. The branching storyline also helps to draw you back in after beating it once.

**The game is based on the D&D Adventure System Board Games**
Do Not go into this game expecting "Baulders Gate" or some type of ARPG, you Will Be Disappointed. If you are unfamiliar with the D&D Adventure System, my advice would be to watch a Twitch stream first, maybe a YouTube video, before you purchase this game. After that, if you think it may be for you, or if like me you enjoy the Adventure System, then this game will provide a very beautiful and challenging experience. A ton of work has obviously gone into this game and the Devs should really be proud of the accomplishment.
*Review Updated to Reflect Current Patch and Content*
Pros:
-Very Good Interpretation of the Board Games
-Very Nice Visuals
-Audio is also well done
-Lots of content, Main Quest Line, Side Quests etc
-Not a bad Crafting System (There is not one in the board game so this is a nice feature)
-In Game Tooltips and Rule Book have made understanding the game rules MUCH easier for new players.
Cons:
-Can get unfair very quick due to random events still going on even while in combat. (Honestly, this is an issue with the system itself and not the fault of the Devs. My house actually made it a rule that no encounters take place during active combat as long as No New tiles are discovered. Of course that is something you can do with a physical board game, make "House Rules".)
-Only 4 Heroes, a New One is on the way. (The Default Heroes for the ToA Board Game, I did not like this line up for the physical game, so that remains a Con from me for the PC version as well. For now.)
- PTW DLCs (This is not the direction the player base wants to see the game go, just read a few reviews and posts on the DLC page to see this. I'm sure the Devs are aware so we will see if this mind set is changed going forward. I am hopeful.)
*A quick word on the Heroes. The primary reason I purchased this game is to add my financial support to the games development. The adventure system has over a dozen heroes from its series of board games and all of them are interchangeable with the different games, i.e. my Heroes from "Temple of Elemental Evil" work in "Castle Ravenloft" or "Legend of Drizzit", that is one of the appeals of the series. I'm sure the reason we have these four Heroes is due to them being the default heroes for the "Tomb of Annihilation" board game itself. I would like to see a better verity of Heroes come to this game and the Devs have said that they are not against the idea of adding Custom Characters as well, which would not only be amazing, but something the board game does not offer, giving the PC version an added feature.*

Chroma Squad is an amazing game where you delve into the makings of a Super Sentai studio. It's like a business tycoon, a tactical RPG, and a customization rainbow stuffed into an amazing masterpiece of a sandwich!
I honestly can't remember how I stumbled across this gem, but when I saw it, I fell in love with it and I had to have it. I'm glad that I did stumble acorss this, 'cuz I've had the funnest time playing Chroma Squad, the most enjoyable game I've come across in a while. In the first week of owning it, this game was what I'd play every night if I wasn't busy. It's extremely addicting, and while the story seems to start out at a good pace, things escalate quickly later on, providing great plot twists that keep the story immensely interesting.
With those opening comments out of the way, let's list the pros and cons.
Pros:
~A great level of customization with a plethora of actors, colors, and equipment to choose from, heck, even the mechs have a good level of customization.
~A great soundtrack. I persoanlly am a big fan of the 8-bit/chiptune style of music, it reminds of the days of arcades and gameboys. Any chiptune lover would listen to the soundtrack over and over again. If you like the music, get the reasonably priced soundtrack. Not only does it help support the devs, but you get to listen to your favorite groovy tunes from the game anytime you want.
~Cool graphics. if you like these kinds of pixely games or pixel art in general, this is a game for you.
~The storyline. I've said it before: It's interesting with a great pace.
~The play time. It took me about 22 hours to get through my first playthrough of the game, on the normal difficulty setting. And that's just for one of 3 endings that the game has to offer. Depending on the difficlty level you're playing and the time spent jamming out to the music, the time to get all the endings can range from 50 hours to 70 hours. Great amount of gameplay.
~The achievements. There's not hundreds of them like their are in other games, and most of them are pretty easy to get, you just need to play the game accordingly. I got over half the achievements on my first playthrough. (Though I guess they could add some ones in the future that require DLC.) If you're not an achievement hunter, that's all right, it could just be a fun side quest. This game has enough play-achievement balance that you don't need to dedicate hundreds of hours to get all of them.
~Difficalty settings. This is always a great feature to have in a game. The difficulties are casual, interesting, and challenging, ehich translates to easy, normal, hard respectively. If you're new to this type of game and/or want to focus on the story, play the game on casual. If you've played these games before and like a nice balance of story and challenge, interesting's your cuppa joe. If you like a challenge, like good planning, and you aren't afraid to lose a little to win a little, challenging is just the right fit.
~Nice balance of battle and management. Not only do you fight with your heroes, you need to check and maintain their gear in order to beat the enemies that get more difficult as time progresses, as well as answer emails from fans, manage production companies, and upgrade your small warehouse studio as time goes on.
~A great price. This game is relatively well priced, and will provide hours of fun and enjoyment that for most of you will be the best entertainment you've had in a while. At 15 American dollars for the game, with 5 additional for the soundtrack DLC, 20 dollars is a great price for this game. (Without DLC, the game is about 10 British pounds, 13 with DLC, for those of you in the UK)
Cons:

It's very important to understand that this game is NOT your pen-and-paper D&D experience, nor is it a successor to Neverwinter Nights or Baldur's Gate.
This is a true-to-form translation of a physical board game experience to a digital board game experience. If you have played and enjoy the D&D Adventure Series board games, then this is for you. If you are unfamiliar with the board game system, you should know a few things.
It's difficult. By design, the board game is inherently challenging. You are meant to face either new monsters or a new encounter (mostly negative but sometimes positive events drawn from a deck of cards) each turn. You are not necessarily going to win each mission on the first try because of this, but you DO keep your treasure and gold, even when you fail. This means you can make progress either way.
That said, this game isn't without its faults.
- You have to unlock the ability to play with multiple characters; from 1 to 2 to 3 to 4, you have to earn experience and gain levels so that you can play with a full party. That said, this goes pretty quickly, but it still feels arbitrary.
- You can't trade items between characters. This makes sense for crafted items (those are essentially buffs to your skills, anyway), but items you discover should be able to be exchanged from one character to another.
- There is no multiplayer. You could theoretically play with a group of friends at home, each making decisions for different characters (just like the board game!), but I'd like to see an online multiplayer mode. Supposedly this in on the agenda.
In the end, I would still recommend this game if you are willing to understand that this is NOT a replacement for your tabletop game or Neverwinter Nights. If you want that, try Divinity 2 for an exciting game with a great GM system. But if you realize that this is a board game, and nothing more, then definitely give this a shot. It's a great execution and it's true to the source.

Enemy Mind is a difficult 2D side-scrolling shoot-em’-up (schmup). It isn’t tremendously long – it has 80 stages, including 8 bosses, taking about 4 hours to complete – but it is definitely quite taxing. Unlike many modern games, this game incorporates a lives system and score system, meaning that if you die, you have to start a set of ten stages over again. This can be very unpleasant if you get a game over on a boss.
The central conceit of Enemy Mind is that you are a mind-hopping parasite who can jump from ship to ship. Each ship has limited ammunition and can take 2-5 shots before going down. Your goal is to use the ships to hop through the battles, taking down all the enemy ships while avoiding being in a ship when it goes down yourself. This leads to fairly unique gameplay, as the ships have a wide variety of attack patterns, both in your hands and in the hands of the AI. This is especially notable in the boss fights, where you must hop around between various ships during the fight to take down the boss without the boss destroying you in the process. Indeed, almost all of the bosses can themselves be mind controlled, resulting in interesting gameplay as you work to destroy the boss while hopping in and out of its body.
The game has a story underlying it – in-between stages, you can listen to enemy chatter over the coms system, as well as having various memories filter into your mind. While delivered via text, the story is interesting as it reveals more about both the mind-hopping parasite and the world you’re inhabiting, and depending on whether you’re controlling a human ship or an Aratus (alien) ship, you get different story messages (and, at the end of the game, a different ending based on which faction you spent more time mind controlling over the course of the game).
Overall, this is a pretty creative game, and is definitely a distinctive entry within the schmup genre. While the game isn’t mind blowing in terms of quality, it works quite well, and it is fun navigating your way through the game and working out what is going on. That said, it is a schmup game, so if that sort of thing isn’t your cup of tea, or if pixel graphics bother you, this isn’t going to change your mind.
Still, if you’re a fan of the genre, this is worth checking out, even if it is quite difficult; judging by the achievements board and high scores, less than 50 people have beaten this game in its entirety.

This is one of the best horror games out there.
First and foremost the sound of the game is probably the best I have ever seen in any game. The amount of detail that can be heard when wearing high quality headphones is impressive and it makes the experience very realistic, besides helping the player project where the enemies are in the darkness of the Asylum.
The graphics are incredible. In some parts of the game, you can stare at a certain spot and think: 'What in this image makes me know that it's a game and not real life?' And a lot of times you can't come up with an answer, that's how realistic the graphics look especially with the night vision on the camera.
The voice acting is another one of the strong spots of this game. The screams and speeches of the patients sound extremely convincing, making the player question whether those are the screams of actors or actually insane patients. That combined with the high sound quality and amazing graphics makes Mount Massive Asylum a very real place and makes playing the game a more than enjoyable experience.
On the other hand, the game lacks a little in story. Not to say that the story is bad, but the dynamics of the game makes the player sometimes forget what he's doing since he's too worried in not dying or getting caught. In other words, it's easy to forget your current objective. This is a very common mistake in horror games, but since Outlast is not very long and since every other aspect is overwhelmingly well done, the lack in story is overlooked by most players.
It doesn't hurt to mention that the player will never feel safe during the game, unlike other games with 'safe spots' such as Resident Evil 7. That forces you to take breaks during the gameplay; it's not easy to clear this game in one sitting even though the game is not very long. The game ends just when it's about to become repetitive so the lenght feels perfect. Not too long and not too short.
In summary, Outlast is one of the best horror games ever made and it is definitely worth your money if you're looking for something that will keep you up at nights for a while. It's not recommended, though, for those easily frightened and that don't know what they're getting themselves into. 10/10

Let me open by saying that this is a fantastic game. It is a classic side-scrolling shooter in the style of games like R-Type. You control a small spacecraft and must navigate through waves of hostile craft, dodging incoming fire while doing your best to dispatch them as quickly as possible.
However, there is some really smart design here which elevates Enemy Mind to the status of a truly great game.
The main thing here is that the game replaces the classic system of power-ups. Rather than boosting the abilities of your craft, in Enemy Mind you are able to project your mind out of your current ship and take control of any other craft in the game. This simple move changes everything.
First, it means that you can take on the powers of various craft with different fire-patterns, health points, sizes and speeds. This adds a deep tactical layer to your choices. Given that all ships have very limited ammunition, you are forced to swap craft every dozen seconds or so and the tactical use of ship hopping quickly becomes a core part of the game.
Second, this allows for a smart and novel approach to bullet hell. Deaths are almost always your fault since there will have always been a chance for you to ship-swap at some given point. If you find yourself in an impossible situation it is because you failed to move quickly enough and not, simply because the game overwhelmed you with attacks.
It is also worth mentioning that the visual and sound design are fantastic. This is a great example of a retro style appearance done right. Everything has character, and the visuals are clear, crisp and informative.
So if you had not yet guessed it I fully recommend this game. It’s one that will be on my playlist for a long time to come and I have no doubt the same will be true for many other people.

I DIG city builder games and I went into this with as positive an attitude as someone possibly could.  After 10 hours of repetitive gameplay unfortunately the experience is incredibly 'lightweight' and disappointing.  Much of my time has been spent alt+tabbing to find the solution to something on a Steam guide, which sometimes turns out to be 'just a bug' or 'guesswork'.
Cons:
- City builder elements are very shallow.  You upgrade Police Stations to put out fires as there are no Fire Stations. Tropico lacks the essential city building elements of its rivals, and it doesn't do a good job of explaining or giving information on the elements that it does have.  There is no 'traffic', and no feedback or information as to how your production network even runs.
- Strategy elements are near non existent.  You plonk down some houses and some farms then after a while you get enough money to plonk down the next thing.  You do get attacked by rebels but there is zero strategy involved with how it plays out.
- A huge issue with lack of information.  How many construction offices do I need?  How many Teamster offices do I need?  How much stock makes up the 'other' stock which is about to be shipped out - why can't I expand that window to see how much I am actually producing?
- Communication ambiguities, for example, 'setting the budget' on a house actually means 'raising the rent', not the budget you give towards the upkeep of houses, like you do for other buildings.
- Housing bugs, for example citizens refusing to live in houses and instead declare themselves 'homeless' even though you have set their salaries high and the rent of the houses low.  No information is given as to why citizens would be homeless, and after searching online though guides, this is possibly a bug.
- Lack of building variety, even with the DLC buildings, which are very unreasonably priced.
- Voice acting is used sparingly.
- 'Advanced trading mechanics' - lol, good one.
- Even when on amicable terms, signing an alliance treaty with the Axis results in them invading you, then you defeating them, and then them immediately agreeing to the alliance after they declared a 'mini-war' on you for initiating an alliance treaty.  That's not what I'd call a believable simulation of the diplomatic and strategic implications of an alliance...
Lastly the population is capped at 2000, you have the option to raise it up to 10000, but raising it above 2000 comes with a warning message about game stability and bug issues.  If I can only populate 10% of an island then where's the fun in that?

If you like co-op gameplay with a team of four like in Left 4 Dead, you will like being a Hunter.
If you like being a lone wolf, proving you are better than 4 other human players combined, you will like being the Monster.
You have 12 Hunters to choose from, 3 for each class.
Medic: Heals / Revives the team.
Support: Gives the team buffs or strategic advantages.
Trapper: Hunts the Monster down using varying skills for each character, and uses the Dome to trap the Monster, forcing it to fight instead of constantly running away.
Assault: The damage dealer, he deals the most damage out of all the Hunters and should generally be in the Monster's face when under the Dome.
Currently there are 3 Monsters with a 4th being worked on as DLC.
Goliath: Ground based brawler, gets in the Hunter's faces.
Wraith: Ground based Assassin / Glass cannon. Sneaky, uses hit and run tactics.
Kraken: Aerial monster. Uses area of effect and ranged attacks.
Behemoth (DLC Monster): Ground based Tank Monster. Massive armor and Health, but slow moving.
Evolve has a team of four human controlled players against one human controlled Monster. The Hunters win by killing the Monster, the Monster wins by killing the Hunters or destroying the Power Relay in each map.
The Monster starts out at level 1, as he eats wildlife on the map, he gains energy to evolve to stage 2 and then to stage 3, when he can wreck the Power Relay. Each time he evolves, the Monster gets stronger, so it is in the Hunter's best interests to find and kill the Monster as quickly as possible. This is the basic game mode, Hunt.
There are other game modes as well.
Evacuation: Instead of a dedicated campaign, you have Evacuation. Where you play a series of game modes you vote on, and the outcome of each match affects the next. Comes with a narrative to guide the story along.
Rescue: Escort AI controlled soldiers to their evacuation point before the Monster kills them.
Defend: Defend generators and the ship refueling depot from non stop wave of level 1 Monster minions, and the enemy Monster at level 3. Win by holding out for enough time as the Hunters, or win by destroying the refueling depot as the Monster.
Nest: Egg hunt mode, find all the Monster eggs on the map and destroy them or kill the Monster to win as Hunters. Kill all the Hunters to win as Monster. The monster can hatch one of the eggs at a time for a Monster minion to help in killing the Hunters.
ALL FUTURE MAPS WILL BE FREE. ALL FUTURE GAME MODES WILL BE FREE.
There are more DLC Hunters and Monsters being worked on, which are not ready yet. If you buy them you can play as them, but if you do not buy them, you can still play with them as your allies in matches. Or setup solo matched where the Monster can be a DLC monster, and your allies are AI DLC characters. Not buying DLC will not separate the online community.
Turtle Rock Studios, the developers have said time and time again, the DLC characters will be balanced, this will not be pay to win. The studio aims for a 50/50 win/loss ratio for all Monsters and hunters. Meaning only skill sets you apart from the average Hunter to win.

The storyline is the usual entertaining farce and the new era system works pretty well in that you have a different feel for each time period in terms of interaction with foerign powers. There's also a new trade system but it just seems different rather than better. The  biggest bugbear is the feeling that it's all been dumbed down. There are fewer micro management options, the almanac has less information (especially regarding politics) and there seem to be less building options. This means that often there feels like there is nothing much to do once a mission gets going and often it's just a case of letting the clock run down, occasionally throwing down some random buildings to fulfil a quest. Great game.  Unfortunately, it might die because it has become fashionable/meme-like to diss this game's DLC practices, and trash it at ever turn, even though I personally don't see what the hullaballoo is about.  Future publishers may want to take note, however--not necessarily because the haters are right, but because they are, at the very least, vocal.  I'll admit my opinion about the DLC/pricing set-up was skewed a bit, mostly because of the vocal hate.  Thankfully, I did some research on my own.  Here's what I've come up with:
This game's DLC is similar model to games such as League of Legends--cosmetic skins and future playable characters will need to be bought.  They have stated that new maps/game-modes will always be free (which will be great as it won't split the playerbase), and you will be able to play against others who own monsters and hunters you don't own.  Pretty much like League and other MOBAs.  The big difference, of course, is that Evolve is 60 USD for the base game, while most games that generate revenue from micro-trasnactions are free-to-play.
That said, Evolve has the graphics, gameplay, sounds, maps of a AAA title.  League, perhaps, is a great game, but it is not sylistically what we've come to expect from a AAA title.
As far as the gameplay, I have no complaints.  Every game has been different, exciting, and I look forward to putting in more hours this week on my medic.  There is a nice sense of progression through the tiers to unlock each hunter/monster.  If you like arena type gameplay, asymetical fighting, and strong group tactics, then you will probably really like this game.
I want to reiterate that NO ONE who purchased DLC day 1 has any advantage of someone picking up the game right now.  All they are getting is skins/monsters/hunters which are to be released in the future.  This is pay2customize, pay2playstyle, not pay2win.  If, perhaps, there is an overtuned monster/hunter that is released in the future that is a "must" own because it is overpowered or whatever, then hopefully the dev's will act quickly to rebalance it, as they seem to have done quite well with the monsters/hunters on release.

Not every game has to have hours upon hours of lengthy storyline, where by the end, you've either tuned out or forgot the original premise.
The Park is short and to the point, which is exactly what I suspect the devs wanted. And they nailed it IMHO.
